comments.body: I don't think that it is counter to how the structure works.  I know that if you just do `x[y] = v` in most languages that doesn't reorder `y`.  But `delete x[y]; x[y] = v` should produce the same outcome everywhere.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Anyone else with a preference for this?

comments.author: phluid61
comments.body:
Given the situation, my preferences are:

1. no change to anything; it's not 100% clear, but the right answer can already be inferred
2. change the wording of the algorithm but keep the implementation the same; @mnot's https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1330#issuecomment-730696699 is okay

@martinthomson:
> I don't think that it is counter to how the structure works.

This issue only became relevant when we decided to let different parties emit the same field name in an unbuffered stream, and give preference to the later ones. (Originally we dropped the subsequent dupe, so first won.) If ordering matters _in that case_ we should be providing explicit reordering tools, so that the later entity can prepend/insert/delete/etc. But we don't. So the later entity either sucks up the fact that the earlier entities decide the ordering, or it buffers the fields and explicitly reorders them.

Aside from all that, we're making a whole lot of fairly substantive changes to a spec that's gone through all its last calls. If it's this wrong, should we pull it back and start over?

issues.title: rfc6265bis empty domain attribute
issues.author: essen
issues.body:
The behavior for when the domain attribute is empty is confusing when there are multiple domain attributes.

The [spec](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-06#section-5.3.3) says:

```
   If the attribute-name case-insensitively matches the string "Domain",
   the user agent MUST process the cookie-av as follows.

   1.  If the attribute-value is empty, the behavior is undefined.
       However, the user agent SHOULD ignore the cookie-av entirely.
```

This means that when there's a single empty domain attribute, and the implementation follows this SHOULD, then this attribute is removed. No problem there. But when there's two attributes including an empty domain attribute, then only the empty attribute is removed. This means that the three following set-cookie headers are equivalent:

```
Set-Cookie: foo=bar; domain=foo.example.org; domain=
Set-Cookie: foo=bar; domain=; domain=foo.example.org
Set-Cookie: foo=bar; domain=foo.example.org
```

When the domain is `foo.example.org` all 3 cookies end up stored. When the domain is `home.example.org` all 3 are dropped.

The first case is confusing because it is in stark contrast with the path attribute where an empty path equals `default-path` and the final path wins, so an empty final path has the effect of "resetting" the path. I would also suggest the first case is not intuitive.

An implementation that does not follow the SHOULD would have undefined behavior. This is the only place in the spec where this is the case I believe. It would be good to get rid of it.

I would suggest first changing the SHOULD into a MUST so as to avoid differing behaviors. I would also suggest either having behavior similar to path, or invalidating the cookie entirely.

(This is a followup to #1136 and the relevant http-state test was as follow:)

```
Set-Cookie: foo=bar; domain=foo.example.org; domain=
Location: http://home.example.org:8888/cookie-parser-result?optional-domain0042
```

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
This test now lives at https://wpt.fyi/results/cookies/attributes/domain/domain.sub.html?label=master&label=experimental&aligned 

https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/489679e4fccedcb37ae4d3e028b5d1a56adbc769/cookies/attributes/resources/domain-child.sub.html#L311-L316
```
        {
          cookie: `test=42; domain=${www1Host}; domain=`,
          expected: "",
          name: "No cookie returned for domain mismatch (with domain mismatch as first domain attribute and second a bare attribute)",
          location: `http://${wwwHost}:${port}/cookies/attributes/resources/path.html`,
        },
```

The test works like so: 

1. open the test page to `http://home.example.org/path/to/file` (using example.org here instead of the variables so it's less confusing)
2. (attempt to) set the following cookie: `test=42; domain=sibling.example.org; domain=; path=/cookies/attributes/resources`
3. The server that sets the cookie will 302 to `http://home.example.org/cookies/attributes/resources/path.html`
4. The test page sees if any cookies are sent

There's disagreement between Chrome (which doesn't set a cookie) and Firefox & Safari (which do) here.

> I would suggest first changing the SHOULD into a MUST so as to avoid differing behaviors. I would also suggest either having behavior similar to path, or invalidating the cookie entirely.

It does seem a little strange that some browsers would send a cookie, I'm not sure if that could be abused though -- if you can modify a domain attribute to make it empty, you can modify it to whatever you want.

Do we keep it as SHOULD? Change to MUST? Thoughts @chlily1 @englehardt?

comments.author: chlily1
comments.body:
I believe the correct behavior (according to the SHOULD) should be to not store a cookie, since the empty domain= attribute should be ignored, leaving the last valid one (domain=sibling.example.org) which doesn't match the current host. I wouldn't mind changing this to a MUST; it seems in line with the definition of "MUST" in RFC 2119.

Agreed that it's weird the Domain attribute behaves like this. In Chromium's parsing code, there's a [special case](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/master:net/cookies/parsed_cookie.cc;l=451-452;drc=ed6c24ca7c5bb5ed377f99fbf24747e127e85490) for empty Domain attributes, different from all the other attributes.

The value of ignoring an empty domain attribute might have been to avoid possible ambiguity in the correct behavior of an empty domain attribute? I don't like either of the alternatives suggested above. Having behavior similar to path (where an empty attribute means filling in a default, in this case the current host) might be dangerous, as it could lead to unintentionally sending the cookie to subdomains which may be less-secure origins. Invalidating the cookie entirely is inconsistent with what happens when other attributes end up with nonsensical values (see issue #933).

I think the most sensible thing is to either continue to ignore empty domain attributes (and make the SHOULD a MUST), or to say that cookies with an empty domain attribute as the last domain attribute behave as host-only cookies (effectively treating `domain=` as an explicit marker of a host-only cookie). These two are different, e.g. in the case of `domain=foo.example;domain=`, which currently ends up as a domain cookie for foo.example, but under the second proposal would end up as a host-only cookie.

### Test Cases and Results
(All to be run on example.com)

**Test case 1**: If the cookie-av is ignored then we should have only the `foo=hostonly` and `foo=nonhostonly` cookies.

Clear all cookies on example.com then run
```
document.cookie = "foo=hostonly"
document.cookie = "foo=nonhostonly; domain=example.com"
document.cookie = "foo=domaintest; domain=other.com; domain="
```

- Chrome 94
   - `foo=hostonly; foo=nonhostonly`
- Firefox 92
   - `foo=nonhostonly; foo=domaintest`

**Test case 2**: If the cookie-av is ignored then we should have only the `foo=hostonly` and `foo=domaintest` cookies.

Clear all cookies on example.com then run
```
document.cookie = "foo=hostonly"
document.cookie = "foo=nonhostonly; domain=example.com"
document.cookie = "foo=domaintest; domain=example.com; domain="
```
- Chrome 94
   - `foo=hostonly; foo=domaintest`
- Firefox 92
   - `foo=nonhostonly; foo=domaintest`

**Test case 3:** If the cookie-av is ignored then we should have only the `foo=domaintest` and `foo=nonhostonly` cookies.

Clear all cookies on example.com then run
```
document.cookie = "foo=hostonly"
document.cookie = "foo=nonhostonly; domain=example.com"
document.cookie = "foo=domaintest; domain="
```
- Chrome 94
   - `foo=nonhostonly; foo=domaintest`
- Firefox 92
   - `foo=nonhostonly; foo=domaintest`

### Summary

So it appears that Chrome is ignoring the cookie-av while Firefox always make the cookie host-only when it encounters `domain=`.
Additionally Firefox rejects cookies when it sees `domain=.` as the last domain attribute, Chrome doesn't seem to mind the `.`.

issues.title: [6265bis] Clarification on cookie size limits
issues.author: miketaylr
issues.body:
https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-07#section-6.1 states:
>    Practical user agent implementations have limits on the number and
   size of cookies that they can store.  General-use user agents SHOULD
   provide each of the following minimum capabilities:
>      *   At least 4096 bytes per cookie (as measured by the sum of the
      length of the cookie's name, value, and attributes).

IMHO, the prose here is a little confusing. It's clearly talking about limits on size, but then says the "minimum capability should be at least 4096 bytes per cookie". That I think can be cleaned up.

In addition, it's worthwhile looking into the current situation of interop on these limits. @chlily1 pointed me at http://www.ruslog.com/tools/cookies.html which has some interesting (older) research on the topic.

Other related links: 

Chrome considers name, =, value, and attributes when checking the 4096 cap:
https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/master:net/cookies/parsed_cookie.cc;drc=b35da1f38c91cbc8a3ec0f934b747360fa9a0f73;bpv=1;bpt=1;l=133

Firefox only looks at name and value when checking the 4096 cap, and not attributes.
https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/ffdb6a4d934b3f5294f18cf0e1df618109ccb36b/netwerk/cookie/CookieCommons.cpp#193-197

But, Firefox enforces a limit on the path attribute:
https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/ffdb6a4d934b3f5294f18cf0e1df618109ccb36b/netwerk/cookie/CookieCommons.cpp#189-191

So neither Firefox nor Chrome are strictly following 6.1 here (but yes, it's a SHOULD).

Need to look at what Safari and other clients do.

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body: I forgot to note that interop here seems desirable to prevent using these differences as a browser fingerprinting mechanism.

comments.author: karlcow
comments.body:
@miketaylr 

WebKit

https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/88278b55563e5ccdc0b3419c6c391c3becc19e40/Source/WebCore/platform/network/curl/CookieUtil.cpp#L143-L144

and MAX_COOKIE_LINE is `5000`

https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/88278b55563e5ccdc0b3419c6c391c3becc19e40/Source/WebCore/platform/network/curl/CookieUtil.cpp#L37-L49

and fwiw the MAX_NAME doesn't seem to be used in the code.

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
OK, to recap, the current the spec text states:

>  At least 4096 bytes per cookie (as measured by the sum of the length of the cookie's name, value, and attributes).

Browsers interpret that "at least" as "at most", so we should change that.

Here's what browsers are doing:

Firefox: sets `kMaxBytesPerCookie = 4096` and adds up the name and value lengths (minus the =), and does not consider attributes. however, it seems there are constraints on the path size (1024 bytes) that can cause a cookie to be rejected. But expires, for example, I believe can add an additional 8 bytes to the total cookie size. And then there's attribute names' length to consider.

Chrome: sets `kMaxCookieSize = 4096;`, and counts the entire cookie string length (that is, everything from `Set-Cookie:` to the first of `kTerminator[] = "\n\r\0";`)

Safari: sets `#define MAX_COOKIE_LINE 5000` and also counts the entire cookie string length (`if (cookieLine.length() >= MAX_COOKIE_LINE)`. But my tests show it only allows a total cookie length of 4096.

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
> MAX_COOKIE_LINE is `5000`
> 
> https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/88278b55563e5ccdc0b3419c6c391c3becc19e40/Source/WebCore/platform/network/curl/CookieUtil.cpp#L37-L49

I'm not really sure if Safari is using that (because I'm not super familiar with the WebKit codebase), but here is where that was added to curl, with a nice commit message: https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/2bc230de63bd7da197280a69d84972b61455cd18

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
My general thinking here is that we should set a minimum for name+value, as well as a limit on attribute values. Perhaps something like 1024 bytes for attributes, and 4096 for name+value (similar to what Firefox does).

We should have some metrics from Chrome to look at in a few weeks to help us determine if this is web-compatible. In theory a domain or path attribute could be much larger than 1024 bytes. Hopefully not in practice?

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
> Safari: sets `#define MAX_COOKIE_LINE 5000` and also counts the entire cookie string length (`if (cookieLine.length() >= MAX_COOKIE_LINE)`. But my tests show it only allows a total cookie length of 4096.

I've since learned this isn't true -- this is curl code that's inside WebKit. Safari seems to bound by the limitations of https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/nshttpcookie which aren't well documented (at least, I can't find good documentation). You can make really, really large cookies because NSHttpCookie supports the Set-Cookie2 comment attribute (up to 28k just for the comment alone).

I admit to struggling to fully grasp the meaning of HTTP representation-data and/or selected representation as it relates to which actual bytes to use as input to the digest function (I was trying to write down how to use the Digest value as part of a simple digital signature scheme for HTTP messages FWIW). 

In an effort to better understand, I went to work through the examples in [Section 10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers-04.html#name-examples-of-unsolicited-dig) but ran into some things that didn't seem right. 

Specifically for the [response in sec 10.8](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers-04.html#section-10.8-6), with some luck and experimentation I was able to reproduce the digest value of `0o/WKwSfnmIoSlop2LV/ISaBDth05IeW27zzNMUh5l8=` from an input of `{"status": "created", "id": "123", "ts": 1569327729, "instance": "/books/123"}` as the body or representation-data. However, the JSON in the body of that example is semantically equivalent to that but formatted differently and consequently has a different digest value:
```
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Digest: id-sha-256=0o/WKwSfnmIoSlop2LV/ISaBDth05IeW27zzNMUh5l8=
Location: /books/123

{
  "status": "created",
  "id": "123",
  "ts": 1569327729,
  "instance": "/books/123"
}
```
Similarly for the [response in sec 10.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers-04.html#section-10.10-6) the digest value in the example was reproducible from `{"title": "Not Found", "detail": "Cannot PATCH a non-existent resource", "status": 404}` but the formatting of the JSON in the example differs:
```
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Digest: sha-256=UJSojgEzqUe4UoHzmNl5d2xkmrW3BOdmvsvWu1uFeu0=

{
  "title": "Not Found",
  "detail": "Cannot PATCH a non-existent resource",
  "status": 404
}
```

I don't think I'm dong anything wrong here. But please correct me, if so. 

I realize there are line length limitations to the textual RFC style output that need to be considered but I do think having examples that readers can easily and reliably follow and reproduce is worthwhile.

I'm porting the old http-state path tests (which were already ported to WPT, but don't actually work) and have a question on what the spec says to do vs what browsers actually do.

The setup is the following:

The browser calls fetch to a test `cookie.py` endpoint and sets a cookie via `Set-Cookie`. The `cookie.py` endpoint then returns a 302 with a `Location` header. However, Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all send a cookie.

Is this consistent with Path-Match as defined in https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-07#section-5.1.4?

Another point to consider, I added a new test which tests a partially URL-encoded `Location` (the API is different, but the test setup is the same as previously described):

> POST and PATCH requests can appear to convey partial representations but are semantically acting on resources. The enclosed representation, including its metadata, refers to that action.

Aren't all HTTP requests "acting on resources"?

> In these requests the representation digest MUST be computed on the representation-data of that action. This is the only possible choice because representation digest requires complete representation metadata (see Section 2).

IMHO, that should be the case for *any* requests (but we already have a ticket for that).

> In responses,
> 
>    if the representation describes the status of the request, Digest MUST be computed on the enclosed representation (see Section 10.8 );
>    if there is a referenced resource Digest MUST be computed on the selected representation of the referenced resource even if that is different from the target resource. That might or might not result in computing Digest on the enclosed representation.
> The latter case might be done according to the HTTP semantics of the given method, for example using the Content-Location header field. In contrast, the Location header field does not affect Digest because it is not representation metadata.

- [x] This is true, but "might be done" is a bit vague. In general, this is the way it is done.

Why do we need this if 6 is about POST and PATCH already?

How is this different from POST?

> In PATCH responses, the representation digest MUST be computed on the selected representation of the patched resource.

- [x] No. General rules should apply here. There is no special case for PATCH.

> Digest usage with PATCH is thus very similar to POST, but with the resource's own semantic partly implied by the method and by the patch document.

issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
The I-D contains the following TODO

> TODO: Discuss if we should add a signal that mitigates this issue. For example,
we might add a SETTINGS parameter that indicates the next hop that the

comments.author: rmarx
comments.body:
I don't think anything additional is needed. We've got the two standard header options to indicate an intermediary is involved, that was the main point of the original discussion in Singapore IIRC. 

I think this won't matter all that much in practice, given warmed up edge-to-origin connections, pops being able to serve cached resources in between, etc. Origin owners really concerned with performance will know if their setup is coalescing or not (then the question is if origin server software allows tweaking prioritization behavior, but that's a general concern). CDN owners seeing bad origin behaviour will probably just overwrite the priority information instead of forwarding in practice. 

In short, I think the current text `if a server knows the intermediary is coalescing requests` should suffice here, as I don't think many servers would support switching to RR when seeing an explicit "warning: coalescing intermediary" signal either way.

issues.title: Third-party cookies
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
In [the current draft's privacy considerations](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html#name-third-party-cookies):

> Given this risk to user privacy, some user agents restrict how third-party cookies behave, and those restrictions vary widly. For instance, user agents might block third-party cookies entirely by refusing to send Cookie headers or process Set-Cookie headers during third-party requests. They might take a less draconian approach by partitioning cookies based on the first-party context, sending one set of cookies to a given third party in one first-party context, and another to the same third party in another.

Is this still true?

comments.author: chlily1
comments.body:
Which part of it are you asking about, specifically?

The part about "grants user agents wide latitude" is certainly true. It allows UAs to [ignore Set-Cookie headers in their entirety](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-07#section-5.3) and [omit the Cookie header entirely](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-07#section-5.5). I suppose it does not technically allow for selectively withholding certain cookies from the Cookie header. (Maybe that should be allowed?)

The part about not endorsing any third-party cookie policy is probably also fine. It gives examples of a third-party cookie policy that drops Set-Cookie and Cookie headers entirely on third-party requests, but I don't think this constitutes an endorsement.

comments.author: jwrosewell
comments.body:
@annevk There may be an agreement among browser vendors and a small number of others within the IETF however the distinction between first / third or cross-site is not recognised by a wider group of stakeholders including the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and the Competition and Markets Authority. See [their joint statement](https://ico.org.uk/media/about-the-ico/documents/2619797/cma-ico-public-statement-20210518.pdf) from May 2021.

> Data is sometimes categorised according to the relationship between the party collecting and processing it and the individual or circumstance it relates to:

> • First-party data: data that is collected by a business through direct interaction with an individual providing or generating the data. For example, data collected by an online retailer regarding purchases made by consumers on its site. 

> • Third-party data: data collected by a business not in direct interaction with the individual providing or generating the data, for example, through business partners. Digital firms that do not have a direct relationship with users frequently rely on third-party data.

> The boundaries between first and third-party data according to the above definition are not always clear, particularly when large companies own a variety of businesses, some of which have a relationship with the user and some of which do not.
Both first-party and third-party data as defined above can include personal and non personal data. Whether information is personal data depends on whether it relates to an identified or identifiable individual. There is no explicit reference to the distinction between first-party and third-party data in data protection law.

> The descriptions of ‘first party’ and ‘third party’ are also used (though with a different meaning) in the context of cookies and similar technologies,10 which collectively form the key means by which information (including personal data) is collected and disseminated in online advertising. A cookie is generally identified as being first-party if the domain of the cookie matches the domain of the page visited and as being third-party in instances where the domain of the cookie does not match the domain of the website. This is not a rigid distinction. Some functions typically delivered through third party cookies can be done via first party cookies, even if a third party’s code and associated service is still involved.

> The rules on the use of cookies and similar technologies are specified in Regulation 6 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations 2003 (as amended) (‘PECR’), and oversight of these rules is one of the ICO’s regulatory functions. PECR provides more specific rules than the UK GDPR in a number of areas such as cookie use. It is also important to note that PECR’s provisions in this area apply whether or not personal data is processed.

This debate in this group consists of browser vendor representatives and a small number of others, agreeing to work with each other to exclude other non browser vendors from the market.

issues.body:
`Cache-Control` header seems a one of confusing point for developer. 

for example, as @mnot noted in [Cache-Control in the wild | Fastly](https://www.fastly.com/blog/cache-control-wild) there are a lot of strange directive combination which says much developer doesn't understand Cache-Control correctly.

So I hope BCP include more important practice around caching.

# private / public

mentioning about adding `private` for private content which must not be stored in shared cache.
and `public` is not a thing for public content because caches are public by default.

# explicit cache-control for heuristic cache

no `Cache-Control` header doesn't mean un-cacheable. browser could cache them under heuristic caching theory.
so if you have any restriction around caching, adding cache-control header for explicit control.

see also [Twitter Direct Message Caching and Firefox - Mozilla Hacks - the Web developer blog](https://hacks.mozilla.org/2020/04/twitter-direct-message-caching-and-firefox/)

# no-cache is not a "don't cache"

already mentioned is draft

# max-age=0 + must-revalidate

it's better to use `no-cache` (almost same bihavior)

```http
Cache-Control: max-age=0, must-revalidate # 👎
Cache-Control: no-store # 👍
```

# s-maxage & proxy-revalidate

`s-maxage` & `proxy-revalidate` are optional when you do different control for shared proxy. so
if `max-age` and `s-maxage` has same value, `s-maxage` is ommitable.
if `must-revalidate` is present, `proxy-revalidate` is ommitable.

```http
Cache-Control: max-age=100, s-maxage=100, must-revalidate, proxy-revaliate 👎
Cache-Control: max-age=100, must-revalidate 👍
```


# throw the kitchen sink

if you really wanna make this not cacheable and avoid store any cache, best choice is to use `no-store` alone.

```http
Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, proxy-revalidate, max-age=0 # 👎
Cache-Control: no-store # 👍
```

throw the kitchen sink is almost meaningless and not only waste bytes but also implementation could cause a problem because `no-store` and other directives are semantically conflicted.

# reload request (max-age=0 or no-cache)

semantically, `no-cache` should works fine when you do like Reloading of browser.
(but I don't know why browser sends `max-age=0` when reloading instead of `no-cache`.
if there are some reason/use-case for `max-age=0` it could be noted here too)

I'll update if I remember more ideas. Correct me if I also misunderstood.
Thanks

issues.title: Support for Partial Hits
issues.author: elithrar
issues.body:
Continuing a discussion with @mnot  - 

The current draft[1] of the `cache-status` header specifies that ""hit" and "fwd" are exclusive; only one of them should appear on each list member.". 

If a "downstream" (user-facing) cache has a partial hit - say, a 2MB chunk of a larger object, it is challenging to accurately map that representation in the cache-status header. 

For example:

1. The user requests a larger video file - say, an 8MB segment
2. The cache has this stored in 2MB (or smaller) chunks
3. The cache closest to the client has the first 6MB, but not the last 2MB, and needs to fetch that from an upstream cache (or the origin; it doesn't know) 
4. The last 2MB chunk is fulfilled by an upstream.

This would be naively represented as `x-cache-status: PARTIAL, HIT`. Without constraints, it could potentially be represented as `cache-status: ExampleCache; fwd=partial; hit`.

In the case the next tier of caching did not have the segment, then it would be `cache-status: ExampleCache; fwd=partial; fwd=miss; hit`. 

That is, a cache may be able to fulfill _part_ of the response, but not all, and this is useful to distinguish vs. a full hit - e.g. from a latency/performance perspective.





[1]: https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-cache-header-06.html

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
I think that `fwd=partial` makes sense, with the semantic that the cache had a partial, fresh response stored that could be used to satisfy part of the request, but not all of it, so the cache needed to go forward for that reason.

`hit` and `fwd` in the same member of `Cache-Status` isn't allowed by the spec right now; allowing that would muddy what the meaning of `hit` is. I know that it's already muddy in existing headers and logs, but this is a good opportunity to crisp it up.

I'll try to clarify this a bit more in the spec.

issues.title: RFC6265bis does not specify what happens to existing cookies when the Public Suffix List changes
issues.author: chlily1
issues.body:
If the user agent is configured to reject "public suffixes", cookies with a `Domain` attribute should be [processed](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-07#page-28) according to the Public Suffix List (PSL), which may change frequently. The spec currently says "Whenever possible, user agents SHOULD use an up-to-date public suffix list", but does not specify what to do with existing `Domain` cookies whose `domain-attribute` becomes a public suffix after a PSL update.

I think the sensible thing to do would be to remove such a cookie from the cookie store entirely. (The alternative would be to convert it to a host-only cookie, but since the storage model doesn't include the origin that set the cookie, there's no way to know whether the cookie originally came from that host.)

Chrome currently keeps such a cookie, but I think that's [a bug](https://crbug.com/1170834). I am not sure what other UAs do in this scenario.

issues.title: RFC 6265bis: Set-Cookie parsing algorithm should enforce more of the syntax requirements
issues.author: chlily1
issues.body:
There is an ABNF syntax given for the Set-Cookie header [in section 4.4.1](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-07#section-4.1.1), however many aspects of this are not enforced in the actual parsing algorithm [in section 5.3](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-07#section-5.3).

The syntax given in 4.4.1 is only a "SHOULD", not a hard requirement for the server:
```
Servers SHOULD NOT send Set-Cookie headers that fail to conform to
   the following grammar:
```

There is an explicit caveat about this in section 5.3:
```
   NOTE: The algorithm below is more permissive than the grammar in
   Section 4.1.  For example, the algorithm strips leading and trailing
   whitespace from the cookie name and value (but maintains internal
   whitespace), whereas the grammar in Section 4.1 forbids whitespace in
   these positions.  User agents use this algorithm so as to
   interoperate with servers that do not follow the recommendations in
   Section 4.
```

The algorithm in 5.3 should enforce more of the requirements given in the recommended syntax, at the very least the requirements on validity of characters/octets (whitespace, control characters, etc.), and specify the intended behavior in these cases. (For context and examples of such discrepancies, see [here](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1136#issuecomment-772872621) and [here](https://crbug.com/1174647).)

comments.author: recvfrom
comments.body:
To call out some of the current differences between the ABNF section and the parsing algorithm (not an exhaustive list - just the ones I've happened to notice):

```
cookie-pair       = cookie-name BWS "=" BWS cookie-value
cookie-name       = 1*cookie-octet
cookie-value      = *cookie-octet / ( DQUOTE *cookie-octet DQUOTE )
```
 - `cookie-name` can be empty
 - `cookie-pair` doesn't have to include the '=' (Ex: cookie with empty name, non-empty cookie value)
 - Double quotes surrounding `cookie-octet` in `cookie-value` are not removed and will be a part of the `cookie-value` if present

```
cookie-octet      = %x21 / %x23-2B / %x2D-3A / %x3C-5B / %x5D-7E
                    / %x80-FF
                      ; octets excluding CTLs,
                      ; whitespace DQUOTE, comma, semicolon,
                      ; and backslash
```

 - The character set used by `cookie-name` is `%x09 / %x20-3A / %x3C / %x3E-7E / %x80-FF` (all octets except for non-whitespace CTLs, `;`, and `=`)
 - The character set used by `cookie-value` is `%x09 / %x20-3A / %x3C-7E / %x80-FF` (all octets except for non-whitespace CTLs and `;`)
 - Whitespace gets trimmed from the beginning and end

```
max-age-av        = "Max-Age" BWS "=" BWS non-zero-digit *DIGIT
                      ; In practice, both expires-av and max-age-av
                      ; are limited to dates representable by the
                      ; user agent.
non-zero-digit    = %x31-39
                      ; digits 1 through 9
```
 - The first digit can be 0 or a negative sign

```
domain-value      = <subdomain>
                      ; defined in [RFC1034], Section 3.5, as
                      ; enhanced by [RFC1123], Section 2.1
```
 - The RFCs for domains indicate that the domain name should not exceed 253 characters, and also indicates that labels (the pieces separated by dots in a domain) should not be more than 63 characters each.  The parsing algorithm doesn't indicate that these restrictions must be enforced, but instead applies the 1024 octet limit for attribute values as an upper bound on the length of `domain-value`.

```
extension-av      = *av-octet
av-octet          = %x20-3A / %x3C-7E
                      ; any CHAR except CTLs or ";"
```
 - the `av-octet` character set is `%x09 / %x20-3A / %x3C-7E / %x80-FF` (all octets except for non-whitespace CTLs and `;`)

comments.author: recvfrom
comments.body:
I've observed multiple instances where the grammar from 4.4.1 is copied into discussions/code related to cookie parsing and used as if it was the syntax that all cookies MUST adhere to.  To mitigate this confusion, I think we should provide a grammar for section 5.3 either in addition to or in place of the one in 4.4.1.

Does anyone have any thoughts about whether there's still value in having the separate, stricter grammar for Set-Cookie headers sent by servers?

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body: Let's make sure anything changing here is well tested and matches reality.

comments.author: kailuowang
comments.body:
Just noticed another discrepancy in section 4.4.1:
```
 cookie-octet      = %x21 / %x23-2B / %x2D-3A / %x3C-5B / %x5D-7E
                       / %x80-FF
                         ; octets excluding CTLs,
                         ; whitespace DQUOTE, comma, semicolon,
                         ; and backslash
```
`%x7F` is also excluded but not mentioned in the comment: It's the question mark character `?`

comments.author: annevk
comments.body:
I hadn't seen this issue before, but it's quite common to have strict requirements for producers and loose-but-still-strict requirements for consumers. E.g., CSS and HTML do something similar.

https://crbug.com/1174647 seems like a solid reason to make changes to the parser, but I think that's a separable concern from what this issue seems to raise as a larger issue, which I don't think is an issue at all.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
Stepping back, I see two aspects to this issue:

a. Whether there should be differences in the producer and consumer grammars, and 
b. If so, how to document them.

It _seems_ like we've come to agreement here that there can be such differences. Not only do we see it in existing specs (e.g., Cookies so far, HTTP with productions like `OWS`, Structured Fields), it's inevitable - ABNF cannot capture all of the constraints that prose (or an algorithm) can express.

(b) is largely an editorial issue about how to capture the delta between the producer grammer and the parsing algorithm. As such, the editors should decide, taking into account input from the WG as they see fit.

Personally: I don't see how having two separate ABNF grammars would help -- it's just as likely to cause confusion, and there's a possilbity of introducing yet more errors. I think it'd be fine if the editors added a note to the top of 4.1.1 noting the relationship with 5.4, much as they already do in the other direction.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: As per above, marking as editorial.

issues.title: backward compatibility for current http-signatures implementations
issues.author: kaniini
issues.body:
There's a wonderful world out there of servers implementing ActivityPub, which already implement HTTP Signatures.

Unfortunately, `draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-01` has completely broken compatibility with current implementations, because it changed `(request-target)` to `*request-target` for the signing string, as well as completely changing the way the `Signature` header works.

Is there any advice for allowing both forms of the signature to exist at the same time?

I know, you're going to say: "deploying internet-draft specifications in production is not good practice", but I didn't make that decision, the ActivityPub community made that decision several years ago based on perceived stability of the spec.

This is a serious problem that blocks any possibility of upgrading to support the latest draft, as it breaks *real world* use of the extension.

comments.author: msporny
comments.body:
> Is there any advice for allowing both forms of the signature to exist at the same time?

Yes, and the expectation is that most libraries can (and will) support the old version and the new version. Presently, while the specification is silent on how to do that, implementers are putting in two code paths -- one for the old version and one for the new version by doing feature detection on the signing string... 

Implementers have options for feature detection. For example, if you see (request-target) -- you use the old algorithm to verify... if you see *request-target, you use the new algorithm to verify. The libraries will also be given the option of generating an old-style signature (which is what ActivityPub uses) and a new-style signature (which ActivityPub can switch to once the official spec is live AND the ActivityPub community has deployed enough infrastructure to be sure that they can support new style signatures without breaking the ecosystem).

comments.author: kaniini
comments.body:
Uhh, how does that work?

The signing string is not known to us ahead of time as we generate it on the verifying side.

Are you saying that we should look for headers="(request-target)" in the Signature header?  What if somebody creates a new signature with `Signature-Input: headers=(...)`?

comments.author: kaniini
comments.body:
It seems to me the best way to go is if `Signature-Input` is in headers: it's a new-style signature, else it's old-style.

I think that's simple enough on the verify side.  I'm working on generalizing my http_signatures python implementation to work with any aiohttp.web application, so I will do this work when I split that out :)

comments.author: msporny
comments.body:
> It seems to me the best way to go is if Signature-Input is in headers: it's a new-style signature, else it's old-style.

Yes, that's possibility as well -- like I said, the spec is almost certainly going to be silent on this, and it'll be up to implementers to do feature detection properly.

Now, speaking as an implementer (not as a spec author) -- I was averse to breaking changes that were not easily detectable... I don't know how much care is going into making sure there is clear feature detection possible, but I expect if we ever hit a state where it creates a huge burden on the ActivityPub community, we'd take a deep breath and serve the needs of people using this stuff in the wild rather than go down the academic purity path. We're not there yet, so I wouldn't worry too much. If we do get there, I expect that you (and I) will complain loudly (and will be heard -- I expect the HTTP WG doesn't have an interest in alienating the implementation base for the HTTP Signatures specification).

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
The `draft-ietf-http-message-signatures` spec is based on input from `draft-cavage-http-signatures` but is not intended to be directly compatible with it.  As the old draft was an independent work and not tied to any standards working group, implementation of it is always an at-risk proposition. Sometimes that risk is worthwhile, but sometimes it can cause pain.

Changes are happening in the draft to address problems with the draft, and these changes will not be hampered by backwards compatibility with the independent draft. This is not simply an exercise of "academic purity" as some might say, but rather driven by a desire to make a specification that works for a wide variety of use cases. While many have adopted the independent draft, and that experience is deeply valuable, it's important to remember that there are also many other communities who have not been able to adopt the independent draft because of limitations. Furthermore, in my personal experience, many of the implementations of the independent draft aren't compatible with each other because they either work against different versions of the draft, or they implement only portions of the draft that seem relevant at the time. Having a stable, engineering-driven RFC will help that. 

I can assure you that the editors of the spec are not blind to the issues that breaking compatibility will cause in some parts of the world, and as said above there are a lot of things we can do to signal developers clearly what's going on. I've personally been a part of several major protocol migrations (OAuth 1 -> OAuth 2, OpenID 2.x -> OpenID Connect), and so I really get where you're coming from. The spec is not likely to be silent on migration issues, in spite of what's said above, but I do agree that we aren't at the point of getting that sorted out yet. It could be something as simple as renaming a header or something more complex like detecting an internal header format, but it's something that this spec won't be blind to. In the end though, it will be worlds better than the current situation where two independent implementations of the individual draft might look like they should work together but in fact might or might not talk to each other depending on a dozen different decisions and variables.

issues.title: Cookies and Fetch
issues.author: annevk
issues.body:
As discussed in #1428 I thought I'd try to note down what Fetch needs:

* `Cookie` header is appended in https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-http-network-or-cache-fetch.
* Currently https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-network-fetch parses `Set-Cookie` headers.

Neither is super precise, especially when it comes to the various cookie policies implementations have, the cookie store, and any potential partitioning of that cookie store.

Furthermore, with `SameSite` I feel like we have a layering violation where the cookie specification makes determinations about cookies that it really needs additional input from Fetch from (i.e., more than a URL). I think it's understandable how that became to be that way, but I think eventually it would be better if that was better abstracted and "site for cookies" and such are instead inputs from Fetch. (Either calculated in fetch before it does things on a thread where that information is no longer accessible or even before fetch is invoked as not all invocations happen from the "main thread".)

None of this seems particularly pressing to me, but I think we should get to it eventually.

(See also https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/693.)

issues.title: Signature: Invalid space in Signature-Input field examples
issues.author: bblfish
issues.body:
I am writing [a parser for RFC8941](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/issues/13) in Scala, to implement the Signature spec. So I am looking very closely at both specs.

We find the following in [2.4.2](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-03#section-2.4.2)

```http
# NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792
   ("@request-target" "host" "date" "cache-control" "x-empty-header"
     "x-example"); keyid="test-key-a"; alg="rsa-pss-sha512"; \
     created=1402170695; expires=1402170995
```

in [§2.4.2.1](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-03#section-2.4.2.1)

```http
"@signature-params": ("@request-target" "host" "date" "cache-control" \
   "x-empty-header" "x-example" "x-dictionary";key=b \
   "x-dictionary";key=a "x-list";prefix=3); keyid="test-key-a"; \
   alg="rsa-pss-sha512"; created=1402170695; expires=1402170995
```

in [§2.5](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-03#section-2.5), and so on.

In each of these cases the attributes for the inner list have a white space after the semicolon. I.e. they have "; " instead of ";". The [Signatures Param](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-03#section-2.5) section refers to [the inner list section of RFC8941](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8941#section-4.1.1.1), but in that section and the next there is no mention of adding a whitespace.

I think the following text from that RFC supports my reading:

> Note that parameters are ordered as serialized, and parameter keys
   cannot contain uppercase letters.  A parameter is separated from its
   Item or Inner List and other parameters by a semicolon.  For example:
   
```http
   Example-List: abc;a=1;b=2; cde_456, (ghi;jk=4 l);q="9";r=w
```

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
ABNF (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941.html#section-3.1.2):

~~~
parameters    = *( ";" *SP parameter )
~~~

Also see the parsing algorithm (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941.html#section-4.2.3.2).

comments.author: bblfish
comments.body:
@reschke yes, that is how I implemented the *parser*. (see [here](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/blob/c5163ed8f3d135f87be0a5091caaed997b2a2522/src/main/scala/run/cosy/http/headers/Rfc8941.scala#L69)).

I am speaking here not about parsing, but about serialization, which is different. Parsing of headers must be lenient, but the output to be signed must be exactly the same for each client and server. So for example `*SP` does not make sense there, as that would not make it possible for servers to verify the signature.

Perhaps a better example would have been from the paragraph just before [Section 3](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-03#section-3)

```http
# NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792
 "@request-target": get /foo
 "host": example.org
 "date": Tue, 07 Jun 2014 20:51:35 GMT
 "cache-control": max-age=60, must-revalidate
 "x-emptyheader":
 "x-example": Example header with some whitespace.
 "x-dictionary";key=b: 2
 "x-dictionary";key=a: 1
 "x-list";prefix=3: (a, b, c)
 "@signature-params": ("@request-target" "host" "date" "cache-control" \
   "x-empty-header" "x-example" "x-dictionary";key=b \
   "x-dictionary";key=a "x-list";prefix=3); keyid="test-key-a"; \
   created=1402170695; expires=1402170995
   ```
   
   This clearly is the string to be signed by the client and verified by the server.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941.html#section-1.2-4>

> For serialization to HTTP fields, the ABNF illustrates their expected wire representations, and the algorithms define the recommended way to produce them. Implementations MAY vary from the specified behavior so long as the output is still correctly handled by the parsing algorithm described in Section 4.2.

So you really can't rely on a specific serialization wrt optional whitespace.

That said, the Signatures spec can of course make additional requirements.

comments.author: bblfish
comments.body:
> So you really can't rely on a specific serialization wrt optional whitespace.

The text I am speaking of is not sent over the wire.  It is calculated by the client and reconstituted by the server and has to be byte to byte identical in order for the signature verification to work.

>  the Signatures spec can of course make additional requirements.

yes, and it quite handily points to the serialization algorithms from RFC8941 for the generated header to be signed. 
That is nice because it saves implementors work: My RFC8941 implementation [has Serialization code](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/blob/c5163ed8f3d135f87be0a5091caaed997b2a2522/src/main/scala/run/cosy/http/headers/Rfc8941.scala#L115) , that I can use for "Signing HTTP Messages". 

There is no deep problem here. It just requires the examples to be fixed, and the associated example signatures to be regenerated.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
I have not re-generated any of the examples yet, we've been focusing on getting the requirements and syntax right. It doesn't surprised me that one or more of the example serializations is off, and I guarantee that the signatures will fail because they haven't been changed with regard to the new signature input string format, yet. Unfortunately that process isn't automated for our draft and I haven't had a chance to do that yet! :) 

With that in mind: the design constraints of the signature draft is to use the serialization algorithms exactly as specified in RFC8941 to provide a single deterministic process. This is why the signature-params specialty parameter value is declared to be re-serialized by verifiers, for example. 

The other consideration is that it's difficult to accurately portray examples that are both human-readable and machine-processable in the spec text which has limits on line width for displays.

comments.body: Examples should all be fixed in -04

issues.title: Signatures: hs2019 algorithm gone from spec v3
issues.author: bblfish
issues.body:
I just noticed that the only supported algorithm `hs2019` present in [message-signatures-02 §5.1.2.1](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-02#section-5.1.2.1) has gone in [message-signatures-03](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-03) replaced by the old style of algorithm specification.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Dropping this is an intentional change. The `hs2019` algorithm identifier definition (itself a late addition to one of the input I-D's) was an artifact of the `alg` parameter being required by the spec, so it was a placeholder that said "ignore the algorithm and go find something else". In other words, it was functionally vestigial. This parameter is no longer required, meaning the behavior of `hs2019` of determining the algorithm from the key, context, configuration, or environment is now the default behavior. The explicit algorithm identifier of `alg` is also allowable in circumstances that require it, but it's overridden by the context (ie: they have to match if both specified). Also the parameters are now signed, which wasn't the case before. This discussion happened over the course of a few different issues and pull requests on here. The discussion is expanded in #1455 and will hopefully be more clear in the next draft being published soon.

issues.title: Signatures: Difficulty verifying B.2 examples
issues.author: bblfish
issues.body:
I [have implemented](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/issues/14)  nearly all of "Signing HTTP Messages v04" and have tested it carefully in [TestMessageSigningRFCFn.scala](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/blob/5339b4200cc5e3f7ec95a9c8b521a0ce0048ef98/src/test/scala/run/cosy/http/auth/TestMessageSigningRFCFn.scala). The 3 problematic cases are commented out here:
- [line 392](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/blob/5339b4200cc5e3f7ec95a9c8b521a0ce0048ef98/src/test/scala/run/cosy/http/auth/TestMessageSigningRFCFn.scala#L392)
 - [line 450](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/blob/5339b4200cc5e3f7ec95a9c8b521a0ce0048ef98/src/test/scala/run/cosy/http/auth/TestMessageSigningRFCFn.scala#L450)

 In each case I am able to sign and verify the headers myself using the Java Cryptography API, using the [rsa-pss-sha512 Signature object](https://github.com/co-operating-systems/Reactive-SoLiD/blob/5339b4200cc5e3f7ec95a9c8b521a0ce0048ef98/src/test/scala/run/cosy/http/auth/TestMessageSigningRFCFn.scala#L328). It may be that I am not using the right signature algorithm, or it may  be that the signatures in the spec are not quite right, or ... Since the spec is still in development I thought I would check here.
 
 This is the signature I tried out:
 ```scala
 lazy val `rsa-pss-sha512`: JSignature =
	//is this the same as JWT PS512?
	//see [[https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518 JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) RFC]]
	val rsapss = JSignature.getInstance("RSASSA-PSS")
	import java.security.spec.{PSSParameterSpec, MGF1ParameterSpec}
	rsapss.setParameter(new PSSParameterSpec(
		"SHA-512", "MGF1", MGF1ParameterSpec.SHA512, 512 / 8, 1))
	rsapss
```	

Where `JSignature` is a just an alias for `java.security.Signature`.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
All the signatures in the spec in -04 were generated and verified using a python implementation (and we're figuring out the best place to release it to), so they should all work as is -- unless I've got a bug in my own implementation! I'm not deeply familiar with Scala, but it looks like you might be checking signature validity by re-generating the signature and then evaluating for equality with the presented signature, is that correct? If so, then that is not going to work for the RSA PSS algorithm (or most elliptic curve algorithms, which we haven't added examples for). The output of the signing algorithm is not the same for each signing, but the definitions of the verification functions take this into account -- you pass in the signature to be verified, the key, and the content to sign over in order to verify. This is what it looks like in part of the python code that generated the examples:

```
# Sign
signed = http_sfv.Item(key.sign_rsassa_pss(str.encode(base), algo='sha512'))

# Verify
verified = key.verify_rsassa_pss(str.encode(base), signed.value, algo='sha512')
```

Here, `key` is our public/private keypair (we could use just the public key to verify, though), `base` is the signature base string calculated from the "minimal" example in B.2.1.

As for the other points:

- yes the list prefix examples should be over a top level list not an inner list, thanks for catching that. Can you please file a separate issue for this?
- the multiple signatures message is given in the example: it uses an incoming signature field but doesn't sign other parts of the request
- yes the space is required, as per the serialization algorithm at https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-04.html#section-2.5-2.2.2.3; you can think of this as 'connect the identifier and content with ": " and then connect the lines with "\n" to get the output' if you want to think in terms of join() functions or the like. In the example generation code we do:

```
base = '';
for c in coveredContent:
    i = http_sfv.Item()
    i.parse(c.encode())
    sigparams.append(i)
    base += c # already serialized as an Item
    base += ': '
    base += coveredContent[c]
    base += "\n"
```

This is followed by adding the `@signature-params` item as the last on the list, so we don't have to account for the final line.

issues.title: Signatures 04: Use lists instead of Inner lists for §2.3 Prefixes
issues.author: bblfish
issues.body:
The [Message Signing 04 $2.3 Prefixes](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-04.html#name-list-prefixes) section gives inner lists as example of a data structure to which prefixes can be applied. 

```HTTP
X-List-A: (a b c d e f)
X-List-B: ()
```

The problem there is that this requires uniqueness of headers as [RFC 8941 Inner Lists](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941#name-inner-lists) on multiple headers fold into [RFC 8941 §3.1 Lists](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941#name-lists). So for example for a Message containing the following headers:

```HTTP
X-List-A: (a b c d e f)
X-List-A: (g h i)
```

would give the following folded header

```HTTP
X-List-A:  (a b c d e f), (g h i)
```

And that seems to be the more fundamental one on which Prefixes need to be applied.

issues.title: signatures and empty fields vs http-semantics-latest
issues.author: ioggstream
issues.body:
## Question

Does the fact that intermediaries can aggregate fields and ignore empty fields impact on the definition of this spec?

See:
- https://github.com/httpwg/http-core/issues/836#issuecomment-826166475 
- https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-latest.html#abnf.extension.recipient

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Combining field values in a deterministic way (which is required for signatures) is iffy at the best of times. There's a defined canonicalization for combining fields which, I believe, comes from the existing definitions in the HTTP core specs -- this might be able to be re-defined. If intermediaries follow the combination rules without dropping, it should be fine. If an empty field is signed by the sender and removed in transit, then that empty field won't be in the target message, meaning the signature would fail. But that's expected behavior because a signed element was removed or modified, it's exactly the time you'd want the signature to fail. If this kind of transformation is a known problem for an application, then the problematic field shouldn't be covered by the signature. This is one of the core reasons why the Signatures draft leaves it to applications and profiles to define required fields.

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
iiuc here is that if this spec supports combining fields, this should be done ignoring empty fields.

About breaking signatures, in general it's very hard to support or anticipate any transformation from intermediaries. I am not sure this brings much value, but I am curious about examples where this is needed.

issues.title: Disabling h2 priorities - nits
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
2.1 says:

> Once the client learns that the HTTP/2 priority scheme is deprecated, it SHOULD stop sending the HTTP/2 priority signals.

'deprecated' isn't the right word here; perhaps 'disabled by a peer'?

Also, here and a few other places refer to 'the HTTP/2 priority signals' without enumerating them. To be precise, that should be done somewhere. I think that means:

* The PRIORITY flag in HEADERS and its associated Exclusive flag, Stream Dependency field, and Weight field
* The PRIORITY frame type

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
How about instead "once a client learns that the server supports this priority scheme, it SHOULD stop sending HTTP/2 priority signals"

After all, this spec can only really have something to say about the stuff it defines and the h2 priority stuff.  (Plus what Mark says about being very clear about what "HTTP/2 priority signals" means.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinthomson I like the suggestion but that does not work as is.

The draft defines two separate concepts: an HTTP/2 SETTINGS flag that allows an endpoint to deprecate the use of H2 priorities, and a different prioritization scheme. While the two are expected to be used together on HTTP/2, they aren't required to.

[The first paragraph of section 2.1](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-priority.html#section-2.1-1) defines the SETTINGS_DEPRECATE_HTTP2_PRIORITIES flag as a way to _opt out of using the HTTP/2 priority scheme, in favor of using an alternative __such as__ the scheme defined in this specification_.

That said, I tend to wonder what @mnot and @martinthomson are suggesting is that the current draft is a bit verbose. At the moment, it uses [one paragraph](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-priority.html#section-2.1-2) to define what "deprecation" means, then the term to define how the client acts when the peer "deprecates."

Hence #1501. I would appreciate your reviews.

> Also, here and a few other places refer to 'the HTTP/2 priority signals' without enumerating them. To be precise, that should be done somewhere. I think that means:
> * The PRIORITY flag in HEADERS and its associated Exclusive flag, Stream Dependency field, and Weight field
> * The PRIORITY frame type

Makes sense.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: That raises a different issue. The setting is phrased in the negative, where it could be positive. That is, I support priority mechanism X. That works equally well and doesn't have issues in the case that we have to design a third scheme.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Yes, I think I would prefer a model of advertising support for (potentially multiple) schemes and then saying that the client SHOULD NOT send more than one scheme on a given connection.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinthomson @MikeBishop While I do not oppose strongly, I think there are number of things that we have to consider:

Technically, we can create a mechanism that allows the two sides of a hop agree on one prioritization scheme. However, that's going to be a bit complicated, because SETTINGS is a frame that is sent by the two endpoints before receiving one from the peer. Therefore, the minimal mechanism would be something like each endpoint sending a list of schemes that it supports, and then both endpoint choose a scheme from a intersection of the two lists using a predefined logic (e.g., client's list of schemes are ordered by its preference, and the most preferred one also supported by the server will be selected).

But before designing a negotiation scheme, I think it's worth asking one question: do we want a negotiation scheme for HTTP/3? If the answer is no, I'm not sure if we need something more than a deprecation scheme for HTTP/2, when what we are trying to do is a back port from HTTP/3.

Even with HTTP/2, there's isn't a necessity to negotiate the prioritization scheme. IIRC, the two reasons we introduced the deprecation flag (which IMO is an optimization) are:
* to reduce the burden of setting up the h2 prioritization tree on the server-side
* to conserve bandwidth

All that said, I think my argument is that having deprecation flag is a good way to punt to the future the cost of designing a solution that we might not need. Because the deprecation flag makes h2 and h3 on par.

If we find that we need to replace the new prioritization scheme in the future, then we could introduce a negotiation scheme that works for both H2 and H3. Note also that the new prioritization scheme is extensible.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Not needing to fully specify how they're selected right now is certainly a valid point.  But the only difference between a deprecation flag and an indication of support is the orientation of the default value.  In HTTP/2, the orientation is that the peer might support that feature, but many don't.  So there's value in being explicit both directions; the honest choice for default is "don't know."  Indicating support for each scheme gives us more leeway in the future, and we can recommend that implementations which don't support the old scheme explicitly disavow it.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Regarding default, I tend to believe that it should be "supports_h2_priorities," because clients should continue sending h2 priorities to h2 servers that do not implement the new extension.

That leaves us to the discussion of orientation. I do not have a strong opinion, though IIRC, some argued that they prefer default value being 0 rather than 1. That's how we ended up with a "deprecate" flag than "preferred" flag.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I agree with all of Kazuho's points. We explored something different in the past (e.g. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-kazuho-httpbis-priority-02#section-4.1) but ended up with what we have today, and I don't think there has been significant new information that would change my opinion.

comments.body: @mnot PTAL at this PR that addresses your comment about describing the signals https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1541/files

comments.body: That looks good, but I wonder if 2.1 should explicitly reference that for the definition of h2 priority signals.

issues.title: RFC 6265bis should allow user agents to block a subset of cookies during third-party requests
issues.author: cfredric
issues.body:
Currently, the relevant wording is:

Section 5.3:
> When a user agent receives a Set-Cookie header field in an HTTP
   response, the user agent MAY ignore the Set-Cookie header field in
   its entirety.  For example, the user agent might wish to block
   responses to "third-party" requests from setting cookies (see
   Section 7.1).

Section 5.5:
> A user agent MAY omit the Cookie header in its entirety.  For
   example, the user agent might wish to block sending cookies during
   "third-party" requests from setting cookies (see Section 7.1).

These indicate that a user agent can block setting/sending **all** cookies during third-party requests. This bakes in an assumption that the user agent considers all cookies to be "third-party" during such a request. Chrome is planning on breaking this assumption in the future (notably for https://github.com/cfredric/sameparty/issues/4): some cookies (those with the [SameParty](https://github.com/cfredric/sameparty) attribute) may be considered first-party, so will not be blocked in those cases.

Therefore, it would be nice if the spec indicated that user agents may block a _subset_ of cookies during third-party requests. Section 7.1 could also explicitly mention that user agents might wish to block a subset of cookies during third-party requests, as an alternative to refusing to send the Cookie header at all.

comments.author: chlily1
comments.body:
There's also this text in section 6.1, which suggests that servers SHOULD be able to handle individual cookies being absent:
```
   Servers SHOULD gracefully degrade if the user agent fails to return
   one or more cookies in the Cookie header because the user agent might
   evict any cookie at any time on orders from the user.
```

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
Section 7.1 is pretty generous here; I don't think any changes would be required to ship a SameParty cookies experiment.

> This document grants user agents wide latitude to experiment with third-party cookie policies that balance the privacy and compatibility needs of their users.  However, this document does not endorse any particular third-party cookie policy.

But making things more clear doesn't hurt. I guess we could update 5.3 to say (emphasis just to show the diff):

> For example, the user agent might wish to block responses to **all** "third-party" requests from setting cookies, **or just a subset, depending on user agent policy or user preference**. (see Section 7.1).

And do something similar in Section 5.5.

I think that would better describe what other UAs are doing today, e.g., Firefox's Standard ETP setting which blocks cross-site tracking cookies vs Strict ETP which blocks all cross-site cookies.

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body: Actually, https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/commit/1f7edb710db72cfc994ab84260334899fcf8aebc landed after this issue was filed, so I'll just add an example to the "Third Party Cookies" section and I think we're good.
