issues.title: RFC6265bis: Standardize maximum Max-Age cookie attribute value/handling
issues.author: recvfrom
issues.body:
RFC6265bis specifies a 1024 octet limit on all cookie attribute values, but given that the Max-Age attribute value is the number of seconds until the cookie expires, a much lower upper bound must be used in practice.  From some experimentation, these limits and the handling of Max-Age attributes that exceed them vary by browser (see below), and in some cases the differences could be used as a browser fingerprinting vector.  It might be worth having the RFC define appropriate maximum values for the Max-Age field in addition to specifying how values that exceed the max should be handled.

Results of Max-Age attribute experimentation:

In Chrome, if the Max-Age value is sufficiently high (Ex: `9999999999999`), the cookie will get set and DevTools shows it as being a `Session` cookie (in other words, it appears that the attribute is effectively ignored).  If the Max-Age value is something smaller like `7999999999999`, the cookie gets set and the Max-Age value appears to get used directly (DevTools shows it as having a huge date like `+255531-07-10T10:45:20.000Z`). 

In Firefox, if the Max-Age value is above roughly `9223372036854775807-Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)`, the whole cookie will fail to be set. Otherwise, the cookie gets set and the Max-Age attribute value appears to get used directly (even to the point where large Max-Age values result in an expiration date with such a large year component that `Invalid Date` is shown under the `Expires / Max-Age` column in the Firefox Developer Tools UI).

In Safari, any Max-Age value above `604800` (one week in seconds) appears to be treated as having a value of `604800`, but very large values for Max-Age (even 1000 digits) still result in the cookie being set.

Versions used for testing:
Chrome:  92.0.4515.131
Firefox: 90.0.2 (20210721174149)
Safari: 14.1.2 (16611.3.10.1.3)

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
> large Max-Age values result in an expiration date with such a large year component that `Invalid Date` is shown under the `Expires / Max-Age` column in the Firefox Developer Tools UI

This is probably worth a bug to Mozilla, if you haven't filed one yet: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/enter_bug.cgi?product=DevTools&component=Storage%20Inspector

> In Firefox, if the Max-Age value is above roughly 9223372036854775807-Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000), the whole cookie will fail to be set. 

According to  https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/12770bd668c0a6bdaa8eb96ad9507c6febe8d23d/netwerk/cookie/CookieService.cpp#1931-1937, the cookie should get set, but there's an overflow if the value is bigger than a [`unit32_t`](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/12770bd668c0a6bdaa8eb96ad9507c6febe8d23d/modules/libpref/init/StaticPrefList.yaml#10528-10533) so it's immediately expired. 

It seems like a reasonable thing to spec here would be to the effect of ~UAs may set a UA-defined cap on Max-Age values. The fact that Safari and Chrome behavior differently for large values isn't super worrying to me, as it's going to take 1 week to observe 

Currently the draft states, in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis#section-4.1.2.2, 

> The Max-Age attribute indicates the maximum lifetime of the cookie,
   represented as the number of seconds until the cookie expires.  The
   user agent is not required to retain the cookie for the specified
   duration.

We could add a clause at the end to the effect of ", and may set a user-agent defined duration limit." and that would more closely match what browsers are doing. I think the fingerprinting vector here is pretty tiny - we could just open a bug against Firefox to see if they would like to do something different than their current behavior to get rid of it.

Thoughts @recvfrom?

comments.author: recvfrom
comments.body:
> > large Max-Age values result in an expiration date with such a large year component that Invalid Date is shown under the Expires / Max-Age column in the Firefox Developer Tools UI
> 
> This is probably worth a bug to Mozilla, if you haven't filed one yet: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/enter_bug.cgi?product=DevTools&component=Storage%20Inspector

My guess is that 'Invalid Date' is shown when the computed expiration date for the cookie exceeds the maximum value for a JavaScript Date object (`Fri Sep 12 275760 20:00:00 GMT-0400`). I wonder if it'd be worth asking Firefox whether they'd prefer to implement a cap on the maximum cookie expiration time before we ask the Firefox DevTools team to support larger dates in the UI?

> It seems like a reasonable thing to spec here would be to the effect of ~UAs may set a UA-defined cap on Max-Age values. The fact that Safari and Chrome behavior differently for large values isn't super worrying to me, as it's going to take 1 week to observe

I think we'd either want to require some cap or at least specify what happens when the Max-Age value causes the cookie expiration date to exceed what the UA is able to handle (i.e. the overflow behavior).  Right now for huge Max-Age values, Firefox immediately expires the cookie whereas Safari uses it's fixed cap and Chrome treats the cookie as a session cookie.  It seems, then, like it's at least trivial to use this to distinguish Firefox from the others immediately and to distinguish Chrome from the others after a site's session has ended.

If the spec is updated to require some cap, should it also require (or at least recommend) a sufficiently high cap?  Maybe a cap that's at least one week since that's what Safari does today?  Also, should this same cap apply to dates provided directly by the `Expires` header as well?

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
>  I wonder if it'd be worth asking Firefox whether they'd prefer to implement a cap on the maximum cookie expiration time before we ask the Firefox DevTools team to support larger dates in the UI?

I think it's worthwhile to make them aware of it.

> If the spec is updated to require some cap, should it also require (or at least recommend) a sufficiently high cap?

I think the interesting thing for the spec to specify is what behavior the UA should take if a value is outside the cap. Immediately expiring/dropping a cookie is immediately visible. Clamping the value or even turning it into a session cookie is much harder to notice (especially given the surprisingly long lives of session cookies).

As for the actual cap, I don't think the spec should take a firmer stance than a recommendation. Not sure as to the actual value, maybe a year or less?

comments.author: arichiv
comments.body: On it, more soon

comments.author: arichiv
comments.body: Re-confirming that I'm working on this

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body: Let's pick a reasonable max value, clamp if servers try to set it higher, and let browsers have policies to pick lower max values if they want.

comments.author: arichiv
comments.body:
I'm proposing a maximum value of no more than 400 days in the future (meaning Safari's behavior is the only one currently compliant).

Why 400 days? The goal was to get close to 13 months so that functions one might perform annually (e.g., selecting insurance benefits for the next year) would work even as specific dates varied slightly. Since Expires deals in a specific date while Max-Age deals in delta-seconds, it seems ideal to select a value with an unambiguous meaning. If the cap were set at 13 months (instead of 400 days) in the future, the maximum TTL varies by the month it was set in and whether or not it's a leap year.

comments.author: sbingler
Chealer
comments.body:
Thank you @recvfrom 
Your report points out several issues which I hope browsers already fixed.

You are right to point out that browsers have different actual limits and that it would be best to at least standardize what happens when exceeding those. [Ignoring cookies with an unsupported expiry date has long caused confusion](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/16626875/google-chrome-maximum-cookie-expiry-date).

This ticket resulted in [a rushed change to the draft](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1732/files), which required user agents to limit the maximum value expiry time of cookies to no later than 400 days (34560000 seconds) in the future. This arbitrary limit would have been very problematic, since (non-session) **cookies have to set an expiry time**. I for one have already had my browsing plagued with lost cookies/sessions, which I deal with constantly (tens of times per week), even though I use a browser which does not follow such a rule (Firefox 145).

This was thankfully [softened in 2022](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1980), thanks to @arichiv and @johnwilander. Still the draft recommends a limit of 400 days. ~~It also says UAs MUST adjust exceeding attributes to (precisely) that limit, which may create a privacy issue, making it difficult for UAs to prevent fingerprinting based on constants.~~

This has already caused both [Google Chrome (104 and ulterior)](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/cookie-max-age-expires) and [Firefox (apparently 140 and ulterior)](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1962986) to massively reduce their cookie retention, to the recommended 400 days, which [immediately caused issues](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/73278956/is-there-any-limit-on-a-browser-cookie-s-expiration-date). The confusion is worsened since both Firefox 145 and Chrome 142 override unsupported expiries fully quietly; there is not even a message logged at the debug level. Before this spreads further, here are options. Please express your preferences by reacting using emoji such as "👍".

comments.author: Chealer
comments.body:
Option 1: Status quo
Limit often platform-dependent, no guidance besides warning:
> In practice, both expires-av and max-age-av are limited to dates representable by the user agent.

comments.author: Chealer
comments.body:
Option 2: Current proposal
Recommend 400 days, mandatory constraining

comments.author: Chealer
comments.body: Option 3: Recommend a duration limit which can at least retain until the current lower logical limit, i.e. [Epochalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_2038_problem) (2038)

comments.author: Chealer
comments.body: Option 4: Recommend implementers choose a specific limit rather than leaving it to platform limits, documenting the potential for fingerprinting, and documenting common limits (such as [Google Chrome >=104's 400 days](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/cookie-max-age-expires))

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body: @Chealer can you elaborate on the fingerprinting concerns? It's not immediately obvious to me what that means.

comments.author: Chealer
comments.body:
@miketaylr: Currently, if using a browser which caps cookie lifespan to―say―2000 days, a privacy-concerned user can complicate fingerprinting by limiting to a variable (possibly random) duration. For example, site example.com could be capped to 1347 days, making it more difficult for that site to guess which browser is accessing. But such a fuzzing strategy would not comply with [the current proposal](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html#section-5.5):

> Expires or Max-Age attributes that specify a lifetime longer than the limit MUST be reduced to the limit.

comments.author: johannhof
comments.body: I still don't understand how the fingerprinting would work here

comments.author: Chealer
arichiv
comments.body: The fingerprinting here is to the resolution of a specific browser engine (or range of versions of a browser)? If so, we should keep that potential in mind but already have many other avenues for that (for example, whether the cookieStore API is available and what parts of it are present).

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body: Or, the User-Agent header.

comments.author: Chealer
miketaylr
comments.body: FWIW, https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html#section-5.5 does not prevent custom caps, or dynamic caps. This is what "the user agent MAY adjust the limit" allows. And 7.2 allows custom cookie policies which means anything goes. It's really up to the user agent, and the tradeoffs it wants to make between interop, security, and privacy. I don't think any changes are needed to allow what you're asking for.

comments.author: Chealer
comments.body:
@miketaylr:
> FWIW, https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html#section-5.5 does not prevent custom caps, or dynamic caps. This is what "the user agent MAY adjust the limit" allows.

I agree that it is not clearly and explicitly prohibited. The paragraph is unfortunately ambiguous. It all depends on how "the limit" is interpreted, and it is not defined explicitly. It is introduced in the first sentence, which is unfortunately incoherent. If the sentence only referred to "cookies", we would infer there is a single (constant) limit. But since it also discusses "*the* cookie", your interpretation is also possible. The constant interpretation is more likely, but I agree that yours cannot be excluded.

> And 7.2 allows custom cookie policies which means anything goes.

The term "policy" has numerous similar senses and can be very confusing, but in general, policies try to make decisions objective and predictable. So it's unlikely that readers would interpret 7.2 as enabling a randomly variable limit.

issues.title: Parsing as Structured Fields: MAY or SHOULD?
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
Right now, parsing of targeted Cache-Control is specified like this:

> Targeted fields MAY be parsed as a Dictionary Structured Field [RFC8941], and implementations are encouraged to use a parser for that format in the interests of robustness, interoperability and security. [...] However, implementers MAY reuse a Cache-Control parser for simplicity.

The idea here is that while we'd like the interop benefits of SF, we recognise that some -- perhaps many -- implementers will have a strong motivation to reuse their Cache-Control parsers.

This seems like it might be the worst of both worlds, in that we now have two possible implementation strategies. Given that there are several [SF implementations](https://github.com/httpwg/wiki/wiki/Structured-Fields) now,  I wonder whether should reconsider this. E.g.,

1) Strengthen the first MAY to a SHOULD, making the field sf-first, or even
2) Require SF, don't allow reuse of CC parsers

issues.title: Use of `Date` for creation time - potential conflict with some caching deployments
issues.author: ezekg
issues.body:
Background: I've added and have been field-testing HTTP response signatures in my business's API, per the earlier [Cavage HTTP draft spec](https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-cavage-http-signatures-12.html). I hope that this is OK to post my issue here — trying to save other teams time in resolving this issue, granted they encounter it. I attempted to deliver a similar message to the ietf-http-wg mailing list, but since I'm not a W3 member, I don't think that's allowed, or at least it doesn't seem like it is.

With that said —

As you all may know, response signatures often utilize the standard `Date` response header to help prevent replay attacks, verify message integrity, among other things. In fact, the Cavage spec even defines the `Date` header as the default test for the response `Signature` header.

I wanted to give a PSA that Cloudflare rewrites the `Date` response header at the edge. Meaning, if a particularly unlucky request leaves a server at `14:01:26.999` with a `Date` header `Thu, 12 Aug 2021 14:01:26 GMT` and takes ~1ms to process at the edge by Cloudflare, the `Date` header from Cloudflare to the client ends up being `Thu, 12 Aug 2021 14:01:27 GMT` (note the change to the time's second). As of this issue, there is no way to disable this behavior.

Obviously, this is problematic when it comes to a cryptographic signature of an HTTP response, since the signature is invalidated once the `Date` header is modified. This ends up causing sporadic, hard-to-debug response signature verification failures, because the server is sending the correct dataset, but the client is not receiving the correct dataset. It's my understanding that the `Date` header is "the date and time at which the message _originated._"

I understand that the original draft spec by Cavage had the default test utilize the `Date` header, so this renders Cloudflare unusable for even the default test if signature reliability is a requirement (and it should be). I'm not sure if [the newer version of the spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures) also defaults to using `Date`, but regardless — if a signature contains the `Date` header and is proxied by Cloudflare, signatures will occasionally be invalidated.

A workaround is to use `X-Date` or similar instead of `Date`, but I do not find that to be a satisfactory workaround. And that doesn't take into account a default test that utilizes the standard `Date` header, which could be implemented more widely granted the draft spec is standardized in the future.

The other solution is to, of course, disable any proxies that behave in this way.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
CDNs are acting as Gateways (by definition of HTTP https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-18.html#section-3.7). In this role they are the origin server.

Cloudflare is not unique in generating a current `Date` header field when they generate the response message, other CDNs do it too. Indeed, using a cached `Date` header can result in serving a date that is not current, leading to user-agents classing the content as instantly stale.

As far as I can tell, draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures includes no examples where the `Date` header field is used to sign responses. 

Replay protections are not mentioned explicitly in draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures  (maybe they should be) but it would seem the parameters defined in https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html#section-2.3.1, namely `created` and `expired`, can allow for that type of thing.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> CDNs are acting as Gateways (by definition of HTTP https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-18.html#section-3.7). In this role they are the origin server.

Sort of :)  Gateways are by definition undefined -- they can do pretty much whatever they want when the glue two protocols together, including when they glue together HTTP and HTTP. It happens to be that a profile of how to do that has gradually emerged over the years that we call 'CDN', but the edges are fuzzy still. That said, they're definitely allowed to update the `Date` header. Whether it's a good idea is another question.

> Cloudflare is not unique in generating a current Date header field when they generate the response message, other CDNs do it too.

That is [true](https://cache-tests.fyi/?id=other-date-update#).

> using a cached Date header can result in serving a date that is not current, leading to user-agents classing the content as instantly stale.

There are two cases to consider here. 

If the CDN is honouring `Cache-Control` and other "normal" HTTP freshness mechanisms, it can leave `Date` alone and HTTP's caching semantics will do their work. However, this has a couple of downsides. First, the responses it serves will have on average a smaller freshness lifetime than if they were served from origin, leading to less cache efficiency. Edith Cohen refers to this as the [age penalty](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2324330_The_Age_Penalty_and_its_Effect_on_Cache_Performance).

Furthermore, when the stored response becomes stale on the CDN, it also becomes stale on browsers, leading to a 'thundering herd' effect, and requiring an end-to-end revalidation of the response (unless something like `stale-while-revalidate` is used). 

The other case is when the CDN has a separate freshness model -- especially when CDN freshness lifetimes are longer than the normal HTTP freshness lifetime, which is often the case. Here, if it doesn't update the HTTP headers (e.g., `Date`), the CDN can _often_ serve an already-stale response, even if its `Cache-Control` says otherwise.

The catch is that by having two separate freshness models (one for the CDN, one for the downstream caches), you have to _add_ them together to understand the maximum amount of time that something can be stored in cache. For example, if I configure my CDN to cache for one day, and "normal" cache-control to allow 12 hours, then something can live in cache for a total of one day, 12 hours. If you have a server-side reverse proxy as well, you have to add it in too.

I suspect many / most web developers don't understand that, and it's a bit of a gotcha if you're relying on expiry for things like rolling out new features. We as an industry could communicate about it better -- perhaps this should be discussed in the targeted cache control draft.

Back to the issue at hand -- I think the root of the problem is that `Date` is being used for more than one thing, and those uses are conflicting (we seem to be re-learning this lesson often ;). The fix is to either use a separate header, or configure your CDN to stop rewriting `Date` (with the caveat of all of the downsides above).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks for the added detail @mnot .

I think the editors can talk with more authority here, but it seems to me that 

```
Creation Time:

    A timestamp representing the point in time that the signature was generated, as asserted by the signer.
```

and `created` are intended to address the ambiguity/dual use of `Date`.

comments.author: ezekg
comments.body:
@mnot Thanks for the in-depth explanation here around the `Date` header's relationship to caching — I didn't think about caching, simply because I'm not using Cloudflare for caching/as a CDN. I'm using CF as a web application firewall. So I guess one of the issues is that, even with caching turned off, CF still modifies the `Date` header.

@LPardue you're right that `created` likely works as an alternative to `Date`. Nearly all examples [in the spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures#section-4.1) include the `Date` header in the signature input (search `"date"` with double quotes and you can find the occurrences). E.g.:

```
 Signature-Input: sig1=("@method" "@target-uri" "host" "date" \
     "cache-control" "x-empty-header" "x-example");created=1618884475\
     ;keyid="test-key-rsa-pss"
```

I foresee more and more people encountering this issue once adoption increases, since CDNs are used so widely.

If `created` is a satisfactory alternative, I think the spec should mention that and forego utilizing the `Date` header entirely, or at least note the potential issues that could occur when utilizing `Date` with a CDN like Cloudflare.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> Nearly all examples in the spec include the Date header in the signature input (search "date" with double quotes and you can find the occurrences)

That's not entirely accurate. There's 11 instance of `Signature-Input:` in the draft, only 3 include `"date"`. The first, in section 4.1, is an abstract example of the `Signature-Input` header field. The other two in the appendices cover only request signatures, not responses. Requests are handled differently.

I agree the spec could be improved by noting deployment considerations.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
The `created` parameter is meant to timestamp the signature itself, where the `Date` header is the HTTP message -- these are two different considerations and could vary for all the reasons listed here plus any number of situations where the signature is applied to portions of a message at a different point than the message itself is fully instantiated. For all these reasons, relying on the `Date` header for both purposes is problematic. It's true that the Cavage draft used `Date`, but we've tried to remove most instances of covering the `Date` header from the examples, and in the two examples that have actual signatures, there's also a `created` field included. They happen to be the same value in the example in question, but that's simple to change if people would even notice that detail. The important thing is that they convey different information.

As it stands, the `created` field is defined for its specific purpose, but we will add language expanding on that discussion. There are a few other fields where similar discussion is needed (the `Host` field comes to mind immediately), and the editors are working on the security and privacy considerations sections currently to include this discussion.

comments.body: @ezekg pls check this old thread https://github.com/w3c-ccg/http-signatures/issues/35 wrt `Date` vs `created` on a previous version of the signature spec. Cavage had a lot of quirks that have been fixed in this spec!

issues.title: what method name to use
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
(opening this so it has a discussion venue)

Currently, the spec uses "SEARCH" (for the reasons given in the spec).

Alternatives:

1) pick a new name
2) use GET with payload (probably unrealistic, just listed for completeness)
3) use POST and find a way to label it as safe
4) re-use another existing safe method that takes a body (PROPFIND, REPORT) (just listed for completeness)

The obvious drawback in "pick a new name" is the forseealke bike-shedding.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
Just my .02. 

Using `POST` is initially attractive because it's familiar; effectively we'd be extending the semantics of the method with a header.

However, I'm not sure it's a good idea. `POST` implies certain guarantees to clients, servers and intermediaries -- e.g., write-through. If an extension can change those guarantees, it's important that they're visible to all components, and an extension (e.g., a header) by nature can't guarantee that.

It seems to me that one of the critical things to do is to get a positive indication from the user agent that the request they're sending doesn't have write-through, so a `POST` extension would need to carry an indication from the client. However, the origin server is also likely to need to convey a cache key and perhaps additional information, which leads this approach to something that's looking complex; the client has to send a certain header, the server has to send a certain header, and an intermediary still might not understand what's going on (which might be good or bad).

So that makes me lean towards the status quo, (1), or (4) as being more straightforward.

Reusing an already-deployed name has been discussed elsewhere; I'm not convinced that it's going to add a lot of value, considering that most traffic is HTTPS now and so intermediaries with fixed lists of supported methods are much less common. If we had data that they'd get through e.g., an enterprise virus scanning proxy whereas a new method wouldn't, I'd be interested to see that.

Still, if `SEARCH` fits the bill adequately, I think it's fine. The real test will be whether folks (especially HTTP API developers) find it compelling enough to use; I'm not sure `SEARCH` quite gets there, but it's in the ballpark.

If we're going to consider new names, I'd suggest `QUERY`.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
If the point of this exercise is to make safe-ness visible to intermediaries, then a method is the right place to put that signal.

I'm comfortable enough with `SEARCH`, though an entirely name would be equally good.

(I think that we should continue discussion about cache keys separately.)

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body: I value a lot the ability for intermediaries to filter out write requests before they reach an application. Reusing `POST` won't have this advantage.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: Interim discussion: switch document to use `QUERY`, which has good support from the attendees, and see how it seems to people who would be adopting.

> This document contains best current practices for the specification

issues.title: Adopt Structured Field Values for HTTP (RFC 8941)
issues.author: MrGossett
issues.body:
[Structured Field Values for HTTP (RFC 8941)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8941) was adopted Feb 2021. It describes a set of data types and associated algorithms that are intended to make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP headers fields, and is intended for use by specifications dealing with HTTP fields that wish to use a common syntax that is more restrictive than traditional HTTP field values.

[draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers v05](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers) provides example values of the `Digest` header which are very similar to the [dictionary](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941.html#name-dictionaries) type defined in RFC 8941. One notable difference is that [section 12.9.1 of draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers#section-12.9.1) allows duplicate keys where RFC 8941 would not allow duplicate keys.

Perhaps it would be useful to borrow some of the formatting rules from RFC 8941, and thus simplify parsing of the `Digest` header proposed here.

Digest values are (for the most part) byte sequences, represented in HTTP header values using base64 encoding. To make parsing easier, and to differentiate strings or bare tokens from byte sequences, RFC 8941 specifies that byte sequences are enclosing with colons (`:`).

So this example header:

```http
Digest: sha-256=bWopGGNiZtbVgHsG+I4knzfEJpmmmQHf7RHDXA3o1hQ=
```

would instead look like this:

```http
Digest: sha-256=:bWopGGNiZtbVgHsG+I4knzfEJpmmmQHf7RHDXA3o1hQ=:
```

And this example header

```http
Digest: sha-256=4REjxQ4yrqUVicfSKYNO/cF9zNj5ANbzgDZt3/h3Qxo=, id-sha-256=X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=
```

would instead look like this:

```http
Digest: sha-256=:4REjxQ4yrqUVicfSKYNO/cF9zNj5ANbzgDZt3/h3Qxo=:, id-sha-256=:X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=:
```

Perhaps it would also be beneficial to adopt RFC 8941 in its entirety. This would imply that [section 12.9.1 of draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers#section-12.9.1) would no longer allow duplicate keys, or the key for a digest would be composed of more than just the digest-algorithm.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Thanks for the suggestion. Switching to Structured Headers has, however, been discussed before and ruled out. The primary reason being that this is a document intended to align RFC 3230 to modern HTTP specs, without really changing any if the wirevprotocol. Changing the Digest field would introduce interoperability problems for implementations that are working to the old definition.

comments.author: MrGossett
comments.body:
Ok, thanks for the explanation.

I had done some searching through issues here to see if this had been proposed before, and I didn't find anything. Perhaps I had missed this issue: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/855.

Is there any other previous discussion I can link here for posterity?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I'm not able to search for anything at the moment I'm afraid, sorry I can't link to some useful background.

#855 is related but is only one small part of the puzzle. 

The proposal here was to turn the entire Digest header into structured headers, which is hard due to legacy. The matter discussed on #855 was specifically about the format of `digest-value`; one component of the Digeat field value. Each digest algorithm defines their own format. base 64 is a common one but there is no universal rule it has to be base 64. New algorithms could pick something else, because it would be expected that implementation either implement the new algorithm or ignore it. If folks really wanted to they could use sh-binary to avoid the base 64 overhead, but that would need new Digest algorithm definitions e.g. "sha512-bin" or something. That work could be progressed independently of this spec.

issues.title: [bcp56bis] recommend "fail safe" semantics for request header fields w.r.t. redirect
issues.author: kaduk
issues.body:
Extracting from #1617 :

> > An application
using HTTP should specify if any request header fields that it
defines need to be modified or removed upon a redirect; however, this
behaviour cannot be relied upon, since a generic client (like a
browser) will be unaware of such requirements.
>
> Should we encourage the application designer to use "fail safe"
semantics for such request header fields in light of the non-guarantee
that application-specific requirements will be heeded? (Possibly in a
later section more focused on header fields or application state rather
than here.)
>
> Editor: That sounds like a substantial new text that would require more WG discussion. Perhaps in the next revision.

Sorry, I don't see how that's a useful justification for not considering a change.  It comes across as something like "once the document has left the WG, no further substantial change is possible", which makes a mockery of the IETF Last Call and IESG Evaluation stages of the document lifecycle.  If significant issues are raised after the document leaves the WG, we still address them, even if addressing them requires making changes that do require going back and having more WG discussion.  Issues that are not sufficiently significant can and do get pushed back to a later revision, but only after discussion and assessment of their severity/significance, a step that seems to have not happened (yet), here.

It seems like we could give some useful guidance here without getting too involved; it migh suffice to note that application designer should consider the risk of removal when choosing what the default semantics for the header field should be.  As this is "consider <topic>" advice rather than "do <specific thing> in <specific way>", it seems like the risk of getting it wrong is rather low.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
I note that this document is now in the RFC Editor queue (and was when you opened this issue); you failed to challenge the reason given when it was in IESG evaluation (the revision history tells me that six days passed between my comment and this issue being opened). Also, I note that the issue you highlight was raised as a COMMENT, not a DISCUSS. By definition, COMMENTs are non-blocking.

I responded as I did because this is not a problem with the specification in terms of interoperability, security or function; it is a suggestion for additional content which you yourself characterise as 'guidance'. As such, I've handled it like any other suggestion by a participant at this stage in the process -- if it's an urgent fix (e.g., the spec has an actual flaw, the spec could be misunderstood), we fix it after WG and broader consultation as needed; if it's purely editorial, we fix it. This doesn't fall into either of those categories. It's asking us to consider and document something genuinely new that hasn't been discussed in the WG, at all. Hence, my reluctance to add text that might not reflect careful consideration and full consensus, or to delay publication unnecessarily.

Turning to the actual issue you raise - what you're looking for is documentation of what is arguably a general property of HTTP fields, not just those defined for APIs, and I note that we don't discuss it in the [most appropriate place for that](https://httpwg.org/http-core/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-latest.html#considerations.for.new.fields). 

However, I don't think this is specific to fields -- it's more a property that any application-specific extensions won't be understood or honoured by software that isn't aware of the application. That includes header and trailer fields, message content, and of course the URI.

We have a whole [BCP about URIs covering this topic](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8820), which is already mentioned in the spec. That's the case because there's a certain moral hazard involved; it's very easy to squat on URI name space and nothing immediately bad happens when you do. 

For fields and message content, perhaps there isn't any existing guidance because a person who attempts to rely on generic software understanding their application's semantics will immediately be faced with the reality of it not working; it's self-policing. As such, documenting this would be unsurprising to almost everyone and ignored by most, I suspect; I don't think it adds much value to the spec to point out the obvious. This issue was mentioned around redirection specifically because the behaviour of clients regarding headers in redirection has until recently been extremely poorly specified, with some variance in implementations. As a result, it seemed prudent to highlight this specific potential pitfall.

So I don't think adding specification text is the right outcome here, and am closing this issue. If you disagree, please request it to be reopened and we can take it to the working group list and/or IESG as @tfpauly and @fpalombini think appropriate.

Finally, I'll ask you to be more thoughtful about use of phrases like 'make a mockery' with regard to process. I don't think that's an appropriate characterisation of what's happening here. I do, however, have reservations about ADs inserting themselves into the process in a privileged way, regardless of good intent.

comments.author: kaduk
comments.body:
Thank you very much for this thoughtful note; it more than addresses my previous concerns!
Your point about phrases like "make a mockery" is well-taken, as well.  To be clear: I was not ascribing that as intent, and agree that it's not what's happening here.

issues.title: RFC6265bis: The Secure Attribute section may be incorrectly warning that a secure cookie can be overwritten by an insecure origin
issues.author: sbingler
issues.body:
[Section-4.1.2.5](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-08#section-4.1.2.5) states "An active network attacker can overwrite Secure cookies from an insecure channel, disrupting their integrity".

This warning appears to be out of date since [Leave Secure Cookies Alone](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-west-leave-secure-cookies-alone-05) updated the spec to disallow insecure origins (schemes) from overwriting Secure cookies set by secure origins.

If there is in fact some other mechanism in which an insecure origin can overwrite a Secure cookie set by a secure origin then section 8.6 should be updated to list it (ignoring any origins which the UA might consider trustworthy, such as localhost).

comments.author: recvfrom

Currently it makes no mention of cookies needing to be set from a secure origin like the [The "__Host-" Prefix](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/blob/cedd1ceeb474468ced197f67a78f81b606184e11/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.md#the-__host--prefix) section does.

issues.title: parameter consistency
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
I noticed that parameters are generally defined in terms of what happened to generate this response, whether or not the next hop was actually contacted.

The exception is `next-protocol`, which says:

> This is only applicable when that connection was actually established.

I think it's potentially valuable for a response to indicate what protocol it was fetched over even if it comes from cache.

The remedy would be to remove that statement and align this with the other parameters by talking about 'this response'. Probably also making that more prominent in `received-status`.

Thoughts, @PiotrSikora?

issues.title: ALPN tokens and TLS usage
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
Spinoff from #1620, a question which I think still needs to be answered in the draft even if we don't add a `next-secure`.  ALPN tokens generally imply that TLS was used, e.g. `http/1.1` or `h2`, and the exceptions are generally called out explicitly (`h2c`).

Do we need language that says whether you can/can't infer the presence of TLS from a particular ALPN token?  If so, do we need to register `http/1.1c` or similar?

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
This was addressed with:

>  Note that the APLN identifier is being used here to identify the protocol in use; it may or may not have been actually used in the protocol negotiation.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
That's not quite the same thing, though.  *ALPN* might or might not actually have been used, as I read that statement.  And that's reasonable -- the token `http/1.1` is often the result of the origin not supporting ALPN, and returning that token even if the server did not accept ALPN (or the proxy didn't offer it) is the correct response.

What's unclear, and what this issue intended to capture, is whether the use of any ALPN token implies that TLS was used, regardless of whether ALPN was.  `h2c` explicitly disclaims the use of TLS, suggesting that the other entries in the registry *do* reflect the use of TLS.

issues.title: Don't deprecate MD5 and CRC32c in Digest Fields RFC
issues.author: zbjornson
issues.body:
The latest draft of the Digest Fields RFC [0] deprecates all non-cryptographically secure algorithms (notably, MD5 and CRC32c). Given that the RFC is "not intended to be a general protection against malicious tampering with HTTP messages," I'd like to propose not deprecating at least these two algorithms, or changing "deprecated digest algorithms MUST NOT be used" to "should be used with caution" or similar.

CRC32c is a very useful algorithm because it is composable (*crc(A+B) == combine(crc(A), crc(B))*). See [1] for an explainer and [2] for an implementation of *combine()* in zlib.

MD5 is ubiquitous. AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage both use it (see `x-goog-hash` [3], which has similar syntax to this RFC except that the crc32c is base64 instead of hex).

[0] https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers.html#name-digest-algorithm-values
[1] http://www.nicst.de/crc.pdf
[2] https://github.com/madler/zlib/blob/cacf7f1d4e3d44d871b605da3b647f07d718623f/crc32.c#L372
[3] https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/xml-api/reference-headers#xgooghash

---

Sorry if this is the wrong forum. I saw some links from the w3c mailing list archive that looked like more discussions were happening here than there.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Hi @zbjornson, this is the right place, thanks for opening the issue.

Do you have a use case where you'd like to use these algorithms with the Digest or Content-Digest header? They are pretty old and pretty bad at their intended purpose - what caution can we offer? 

The statement 

> "not intended to be a general protection against malicious tampering with HTTP messages,"

comes from https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers.html#section-10.1, which is really about making it clear that applications do care about protecting messages also need to apply signatures that protect HTTP header or trailer sections. Otherwise, an attacker could just change the `Digest` header at the same time as changing the representation.

comments.author: zbjornson
comments.body:
Thanks for the fast reply.

My use case is for detecting file corruption in internal HTTP communication, where we trust the network/server/client. Since it's internal, we don't have to obey a standard, but I was hoping to provide the CRC32C and MD5 that we already store to our end users -- provide *something* instead of nothing. Those algorithms provide an adequate level of error detection by our rough calculation (considering that TCP and other layers also checksum). Intel's implementation of CRC32C [0] runs at >19 GB/s, whereas SHA256 runs at only ~360 MB/s. We also take advantage of the ability of CRC32C to be combined, so we can concatenate files in O(1) time and get their CRC32C without calculating a SHA256/512 or MD5 over the whole content.

We serve some millions of files. Google Cloud Storage and AWS S3 probably store many trillions of files and provide CRC32C+MD5 and MD5, respectively.<sup>1</sup> It would be pretty impactful for servers to be able to pass along these digests and might make it worthwhile for browsers to start verifying digests for downloads (e.g. revive [1]).

I might be under-appreciating the security intents of this RFC, but there is clear mention of the other benefits of the RFC (below), which are ones that non-cryptographically secure hashes are often good enough for.

> offering the potential to detect programming errors and corruption of data in flight or at rest. They can be used across multiple hops in order to provide end-to-end integrity guarantees, which can aid fault diagnosis when resources are transferred across hops and system boundaries

[0] https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/white-papers/fast-crc-computation-generic-polynomials-pclmulqdq-paper.pdf
[1] https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=232030

---

Edit: <sup>1</sup> Clarification: The S3 object `ETag` is an MD5 in many scenarios, and S3 uses `Content-MD5` for integrity checks during uploads. They do not explicitly store the MD5 for all objects though.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Corruption in the network does happen, but HTTPS is a far better way of managing that risk.  I know that you say that you trust them, but I would be worried about the network/server/client being - or becoming - untrustworthy.  Obviously, if you are into high-volume transfers of bulk data, you are going to do what you need to do; specialized applications have specialized constraints.  But that doesn't make unsecured transfers any less inadvisable; I'd stand by the deprecation here as a general statement.

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
Hi @zbjornson. Thanks for joining the discussion! Let me clarify one point:

> Given that the RFC is "not intended to be a general protection against malicious tampering with HTTP messages

This just means that the part protected by Digest (the representation) is only a subset of an HTTP message.

For the rest, while I agree on some of your considerations, eg.

> Intel's implementation of CRC32C [0] runs at >19 GB/s, whereas SHA256 runs at only ~360 MB/s.

we had a very long discussion on that https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues?q=is%3Aissue+crc32+is%3Aclosed

Maybe, since crc32 & co - while deprecated - are still  defined in the digest algorithm table, I think that you wouldn't have particular interoperability issues if you need to use them in a specific environment.

comments.author: zbjornson
comments.body:
Thanks @ioggstream for the pointers to the earlier discussions. I'd thought I'd searched but somehow missed those.

I'll yield, although I remain in favor of saying these "SHOULD NOT" instead of "MUST NOT" be used at least because of their ubiquity, performance and the composability of CRCs. 

One last question: does the Digest header provide better security than, or any additional beyond, what TLS provides? My reading of the RFC is that TLS is the typical primary protection layer (since `Digest` doesn't protect headers; indeed, `Digest` itself could be altered) and `Digest` is primarily useful for finding ~bugs.

(PS: I really like the `id-xxx` digests, nice idea.)

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
@zbjornson you've made some good points. Adding accommodation for these algorithms, given the proliferation of e.g. MD5 for this kind of integrity checking could be better than nothing, or hoping that everyone would run a SHA-algo over all of their existing assets.

The thorny part is how to square the circle on relaxing the rule and providing clear, meaningful guidance to implementers.

The MUST_NOT helps set a clear bar, this means its unambiguous what the spec thinks about the relationship of Digest to secure usage scenarios. Anything else needs careful wording and is hard to get right.

The current MUST_NOT is slightly odd in so far as we don't state the ramifications if it is used. Part of that is a product of how Digest has been defined and how apps use it

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
@zbjornson 

> does the Digest header provide better security than, or any additional beyond, what TLS provide ?

The actual work on digest was driven by its usage in signing http messages (eg https://github.com/WICG/webpackage/blob/main/draft-yasskin-httpbis-origin-signed-exchanges-impl.md and https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html )

This is at a different layer wrt TLS. So you can see Digest as a building block for creating non-repudiable
HTTP exchanges without altering the payload (since signatures are conveyed via http headers).

Hth, R.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
Personally -- I think there's something here worth considering. 

AIUI the primary use case for `Digest` headers is _not_ adversarial -- it's end-to-end (i.e., through various intermediaries, toolkits, perhaps a data store) integrity. If someone has lots of content they've calculated CRC or MD5 for, it seems reasonable to allow them to use it in `Digest`; not only is it more efficient, but it saves them recalculating a value for all of that content (and possibly getting it wrong -- that's effectively "end-to-end over time").

OTOH, there are adversarial use cases for `Digest` too -- mostly, signing the digest as a proxy for signing the content. Here, using CRC or MD5 can be bad, and shouldn't be encouraged (or perhaps allowed) by the spec.

This leads me to think that deprecating them isn't the right thing to do; instead, what about marking them as insecure in the registry, and putting language into the spec to explain how to use that?

If folks think that's a good idea, I can do a PR.

comments.author: zbjornson
comments.body:
Thanks for the background @ioggstream .

@mnot @LPardue I think that sounds reasonable to state something like "insecure digests {MUST NOT be used|are not suitable} for protection against malicious actors." The final part of this I think would be allowing `id-xxx` for the insecure digests.

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
I like @mnot idea of introducing "insecure".

It's not trivial how to state that insecure algorithms must not be used in signatures/adversarial use cases.

I'm waiting for Mark's proposal :)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Maybe "Checksum Only" to imply a more narrow purpose.  "Insecure" is not the opposite of "secure".

issues.title: Alt-Svc and multi-CDN
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
An Alternative Service is bound to a location for a specified period of time; with the header filed, the `ma` parameter.

That works reasonably well when the alternative service is relatively stable. However, it causes a problem when the origin uses DNS to distribute traffic to many servers -- e.g., when a server is using more than one CDN for its traffic (so-called 'multi-CDN', which has become common for large sites).

In these cases, there's a strong motivation to give the alternative a long-ish lifetime, especially when alt-svc is being used to advertise QUIC. However, multi-CDN typically uses fairly short DNS TTLs, which leads to a client who has been balanced to a new CDN applying alt-svc policy for the old one.

In the best case here, multi-CDN doesn't distribute traffic in the manner that the site wishes. In the worst, requests go to the wrong node and they `421` or even show a user-visible error.

While the `HTTPS` RR might address some of these issues, it would be good to clean up the Alt-Svc mechanism too. One possible way forward would be to advise that alt-svc information is scoped by the resolution of the origin name -- when it changes, the cache should be dropped.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
So you would perform a DNS query for the origin name and only proceed if it were the same as it was on the connection on which you learned Alt-Svc?  Or the last time you connected to that origin (under any service)?

Is this just an extension of the rule that says if your environment changes, drop the cache?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Yes, this is a problem; I'm not sure this is the path to solve it.  The resolution could easily wind up with a different IP later simply due to mapping changes or load balancing even within the same CDN.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Is this something that can be addressed by refining the "persist" flag (or really something that is nearly the opposite of it)?  On the "persist" end of things, changes in all aspects of topology/configuration are ignored.  This is asking clients to be more sensitive to changes.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: That's an interesting thought, particularly for the clients who say they can't realistically implement "persist".  At the least, this should be mentioned as a way the flag could be implemented if you don't have visibility into topology changes.

comments.author: ddragana
comments.body:
I am not sure how clients can detect topology change. I am worried that it is hard for a client to detect it.
Would something like this be possible:
- look at the cache and choose a ALtSvc. The altsvc entry have a parameter "valid-for-ip-range"
- do a DNS lookup for the AltSvc origin and find out its IP address. if the IP address is not in the range drop the altsvc.

I know that IP address ranges are not the best solution. Would CNAME maybe work?

Note: I do not like the idea of doing DNS query before decided to use an AltSvc record, but that does not work according to [this comment](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1673#issuecomment-920043555)

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I agree that this is a problem. I think the case can be worse than @mnot describes when it comes to QUIC. Under certain circumstances, depending on client implementations, Alt-Svc caching can lead to clients attempting QUIC handshakes that might get blackholed, which could cause delays until fallbacks kick in. This wouldn't manifest directly as a user visible error but an annoying intermittent delay that could cause some diagnosis headaches. This could be treated as a failure from a performance perspective.

comments.author: sc0ttbeardsley
comments.body:
Pinterest is still interested in a solution to this as it would allow more adoption without the latency regression. Referenced in [our blog post](https://medium.com/pinterest-engineering/pinterest-is-now-on-http-3-608fb5581094). 

We have made great progress in pushing CDN vendors to allow modifications to `alt-svc` response headers but it is pretty awkward given we really only should be allowed to modify `ma` since CDN vendors want to control the protocol ids (as they should). 

Note: we were able to launch by setting `ma` to 10m but would love to be able to set for as long as a month or year.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: @sc0ttbeardsley just in case you're not tracking the HTTP WG too closely, we've been actively discussing an "Alt-Svc plan B" that might provide a solution, the latest update was given at IETF 115; see https://github.com/httpwg/wg-materials/blob/gh-pages/ietf115/alt-svc.pdf.

comments.author: sc0ttbeardsley
comments.body: Thanks for the pointer @LPardue ! I will try to get more hooked in to what is happening with plan b. It looks reasonable so far but I have some concerns some of the details like CNAME chains and willingness/ability of endpoint owners to provide the necessary features to domain owners.

comments.author: LPardue
sc0ttbeardsley
comments.body:
@LPardue sure! wasn't sure if we should have the conversation here or elsewhere... 

My assumption and understanding of "alt-svc plan b" is that endpoint operators control the dns records which are consulted by clients... for instance assuming this dns chain:

```
www.pinterest.com -CNAME-> pinterest.examplecdn.com -A-> [10.1.1.1, 10.2.2.2]
```

Assuming a config of `alt-svc: h3=:443;ma=3600` This DNS record would be consulted:

```
_443._https.pinterest.examplecdn.com
```

**Endpoint operators (aka CDNs)**: care about things like the protocol ids and ports. Endpoint operators might also care about maximum possible value for the `ma` param so that they have a path to retire old protocol ids and introduce new protocol ids.

**Domain owners (aka me and other CDN users)**: care about `ma` and perhaps the `persist` values. Domain owners need to roll out new protocols (like H3) and typically want to experiment with the `ma` duration to prevent clients getting into a bad state for too long. Eventually, once adoption of new protocols is complete, they might want this to be some large value to allow it the best opportunity to be used for return clients. Again, this is all in the interest of the domain owner and the endpoint owner couldn't care less.

Does "alt-svc plan b" assign control of these components of `alt-svc` to their respective owners? If we make everything just move to a DNS record controlled by the endpoint operators this solves the multi-endpoint problem by allowing each endpoint operator to have distinct values independent of other endpoints which solves the problem of load balancing across multiple vendors. However the problem of control of the `ma` param is not solved and is left to endpoint operators to figure out how best to expose to the domain owners. Every CDN would need to agree to implement some configuration option to allow me (domain owner) to modify *only* the `ma` portion of the DNS answer at `_443._https.pinterest.examplecdn.com`. We've had trouble getting CDNs to allow us to modify the `alt-svc` response headers (rightfully so! we can potentially cause havoc through protocol id mismatches) so this separation of interests and outlining exactly how endpoint operators *should* implement this is important to us.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks Scott, having some concrete use cases from what you `Domain owners` really helps. I'm sure vendors are happy to continue talking to customers in more confidential channels where its needed but this seems broad enough not to require it.

To oversimplify "Alt-Svc plan B", (spec: https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-thomson-httpbis-alt-svcb-00.html), roughly what we in mind is to deprecate the Alt-Svc header and push people towards using the DNS as a better source of truth. A new header, WIP name alt-svcb, provides a prompt to the best place in the DNS to start looking. 

Part of the outcome of this proposal is to get rid of caching based on `ma`, and instead let it be handled by DNS aspects like TTL.  So for example, say a client were to rely on the SVCB HTTPS RR for discovering that HTTP/3 was available. This aligns well with DNS-based steering strategies. 

Alt-Svc `persist` is an odd parameter in practice, so we have deprecated that. Even without, clients will still be able to use their own local knowledge together with the advertised configuration(s) to determine if a protocol is a good selection or not.

With this design, your question of configurability probably then comes down to DNS configurability.

comments.author: sc0ttbeardsley
comments.body: Thanks deprecating `ma` and relying on DNS TTL makes perfect sense. I agree this comes down to DNS configurability of the endpoint-owned records. I worry about CDN vendors providing this configurability consistently but if there is some recommendation and everyone gets on board my concerns mostly go away.

issues.title: When SETTING deprecate H2 priority, is extensible priority mandatory?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Above, you indicate any scheme can be used, with this being just one option. 

This does make guidance about PRIO_UPDATE frames/header field more difficult later, so maybe some other textual adjustment is needed earlier:

e.g., for the remainder of this text ,we assume the use of the scheme defined in this document as the alternate

Or, move the following text from below up and adjust a bit 
> Where both endpoints disable RFC 7540 stream priority, the client is expected to
send this scheme's priority signal

_Originally posted by @rmarx in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1601#r708087994_

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: The text isn't amazingly clear if endpoints have to use Extensible priority when they explicitly disable H2 priority. I suggest we state they do. If anyone really wants to invent a new scheme, they will need to deal with negotiation.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> The text isn't amazingly clear if endpoints have to use Extensible priority when they explicitly disable H2 priority. I suggest we state they do. If anyone really wants to invent a new scheme, they will need to deal with negotiation.

Yeah I see two somewhat contradicting statements:
* _Endpoints are expected to use an alternative, such as the scheme defined in this specification._
* _Until the client receives the SETTINGS frame from the server, the client SHOULD send both the HTTP/2 priority signals and the signals of this prioritization scheme (see Section 5 and Section 7.1)._

I would argue that the former is precise, and that the latter is a bit misleading in recommending endpoints send Extensible Priorities rather than _any_ alternative to H2 priorities.

The rationale is as follows.

In principle, negotiation is a hop-by-hop mechanism and therefore cannot be used for negotiating the use of an end-to-end signal, which includes the header-field variant of Extensible Priorities. To paraphrase, in a world where end-to-end signals are used for prioritization, multiple signals are expected to co-exist.

IMO, SETTINGS_DEPRECATE_RFC7540_PRIORITIES is no more than an optimization, that allows clients to conserve bandwidth (by omitting the PRIORITY frames), servers to reduce complexity (by ignoring PRIORITY frames being received). These benefits are stated correctly in the section.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks Kazuho. I tend to agree. The thing I also wanted to avoid is endpoints disabling RFC 7550 stream priority and then not providing any suitable replacement by accident. I think there is agreement that not doing scheduling is pretty bad. But we also highlight that other inputs, beyond this scheme and beyond anything that would be standardised are fine to use too.

I'm getting an idea of how we could change the text to address the points made on this issue.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Reading again the current text

> Where both endpoints disable RFC 7540 stream priority, the client is expected to
send this scheme's priority signal. Handling of omitted signals is described in
{{parameters}}.

This is effectively a differently worded restatement of the guidance for implementers of Extensible Priorities 

> This document defines the urgency(`u`) and incremental(`i`) parameters. When
receiving an HTTP request that does not carry these priority parameters, a
server SHOULD act as if their default values were specified.

That is, imagine both endpoints send SETTINGS_DEPRECATE_RFC7540_PRIORITIES and a client wants the default prioritization for a request (u=3,i). It can omit the Priority header field and have some expectation that a server implementing Extensible priorities will interpret that as a signal to apply the default.

The simple action here is to make SETTINGS_DEPRECATE_RFC7540_PRIORITIES independent from any advice to use a specific alternative.

issues.title: "Want-Digest" and Bad Request
issues.author: MikeBishop

The Digest mechanism seems to be oriented such that it's always optional -- senders can disregard receiver preferences; receivers can disregard digests in unsupported formats, or disregard them entirely.

As such, the example in https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers.html#appendix-C.3 is a bit confusing.  It shows a server responding with a 400 because the client would prefer to receive a digest in a format the server does not support.  However, I don't see any text in this document stating that servers SHOULD/MUST/SHOULD-NOT, etc. reject requests on the basis of requested digests.

Am I just missing it, or does this need more explanatory text?

comments.body:
I agree this is an overloaded example. I think we need to explain more and/or split out the cases.

An alternative interpretation of this example is that the server required a digestvwith the request. There's some ambiguity. I kind of dislike want-digest but we're sort of stuff with it.

2. https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/blob/main/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers.md#server-does-not-support-client-algorithm-and-returns-an-error shows that the receiver is free to enforce a given policy
