In that light, 201 seems a very strange response.  The client did not ask the server to create anything.

The use-case that I envision is using this for a refresh with fewer bytes on subsequent requests. If anything should be said about this, I think it belongs in section [4.2.1 of the HTTP specification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-4.2.1) which may cover this well enough already:

> This definition of safe methods does not prevent an implementation from including behavior that is potentially harmful, that is not entirely read-only, or that causes side effects while invoking a safe method.  What is important, however, is that the client did not request that additional behavior and cannot be held accountable for it.

comments.author: IamfromSpace
comments.body:
I feel like one interesting aspect of this is that returning a `Location` or `Content-Location` header does have some differing meanings.  A `Location` might indicate that there is a _resource_ that was found, that can now be located, and might support all sorts of representations.  And a `Content-Location` header would indicate a permanent place to view this particular _representation_ of the resource discovered by the `QUERY`.  Arguably, both could make sense.

I don't think that either could/should imply that the location is an "immutable snapshot."  They're simply discovery of resources.

From that standpoint, I think `201 Created` only makes sense if you are in fact directing the user to an immutable snapshot of the result.  Other resources discovered should already exist, the only think we could create is resource that represents this query.

I don't personally think that creating a snapshot is an oxymoron for a safe method.  The resource you interacted with is not invalidated, something else is just there now too.

However, I think it would be confusing to use `Location` to mean two different things (200: "Here's the resource you found," 201: "Here's a permanent location for the response to this query.").

Just wanted to throw a couple thoughts into the ring :)

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
Oh dear. Let's not mix things up.

The request method defines what is requested, not what the server does. 201 is always a valid response when a resource is created, even if the user agent didn't request it, but providing a Location without some corresponding defined semantics for what it identifies would not be very useful. QUERY could define such semantics for Location in any successful response, not just 201, as defined in 

   https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-location

so that Location could be used in a 200 response to indicate a pre-existing resource, or in a 201 to indicate a new one. Such a relationship defined by Location does not necessarily have anything to do with the content in the response, unless that's what the method specifies.

Content-Location, on the other hand, is a relationship between the content in the response and a resource that provides the same content in response to GET. Note the emphasis: It is the **same content**, not the same service. It is not an equivalent URI to repeating the same QUERY parameters again in the future.

For example, if I were to QUERY a resource that provides the weather for Tustin today, like
```
QUERY /weather?city=Tustin HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
```
and I received back
```
200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Location: /weather/us/ca/tustin/20240524
Location: /weather/us/ca/tustin/

Sunny 66°F
```
then the Content-Location identifies a resource that should always respond with "Sunny 66°F" no matter what the weather might be in the future. IOW, it provides a representation of that past result, not a repeat of the same query.

In contrast, the Location might identify a resource identifier that could be used in the future to perform the same query using a GET without unsafe parameters, if that's how Location on a 2xx response is defined by Query.

Yes, there is some overlap here with 303. The difference is that 2xx supplies a representation of the query result, whereas 303 does not -- it instructs the client to GET a representation over there.

Regarding cache semantics: I strongly recommend against any attempt to use the result of a QUERY as if it were a cached copy of some other resource. If you want those semantics, respond with 303. The 303 forces the client to perform a GET through consistent mechanisms for the service, including CDNs, filters, pipes, security, context, etc.

Caching QUERY directly and reusing it for a later GET is guaranteed to result in security holes somewhere along the service chain, either because something doesn't implement QUERY, or there is layered processing that is bypassed by QUERY, or there are access controls that don't know about QUERY, or it's Tuesday, or it's a beach day, or ... I could literally spend the next two weeks explaining how I could trojan horse any CDN that assumes a given path had processed the result of a GET. Don't do that. 303 works fine and is already deployed.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
@royfielding, I don't necessarily have a problem with the mapping that Location enables repeating the query and Content-Location points to the historical information. Indeed, I can see the case that the historical query data might be the "most specific resource" in the sense that "at a specified instant" is more specific than an ever-changing now.

Based on 9110, I'm reading Location as being a resource that's related to the response with semantics defined by other elements of the request/response, so the Location can be basically whatever we define it to be for QUERY. Content-Location is a resource which currently has the representation carried in the message body.

> The "Content-Location" header field references a URI that can be used as an identifier for a specific resource corresponding to the representation in this message's content. In other words, if one were to perform a GET request on this URI **at the time of this message's generation**, then a [200 (OK)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#status.200) response would contain the same representation that is enclosed as content in this message.

That's what pointed me in the direction of Content-Location repeating the query -- the response body contains the representation of the query's *current* results. 9110 makes no statement about the content of that resource in the future that I can find.

Regardless, I don't think either spelling is inherently wrong; we just need to agree on one.

> Ok, I re-read the thread over here and in the PR.

Yes, though trying to pre-cache this response as if it were a GET on the Location is a separate concern

> I'm not convinced that your description of `Content-Location` is actually backed by the HTTP spec:

>

That is literally what it says. The Content-Location is a location for this content, not the location of an equivalent query.
An equivalent to query would have to be defined elsewhere for any content that varies over time/context, and the elsewhere pointer is traditionally provided by Location when defined as such by the method and/or status code.

> But if switching to `Location` allows us to move forward, so be it.

> What we should agree on is:
>

The method should explain what the Location means on a 2xx response. So, yes, an update would be appropriate, or you could just implement it that way and standardize it later.

We really don't need to flip any coins. Please do not get hung up on one sentence read out of context. The 9110 spec is correct as written. Read it in the context of the section being described. 

Content-Location was defined for email. It has the same meaning regardless of the status code. If you were to get a 500 response from Twitter with a fancy fail whale image, the Content-Location points to the fail whale resource. It might have nothing to do with the original request resource aside from being a response from the same gateway server. 

Content-Location might apply to any message, both requests and responses.

It does not need to be clarified further, unless someone wants to write a book about HTTP.

issues.title: PRIORITY_UPDATE buffer limits need stronger advice
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Regarding the number of PRIORITY_UPDATE frames that a server should buffer, I think we need to state three things:
* Most recently-received PRIORITY_UPDATE frame for each request stream yet to be opened SHOULD be buffered.
* There should be enough slots in that buffer, so that prioritization information would not be lost when the client tries to fully utilize the concurrency.
* The number of slots MUST be bounded to avoid attacks.

I think that the first two points are already stated in Section 7. Regarding this paragraph, I think the problem with the text that we have is that it is discussing interoperability issues rather than security issues. This is Security Considerations section and what we need to state here is the attack and the mitigation (i.e. the third bullet point).

EDIT. Regarding what we do in h2o (our HTTP/3 stack), we [error-close the connection when receiving a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame carrying a Stream ID that it above the current limit](https://github.com/h2o/h2o/blob/6f6ecfc734dfaf30f3be9d62de81b7a327259ea9/lib/http3/server.c#L1441-L1443). But as you might have pointed out, QUIC stacks might not provide an API that allows HTTP/3 clients to prevent such PRIORITY_UPDATE frames from being sent.

_Originally posted by @kazuho in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1740#discussion_r727746109_

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I think that the rule for *sending* PRIORITY_UPDATE should be that you not send one prior to having *opened* the stream that you plan to use.  That ensures that you never violate stream limits.

The general requirements for the receiving side are fine.  It's OK (ish) if these signals are lost, so you are just balancing the desire to retain information against the need for endpoints to protect themselves.

Our implementation accepts the frame and does not allow it to be for a stream that exceeds the application MAX_STREAMS value, just like @kazuho.  Following the above advice is sufficient to avoid the stated problem.  Allowing for that rule to be enforced is fine; I would be opposed to *requiring* enforcement as it depends on an interface that doesn't exist in the QUIC spec.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> I think that the rule for _sending_ PRIORITY_UPDATE should be that you not send one prior to having _opened_ the stream that you plan to use. That ensures that you never violate stream limits.

While I'll be more than happy to require all implementations adhere to such rule, I'm not sure if that is achievable under the API provided by every QUIC stack.

The problem here is that while the QUIC specification requires endpoints to refrain from sending references to streams above current limit, there is nothing that prevents QUIC stacks from internally generating a reference to a stream with a Stream ID above the limit and providing that Stream ID to the application.

When a client behaves as such, it might send PRIORITY_UPDATE frames carrying a Stream ID above the current limit that is only known to the QUIC stack.

To paraphrase, in order to prohibit clients from sending PRIORITY_UPDATE frames carrying a Stream ID above the limit, there has to be some API on the client-side that either delays the generation of a stream until the QUIC stack learns that a new stream can be opened, or indicates to the application when the limit is raised.

Are we fine with that?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I was going to say: why can't you rely on the stream being created, but https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/rfc9000.html#name-operations-on-streams doesn't say that applications can create streams.  Seems like a bit of an oversight.

Any interface that allows an application to create a stream, for which sending stuff might never be permitted, is probably not a good idea.

I think that your proposed interface is about right though.  I would probably choose to define an API where an application can request the next unused stream, which fails if there are none that can be immediately created.  You might add some way to learn when more streams become available (we don't have that API, but we probably just haven't encountered the need just yet).

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I think we are almost on the same page.

While some clients might send PRIORITY_UPDATE frames carrying Stream IDs that are out of the limit advertised by the server, we can assume that well-designed clients will not. That is because assigning Stream IDs to streams before they can be sent causes head-of-line blocking.

In HTTP/2 and QUIC, endpoints are allowed to open streams in the order of Stream IDs. The reason we have  Urgency parameter in Extensible Priorities is to allow HTTP requests generated at a later moment to have precedence over others that are created at an earlier moment.

Based on this observation, I think that current text is correct in stating that servers can _ignore_ PRIORITY_UPDATE frames. When a server receives a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame carrying a Stream ID out of the concurrency limit, we know that the client is badly designed and will likely suffer from head-of-line blocking. What we should do is discourage such clients getting developed, rather than trying to mitigate priority handling of such clients.

If we want to be clear, we can say that:
* Clients SHOULD send PRIORITY_UPDATE frames carrying Stream IDs within the concurrency limit advertised by servers.
* If the Stream ID conveyed by PRIORITY_UPDATE frame refers to a stream yet to be opened but is within the current limit advertised by the QUIC stack, servers SHOULD buffer the information carried by the PRIORITY_UPDATE frame.
* If the Stream ID is above the advertised limit, servers can ignore the PRIORITY_UPDATE frame.
* Servers SHOULD limit the number of PRIORITY_UPDATE frames to avoid resource exhaustion attacks.

WDYT?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
That sounds reasonable to me.

P.s. I don't think it would much work to add an API to Cloudflare quiche to
allow applications to query the concurrency limit. And I would likely do so
while introducing PRIORITY_UPDATE frame support

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I don't think that endpoints should be free to send PRIORITY_UPDATE for arbitrary streams.  It should be possible for applications to avoid sending the frame for streams that cannot exist yet.

(Right now, our implementation would generate a connection error if a peer did that, and I think that is entirely reasonable.)

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body:
> I don't think that endpoints should be free to send PRIORITY_UPDATE for arbitrary streams. It should be possible for applications to avoid sending the frame for streams that cannot exist yet.
> 
> (Right now, our implementation would generate a connection error if a peer did that, and I think that is entirely reasonable.)

Strong +1 to both of these points.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> I don't think that endpoints should be free to send PRIORITY_UPDATE for arbitrary streams. It should be possible for applications to avoid sending the frame for streams that cannot exist yet.

I'd be fine with going in that direction. As stated previously, such clients have head-of-line blocking. One of the goals of HTTP/3 and QUIC was to eliminate head-of-line blocking.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Head-of-line blocking only occurs to the extent that no new streams can be created.  In other words, this is a deliberate choice made by a server to limit resource usage.  That still allows for concurrency (and no blocking) up to a stream limit, which is enough for requests.  That should be enough for prioritization of requests.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Coming back to this, I'll note that there is already text in https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-priority.html#section-7.1 and https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-priority.html#section-7.2 that states requirements for senders of PRIORITY_UPDATE frames.

The rules for detecting "concurrency limits" vary between H2 and H3. In H2 we say that 

> The number of streams which have been prioritized but remain in the "idle" state plus the number of active streams (those in the "open" or either "half-closed" state; see Section 5.1.2 of [HTTP2]) MUST NOT exceed the value of the SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS parameter. Servers that receive such a PRIORITY_UPDATE MUST respond with a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.

and H3 we say 

> The Stream ID MUST be within the client-initiated bidirectional stream limit. If a server receives a PRIORITY_UPDATE (type=0xF0700) with a Stream ID that is beyond the stream limits, this SHOULD be treated as a connection error of type H3_ID_ERROR.

Based on the current text, I would argue that by design we do bound the commitment. The difference is that in H2 we say MUST error, and in H3 we say SHOULD. This is because of the fact that servers might not know their own concurrency limit due to QUIC APIS. That rationale was buried all the way in the security considerations, so in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1755 I just move it to a better place.

I am struggling to see any additional changes that are needed here, either normative or editorial in nature. So unless someone can explain clearly what they want changed (or even better, make a PR) then I don't think there's anything to do.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Closing this as there does not seem anything to do (as noted previously).

issues.title: WebSockets supports indication in HTTPS RR
issues.author: ddragana
issues.body:
To use WebSockets over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, clients needs to wait for the settings to be exchange on a connection before they can dispatch a WebSocket on a connection. It would be useful if the supports is indicated in HTTPS RR record and the clients could skip trying to use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.

The clients still needs a mechanism to re-dispatch a WebSocket request to HTTP/1.1, if the server do not support WebSockets although it advertise the support.  

I am interested what people think. I can write a draft if this is useful.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
This is interesting. It reminds me a little bit of the motivating case for https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-pardue-alt-svc-ext-unsupported-00, whereby a client gets mistakenly alt-svc'd from a H2 WS-supporting endpoint to a H3 non-WS-supporting endpoint and vice-versa

Indicating the properties of the endpoints like you suggest would seem like a good way to avoid such a situation.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
For H2, deploying it via DNS seems both unnecessarily hazardous to deploy on the server (the server needs to configure something via DNS, and worry about rollout considerations if the server has multiple instances) and unnecessary complexity on the client (we need to handle DNS/server out-of-sync cases by retrying with HTTP/1.1). Rather, it seems all of this can be done more robustly in-band:

First, the problem case is if there isn't an existing connection available and we wish to make a wss:// request. We want the server to negotiate HTTP/2 on the new connection if and only if the server supports WebSockets over HTTP/2. This can be done by simply integrating with ALPN. It's a little janky, but we can define an `h2+wss` ALPN token, which is exactly the same as `h2` except the server must support WebSockets. Then, for wss:// connections, the client sends an ALPN list of `http/1.1`, `h2+wss`, without `h2`. (If this starts needing to explode, we can define a single `h2+exts` value, which cross-references a separate "mandatory extensions" client extension.)

Second, when there is an existing HTTP/2 connection available, there is a short window of time when we have the connection but don't know that it is WebSockets-capable. Clients may then unnecessarily make new HTTP/2 connections. If we care, we can optionally eliminate this gap with something like [ALPS](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-vvv-httpbis-alps). That guarantees that, as soon as the HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection is available, the client knows that WebSockets are supported.

Then again, for H3, we have to do it out-of-band regardless.

comments.author: ddragana
comments.body:
ALPN will not resolve this as well, not all case.

Scenario: wss:// request comes first and the browser try to make connection with http1.1, h2+wss. After that comes a https:// request to the same domain. Should browser wait for the first connection to be established and see if h2 is negotiated or should it open a new connection.
Our current wss implementation tries h2 and queues wss request until settings are received and then decide to open a new http/1.1 connection if needed. With h3 (we do not have an implementation yet) this is a long wait h3->h2->http/1.1 (or skip one of them)

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Does making progress on this requiring making any changes to the h3-websockets specification?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Unless I'm *badly* mistaken, this is something that can (and should) be pursued separately.

comments.author: ddragana
comments.body: I see one issue and that is what should happen if server advertise support for the extended connect but does not support WebSockets. I will open a separate issue for that.

issues.title: RFC6265bis: Minor improvements to the Max-Age attribute parsing algorithm
issues.author: recvfrom
issues.body:
The current wording of the Max-Age attribute parsing algorithm could be improved so that `Max-Age=-` is handled better (right now, the instructions would lead to attempting to convert `-` to an integer).

Also, it might be worth mentioning that digits should be converted to an integer using base 10 (so it's clear that `Max-Age=0111` should be the same as `Max-Age=111` and not `Max-Age=73`).

I did some quick testing in recent versions of Chrome, Safari, and Firefox by setting cookies using `document.cookie` in the console, and these cases are all handled as expected.  Implementing the improvements above would be some nice dotting of i's and crossing of t's, though.

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body:
Assuming browsers behavior interoperably here, it would be nice to document that (and ensure we have WPTs).

(perhaps after https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1732 lands, so to avoid any merge acrobatics)

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body: Yeah, let's wait until 1732 lands. I can take this one once it does.

comments.author: recvfrom
comments.body:
As part of this, let's also better specify how an empty Max-Age value (from using `Max-Age=;` or `Max-Age;`) should be handled (the current instructions would lead to attempting to convert the empty string to an integer)

Looks like Chrome and Firefox both treat `a=b; max-age=11111; max-age;` as a session cookie (at least when set via `document.cookie`)

comments.author: johannhof
comments.body:
Testing on WebKit it seems like it differs from Firefox and Chrome:

Setting `a=b; max-age=11111; max-age;` (or `max-age=bla`) will result in WebKit ignoring the 2nd attribute and thus not setting a session cookie, but a cookie with expiry + 11111.

Looking at https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html#section-5.4.2 the WebKit behavior actually seems much closer to spec and might be less confusing to web authors as well (invalid attributes get ignored, not turned into session somehow despite valid attributes being present).

I'd like to add tests for this but might need to add better infrastructure first for getting better information than cookie set/not set in WPT.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body: The issue of what to do with an invalid attribute (ignore the attribute completely, ignore and use last valid, abort the cookie) has come up a few times now. It's probably worthwhile to come up with a story for how to handle this in general.

issues.title: RFC6265bis: Handling a trailing dot in the domain attribute
issues.author: recvfrom
issues.body:
@miketaylr I vaguely remember us having a discussion related to this from a few weeks ago, but I stumbled across it again today when reading the spec and figured I'd open an issue for it.

There are multiple places in the spec that say:

> Note that a leading %x2E ("."), if present, is ignored even though that character is not permitted, but a trailing %x2E ("."), if present, will cause the user agent to ignore the attribute.

I doesn't look like there's a step in the domain attribute parsing algorithm to actually ignore the attribute if a trailing dot is present, though.  My first thought was maybe this is implicitly handled by the domain-match algorithm.  It's unclear to me what the canonicalized version of `www.example.com.` would be, and whether that'd domain-match with `www.example.com`.  Assuming they don't domain-match, the algorithm states that the whole cookie should be ignored instead of just the attribute being ignored.  Assuming they do domain-match, then the attribute wasn't ignored.

Are we missing a step that would cause the attribute to be ignored in this case?

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
A quick test of Chrome indicates that we're failing the domain match and dropping the entire cookie, rather than ignoring the attribute.

> I doesn't look like there's a step in the domain attribute parsing algorithm to actually ignore the attribute if a trailing dot is present, though

I suspect section 5.5, step 7 is meant as the instruction to ignore the cookie. But it's not particularly commanding.

I can take this one.

comments.author: annevk
comments.body:
Almost universally throughout the web platform trailing-dot domains are treated as distinct from non-trailing-dot domains. If anything it seems to me that the note is wrong as the attribute should not be ignored if the user is actually visiting a trailing-dot domain, such as `example.com.`.

So I think we should update this to not state anything about trailing dots. (Domain matching should already do the right thing.)

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
> Almost universally throughout the web platform trailing-dot domains are treated as distinct from non-trailing-dot domains

Thanks for the extra context Anne. That's good to know.

> So I think we should update this to not state anything about trailing dots.

To clarify, you're suggesting to remove 

> but a trailing %x2E ("."), if present, will cause the user agent to ignore the attribute.

within
```
 1.  Let the domain-attribute be the attribute-value of the last
        attribute in the cookie-attribute-list with both an
        attribute-name of "Domain" and an attribute-value whose
        length is no more than 1024 octets. (Note that a leading %x2E
        ("."), if present, is ignored even though that character is not
        permitted, but a trailing %x2E ("."), if present, will cause
        the user agent to ignore the attribute.)
```
rather than correct it?

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: I expect that removing it would be the correction as it is treated as significant by user agents. It's just that in most cases end users are not visiting trailing-dot domains so domain matching ends up failing. However, if the specified domain is `example.com.` and the end user is visiting `example.com.`, it'll work.

issues.title: Clarify how endpoints use NO_RFC7540 setting
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body: Paraphrasing feedback from @rmarx, the section explains the setting just fine but could be clearer on how the client or server might use this setting

issues.title: Urgency section's description of sender is mildly ambiguous
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Paraphrasing @rmarx feedback, in S 4.1 we say 

> This parameter indicates the sender's recommendation, based on the expectation that the server would transmit HTTP responses in the order of their urgency values if possible. The smaller the value, the higher the precedence.

we might consider clearer statements about the actors are i.e. who sends this parameter, and who actions it.

comments.author: rmarx
comments.body: For clarity, it's mainly the term "sender" in "sender's recommendations" that I find unclear here, since the server can also "send" Priority information, where it doesn't always reflect the server's "recommendation" when doing so (e.g., sometimes it's just echo'ing the client's value).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: We don't really need to hammer home the "recommendation" concept, that's explained elsewhere in the document. I'll propose an editorial change to this text to focus on the thing we care about

issues.title: The use of the term "parallel" can be misleading
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Paraphrasing @rmarx, in S 4.2 we say

> If a client makes concurrent requests with the incremental parameter set to false, there is no benefit serving responses with the same urgency in parallel because the client is not going to process those responses incrementally.

Resources are not sent in parallel (implying "at the same time"), but rather multiplexed vs sequential. We don't want to leave the impression that setting i=1 would give better perf due to actual "parallel" sending.

issues.title: Talk more about a case of same urgency: mixed incremental and non-incremental
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Paraphrasing @rmarx, S 10 is still somewhat ambiguous on what to do if you have both non-incremental and incremental resources at the same urgency level. There is no single correct answer here, and the "starvation" text partially addresses this,
but I'm not sure that's enough. Maybe explicitly pointing out the situation and saying no guidance is given?

Editors suggestion here is NOT to add any more normative guidance but to provide a better linkage between the the paragraphs that touch on these matters.

comments.author: rmarx
comments.body: I still personally feel it would be good to call out this specific situation, since it's an edge case you probably -will- encounter and for which you need to (in my opinion) make a conscious decision. The starvation text already calls out other examples, so I feel this edge case could also use some text.

issues.title: Server advertise support for extended CONNECT but does not support websocket as a :protocol
issues.author: ddragana
issues.body:
I think this is an issue. and we need graceful way to fall back to fallback. 

I do not believe that HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED and 421 response code are the right solution.

I think it would be good to make this part of WebSockets over HTTP3 spec.

edit: remove double negation -> I think that   HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED and 421 response code are not the answer.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I agree the options we have today are not the right fit. This document could provide that and update RFC 8441.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: The server could just close the stream with H3_VERSION_FALLBACK. Is that not sufficient?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Perhaps for WebSockets, but there's a more general question here.  When a client uses Extended CONNECT with an unknown protocol, what is the correct failure mode?  There's no guarantee that HTTP/1.1 would support an arbitrary requested protocol, even if it might be more likely to work with WebSockets.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I'm not sure we need a general solution, because it isn't clear that we have a general problem. The answer here will depend on why the client is using this protocol in the first place. For example with MASQUE, the client will know which proxy to connect to thanks to out-of-band configuration, so the proxy operator is responsible for ensuring its HTTP servers are in sync with its config servers. For WebSocket on the other hand, the issue is that WebSockets were originally designed for h1 and there exist servers that are gradually deploying h2 or h3 for GET but don't yet support WebSocket there. For those, H3_VERSION_FALLBACK should be sufficient.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
> For example with MASQUE, the client will know which proxy to connect to thanks to out-of-band configuration, so the proxy operator is responsible for ensuring its HTTP servers are in sync with its config servers.

That's nice in theory.  We should still say what happens when the proxy operator makes a mistake.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
> We should still say what happens when the proxy operator makes a mistake.

Why is this specific to extended CONNECT then? A server operator could make a mistake and end up with some GET resources not working on h3 too, right?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The example I would use here is a server that  supports masque on H3 and H2 CONNECT. If for some reason a proxy operator gets desyncd with the config that it may or may not be responsible for, then things could go wrong. In a scenario where version fallback to HTTP/1.1 is not desirable, articulating such an error is underspecified.

Similarly for H2 and H3 websocket, telling client the resource is not available or the stream was reset with the fallback error code is misinformation.

issues.title: Message signatures: Pre-signed URLs
issues.author: benkehoe
issues.body: A useful feature of AWS's SigV4 implementation is to allow, at least for certain services, URLs to be created that include the signature as query parameters. This enables, notably, authorized Amazon S3 uploads and downloads scoped to a particular object as URLs that can be shared with another party. If I'm reading the current (-07) HTTP Message Signatures draft correctly, this sort of delegation would only work with message signatures if the client was able to receive a URL and the `Signature-Input` and `Signature` headers as separate values and construct the HTTP request accordingly. Is this correct, and if so, is there any potential for optionally allowing those two header values to be provided through query parameters instead?

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
This is correct - this draft is purposefully not intended to support URL signing like that, but instead to be completely HTTP-focused, taking advantage of all of the parts of HTTP. That's also why we didn't use the `Authorization` header like other signature methods have used.

While signed capability-style URLs have their uses, I believe those uses are distinct enough that support would warrant a different draft to define them. Such a draft could re-use the message normalization, base string generation, and even the header field format for the query parameter values. However, the application of all of that to a pure URL-based delivery context is substantially different from a full HTTP message, and so I don't think that feature belongs in the core draft.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Closing as there are no plans to add this capability within this specification.

issues.title: clearer advice on server interpretation
issues.author: icing
issues.body:
In rfc7540, the 'exclusive' priority description gave explicity advice on when it needs to be disregarded:

```
rfc7540 5.3.1
 ...
 Inside the dependency tree, a dependent stream SHOULD only be
 allocated resources if either all of the streams that it depends on
 (the chain of parent streams up to 0x0) are closed or it is not
 possible to make progress on them."
```

I feel the new priorities draft is not explicit enough on this and implemenations might misinterpret its requirements as in

```
draft: 10.
 Therefore, non-incremental responses of the same urgency SHOULD 
  be served in their entirety, one-by-one, based on the stream ID[...]
```

I propose to change:

```
draft 10.
 It is RECOMMENDED that, when possible, servers respect the 
urgency parameter (Section 4.1), sending higher urgency  responses 
before lower urgency responses.
```

to

```
 Connections SHOULD be progressed whenever response data is available 
 and urgency/incremental information MUST not prevent use of downstream 
 bandwidth. Given that, it is RECOMMENDED that servers respect the urgency 
 parameter (Section 4.1), sending higher urgency  responses before lower 
 urgency responses.
```

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
So IMO RFC 7540 had to say what you quoted because it had the explicit flag. Extensible priorities is a lot less rigid in the relationship between requests. 

I'm not a fan of the suggestion to say "urgency/incremental information MUST not prevent use of downstream 
 bandwidth" because 1) it is a strong requirement (MUST), which is opposed to the general theme of section 10 and 2) it is not clear which actor the requirement is levied upon.

As an alternative suggestion, we could add some more flavour text to highlight that it is generally more beneficial for servers to fill the pipe's bandwidth than let it go quite do to any combination of scheduling decisions whether based on the RECOMMENDations in the section or not. That could be something like a new paragraph at the top of section 10 like


> Server scheduling determines how connection resources such as bandwidth are used. It is generally beneficial for the server to maximise its use of available bandwidth when serving concurrent requests. Therefore, use of bandwidth is one form of input to a prioritization process that considers other inputs. This section describes considerations that servers make when scheduling.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Rereading this issue, I think that the existing text could be misinterpreted in several ways:
* that once the server has started sending a non-incremental response of low urgency, it should continue sending it until the end even when a response of higher urgency becomes available to the server (point raised by @icing),
* that when the non-incremental response cannot fulfill the bandwidth, other responses of same or lower urgency should be sent as well (point raised by @LPardue).

At the moment, both @LPardue's and my text being proposed in #1803 fixes the latter, but not the former.

For the former, I think the question is if we need phrases like "one-by-one" or "entirety." I would argue that maybe changing:
> Therefore, non-incremental responses of the same urgency SHOULD be served in their entirety, one-by-one, based on the stream ID, which corresponds to the order in which clients make requests.


to
> Therefore, non-incremental responses of the same urgency SHOULD be served in the ascending order of the stream ID, which corresponds to the order in which clients make requests.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Not sure why I reopened this issue back in December, it was resolved by the linked PR.

issues.title: TSVART review - editorial comments
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Comments from Bob Briscoe's review:

General (all sections).

- [x]  E#0a) Are precedence and priority interchangeable with urgency?

It's called a priority field, and the parameter is called urgency, but
sometimes the term priority or precedence is used to describe urgency. Please
go through the draft using priority or urgency consistently, and remove
precedence unless it's there for good reason.

§1. Introduction

- [ ] E#1a) The "For example" in para 2 is actually the general point not the
example, whereas the example is in the previous para.

- [x] E#1b) The last para "   The prioritization scheme and priority signals defined
herein can act as a substitute for RFC 7540 stream priority." would fit better
3 paras earlier, just after "HTTP/2 [HTTP2] has consequently deprecated the use
of these stream priority signals."

- [ ] E#1c) It would help to state what the interaction model is for the priority
field. I believe it's not as simple as just "e2e" (see technical comment
earlier about §5). Although I've suggested that normative text about this ought
to be in the §5, it needs to be stated early on (probably in the intro, not
just the abstract), because the reader needs it to understand §§2 & 4.

§1.1.  Notational Conventions

- [ ] E#1d) Was HTTP/2 priority only from C-S?

   The term HTTP/2 priority signal is used to describe the priority
   information sent from clients to servers in HTTP/2 frames;

Neither RFC7540 nor the http2bis draft says that an HTTP/2 priority signal
cannot be sent by a server. It may be that this was the unstated intention but,
if it wasn't, the above sentence is incorrect.

§2.  Motivation for Replacing RFC 7540 Priorities

- [x] E#2a) Not just absence

CURRENT:

   compatibility (see Section 5.3.2 of [HTTP2]), which means that they
   might still be used in the absence of alternative signaling, such as
   the scheme this document describes.

PROPOSED:

   compatibility (see Section 5.3.2 of [HTTP2]), because they
   might still be used by other nodes.

REASONING:
7540 priority fields are not only used in the absence of alternative
signalling. They are used by the client in parallel to extensible priorities
before it receives the server's SETTINGS frame.

2.1.1. Advice when Using Extensible Priorities as the Alternative

- [ ] E#2b)
CURRENT:

   might be useful to nodes behind the server that the client is
   directly connected to.

PROPOSED:

   might be useful to a server behind the directly connected node.

REASONING:
Removes ambiguity - I initially read this as "nodes (behind the server) that"
rather than "...the server that".

§3.  Applicability of the Extensible Priority Scheme

- [x] E#3a)

   The priority scheme defined by this document considers only the
   prioritization of HTTP messages and tunnels, see Section 9,
   Section 10, and Section 11.

Is this sentence meant to be as mysterious as it sounds? If this document only
considers messages and tunnels, what else doesn't it consider? Is 'HTTP
messages' deliberately used instead of 'HTTP responses'? If it is wider than
just responses, then all the places in the draft where it says it is about http
responses need to be generalized (e.g. §4.1, §4.2, §8, §10 §14). But will this
make the draft so abstract that it becomes incomprehensible? Perhaps better to
explain here that it is applicable to a few other odd messages and tunnels, but
it is primarily about responses, so where the draft talks about responses, it
is not intended to preclude the other less-common cases.

It's not clear what the references to §§9,10,11 are there for. Are they further
info about tunnels (only §10 has one sentence on tunnels)? Or are they meant to
list all the sections about scheduling things? if so, why not also §12 on
scheduling retransmissions?

- [x] E#3b)
CURRENT:

   they can also define how this priority scheme
   can be applied.

PROPOSED:

   they can also define how the present priority scheme
   can be extended to support the new extension.

RATIONALE:
I think this is what was intended?

§4.  Priority Parameters

- [x] E#4a) First use of reprioritize
Ought to explain long-hand why reprioritization might be needed here, given it
hasn't been mentioned yet.

- [x] E#4b)

   Note that handling of omitted parameters is different
   when processing an HTTP response

When what processes an HTTP response? The client? An intermediary? Both?

§4.1. Urgency
- [x] E#4c)

   integer between 0 and 7, in
   descending order of priority

   The smaller
   the value, the higher the precedence.

Suggest the latter is moved up 2 paras.
(BTW, what possessed anyone to define this in the most illogical way possible?
So that the highest numerical urgency means the lowest urgency?)

- [x] E#4d) Priority = Precedence = Urgency?
This section interchanges the words 'priority', 'precedence' and 'urgency'. Why
not just use urgency throughout? Otherwise you have to define that priority and
precedence mean exactly the same as urgency.

§4.3.  Defining New Parameters

- [x] E#4e) Not new parameters for everything

Suggested replacement section heading: "Defining New Priority Parameters"

s/   When attempting to define new parameters,/
 /   When attempting to define new priority parameters,/

§4.3.1.  Registration

- [x] E#4f)

s/in Structured Fields Dictionary/
 /in the Structured Fields Dictionary

§5.  The Priority HTTP Header Field

- [x] E#5a)

s/carries priority parameters Section 4./
 /carries priority parameters (Section 4)./

- [x] E#5b)

s/As is the ordinary case for HTTP caching [CACHING], a response with a
  Priority header field might be cached /
 /A response with a Priority header field might be cached [CACHING]/

§7.  The PRIORITY_UPDATE Frame
- [x] E#7a)

s/which can can be bound by/
 /which can can be bounded by/

(Oxford dictionary example '‘the ground was bounded by a main road on one side
and a meadow on the other’')

§8.  Merging Client- and Server-Driven Parameters

- [ ] E#8a)
First para: The 2nd example isn't a particularly good example of 'server knows
best'; it even admits that it's the visual-ness of the client that determines
the priority.

- [x] #8b) What is 'the logic being defined' meant to mean?

s/This is different from the logic being defined for the request header field,/
 /This is different from the approach for the request header field,/

Perhaps?

§10.  Server Scheduling

- [x] E#10a) No guidance is provided,... except for a page and a half

   No guidance is provided about how this can or
   should be done.  ...
   For these reasons, ... this document only provides some basic
   recommendations for implementations.

(Contradictory.)
It seems like the rather over-negative caveats in the first 3 paras need to be
revisited now that the page and a half of recommendations (some normative) has
been added after them.

§10.1.  Intermediaries with Multiple Backend Connections

- [x] E#10b)
s/inflight/in flight/

§11.  Scheduling and the CONNECT Method

- [x] #E11a)

   A
   client that issues multiple CONNECT requests can set the incremental
   parameter to true, servers that implement the recommendation in
   Section 10 will schedule these fairly.

s/...true, servers.../
 /...true. Servers.../

There are 3 recommendations in §10. Which one?

Given §10 starts with a load of caveats about how hard this stuff is to get
right, is it appropriate to assert with such certainty that scheduling will be
fair?

§12.  Retransmission Scheduling

- [x] E#12a)

s/Section 6.2.4 of [QUIC-RECOVERY], also highlights/
 /Section 6.2.4 of [QUIC-RECOVERY] also highlights/

§13.1.  Coalescing Intermediaries

- [x] E#13a)

   It is sometimes beneficial for the server running behind an
   intermediary to obey to the value of the Priority header field.

This seems an odd sentence to have in this draft. I think it is meant to be in
the context of the previous sentence about coalesced requests with priorities
set by different clients. Needs rewriting, I think.

s/obey to/
 /obey/

s/the Priority header field/
 /each Priority header field/

s/as another signal in its prioritization decisions./
 /as another input in its prioritization decisions./

§14.  Why use an End-to-End Header Field?

- [x] E#14a)

s|Contrary to the prioritization scheme of HTTP/2|
 |In contrast to the prioritization scheme of HTTP/2|

Contrary in this form has an implication that HTTP/2 was wrong. That might be
intended. But 'in contrast to' has less of a 'know-it-all' feel.

- [x] E#14b) Answering a different question

   rather
   than how relatively urgent each response is to others.

This seems to be a (weak) rationale for relative rather than absolute
priorities, whereas the section heading promises the rationale for an e2e
header. I suggest the whole first sentence of this 2nd para is deleted, because
the next sentence gives a sufficient rationale.

- [x] E#14c) Answering another different question

   It should also be noted that the use of a header field carrying a
   textual value makes the prioritization scheme extensible; see the
   discussion below.

This is also not a rationale for an e2e header. Perhaps it belongs in the Intro?

Alternatively, the section title could be changed to "Rationale for Priority
Protocol Design" or something. Then it could give rationale for absolute
priority values and textual values as well as e2e header fields.

- [x] E14d) see what "discussion below"?

Perhaps this refers to the sentence in Security Considerations that refers to
[STRUCTURED FIELDS]? If so, it's hardly a "discussion".

§16.  IANA Considerations

- [x] E#16a)

   populate it with the
   types defined in Section 4; see Section 4.3.1 for its associated
   procedures.

I suspect IANA will prefer the exact text they should use to be written here.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
We've been working through these editorial issues with the various associated PRs. To help track progress, here is the current (at the time of writing) status of open items on the issue based on my take:

* Precedence, Priority, Urgency (E#0a, E#4c, E#4d)
  * Fixed in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1827
  
* E#1a
  *  Since this priority scheme is for HTTP in general, anything the refers to HTML is only an example of how the scheme applies. Not seeing any action required here.
  
* E#1c
  * The Priority header field is a signal. How it is used by clients, servers and intermediaries is described in the intro. That text was added in response to WGLC. I don't feel that expanding the text here as suggested would improve the document because it relies on text elsewhere in the document to understand all the details.

* E#1d
  * RFC7540 server-to-client signals seem like something that was technically allowed but never used by anyone in practice. There is a 7540bis activity underway, I raise an issue for this https://github.com/httpwg/http2-spec/issues/1000. With respect to this document, we are defining our own terms for the benefit of this document. The term is consistently applied in the document with this in mind. I'm happy keeping things as is.
  
* E#2b
  * The current text is accurate. The header might be useful to nodes behind the server (imagine a front-end HTTP server that talks to some other process via CGI etc)

* E#3a
  * Agreed. See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1806 for changes to address this.
  
* E#3b
  * The intent here is that "things we don't know about" might or might not be able to apply this scheme. Take for example HTTP/3 datagrams - we can't say that they just need to extend the scheme (they might not!) and we can't assume the scheme will work for them (otherwise we'd have to write some scheduling considerations). So the responsibility is on the extensions to state how they think they fit with this scheme. The text has changed a bit in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1806 (targetted for E#3b) but the intent remains the same.

* E#4a
  * See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1812

* E#5b
  * See  https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1815

* E#8a
  * This example seems fine to me. An operator could know that the font will block text rendering and want to prioritize that for web page performance or QoE reasons.

* E#11a
  * See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1816

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: closing this now that we addressed the items we decided to. Any remaining open tasks are to be left without action.

RFC Editor recommends either:

issues.title: Define fairness
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
From the TSVART review, Bob says:

> §13. Fairness
> 
> T#13a) Please define fair. Seriously.
> 
> A prerequisite question is, "What parameters does a server scheduler
> manipulate?" The text implies the server can only control the order in which it
> starts a response to each request, and whether responses start while other
> responses are in progress or wait for their completion. If so, I'm not sure
> what fairness could mean.
> 
> Presumably a server can also determine the relative rate at which it sends
> different streams. And it could stall a stream to allow another absolute
> priority. In this context, fairness might mean instantaneously equal rates. But
> that's not fair if the objects are of different sizes.
> 
> So we genuinely do need to see a definition of what fairness means here.

We should address this.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I think there's confusion here.

Section 13 discusses fairness of bandwidth allocated between end clients, not requests. I think clarifying this might help.

issues.title: Why does the IETF have anything to say about scheduling across mutliple connections?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
As part of the TSVART review, Bob said

>  T#13b) Why not make scheduling decisions across different clients?
> 
>    As a general guideline, a server SHOULD NOT use priority information
>    for making scheduling decisions across multiple connections, unless
>    it knows that those connections originate from the same client.
> 
> Why does the IETF have anything to say about this? It's surely an operator
> policy decision.

This seems like a fair point and we likely shouldn't say anything. We can remove this statement entirely but it is normative text so it'll be a change.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I initially thought the same, but now I have a counter-argument.

This section (Section 13. Fairness) discusses distributing bandwidth between multiple connections.

13.1 and 13.2 cover considerations when intermediaries coalesce requests originating from multiple connections onto a single backend connection, or split requests being received on one connection to multiple backend connections.

Section 13.3 distributing bandwidth between multiple connections that might share same path. 

I would argue that all of these belong to IETF, and that they should be covered in the document.

We can probably improve the explanation to avoid confusion.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: OK that works for me too, could you tackle that?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: :+1: Will do alongside #1819.

- Here's a set of examples where the content-digest and digest are the same
  - A response message without content encoding
  - A request message without content encoding
  - A request and response pair at an API (json in, json out)
- Here's a set of examples where the content-digest and digest are different
  - A response message with content encoding
  - A request message with content encoding

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks for elaborating Justin.

The problem I have is that examples will never be exhaustive and are not suitable as a comprehensive set of test vectors. In some folks view the appendices are already too long. Adding even more things makes it worse.

As an alternative, maybe we could speak to your comments in a different way. How about a short section of its own that compares content digest and representation digest directly? It could contain one or two examples that drive home the differences but stay shy from every possible permutation.

comments.author: jricher
LPardue
comments.body:
Content-digest is really simple. It's just calculated over the content. If you don't have content or you don't want content digest, there's really no need for the header. 

Adding Content-digest to all applicable examples is possible. But it might be inferred that endpoints are expected to use both. That's not the case, they can choose either. Furthermore, sending both only makes sense in a limited set of cases like the content-digest of a chunk along with the representation digest of the whole think.

I can take another look at the examples to see if there's opportunity for what you suggest. I just worry that people take the examples as verbatim and start inferring meaning from them that is not intended.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
It's the fact that "Content-Digest is simple" that I want to make sure we convey. Right now it seems like the exception, since so much of the draft is given to showing Digest and its complexities. I think we want to steer developers to using Content-Digest most of the time since they're more likely to get it right. I'll say that for my implementations of 3230, I was pretty much always already doing what Content-Digest says to do, but it worked because I wasn't dealing with Content-Encoding or ranges or the other things that allow it to differ from Digest.

You don't have to put both headers in each example in a single message -- I was picturing having two separate examples, or having a note that says the calculated value is valid for both of them at the same time. What I was describing above is something like these:

B3
----

Take the response message:

```
HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Range: bytes 1-7/18

"hello"
```

The digest is calculated across the whole object of

```
{"hello": "world"}
```

Giving a value for of:

```
Digest: sha-256=X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=
```

However, the content of the message contains only the indicated range of bytes:

```
"hello"
```

Which gives a value of:

```
Content-Digest: sha-256=Wqdirjg/u3J688ejbUlApbjECpiUUtIwT8lY/z81Tno=
```

B1
----

Take the response message:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"hello": "world"}
```

Since the content is the same as the representation, both the digest and content-digest sha-256 hashes are the same for this message:

```
Digest: sha-256=X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=
Content-Digest: sha-256=X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=
```

----

All of that information is technically in the examples right now but I had to dig around to see it more clearly. I'm not necessarily asking for more or different examples, I'm asking for a clearer (to me at least) presentation of the examples and values. I find separating the calculated values from the message that they are embedded in is helpful, but others might not.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks for taking the time @jricher, I have a clearer understanding what you mean now and it seems reasonable. I'll take a task to prepare a PR along the lines you suggest.

Edit: reasonable in the British sense. In other cultures they might say "this is a great suggestion, thank you"

From @jricher WGLC review:

issues.title: Signing Empty / Absent Headers
issues.author: jricher
issues.body:
Currently, an empty header can be included, but an absent header can't be guaranteed. 

Proposal: add a boolean parameter for header field identifiers to mark a specific field as "not present" in the target message. Its value is an empty string. (Or should it be some special flag?)

If the verifier finds any header value with that name in the target message, throw an error.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
My understanding of the design was that the signature covered the message you receive.  This would be a departure from that in that it encodes the *value* associated with the field into the signature description.

I see that the current algorithm fails with an error if a field is listed but absent from the message.  You could change that easily enough and encode absent fields[^1].  Then, if you want to prevent the inclusion of a field, you would list it in `Signature-Input` but not include that field in the message.

Note that fields that are present but empty are not absent. These can be encoded already.

[^1]: One simple way to encode an absent field is to include the field name on an empty line. That is, omit the colon, space, and value.  That should be easily distinguishable.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Copying from the PR where @jricher [says](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1976#issuecomment-1144168848):

> After review of the previous discussion following the interim, I still think this is something we should not add.
>
> I am strongly against the proposed alternative of having a signer include a covered component that does not exist by using the same syntax as a covered component that does exist, and having that process create a valid signature.

After that discussion and some consideration, I find I agree with the conclusion here.  We shouldn't build in the ability to sign an absence.

If you want something absent, then not signing it is sufficient.  This is primarily because not signing something should -- ideally -- ensure that the recipient who depends on that signature will treat these extra pieces of the message as absent when it comes to processing messages.  Even if they have been added, they are not signed and should not alter how the message is processed by the recipient.  See [Section 8.1 of RFC 3275](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3275#section-8.1) and subsections (reading the titles should suffice) for a succinct treatment of that.

I was originally of the view that an approach where you have a specification of what is signed that is fixed no matter what the message is would be useful.  For instance, if you believe that signing the X field is important, it might be useful to include that in `Signature-Input` even in cases where messages don't include the X field.  But I'm OK with having signers adapt the value of `Signature-Input` to the specific message they are signing.  There are hazards in that approach in terms of implementation complexity and robustness, but it is not much more than the specification already demands of implementations.

(I still disagree with the second sentiment, but we can happily continue to disagree on that point without consequence, because it is moot.)

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
I think that we've incorporated the warnings on the need to cover important elements with a signature in the security considerations: https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-10.html#name-insufficient-coverage

Unless there's significant pull to do otherwise, I'm going to plan to close this issue and the associated PR with no action in the next week.

issues.title: Signatures: Move keys to PKCS#8 PEM Format
issues.author: bblfish
issues.body:
1. Neither Java nor JS subtleCrypto come out of the box with PKCS1 PEM support.  (for java [see here](https://stackoverflow.com/posts/6560187/revisions)).
2. It is not immediately obvious to work out that the PEM formats of the private key in in PKCS1 format (the spec could point that out).
3. When building an implementation it helps to have the test suite clearly map to the data in the spec (e.g. [here](https://github.com/bblfish/bobcats/blob/ab9c7fa1759f3fc58abdbf10e8c5431451a045a0/core/shared/src/test/scala/bobcats/SigningHttpMessages.scala#L256)) so as to make error reporting clearer. That is even though using the following openssl command to convert the keys work, it makes it difficult to see if an error was introduced at some point.
```zsh
$ openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -in spec.private.pem -out private.pem -nocrypt
```
4. To support PKCS1 the developer has to depend on further less well tested libraries and add additional code (as I [did here](https://github.com/bblfish/bobcats/blob/main/core/jvm/src/test/scala/bobcats/util/BouncyJavaPEMUtils.scala)) leading possibly to new bugs. Furthermore, I will need to go through the same process for JavaScript now, doubling the work.

Since PKCS8 is as expressive as PKCS1 ([according to this article](https://www.starkandwayne.com/blog/credhub-keysmust-be-pem-encoded-pkcs1-keys/) and see [this nice StackExchange answer](https://stackoverflow.com/a/48960291/396079)), it would make life easier for devs if the keys were all in PKCS8 format. Unless there really is something that PKCS1 offers that PKCS8 does not?

I will try doing this using the Web Crypto API next. But there we find that [importKey](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SubtleCrypto/importKey) supports the PKCS#8 format.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
@bblfish Since this all has to do with the examples in the text and not the spec itself, I think we'd be fine with having the keys in multiple formats if it's useful for developers. However I'll note that in many code libraries you need to add the PEM headers of `---- BEGIN EC KEY ----` and `---- END EC KEY ----` for their compliant parsers to parse an EC key in PEM format, for example. I've been able to parse these keys in both Java and Python, and in fact all the examples are generated using a python script: https://github.com/bspk/sig-example-scripts/blob/main/http_sig_examples.py

Also, note that RSA-PSS and ECDSA are non-deterministic signatures that incorporate a source of randomness into the signature calculation. This might be why you're getting valid signatures that look different from the examples -- you shouldn't expect to replicate the exact signature values. RSA 1.5 is deterministic, and will always give this same signature for the same input (as will HMAC). This is just one of the reasons why it's not recommended in many environments. I think we can add some text in the examples sections that points this out, if that would be helpful.

issues.title: Client scheduling applies to what message?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Section 9 says:

> A client MAY use priority values to make local processing or scheduling choices about the requests it initiates.

Bob Briscoe asked if this is supposed to be "responses to the requests that it initiates". Another interpretation could be that it applies to both requests that are sent and responses that are received.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
It has always been my position that this applies to requests.

To be specific, this statement matters to intermediaries that forward requests to backend servers, especially when the request-level concurrency to back-end servers is smaller than that of the front-end connection. In such deployment, pending requests can get queued up within the intermediary. Then, when picking up the next request to be forwarded from that queue, it makes sense to pick up one that has the highest priority.

This statement also matters to end clients but to a lesser extent, because end clients do not need to (or probably not use) the signalling method being defined by a standardization organization that governs protocols but not internal behaviors.

comments.author: bbriscoe
comments.body: The subject of the sentence is the client, not intermediaries.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
In [HTTP terminology](https://httpwg.org/http-core/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-latest.html#terminology), intermediary is a node that acts as both client and server, forwarding HTTP messages.

What I argued in my previous comment is that existing text is correct to cover both user agents (i.e., clients that initiate requests) and intermediaries (clients that forward request), but it matters more to the latter.

comments.author: bbriscoe
comments.body:
Of the 84 occurrences of 'client' in the draft, I suspect a number were actually intended to mean 'user agent'. This one in §9 seems to be one of them, because in §5 it says
> Guidance for how endpoints can act on Priority header
> values is given in Section 10 and Section 9." 

Also, I noticed that there is a list of [Considerations for New Fields](https://httpwg.org/http-core/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-latest.html#considerations.for.new.fields) in §16.3.2 that would have been useful to follow for the new Priority field.

issues.title: Signatures: 2.1.3 Dictionary Structured Field Members
issues.author: damz
issues.body:
In section 2.1.3 we have:

https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/blob/28685efd422e2512bec9cc7326e1c9882b84575d/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.md?plain=1#L285

> An individual member in the value of a Dictionary Structured Field is canonicalized by applying the serialization algorithm described in {{Section 4.1.2 of RFC8941}} on a Dictionary containing only that item.

I assume this meant to reference the list serialization of SFV instead. Something like this:

> An individual member in the value of a Dictionary Structured Field is canonicalized by applying the serialization algorithm described in {{Section 4.1.1 of RFC8941}} on a List containing only that item.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: On closer read, it needs to be serialization on the Item itself, not a single-member Dictionary or List. It's an artifact that a single-member List and an Item are the same, though I think that's actually more confusing.

comments.author: damz
comments.body:
The Structured Field Values specification is quite peculiar. The serialization described in [4.1.3. Serializing an Item](https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-header-structure-19.html#ser-item) only supports bare items. But dictionaries and lists do support inner lists as values (as well as bare items).

To do what you want to do here, you need to take the item, put it in a list and serialize the list, which is the language I am suggesting above.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Text should be fixed by cleanup in #1903: I pointed to the dictionary section 4.1.2 but without the call for it to be a "single-member dictionary". I think the single-member list is accurate but confusing here, so the new text says to serialize the member item itself. Leaving this open to see if this can be made even clearer.

issues.title: Security Consideration: Lazy header parsers
issues.author: jricher
issues.body:
It's been reported that the HTTP header parsers on some platforms are particularly lazy in what they allow for header content, including allowing header field names to start with the `@` symbol. If an implementation of HTTP Signatures uses one of these platforms naively, that implementation could end up in a situation where an attacker could try to override one of the derived content values, like `@method` by sending a fake header in the request to override the actual value derivation.

Advice in both processing algorithm and security considerations will be to check the first character and only look for header field values if it's not the reserved `@` character.

issues.title: Signatures: "Related response" feature
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
I think the "related response" feature, as in:

>If used in a related-response, the `@path` identifier refers to the associated component value of the request that triggered the response message being signed.

is not a good idea, for two reasons:

* It only applies (and can only apply) to specialty/derived components, and cannot apply to normal headers and query params which people might also want to bind between requests and responses.
* It is subsumed by the `@request-response` feature, and request-response is simpler and more secure. You decide once which request fields need to be signed, and the response is then bound to the entire verified request.

So I would suggest to remove this feature, and allow `@path` and similar to only apply to requests.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: It's not entirely subsumed by request-response, since this requires the client to sign the initial request, which the server has no control over. That said, it may be safer to have that restriction.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
On second thought, there may be cases when the client is unable to sign, because its public key is not trusted by the server. So the server is doing the signing for both of them. Strange.

This still doesn't address my first point. Specifically, if the whole semantics of the request is in the message body, there's no way for the server to bind the response to the Digest of the request.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
You are correct, there's no way to bind a header from the request into the related-response method if you're doing it server-only. The editors discussed this and felt like it would be a very complicated path for people to get right, and it could lead to confusion and potential security issues. With the derived content, there's at least no ambiguity as to what the source of the data is -- if it's a request-only value and you're looking at a response, you know it came from the triggering request.

That said, this whole feature is more of a "nice to have" in my own book. I think it makes sense, but I'd like to hear more from implementors who would actually use this, or not. It's entirely possible that for real-life use cases the request-response derived content is sufficient for systems that would be able to make sense of such an advanced use case anyway.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
Just to throw it out there, I would have loved a more explicit construction. Such as:

* `@related/x-My-Header`
* `@related/@query`

I haven't checked if the `/` character is even allowed.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Thanks for that idea, it's something the editors considered. If we did that, the syntax would just use structured field parameters, like `"@related"; field="x-header"`. Things start to get really weird when you allow signing elements that have their own parameters, though. We started down that path to get the "request-response" functionality originally, since you could sign a "related" signature header, but we really didn't like the complexity that arose very quickly from that construct. The narrowly defined derived components were our way around that. I agree that they're still complicated and it's a reasonable question whether the functionality is worth it or not.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
As discussed in the meeting today, in HTTP the corresponding request is necessary to fully understand and contextualise a response. while `@request-response` does that, as @jricher points out that doesn't work in the case when the client doesn't sign the request. 

My tentative suggestion would be to collapse `related-response` into `response` and distinguish request headers from response headers with prefix other than `@`.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
I personally don't like the idea of having a prefix that namespaces headers like that because then you need to do parsing within the string. Right now it's more of a direct string match, which is less error prone.

That said, @richanna has suggested that we can do something like:

```
"x-my-header";req: Request Header value
"@query";req: ?request-query
"@status": normal response status
```

This approach would require more error checking and explicit testing for combinations with and without the `req` flag, but I think it would lead to clearer code paths than a prefix.

If we did this, we could also ostensibly get rid of the `@request-response` derived header entirely, because it would amount to signing:

```
"signature";key="sig1";req
```

inside the response. If we have the discussion about the use case for this clear in the document, I think it could work. Thoughts on this approach?

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: I like both the `;req` proposal as well as getting rid of the special-case `@request-response`.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: WFM - not hung up on syntax.
