issues.title: Upload progress via informational responses
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
In a message to the mailing list (https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0006.html), Austin Wright (@awwright) proposed to use informational responses to send information about the upload progress from the server to the client. During the Upload Creation Procedure and Upload Appending Procedure, the server could regularly send an informational response with the latest offset in the Upload-Offset header.

The value should reflect the amount of data that has been received and safely stored by the server. This way, the client knows what data has been successfully transmitted and is not needed for resumption anymore. Any resources attached for this data (e.g. memory buffers) can be released then. In contrast, If the client only monitors which,data it has sent, it cannot be sure if the server properly stored it yet.

There is a short example of this how communication could look like (note: it uses server-generated upload URLs (https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2292), but it could also be done using client-generated tokens, of course):

```
:method: POST
:scheme: https
:authority: example.com
:path: /upload
content-length: 300
[content (300 bytes)]

:status: 104
location: https://example.com/upload/b530ce8ff

:status: 1xx
upload-offset: 100

:status: 1xx
upload-offset: 200

:status: 201
location: https://example.com/upload/b530ce8ff
upload-offset: 300
```

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I think doing this is fine, and I agree that it has benefits as pointed out above.

General guideline of HTTP is that servers are allowed to send any number of informational responses. There's no reason to not use that.

Regarding the status code, I think we can reuse 104.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: +1 Kazuho

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
I think we need some communication between client and server to enable this. The protocol is designed to avoid depending on 1xx status codes.

* Does the client need to explicitly opt in to this?
* Can the server opt out?
* What if the server doesn't support 1xx?

If we want to keep this optional without adding a new header field, a possible design is:

```
:status: 104
location: /upload/token
upload-offset: 0

:status: 104
upload-offset: 10000
```

If the server wants to send periodic updates, it can start by doing so in the initial 104. The client can enable additional buffering behavior based on this information (but it might have already dropped some bytes by the initial 104). This is a server driven solution and the client won't be able to opt out.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Or maybe https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc2518.html#STATUS_102

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I'm not fussed on the specific response code value but the 102 seems deprecated, for whatever that means, and the linked wording seems at odds with the system design we want

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
It's not deprecated, but wasn't carried over to WebDAV-bis due to lack of implementations.

It's in the registry, so it's a real HTTP status code.

That said, I now agree it doesn't fit well, as 102 is for situations where the client is actually *waiting* for a response (as opposed to still sending).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> It's not deprecated, but wasn't carried over to WebDAV-bis due to lack of implementations.

I guess that's accurate to the historical record, after a very cursory delve into RFC 2518 and 4918. But I wonder how clear that interpretation is to the broader HTTP world. MDN has a perspective you might want to follow up on.

> 
> It's in the registry, so it's a real HTTP status code.
> 
> That said, I now agree it doesn't fit well, as 102 is for situations where the client is actually _waiting_ for a response (as opposed to still sending).

Yeah this is where I'm hitting a hard edge. A registered status code, where the behaviour, the important stuff,  is described in an obsoleted RFC doesn't really seem great.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
FWIW, I would push back hard on that line of argument. The code is registered, so it's a valid status code.

And yes, a spec that wants to *use* might want to either include an updated definition, or make sure the definition is moved to a separate new document.

comments.author: awwright
comments.body:
I also think that 102 is OK to use here (but maybe a new status code is still warranted, see below). The 102 isn't depreciated as a bad idea or because of another better solution, it was merely omitted from recent updates to the WebDAV specification for lack of implementations. I imagine another specification could take over ownership of the definition/registration.

I think the only reason I didn't specifically write 102 in my email is, I've [previously (2019) experimented with using it](https://awwright.github.io/http-progress/draft-wright-http-progress.html) to indicate "upload complete, the server is now performing additional processing" and it may be useful to distinguish this signal from "upload has been partially received and committed to storage". The former is probably closer to the intended usage, so it may still be good to mint a new status code for the latter usage.

Alternatively, both cases might be distinguished by the HTTP fields that are returned, and maybe servers want to indicate both at the same time ("50% committed to disk, 20% processed").

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I share the view that 102 does not fit very well here. It would be awkward to send an URI to which the missing part of the request should be sent, while indicating that "the server has accepted the complete request" ([RFC 2518 section 10.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2518#section-10.1)).

If we are to choose from an existing status code, 100-continue might be a better choice, though I would prefer using a new status code considering that we did so in introducing 103. All 1xx codes are interim and therefore kind of implies continuation. We can burn a new status code for a particular case of contiuation, which Resumable Upload is.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: I opened a PR for this in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2664.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
I think this would be a good addition to the spec as long as it's not mandatory for the server to send this data. As previously stated in this thread It would help the client to discard in-memory data that is no longer required to resume.

Would it make sense to also include the location header in the additional 104 responses? This would make the solution more robust in case one (or several) of the 104 responses get lost and the extra header field would not add any significant amount of extra bytes in each request.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> I think this would be a good addition to the spec as long as it's not mandatory for the server to send this data.

Yes, this would be optional.




> Would it make sense to also include the location header in the additional 104 responses? This would make the solution more robust in case one (or several) of the 104 responses get lost and the extra header field would not add any significant amount of extra bytes in each request.

I am unsure how big the benefit would actually be. This would only help if a 104 is lost without the connection being destroyed, so the HTTP response is still open and a subsequent 104 could be received. Maybe this is possible with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, but I don't know that. Other than that, repeating Location would be redundant.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: 1xx response are allowed to be dropped by intermediaries. But I'm not aware of any that would drop _some_ in a request. Typically they just swallow all or pass all.

comments.author: kazuho
MikeBishop
comments.body: I suspect what @LPardue meant to say is that some proxies _do_ drop 1xx responses, whether they're allowed to or not. Also, some HTTP libraries consume all the 1xx responses without exposing them to the caller, even if the library itself doesn't do anything with that particular 1xx code; such a library is indistinguishable from a poorly-behaved intermediary.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
> I am unsure how big the benefit would actually be. This would only help if a 104 is lost without the connection being destroyed, so the HTTP response is still open and a subsequent 104 could be received. Maybe this is possible with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, but I don't know that. Other than that, repeating Location would be redundant.

> 1xx response are allowed to be dropped by intermediaries. But I'm not aware of any that would drop some in a request. Typically they just swallow all or pass all.

My concern isn't so much proxies dropping one or more response as much as e.g. switching network and losing one or more of the 104 response (think spotty Wi-Fi moving over to 4G). Another input here would be consistency, especially if we add the `Upload-Offset: 0` header to the first 104. I agree that the benefit might not be huge but it's not zero either. It does however seem like the consensus in Prague was that this is not needed and I can get behind that.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> e.g. switching network and losing one or more of the 104 response (think spotty Wi-Fi moving over to 4G)

One or more of the 104 responses could be dropped, along with the final response, due to the connection being interrupted, but _selective_ 104s can't be dropped due to network issues. Clients need to deal with failed connections no matter what, so  I don't see how this is an issue.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body: @mnot Right, then this is a non-issue that can be skipped. I just wanted to bring it up so that we do not miss aspects. :)

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thanks for the feedback! I adjusted https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2664 to clarify what header fields can be present in 104 responses.

issues.title: Retry-able upload creations using Idempotency-Key
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
The current draft -00 of the resumable upload protocol uses a client-generated token to identify which procedures belong together. In https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2292 an alternative approach is proposed where the server generates an upload URL and return it to the client in the response for the Upload Creation Procedures. Details can be found in the PR.

The original approach with the client-generated tokens allowed the client to resume an upload even if it never received an response for the Upload Creation Procedure. The client could just perform an Offset Retrieving Procedure and resume based on the corresponding response. This is obviously not possible anymore with the server-generated URLs because the client does not know these URLs until it received a response.

So, Austin Wright (@awwright) had the idea to use the Idempotency-Key header to allow retrying the Upload Creation Procedure if the response was not received (see https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0004.html). There is currently a draft for the Idempotency-Key header being discussed by the httpapi working group: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/. Based on this idea, a retry-able upload creation could look like this:

- If the client knows that the server supports the Idempotency-Key, it can generate a value and include it in the Upload Creation Procedure.
- If the connection was interrupted and the client did not receive an upload URL (either through an 1XX or 2XX response), it can choose to try the entire Upload Creation Procedure:
  - The client sends the same Upload Creation Procedure again, including the same Idempotency-Key and Upload-Incomplete header. The client should also send the same request body.
  - If the server receives an Upload Creation Request with an unknown Idempotency-Key value, it should just create a new upload resource as usual.
  - If the server receives an Upload Creation Request with a known Idempotency-Key value, it should not create a new upload resource and instead use the existing one. If the request contains a body, the server should append any data that exceeds the current upload offset (e.g. if the server received 100 bytes in the first Upload Creation Procedure and the client sends 200 bytes in the retried Upload Creation Procedure, the server should ignore the first 100 bytes because it already received them. Only the second 100 bytes should be appended).
  - In the end, the server should send the appropriate response, as usual.
- This allows the client to retrieve the same upload URL that was created in a previous Upload Creation Procedure, for which it did not receive the response.
- This also allows client to upload small files in a single, retry-able request. Based on the client's desire, it can choose different ways to upload:
  - If the client wants to upload a big file, where an additional request for the Upload Creation Procedure is of no concern, it can send an Upload Creation Procedure with no additional data. The Idempontency-Key can be used to obtain the upload URL if the connection fail here. After this, the Upload Appending Procedure is used to transfer the actual data.
  - If the client wants to upload a small file, where additional requests should be avoided, the client can send an Upload Creation Procedure and include the entire file representation in the request body alongside the Idempotency-Key. If the transmission fails, the client should retry (not resume) the entire request include the entire file representation. In the best case, the client can upload in a single request. In the worst case, it must retransmit the entire file. But this is not a big concern because of the small file size (whose definition depends on the situation).

Finally, retry-able requests and resumable uploads are not the same. However, in this case, I believe they work hand-in-hand to deliver reliable uploads, which is the entire goal of this adventure.

What do you think about this?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: During IETF 115 the feedback was largely uniform against including this in the draft. Since Idempotency-Key is its own draft in the httpapi WG, people can still choose to use this header for their applications if they like to do so. Maybe in the future we will revisit this topic if we have seen that Idempotency-Key proved helpful in real-world scenarios.

comments.author: awwright
Acconut
comments.body:
> I'm not sure what _part_ of the idea is disfavored, could you please discuss this on list?

IIRC, the disagreement was more about `Idempotency-Key` on its own, rather than the concept of idempotency itself. It would be very similar to the client-generated `Upload-Token` that was used in earlier versions of the resumable upload draft. Such client-generated tokens are generally a bit more problematic to handle as previous discussions of client vs server-generated identifiers showed.

> The important thing I'm pointing out is that resumable uploads are necessarily idempotent.

I agree that a resumable upload in its entirety should be idempotent. However, this does not mean that each operation of a resumable upload has to be idempotent. For example, the same Upload Appending Procedure cannot be retried without running into errors, making it not-idempotent.

That being said, I want to bring up the topic of error handling for Upload Creation Procedure again.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2596

issues.title: Non-cachable HEAD responses
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
In a message to the mailing list (https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0006.html), Austin Wright (@awwright) voices concerns of the inability to cache HEAD responses from the Offset Retrieving Procedure:

> GET/HEAD is supposed to be cachable (and so returning a client-specific Upload-Offset would be dubious)

In fact, the current draft -00 recommends the server to disallow caching the response header:

> The response SHOULD include Cache-Control: no-store header to prevent HTTP caching.

Is this a conflict between the intended usage of HEAD requests and its actual usage inside resumable uploads? Or is this not a problem?

comments.author: jrflat
comments.body:
I don't think this is a huge conflict, but if we are concerned we could potentially look into something like a RESUME method like Austin suggests in his email. I also think the "non-intended" usage of HEAD is mitigated when using server-generated URLs (#2292) rather than client-generated token. It feels more natural to respond to a `HEAD /upload/unique-identifier` with an `Upload-Offset`  header as opposed to responding to `HEAD /upload` with different `Upload-Offset` values based on the clients' tokens.

If a middlebox doesn't abide by the `Cache-Control: no-store` rule, having the unique server-generated paths would at least isolate the issue to a single upload session. The client also has the chance to get at least 1 valid `Upload-Offset` from the server before running into issues with a cached value. If the client receives the cached value later at some point and tries to resume, it would get a `409 Conflict`, so maybe the client could just retry the upload entirely at which point it receives a new upload URL? We could also just recommend using HTTPS.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: I agree that there seems to be little concerns about this issue, so we can close it for now.

issues.title: Use of Prefer header for request identification
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
In https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2243#issuecomment-1264586690, @reschke mentioned that the `Prefer` header could be used by the client to indicate its interest for performing a resumable upload. The server could use this header to identify a request as the Upload Creation Procedure.

In the current draft -00, the `Upload-Token` header can also be used to identify the Upload Creation Procedure (https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-00.html#name-request-identification). However, depending on the outcome of https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2292, this header might not be present in future drafts. So a `Prefer: resumable-upload` request header could be a great replacement for this.

This could require adding a new entry for resumable uploads to the Registry of Preferences: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7240#section-5.1

Other options are:
- `Expect: 104-upload-resumption-support`: Problematic due to conflicts with `Expect: 100-continue` and strict specification (see https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2243)
- Require a custom header, e.g. `Upload-Incomplete`. That seems inferior if the Prefer header already fits our needs.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: This can be closed for now. Upload creation and upload append requests must include the `Upload-Complete` header, which can be used for identification.

issues.title: how to get the response after upload is complete
issues.author: kazuho
issues.body:
IIUC, with #2292, we have two resources. One being the resource to which the transaction is started (A), and another to which the chunks are sent (B).

Assuming that responses that we get for resource B is that for resource B, how do we obtain the response for resource A when the upload is complete?

To give an example, consider the following case:
* Client starts a POST to /foo, and server sends a 1xx response specifying a transaction resource /transaction/1234.
* The clients uploads the final chunk to /transaction/1234, and gets a 500 response.

Does this 500 mean that the upload of the final chunk failed? Or is it a response for the original request (for resource A)?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: IMHO, one way of fixing this ambiguity issue would be to define a method to commit the transaction, that would target the original URI (A), even though chunks can be uploaded through a different URI (B).

comments.body: This is a really good point. Currently, responses to Upload Appending Procedure include the upload offset. We could say something like "if the offset is equal to the size of the upload, treat this response as the final response and don't retry".

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> "if the offset is equal to the size of the upload, treat this response as the final response and don't retry".

I like this idea, yes. However, what should the client do if it does not receive the response for the last Upload Appending Procedure? Should we add a mechanism where the client can retry fetching the response for the last Upload Appending Procedure?

comments.body: If they don't receive the response, performing an offset retrieving and attempting a resumption (even if it's a 0-length resumption at the end) should be sufficient I think.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Sure

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> If they don't receive the response, performing an offset retrieving and attempting a resumption (even if it's a 0-length resumption at the end) should be sufficient I think.

:+1: this sounds good to me. Thank you for the efforts.

The flip side of the resolution is that, once the server receives the entire upload, the server is expected to generate a response and cache it for certain amount of time, because the client might fail to receive the response and re-issue a PATCH request that is possibly zero-length.

As the PATCH request (or the original POST / PUT request that initiates the upload) is not idempotent, a response for a Resumable Upload request cannot be resumed (like we do for file downloads). But that's probably okay, most HTTP responses for Resumable Upload is going to be tiny.

comments.body:
> The flip side of the resolution is that, once the server receives the entire upload, the server is expected to generate a response and cache it for certain amount of time

comments.body:
The server could also include the location of the response, either:

- as a Content-Location when the client uploads the final chunk, alongside actually sending the response
- as a Location when the client queries the status of a completed upload resource

Once the client has the URL of the response, even if it's large and interrupted, it can perform traditional resumable downloads on it for as long as the server is willing to keep it around.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: I agree with the feedback from Prague that Content-Location would be a great fit to solve this problem. The server can sends a URL using Content-Location during the upload. The client can then use this URL to query a potential result of the upload process. I will open a PR to add a note explaining this possibility.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
I have updated the [tusdotnet POC](https://github.com/tusdotnet/tusdotnet/tree/POC/tus2) to add support for Content-Location. For now it will call [user code](https://github.com/tusdotnet/tusdotnet/blob/POC/tus2/Source/TestSites/AspNetCore_netcoreapp3.1_TestApp/MyTusHandler.cs#L73) each time the Content-Location is requested and the user code can determine if it wants to provide a CL or just ignore the call (resulting in no header returned to the client). 

Some thoughts on Content-Location that are probably not really thought through:

* Can it change once set? Can it differ between HEAD/POST/PATCH responses? 
* Can the header be returned directly when the upload is created or can it only be returned once the upload is complete?
* The URI pointed to by Content-Location - is it allowed to return different data during processing? Based on the below section I would say yes.
> "Otherwise, such a Content-Location indicates that this payload is
>       a representation reporting on the requested action's status and
>       that the same report is available (for future access with GET) at
>       the given URI.  For example, a purchase transaction made via a
>       POST request might include a receipt document as the payload of
>       the 200 (OK) response; the Content-Location field-value provides
>       an identifier for retrieving a copy of that same receipt in the
>       future." - https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-3.1.4.2

issues.title: Test Suite for Signature? Space to discuss corner cases?
issues.author: bblfish
issues.body:
Hi, I was thinking that [Signing HTTP Messages](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html) could do with a an extensive test suite. The test suite in the doc is pretty good, but more may be better here...

Such a suite could consist of a set of data in some format each consisting of

* a (request response) pair, max one of them being optional
* a `Signature-Input` description
* the resulting signature base
* a signature, using one of the keys
* whether the signature is valid, and if not why not (eg,

Then one could have all kinds of corner cases such as HTTP requests with URLs such as `example.COM`, and cover many more problematic cases like dates where the signare and all are correct but the semantics are wrong (eg. date does not exist)... That would allow one to collect difficult cases. 

IT would also be good if there were a channel to discuss these cases, such as perhaps the IETF [Zulip Http Signature](https://zulip.ietf.org/#narrow/stream/225-httpbis/topic/Signing.20HTTP.20Messages) stream? If we can publicize it for implementors we may get some interesting feedback that way? 

Here is a little question I have for example. The spec says in §2.2.5 that for a request

```HTTP
CONNECT www.example.com:80 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
```

the  `@request-target` attribute should have as value the content of the string "www.example.com:80" . Is that specific
to `CONNECT`? What should the value be for?

```HTTP
GET http://example.com:80/hello HTTP/1.1
``` 
should it be "http://example.com:80/hello" or "http://example.com/hello" because the 80 is the default port for `http`.
If I am asking myself questions here, I guess many other implementors will too, and they may come to different conclusions.

It could also be useful to have a forum or DB where people can explain problems with intermediaries that comes with experience deploying this.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Henry, this repo is for issues against the spec itself. If you want to have a discussion like this, the best place is on the mailing list. Thanks!

issues.title: message-signatures: requirement for field value concatenation
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
https://www.ietf.org/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-15.html#section-2.1-3

> Unless overridden by additional parameters and rules, HTTP field values MUST be combined into a single value as defined in [Section 5.2](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-5.2) of [[HTTP](https://www.ietf.org/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-15.html#HTTP)] to create the component value. Specifically, HTTP fields sent as multiple fields MUST be combined using a single comma (",") and a single space (" ") between each item.

I don't quite get the reasoning for the second "MUST". Why does it matter? What would break if the client uses a single comma, which is also allowed by HTTP?

IMHO the exact delimiter sequence here does not matter at all, as long as it is allowed per HTTP. Note that HTTP allows *combining* field values, it does not allow splitting them afterwards.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: This isn't combination at the HTTP level by the client or intermediary, this is combination by either the signer or verifier when making the signature base. It's a MUST here because there needs to be only one way to do it at that step. If the lines are already combined then leave them combined.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
hm. ok.

So one confusing thing here is that HTTP 5.2 is already only about combining field values. So the "Specifically" is a distraction.

Also, 5.2 does *not* mandate using COMMA SP. The section doing *that* is 5.3.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Also...:

> Where that approach is not possible and multiple instances of a field need to be sent separately, it is RECOMMENDED that signers and verifiers process any list-based fields by parsing out individual field values and combining them based on the strict algorithm below, to counter possible intermediary behavior.

I think I misread that as a recommendation to parse individual field values into a list, before recombining everything. Maybe "parsing out individual field values" needs to be rephrased.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
You would only parse out individual values if you:

1: Know the overall syntax/grammar of the field
2: Know that it's a list separated by commas
3: Can't send everything as a single field line
4: Know that an intermediary is going to mess with things sent as multiple lines in a way that you don't want

The recommendation is really only for that one corner case, not for every value.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: I agree with that, but the spec really needs to be clearer here.

issues.title: message-signatures: requirement to 'separate' values
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
https://www.ietf.org/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-15.html#section-2.1-5

> 1. Create an ordered list of the field values of each instance of the field in the message, in the order that they occur (or will occur) in the message. If necessary, separate individual values found in a field instance.

This does not work. It's impossible to split multiple values (be it a list-based field or not) without knowledge of the field value's grammar.

For example, what is the canonicalized value for:

~~~
If-None-Match: W/"1,2", "3"
If-None-Match: "bar"
~~~

?

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
The value would be

```
"if-none-match": W/"1,2", "3", "bar"
```

Since it was sent as two instances, you combine the instances with a comma and space.

The language to split the field values was added late based on several conversations about list type fields and how they can be combined, but we can remove this. If someone needs additional armoring they can use the "sf" flag on a list formatted field.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Ok, but what the spec currently says would result in:

~~~
"if-none-match": W/"1, 2", "3", "bar"
~~~

...so that sentence really needs to go.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: No, it would not result in that, because as you point out those are not separate field values that can be separated.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
So what does:

> If necessary, separate individual values found in a field instance.

mean then? When is it "necessary"? How does the code know that for any given field name?

comments.author: bblfish
comments.body:
I think what is meant is that you take a list of the values of a given field (one member of the list for each header line) and then concatenate them by separating them with ", ". 

In scala this is 
```scala
headerValuesList.mkString(", ")
```

or just to make it explicit
```scala
$ scala
Welcome to Scala 3.2.1 (17.0.4.1, Java OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM).
Type in expressions for evaluation. Or try :help.

scala> val headerVal1 = """W/"1,2", "3""""
val headerVal1: String = W/"1,2", "3"

scala> val headerVal2 = """"bar""""
val headerVal2: String = "bar"

scala> val values = List(headerVal1, headerVal2)
val values: List[String] = List(W/"1,2", "3", "bar")

scala> values.size
val res0: Int = 2

scala> values.mkString(", ")
val res1: String = W/"1,2", "3", "bar"
```

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Thanks @bblfish - I get that, but that doesn't address the question I asked...

comments.author: bblfish
comments.body:
Ok, I see the problem is:
> If necessary, separate individual values found in a field instance.

I would not know how to do that, whereas I do know how to seperate the fields in the list.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: We need to be very clear with the terminology. What do you mean by "seperate the fields in the list"? Do you have an example?

comments.author: bblfish
comments.body:
If you are talking to me, I meant what the code above showed: the list is the list of header values (for a given header name). And I meant seperating the values of that list. 

I don't know how to write that up well in the spec though...

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Ok, AFAIU: just drop "If necessary, separate individual values found in a field instance." from the spec.

issues.title: ABNF
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
As discussed during adoption, we want to reconsider our use of ABNF in this specification.

Uncontroversial was removing the recommendation to define new fields using ABNF; that can be easily accommodated and I'll do that in a commit to `main` shortly.

More discussion is needed about completely removing ABNF from the definitions of the types, and other potential changes to the use of ABNF.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Personally -- I believe the best, least confusing thing to do is remove ABNF from this specification. It leads developers down the path of ignoring the algorithms, which is very bad for interoperability and counter to the purpose of this specification. We've seen this in Julian's comments about finding the ABNF valuable as an aid in implementation, and others' comments about converting the ABNF into regex.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I completely disagree.

FWIW, I have implemented structured fields based on the given algorithms (and it passes all tests from the non-official test suite): https://github.com/reschke/structured-fields

So this is implementor (not just spec reader) feedback: the ABNF is extremely useful (for those who speak ABNF) to quickly see what the syntax of a construct in the syntax is. Reading prose or algorithms expressed in prose doesn't work as well.

I'll also note that removing the ABNF was *removed* from the scope of this work; compare https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0013.html with https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0051.html (which only says: "Add clarifications to the use of ABNF in the document (for example, emphasize that they are not normative), subject to WG discussion").

I'm fine with clarifications - and that's exactly what the call for adoption mentions.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: What about keeping the ABNF, but moving all of the ABNF definitions to an appendix all in one place, and mark the whole thing as non-normative? That seems like it would retain the value for implementors who are fluent in ABNF while not adding extra bulk or confusion to the main document.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: That's a compromise, yes. I'd prefer to remove them but that might mitigate the risks.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> What about keeping the ABNF, but moving all of the ABNF definitions to an appendix all in one place, and mark the whole thing as non-normative? That seems like it would retain the value for implementors who are fluent in ABNF while not adding extra bulk or confusion to the main document.

The spec already says that the ABNF is not normative (in that if there's a conflict, the prose algorithm wins).

WRT moving to an appendix - that could be done, but it de-values the ABNF and I still do not see a good reason for that. It would be really helpful to have an example where readers of the original spec got confused by the presence of the ABNF.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
As an anecdote, I've seen people that want to implement SF pick up the spec, more or less skip sections 1 and 2 and going to section where the types are defined (3 and 3.x). They see the ABNF and start building up a mental model of what things to do (governed by if they are a producer or consumer) and might not be aware that section 4 is where they should be investing their efforts. That risks an incorrect model or annoying the reader.

Moving the ABNF later in the document (such as the appendix), and more actvely promoting the relevant serilizing/parsing sections as each type is introduced might do better to promote the intention that the document had.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I hear you.

But then, it is impossible to optimize specs for people who are not reading the important parts.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: So why does the ABNF deserve to be in section 3? Section 3 is about the abstract types but then we immediately jump to a concrete on-wire protocol expression. That seems odd, especially if we're considering other representations of SF types like binary structured fields.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
If Section 3 is just about abstract types, why does it contain statements like "Each member is separated by a comma and optional whitespace."?

(If we want to ship quickly, I would highly recommend to avoid changes that are controversial)

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: @reschke I'm not hearing a ton of other opinions for keeping the ABNF where it is. While I get that removing it entirely would be a problem, I don't see how having a dedicated section for the ABNF mappings hurts the implementers that want to reference that. Could you live with the ABNF being in its own section/appendix as a compromise between the positions here?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I've been in the rough before...

No matter what we do, we have to double-check the prose for potential inconsistencies with the ABNF, as mentioned in another ticket.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @tfpauly are we OK to merge?

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: Left a comment on that PR, but yes I think so in general.

issues.title: sfbis: ensure prose introductions are in sync with ABNF and parsing algorithms
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
Example:

> [3.1.](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis-latest.html#rfc.section.3.1) [Lists](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis-latest.html#list)
>
> Lists are arrays of zero or more members, each of which can be an Item ([Section 3.3](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis-latest.html#item)) or an Inner List ([Section 3.1.1](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis-latest.html#inner-list)), both of which can be Parameterized ([Section 3.1.2](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis-latest.html#param)).
>
> The ABNF for Lists in HTTP fields is:
>
> sf-list       = list-member *( OWS "," OWS list-member )
> list-member   = sf-item / inner-list
>
> Each member is separated by a comma and optional whitespace. (...)

The last sentence is in conflict with both the ABNF and the parsing algorithm - it needs to say "Each member is separated by _optional whitespace,_ a comma and optional whitespace"

(there may be more cases like this)

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
Strongly disagree. The prose is not in conflict (it doesn't say anything about ordering or cardinality). 

Right now the prose is clearly an overview and not specific. If we add that level of precision to the prose, it will lead to ambiguities that will cause issues.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Wait - I think this is clearly a bug.

If you have prose describing what a datastructure is, *either* just describe the structure, or include the syntax. If you include the syntax, it needs to reflect reality.

This is not editorial - reopening.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
In the original drafting, we qualified these statements with "in the textual representation..." or similar.

I think the options are:

a. Reintroduce that framing, to make it clear we're not talking about the abstract data model, just one expression of it
b. Remove anything about the serialisation-specific syntax and just stick to the abstract data model.

Thoughts?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
The first option sounds good to me.

We may also have to say somewhere that right now, there's just that one representation, but that this might change in the future.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Waiting for #2338...

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
[62a67d0](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/commit/62a67d0a4471e322f1b552bb980d2e540c9504c1) attempted to do that. 

We might also do one or both of:

1. Introducing subsections in each of the abstract data model to separate those summaries of the textual form from the abstract model
2. Add more summaries of the textual forms (but the ones that are missing are pretty obvious)

On balance, I think neither of these is necessary, and they'd add noise to the document without corresponding value. 

Opinions?

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Closing, but please give more feedback if necessary.

issues.title: explore solution space for non-ASCII characters in Strings
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
RFC 8941 does not support non-ASCII characters in sf-string (but recommends to use sf-binary when non-ASCII characters are needed).

The solution space is roughly:

1. No support at all
2. No support, but addings hints about workarounds, such as
2.1 Using sf-binary (approach in RFC 8941)
2.2 Using RFC8187 parameter encoding (works only for parameters at it uses the "*" marker)
2.3 Using an escaping mechanism inside sf-string (with out-of-band info to indicate that it is in use) - currently proposed for the "Problem" header field (see https://github.com/ietf-wg-httpapi/rfc7807bis/commit/ebf9465504713876e6cd507629511313bdbce39c)
3. Direct support
3.1 By extending sf-string to allow native UTF-8
3.2 By extending sf-string to support a new escaping mechanism (for instance, by introducing new backslash escapes)
3.3 By adding a new type ("sf-ustring") that somehow supports non-ASCII codepoints (NOTE: this used to say "characters")

Note that the question whether non-ASCII octets appear in the field value (obs-text) is somehat orthogonal, expect if 3.1 would be chosen.

comments.author: bsdphk
comments.body:
Your point 1 is disingenious and misleading: As long as we allow two distinct glyphs in sf-string, people can transfer any bit-sequence they want to with it and sf-binary allows them to transfer any byte sequence.  Please remove it.

Anything which changes the definition of `sf-string` is a hard no from me, because:

A) It will dilute retrofit
B) It will enable emojis in `sf-string` by default, unless spec-writers explicitly forbid them.

There goes your 3.1 and 3.2.

Anything which requires general-purpose SF serializers or parsers to know anything about time-variant registries of human politics or other foibles, for instance MIME, UniCode, Codepages, TimeZones, LeapSeconds etc. are a hard no from me, as a matter of principle.

That takes 3.3 out, because without access to a registry, there is no way to tell what might or might not be a "character".

For all I care, people can use any of your 2.1, 2.2 or 2.3, or anything else they come up with.

If anything need to be said about that, it should obviously be said in RFC8187(bis) since it already occupies precisely that topic on the standards track.

In particular I do not want 2.3, not even as an appendix, because of the risk that it "leaks" and `%xx` unintentionally is interpreted in places where that is not explicitly allowed (See also: The "../" hole, Log4J, etc.)

So with all due respect Julian:  Stay in your lane, this stuff belongs in your own RFC, not in SF

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> Your point 1 is disingenious and misleading: As long as we allow two distinct glyphs in sf-string, people can transfer any bit-sequence they want to with it and sf-binary allows them to transfer any byte sequence. Please remove it.

Not helpful. If we follow that line of argument to the end, we just need sequences of "0" and "1", and the whole idea of "structured header fields" is useless.

> Anything which changes the definition of sf-string is a hard no from me, because:
>
> A) It will dilute retrofit

That's an interesting point.

> B) It will enable emojis in sf-string by default, unless spec-writers explicitly forbid them.

I don't see why that is a problem in a string datatype.

> There goes your 3.1 and 3.2.
>
> Anything which requires general-purpose SF serializers or parsers to know anything about time-variant registries of human politics or other foibles, for instance MIME, UniCode, Codepages, TimeZones, LeapSeconds etc. are a hard no from me, as a matter of principle.

Strawman. To understand UTF-8, you need RFC 3629. That's it.

> That takes 3.3 out, because without access to a registry, there is no way to tell what might or might not be a "character".

I'll rename it to "codepoint" if that makes a difference to you.

> For all I care, people can use any of your 2.1, 2.2 or 2.3, or anything else they come up with.

All of these need out-of-band signals, and will not be supported by tooling. If you believe that's unimportant, then why add sf-date?

> If anything need to be said about that, it should obviously be said in RFC8187(bis) since it already occupies precisely that topic on the standards track.

RFC 8187 applies to parameter syntax; thus it wouln't help with bare strings.

> In particular I do not want 2.3, not even as an appendix, because of the risk that it "leaks" and %xx unintentionally is interpreted in places where that is not explicitly allowed (See also: The "../" hole, Log4J, etc.)

I happen to agree that an approach is problematic if there's no in-band signal that shows that is in use. It causes confusion about when to unescape and when not to.

> So with all due respect Julian: Stay in your lane, this stuff belongs in your own RFC, not in SF#

I continue to disagree with that.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: As far as I can see this is out of the scope we agreed to when we started this work, and would represent a potentially signficant delay to it. I'm going to wait for @tfpauly to say whether we should be working on it before I spend any time responding.

comments.author: awwright
comments.body:
@reschke Is this related to [RFC 8187](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8187) at all? I like the formatting described there. (Edit: Yes it is, sorry I missed the link above. I suppose my question is: is this relevant to 3. Direct Support; could this be implemented in a new type, perhaps indicated with a single-quote rather than a double-quote?)

This seems like a significant question. I've had some trouble figuring out how to implement the encoding/decoding step in Problem, and I don't see why such an extra step should be necessary.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: @awwright - RFC 8187 is one possible approach here; but it would only work for strings that appear as parameter values /such for "Problem" it would be good enough). To make it "automatic" when using an SF parser, the spec though would have to change to require that.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body:
@reschke, all:

Given the scope of the revision that the group agreed upon when embarking on 8941bis, I don't think this kind of change fits within "minor technical issues and editorial fixes":

> - Add the Date type, currently in draft-ietf-httpbis-retrofit
> - Make the "Defining New Structured Fields” section align with the style guide (https://httpwg.org/admin/editors/style-guide#structured-fields), to not recommend the use of ABNF in new header definitions
> - Add clarifications to the use of ABNF in the document (for example, emphasize that they are not normative), subject to WG discussion
> - Address minor technical issues and editorial fixes

Expanding the scope would require a new consensus call to see what the WG thinks about the scope of this kind of change. We can do that if necessary, but I am concerned that this level of change is not in the limited spirit of the revision.

@reschke at this point I'd prefer to see a document/proposal with motivating use cases written up, separate from 8941bis.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
The use cases are on the table:

- The HTTPAPI problem format document invents yet another way to embed non-ASCII
- Retrofit essentially proposes parser switches
- We need to decide how the sfbis document affects existing documents that refer to the older revision

I don't believe that writing another document that captures these discussions is productive; what we need to do is address these issues.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body:
(Speaking as chair)

While I acknowledge that draft-ietf-httpapi-rfc7807bis does define a way to encode UTF-8 within ASCII strings that is not sf-binary, I don't see that as a reason to expand the scope of the sf-bis effort that the WG agreed to initially.

My impression is that the sf-bis document doesn't affect existing documents that refer to the original RFC at all in the current state of things, since sf-string's definition wouldn't change. The only semantic change the WG agreed to was the addition of sf-date, not modifying existing types or adding new types.

The issue of how to handle non-ASCII field values, as far as I can tell, is made no better nor worse by sf-bis; it is maintaining the definition of sf-string and sf-binary, which are tools that field definitions can choose to use. Changing the definition of those types or adding a new type is a larger, unrelated change that doesn't fit in the defined scope.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I would love to see a discussion about whether it makes sense to support arbitrary strings in fields (as opposed to just ASCII strings).  However, I agree with @tfpauly that this is not appropriate to include in the scope of the current change.

It's true that the changes we're considering here suggest that further changes might be possible or even appropriate.  But the scope of a change was deliberately small and it should remain so.  Then we'll have a chance of shipping an incremental improvement that is meaningful in a reasonable period.

Doing arbitrary strings won't be easy.  I can see that there are pressures to do, so I don't object to starting that work.  In parallel.  If that work resolves quickly, we can discuss how that might be integrated into the whole.  But that discussion isn't so mature.

issues.title: Client-Cert HTTP Header: call out resumption risks in security considerations
issues.author: enygren
issues.body:
It would also be good to add some notes to Security Considerations on the risks associated with resumption, ie for implementations that do try and use client cert information following a resumed session.  While there's mention here in 3.3. TLS Session Resumption, the risks are very non-obvious and subtle.  Especially if there's not an RFC that describes how to convey client cert information across session resumption safely (covering TLS 1.2 and 1.3) it  seems like much stronger ("should not" / "must not") guidance may be applicable.  Some risks might include:

* Anyone with access to an STEK can also create a session claiming to be authenticated by any client cert and chain they want.  This is unavoidable, but may not be an obvious risks.
* Client cert and trust chain information must be fully protected and bound cryptographically into the session ticket.  Are there subtle exposures in TLS 1.2 as well here? 
* ...  this area may be worth further analysis/guidance from TLS experts

comments.author: enygren
comments.body: See #1992 for discussion leading to the current text.

comments.author: bc-pi
comments.body: I am nowhere near competent enough in TLS or implementations thereof to write such security considerations so am going to need a lot of help. By which I mean a PR or proposed text.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
These seem to be general TLS concerns, and not specific to this header, no?

> Client cert and trust chain information must be fully protected and bound cryptographically into the session ticket. Are there subtle exposures in TLS 1.2 as well here?

That's not quite right. That is a valid implementation strategy, but there are others, particularly if you want to avoid ballooning the ticket size. See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1992#issuecomment-1061898656

comments.author: bc-pi
comments.body: Thinking about this a bit more and, to David's point, aren't these concerns applicable to resumption w/ client certs in TLS in general?  Any discussion in this draft should probably be couched in that context. Or refer to discussion elsewhere.

comments.author: b---c
comments.body: Draft is in the RFC Editor queue https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-client-cert-field/ so past the window for changes.

issues.title: Client-Cert HTTP Header: guidance for layered usage
issues.author: enygren
issues.body:
A common usage pattern is likely to be:

1) Client authenticates to a CDN which validates the client cert and passes along this information in a header
2) CDN authenticates to an origin TLS-terminating load balancer or ingress gateway which passes along this information in a header to the app server

In this case, the app server probably cares about (1) but may also need to validate (2) as well.  Or alternatively, only pass along (1) when (2) is validated.

Trying to add semantics here into the headers seems like way more complexity than we want to take on,
so allowing the use of alternate pre-arranged header names may make sense.

Taking an approach from RFC 9213 (Targeted HTTP Cache Control) might be an option, such as having
a short section that describes this scenario and says  "implementations MAY prefix with an identifier 
by prior arrangement".

comments.author: bc-pi
comments.body:
**I somehow missed this - apologies for coming to it months later...**

With the goal of keeping this draft simple and reflecting current practice, such layered cases are out of scope of this document. There's text in the last paragraph of the intro that attempts to capture that https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-client-cert-field-04.html#section-1-4 FWIW 

> While there may be additional proxies or hops between the TTRP and the origin server (potentially even with mutually-authenticated TLS connections between them), the scope of the Client-Cert header field is intentionally limited to exposing to the origin server the certificate that was presented by the originating client in its connection to the TTRP.

Nothing in the document would prohibit using alternate prearranged header names in such a situation. But If you'd like to propose or PR some non-normative text for an appendix that describes the scenario with general guidance (the alternate header(s) would be used for (2)), that seems like it'd be okay/appropriate for the doc.

comments.body: Draft is in the RFC Editor queue https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-client-cert-field/ so past the window for changes.

issues.title: Signature: error in 4.3 examples
issues.author: bblfish
issues.body:
The first example signature from [§4.3 of message-signatures-15](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-15#section-4-3) fails signature verification. 

```rfc
POST /foo?param=Value&Pet=dog HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Date: Tue, 20 Apr 2021 02:07:55 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Digest: sha-512=:WZDPaVn/7XgHaAy8pmojAkGWoRx2UFChF41A2svX+T\
  aPm+AbwAgBWnrIiYllu7BNNyealdVLvRwEmTHWXvJwew==:
Content-Length: 18
Signature-Input: sig1=("@method" "@authority" "@path" \
  "content-digest" "content-length" "content-type")\
  ;created=1618884475;keyid="test-key-rsa-pss"
Signature:  sig1=:LAH8BjcfcOcLojiuOBFWn0P5keD3xAOuJRGziCLuD8r5MW9S0\
  RoXXLzLSRfGY/3SF8kVIkHjE13SEFdTo4Af/fJ/Pu9wheqoLVdwXyY/UkBIS1M8Br\
  c8IODsn5DFIrG0IrburbLi0uCc+E2ZIIb6HbUJ+o+jP58JelMTe0QE3IpWINTEzpx\
  jqDf5/Df+InHCAkQCTuKsamjWXUpyOT1Wkxi7YPVNOjW4MfNuTZ9HdbD2Tr65+BXe\
  TG9ZS/9SWuXAc+BZ8WyPz0QRz//ec3uWXd7bYYODSjRAxHqX+S1ag3LZElYyUKaAI\
  jZ8MGOt4gXEwCSLDv/zqxZeWLj/PDkn6w==:

{"hello": "world"}
```

By changing the validity date from 1618884475 to 1618884473 the validation succeeds.  I guessed that date as it is the one used in all the other signatures. So I guess that is a typo. (It would have been good to have a different created date, just to make testing less mechanical, but then the signature needs to be changed).

There is then perhaps a logical mistake in the next example. 
The story goes that the proxy receiving the above request alters the message and signs it before sending it on. The original signature is kept and added as part of the signature. The proxy alters the `Host` header and adds a `Forwarded` header along with a new Signature.  But by changing the `Host` the proxy makes it impossible for the recipient to verify the initial signature, since that includes a `@authority` component which was changed. 

```
POST /foo?param=Value&Pet=dog HTTP/1.1
Host: origin.host.internal.example
Date: Tue, 20 Apr 2021 02:07:56 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Digest: sha-512=:WZDPaVn/7XgHaAy8pmojAkGWoRx2UFChF41A2svX+T\
  aPm+AbwAgBWnrIiYllu7BNNyealdVLvRwEmTHWXvJwew==:
Content-Length: 18
Forwarded: for=192.0.2.123
Signature-Input: sig1=("@method" "@authority" "@path" \
    "content-digest" "content-length" "content-type")\
    ;created=1618884475;keyid="test-key-rsa-pss", \
  proxy_sig=("signature";key="sig1" "forwarded")\
    ;created=1618884480;expires=1618884540;keyid="test-key-rsa"\
    ;alg="rsa-v1_5-sha256"
Signature:  sig1=:LAH8BjcfcOcLojiuOBFWn0P5keD3xAOuJRGziCLuD8r5MW9S0\
    RoXXLzLSRfGY/3SF8kVIkHjE13SEFdTo4Af/fJ/Pu9wheqoLVdwXyY/UkBIS1M8\
    Brc8IODsn5DFIrG0IrburbLi0uCc+E2ZIIb6HbUJ+o+jP58JelMTe0QE3IpWINT\
    EzpxjqDf5/Df+InHCAkQCTuKsamjWXUpyOT1Wkxi7YPVNOjW4MfNuTZ9HdbD2Tr\
    65+BXeTG9ZS/9SWuXAc+BZ8WyPz0QRz//ec3uWXd7bYYODSjRAxHqX+S1ag3LZE\
    lYyUKaAIjZ8MGOt4gXEwCSLDv/zqxZeWLj/PDkn6w==:, \
  proxy_sig=:G1WLTL4/9PGSKEQbSAMypZNk+I2dpLJ6qvl2JISahlP31OO/QEUd8/\
    HdO2O7vYLi5k3JIiAK3UPK4U+kvJZyIUidsiXlzRI+Y2se3SGo0D8dLfhG95bKr\
    6ukYXl60QHpsGRTfSiwdtvYKXGpKNrMlISJYd+oGrGRyI9gbCy0aFhc6I/okIML\
    eK4g9PgzpC3YTwhUQ98KIBNLWHgREfBgJxjPbxFlsgJ9ykPviLj8GKJ81HwsK3X\
    M9P7WaS7fMGOt8h1kSqgkZQB9YqiIo+WhHvJa7iPy8QrYFKzx9BBEY6AwfStZAs\
    XXz3LobZseyxsYcLJLs8rY0wVA9NPsxKrHGA==:

{"hello": "world"}
```

So the spec has to either remove the `@authority` component from the client request, or change the text at the end of the section which says

> The proxy's signature and the client's original signature can be verified independently for the same message, based on the needs of the application.

Note:   the proxy's signature does verify for me with the timestamp of the client as it appears in the spec.

comments.body:
Verification of claim above:

The test on line 173 of [VerifySignatureTests.scala](https://github.com/bblfish/httpSig/blob/96b8cca8dff46d57a66031f27338b09991057f77/ietfSigTests/shared/src/main/scala/run/cosy/http/auth/VerifySignatureTests.scala#L173) had to be disabled for my tests to pass on the JVM  (JS tests coming soon).

The whole point of the story is that the proxy verifies the first signature, and the service behind the proxy verifies the proxy's signature. If we can make that story more clear, I'd be glad to!

comments.author: bblfish
comments.body:
> The whole point of the story is that the proxy verifies the first signature, and the service behind the proxy verifies the proxy's signature. If we can make that story more clear, I'd be glad to!

It is indeed an option to have the final recipient rely on the signature of the proxy as a verification of the originally signed message.  

But the text currently says "The proxy's signature and the client's original signature can be verified independently for the same message, based on the needs of the application." 

The "independently" reads to me as if the application (that is the server receiving the signature) should be able to verify both signatures. If you want the full set of interior names across a chain of multiple CNAME records I don't believe you can retrieve that with `getaddrinfo`.

I think AI_CANONNAME is important historical context here.  You can't

issues.title: draft-ietf-httpbis-alias-proxy-status: Omit trailing dots from FQDNs
issues.author: edmondsfastly
issues.body:
The draft currently has this example:

```
Proxy-Status: proxy.example.net; next-hop=2001:db8::1
    next-hop-aliases="tracker.example.com.,service1.example-cdn.com."
```

I'd suggest always omitting trailing dots since it's clear that these names will be FQDNs, i.e.:

```
Proxy-Status: proxy.example.net; next-hop=2001:db8::1
    next-hop-aliases="tracker.example.com,service1.example-cdn.com"
```

issues.title: draft-ietf-httpbis-alias-proxy-status: Use of "alias" differs from DNS term "alias"
issues.author: edmondsfastly
issues.body:
This draft (-00) is using the term "alias" in a slightly different way than used in DNS:

> The next-hop-aliases parameter's value is a String that contains one or more DNS names in a comma-separated list. The items in the list include **all names received in CNAME records** [DNS] during the course of resolving the next hop's hostname using DNS. […] The aliases SHOULD appear in the order in which they were received in DNS; that is, **if a name has a CNAME record with a first alias, which has a CNAME record for a second alias, the aliases should appear in that order.**

A CNAME record has two names, the owner name on the left-hand side or "alias", and the target name on the right-hand side or "canonical name".

RFC 8499 (DNS Terminology):

```
   Alias:  The owner of a CNAME resource record, or a subdomain of the
      owner of a DNAME resource record (DNAME records are defined in
      [RFC6672]).  See also "canonical name".

   Canonical name:  A CNAME resource record "identifies its owner name
      as an alias, and specifies the corresponding canonical name in the
      RDATA section of the RR."  (Quoted from [RFC1034], Section 3.6.2)
      This usage of the word "canonical" is related to the mathematical
      concept of "canonical form".

Hoffman, et al.           Best Current Practice                 [Page 9]
RFC 8499                     DNS Terminology                January 2019

   CNAME:  "It has been traditional to refer to the [owner] of a CNAME
      record as 'a CNAME'.  This is unfortunate, as 'CNAME' is an
      abbreviation of 'canonical name', and the [owner] of a CNAME
      record is most certainly not a canonical name."  (Quoted from
      [RFC2181], Section 10.1.1.  The quoted text has been changed from
      "label" to "owner".)
```

In other words, to use the example in the draft:
```
Proxy-Status: proxy.example.net; next-hop=2001:db8::1;
    next-hop-aliases="tracker.example.com.,service1.example-cdn.com."
```

Which might correspond to a DNS response that looked something like:
```
proxy.example.net.          CNAME   tracker.example.com.
tracker.example.com.        CNAME   service1.example-cdn.com.
service1.example-cdn.com.   AAAA    2001:db8::1
```

`proxy.example.net` and `tracker.example.com` are DNS **aliases** (because there are CNAME records with those owner names) whereas `service1.example-cdn.com` is a DNS "canonical name" without an alias. But `service1.example-cdn.com` is included in the `next-hop-aliases` example in this draft.

This might be confusing for the DNS name at the end of the CNAME chain (which is not an alias from a DNS perspective), so I might suggest changing:

> Description: A string containing one or more DNS alises used to establish a proxied connection to the next hop.

to something like:

> Description: A string containing one or more DNS aliases or canonical names used to establish a proxied connection to the next hop.

issues.title: signatures: clarify dependency on structured fields
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
IMHO we need to be clear what the requirements of SF support are. The way the spec currently is written (referencing RFC 8941) means that SF-shaped field values using the new sf-date format are not supported.

I don't think this is what we want, so unless we want to wait for sfbis to be ready, we'll need to add some consideration of how compat with SF extensions/revisions is supposed to work.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: The intent of the current text is not to limit the use of the `sf` flag to only the currently defined formats. New formats are supported if the signer and verifier support the formats. The agreement of what format to use for a particular field is out of scope for this specification, and needs to be agreed upon by the signer and verifier outside of the signature process. This is true for all the current types and will remain true for any additional types defined in the future.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
On a high level, this sounds right.

As an implementer of a signature library, calling an SF library, what is your expectation what it'll do with sf-date once the spec is published?

What if the sender want to sign an integer param in a dictionary, but the field instance contains another param using sf-date?

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: I would expect a library of that nature to publish its mapping between field names and SF types, and ideally allow that mapping to be edited by the caller of the library. Otherwise, how would a user of the library be able to provide a type mapping for a custom field that the library doesn't know about, let alone a new sf-type?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Understood. Different layers of libs.

What I meant is a *generic* SF library, that just parses/serializes SF fields.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Then you need to know what you're parsing it in to. SF fields aren't entirely discoverable from the syntax alone, you need to know the type explicitly. I ran into this when implementing my own signature libraries. So the signature library needs to have that mapping, and if the underlying SF library doesn't support some new type, then you can't map to it. Once the dependencies are updated, you can provide that feature up the chain. It all seems pretty standard and simple to me, honestly.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> SF fields aren't entirely discoverable from the syntax alone, you need to know the type explicitly.

How so?

I still don't see the path to interop for any update of the structured field syntax, unless this spec at least provides some hints.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
You need to know the top-level type (Dictionary, List, or Item) for each field. The consequence of that (AIUI) is that a recipient wishing to validate a signature that uses `sf` will need to understand the top-level type of each `sf`'d field in the signature.

It'll also need to support the permissable types in those fields -- e.g., if a field allows Date, the recipient needs to be able to handle that.

As a result, it won't be possible to reliably verify a signature if your processor doesn't have knowledge of the top-level type, or if it doesn't have support for an extension type in use in one of those fields. However, there is a *chance* of verifying it still, if the SF-produced form is sent on the wire and not changed at all in transit, and the processor just ignores `sf` processing (and in some ways, this is worse than reliably failing).

I think this all can be reasoned out by reading the specs appropriately. Documenting it as a tripping hazard would help users avoid interoperability issues, but this specification is already long and dense, and if we also make it a user guide, it will risk becoming unusable.

So, speaking personally -- if the above summary is correct, I could see adding a sentence or two to section 2.1.1 at the most; I could also see leaving it to a separate profile/user guide.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
[ chair hat on ]

This issue is the last thing holding the Signature spec going to IETF LC. @jricher @reschke please respond to above, particularly:

1. whether such text is necessary
2. whether such text will address the issue
3. when such text, if necesary, would need to be incorporated (before/after LC).

Thanks,

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I believe it would be good to have such text; and that it should be in the spec, not in a guide that is unlikely to materialize.

It should be incorporated before LC (I hope you mean a new WGLC here...?). Given the amount of changes, we really should spend some time reviewing all that changed, and to verify that the open issues have been addressed properly.

comments.author: mnot
reschke
comments.body:
> @reschke can you propose something?

I would prefer to see your proposal :-).

> I don't see any reason to rerun WGLC, based upon the current PRs; there are some changes (especially in one or two), but they're based on AD review and can be discussed during IETF LC.

The RFC diff since the last WG version has 143 change blocks:

https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/sig-diffs.html

We also currently have 17 open issues/PRs:

https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/labels/signatures

IMHO we need to get these closed (can be rejecting or fixing), and also have a look at those that we raised since -13 and closed in the meantime. I don't think we do the community a service by sending this to IETF LC right now.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
@reschke you are grossly misrepresenting the state of the document. For one, the last WG version, and the one that went to the AD, is -15, not 13, so your diff above is misleading at best. The changes since then have largely not been substantive in nature, and all have been made publicly with the view and input of the WG.

The open issues are nearly all addressed by open PRs, which I am waiting for AD feedback before merging (I'm not sure if the AD wants to review the PR text or the merged draft that results). What remains is this issue, as @mnot pointed out above.

To answer @mnot 's question about how to resolve this: I think pointing out as a potential tripping hazard is not necessary but would not be harmful. The precondition to know the type is already in the text as the first sentence about the `sf` flag in section 2.1.1:

> If the value of an HTTP field is **known by the application to be a structured field** ([[STRUCTURED-FIELDS](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-15.html#STRUCTURED-FIELDS)]), and **the expected type of the structured field is known**

Additionally, the lack of knowledge of the type of the field is already called out explicitly as a required error condition in section 2.5:

> implementation MUST produce an error [... if:... ]The component identifier indicates that a structured field serialization is used (via the sf parameter), but the field in question is known to not be a structured field **or the type of structured field is not known** to the implementation.

I would propose we simply add a note to 2.1.1 of the form:

> If the application does not know the type of the field, use of this flag will produce an error.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> The open issues are nearly all addressed by open PRs, which I am waiting for AD feedback before merging (I'm not sure if the AD wants to review the PR text or the merged draft that results). What remains is this issue, as @mnot pointed out above.

Well, it's hard to say what remains to be done until an issue is actually closed. We're all volunteers here, so it's good to make things as easy as possible to reviewers. 

So, trying to rephrase: let's get all open issues closed (one way or the other), and let the people who raised the issues give an opportunity to provide feedback before sending this back to the IESG.

(I, for once, am not convinced that I agree with the proposed solutions, but due to the type of diffs (long lines) it's a bit tricky to understand what actually changed)

2.1.1 works for the sending side; but what is a recipient supposed to do when the sf flag is present and the field value does not parse due to sender and receiver disagreeing about the SF version?

Also, that only affects the *toplevel* type of the structured field. It does not address the case where an extension parameter is added is an sf-date (or any future new type).

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: @reschke until you propose text, it will be hard to say what kind of text you think would close this issue.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> I don't think we do the community a service by sending this to IETF LC right now.

Except for this issue and two others recently raised by you (which will be considered as IETF LC issues), all of the issues and PRs you mention were generated by the AD review before IETF LC; this is a normal part of the process that does not require going back to WGLC unless the AD asks for WG review, which [has not happened](https://www.w3.org/mid/AS1PR07MB861690BC64D82F95C29D935A98D19@AS1PR07MB8616.eurprd07.prod.outlook.com).

@jricher made a reasonable proposal. If you disagree with it, make your own.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
If the proposal was:

> If the application does not know the type of the field, use of this flag will produce an error.

Then this isn't sufficient as it only applies to the toplevel type (see https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2362#issuecomment-1412160551).

@mnot - I believe you are in the best position to make a proposal; but that said; I can *try* something later today.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
So, we have in 2.1.1:

> If this parameter is included with a component identifier, the HTTP field value MUST be serialized using the rules specified in [Section 4](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941#section-4) of [[STRUCTURED-FIELDS](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html#STRUCTURED-FIELDS)] applicable to the type of the HTTP field.

This implies that the "sf" parameter can only be used on fields that conform to RFC 8941, no extensions allowed.

I would suggest clarifying that, at the end of 2.1.1, with:

"Note that the normative requirement to use the SF serialization algorithm precludes any use of future extensions of the structured field syntax. Support for future versions of SF will require an update to this specification."

I *believe* this matches what @mnot suggested.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
Except that *your proposed text is incorrect*. The implication you are drawing is not true, nor what others have taken from that text. The use of the `sf` parameter does not preclude extensions to RFC 8941, as has been discussed at length here and on the mailing list. Extensions to sf types would not require changes to the signatures spec.

I propose closing this issue without change to the signatures spec.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Sorry. Mark asked me to propose text, and that's what I did.

The text has a normative requirement to use an RFC8941 serializer, so the proposed text is correct. That we disagree here is *proof* that a clarification is needed.

If you feel that that p.o.v. is too restrictive, we'll have to somehow relax the requirement on the serializer (for instance, by stating that the serializer needs to implement 8941 or a successor RFC  - that is an RFC that obsoletes 8941).

> Extensions to sf types would not require changes to the signatures spec.

FWIW, I agree that this would be good. But it is not what the spec says.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
No, we reference the current document and if that document is updated or obsoleted by something else after publication then you as an implementer go and follow that. That's how updating RFC's already work. All the specs and systems that implemented RFC2616 didn't suddenly break and become invalid when 7230 or later 9110 came out. Here, It's up to the updaters of 8941 to make sure there's A serialization section. 

Your view of specification dependency is not at all in line with reality.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I see where you're coming from; I'd appreciate if you would do the effort to understand where I'm coming from.

The difference here is that any spec that extends 8941 with new types by definition is *not* backwards compatible. This is because 8941 has no extension points, has drastic error handling and thus requires a wholesale spec update for new things. This is very different from most other RFCs that we're using here.

If there is agreement about what we want, why don't we just say it?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: To illustrate further: RFC8941-vs-8941bis is like XML1.0-vs-1.1 or HTTP1.1-vs-2.0, not like RFC2616-vs-RFC9112.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> The difference here is that any spec that extends 8941 with new types by definition is not backwards compatible. This is because 8941 has no extension points, has drastic error handling and thus requires a wholesale spec update for new things. This is very different from most other RFCs that we're using here.

That's a very specific definition of 'not backwards compatible' and one that I suspect many would be surprised by. Just because there are no explicitly nominated extension points doesn't mean you can't evolve the specification in a backwards-compatible fashion; the key requirement is that valid inputs per the 'old' version are also valid inputs per the 'new' revision. That is the case for sf-bis.

It is true that an *invalid* input for RFC 8941 will now become valid; specifically, a type value beginning with '@' used to generate an error, and now will not (provided that the following characters are appropriate).

The reasonable question to ask at this point is whether it's realistic / probable that an application will be depending upon that error being thrown to operate. Can you suggest when that might be the case? Because I find it doubtful in the extreme that this will cause real-world problems.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I agree that this wouldn't cause real-world problems. I just also wish that our specs actually say what we think should happen, instead of requiring people to figure out.

So in this case, I think we can solve this by saying "RFC 8941 or a revision obsoleting it".

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Since @reschke acknowledges that this doesnt affect interoperability and this is merely a "wish", @jricher why don't you go ahead and incorporate your proposal so we can ship this spec?
