issues.title: AD review: advice for when a client asks for digest and it doesn't get one
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Murray asked:

>    General:

>    * I may be showing some ignorance of this space here, or I may have missed something, but I'll ask anyway: Is there any advice to be given for a situation where a client requests digest(s) but the server provides none, especially when that client has reason to expect that this specific server implements this specification?  i.e., "Hmm, I asked for the digest(s), and they ought to be there but aren't, that's weird..."

on the email thread, I responded with 

> We fall into the general realm of HTTP feature negotiation here, which has some well-trodden problems. If the client and server have some prior knowledge or OOB channel that lets them build an exception for digest, they can define their own rules for how to handle its absence - I don't want to go too far down the path of trying to describe that. I think what is useful is to highlight, with an editorial change, the very real possibility that an endpoint sends "want-*-digest" and the peer ignores it and doesn't provide any "*-digest" at all. Then all we should say is that dealing with this situation is an implementation decision.

To which Murray confirmed it would be a reasonable resolution.

Lets get this fixed as discussed

issues.title: 6.5 Usage with Encryption - it isn’t clear what layer of encryption is assumed (representation, content)
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
James Manger wrote:

> In “6.5 Usage with Encryption” it isn’t clear what layer of encryption is assumed (representation, content). I guess it is assuming a Content-Encoding that encrypts, such as “Content-Encoding: aes128gcm” from RFC 8188. And the security consideration is pointing out that if the encryption is performed multiple times to respond to multiple HTTP requests then the ciphertext (& hence Content-Digest & Repr-Digest) is likely to change each time, as each encryption (of the same plaintext) is likely to use a different nonce and/or key.
> 
>  This issue could occur without encryption. For instance, compression algorithms often have different “levels” (eg 1=fast, 9=best). So the representation could change if the level changed between requests. Maybe that will be rare enough to ignore?
> 
> I thought “6.5 Usage with Encryption” might be warning against including a digest of the plaintext if encryption was applied as, say, a transfer-encoding (not sure if there are encrypting transfer-encodings). That would be insecure.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: yeah I think  RFC 8188 was the target of the section here. @ioggstream can you recall? What can we add to make this section a bit more clear?

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body: That's correct. And the suggestion wrt different compression levels is correct to! This is worth mentioning and maybe highlight that it applies to a specific kind of content codings.

From James Manger:

This is particularly important as checksums were conveyed in decimal and hex in Digest, but will now be base64-encoded in Content-Digest & Repr-Digest. Do you base64-encode the decimal digits from, say, cksum; or base64-encode the 32-bits (most significant byte first?) they represent?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Yeah I think this identifies some ambiguities. But addressing those with examples alone doesn't seem right. If people to run a hash algorithm and calculate an output, but disagree on using the underlying bytes or the presentation format of that output *before* it is converted into a Byte Sequence, then that seems like a potential interop problem.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I think the simplest thing to do here is to state clearly that the value sent on the wire is the base-64 encoding of the actual bytes produced by an algorithm (and pick MSB or LSB).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Another option here is to add some test vectors to the document. That way we could be exhaustive for all algorithms that populate the IANA table, without having to generate lots of examples.

issues.title: Newlines at the end of JSON bodies
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
From James Manger:

> No newlines are included at the end of the JSON bodies, though that is never mentioned. “Content-Length: 18” on the first {"hello": "world"} example could indicate that. Not including newlines is okay for 1-line JSON values (even though they have extraneous spaces so they aren’t “compact” JSON). No final newline on the multi-line JSON examples is a bit nasty.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
A few responses:

- The string `{"hello": "world"}` is 18 characters long, hence the associated `Content-Length: 18`.
- Single line examples using spaces are consistent with the [Signatures draft ](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html)
- Multi line examples are not JSON files but more like JSON API responses. Omitting a trailing newline seems just fine to me.

At this stage in the document standardisation, changing the example message content is disruptive since we'd have to regenerate the hash values (and signatures if they decided to try to be consistent). Change risks breaking the examples that are intended to demonstrate aspects of integrity, not aspects of JSON.

I propose closing with no action.

In which case copy & paste wouldn't work anymore.

> .... If we're going to that extent, I would entertain adding an explicit trailing linefeed to make the JSON less weird for folks that find it that way.

Just to be clear. The spec does have trailing LFs. The problem is that the examples were computed without them.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Ok this is news to me. RFC 9110 does seem to be consistent with this view - https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-3.9 at least says it includes a CLRF and the content-length matches, while https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-426-upgrade-required doesn't include such a statement but the content-length covers the CLRF. It wouldn't surprise me if others had been caught out by this behaviour in the past in other specs. 

So lets whittle this down a bit:

* Where examples include message content, there is an implicit CLRF. Examples are not correctly accommodating this in either their content-length or digest values.
* Incorrect examples are confusing and dangerous for interop.

Based on this, I think our only recourse is to pick through all the examples and ensure they are correct, including regenerating digests. This may affect @jricher and the signature draft too.

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
Hi folks. Since this can be confusing, I think the best option here is not using JSON content. Instead I would replace it with the `Hello world.` string. JSON serialization is out of scope for Digest Fields: let's keep it simple. 

Another option is to always use HEX encoding even for text (e.g.) 

```
7B 22 68 65 6C 6C 6F 22 3A 20 22 77 6F 72 6C 64 22 7D
{  "  h  e  l  l  o  "  :     "  w  o  r  l  d  "  }
```

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
IIUC the problem is that any form of example can include the LF due to how our tooling works.

Having to state everywhere that LF isn't included and showing that via a hex rendering hurts the legibility of the examples IMO.

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
The problem here is that if every line ends with LF, readers will think that they should add LF at the end of any content before computing the digest. IIUC this is not true (but maybe I haven't understood correctly).

A better solution to me is this one, taken from RFC9110: using the following content for all the non-hex examples

```Hello World! My content includes a trailing CRLF.``` -> C-L: 51

see https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-3.9-4

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Examples are by their nature limited. It is always up to implementers to determine how to apply the spec to their own work. 

That example in RFC9110 just states in the content itself what I already attempted to communicated in PR #2458.  If we're clear about what the input bytes are in the scope of an example, then that seems good enough to me.

Changing away from json is quite a significant change that would require additional validation of the examples themselves. I don't think redesigning the examples is a good use of time at this stage in the process, hence the approach in #2458. Furthermore, changing the content to a single line also risks not covering cases of multiline text, which is common.

issues.title: Can 2 algorithms have the same preference?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
From James Manger:

> Can 2 algorithms have the same preference? For example:
Want-Repr-Digest: sha-512=5, sha-256=5, unixsum=0

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Good question. Syntactically, Structured Fields allows dictionary members to have the same value. We say the value conveys an ascending, relative, weighted preference. So members with the same value are relatively the same.

The intention here is to emulate RFC 3230's `q` parameter, based on HTTP "Quality Values" aka `qvalue`, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-quality-values. We just apply a much smaller range. Partly because we never got much feedback on whether RFC 3230's Want-Digest or its `q` parameter was used in the wild. Partly because the thing is just a hint and the server can do what it wants anyway. 

AFAICT, RFC 9110 says nothing about how to treat quality values that use the same number. Maybe @mnot @royfielding or @reschke have an opinion on the matter. 

Since RFC9110 is quiet on the matter of same qvalue number, I'm inclined to stay quiet here.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Right, same value is same value (there are fields that range "simpler" values better (Accept?) - but that doesn't seem to apply here).

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body: +1 on quiet

comments.body: Based on this discussion, closing with no action

issues.title: Date as an extension in 8941-defined fields
issues.author: mnot
issues.body: As pointed out on list, we need to warn people against just using Date as an extension in a field that was defined using 8941.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: The warning helps, but it IMHO does not address the larger extensibility problem we have.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @reschke can you articulate that (here or in another issue, if it's substantially different / larger)?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I'll try.

The main selling point for structured fields IMHO is "a unified parser". You know that a field value is SF-shaped, drop it into the parser, and get a more or less self describing data structure. Great.

Now once we add extensions to SF, this get's harder.

Starting with the the current proposals:

1. A recipient of a field does not only have to know which top-level field type to parse for, but also whether to switch on support for SF-date or not. Or we would need to say that even when a spec defines a field using 8941, it still's ok to parse it with an sf-date-enabled parser. In that case, it would be up to the recipient to either ignore sf-date-typed extension parameters (if the field definition already allowed future extension), to convert them to an integer, or to reject the parsing result altogether.
2. Retrofit parsing flags: I hope we have consensus that preprocessing values *before* passing them into the parser will be fragile. So a retrofit-supporting SF parser will either need modes, or the wire syntax for SF *could* be relaxed so that retrofit would need no new mode.

The common concern here is that SF in theory is simple to extend, the process is extremely hard both process-wise and deployment-wise. Ideas:

- we could simply avoid doing extensions; sf-date is only a "lipstick" flag so that tools can switch on a special display mode - maybe we don't really need it?
- we could try to define what future extensions mean for specs that are written for the current version of the spec

My concern with the current state of things is that a parser implementation will need a *set* of flags, and each new flag will add complexity not only with respect to the parsing code, but also to API and documentation (how do I get the user to select the right mode, or will she always just select *all* extensions - and why would that be bad...?), and to test coverage (we need a parametrized test suite, right?).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
> it would be up to the recipient to either ignore sf-date-typed extension parameters (if the field definition already allowed future extension), to convert them to an integer, or to reject the parsing result altogether.

I think that this is a reasonable outcome.  Using sf-date before a recipient is prepared to process it can result in the field being dropped.  Now, this isn't entirely satisfactory, because an extension *within* a field will be dropped by a date-unaware SF parser, but that risk can be documented.  Extensions to structured fields defined against RFC 8941 probably don't get to use dates then, at least until sf-date-aware parsers are widely enough deployed that the risk is negligible.

Documenting this as a caveat is worthwhile; it's only the current set of structured fields that are affected in this way.

I don't think that a flag is necessary for sf-date.

(I haven't thought much about your retrofit points just yet, I just wanted to put this there as a potential way forward for sf-date.)

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> I think that this is a reasonable outcome.

Just to clarify: any of these three?

> I don't think that a flag is necessary for sf-date.

Which means that updated parsers will accept sf-date, and thus not be compliant to 8941 anymore. (I'm personally ok with that, but we really should be clear about that)

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> it would be up to the recipient to either ignore sf-date-typed extension parameters (if the field definition already allowed future extension), to convert them to an integer, or to reject the parsing result altogether.

Yes, that had been my assumption -- a recipient is always going to need to check whether or not the types it recieves are the ones it expected; e.g., if a field is defined to only allow Strings and it receives an Integer, it needs to deal with that. Same for Dates, in this case.

> Which means that updated parsers will accept sf-date, and thus not be compliant to 8941 anymore. (I'm personally ok with that, but we really should be clear about that)

I don't think that non-compliance has any significant impact, as discussed above. Happy to clarify it, but I seriously doubt whether it will have any real-world impact to do so.

In the case where a field that specifies (or allows through extension) a Date, the appropriate spec needs to refer to the updated RFC so that an updated parser is used. The extension case is a little less obvious, so we're talking through the text to highlight that now.

Regarding retrofit -- I don't think preprocessing is seriously considered by anyone at this point; the question is whether we make it a flag in sf-bis, or 'monkey patch' the spec from afar, just for the purpose of retrofit. So far we seem to be leaning towards the former, but there are risks (as discussed). Note that if we have flags, they're in the parser, but they needn't be exposed to people doing end-user parsing of fields. Or, as discussed elsewhere, we could decide to drop those compatibility fixes. Let's keep discussion of that on issue #2235. 

> We could simply avoid doing extensions; sf-date is only a "lipstick" flag so that tools can switch on a special display mode - maybe we don't really need it?

I'm not unsympathetic here. I was much more excited about a Date that looked developer-friendly in HTTP/1; now I fear it's not going to be adopted (the HTTPAPI is very lukewarm about it).

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> Yes, that had been my assumption -- a recipient is always going to need to check whether or not the types it recieves are the ones it expected; e.g., if a field is defined to only allow Strings and it receives an Integer, it needs to deal with that. Same for Dates, in this case.

Ok, here's an implementation question. In the branch for sf-date, https://github.com/reschke/structured-fields currently handles dates as extensions of integers. So somebody expecting an integer would actually see an integer, unless when aware of the new type https://github.com/reschke/structured-fields/blob/sfdate/src/main/java/org/greenbytes/http/sfv/DateItem.java (extending NumberItem).

Would you consider that a problematic approach? (I got there just because of code re-use from integers, AFAIR it was not a conscious decision (yet)).

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: It'd be problematic if the implementation didn't have any way of distinguishing Dates from Integers, because that would be impossible to round-trip -- the serialiser wouldn't know which form to pick.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: See linked PR.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> It'd be problematic if the implementation didn't have any way of distinguishing Dates from Integers, because that would be impossible to round-trip -- the serialiser wouldn't know which form to pick.

Well, if the caller knows about the new types, it will be able to check. The serializer does know about the new types, so round-tripping would happen correctly even if the user of the API wasn't aware of the extension.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Ok, the PR makes things clearer, in that:

1. you can't use sf-date, even inside an extension parameter, unless you update the spec defining the field, and
2. code calling an SF parser will now have to specify which version of SF to use (that's ok with just the three top-level types and one additional flag, but it will get messy if more extensions are being defined)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I would like to avoid the second if possible.  That is, you can process with a newer SF version, but you can't produce with a newer SF version.  That means that rejection by a receiver isn't guaranteed, but it offers a path toward upgrade at some point (we could decide, collectively, that it is OK to use sf-date in an extension for an older field definition.  We might do that based on adoption rates for the new SF version, and memorialize it with an update to the field, but we wouldn't necessarily need to pick a new field name in order to avoid the compatibility risk (we'd just be managing the probability of it happening).

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: It would be interesting to see more feedback from people defining APIs for SF support...

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> code calling an SF parser will now have to specify which version of SF to use (that's ok with just the three top-level types and one additional flag, but it will get messy if more extensions are being defined)

How does the PR imply that?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Well, if a spec refers to an SF-shaped field based on RFC 8941, parsing it with an 8941bis parser (allowing sf-date) would be incorrect. RFC 8941 requires draconian error handling, after all.

When we defined RFC 8941, we consciously specced draconian error handling + no extension points (until the spec is updated), so that's the consequence.

I fear that we are in a very fundamental disagreement about how extending the structured field syntax is supposed to happen given the constraints we put into 8941.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Perhaps it would be best to take this to the list. I don't see anyone else who yet shares your point of view, so it would be good to circulate it with a wider audience.

issues.title: signatures: structure 2.1
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
Strictly editorial: Section 2.1 is way too long; moving a few more things into sub sections might be good.

(I can provide a PR if desired)

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: As editor, I disagree with this. The section consists of the definition, the caveats (which are several because HTTP fields are super weird), some general examples, and a listing of the flags that are explained in the next sub-sections. I personally see no value to split any of those out into sub-sections, as the narrative flows between them and they're tied together under a single topic.

issues.title: signature: canon. algorithm
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html#section-2.1-5:

> If the correctly combined value is not directly available for a given field by an implementation, the following algorithm will produce canonicalized results for list-based fields:
>
> 1. Create an ordered list of the field values of each instance of the field in the message, in the order that they occur (or will occur) in the message. If necessary, separate individual values found in a field instance.

So, what does "If necessary, separate individual values found in a field instance" actually mean? Split by comma? This will cause multiple valid values to have the same signature.

Consider:

~~~
"a , b , c" 
~~~

and

~~~
"a,b,c"
~~~

So if this is indeed what's suggested we should note that this will mangle values, and that multiple different values might have the same signature.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: This appears to be addressed by https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2380

issues.author: reschke

Was support to sf-list (in addition of sf-dictionary) considered? (If yes, it might be good to state somewhere why it was not included).

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Yes, it's already supported like any other sf-type. Are you looking for some specific form of support, like sub-indexing? That specifically was in an earlier version of the draft but was removed due to very valid WG feedback.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: If sub-indexing is what's described in [2.1.2. ](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html#section-2.1.2)[Dictionary Structured Field Members](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html#name-dictionary-structured-field) - then yes, that's what I was looking for. Do you have a pointer to that feedback?

issues.title: sf: (potentially) clarify strict error handling
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis.html#section-2

> When parsing fails, the entire field is ignored (see [Section 4.2](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis.html#text-parse)); in most situations, violating field-specific constraints should have the same effect. Thus, if a header is defined as an Item and required to be an Integer, but a String is received, the field will by default be ignored. If the field requires different error handling, this should be explicitly specified.

It appears that some read the last sentence:

> If the field requires different error handling, this should be explicitly specified.

as saying that the generic draconian handling of parsing errors can be relaxed.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: It's saying that a generic parser will fail, but the field-specific handling of that failure might do somthing else, including try to parse the field using an alternative method. SF cannot constrain what a field does with the output of parsing.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
That sounds like "we require draconian error handling, but if there's an error, you are free to do something else".

Of course we can't force anybody not to do that, but we should be clear that this is not what the spec says.

issues.title: Hashes of uploaded files
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
At IETF 115, Hans-Jörg Happel mentioned the idea of an extension to add checksum mechanism to resumable uploads.

One option is that the server calculates a checksum of completed uploads and provides it to the client, which can compare this checksum with an expected value. If the values do not match, the client can error out or retry the upload.

Another option is that the client tells the server the expected checksum in the beginning, and the server verifies the checksum once the upload is complete.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
[HTTP digests](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers.html)  can probably deal with both of these options. I would be resistant to implementing something new just for resumable uploads.

The question for me is how much, if at all, resumable uploads should discuss this kind of scenario. Maybe just mentioning the possibility of HTTP digeat, or maybe some examples if the sequence if messages is non-obvious. But we should try to keep text lean IMO.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
HTTP digests seems to fit very well here. There is also some discussion in https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0067.html around this topic. 

> Maybe just mentioning the possibility of HTTP digeat, or maybe some examples if the sequence if messages is non-obvious. But we should try to keep text lean IMO.

I agree. Such a mention and a few examples should be sufficient.

issues.title: message-signatures: addition of leading or trailing whitespace to a field value
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
1.3:

> As mentioned earlier, HTTP explicitly permits and in some cases requires implementations to transform messages in a variety of ways. Implementations are required to tolerate many of these transformations. What follows is a non-normative and non-exhaustive list of transformations that could occur under HTTP, provided as context:
> ...
>  -  Addition or removal of leading or trailing whitespace to a field value.

This is misleading. No HTTP permits *addition* of leading/trailing whitespace. Leading/trailing whitespace in field values by definition is invalid.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: While technically true, many (including implementers) won't understand the nuance Here. Given the impact, it's better to be over-inclusive, I think.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: If invalid changes are included, then it might be best to either say that some of these changes might be invalid or point specifically to those that are.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Yes, my proposal would be to split the list into two; the second just listing the transformatios that might happen in reality despite bing forbidden.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: @reschke I agree that we need to prepare developers for the messy reality of HTTP in addition to what's strictly allowed. What else would appear in this second list?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: The only other thing that I can see right now is addition of obs-fold.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Speaking of which: there are other transformations like parsing and re-serializing field values, which are certainly allowed. Shouldn't these be mentioned here as well?

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: @reschke Re-serialization of a field value by an intermediary would likely break things in an expected way. It was my impression that this was not allowed by intermediaries in general. A structured field does help this, and the `sf` flag protects against that kind of transformation, as mentioned in the section.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I don't think we have a rule anywhere that would keep an intermediary from parsing and re-serializing fields.

And even if that was the case, the same would be true for the original point (addition of leading/trailing WS), so I'm trying to understand where we draw the line.

issues.title: message-signatures: obs-fold
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
The spec several times refers to the term obs-fold, but doesn't say where it's defined (-> https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-5.2).

Furthermore, in 1.3 it claims that *addition* of obs-fold could be permitted under certain circumstances. That IMHO is incorrect.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Adding the reference makes sense. The signatures spec doesn't change how the messages are created, nor does it make `obs-fold` more allowed than it is now, it just tells people what to do with the messages that they have even if they have `obs-fold` in them.

issues.title: message-signatures: requirements on sf dictionary parsing
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
2.1.2 says:

> Each parameterized key for a given field MUST NOT appear more than once in the signature base. Parameterized keys MAY appear in any order in the signature base, regardless of the order they occur in the source Dictionary.

How is an implementation supposed to verify that, given the fact that a SF parser will happily parse the field value (see RFC 8941, Section 4.2.2, step 2.4)?

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: This is checked fairly simply by checking the input of the signature components. If you've got two field entries with the same key parameter, you throw an error and stop creating the signature base. That's true for both the signer and verifier. The reason for this is exactly because of the expected behavior of a dictionary parser -- it's an ambiguity that can't reliably be covered by a signature because only the "last" element with a key gets used by the data structure in spite of other things getting shadowed.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Ah, sorry, I misread that and was confused by the MUST requirement here. In practice, a key appearing multiple times would be completely harmless, no? (because, by definition, it would always have the same value).

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Correct, so it's a prohibition on the input behavior more than anything to avoid a possible ambiguity or rough edge for implementers.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: OK,  I'm not sure this mandates a MUST requirement then; the reason I was confused was that I thought "otherwise something bad will happen", but that does not seem to be the case. Switching to "editorial".

issues.title: message-signatures: ASCII restriction in field-value to byte sequence
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
in 2.1.3:

> Encode the bytes of the resulting field value's ASCII representation as a Byte Sequence.

What if the field value contains non-ASCII characters (from obs-text)?

Of course that could be considered an error, but I believe the intention is to be able to represent anything here. So the text should refer to the field value as byte sequence, in which case the encoding step would not be needed.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: This text was added in response to a comment about needing to know which encoding to put into the byte sequence input, and the commenter suggested ASCII as the base for it. If field values have a well-defined byte sequence that isn't ASCII characters only, then we should refer to whatever that is from the HTTP docs.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Well, field values in HTTP can be anything. It's obsolete, it's deprecated, but that's what it is. So we need to deal with it one way or another.

I could live with UTF-8, and a note that if the octet sequence does not decode as UTF-8, you can't sign it.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: @jricher - yes, you can merge and close issues as you wish, you are the editor. But by all means do not submit a new draft until the changes have been reviewed by those who opened the issue. (cc chairs @mnot @tfpauly )

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: As far as I can tell, the changes require percent-encoding only for non-ASCII values. That is, the character U+0080 would get the same encoding as a verbatim "%80" in a field value. I believe this is a problem.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
This issue has been addressed. There is no percent encoding needed in this section since the value is taken directly from the bytes of the field in a binary-wrapped representation, and the bytes are encoded using the base64 serialization of a Byte Sequence from Structured Fields:

> Encode the bytes of the resulting field value as a Byte Sequence. Note that most fields are restricted to ASCII characters, but other octets could be included in the value in some implementations.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: I'm talking about the simple case, not the one where Byte Sequence encoding is used (yes, the issue title doesn't match anymore).

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Ok, opened new issue https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2513

issues.title: message-signatures: query parameters vs encoding
issues.author: reschke
issues.body: In 2.2.8, it might be good to mention that the referenced algorithm only supports query parameters using (percent-escaped) UTF-8 encoding (this came as a surprise to me because I assumed it works the same as the algorithm used for forms decoding).

issues.title: message-signatures: format of signature base
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
2.5:

> The signature base is a US-ASCII string containing the canonicalized HTTP message components covered by the signature.

This seems to be inconsistent with Section 2.2.8 ("Query Parameters"), which could create non-ASCII component values.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: FWIW, a query parameter (after application of https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#application/x-www-form-urlencoded) could contain CR, LF and other control characters.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: So we likely need to serialize information extracted from query parameters using some kind of encoding; maybe an SF Byte Sequence.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
This is tricky -- originally the query parameters were kept in percent-encoded form but from WG discussion we changed that to just use the unencoded value instead since several percent-encoded forms could be used. However it does look like the unencoded form could end up with problematic values here, so maybe we need to go back to that.

I'd rather us use an encoding native to the value rather than inventing something to put on top of it, even trying to re-use the `bs` flag we've already got defined for headers.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
And we did that because to extract query parameter values, we need a query parser, and that is defined the way it is. I believe that decision was good, we now just need to figure out out to transform the extracted values so that they can be used in the signature base.

(And, FWIW, at the end we also should have an example for a case like that in the spec).

issues.title: Support SM2/SM3 algorithms
issues.author: SunFulong

@SunFulong my question was about which specification you are referring to.  There are multiple specifications in this repository.  I doubt that this applies to [the retrofit work](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-retrofit.html), for example.

If your goal is to request the addition of SM3 and SM2 to a particular specification, we need to know which.  If this is a more general inquiry, then [our mailing list](mailto:ietf-http-wg@w3.org) is probably a better place to start.

In cases where there is no chain, is it advisable to send the empty string to indicate this, rather than omitting the parameter? comments.body: That's a good question! I don't think there needs to be a normative requirement here, but I think it's reasonable to have `""` signify that there were no aliases.

issues.title: message-signatures: HTTP Signature Algorithms names
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
6.2.1:

> Algorithm Name:
>    An identifier for the HTTP Signature Algorithm. The name MUST be an ASCII string consisting only of lower-case characters ("a" - "z"), digits ("0" - "9"), and hyphens ("-"), and SHOULD NOT exceed 20 characters in length. The identifier MUST be unique within the context of the registry.

1. Can it start with a hyphen?
2. Under which circumstances would be more than 20 characters ok?
3. Uniqueness seems to be evident, given that we talk about a registry.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
1. Sure, why not?
2. If you try to get the name down under 20 and it doesn't make sense, is misleading to implementors, or isn't unique.
3. Yes.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: 1. It's ... uncommon in identifiers.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Is "uncommon" enough to make it prohibited? It seems like the DE would question that decision prior to registration.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: I'm just surprised that the rules are very different from other related HTTP registries, and I wonder why that is the case.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: There's not a compelling reason for the rules to be different for this element. What rules would you propose for algorithm names?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Ok, I now realize that this applies to most or all registries introduced here.

That said, why not just use HTTP's "token" ABNF?

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
If anything, the restriction should be the contents of `sf-string`, of which this is already a subset. I don't think adding uppercase characters is a good idea, because you're going to run into practical problems if `RSA`, `rsa`, and `rSa` all mean different things in the registry, even if the value is case-sensitive by nature.

I see no compelling reason to expand the character set beyond what's already allowed in each registration.

issues.title: Make sure u= is not a tracking vector
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body: Right now the document contains the `u` (user ID) parameter. Thinking about it some more, this is more about describing the key than the user, see httpwg/http-extensions#2431. In addition to that change, we should add text warning about the tracking risks or this and how to avoid these issues.

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body:
It seems to me that there's room for both user-ID type uses for the "u" (in the employee remote access model, e.g.) as well as the more indirect key-indicator type uses (in the Internet Freedom model of distributed communities).  I'm especially interested in the latter - use cases where users can prove they are in possession of a valid secret without requiring a hard user identifier (one that attaches them to a permanent/billable/irrevocable external identifier).  The draft does not currently provide an Authentication Scheme that directly offers this latter capability, however (though it's possible to overload on the "u"/"k" parameter if the server and client agree on the scheme for doing that). 

I'm unable to steelman the case for "u" (or "k") being a "super-cookie".  The imagined use cases in my head have this scheme tied to a single service provider and employed on the first hop.   I don't understand the language being used in the list commentary on this topic (e.g., "Each site (*) could get a different key pair and key identifier.").  My assumption has been sites issue credentials as they see fit without reference to any other site.  The commentary implies to me that there is some overriding entity distributing credentials to many sites (a la Privacy Pass). I did not think Unprompted Authentication addresses that space.  Further, if indeed we need to address that space, it seems to me the "super-cookie" burden of proof is then with THAT scheme, not Unprompted Authentication.  

The "document it" point might be the salient one: "This is probably another case where documenting a little more detail about the usage context could help.".   Here's a start:

Sites offering Unprompted Authentication are able to link requests from individuals clients via the Authentication Schemes provided.  However, requests as not linkable across other sites if the credentials used are private to individual sites.

issues.title: Explain use cases
issues.author: chris-wood
issues.body: The draft could benefit from some example use cases up front in the introduction.

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body:
Concise Use Case Description:

Unprompted authentication, as defined here, serves use cases in which the provider of a service or capability wants only "those who know" to access it while all others are given no indication the service or capability exists.  The conceptual model is that of a "speakeasy".  For example, a company might offer remote employee access directly via its website, or access to limited special capabilities for specific employees.  Members of less well-defined communities might acquire metered access to geography- or capability-specific resources by an entity whose user base is larger than the available resources can support.  Unprompted authentication is also useful for cases where a service provider wants to distribute provisioning information to its resources without exposing the provisioning location to non-users. 

Edits/Additions welcome

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body:
Version 2:

Unprompted authentication, as defined here, serves use cases in which the provider of a service or capability wants only "those who know" to access the service or capability while all others are given no indication the service or capability exists. "Knowing" is via an externally-defined mechanism by which user identifiers (required here) are distributed. The conceptual model is that of a "speakeasy". For example, a company might offer remote employee access to company services directly via its website, or offer access to limited special capabilities for specific employees, while making discovering (probing for) such capabilities difficult. Members of less well-defined communities might acquire access to geography- or capability-specific resources by an entity whose user base is larger than the available resources can support (via that entity metering the availability of user identifiers temporally or geographically). Unprompted authentication is also useful for cases where a service provider wants to distribute user-provisioning information for its resources without exposing the provisioning location to non-users.

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body:
Version 3:

Unprompted authentication, as defined here, serves use cases in which a site wants to offer a service or capability only to "those who know" while all others are given no indication the service or capability exists. The conceptual model is that of a "speakeasy". "Knowing" is via an externally-defined mechanism by which user identifiers are distributed.  For example, a company might offer remote employee access to company services directly via its website using their employee ID, or offer access to limited special capabilities for specific employees, while making discovering (probing for) such capabilities difficult. Members of less well-defined communities might more ephemeral identifiers to acquire access to geography- or capability-specific resources, as issued by an entity whose user base is larger than the available resources can support (by that entity metering the availability of user identifiers temporally or geographically). Unprompted authentication is also useful for cases where a service provider wants to distribute user-provisioning information for its resources without exposing the provisioning location to non-users.

issues.title: Consider refining scope to the origin
issues.author: chris-wood
issues.body: [WebAuthn](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-2/#sctn-authenticator-data) signatures are computed in a way that binds them to the origin which accepts the authenticator. While it's true that the nonce is a per-session concept, and the session is bound to a specific origin (by virtue of the TLS SNI), it seems possible for bugs to be introduced in settings where a TLS-terminating server supports more than one origin. Maybe the server accidentally sends an authenticator computed in a session for one origin to another, or something. I would follow in WebAuthn's footsteps here and sign something that's specific to the origin.

comments.author: ilaril
comments.body:
HTTPS sessions are not bound to a specific origin.  There is no requirement for client to only use one origin on connection, and even if there was, TLS SNI is not fine-grained enough, as e.g. https://foo.example and https://foo.example:8443 are different origins, but have the same TLS SNI.

Extending the idea of throwing some stuff into the context from httpwg/http-extensions#2429, one could throw the origin (host/:authority) in as well (the contexts can be up to 65535 bytes, so there is plenty of space). This would bind the signatures to origin, would still work if host gets remapped somewhere, and could mitigate some tracking vectors. And it would still retain the no explicit configuration / no algorithm support property.

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: Oh, right, duh. We have connection coalescing! Throwing in the origin as you suggest seems like it work, and as in httpwg/http-extensions#2429 perhaps doing it above nonce generation is best.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Discussed at IETF 116, it seemed like the proposal most likely to succeed was to add the [realm](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-11.5) to the context

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Regarding the question on [presentation at IETF 116](https://github.com/httpwg/wg-materials/blob/gh-pages/ietf116/unprompted-auth.pdf), asking if origin and also URL should be part of the context.

[RFC 9110 section 11.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-establishing-a-protection-s) says, quote "unless specifically allowed by the authentication scheme, a single protection space cannot extend outside the scope of its server."

So as @ilaril points out, we should include the origin.

[Section 17.16.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-protection-spaces) discusses the danger of using the same context for different URLs belonging to the same origin, pointing out that it is an problem that already exists and explaining the mitigations (such as not forwarding the Authorization header to the application running on top of HTTP). Assuming that we would switch to using the Authorization header, I think we can rely on that.

To paraphrase, there is no need to include URL in the context.

In addition, we can<sup>1</sup> include "realm" in the Context, so that there can be multiple "protection spaces" inside one origin. In the Unprompted Authentication scheme, there is no way for a server to signal the realm to be used. Therefore, as @martinthomson pointed out, there has to be a default value that would be defined by the specification. Clients and servers can agree out-of-band to use a different value.

1: During the meeting, I asked as a pure question how Realm is to be used. In the follow-on discussion at least assumed that "realm" has to be part of the Unprompted Authentication as it is to use the Authorization header. However, reading RFC 9110 I realize that not all authentication schemes are required to support realms (i.e., having multiple protection spaces within an origin). Hence the "can."

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: OK wrote up #2572 to address this

issues.title: Per-authenticator context labels
issues.author: chris-wood
issues.body: I would recommend making the TLS exporter labels specific to the type of algorithm in use. For example, rather than use "EXPORTER-HTTP-Unprompted-Authentication-Signature" for signature-based authenticators, I might use "EXPORTER-HTTP-Unprompted-Authentication-Signature-Ed25519" for authenticators using Ed25519.

comments.author: ilaril
comments.body:
This would seem to have the drawback of making it complicated for intermediates to forward the authentication nonce.

The alternative being for intermediary to implement the validation itself, which has its own drawbacks.

Thinking why would one want to do something like this, I came up with vague ideas about possible cross-key tracking vectors. However, making labels algorithm-specific would not help if both keys happen to have the same type. One idea would be to mix the key id as context input, which would make the nonces be pretty much per-key in a way that is feasible for the first intermediary to calculate with no explicit algorithm support nor configuration.

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: An alternative proposal would be to just use a single context string for exporting the nonce but then somehow bind additional information into the signature computation at a higher layer. This would address the issue without complicating the intermediary story, I think.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Any case that involves intermediaries forwarding tokens will necessarily involve some amount of trust in the intermediary.  The intermediary can provide the exporter output when it forwards the token, which would allow the signature to be verified, but the recipient is going to have to trust that this isn't copied from some other request.

I definitely think that the context string is the right place to include origin, key identifier, algorithm choice, and maybe even some context from the request (URL).  That latter depends on how heavily people intend to lean on the intermediation case.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Discussed at IETF 116, sense of the room appeared to be that adding the key identifier and algorithm to the context made sense. We can skip URL and instead add realm, see #2428

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: OK wrote up #2572 to address this

issues.title: Signature optional
issues.author: chris-wood
issues.body: Is there a reason why the signature parameter in the header field is listed as optional? That seems fairly essential for this thing to work.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Presumably the signature algorithm is determined by the key that is used, which is either implicit (`u=` is optional too) or indirectly identified via `u=`.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: That's correct. We can add some editorial text to make this clearer

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: I think making it optional probably requires some analysis to ensure it's safe. This feels like a sharp edge. I would recommend making it mandatory for now and then possibly let it be optional if we have evidence it's safe.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @chris-wood I think you're misunderstanding the draft. `s` is OPTIONAL in general because it's only used by `Signature` but not by `Hash`. `Signature` requires `s`. Can you re-read to double-check this and see if you still have concerns?

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: That matches my understanding. My point is that if the algorithm actually requires a signature to be provided, then I think it MUST be included, not left up for interpretation by the receiver. Specifically, if authenticating with a digital signature and not a MAC, then I'm suggesting this parameter to be mandatory. I understand that it's not needed by the other variants.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
@chris-wood that's what the draft already says:
> The "Signature" HTTP Authentication Scheme uses asymmetric cryptography. User agents possess a user ID and a public/private key pair, and origin servers maintain a mapping of authorized user IDs to their associated public keys. When using this scheme, the "u", "p", and "s" parameters are REQUIRED.

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: Great! In that case, we can close this.

issues.title: Consider renaming "u" to "k"
issues.author: chris-wood
issues.body: The user ID parameter "u" effectively identifies the keying material that servers might use to verify the authenticator sent in the header. As noted on the list, this is more or less a key ID, and I think leaning into that framing could be helpful. For example, beyond avoiding the confusion raised on the list, it might also be more ergonomic for different types of authenticators. One could imagine using a [ring signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_signature) for unprompted authentication where the server only learns that someone with a valid private key produced the authenticator but not necessarily which one.

issues.title: New header field vs existing Authorization header
issues.author: chris-wood
issues.body: Is there a technical reason why the `WWW-Authenticate` header was not chosen for this draft? That can be sent without a corresponding challenge (in an unprompted way), as we note in the [HTTP authentication scheme for Privacy Pass](https://ietf-wg-privacypass.github.io/base-drafts/draft-ietf-privacypass-auth-scheme.html). It seems like that would work in this context, too.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: Is this rather about using the Authorization header?

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: 🤦 Yep!

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @chris-wood can you elaborate on "as we note in the [HTTP authentication scheme for Privacy Pass](https://ietf-wg-privacypass.github.io/base-drafts/draft-ietf-privacypass-auth-scheme.html)"? I skimmed through that draft and it seems to clearly require a TokenChallenge before sending a Token.

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: I thought we had text that described it, but I can't find it. In any case, I think one can send the Authorization header unsolicited, so I think this draft ought to do that instead of rolling a new auth header.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Fair enough, let's discuss this at 116.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: FWIW, I agree that unprompted "Authorization" is permissible in this context, but I think "Unprompted-Authorization" could be useful for clarity when reading logs, etc.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Discussed at IETF 116, sense of the room appeared to be that switching to Authorization made sense.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: OK wrote up #2571 to address this

issues.title: Intermediaries: suggest having the intermediary send the nonce as an alternative to validation
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body:
Ilari suggests on the [list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JanMar/0069.html):

comments.author: chris-wood
comments.body: 👍 to this. It's been implemented for exported authenticators and isn't too challenging.

issues.title: Comments on the updated draft
issues.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
issues.body:
Thank you for the draft updates, @DavidSchinazi.  Here's a shot at a "validating scenario" for HTTP Unprompted Auth:

We seek to emulate the phenomenon of the "speakeasy" in Prohibition America, with a bit more rigor to support higher levels of usage.  

Imagine a back alley deep in a maze of warehouse buildings in 1920s Chicago USA.  A person stands in front of door beneath a dimly lit bulb. Another person arrives and says "Is this the club where they serve free beer?".  The person answers "I don't know what you mean" and the man leaves. Another person arrives later and, without being asked, nods their head to the side and says "Whiskey Tango Foxtrot".  The person is let in the door.  A third person, arriving much later, emulates the second person but is told "I don't know what you mean".  

The second person in this scenario knows the speakeasy's location, knows the code and knows to provide it without being asked.   Everyone else fails to gain access and learns no information about the failure.  As a secondary measure, anyone who re-uses a previously-used code similarly fails to gain access and learns no information about the failure.  This secondary measure assures the code itself can not be shared along with the location. 

In an HTTP use case, certain resources provided by an origin require a mechanism for differentiating valid users from invalid ones. Validity is determined by perhaps account settings, expressed preferences or fees. These resources are valuable and, if the origin was known, it could be flooded with invalid requests, rendering the resources unusable by all.  Therefore the resource location is provided only to known valid users.  However, to prevent unwanted sharing of the location with invalid users, a mechanism is necessary to allow valid users to gain entry in a manner that does not indicate (a) the resource's location has been found or (b) that a special authentication is required.  The mechanism proposed by HTTP Unprompted Authentication supports this scenario by (a) using per-connection private data combined with pre-agreed or pre-generated authentication tokens and (b) generic failure codes.

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body: If it's useful to present "real world use cases" and further if you think it's safe to provide Internet Freedom use cases, I think VPN access and configuration are good examples.  Someone at IETF115 mentioned access to Tor bridges. There are several different mechanisms where it would be useful just looking at Tor.  Pluggable Transports - which require another level of proxying, and are not specific to Tor - are another example.  Realistically, all the VPN providers need to wrap what are in reality a small number of network tunnel technologies (OpenVPN, Wireguard, Shadowsocks, etc) in configuration and access techniques that discriminate valid from invalid users.  And as they are, in many cases, under attack, anti-probing is very useful.

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body: I recall that key exporters require that both sides use the same bit pattern when requesting the export (which serves to assure the same output hash is provided to both).  That's just a text string and in our case is the string name of the authentication scheme used.   Thus Signature and HMAC will generate two different hashes on output.  Should we indicate specifically that, as long as both sides agree in advance (the case of a "captive" client and server, as with VPN use cases) then in reality ANY agreed string can be used, in addition to the offically-registered schemes?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
Regarding the validating scenario, I think that having that example is really helpful in the discussion of whether the HTTPBIS WG should adopt the draft, but maybe it might be best to avoid it in the draft to reduce the odds of folks trying to block this.

For the key exporter, what's the benefit of using another string? Conceptually it's another shared secret which would be redundant with the keys we already have?

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body:
Yes, the scenario was for verbal discussion (I can't remember who said "we need a good use case"). 

Re the key exporter: I remember when you call the OpenSSL function you provide a string as input and it's hashed with the session key to give you a new exported key.  So, that string matters - both sides have to use the same string to extract the same value and this draft proposes to use the name of the authentication type being used.  It makes sense to register the two auth schemes defined in the draft, but in Internet Freedom use cases, others might want to use different auth schemes "privately" (that is, the application authors define a scheme name and an auth process that they use for their own app.  I'm just thinking we should highlight the fact that this is possible, or maybe even a feature.  E.g., a vendor might develop a private Zero Knowledge authentication scheme that requires the vendor to have very little actual identifying information about the user.  I'm talking about a half-way point between something like Tor that doesn't require any user authentication and a VPN that has (possibly billed) customers with emails or phone numbers.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I still fail to see why changing the string accomplishes anything? Why not change the key instead? This schemes allows you to use the same key for all users if you'd like.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @m4mb01t4l14n0 ping?

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body: @DavidSchinazi re the authentication type string - I am happy to drop discussion of this topic completely.  I think the change suggested ( u -> k) is effectively the same, as in the example cited in #2431.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
Thanks. I think we can close this and use
* #2427 to discuss use-cases
* #2428 and #2429 to discuss what goes into the TLS exporter context/label

issues.title: Describe server handling
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body:
From @nharper on the [list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0028.html):

> There's no mention of how a server should process this header and respond to it. Given that the purpose is to be unprobable, the draft should probably say something to the effect of "if a server receives a header it is unable to validate, it should process the request as if the header were not present". The security considerations should also discuss ways that a server might inadvertently reveal that it serves resources protected by this mechanism.

issues.title: Discuss security properties of keys
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body:
From @nharper on the [list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0028.html):

> The draft is very light on details about where the user's key (private or symmetric) comes from. I assume that key generation/distribution/registration/etc is out of scope for this draft, but the draft should address the security properties expected of said key, e.g. can a key be used for Unprompted Authentication and another use?

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body:
The conservative thing to do here would be to insist that the key be unique to the protocol. 
We have domain separation in our outputs, so we don't need to worry about unprompted auth messages being used in cross-protocol attacks, but a different protocol (that doesn't use context strings) could possibly be induced to generate unprompted auth messages. We also need to worry about key compromise.

Imagine a protocol that leaks the private / secret key, that shares a key with unprompted auth. This doesn't even need to be a bug, it could be a commit-before-reveal style protocol. (Obviously that's a pathological example, but it shows we can't assume composability with all protocols) 

If we want to do a formal analysis (which I do) I think we need to be conservative here.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: SGTM

issues.title: Consider contextualizing signatures
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body:
From Ilari Liusvaara on the [list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0027.html):

> The signatures do not appear to be contextualized in any way, which is questionable. For example, one could use the same contextualization mechanism that TLS 1.3 uses (which prepends 64 spaces, a context label and NUL [one zero octet]).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I think that I might disagree with Ilari here for this application.  Key separation is probably a better model to employ here, though as soon as someone even hints that they might want to share client certificate keys and these keys then this sort of protection probably makes sense.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi

issues.title: Signature hash algorithm is ambiguous
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body:
From Ilari Liusvaara on the [list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0027.html):

> There is no requirement to include hash algorithm in signatures. There are TLS signature algorithms that mean totally different things depending on hash function, and more of those could appear in the future. E.g, signatures 7 and 8 already have double meaning (EdDSA [hash 8] and some Chinese stuff [hash 7]).

From @nharper on the [list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2022OctDec/0028.html):

> I agree with Ilari - do not use the TLS SignatureAlgorithm and HashAlgorithm registries that were orphaned by RFC 8447. For (asymmetric) signatures, you could use the 16-bit TLS SignatureScheme registry (https://www.iana.org/assignments/tls-parameters/tls-parameters.xhtml#tls-signaturescheme).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Maybe also consider [JWA](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7518#section-3) for identification.  That's not perfect, because of the "none" thing, but it might be a better fit.

The TLS schemes are generally OK provided that you only use the recommended ones (of which there aren't many).

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I don't love JWA since [it doesn't currently have an entry for Ed25519](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml#web-signature-encryption-algorithms), but using TLS SignatureScheme with a requirement to only use the recommended ones sounds good to me.

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body: @DavidSchinazi Doesn't it define the algorithm `EdDSA` and then define the subkey types `Ed25519` and `Ed448` in [RFC 8037](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8037.html#section-3.1)?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
@jhoyla that could be made to work though it's quite clunky since it requires a separate string parameter for "alg". Overall I think the [TLS SignatureScheme registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/tls-parameters/tls-parameters.xhtml#tls-signaturescheme) is a much better fit for signatures here. We already tightly integrate with TLS but not JWA. All that said, the closest option for hashes is the [TLS HashAlgorithms registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/tls-parameters/tls-parameters.xhtml#tls-parameters-18) and that's been orphaned by RFC 8447.

At this point I guess we should bite the bullet and define a new registry. Perhaps we include as current values:
* hmac-sha256
* hmac-sha384
* hmac-sha512
* signature-rsa_pkcs1_sha256
* signature-rsa_pkcs1_sha384
* signature-rsa_pkcs1_sha512
* signature-ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256
* signature-ecdsa_secp384r1_sha384
* signature-ecdsa_secp521r1_sha512
* signature-rsa_pss_rsae_sha256
* signature-rsa_pss_rsae_sha384
* signature-rsa_pss_rsae_sha512
* signature-rsa_pss_pss_sha256
* signature-rsa_pss_pss_sha384
* signature-rsa_pss_pss_sha512
* signature-ed25519
* signature-ed448

Of course this requires to paint the bikeshed one of two colors:
1. HMAC and Signatures in the same registry, using a single new auth scheme
2. Separate registries, using separate auth schemes

Thoughts? At this point I suspect this issue will need WG discussion at IETF 116.

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body: I had to implement rsa_pss_pss_shaX algorithms to produce test vectors for DCs, and unless there's a really compelling reason to include them, I'd really rather not. They're just such a pain to use, and the support for them is very poor (thus me needing to implement them).

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: FWIW, adding an entry in the registry doesn't mean it'll be mandatory to implement so there's not much of a cost. But I don't feel strongly about this one so I'm happy to not include it if it's the WG's preference.

comments.author: seanturner

Just saying here's a registry that you might could co-opt:
https://www.iana.org/assignments/hash-function-text-names/hash-function-text-names.xhtml#hash-function-text-names-1

Defined by https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8122/

issues.title: Double-check security of reusing the signature key multiple times in one connection
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body: @jhoyla and @martinthomson have pointed out that there be dragons in reusing keys. We should check to see if we need to add a signature index or some other addition to the nonce to avoid reuse.

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body: Maybe the right approach is to add an `opaque request_context<0..2^8-1>` field?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @jhoyla can you elaborate on what the exact issue is? If the key and nonce are reused without changing anything else, what is the exact problem?

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body:
I guess the threat model has to be a Person-In-Browser attacker, because we're assuming TLS is already defeated. 
One issue would be if the key and nonce were reused with a different identity, for example if the first attempt was rejected / failed.
This can (in some contexts) be used for a key recovery attack, which would allow the attacker to possibly sign things they otherwise couldn't. 
The other issue is that the identity is not bound to a single authentication. I don't think Frames have to cause an idempotent response from the server? It could be that (correctly) authenticating twice would have some side effect. A authentication might cause the server to take some action with a side effect "send the money" style.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I see. Would adding the identity to the signed data be sufficient? (I'm happy to add a request context if needed but I want to understand the details)

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body:
I don't think so, because it doesn't stop an in-browser attacker replaying the credentials to try and perform some action twice. Also in the Intermediary case, I was wondering if we could structure it such that the intermediary shares the exported key with the server, which allows the server to validate the credential. The goal would be that the server doesn't have to trust that the intermediary isn't making stuff up. I'm not sure if it's sensible or secure, because even though the shared key is independent from any of the other TLS keys shared between the client and intermediary, maybe it's possible for the intermediary to lie about the key and thus change the meaning of the message. 
(The connection here being that in the case of origin validation with an intermediary, we don't want the intermediary to be able to replay requests.) 
The more I think about the signature case the closer it seems to get to a version of EAs that allows client-initiation. I need to sit down and think a bit more about what we can learn from the security model of EAs. One question that springs to mind is "do we need a `Finished` message / MAC here?" 
If not, why do we include it in EAs? 
Sorry, I'm starting to ramble. I'll leave it there.

comments.author: m4mb01t4l14n0
comments.body: I have not looked at the code in a long time (SSL_export_keying_material). Do repeated calls to the key exporter - on the same TLS connection - generate the same value?  SCRATCH THAT, of course not.

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body: According to RFC 8446 it should, unless there has been a resumption or a rekeying.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
To clarify, in TLS 1.3 repeated calls to the key exporter with the same parameters (label, context, length) will always generate the same value. In TLS 1.2 there are dragons when it comes to resumption and rekey as Jonathan points out but we can add text explaining what not to do.

I'm not convinced that an in-browser attacker is part of the threat model here, but I'm not opposed to adding a counter to the signed data in addition to the nonce to solve that attack.

Regarding intermediaries, I like the idea of having the intermediary share the nonce with the backend. I'd be inclined to mention both options (sharing the nonce and having the intermediary check auth) in that section, but I'd rather not define how that's done until someone has a use-case for it.

From looking at TLS exported authenticators (EA) it's not clear to me what purpose the Finished message serves there.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I had a quick chat with @grittygrease and @davidben about this and the conclusion was that the Finished message in EA doesn't bind any more secrets together but it allows reusing the security proofs from TLS.

issues.title: Next-hop aliases: Escaping "."
issues.author: bemasc
issues.body: The "[unreserved characters](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-2.3)" set includes ".", but we actually need to escape "." to avoid [Period Injection](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.05439.pdf) attacks.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body:
Hm, my impression is that this attack is about making a period within a label look like a label separator.

By the time that you have a string for a name, it would already need this kind of escaping done. Put another way, the "." characters we have in the string are indeed label separators already.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
The draft doesn't specify how to construct the DNS name string (and in general there is not a great specification for this).  The most common convention (noted in RFC 1035 Section 5.1) is to precede "." inside a label with a backslash.  This draft would then percent-escape the backslash, but not the ".", so there would indeed be a "." character that is not a label separator in the final header field value.

Whatever escaping convention you choose, this is sufficiently non-obvious that I think a very clear specification and some examples are probably in order.

(This whole rigmarole is normally not a problem because URIs are restricted to contain only "hostnames", which cannot have weird characters in the labels.)

issues.title: Extend next-hop alias security considerations to cover trust in DNS resolution
issues.author: chris-wood
issues.body: Without going through a proxy, clients implement CNAME cloaking mitigations on the basis of DNS information they see during resolution, which is totally reasonable. If resolution is subverted (or whatever) and the CNAME information is modified, these client checks might not work. When going through a proxy, the proxy is the one doing DNS resolution, so it seems like any sort of funny business that one might do to DNS answers for the proxy might affect the client's ability to implement cloaking mitigations correctly. The security considerations might benefit from a bit of expansion to cover this additional aspect of the threat model.

issues.title: Unprompted Auth: Freshness & Signature Binding
issues.author: dennisjackson
issues.body:
In the current draft, the header is composed as: 
```
{key_id}, {sig_alg}, {hash_alg}, {signature_over_nonce}
```
The server computes the nonce from the TLS key material exporter and verifies the signature. 

This doesn't actually guarantee freshness, because its possible for parties to construct signatures which are valid for any message/nonce. This means that a party which does not have access to the TLS Export material can still inject a valid Auth header. I don't think that's a major problem, but it is a bit unintuitive and its hard to predict how drafts like this will eventually get deployed. 

A simple fix would be in to add an additional parameter, say `v` which is `hash(seperator || nonce)` or similar and have servers check its been correctly computed. This ensures that only parties that can access TLS key material can inject valid headers. 

Behind the scenes, this attack / fix works because hash functions have to be collision resistant for all inputs, whereas signatures don't have to satisfy **any** properties if the associated public key was generated maliciously. [Seems Legit](https://dennis-jackson.uk/assets/pdfs/signatures.pdf) has a longer discussion.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Thanks! This sounds like an easy fix. Instead of a hash, we could also generate more bytes from the key exporter and use some for the nonce and some for the `v` parameter
