issues.title: Supported Range of Dates
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
Implementing Date in Python as a `datetime.datetime` object has an issue -- Python dates are limited to a specific range. 

Given that it's good to expose SF as idiomatic data structures wherever possible, I poked around a bit for limits on date/time objects in libraries, and found (all expressed as limits on years, as that's the most significant bit):

* Python - [1-9999](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#constants)
* Rust - [262145-262143](https://docs.rs/chrono/0.4.26/chrono/naive/struct.NaiveDate.html)
* Go - [0-9999](https://pkg.go.dev/time#Parse)
* PHP - [64bits](https://www.php.net/manual/en/intro.datetime.php)
* JavaScript - [-271821-275760](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date)
* Ruby - [unbounded](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15988539/what-is-the-range-of-the-ruby-date-or-datetime-object)
* Java - [-292269055-292278994](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3598091/java-min-and-max-date-range)

Should we specify a minimum range of dates that an implementation should support (likely 1-9999) so that developers can be confident of them (as we've done for other data types)?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Hm. Do these differences affect other parts of HTTP as well, such as processing the "Date" field (or fields specific to caching...?).

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: One would imagine that people put HTTP dates into these structures from time to time, yes.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: (it's just that HTTP dates rarely go outside the range 1970 - "forseeable future")

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Restricting to a year-based range would IMHO make sense if we actually would be using calendar dates (which we do not).

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
To be clear, I'm not proposing we restrict it -- just require implementations to support at least a particular range of values, just as we do with many other types.

Don't get stuck on years, that's just a rough sizing to get an idea of what we're looking at. I think we'd express it in integer values.

comments.author: bsdphk
comments.body:
I've commented in the PR that I dont like this, but let me add a bit of context:

Handling of time, in real life and in computers, is incredibly messy and one of the most unreadable scientific books of all time is "Calendrical Calculations" which is our best shot at that subject matter.

I really do not want us to wade into this tarpit, because everybody who has ever done so, has just added more tar in the process.

My really strong preference is if Date was defined as "Seconds since Epoch" according to POSIX" with the full range of signed 15 decimal digits we inherit from Integer, so that we in no way adds any further complexity.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> My really strong preference is if Date was defined as "Seconds since Epoch" according to POSIX" with the full range of signed 15 decimal digits we inherit from Integer, so that we in no way adds any further complexity.

That's effectively what we have, even with this addition. This text is just requiring implementations to support _at least_ a certain range, so that it can be relied upon for interoperability.

issues.title: ABNF sf-dictionary and sf-list do not allow empty lists
issues.author: reschke
issues.body: ...which are disallowed in serialization (as fields), but allowed in prose and in parsing.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Proposal:

~~~ abnf
sf-dictionary  = [ dict-member *( OWS "," OWS dict-member ) ]
~~~

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Does this apply to `sf-list` as well?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Yes, it does.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
As discussed elsewhere (somewhere; maybe last time around?), the ABNF is used to

> illustrate expected syntax of Structured Fields

Given that the first step of [Serializing Structured Fields](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis.html#name-serializing-structured-fiel) is:

> 1. If the structure is a Dictionary or List and its value is empty (i.e., it has no members), do not serialize the field at all (i.e., omit both the field-name and field-value).

This _is_ the "expected syntax."

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
That's a pretty fine distinction to draw, but I think that this is mostly OK in that case.

These look problematic in that case:  "[No structured data has been found; return members (which is empty).](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis.html#section-4.2.1-2.3.1)" and "[No structured data has been found; return dictionary (which is empty).](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis.html#section-4.2.2-2.3.1)"

My view is that this is an error condition instead.  I don't recall a decision to be tolerant of this particular deviation from the serialization process.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: I don't see that as an error condition at all -- an empty structure is valid, but the correct way to serialise that in HTTP/1.1 is to omit the field.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Are you saying that because the current definition does allow for variant serializations in some cases, this is just another case where the serialization is stricter than the parsing?

Maybe that ship has sailed already, but I can't see any good thing to come from empty fields.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: I'm confused by your statement, that's not where I was going. However, I agree regarding _no good from empty fields_ -- which is why the ABNF shouldn't include them.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Oh, I moved on, sorry.  I'm talking about the parsing being lenient about empty fields (for list and dictionary).  It doesn't need to be.  In which case the ABNF question resolves itself cleanly.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Ah, I see. Yes, I suspect the ship has sailed.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: I think we can close this issue - any more discussion?

issues.title: Support matching on fetch destination
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
In addition to matching dictionaries based on URL, it would be beneficial to be able to specify an optional [fetch destination](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-request-destination).

Not 100% sure it is necessary since a site-wide dictionary could still be used without specifying that it should only be advertised for documents as long as the origin only applies them on appropriate responses but it could be useful. A site-wide HTML dictionary was the use case referenced (which would only really be useful to be used on `document` requests).

Maybe as a `match-dest` field on the `Use-As-Dictionary` response.

issues.title: Strings, Tokens, and Display Strings
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
Display Strings are a superset of Strings, which are a superset of Tokens. This makes APIs more complex, and makes designers have to think about which structure to use.

A couple of thoughts:

1) Should we define best practice, that e.g., you should specify Token or String when you specify String -- similar to HTTP?

2) Should we define a new TokenOrString type to encourage this pattern (both in header definitions and APIs)?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Not sure it would be always a best practice, but there are certainly cases where it is. Thus describing the pattern and making it easier to use it sounds right to me.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body: I'm probably missing something, but why would we want header designers to use TokenOrString? Given, as you say, string is a superset, if you needed to use a string, why allow tokens too when you can just define the header to simply take string?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: For brevity. It happens in legacy header fields all the time (dunno whether that's a good reason, though).

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
This is because legacy fields didn't actually believe token and string are different types, right? Just that strings were optionally unquoted when you don't need quotes.

But guidance on the types is for new fields. And, for better or worse, structured fields went with a data model where quoted and unquoted are different types, rather than alternate encodings of the same types. Now that we've made them different, if you're making a new field that needs to represent string values, use strings.

It's true this means designers must pick between two similar types. Perhaps making them different was a mistake. (Though making them the same would mean multiple encodings, which is differently bad.) But we've already done that. It's too late to fully merge them because we'll break everyone who was told structures fields was ready to use and treated them differently. Without fully merging them, generic structured fields APIs are stuck using different types for them. So merging them back needs to be a per-field thing, which means fighting with your SF APIs. Instead, the best simplification we can manage is to *discourage* the TokenOrString half-measure in new fields and say you should just use one or the other.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body: To the first half of the bug, yes definitely define best practice! Just if the best practice we pick does not align with the data model we picked, we have done something seriously wrong.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
We already have best practice about Display Strings in the spec (in that we steer people away from them if they don't need them).

We have a separation between Tokens and Strings because they were visible on the wire in pre-existing headers, and we wanted to be able to retrofit / 'pave the cowpaths'. In _some_ cases, they are interchangeable; in others, they are not.

I suspect that if we documented best practice for new fields, we'd say "probably use Strings most of the time" because of the underlying reason I raised this issue for -- APIs have very natural mappings for Strings, but for Tokens you probably need some sort of wrapper object or equivalent strategy, so that you can distinguish them from Strings.

I'll put together a PR nudging people that way.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
Sounds good! So I guess the decision tree is then:
1. Do you need display strings? If yes, use that and only that.
2. Do you have a legacy reason to use tokens? If use, do whatever your legacy reasons need.
3. Otherwise, just use ASCII strings.

issues.title: Retrofit etag mapping: string, not byte sequence?
issues.author: bathos
issues.body:
Was [byte sequence](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis.html#name-byte-sequences) / `sf-binary` considered for [mapping ETag](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-retrofit.html#section-3.3) (or more precisely, mapping [opaque-tag](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.etag)) in the retrofit? Currently this uses [string](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-sfbis.html#name-strings) / `sf-string`, but:

1. Semantically, an `opaque-tag` value is opaque data, not string data.
2. The `opaque-tag` production permits [obs-text](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#fields.values), and `sf-string` cannot represent octets in that range.

This may well be a motivated decision rather than an oversight, but I couldn’t turn up any information about how the decision was made. I would have guessed that the general goal for mappings would be to choose the SFV type whose value space covers the widest range of pre-retrofit valid values possible and/or the SFV type with the closest semantics, though, and afaict that would be “byte sequence” in both cases here.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
obs-text and similar are there only for 'historical reasons' -- they're not to be encoraged, or considered 'normal' HTTP.

Every SF mapping has edge cases where technically valid values will fail SF parsing, and that's fine -- the idea isn't to match the original ABNF, because that's not possible in most cases, and also because the variance between the ABNF and real world are considerable.

issues.title: hash agility
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
The draft has a whole thing where you negotiate what hash function to use.  That seems overwrought.  Yes, you need to plan for the possibility that your chosen hash function is no longer considered good.  

For this use case, even a broken SHA-256 would still likely be fine, so I would instead advocate for a different strategy: if SHA-256 cannot be used, we'll build a new set of fields.

Then you can drop the whole negotiation mechanism and simplify things.

issues.title: Consider standardizing 7-day max-age cap for cookies set via JavaScript
issues.author: arichiv
issues.body: Two browsers are already doing this ([Safari](https://webkit.org/blog/8613/intelligent-tracking-prevention-2-1/) and [Brave](https://brave.com/privacy-features/#:~:text=Brave%20caps%20the%20life%20of,clear%20cookies%20at%20any%20time.)). It might be worth documenting in the standard.

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: cc @johannhof @johnwilander @bvandersloot-mozilla

comments.author: johannhof
comments.body: Given that two other browsers are explicitly deciding against this I'd be okay with providing the spec with a standardized means to do this but leaving the decision up to the implementer :)

issues.title: Add dictionary URL to sec-available-dictionary requests - Raised by Vlad Krasnov
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
I think it would make the proposal easier to support from a CDN POV if the Sec-Available-Dictionary included the dictionary URL and Etag, otherwise it requires too much state keeping.

Given a URL and an Etag it is pretty easy to have a best effort dictionary compression.

[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0091.html)
cc @vkrasnov

Moved from private ID [issue #9](https://github.com/pmeenan/i-d-compression-dictionary/issues/9)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
That would necessarily couple the use of a dictionary with the negotiation of the storage. They way it is currently set up, "use-as-dictionary" is one way to populate the dictionary but the dictionaries could also be pre-loaded into a client or otherwise negotiated.

As far as state, if you're passively observing traffic to compress and not actively managing the dictionaries, doesn't something like this work?

1. See response with "use-as-dictionary" response header
1. Store dictionary in key-value store, using the hash of the payload as the key
1. See request with "sec-available-dictionary" request header

For supporting static, offline resource compression:

* If a version of the resource is in cache compressed with the requested dictionary, serve it
* If not, kick off an async task to compress the cached full response with the dictionary (if one is available in KV)

For dynamic responses:

* If the dictionary is in KV, use it to compress the response

The main "state" that needs to be managed is the storage of the dictionary keys, indexed by the appropriate hash.

If the CDN is generating the dictionaries (or adding the headers) there's not much more state than that either.

I'm sure I'm probably hand-waving a lot of things that need to be done at scale when handling thousands of dictionaries and thousands of simultaneous requests for the same dictionary but I'd hate to add complexity to the negotiation itself if it isn't absolutely necessary.

[listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0092.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
One area I could see benefitting from reducing some overhead would be around the hash of the dictionary contents since it could be expensive to calculate.

One thing we could do there is have an additional (optional) field in the use-as-dictionary response where the origin could populate the hash as "hint" so caches or clients could use the advertised hash to determine if it needs to store the dictionary or if it already has it.

The language would have to be careful to require that the actual hash still be calculated before storing (or use) to be sure that the has represents the contents accurately but the hint could make the processing lighter weight, particularly in the CDN flow.

[listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0093.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
[listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0094.html) from @vkrasnov:

There are many possible architectures that can work of course, but the simplest one and most generic one is to hope the dictionary is present in your local cache and fetch it (with Cache-Control: only-if-cached; If-Match: etag).

I would definitely avoid using a KV for a generic solution, maybe in the far future for high value use case.

I can't simply store an arbitrary number of dictionaries in KV, this can very well explode, and some intelligent eviction is needed.

We also don't want to store multiple versions of the same resource compressed with different algorithms, even for statically compressed assets. It consumes valuable space that could be used to cache other assets instead.

In any case, having the URL and ETag (and obviously ETags are not always present either) allows us to have something in production almost out of the box, having just the cache requires building new stuff, which is a much higher bar for entrance.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
I have a few concerns with making the URL available (for URL-delivered dictionaries). It's possible we could add another optional header as a request hint but there's a risk of middle-boxes holding it wrong.

* You would still need to verify that the hash of the dictionary matches the requested hash before using it. Re-calculating the hash on every access could be pretty expensive (feels like verifying the hash before writing would be hit less often).
* The same URL could represent multiple dictionaries with different hashes (think a well-known URL like fb.js that does in-place upgrades).

Indexing the entry by URL and hash could potentially solve the issues but could it not just as easily be indexed by the hash without the URL since the hash is the unique index?

issues.title: CORS is inappropriate - Raised by Roy T. Fielding
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
For the existing draft, there is a lot of unnecessary confusion regarding features of fetch, like CORS, that don't make any sense from a security perspective. That's not what CORS is capable of covering, nor how it is implemented in practice, so reusing it doesn't make any sense.

[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0130.html)
cc @royfielding 

Moved from private ID [issue #7](https://github.com/pmeenan/i-d-compression-dictionary/issues/7)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
CORS covers privacy from a browser perspective as far as the readability of responses relative to the origin of the containing document which is exactly the context that it is needed for here.

The concern that it takes care of is to make sure that responses that shouldn't be readable from the document context of the client can't be exposed to oracle timing attacks (because there won't be any client-opaque responses).

HTTP itself doesn't really have the same document framing context and need for protecting read access of individual responses on a shared connection by clients running in different document contexts.

[listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0131.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
From @royfielding:

I still don't see how CORS applies to the draft.

If the origin is choosing both the available dictionaries and whether or not to apply them to a given response, why is the context of a request relevant to the nature or credibility of the compressed response? Neither one is controlled by the context. The origin server isn't going to attack itself. The client might choose not to advertise an available dictionary based on the context, but I don't see how ignoring a server's valid response makes a difference.

I assume the content of the response after decompressions would still be restricted by CORS, but that should already be defined by fetch; I wouldn't expect this document to specify it.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
The concern raised by the security team is that a client could abuse dictionary compression and a timing attack to expose the contents of a CORS-opaque response. The contents themselves would already be prevented from being exposed directly but there's a theoretical risk that an origin serving private data through dictionary compression could expose that data unexpectedly in a cross-origin timing attack.

I don't know enough about the practicality of timing-based oracle attacks using dictionary compression and the level of control that an attacker would need to have on either the payload of the response or the payload of the dictionary but in an abundance of caution we are recommending that servers avoid the problem entirely and don't use dictionaries in cross-origin opaque responses (even if it would be blocked from being processed in the client).

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
The shared-brotli draft has a fairly good write-up on the CRIME attack concerns which is what the CORS mitigations prevent (by making sure there is no mix of public and private data and only allowing for public data):

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-vandevenne-shared-brotli-format-08#section-10

Most of the CORS protections are on the client side and not something that needs to be exposed to HTTP or for origins to be concerned about.  If a server never mixes public and private data or doesn't talk to a client that needs to partition that kind of data (i.e. not serving to a browser) then it can also ignore the one remaining case called out in the spec.

If there's a chance that public/private data will me mixed AND the server is serving content to a browser (or other client that implements CORS) then there is a risk of a timing attack being able to reveal the private content if the crossorigin not-allowed case uses dictionary compression.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Closing this as the need for CORS for the client protection should be well documented at this point (and mostly applies to the WHATWG side of things in fetch processing but there is one case here where people should at least be aware of a possible attack vector if not handled).

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
I have no problem with this being a requirement for the fetch implementation (or for script-enabled browser implementations in general). However, I still don't understand how the requirements in 9.3.2.* will pass muster for the IESG and RFC Ed reviews without a normative reference to the Fetch spec. A link to a web page isn't enough.

Personally, I think these details should be moved to the fetch spec (where the right people will read it). The bits needed for the IETF are covered in 9.3.1 and the first two paragraphs of 9.3.2:
```
9.3.1.  Cross-origin protection

   To make sure that a dictionary can only impact content from the same
   origin where the dictionary was served, the URL Pattern used for
   matching a dictionary to requests (Section 2.1.1) is guaranteed to be
   for the same origin that the dictionary is served from.

9.3.2.  Response readability

   For clients, like web browsers, that provide additional protection
   against the readability of the payload of a response and against user
   tracking, additional protections MUST be taken to make sure that the
   use of dictionary-based compression does not reveal information that
   would not otherwise be available.

   In these cases, dictionary compression MUST only be used when both
   the dictionary and the compressed response are fully readable by the
   client.
```
and then everything else in 9.3 (and below) can be a replaced by a non-normative reference to fetch.

Otherwise, this should be a normative reference and the several links to fetch replaced with an appropriate [FETCH] entry in 11.1.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body: To be clear, I don't object to moving forward with this as is, but I don't believe will be allowed as is, unless the chairs have some extra special hand-waving skills I haven't seen yet.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: I almost take that as a challenge...

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
There is processing model stuff that is browser-specific that will be in fetch but the parts in 9.3.2.1 and 9.3.2.2 are the things that are required from any HTTP server that might be used to serve sensitive information to a browser.

I stripped out as much as I could but there is a timing attack that can be performed in fetching cross-origin content that would allow a client to "read" the response even if it doesn't have access to it on the client side and the only way to prevent it entirely is to not serve a response in the first place. By making it only a requirement when the CORS headers are present, it allows servers that never talk to browsers to not have to consider it but it really does need to be considered carefully for any server that might serve responses to a browser (or anything else that implements cross-origin readability restrictions).

Making the protection non-normative would make the privacy protections optional and risk servers not being aware or necessarily implementing it (and it is the same side-channel timing attack that killed SDCH).

If we're comfortable making that change then I can make the fetch spec parts authoritative about the CORS restrictions on both clients and servers but it would probably have to be a normative reference.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
Oh, I see, the server description contains things a server MUST do (or not do) based on the values received in those fields when they indicate a cross-origin request. I was reading them as things a client would verify after receipt of the Response, since we usually don't rely on a bad client sending "I'm good" information in request header fields.

[BTW, this is why the main HTTP specs always target requirements to a role instead of making them neutral requirements on a message.]

In that case, these are definitely normative requirements, similar to conditional requests. HTTP servers don't normally parse CORS header fields, since pre-flights and such are handled by back-end applications (not httpd).

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
I'll make another pass over the CORS language tomorrow to make it clearer
and make sure it only covers the parts that servers need to handle for
fetch-compliant clients. The client bits can and should be in fetch.

issues.title: Should not use Content-encoding - Raised by Roy T. Fielding
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
I think implementation of such through content-codings is fundamentally misguided because it changes the resource itself and impacts all caching along the chain of requests in ways that are non-recoverable. That is due to the lost metadata and variance on whatever request field is used to indicate that some downstream client can grok some possible dictionary.

In short, it looks like an easy solution for a browser, but will wreak havoc with the larger architecture of the Web.

The right way to do this is to implement it as a transfer encoding that can be decoded without loss or confusion with the unencoded resource, which would require extending h2 and h3 to support that feature of HTTP/1.1.

[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0130.html)
cc @royfielding 

Moved from private ID [issue #6](https://github.com/pmeenan/i-d-compression-dictionary/issues/6)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
The decoded version of the resource is unchanged. It's not fundamentally different than brotli which happens to include a default dictionary and the caching is guaranteed to be maintained in a consistent way as long as "Vary" works on "Accept-Encoding" as well as whatever header negotiates the dictionary.

Even without the dictionary, if something in the middle doesn't know how to process one of the content-encodings (and needs to be able to access the content) then the accept-encoding should be modified to only include encodings that it knows how to work with.

This isn't really notably different than "br" or "zstd".

Moving the compression down into the transport layer is what we tried before but failed to navigate the browser security issues because the transport layer doesn't have the context of which responses need to be opaque, which responses are partitioned across document or frame boundaries, etc and that the dictionary compression could be used to perform oracle attacks across those boundaries.

[listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0131.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
@royfielding if the response includes the hash of the dictionary that was used for the compression so that the response is self-contained and independent of the request, would that address your concerns?

That is being discussed in #2636 and would allow for other ways of negotiating dictionaries (but would require a new header to identify the used dictionary).

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
The choice of dictionary is one of the things, but I think overall this is a much larger problem and I don't know if it was sufficiently discussed at the meeting (I missed). Part of it is not knowing when this feature will be used, or specifically how common the variance will be.

In general, a new content-coding causes potentially significant harm to shared cache storage just because it exists.

1. Servers have a new variance on choice of coding
    I.e., it saves bytes so that must be good, right?  No, it's bad because it only saves bytes in aggregate if only the best coding is chosen per resource, and that coding is implemented by every client requesting that resource; if not, there's a threshold where the number of encodings that have to be sent/stored downstream are more of a burden than the improvement gained by one better encoding.

2. Clients have a new variance on Accept-Encoding
     When user agents support different encodings (or even just a different order in Accept-Encoding), the caches have difficulty following the rules for Vary. This is a problem of permutations, so going from N=3 to N=4 (or in this case N=4 + number of allowed dictionaries) is an exponential increase, and that will get very expensive very fast.
     We could make that argument for brotli because "one more encoding" with a standard dictionary would be commonly implemented (in practice) as a per-resource replacement rather than "yet another choice". This does not seem to be the case for the current draft, which would allow for the same resource to be compressed using different dictionaries, presumably based on whichever dictionary the client already has in cache that matches for the target URI.

3. The existence of other potential encodings requires that Vary encompass all potential variances and that ETag values include the variation chosen for this representation (usually this means identifying the coding/dictionary inside the entity-tag). This, in turn, has significant ramifications for conditional requests, range requests, and cache evictions because it is now much harder to know when a new variant represents new content, meaning all the existing ones are stale, or just a new variant of the old content.

4. Facts about how the content is encoded (and even what the metadata looked like before it was encoded) can be included as new header fields (if needed before receipt of the content) or within the leading parts of the encoding. Either one is self-descriptive. But that increases the amount of data sent, which might overwhelm the benefit received from a better encoding.

We could spend ages finding ways to work around or limit implementations such that a new coding is justifiable as an addition to HTTP. I have no doubt that it would be possible. However, I think it is the wrong approach unless we are very clear that the goals for this compression are resource-specific rather than on-the-fly performance improvement.

Transfer-Encoding does not have these problems. It was designed for on-the-fly performance improvement without changing the response metadata (other than requiring that it be decoded as part of processing). It has a separate problem, being that chunked is necessary when used over 1.x, but that usually comes with benefits of its own. It is much harder to deploy across intermediaries, but possible to deploy on one side of an intermediary without impacting the other side. Those are the trade-offs for on-the-fly compression.

The question I have boils down to whether this compression is expected to be highly variable per resource or just specific to each resource. Will it be N=4 or N=4+, and is the cost of 3->4 really worth it?

I can see the draft going either way, and that scares me.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
For the scale of improvement (for the resources impacted), we see results that are 60-90% smaller than brotli which is orders of magnitude bigger than we get from deflate -> brotli (for example). A few bytes added to headers or elsewhere aren't going to make a difference and, honestly, if it does then those resources are probably not appropriate for dictionary compression in the first place.

## Variants
As far as the variants, we added the `ttl` param to minimize the number of different dictionaries that will be in the wild at a time and recommend that it be adjusted based on release cadance of the dictionaries but it currently defaults to 1 year. We could go the other way and default to a short ttl (say, 7 days) and require origins to be explicit if they want longer-lived dictionaries.

The variants introduced by the encodings themselves should only be present when a matching dictionary is provided (e.g. `br-d` would not be advertised unless there is also an `Available-Dictionary`). The main cause of variants that they would introduce would be from clients supporting a different set of encodings or ordering them differently (as they do today).

We could improve that situation by requiring that the encodings be in alphabetical order when dictionaries are being used which would help get cross-client consistency in the accept-encoding header. It would still vary by the encodings supported by the clients but the new dictionary encodings wouldn't add any permutations. We could also require that the base encoding be present if the dictionary variant is present (`br-d` requires that `br` also be supported).

## Encoding
The encoding itself has a few different deployment models that also favor using Content-Encoding over Transfer-Encoding.  In the dynamic compression case where the edge is doing the compression, it doesn't make much difference between the two from a complexity or performance perspective (though there are HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 complexities around transfer-encoding).

The more interesting case for the Content-Encoding side is when the compression is done at build/publish time. The static artifacts (css, js, wasm) can be compressed using previous releases as dictionaries and stored on-disk as dictionary-compressed artifacts with the hash as part of the file name. At serving time, it can be a quick lookup at the origin to see if the asset is available with the `Available-Dictionary` hash as part of the file name and fall-back to the full file if it isn't. This eliminates the compression from the serving flow and largely just requires cache support (as long as the boxes along the path aren't trying to inspect the contents).

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
> We could improve that situation by requiring that the encodings be in alphabetical order when dictionaries are being used which would help get cross-client consistency in the accept-encoding header. It would still vary by the encodings supported by the clients but the new dictionary encodings wouldn't add any permutations. We could also require that the base encoding be present if the dictionary variant is present (`br-d` requires that `br` also be supported).
> ##

What about leaving the Accept-Encoding as the base encoding and defining Available-Dictionary as implying br-d if br is present for A-E? A response that used br-d would Vary on A-E and Available-Dictionary, whereas a response that used the standard dictionary would only need to Vary on A-E.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body: I should add many of the worrisome questions don't matter for content > 10MB (or so) because they would be evicted too fast, so a custom dictionary is going to be a huge benefit for those resources, regardless of variance.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
> What about leaving the Accept-Encoding as the base encoding and defining Available-Dictionary as implying br-d if br is present for A-E? A response that used br-d would Vary on A-E and Available-Dictionary, whereas a response that used the standard dictionary would only need to Vary on A-E.

If A-E only had the base encodings then an Available-Dictionary request would match a cached standard dictionary response that had only varied on A-E.  By having the dictionary-specific encodings on A-E then it will require the dictionary compression be taken into account.

If there's no dictionary-compressed version of the asset then it will end up generating a duplicate cache entry (on middle boxes) but I think we'd be better off if we could focus on minimizing those cases by specifying match pattern capabilities and defaults that encourage dictionaries to only match the requests that are very likely to be dictionary-compressed.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
> If A-E only had the base encodings then an Available-Dictionary request would match a cached standard dictionary response that had only varied on A-E. By having the dictionary-specific encodings on A-E then it will require the dictionary compression be taken into account.

If both are available, the match would go to the smaller encoded variant. If only the standard compression is available, a cache would be able to deliver the one it has, whereas the origin server can choose whether to use the standard dictionary or the available dictionary as it sees fit. I don't see any downsides.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body: Well, the downside would be that the sender of Available-Dictionary would have to accept both standard and custom dictionaries in response, for any of the standard dictionary encodings (with -d alternatives) that it sends in A-E.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Assuming we're talking about a cache in front of whatever generates the responses, if a dictionary-compressed response was not generated before a standard-dictionary response got cached then the dictionary-compressed response would never enter the cache since the standard-dictionary response would always match.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
> Well, the downside would be that the sender of Available-Dictionary would have to accept both standard and custom dictionaries in response, for any of the standard dictionary encodings (with -d alternatives) that it sends in A-E.

That's likely to be the case all of the time anyway for when the server can't generate a dictionary-compressed response. I guess it could fall back to gzip or a different encoding but the same client code that decompresses the dictionary schemes can also decode the non-dictionary schemes.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
> Assuming we're talking about a cache in front of whatever generates the responses

No, an origin server (including CDN) can do whatever it wants in terms of selecting a representation. This would only make a difference for shared caches for which there was no specific origin config, and in those cases the origin can choose to add Available-Dictionary to Vary on a standard dictionary response if they want the request to be passed through.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
> No, an origin server (including CDN) can do whatever it wants in terms of selecting a representation. This would only make a difference for shared caches for which there was no specific origin config, and in those cases the origin can choose to add Available-Dictionary to Vary on a standard dictionary response if they want the request to be passed through.

Ah, yes, sorry.  Then the only concern would be assuming `zstd-d` support could be inferred by `gzip, br, zstd` and `Available-Dictionary`.  It's likely to be the case but, for example, Chrome 117 supports zstd but only dictionaries on brotli (118 added zstd-d).

Other than the added bytes on the request, there shouldn't be any difference on the variants by including `zstd-d` and `br-d` on the requests, particularly if we require the standard version be supported when the dictionary versions are and that the ordering be deterministic.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
Working through the edge cases here, the PR above has some tweaks to reduce the default variations (lowerd default dictionary expiration to 7 days and require clients to normalize the accept-encoding header so they are more likely to be consistent across clients).

For range requests I'm thinking it makes the most sense to just not allow range requests to be make using dictionary compression. Browsers already don't allow anything except for identity for range requests so it would just be making it explicit for all clients.

For etags, there's not a technical issue since the HTTP RFC requires the etags represent each encoding separately but I can see where that would be difficult in a revalidation case to keep track of the different etags and know if they represent the same resource or not (when applying compression somewhere other than the origin). It's not really different that the case of gzip but it does add more variations and the variations may be opaque. 

Would it be useful to not allow `Content-encoding:` of a dictionary encoding type to also carry `Etag:` and if they are both provided to ignore the etag on the client, not use it as a validator and not request dictionary encoding when revalidation a previous resource that was delivered with an etag? It doesn't feel like either of those would be too restrictive for apps and it would avoid propogating more confusion around the interaction between etags, caches and content-encoding.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
We talked about parts of this at IETF 118 today and the decision was made to not add any encoding normalization and that caches should be normalizing the `Accept-Encoding` and managing their caches.

As far as the original topic about `Content-Encoding` (CE) vs `Transfer-Encoding` (TE), I think we've addressed why CE is appropriate since origins will be pre-compressing resources with dictionaries and storing the variants which is appropriate for CE and not TE.

If there are specific concerns that still remain around etags or otherwise making it easier for caches to work well, please open up separate issues and we can work though those in isolation.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body: Already closed, but I wanted to note that I looked through this again for draft 04 and I don't have any more concerns after the proposed change in #2787. The use of CE is justified by the use cases and excessive cache variance will be avoided by only sending the dictionary-aware content-codings when the client has a matching dictionary and wants it to be applied.

issues.title: Response should include dictionary used for encoding - raised by Martin Thomson
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
I don't understand how a client determines which dictionary was used by the server. It seems like the response depends on the request, which is fragile (and doesn't allow clients to advertise multiple dictionaries, which seems likely with Use-As-Dictionary as it is).

[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0102.html)
cc @martinthomson 

Moved from private ID [issue #3](https://github.com/pmeenan/i-d-compression-dictionary/issues/3)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
For identifying the dictionary, it's worth noting that the spec requires that the client advertise a SINGLE dictionary that it supports but yes, the response depends on the dictionary identified in the request. This also helps with minimizing the variants that caches would need to store since the response needs to be varied on the request's available dictionary (and multiple would explode the permutations). It wouldn't hurt to echo the dictionary hash in the response which would allow for other mechanisms of advertising dictionaries but that also carries the cost of complicating the vary logic (would need to vary based on whatever request header was used to negotiate the dictionary that ended up being used).

[Listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0104.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Dictionary hash used is now in the response headers.

issues.title: Split into two documents - Raised by Martin Thomson
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
Would it be worth considering a split for Use-As-Dictionary? Or do we just need more information? I have far less confidence in that component myself.

If this all stays as experimental, a single document is fine. However, if delta encoding ends up being a slam dunk and we need more information on Use-As-Dictionary, then it might be good to take delta encoding as a proposed standard and leave Use-As-Dictionary as an experiment.

[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0103.html)
cc @martinthomson

Moved from private ID [issue #5](https://github.com/pmeenan/i-d-compression-dictionary/issues/5)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
It could make sense since setting the dictionary in a response doesn't have to be the only way that client's populate available dictionaries but the dictionary selection is somewhat entangled with the subsequent request.

There's a good chance that fields will need to be added to Use-As-Dictionary (I just added "type", for example, to allow for forward-compatibility with non-raw dictionaries) but some of those changes will also cascade to the content encoding. Zstandard-specific or Brotli-specific dictionary formats, for example, would require new content encodings as well as some explanation for what to send in the Accept-Encoding when using format-specific dictionaries.

[listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0104.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Closing this as we have been evolving the various parts of the draft together and it has been working well to keep it all combined.

issues.title: Match URLs should not allow full URLs - Raised by Ilari Liusvaara
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
Allowing absolute URLs in match is a footgun, since dictionaries are restricted to same-origin. I don't think any of the usual URI productions are suitable here.

I think most suitable would be 'segment *( "/" segment )', where segment is the production from RFC 3986.

[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023AprJun/0309.html)

Moved from private ID [issue #2](https://github.com/pmeenan/i-d-compression-dictionary/issues/2)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
Even though the URLs must be same-origin, there's some benefit to allowing arbitrary URL formatting to allow for the clean use of relative URLs. They are all going to be expanded to absolute URLs anyway and it wouldn't break anything if someone chose to include the protocol and host parts (though there's no benefit to sending them).

[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023AprJun/0312.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
There is talk about using [URLPattern](https://wicg.github.io/urlpattern/) with an implicit base URL.

The current plan would be to use the version that takes a patternString and have the baseUrl be set automatically to the URL of the request (and to limit the supported tokens).  That mode would still allow for full URLs.

There is also the possibility to break up the `path` and `search` components into different `use-as-dictionary` keys in which case it would prevent full URLs. There's some discussion of what the default `search` pattern behavior should be if one isn't specified though (match all or only match an empty search string).

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
It is really hard to imagine why we would go to all the trouble of optimizing data compression and yet not care about repeating the origin data in the header fields (even though the client is already known to have that data and is required to ignore it if provided). If we don't need it, don't send it on the wire.

It is a foot gun because a lazy implementer (the kind of person who never reads an RFC) will use the full URL provided for the match because it's easier than remembering (or finding) the request context. I know it's silly, but I have seen a lot worse.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Closing this now that we have switched to using URLPattern and the path and query components are explicitly split (and the only settable components).

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Re-opening this because the [URLPattern integration changes](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2689) don't allow for explicitly preventing the origin from being included in the match string.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Closing this again as we are sticking with the URLPattern change. While it allows for users to waste bytes by specifying an origin, a hard requirement on not allowing it is not worth the complexity change of not using URLPattern.

issues.title: Wildcard matching - Raised by Martin Thomson and Roy Fielding
issues.author: pmeenan
issues.body:
From @martinthomson:

For what it's worth, I like Roy's idea of prefix+suffix matching in place of arbitrary wildcards. Pattern matching is more expensive than simple prefix/suffix matches.

Also, "*" is a valid path character in HTTP. Maybe that was unwise, but that's what RFC 3986 says. Probably not a big deal (you can avoid using it if you plan to use this feature), but still.

Moved from private ID [issue #1](https://github.com/pmeenan/i-d-compression-dictionary/issues/1)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
[Original listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0130.html) from @royfielding:

Using * as a wildcard in arbitrary URL references is a foot gun. It would make more sense to have two attributes, prefix and suffix, and have them only match within the URL path (i.e., exclude the origin and query portions, preventing matches on full URIs or user-supplied query parameters). That is far more likely to get right than allowing things like "//example.com/////****"

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
The origin is already excluded from being configurable. There is some discussion about only supporting relative paths but allowing for full URLs just made it easier to reference the existing URL RFC without having to re-define just the parts we need to support.

Query params can't necessarily be excluded and some sites are going to want to allow for either fixed query param matching or wildcard (and maybe for both the static and dynamic use case). Allowing for * allows for some flexibility in site URL structure while still keeping the matching relatively simple and without the complexity of [URLPattern](https://github.com/WICG/urlpattern/blob/main/mdn-drafts/QUICK-REFERENCE.md)

[listserv response](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023JulSep/0131.html)

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
From @royfielding:

I get really nervous when I see shell syntax mixed with URI syntax as a form of pattern matching. We usually don't do that on servers. Regular expression syntax is an even bigger foot gun, but we already have that implemented. Alternatively, the URI Template syntax is a form of pattern matching that is more specific than a wildcard.

If prefix/suffix is insufficient, then maybe "contains" could be there as well, though I'd seriously question why a site would want this much flexibility.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
@royfielding Not sure that it helps any, but the server wouldn't be doing any path matching. It just provides the path string as a hint to the client for where the dictionary would be usable (doesn't need to be validated on the server side at request time - no harm if a resource outside of the path is compressed).

I'll do some browsing over the next week or so and build up a library of URL patterns for static resources and "similar" HTML pages and see what things look like in the wild.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
Sorry, took me a bit to get back to the pattern matching search.

For HTML content things are kind of difficult if you also want the root page on your origin compressed. If we allow for matching on the `destination` (#2625) then it could do something like `use-as-dictionary: match: "/*", match-dest: "document"`. Otherwise, if you want a separate dictionary for product listing pages vs search pages, Amazon (for example) has a `/dp/` in the path but it's not always at the beginning.

I looked at a really quick sampling of subresource URLs in the HTTP Archive and didn't take long to find lots of cases that have more complicated patterns with versions and hashes on either side of parts of the URL.

```
https://www.nadri4u.com/shopimages/ss2565/template/work/3162/common.css?r=1523930855
```

would probably need something like `../*/common.css*`. This case if we allowed separating out the path and search string we could treat as a suffix but there are lots of other cases where it isn't as simple.

```
https://api.manufaktura.cz/api/tenantboot/2_XBBZ/app~80a78feb.css
```

Would need something like `/api/tenantboot/*/app~*.css` or `../*/app~*.css`

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
The server config is where the hint would be coming from, which is why I am concerned from a origin server standpoint, but I should just get used to people using the * as a wildcard. We do use it, but frequently fail to define exactly what it includes (or excludes), and almost always end up having to provide full regex eventually.

However, wildcard * seems to be more common these days in CDN/AWS configs.

I think if the document is clear that it applies to the path and optional query component only, then we transmit fewer characters and limit possible abuse. Specifically, that would be the [origin-form of RFC9112](url)
```
  origin-form    = absolute-path [ "?" query ]
```
as would appear in HTTP/1.x origin requests after being extracted from the target URI.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Closing this as we have moved to use URLPattern as discussed at IETF 118.  Feel free to open a new issue if there are concerns specific to how URLPattern is being used.

issues.title: ZSDCH
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/learnmore-zsdch-compression

There are aspects to this design that are appealing to me.  (The uncoordinated deployment of this technology is a matter that I'll be taking up with colleagues at Microsoft.)  It would be good to explore how this differs from the proposed design in the current draft, along with the consequences of that (for implementation, deployment, performance, architecture, etc...).

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
FWIW, I talked to the team at MS that had implemented it and, as far as I understood, they were exploring migrating to compression dictionaries instead.

It looks like it is very similar to the original SDCH except it is no longer blocking in the request path and uses zstd instead of vcdiff+gzip.

Fundamentally it is very similar to the dynamic use case for compression dictionaries but there are some key differences:
* Dictionaries appear to be scoped to the full origin.
* Multiple dictionaries can be advertised as available (we intentionally prevented that to keep Vary permutations in check).

I'm pretty sure that the implementation and use cases are close enough that they can be handled by the compression dictionaries work (and we'd be happy to get input for any areas where the zsdch implementation is easier to work with).

It's particularly interesting that both were developed independently around the same time, largely from teams that miss having the benefits that had come with SDCH before it was turned down.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Closing this out as all of the relevant parties are involved in the compression dictionary draft and experimenting with the Chrome origin trials.

issues.title: Signatures - Clarify usage of plus character when encoding query parameters
issues.author: robelcik
issues.body:
Hello,

In the section **2.2.8. Query Parameters** we can read that:
> Encode the nameString or valueString using the "percent-encode after encoding" process defined by the "application/x-www-form-urlencoded serializing" section of [[HTMLURL](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#application/x-www-form-urlencoded)], which results in an [[ASCII](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc20)] string.

As I understand the referred specification, spaces should be replaced by plus character, which is indicated by the last word below, which is "true":
(note, that it's different than encoding described in RFC 3986)
> Let value be the result of running [percent-encode after encoding](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#string-percent-encode-after-encoding) with encoding, tuple’s value, the [application/x-www-form-urlencoded percent-encode set](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#application-x-www-form-urlencoded-percent-encode-set), and true.

However, the example in 2.2.8. shows that "+" characters are replaced by "%20".

Could you please, clarify it?

Also, it would be nice, I think, to add more examples. For example "raw" GET requests containing sequences like "-", "%2D", "%48".

Also, path and query encoding could be mentioned in `@target-uri` and `@request-target`. But I'm not sure whether that is relevant.

Thank you in advance for reply.


Regards,
Robert

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
Hi Robert - The signatures spec is with the RFC editor and the text is, for all intents and purposes, final and will not be changed. To answer your specific questions though:

The canonical encoding from HTMLURL's query parameters doesn't use "+" for spaces, it uses "%20". However, it's acceptable to parse a "+" as a space. Consequently, to get to a canonical form, the signer and verifier are required to take the nameString and valueString values and first parse them into raw values then re-encode them, so that corner cases like this can be handled in a consistent manner. The example in question was specifically chosen to show this very property.

More examples are always nice, but in the end you have to balance the length of the document with the number of examples you include. One thing that I'd like to do though is put more examples on the playground website, https://httpsig.org , for people to play with directly, and we can show some of that encoding in play from a real library.

The target-uri and request-target components don't apply any additional encoding beyond what's specified, so what's in the text is what's expected. That means that a URL or query coming in with a "+" treats that as a "+" and not a space, since since that's the character that's actually passed in.

I hope this helps clarify things. I am closing the issue because the signatures specification is not in a position to take any additional changes.

comments.author: robelcik
comments.body:
Hello!

Thank you for explanation. Now I understand your intentions, 😃 

However, I'd like to nitpick a bit. I asked the initial question because I was confused. In section 2.2.8., there is a reference to "[application/x-www-form-urlencoded serializing](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#urlencoded-serializing)". That section says, as far as I understand, that _spaceAsPlus_ should be _true_.
![image](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/assets/12409950/0432ab4d-5094-445b-9a69-a5f6e17c3ae0)

When looking at section "[Percent-encoded bytes](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#percent-encoded-bytes)", one can see that default value of _spaceAsPlus_ is _false_ which, I assume, is what you refer to speaking of "canonical encoding".
![image](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/assets/12409950/85b3c362-e5cd-4efb-860e-75c2eeb80a7b)

I was thinking that someone could get confused as I was, 🤓 

Regards,
Robert

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: Yes, the intent in the text is to refer to the percent encode after encoding with the space as plus set to false, its default value. I can understand the confusion here, so I'll see if we can add any clarifying text to the section during final RFC editor review, whenever that happens.

issues.title: Change of "origin"
issues.author: kazuho
issues.body:
At the moment, section 1.2 (Problems) start with the following sentence:
>    Classic HTTP CONNECT proxies are identified by an origin.  The proxy does not have a path of its own.  This prevents any origin from hosting multiple distinct proxy services.

I totally get what it tries to say, but it is confusing if not incorrect.

[RFC 9110 section 9.3.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-connect) states that a CONNECT request is handled by a "proxy" and the target specified by the "host:port" tuple is the "origin."

Therefore, HTTP CONNECT proxies are not identified by an origin. Rather, they are identified by the user's proxy settings.

I think we'd better update the problem statement, and might also consider pointing out that the definition of "origin" will be different between CONNECT and connect-tcp (or use different terms to identify the CONNECT target and the entity that creates a tunnel in order to avoid confusion, maybe?).

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: PS. Practical example showcasing the side effect of the change to the definition is that the way to authenticate becomes different; when a client tries to establish a CONNECT tunnel with authentication, it uses "proxy-authorization" header, whereas when a client tries to establish a connect-tcp tunnel, it uses "authorization." I think it's worth noting.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I'm realizing that this spec has the opportunity to fix the origin issues present in regular CONNECT. While we're there it'd be great to clarify how connect-tcp interacts with Alt-Svc because it's unclear for CONNECT. I sent some more [details to the mailing list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2023OctDec/0132.html) about why it's unclear for CONNECT.

issues.title: [rfc6265bis] SameSite=Strict cookie isolation on cross-site windows
issues.author: Pedro-Bernardo
issues.body:
We are reporting on the behavior of `samesite=strict` cookies on cross-site windows opened through `window.open` that goes against our assumptions (implied by the current specification) on when and how `samesite=strict` cookies should be isolated. Breaking these assumptions can lead to security issues, allowing the bypass of `samesite=strict` cookies as a defense mechanism against CSRF and XS-Leak attacks.

## 1. Overview

The following table shows  when `samesite=strict` cookies are attached to requests associated with `iframe`s and pages opened through `window.open` (where :x: stands for *not attached*/*not accessible* and :white_check_mark: for *attached*/*accessible*):

| Action/Element        | iframe | window.open        | 
| --------------------- | ------ | ------------------ |
| page load             | :x:    | :x:                |
| document.cookie       | :x:    | :white_check_mark: |
| subresource load      | :x:    | :white_check_mark: |
| user-initiated reload | :x:    | :x:                |
| JavaScript reload     | :x:    | :white_check_mark: |

The behavior of `samesite=strict` cookies regarding page reloads for pages opened through `window.open` from a cross-site position is evident from the [specification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-12#section-8.8.5):

> **Requests issued for reloads triggered through user interface elements** (such as a refresh button on a toolbar) **are same-site only if the reloaded document was originally navigated to via a same-site request**. This **differs from the handling of other reload navigations, which are always same-site if top-level**, since the source navigable's active document is precisely the document being reloaded.
> This special handling of reloads triggered through a user interface element **avoids sending `SameSite` cookies on user-initiated reloads if they were withheld on the original navigation** (i.e., if the initial navigation were cross-site). 

Currently, the specification mandates blocking cookies on user-initiated page reloads but not on reloads performed through JavaScript. We think that `samesite=strict` cookies should also be blocked in this scenario, as this interaction between JavaScript navigations and `samesite=strict` cookies allows attackers to bypass the restrictions imposed by `samesite=strict` (see 2.1). Additionally, we verified that `samesite=strict` cookies, even when not sent in the top-level request that loads a page, are still attached to requests that load subresources for that page. This behavior is not explicitly defined in the specification. However, its counterpart (setting a cookie) is defined as follows:

> The "SameSite" attribute affects cookie creation as well as delivery. Cookies which assert "samesite=lax" or "samesite=strict" cannot be set in responses to cross-site subresource requests, or cross-site nested navigations.

Although these requests are not cross-site, they are performed implicitly by a page navigated from a cross-site context, effectively enabling an attacker to perform authenticated cross-site requests (see 2.1), or cookie tossing attacks.

> **If the reload navigation were instead considered same-site, and sent all the initially withheld `SameSite` cookies, the security benefits of withholding the cookies in the first place would be nullified**

Following this argument, when considering that user-initiated page reloads are deemed cross-site and therefore do not attach `samesite=strict` cookies, it seems reasonable to assume both JavaScript navigations and subresource loads should also not attach `samesite=strict` cookies, as they are also transparent to the user.

## 2. Security Implications
### 2.1 samesite=strict cookies bypass and CSRF

It is possible to abuse the previously described behavior to bypass CSRF protections An attacker can forge same-site requests starting from a cross-site position by abusing gadgets that result in secondary same-site requests. An example of one of these gadgets is a JavaScript-based redirect that performs a redirection using attacker-controlled data. Here is a possible attack flow:

1. Victim visits https://good.com/set, setting the cookie `foo=bar; samesite=strict` cookie for domain `good.com`.
2. Victim then visits https://attacker.com/, which executes `window.open("https://good.com/redir?q=/")`
	1. The request to https://good.com/redir?q=/ is cross-site, so it does not attach `samesite=strict` cookies
3. https://good.com/redir?q=/ performs a navigation to the value of the URL parameter `q` through `document.location.href = '${parsedURL.query['q']}'`
	1. This triggers a request to https://good.com/, which attaches `samesite=strict` cookies, allowing an attacker to make authenticated requests from a cross-site position

A similar scenario was discussed in this [post](https://portswigger.net/web-security/csrf/bypassing-samesite-restrictions#bypassing-samesite-restrictions-using-on-site-gadgets).

Besides JavaScript redirections, other requests, such as subresource loads, could also be exploited to subvert the security assumptions granted by `samesite=strict` cookies.

### 2.2 XS-Leaks 

`samesite=lax` cookies effectively defend against certain classes of XS-Leaks attacks. However, `window.open`-based attacks are still possible since `samesite=lax`cookies are attached to top-level cross-site requests. Since `samesite=strict` cookies are not attached to top-level cross-site requests,  they have been deemed an effective mitigation against `window.open`-based XS-Leaks. 

As discussed in 2.1, gadgets that allow attackers to forge same-site requests from a cross-site position can be leveraged for XS-Leaks. An example would be a page that performs a stateful subresource load, which modifies the page DOM. If an attacker opens this page through `window.open`, `samesite=strict` cookies will not be attached, but following subresource loads in the new page will attach these cookies, leading to state-dependent changes to the DOM, which could be measured by the attacker (through frame counting for example).

Best regards

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
Thanks for your well researched issue! I’ll try and address some of the points you brought up.

First and foremost, SameSite is meant as only one layer in a defense in depth strategy, its design and implementation tries to balance our security and privacy goals with the realities of the web as it exists today. This ultimately means that it must be used with smart site design that leverages the other security tools and features available.

### Similarities between window.open and navigating
`window.open` differs from the original site (let’s call it a.example) navigating itself by allowing a.example to continue to hold and manipulate a reference to the new window. But, every navigation a.example makes on that reference will have an initiator of a.example (On Chrome at least, I haven’t checked other browsers, but I believe it’s true for all).
This means that, as far as SameSite is concerned, an a.example window navigating itself directly or opening a new window and navigating that instead are all the same type of top-level navigation. This appears to hold true for all the examples and notes in your post.

### Addressing your points

> Currently, the specification mandates blocking cookies on user-initiated page reloads but not on reloads performed through JavaScript.

This was a purposeful decision. We wanted to allow the site to be able to operate specific “landing pages” in order to allow third-party entities (maybe a sign in flow or payment processor) to navigate the user back and then the landing page could refresh to allow access to cookies in order to complete the process. Since the reload must be explicitly initiated by the page it would require the site developer to “opt-in” to the behavior and hopefully design the landing page with that behavior in mind.

Conversely, we disallowed user initiated reloads because that doesn’t show an intention on the site’s behalf that it wants or needs cookies following that cross-site navigation. Users have been taught over the years to try reloading if a page looks broken, something that could occur if cookies aren’t present. Continuing to block cookies helps prevent users from inadvertently weakening their own security.

> Additionally, we verified that samesite=strict cookies, even when not sent in the top-level request that loads a page, are still attached to requests that load subresources for that page. This behavior is not explicitly defined in the specification.

That’s expected and intended. Samesite operates on a per request basis (or on a per JS call basis) so all requests, sub-resource or otherwise, are subject to the same rules. See [here](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html#name-same-site-and-cross-site-re).  
The spec assumes that since the page loading the same-site resources is in control of what it loads, it shouldn’t load anything that makes harmful changes.

> abusing gadgets

You’re correct that if a site exposes an API like you’ve given in 2.1 then it’s possible to give an attacker control + access to SameSite cookies. But to me it appears that the gadget is the footgun and I’m not sure how/if SameSite should solve this. Allowing any cross-site entity to make requests as yourself is a dangerous tool!

> Besides JavaScript redirections, other requests, such as subresource loads, could also be exploited to subvert the security assumptions granted by samesite=strict cookies.

I mentioned above that pages are in control of what they load and as long as they only load safe resources that they’re expecting they should be fine, but if you have any examples to the contrary I’m very interested in hearing about them.


> However, window.open-based attacks are still possible since samesite=laxcookies are attached to top-level cross-site requests

Going back to how `window.open`s are basically the same as any other top-level navigation, this is the intended behavior. Lax cookies shouldn’t be used for anything that can allow changes to anything important.

> leading to state-dependent changes to the DOM, which could be measured by the attacker (through frame counting for example).

Agreed, it’s definitely possible to leak state this way. I’m not familiar with the reasoning with why the single-origin policy allows `window.open` references to read `window.length`, but I’m sure the spec writers had a good reason.


Hope that helped clear things up, let me know if you have any other questions or concerns.

comments.author: lavish
comments.body:
Hi @sbingler, thanks (as usual) for the kind and thorough response!

I did a bit of additional investigation and found some discussions that we missed before opening the issue: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1459321 and https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/628

As far as I understood, the current behavior concerning page reloads has been defined only recently (2021). Before that, different browser vendors had [conflicting security concerns](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1459321#c3). Even nowadays, browsers do not seem to fully agree on the intended behavior, or at least Firefox is inconsistent with Chrome's behavior since it does not attach SameSite=strict cookies after a call to `location.reload()`. Some confusion on this matter is justifiable. :)

I now see the rationale behind the design that enables specific pages to opt-in to SameSite=strict cookies upon a self-initiated reload. I always thought SameSite=lax cookies ensured compatibility with SSOs and payment flows, as lax cookies are attached to top-level navigations. But this "strict + reload hack" (so to say) puts the webpage in control instead of attaching cookies to all cross-site top-level requests. The downside of this behavior, as discussed, is that JS-based open redirectors become a gadget for bypassing SameSite=strict cookies. I'm not sure if the benefits outweigh the risks, but probably, the spec would benefit from a more explicit discussion of this trade-off.

> The spec assumes that since the page loading the same-site resources is in control of what it loads, it shouldn't load anything that makes harmful changes.

Concerning subresource loading, I would argue that in general this is not a valid assumption. In principle, here we have an untrusted context (the cross-site page opened via `window.open()`) that automatically loads authenticated resources. This is somehow the dual of SRI, CSP, mixed content, and other security mechanisms that prevent a trusted context from loading untrusted resources that an attacker could abuse. We have not measured the prevalence of security issues caused by this behavior in the wild (i.e., xs-leaks introduced by an authenticated subresource being loaded), but I would expect a non-negligible number of affected instances.

The current behavior surprised me, and it is possible that developers who care about protecting from xs-leaks are also unaware of the potential risks. For instance, the [xs-leaks wiki on SameSite cookies](https://xsleaks.dev/docs/defenses/opt-in/same-site-cookies/) states that:

> Strict cookies provide the strongest security guarantees, but it can be very difficult to deploy Strict same-site cookies in an existing application.

citing only other reasons (e.g., the 2 minutes exception rule) as major limitations of SameSite cookies.

To conclude, we just wanted to discuss this issue after encountering a behavior that diverges from our mental model of SameSite cookies and that we could not entirely justify it after reading the spec. As for JS-initiated reloads, if the behavior is here to stay, I think the spec could mention these limitations more explicitly to prevent developers from building their applications based on wrong assumptions.

Thanks again for the discussion!
Marco

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
Hi @lavish,

As you found in those discussions, reload behavior wasn’t well aligned previously and I’m not sure how purposeful each UA’s behavior was at the time.

> Firefox is inconsistent with Chrome's behavior since it does not attach SameSite=strict cookies after a call to location.reload().

I know Firefox has a number of SameSite related behaviors behind default disabled configs, this could be as well. I don’t have easy access to Firefox at the moment but I believe the nightly builds have these flags enabled. What happens if you try testing on a nightly build?

> Concerning subresource loading, I would argue that in general this is not a valid assumption.

The issue here is that a page may still load sub-resources that require SameSite=Strict auth cookies even if the initial request didn’t include those auth cookies?

Plainly, any site that allows unauthenticated access to a page which loads authenticated sub-resources is incorrectly using SameSite. Sites should return a 401 error, or some other denial, if the initial request does not include the appropriate cookies. 

Sadly though, I agree with you that there are probably sites that do not.

> To conclude, we just wanted to discuss this issue after encountering a behavior that diverges from our mental model of SameSite cookies and that we could not entirely justify it after reading the spec.


Just to confirm, the behavior you’re talking about are:
