comments.author: nicowilliams
comments.body:
Making it a `MAY` would go a great deal of the distance to assuaging my concerns :)

I'd still like to first note that there is a big difference between middleware applying codec conversions (e.g., content encoding compression function changes[^1]), or data serialization rules changes[^2]) and making changes to the _actual contents_ rather than its encodings.  The latter seems so unlikely to happen that I think you should also just consider removing all text about query normalization.

Back to the SQL normalization example, suppose the content-type were a JSON-encoded AST of the actual SQL.  Then we could say that removing interstitial whitespace would be a form of normalization, though what to do about normalization of real numbers would remain a thorny issue.  That would be very reasonable, but it would require a client application that could generate that AST.  And that brings me to: I think the best place to do normalization is on the user-agent!  If the user-agent is real dumb and the query is just taken from a text input widget on the page and user input, then the user-agent can't normalize, and really neither can any middleware -- only the server can, and the middleware can learn nothing about how to normalize future queries.  If the application is smart on the client side (e.g., it runs JavaScript programs that parse user-input queries and turn them into ASTs) then the application can also be smart enough to perform some sorts of normalization -- at least those sorts that are feasible.

Thus as I think about it I believe the only places where query normalization can be performed are:

- the client-side (and then the middleware need not know anything about query forms)
- the server-side, though this does not help middleware unless we had a verb for normalizing queries, then middleware could pre-flight a `NORMALIZEQUERY` request for every `QUERY` so that it could check the cache.

I think perhaps if query normalization is a valuable and feasible thing, and caching canonical queries were equally desirable, then you might want a `NORMALIZEQUERY` verb!

Even if query normalization were non-trivial, having a `NORMALIZEQUERY` verb might still be desirable, even if most applications would only ever produce a `501`.

[^1]: Trivial and application-independent.  Just decompress and re-compress.
[^2]: Less trivial because the middleware must be able to identify the application's request body content schema, unless the codec change were for a self-describing encoding like BER->DER, or DER->CER, etc.  But still feasible because the middleware need not understand the application's semantics, and the middleware need not be a part of the application.

comments.author: vidraj
comments.body:
> I don't think the overhead of adding an opt-out mechanism from normalisation is worth it here, especially considering how narrow the use case is. The opt-out mechanism already exists for transforming proxies and implementing it is a MUST (See [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-7.7)). For a good reason. In my opinion, implementing this mechanism for QUERY is also already a MUST, you just didn't spell it out clearly, because any proxy that implements the cache key transformations as outlined in the QUERY spec is technically a transforming proxy from the point of view of the client. It's just a really bad one, because it sometimes performs transformations, sometimes it doesn't, and it transforms the content in a really weird way that sometimes optimizes it and sometimes pessimizes. And all of this happens without involving the server, so you might have a service which sometimes fails to work correctly, but the operators of the service don't see anything wrong on their end. Perhaps another thing you should consider is to require that a proxy that transforms request bodies for the purpose of caching also sends the canonical representation to the server instead of the original. That way, the transformation is always applied, the server operators see its results and all clients get the same response no matter who sent their request first. This doesn't impose any additional requirements on the proxy beyond handling the first request in the same manner as subsequent ones (e.g. fully buffering the body before sending it on and calculating the transformed body immediately as opposed to lazily). --- To summarize my argument why an opt-out is necessary in a general way: The semantics of a request body can't be inferred from the content type. A few examples: - Whitespace in a JSON request is sometimes significant (because error messages want to point to an exact line+column). - The exact bytes of any request are sometimes significant (because the service in question is a cryptographic digest calculator, to be used e.g. before contacting a banking API, which requires each request to contain a correct digest; or because the service *is* the banking API and requires correct digests to be present). - Sometimes, the following `text/html` bodies are identical: ```html

Hello, world! ``` and ```html

Hello, world!

``` But if the service in question accepts an HTML snippet and returns a full page with the snippet embedded, then embedding the second one makes the generated web page invalid. If the service checks that, it might send an uncacheable error back, but not all services do. Or perhaps the service was originally made to process `application/xhtml+xml`, but as an extension (and in accordance with Postel's law), it also allows clients to make HTML requests, as long as the text is trivially convertible to XHTML, which the latter is, but the former isn't. - Sometimes, sending a JPEG image file with metadata, or sending the same pixels in a different JPEG file without metadata makes no difference. If the service is supposed to add a fancy border and burn any ImageTitle and Photographer tags into the bottom part, the metadata will make a difference. Both requests with metadata and without are fine, neither will result in an error, just an image without the desired title, or (perhaps worse) with a different title than intended. - Sometimes, losslessly reencoding a JPEG image into JPEG-XL image is inconsequential. Not if you want to show the result in a browser, though, because browsers generally support JPEG, but don't support JPEG-XL. The service might process a JPEG-XL just fine, sending another JPEG-XL back, because it doesn't know whether you need it to be browser-compatible or not. - Sometimes, a `text/plain` document with DOS-style CRLF newlines is equivalent to a document with UNIX-style LF newlines. But not if the service is a typesetter that requires the CRs to be present, otherwise it makes all text gradually shift right. This probably won't result in any errors either, just in a broken document. - Sometimes, the C program ```C int main(void) { int x = 1; return 0; } ``` is equivalent to the program ```C int main(void) { return 0; } ``` and to ```C int main(void) { return 0; int x = 1; } ``` But not when compiled with `-Wunused-variable -Werror`, because that makes the first and third program not compile, and not when the compiler processes C89 only, because there the third program is invalid. This might again not result in any errors getting returned from the back end, because if the service in question is Compiler Explorer, it's not there to *actually compile* your programs, it's there to *show you the compiler output*. Which it did, 200 OK. (Of course, it's difficult to imagine a web proxy that understands `text/x-csrc` at the required level, but it's allowed to.) I could go on, but hopefully you get the gist of my argument. > Without normalisation you lose most of the benefits of caching anyway, unless you have a highly homogenous client population -- which isn't the web as deployed. So, you might as well make the response uncacheable or use POST. Counterpoints: - One user typically only has a single client, so even in the worst case, caching in the user-agent will always work. The same argument can be applied to most forward proxies. - Even big deployments with heterogeneous clients (YouTube? Facebook?), typically have one major official client (the JavaScript on the official web pages), potentially two (a desktop/mobile app), but both controlled by the same entity. They can just generate good requests in the first place. The small amount of not-very-well-cacheable requests coming from other clients can mostly be ignored. - An open API (ActivityPub?) can have documented best practices that lead to optimal caching. Also, this problem already exists with GET requests and the ordering of the query parameters and the developers who care solve it through documenting the preferred order. There were proposals for opt-in automatic reordering, but AFAIK they went nowhere, because making such transformations work well is difficult. > Furthermore, developers can (and will) adapt to avoid such assumptions in their error messages. I'd say that's impossible. Both technically impossible (in well-formed XML or JSON, you can identify error positions by their path, as e.g. XPath or `jq` would, but if the file is not well-formed, you already have a problem – and many file formats are not strictly tree-based and therefore don't have such a path mechanism) and socially impossible (good luck persuading the GCC authors to rewrite their compiler to use something else than file:line:column). > I'd still like to first note that there is a big difference between middleware applying codec conversions (e.g., content encoding compression function changes1), or data serialization rules changes2) and making changes to the actual contents rather than its encodings. The latter seems so unlikely to happen that I think you should also just consider removing all text about query normalization. I'd say even the former is problematic, because the proxy can't really know which encodings are supported by the server – this is one area where requests are very different from responses.

comments.author: nicowilliams
comments.body:
@vidraj

> > I'd still like to first note that there is a big difference between middleware applying codec conversions (e.g., content encoding compression function changes1), or data serialization rules changes2) and making changes to the actual contents rather than its encodings. The latter seems so unlikely to happen that I think you should also just consider removing all text about query normalization.

> I'd say even the former is problematic, because the proxy can't really know which encodings are supported by the server – this is one area where requests are very different from responses.

Sure it can:

- user-agent sends a `GET` of some resource with `Accept-Encoding: br`
- the proxy does not respond immediately but does a `GET` of the same to the origin with `Accept-Encoding: br, gzip` (etc.)
- the server responds with `200` w/ `gzip` encoding
- the proxy decompresses and then recompresses to `br` and responds with `200` and the re-compressed response body.

(The server can also respond that there are no acceptable encodings in `br, gzip`.)

This is possible precisely because encoding transformations are not semantic ones.

Though as RFC 9110 section 7.7 1st paragraph notes, even an encoding transformation can break "integrity checks or digital signatures".

> The opt-out mechanism already exists for transforming proxies and implementing it is a MUST (See [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-7.7)). For a good reason.

Sadly that is a _response_ transformation opt-out mechanism.  I don't see an opt-out mechanism for _request_ bodies:

> A proxy MUST NOT transform the content ([Section 6.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#content)) of a response message that contains a no-transform cache directive ([Section 5.2.2.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111#section-5.2.2.6) of [[CACHING](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#CACHING)]). Note that this does not apply to message transformations that do not change the content, such as the addition or removal of transfer codings ([Section 7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-7) of [[HTTP/1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#HTTP11)]).
> 
> A proxy MAY transform the content of a message that does not contain a no-transform cache directive. A proxy that transforms the content of a [200 (OK)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.200) response can inform downstream recipients that a transformation has been applied by changing the response status code to [203 (Non-Authoritative Information)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.203) ([Section 15.3.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.203)).

I do think a _request_ content transformation opt-out mechanism is required, but it's very difficult to add such a thing now, and certainly it's difficult to do so _here_.  (EDIT: I mean that adding a generic request body transformation opt-out to HTTP in an RFC that adds a verb might be _politically_ difficult.)

I remain skeptical that any `QUERY` request body normalizations are practical.  I'm also skeptical of the rationale given for such normalizations because what are the chances that two or more users will be using semantically the same queries with a service with a huge space of possible queries?  @reschke's and @mnot's willingness to drop the `SHOULD` helps make `QUERY` grudgingly acceptable, but I think they would be better off removing all text about `QUERY` request transformations _except_ for the Security Considerations text.  If it turns out that such normalizations are possible, desirable, and actually deployed to good effect then the `QUERY` RFC could always be updated later to note that.  There is no harm in waiting, especially when you recognize that you don't know how to canonicalize queries to begin with beyond removing insignificant whitespace (which is still non-trivial when you consider the space of possible query languages) -- at the very least you could add text to note that you only have such insignificant whitespace deletions in mind.

>

> (The server can also respond that there are no acceptable encodings in `br, gzip`.)

Yeah, with responses, this design space is explored well. It's not always a transparent transformation, but many proxies do it anyway and it mostly works. And since `TE: gzip` etc. never got off the ground, repurposing Content-Encoding for that purpose is a pragmatic decision.

But for request bodies, there is no `Accept-Encoding`. When I write a client that sends a request with a Content-Encoded body, I have to use some out-of-band protocol to learn which encodings are accepted by the server. Typically, that protocol is “reading the documentation” and the choice gets hardcoded into the software. This is viable for service-specific clients or perhaps reverse proxies, but not for general-purpose clients (the most common general-purpose clients – web browsers – AFAIK don't support compressed requests even with JavaScript scripting) and certainly not for forward proxies outside of some very specific deployments.

It would be theoretically possible to either:
1. use `Expect: 100-Continue` in the request to allow the server to send a `415 Unsupported Media Type` before sending the body, or
2. use an `OPTIONS` request to learn the possible representations ahead-of-time,

but both of these have limited support, especially in web browsers. I'm using `100 Continue` for server-to-server API access and it works well, the server-side support is there, but AFAIK browsers don't have a way of requesting it. I don't expect proxies to start doing either any time soon.


> > The opt-out mechanism already exists for transforming proxies and implementing it is a MUST (See [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-7.7)). For a good reason.
> 
> Sadly that is a _response_ transformation opt-out mechanism. I don't see an opt-out mechanism for _request_ bodies[.]

I believe that's an unintended omission or perhaps an outright typo, as the older [RFC 2616](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec14.html#sec14.9.5) specifies it for all messages.

(Tangent, not relevant for QUERY:)
That said, it's not clear from either RFC whether specifying `no-transform` in a request applies the directive to the response as well. RFC 9111 just says “avoid transforming the content”, but it's not specified *which* content it refers to. Since the exact same wording is used for both requests and responses (where it is clear), I assume this is, again, an omission and we should not read too much into it. There is probably no strong intent behind the wording there.


> > A proxy MUST NOT transform the content ([Section 6.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#content)) of a response message that contains a no-transform cache directive ([Section 5.2.2.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111#section-5.2.2.6) of [[CACHING](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#CACHING)]). Note that this does not apply to message transformations that do not change the content, such as the addition or removal of transfer codings ([Section 7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-7) of [[HTTP/1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#HTTP11)]).
> > A proxy MAY transform the content of a message that does not contain a no-transform cache directive. A proxy that transforms the content of a [200 (OK)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.200) response can inform downstream recipients that a transformation has been applied by changing the response status code to [203 (Non-Authoritative Information)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.203) ([Section 15.3.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.203)).
> 
> I do think a _request_ content transformation opt-out mechanism is required, but it's very difficult to add such a thing now, and certainly it's difficult to do so _here_. (EDIT: I mean that adding a generic request body transformation opt-out to HTTP in an RFC that adds a verb might be _politically_ difficult.)

The mechanism is already present, proxies are already required to honor it (even if many don't – Opera Turbo certainly didn't, back in the day, and it was a problem), it's just necessary to make it clear in the QUERY spec that what the proxy is doing there is really a transformation (this is my interpretation, but it is what it looks like from the point of view of the client) with all it entails, including the requirement to honor these directives.

comments.body:

Oh, sorry, I should have checked.  You're absolutely right then I think.  @reschke @mnot please see this.  There already is an opt-out.

It ought to be possible for the user-agent to express a preference or requirement for one of two resulting URI behaviors:

 - URI that encodes the request body
 - URI that does _not_ encode the request body

The latter is what section 5 calls for right now, but the former might be useful too.

If a `NORMALIZE` method were also added, that might help user-agents convert between, e.g., SPARQL and an encoding of simple SPARQL queries in URI q-params.  The user-agent could use a URI w/ q-params and request conversion to SPARQL, or request conversion of SPARQL to URI w/ q-params, or just SPARQL to SPARQL.

Not just knowledgeable users like you or me, but I'm sure you know -I do!- people who are not so knowledgeable who edit q-params in URIs.

issues.title: QUERY: Difference between `Location:` and `Content-Location:`?
issues.author: nicowilliams
issues.body:
In the [I-D section 4.2 example](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-05.html#section-4.2) we see:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/csv
Content-Location: /contacts/responses/42
Location: /contacts/queries/17

...
```

Questions:

 - why should the `Location:` header be present in a `2xx` response?
 - why should the `Content-Location` differ from the `Location` in this example?
   Surely a `GET` of either should produce the same response, no?  I would think so.

IMO `Location:` SHOULD be present in all responses unless the server does not want the query cached, and `Content-Location:`, if it is present, SHOULD be the same as `Location:`.

Question: shouldn't the server use `201` for direct responses when it "creates" a URI for the query??  I would think so (though the issue that might then arise is: is `QUERY` truly safe? but I think it the answer to that would be "yes").

IMO `200` should be for direct responses w/o a `Location:`, and `201` should be for direct responses with a `Location:`.

comments.author: nicowilliams
comments.body: One possibility for why `Location:` and `Content-Location:` should be different is that one can be for "this query" and the other for "this particular response to executing that query".  However, it's not likely that the server will be able to re-compute a particular response to a long-ago execution of a particular query, and if that is desired then perhaps the ability to create a persistent response should be a separate operation (though possibly bundled in one request that creates both resources).

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
These are questions that we tried to address in [Section 2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-05.html#section-2); if they're not clear there, we can try to make them more pointed.

**Why does a 200 have a Location?**

The semantics of Location are defined with respect to the method and the status code. Nothing says that a Location header can't have defined semantics for a 200. Section 2 describes the semantics in this case.

**What's the difference between Location and Content-Location?** 

> A successful response to a QUERY request can include a Content-Location header field ([...]) containing an identifier for a resource corresponding to the results of the operation. This represents a claim from the server that a client can send a GET request for the indicated URI to retrieve the results of the query operation just performed. The indicated resource might be temporary.

>
> A server MAY create or locate a resource that identifies the query operation for future use. If the server does so, the URI of the resource can be included in the Location header field of the response ([...]).

That is, Content-Location (if present) will return the result of the query from the time it was executed, while Location indicates where the same query can be re-performed against up-to-date data. So no, they will essentially never be the same resource if both are present.

The apt example from another issue was that Content-Location might point to weather records of a particular date and time, while Location would point to the current weather for the same location. As you say, it's not going to be the case that both (or either!) exists for every server and every request, but the mechanisms exist to convey them if they do.

**How is this "safe"?**

> QUERY requests are both safe and idempotent **with regards to the resource identified by the request URI**. That is, QUERY requests do not alter the state of the targeted resource. However, while processing a QUERY request, a server can be expected to allocate computing and memory resources or even create additional HTTP resources through which the response can be retrieved.

**Shouldn't it be a 201?**

The server might reasonably send a 201 if it created a new resource to track the query. Or, for frequent queries, one might already have existed and it's merely supplying a pointer. But ultimately, the client doesn't care. The client isn't requesting the creation of such a resource; these are merely affordances for the server to reference them if they exist / it creates them.

comments.author: nicowilliams
comments.body: Thanks.  I should have read section 2 more carefully.  I note the lack of normative language regarding this ("can" instead of "MAY").

issues.title: QUERY: Why should a server ever prefer direct or indirect responses?
issues.author: nicowilliams
issues.body:
For that matter, if a user-agent could request a preference or requirement for direct vs. indirect responses, why should it prefer one or the other?  That is, what guidance can the I-D give for when to use direct responses and when to use indirect responses?

Indirect responses have the benefit of allowing the user-agent to get a URI for its query without executing the query, and then also any subsequent `GET` of that URI will be cacheable as usual.  Whereas direct responses mean executing the query immediately.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I don't think you can guarantee that the query wasn't executed simply because the response was indirect. You've gotten a URL that identifies where the results can be retrieved. Caching is the primary reason why, as using the response to a QUERY request to satisfy a subsequent GET request can have additional complexity. At the cost of a round-trip, you have something whose cache semantics are easier to reason about.

comments.author: nicowilliams
comments.body:
Certainly knowing a URI for the query/response would be handy for a cache, thus the need for `Location:`/`Content-Location:`, but that doesn't require a second round trip.  I encourage you to write some text about why the server should prefer an indirect response.  One possibility is to allow the user-agent to get a URI for the query and/or for one response to it without first executing the query -- the server _could_ delay execution till the `GET` in the follow-up request, and that seems like a reasonable thing to do.

In a way an indirect flow allows the user-agent to "normalize" queries by obtaining URIs for them.  This is why I think another new method, or request headers to influence the response's directness would be useful.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
@nicowilliams - could you elaborate why

> the server could delay execution till the GET in the follow-up request, and that seems like a reasonable thing to do.

would be useful for the server?

My preference is not to add new protocol elements unless it is crystal clear that they are useful.

comments.body: Per discussion on #2897, this is orthogonal to QUERY -- it's applicable to other methods too.

issues.title: Divide and conquer with the existing is a clean alternative to the proposed HTTP QUERY method
issues.author: rafageist
issues.body:
Instead of introducing the QUERY method for complex queries, I propose a divide-and-conquer strategy using existing methods. This allows handling complex payloads without introducing new HTTP methods.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Complex queries are intended for sophisticated backend systems capable of processing and storing such requests. Both the proposed QUERY method and my example are meant for advanced scenarios, not simple use cases. So we are talking about the same context, the same problem and different solutions.

Here is the approach with a hypothetical example:

> [!WARNING]
> You don't need to make 2 requests for each query, the first time is enough if you get creative. The example sends a query template that dynamically generates a URL for subsequent queries, allowing you to reuse the query results efficiently.

## Tell the server that you need to make a complex query and receive a response that your query was registered. 

You can optionally tell it which path you want to consume or return a UUID.

Request:

```http
POST /query
{
  "desiredUrl": "/productos/stock/dell-apple-hp/laptops-500-1500/ratings-4plus-ram-8GB-16GB/{{page}}",
  "page": "{{page}}"
  "filters": {
    "category": "electronics",
    "subCategory": "laptops",
    "priceRange": {
      "min": 500,
      "max": 1500
    },
    "availability": "in_stock",
    "brands": ["Dell", "Apple", "HP"],
    "sort": {
      "field": "ratings",
      "order": "desc"
    },
    "attributes": {
      "screenSize": ["13-inch", "15-inch"],
      "processorType": ["Intel", "AMD"],
      "ram": ["8GB", "16GB"]
    }
  }
}
```

Response:
```http
Content-type: application/json

{
  "query_uuid": "89fbf974-4565-4bf6-8e9e-e1fd8585a0dc"
}
```

## Ask the server about the results of your request

Request:
```http
GET /productos/stock/dell-apple-hp/laptops-500-1500/ratings-4plus-ram-8GB-16GB/1
```

Response:

```http
Content-type: application/json

{
  "totalPages": 100,
  "page": 1,
  "products": [
    {
      "id": 101,
      "name": "Dell XPS 13",
      "category": "laptops",
      "price": 1200,
      "availability": "in_stock",
      "brand": "Dell",
      "rating": 4.5,
      "attributes": {
        "screenSize": "13-inch",
        "processorType": "Intel Core i7",
        "ram": "16GB",
        "storage": "512GB SSD"
      }
    },
    {
      "id": 102,
      "name": "Apple MacBook Air",
      "category": "laptops",
      "price": 1500,
      "availability": "in_stock",
      "brand": "Apple",
      "rating": 4.7,
      "attributes": {
        "screenSize": "13-inch",
        "processorType": "M1",
        "ram": "16GB",
        "storage": "512GB SSD"
      }
    },
    {
      "id": 103,
      "name": "HP Spectre x360",
      "category": "laptops",
      "price": 1400,
      "availability": "in_stock",
      "brand": "HP",
      "rating": 4.3,
      "attributes": {
        "screenSize": "15-inch",
        "processorType": "Intel Core i5",
        "ram": "8GB",
        "storage": "256GB SSD"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

I hope these examples have clarified how complex queries can be effectively handled using existing methods. This method offers flexibility to handle sophisticated queries on advanced backends, requests that can be pre-processed, optimized, cached, return an early error, reused, etc.

I welcome any comments and feedback from the community. Thank you for considering my idea and I hope it has contributed to the ongoing discussion.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
From a quick glace, this misses the point of QUERY - having a method that can pass data in the request body which is "safe".

If "safeness" of the request is irrelevant, then yes, you can POST.

comments.author: rafageist
rafageist
comments.body:
> From a quick glace, this misses the point of QUERY - having a method that can pass data in the request body which is "safe".
> 
> If "safeness" of the request is irrelevant, then yes, you can POST.

@reschke  Re-reading your comment made me realize something important.

The "point of" QUERY cannot simply be the creation of the method itself. There must be a stronger, more meaningful reason behind its existence, something that provides unique value that cannot be achieved with current HTTP methods or through architectural improvements. Creating a new method just because you want to combine features of GET and POST is not a sufficient reason. The purpose of QUERY should clearly answer why it is needed and what its real value is.

When designing something in software engineering, or any other technology, we typically ask ourselves three questions: 

- What are we trying to achieve? 
- How should it be implemented? 
- Why do we need it? 

In this case, while QUERY answers the “what” and the “how,” I think the “why” is still unclear. What real benefit does QUERY provide that can’t be solved by better architecture or existing methods like POST or GET?

If the purpose of QUERY is to allow more complex queries by sending a body in the request (it is possible now, but not official), a simpler solution would be to simply allow bodies in GET within the HTTP specification, rather than introducing a new method. This would keep the semantics clear, avoiding the need to create a new method that could cause confusion and bad practices. In the end, the question is whether we really need a new method or whether we can adjust the existing rules to achieve the same goal.

Now ask yourself why no body has been specified for the GET?

The designers of the HTTP protocol originally decided not to allow bodies in GET because its purpose is to request resources without altering the state of the server, and bodies were considered unnecessary for that. By keeping GET bodyless, the simplicity and clarity of the protocol is preserved, avoiding complications with caching semantics and idempotence. However, it is unclear whether, in the current context, this decision could be revisited, as allowing bodies in GET could solve many problems.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
That topic has been discussed multiple times in the past, and the result always was: don't. See https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.1-6.

As stated earlier, that's the reason why QUERY is being defined.

comments.author: rafageist
comments.body:
> That topic has been discussed multiple times in the past, and the result always was: don't. See https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.1-6.
> 
> As stated earlier, that's the reason why QUERY is being defined.

@reschke The HTTP protocol (RFC 9110) specifies that the GET method refers to a URI, and the URI specification (RFC 3986) does not impose a size limit on these identifiers. Therefore, any limitation on the length of parameters in the URL **is not a deficiency of the protocol**, but of the intermediate implementations (browsers, servers, proxies). Rather than changing the protocol with methods like QUERY, it would be more logical to optimize the ecosystem to handle longer query parameters or implement better solutions as this issue proposes.

>[!IMPORTANT]
>The HTTP QUERY proposal attempts to solve a problem in the protocol that is not part of the protocol, when it is an ecosystem problem and must be solved in the ecosystem.

Therefore, the topic you reference reinforces my point even more. The reason for not allowing a body in GET is well-established, and creating a method like QUERY seems forced. **You’ve dismissed the rest of the arguments, focusing only on the lack of a body in GET**, but haven't provided a solid reason why QUERY is needed and **the proposal is vague in its rationale**. 

The only justification seems to be the risk of URL truncation, which is not a deficiency of the HTTP protocol itself, but of the points along the request path and the ingenuity of developers in structuring URLs and optimizing the systems they implement.

The HTTP QUERY proposal brings more problems than solutions to this world: 

- network overload
- performance degradation
- security vulnerabilities
- unnecessary complexity
- redundancy
- cache inefficiencies
- breaking HTTP semantics
- misuse and bad practices
- lack of backward compatibility
- implementation challenges

An article will be written and published recommending the solution given in this issue and the concerns regarding the HTTP QUERY proposal. All those possible problems will be detailed.

Thanks for your time.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: FWIW, I disagree with this characterization in its entirety.  Making the safe-ness of a request visible to intermediaries is justification enough to use QUERY over a POST, even if a POST could carry most of the same semantics if a resource were configured that way.

comments.author: MikeBishop
rafageist
comments.body:
Thanks for your feedback. 

While structured bodies can be useful, I believe the current issue can still be addressed by using existing methods like POST & GET combined with multiple requests if needed. We've seen 'gaps' between methods like PUT and PATCH, or HEAD and GET, and rather than creating new methods, we combine or layer requests as necessary. Solving everything in a single request isn’t always essential, especially if a combination of methods can achieve the same outcome more effectively.

For example, GraphQL uses POST for everything because it needs to send the query in the body, but that doesn't mean that the whole body needs to be sent multiple times. Maybe you're only interested in changing small parts. 

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7aa2c54d-93c6-432c-b188-0b32afefc6d8)

GraphQL could use the HTTP protocol well, sending a POST with a query-template first (or every time you need to change the template) to prepare future requests and then use GET for subsequent responses. It occurs to me that templates can be reused between different clients.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/095c51ef-5a43-4d94-8390-cb82dd7ea4fe)

This approach takes advantage of the flexibility of multiple requests instead of relying on a single new method like QUERY. The focus of this issue is to break the pattern of wanting to solve the above in a single request.

And this is just one of the solutions I can think of, there may be more that ARE NOT a GET with a body or a secure POST. But quite the opposite, a GET and a POST working together and respecting HTTP.

In a general sense, I have thought of a proposal that says there is no solution for the problem it aims to solve, when in fact it can be solved respecting HTTP. 

If what is desired is to solve it in a single request with the existing methods, then maybe that is not possible right now. But the fact that it cannot be solved now in a single request does not mean that your architecture is correct, and the protocol is incomplete.

It is possible that if it cannot be solved that way, then something is wrong with your architecture. And that is the central point of this issue.

We could try to clarify with something like ``the list « "`a`" » ``.

We could just throw up a "This document depends on Infra" line, like https://johannhof.github.io/draft-annevk-johannhof-httpbis-cookies/draft-annevk-johannhof-httpbis-cookies.html#name-conventions does. That is probably a good idea anyway, since we're taking, e.g., our definition of strings from there. Or maybe even "This document depends on Infra, including the depiction of list literals using « » syntax."

One could imagine using different punctuation, like `(` and `)`, but that seems gratuitously divergent with the existing spec ecosystem to me. If there's precedent to point to in IETF specs though, then maybe it's fine.

I welcome any advice from the IETF community, including @martinthomson who originally filed this over in https://github.com/jeremyroman/http-no-vary-search/issues/4.

comments.body:

Precedent probably doesn't help much here.  It's only relatively recent that non-ASCII codepoints could be used in text, so this list notation would not have been possible in the past.  I will say, it's very annoying to type though.  Given how few instances there are, the `a list with a single element "a"` option is probably what I would do personally.

comments.author: jeremyroman
comments.body:

> This document also adopts some conventions and notation typical in WHATWG and W3C usage, especially as it relates to algorithms. See [[WHATWG-INFRA](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-wicg-http-no-vary-search-01.html#WHATWG-INFRA)].

issues.title: connect-tcp: should capsules be negotiated or always on?
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body:
We started this discussion in the comments of #2921 but it deserves its own issue. Now that #2921 has landed, capsule support is mandatory for servers but clients can decide whether or not to use it by sending the `Capsule-Protocol = ?1` header. Another way forward would be to just say that connect-tcp always uses capsules. Some reasons why:
* it simplifies server implementations
* it simplifies client implementations that want capsules
* it would be consistent with every other `:protocol` that uses capsules
* it avoids reusing `Capsule-Protocol` to mean something different from what was intended in RFC 9297

Since I don't see any real-world reason to use `connect-tcp` without capsules, this sounds like the best path forward to me

cc @bemasc @LPardue @tfpauly

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I'm sympathetic to the argument that there may be cases where someone wants templates tcp without the overhead of capsules. So how about we move the capsule negotiation to the upgrade token? I.e. one token if you want capsules, another if you don't. Then it makes the use of capsule-protocol header more consistent with how it's already used in other connect-foo docs.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
That's a good compromise. That allows me to only implement the upgrade token that enables capsules and not have to deal with the complexity of negotiation.

Another option would be to say that if `capsule_length == UINT64_MAX` then the capsule extends to the end of the stream. 
That works because stream offsets only go to UINT64_MAX so that length cannot ever be valid. It's a shame we didn't do that in 9297 though

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> Another option would be to say that if `capsule_length == UINT64_MAX` then the capsule extends to the end of the stream.

I think this approach works for the sender to indicate its disinterest to use capsules. But it does not allow the receiver to refuse use of capsules by the sender.

By saying using connect-tcp without capsules, I think we are referring to endpoints that do not want to implement capsule support at neither send-side or receive-side.

Assuming that is the case, I think using different upgrade token is the way to go, if somebody asks for connect-tcp without capsules.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: OK, PR up: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2926.  Please review.

```
   name-segment        = ("[" name-selector "]") /
                         ("." member-name-shorthand)
   member-name-shorthand = name-first *name-char
   name-selector       = string-literal
   string-literal      = %x22 *double-quoted %x22 /     ; "string"
                         %x27 *single-quoted %x27       ; 'string'
```
hyphen-minus is not a name-char, so a member-name-shorthand like

```
@.doc-id
```

is a syntax error, as is

```
@.doc\u002did
```

Instead,

```
@["doc-id"]
```

or

```
@['doc-id']
```

is the correct way to use this member name in a name-segment.
The string-literals inside a name-selector also allow escapes like \u002d, but there is no point for hyphen-minus.

issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
1) "#mediatype (for consistency, for example, with PATCH: https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc5789.html#accept-patch)
2) Structured Fields, because that's how we define new fields (and one could argue that we shouldn't make up reasons not to use that format)

comments.body: I am in favour of 2)

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: We'll use SF in the next draft, and see whether somebody complains...

comments.author: zenomt
comments.body:
sorry for not chiming in sooner. i'm in favor of (1) `#media-range` (not `#media-type`, to allow for wildcarding), both for consistency with `Accept`, `Accept-Patch`, and `Accept-Post`, as well as that if it's a structured field with a list of tokens (as proposed by Martin), then a media type _and its parameters_ is essentially an opaque string, and

    application/something; param1="foo"; param2="bar"

would be distinct from

    application/something; param2="bar"; param1="foo"

even though they are semantically the same, and still require parsing a `media-range` out of the SF value.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Good point. @martinthomson - why exactly would you want the parameters be part of the string item? That would make parsing harder than it has to be.

(I assume there was a good reason for your proposal, but which?)

comments.author: zenomt
comments.body: notwithstanding the issue with parameter order i just mentioned, if this is a structured field, then you need to do the SF parsing to get tokens, and *then* parse each one as a `media-range` anyway. so why not just `media-range`s without an extra SF wrapper?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: One reason we (for some value of "we") prefer SF is that we've been consistently telling others not to define new fields in a non-SF syntax - even for consistency with other existing fields.

comments.author: zenomt
comments.body:
my reading of RFC 9651 suggests that a SF that is a List of Token Items (each of which can be parameterized) is syntactically equivalent (and mostly semantically equivalent) to `#media-range` (from RFC 9110). that is

    Accept-Query: application/something; param1="foo", application/other; profile="bar"; param="baz"

conforms to both `#media-range` from RFC 9110, and `sf-list` from RFC 9651 where the `sf-item`s are `sf-token parameters`.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The reason that I suggested parameters as part of the string/token is that I'm not 100% confident that media type parameters fit the SF parameter syntax.  If you do the analysis and conclude that it is OK, then that might be OK.  Finally, I see `q=0.9` being a field value extension, whereas `charset="utf8"` is a media type extension, so maybe having distinct means of extension makes that separation possible.

comments.author: zenomt
comments.body: i think there is a complication in the syntax: the SF ABNF only allows parameters to be separated from each other by `SP` and with no `SP` before a semicolon, whereas `media-range` allows `OWS` (`SP` and `HTAB`) to separate parameters and to occur before semicolons too.

comments.author: zenomt
comments.body: the SF Token Item production is compatible with `media-range` though. i wouldn't object to the definition of the field being that it encodes a "media range and its parameters" as an `sf-list` of SF Token Items and their parameters, rather than requiring the field itself to be `#media-range`. but i do think it's objectionable to have a `media-range` inside an `sf-string`, since that still requires separate parsing of each string value as a `media-range`, and (at the SF layer) destroys the semantic distinction of the parameters.

comments.author: reschke
zenomt
mnot
comments.body: The problem is that if the difference between tokens and strings is semantically significant, an implementation needs to be able to represent that in its API, which can be unpleasant/unidiomatic (e.g., putting one of them in a wrapper class).

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Discussed with @reschke offline. Make it a Token or String, with explicit semantic equivalence between them. Allow Parameters that have Strings (only) as values.

comments.author: zenomt
comments.body:
> Make it a Token or String, with explicit semantic equivalence between them. Allow Parameters that have Strings (only) as values.

from context i assume "it" is the `type "/" subtype` part of a `media-type` or `media-range`.

it seems to me that the point of the `Accept-Query` field is to convey one or more _parameterized media types/ranges_ that the URI understands for a `QUERY`, just like `Accept`, `Accept-Post`, and `Accept-Patch` do for their purposes. since a media type/range has an established meaning and syntax in a larger ecosystem beyond this one field, i think that if this field **has** to be a Structured Field, then in the spirit of @mnot 's [Retrofit Structured Fields for HTTP](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-retrofit.html) we should impose only the _minimum necessary constraints_ on serializing a media type/range to conform to the syntax and semantics of a SF, while not expanding the field syntax to be incompatible with `media-type` or `media-range`.

i think the minimum necessary constraints on a media type or range would be "the top-level `type` can't begin with a digit" (which no IANA-coordinated top-level media types currently do), "no spaces before a parameter's semicolon", "only spaces, no `HTAB`s, between a semicolon and a parameter", and "otherwise a valid `media-type` or `media-range` according to the ABNF of RFC 9110". a parameter's value should be able to be a token or a quoted string, because it's not _necessary_ to constrain it to only a string and still be a SF (and it can't _only_ be a token because media-type parameters can have spaces and other non-token characters).

likewise, the `type "/" subtype` top-level type and the subtype, or `top-level/*`, or `*/*`, should not be able to be a quoted string, because that would be incompatible with the existing syntax of a media-type or media-range.

comments.author: zenomt
comments.body: @mnot if i misunderstood what you meant, and what you actually meant was that "a parameter's value is a string, which can be serialized as a token or a quoted-string with no semantic difference", then i'm on board with that.

issues.title: Better name for the "expires" attribute in Upload-Limit
issues.author: guoye-zhang
issues.body: Expires typically is an absolute timestamp, but it is a number of seconds in Upload-Limit. It might be better named as `timeout` or something similar.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Some possible inspiration maybe?

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers-08.html#section-3.1.3

> The "w" parameter value conveys a time window applicable to the quota ([Section 3.1.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers-08.html#ratelimitpolicy-quota)). The time window MUST be a non-negative Integer value expressing an interval in seconds, similar to the "delay-seconds" rule defined in [Section 10.2.3](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-10.2.3) of [[HTTP](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers-08.html#HTTP)]. Sub-second precision is not supported.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
Maybe we could use `max-age` as it is already used in other standards? Not a perfect 1:1 match but close enough?

`max-age` in RFC 9111 - https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#name-max-age-2
>The max-age response directive indicates that the response is to be considered stale after its age is greater than the specified number of seconds.

`access-control-max-age` in CORS - https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-access-control-max-age
>Indicates the number of seconds (5 by default) the information provided by the `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` headers can be cached.

Another idea could be `expires-in` but that is not in the list of registered IANA headers so might be more work than it's worth?

`TTL` could also possibly be used with the same argument as `max-age`? 

`TTL` in RFC8030 - https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8030.html#page-11
>  An application server MUST include the TTL (Time-To-Live) header
>  field in its request for push message delivery.  The TTL header field
>  contains a value in seconds that suggests how long a push message is
>  retained by the push service.

EDIT: On the other hand, these do not really convey the same thing. Upload-Limit -> Expires is the amount _left_ before the upload expires while e.g. `max-age` is the total time and will be constant on each request while `Expires` will be smaller (or possibly larger) on each request.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body: Another solution would be to change expires into a sf date: https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc9651.html#name-dates

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7838.html#section-3.1

> Syntax:

   ma = delta-seconds; see [[RFC7234], Section 1.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7234#section-1.2.1)

   The delta-seconds value indicates the number of seconds since the
   response was generated for which the alternative service is
   considered fresh.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Another solution would be to change expires into a sf date: https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc9651.html#name-dates

When we first discussed the Upload-Limit, the WG argued that relative durations are preferable to absolute timestamps as durations also work if the client and server don't have aligned clocks. That makes sense, so I would vote for keeping the current value but choosing a different name.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Personally, I think

- max-age,
- expires-in, and
- timeout

are all good options. `max-age`/`ma` is already used in HTTP, although in the area of caching. `expires-in` is the most descriptive for me and would be my preference, but I can live with any other option as well. What is your preference?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: "Expires-In" doesn't have an intuitive meaning for me.  My immediate thought was "What does it expire in? A bucket? The back of a fridge?"  "Expires-After" perhaps.  However, why come up with NIH terminology where there is already a clearly established pattern that says "max-age" is the validity duration of a thing.  We use that for more than just `Cache-Control`.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thank you for the input, Martin. Given that, it makes sense to reuse the terminology and I opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3012 to change the name.

The current text could be interpreted as applying to other HTTP versions, which is not the intent.

issues.title: Consider impact of proxy-initiated close on HTTP 407
issues.author: bemasc
issues.body:
@ekinnear noted today that the performance impact of proxies closing the connection after returning HTTP 407 are not merely hypothetical, and are significant in practice.  This draft currently says that proxies MAY adopt this behavior as a mitigation for potential misbehaving clients.

Some things we could do:
* Remove this MAY.  After a closer look at some earlier anecdotes, we have not actually found a client that exhibits the misbehavior.
* Conduct some kind of study or outreach to see if we can find any misbehaving clients (i.e. CONNECT clients that send first-flight payload data without waiting for the 200 response).
* Define a request header like "Vulnerable-To-Request-Smuggling: ?0", by which the client promises that it is proxying TCP connections for a trusted TCP client or delaying payload data until after the success response, so there is no need for defensive measures.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
Definitely not the last one -- too close to the Evil Bit. I'd be inclined to leave this as MAY, but not stronger, and expand on the text a little bit. It's a defense that has a performance cost, and implementers need to decide whether they're willing to pay the price to have that defense. That's what MAY is -- we don't endorse it, we just note the option.

The right solution is to use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, where this won't be an issue.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
By [trolling through Github](https://github.com/search?q=%2F%28%3F-i%29CONNECT.*HTTP%5C%2F1.1%2F+language%3APython+&type=code), I was able to find many examples of proxy clients that appear to have the wrong behavior:
* https://github.com/lonely-caat/stuff/blob/100daaee4d1707900abdb24300fcdc30356adb60/proxyssl.py#L54
* https://github.com/mzdluo123/bypass_block/blob/002dd2975615eb675a7c0dd8e65b15f79ace35ec/socks_client.py#L65
* https://github.com/qwj/python-proxy/blob/c3a8446c415d53a7a8addfbc5ea37ea27de80504/pproxy/proto.py#L331
* https://github.com/binux/pyproxy/blob/fc6050fdce364dc525b8ae8be51b2088e13b6fcd/pyproxy.py#L194

Most of these are not an "early send" optimization as I expected.  Instead, most of them wait for the response but assume a "200 OK" without checking the status code.

These clients might all be intended to be used in contexts where this behavior doesn't create a vulnerability, but it does seem to suggest that there is an easy mistake here that justifies the MAY.

Should we mention this possibility explicitly in the resumable upload draft or is it not necessary since RFC 9110 and RFC 6265 cover this already?

comments.author: Acconut

issues.title: Resumable Uploads: POST for appending data?
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
In https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/httpbisa/m-iXTJQGdb8XpxGjZWxXGj6Siic/, Roy Fielding suggests POST to be used instead of PATCH + application/octet-stream for appending data to an upload resource:

> For example, use of the method PATCH for appending opaque data is incorrect. PATCH already has a defined semantic that could be used in parallel (e.g., another extension might use PATCH correctly). The resumable upload extension does not use a patch format, so both use of PATCH and creation of a new media type "application/partial-upload” are inappropriate.
>
> POST should be used for appending data to the upload resource. This matches the semantics of POST and is easier to deploy in practice. Each POST can use “application/octet-stream” (or not send any Content-Type, since it has no role to play in processing).

Since we define the upload resource in the first place, we can also specify the meaning of a POST request against it and don't have to use PATCH with a custom media type to define the message's semantics.

Personally, I think both methods (POST or PATCH) are fine. What do others think about this?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I'd rather not do both.

Avoiding creating a media type has the positive of saving some effort. 

I tried to trace back the history of using PATCH in the first place and could not find a good answer. Does anyone have one?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
I believe that @reschke suggested using PATCH and defining a new media type initially.

Personally I don't have a preference, either.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
On 26.11.2024 04:48, Guoye Zhang wrote:
> I believe that @reschke suggested using PATCH and defining a new media type initially.
>
> Personally I don't have a preference, either.

I'm not sure I did, but yes, that seems to be the right thing to do.

Best regards, Julian

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
Right, if we're going to use PATCH, the media type should describe how to handle the request content in a generic way. E.g., `application/append-these-bytes`.

That implies that it might be good to do so in a separate document, so it can be reused by other applications, rather than being perceived as specific to resumable uploads.

If that's thought of as too much work, POST is probably the right answer (with the semantics being defined by the specific resource type that's being baked into the resumable uploads spec).

But how could you resist creating a media type with a name like that?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: If its worth doing, it's worth doing right

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: But also, didn't we have some of this discussion in the WG wrt https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-patch-byterange/

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
@LPardue We did. Both on the mailing list and on Github. 

https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2501 (byte range patch discussions)

https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/httpbisa/UXTmMZaDNgtkMyA7broHeKL6vhg/ (contains discussions on POST vs PATCH)

https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/httpbisa/aAfI1cZZDHnqhykFx4DoFClFocw/ (content type of PATCH and discussions if we can use it at all)

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Right, if we're going to use PATCH, the media type should describe how to handle the request content in a generic way. E.g., `application/append-these-bytes`.
> 
> That implies that it might be good to do so in a separate document, so it can be reused by other applications, rather than being perceived as specific to resumable uploads.

The current draft (-05) intents to define the `application/partial-upload` media type (https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-05.html#name-media-type-application-part) for use in PATCH requests when appending data, but this media type is specific to uploads and not very generic. We can consider renaming the media type and update its description to make it usable in other situations as well.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: If it's spec-specific, that's good enough, I think.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
This topic was discussed during IETF 122. The feedback was that while POST and PATCH both fit semantically for appending to an upload resource, there is no strong reason to move away from the current PATCH + application/partial-upload media type.

Hence, I'll close this for now.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Actually, I strongly disagree with the closing of this issue. This requirement of `PATCH` requests from [RFC 5789 section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5789#section-2) is highly unfavorable for resumable uploads:

> The server MUST apply the entire set of changes atomically and never provide (e.g., in response to a GET during this operation) a partially modified representation.

I am looking to implement a server that accepts resumable uploads and allows other clients to stream a download of the file while another client is uploading it. This would save users a lot of time on very large files. If `PATCH` instructions MUST be atomic, I'm under the impression that would violate RFC 5789. If that's an intentional property of this protocol's design, I would like to understand why, because that would forbid this real-world use case.

Sure, the client could just make the upload across multiple `PATCH`es so that each atomic `PATCH` can be observed by other clients after it's completed. But that shouldn't be a requirement to achieve this functionality. If resumable uploads continue to use `PATCH` requests, I will probably just violate the spec here and not treat the `PATCH` atomically.

It could also be argued resumable uploads inherently violate this requirement already, because resumable uploads are certainly not atomic.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Should I open a new issue to express this concern?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: @GrantGryczan The draft explicitly mentions that partially received patch documents can also be applied because that's safe to do for this media type with an upload resource. This is also explained in https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-2. Does that address your concerns?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: I thought of that, but that really seems contradictory to the semantics of `PATCH` being atomic in general, and I would still strongly argue against it. It's counterintuitive to define a `PATCH` media type that says "ignore the usual semantics of `PATCH` requests; I work differently", if that's even allowed. I assumed it's not allowed.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
This exact wording of RFC 5789 was discussed at IETF 119 as well :) Please take a look at slide 7 of https://httpwg.org/wg-materials/ietf119/resumable-uploads.pdf, the corresponding minutes at https://httpwg.org/wg-materials/ietf119/minutes.html#resumable-uploads or alternatively the recording at https://meetecho-player.ietf.org/playout/?session=IETF119-HTTPBIS-20240319-0730.

The outcome was that the use of PATCH falls within the intentions of RFC 5789, which aim to ensure that a representation or resource is not left in an invalid state. This is the case for an upload resource after applying a PATCH request with a partially received body. The client is always able to continue the upload and interact with the upload resource.

Furthermore, RFC 5789 gives some room for when a PATCH is applied successfully:

> The determination of what constitutes a successful
   PATCH can vary depending on the patch document and the type of
   resource(s) being modified.

Hence we believe the use of PATCH is compatible with RFC 5789.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Thank you for the pointers. I believe that only addresses the last line of my comment:

> It could also be argued resumable uploads inherently violate this requirement already, because resumable uploads are certainly not atomic.

But I believe this fails to address my main concern. In fact, see this comment from the discussion:

> Martin Thomson: Agreed. Can go further and just say that any change in flight you will not see the partial change when querying the resource from elsewhere, which won’t violate the RFC.

This is exactly what I hope to avoid. I _want_ partial changes to be visible elsewhere, so that one client can stream a download of a resource while another client uploads it. Sure, you can define your partial upload media type such that it's considered "complete" to only apply part of it. But you can't define it such that each part of it being incrementally applied is its own atomic "completion" that can be observed from outside. Otherwise, it's inherently not atomic.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: The resumable uploads draft does not address in what form or way the uploaded representation is made available to others. The processing of the representation is controlled by the resource that was initially targeted and the semantics of the corresponding request.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Yes, but incrementally making parts of a single PATCH available to others while the patch document is processed seems to violate the PATCH spec, and that's something I think is important to be allowed to do. I'm not sure what your point is.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
@GrantGryczan I think we should follow the spirit of the requirement rather than focusing on the exact wording. The atomicity requirement of PATCH is to prevent exposing intermediate states that might result in data corruption or expose security vulnerabilities. However, incrementally processing the request body during a resumable upload is no worse than processing a regular request body stream.

The requirement of PATCH is that the partially modified representation cannot be exposed outside. There is no requirement that we can't incrementally process the partially modified representation. Can we instead consider the entire series of PATCHes atomic for a resumable upload?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
guoye-zhang
comments.body:
@GrantGryczan This was the very first presentation about resumable uploads: https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/114/materials/slides-114-httpbis-resumable-uploads-01.pdf We did not use PATCH back then, but switched to PATCH based on the suggestions from the workgroup sessions and mailing list discussions.

POST is disliked by most people because it has very little defined semantics. It’s a catch all upload method that people use when taking a shortcut.

IMO PATCH can define the semantics of the resources being patched, but it cannot define the semantics of other resources. As long as we don’t serve the partial content from the temporary upload resource, it is OK to define a different resource or process the incremental content elsewhere. E.g. it can’t force a different process running on the same machine to not see the file actively being patched.

That being said, I personally don’t care much what method we use since it’s a trivial change as an implementer. If you think it’s an important enough issue to reopen and discuss during the workgroup session, we could.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: I wasn't aware that many others find POST unfavorable. If the consensus is to prefer PATCH, then my objection is probably not important enough to warrant reconsideration (even though I personally stand by it). Nevertheless, I appreciate the time you spent on this discussion!

issues.title: explicitly call out what to do with empty name string in Set-Cookie (rfc6265bis)
issues.author: adamse
issues.body:
What should a user agent do with the "set-cookie-string" `=hej`?

The current RFC says that the name string can be empty and then in a subsequent step to ignore that cookie. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265#autoid-27

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
Hi, 

[6265bis Section 5.6 Step 3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis#name-the-set-cookie-header-field)  instructs 

>If the name-value-pair string lacks a %x3D ("=") character, then the name string is empty, and the value string is the value of name-value-pair.
Otherwise, the name string consists of the characters up to, but not including, the first %x3D ("=") character, and the (possibly empty) value string consists of the characters after the first %x3D ("=") character.

which covers the case of a nameless cookie such as `=hej`. I think clarifying, similar to the value string, that the name string could be possibly empty would improve readability, I'll make that change.

comments.author: adamse
comments.body: Thank you @sbingler. This means there is a change in the recommended parsing algorithm: now empty named cookies are ok. Is that intended?

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
That's correct. Even though it's strongly  not recommended we found that servers still produced unusual set-cookie strings, including empty cookie names, and many UAs accepted them. So the parsing change is meant to standardized behavior so that UAs can at least all do the same thing with them.

I still _strongly_ recommend that any sites only use cookies with a non-empty name that conforms to [Section 4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis#name-server-requirements)'s syntax. Same for the value field too, now that I'm mentioning it. It'll probably work otherwise, but why make your life harder?

issues.title: Proposal: Seamless Domain Transitions Using Shared TLS Certificates
issues.author: fra-iesus
issues.body:
### Problem
Currently, seamless navigation or resource sharing between different domains is not possible even if both domains share the same TLS certificate. This limitation results in degraded user experience and increased complexity for multi-domain applications. For instance, users often face unnecessary page reloads or session resets when transitioning between domains controlled by the same operator.

### Proposed Solution
If two domains share a valid TLS certificate, they should be treated as belonging to the same trusted entity. This could allow for seamless cross-domain transitions, such as:
- Maintaining session state across domains without the need for custom mechanisms (e.g., cross-domain cookies or local storage hacks).
- Enabling browser caching across domains for shared resources.
- Avoiding full page reloads during cross-domain navigation.

This could involve:
1. Extending the HTTP specification to allow session context or caching to be shared between domains with the same TLS certificate.
2. Collaboration with TLS standards to ensure the validity and security of shared certificates.

### Why It Matters for HTTP
The proposal would directly impact how HTTP handles sessions, caching, and cross-origin policies. By treating such domains as part of the same entity, it aligns with the principles of seamless and efficient web experiences.

### Call to Action
I’d love to hear the community’s thoughts on this idea. Is this feasible within the scope of HTTP? What potential security or privacy concerns would need to be addressed? Would collaboration with the TLS Working Group be necessary for implementing this?

Thanks in advance for your feedback!
Lex

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: This issues list is for currently adopted WG drafts. If you want to make a proposal for new work within the WG's scope, the best place to do that is either on the WG mailing list or as an Internet-Draft. Thanks!

issues.title: Sorry I didn't see this when you first filed it.
issues.author: Burberrysmart
issues.body:
Sorry I didn't see this when you first filed it.

> I understand that @mikewest still prefers cookie priorities, but no one at Mozilla has
> any interest in that solution and it didn't seem to get any traction when we discussed

I'd rephrase this a bit. :) The relevant claim here is less that I prefer `Priority` (though I do), and more that Chrome has been shipping the `Priority` attribute for years and I have personal knowledge of Google's internal dependency on the attribute for the corporate intranet. I have anecdotal stories of similar dependency in other companies, but nothing I can point to public statements to justify.

I recognize that other vendors are unlikely to ship the attribute. I'm very open to reviewing the results of y'all's experimentation to see if the results in other browsers show that we're making the wrong choice in Chrome, but my (biased) opinion at the moment is that `Priority` solves this problem in a way that puts developers more directly in control of the eviction process, and that that control is concretely valuable in scenarios that run up against the vendor-specified limits on a regular basis.

issues.title: Retrofit: X-Content-Type-Options is a list, not an item
issues.author: lidaobing
issues.body:
Reason:

1. The standard for X-Content-Type-Options is specified in the Fetch Standard, which treats it as a list (currently with only one valid option).

https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#x-content-type-options-header

> To determine nosniff, given a [header list](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-header-list) list, run these steps:
> 1. Let values be the result of [getting, decoding, and splitting](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-header-list-get-decode-split) `[X-Content-Type-Options](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-x-content-type-options)` from list.
> 2. If values is null, then return false.
> 3. If values[0] is an [ASCII case-insensitive](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#ascii-case-insensitive) match for "nosniff", then return true.
> 4. Return false.

2. Some websites, such as IANA, use multiple X-Content-Type-Options headers.
Example:
```
$ curl -si https://www.iana.org/help/example-domains | grep -i x-content
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
```

3. The field name is X-Content-Type-Options, not X-Content-Type-Option, implying that there is a possibility of adding more options to this field in the future.

Thanks,

issues.title: SHOULD NOT
issues.author: sbingler
issues.body:
_Comment by @fpalombini_

[Section 3](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-19.html#section-3):

> Origin servers SHOULD NOT fold multiple Set-Cookie header fields into a single header field.

I wonder why this is a SHOULD NOT and not a MUST NOT. I do see this was a SHOULD NOT in the original RFC 6265. If it's the case that it has been kept as a SHOULD NOT because existing implementations do it despite this recommendation, I suggest explicitly motivate it here (for example by adding a note, as it has been done in other sections of the document).

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
@mikewest 

Do you have any more context as to why this is a "SHOULD NOT" instead of a "MUST NOT"?

Looking at the mail list for RFC6265 I found https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/http-state/FwQWLsmRynEwtCKxOgUOWjFa7gE/

>>>> [S3 P4] It seems like there should be an all-caps requirement here, e.g., that "Origin servers MUST NOT fold multiple Set-Cookie header fields into a single header field".
>>> 
>>> Origin servers certainly can fold multiple Set-Cookie header fields
>>> into a single header field if they desire.  However, doing so changes
>>> the semantics.  Given the bytes on the wire, there's no experiment we
>>> can run to see if the origin server did or did not perform this
>>> folding.  Therefore, a MUST-level requirement is inappropriate.
>> 
>> As I understand it, folding would cause multiple Set-Cooking header values to be considered instead as setting one cookie with many attributes.  Is there a situation where this is "acceptable or even useful", to quote RFC 2119?  It seems to me like folding is virtually guaranteed to be a bug.
> 
> Ok.  I've changed this to a SHOULD.  I suspect, actually, that this
> requirement already exists in the document (in an obtuse way) because
> the recommend grammar for servers won't produce a "," in the right
> syntactic surrounds to be a folded Set-Cookie header.

Sounds like it's this way because it's a bad idea but we can't check/enforce that it hasn't occurred.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: For what it's worth -- SHOULD vs MUST does not depend on whether it can be tested/enforced; it's whether there are exceptions to the rule.

comments.author: mikewest
comments.body:
I agree with the position in that thread that there's no reasonable way to ensure that clients parse header-folded cookies in the way servers meant them to, and that this change in semantics runs against the grammar of the `set-cookie` header defined in [4.1.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis#section-4.1.1).

I'd note, though, that that grammatical definition's section also suggests a number of SHOULDs that would ideally be MUSTs: "Servers SHOULD NOT send Set-Cookie header fields that fail to conform to the following grammar", "Per the grammar above, servers SHOULD NOT produce nameless cookies", "Servers SHOULD NOT include more than one Set-Cookie header field in the same response with the same cookie-name.", and so on.

I think I'd be comfortable being more prescriptive in the "well-behaved profile" that section 4 defines, and changing many these to hard requirements. I don't think that would require any changes to the client-side behavior that's more accepting of deviations from this profile (and would therefore have no practical effect on the world...), but could usefully increase the predictability of the profile.

I'll put up a PR to discuss.

> When possible, developers should use a session management mechanism such as that described in [Section 8.8.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-19.html#section-8.8.2) to mitigate the risk of CSRF more completely.

We could reframe this to "Developers can more completely mitigate CSRF through a ..." without losing any meaning.
