issues.title: Would it help to mention the end user threats caused by opportunistic data payload with CONNECT?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Not a rhetorical question 😉 . 

It crossed my mind that conventional TCP (ignore TFO) requires a 3-way handshake before application data can be sent. HTTP CONNECT breaks that model, the client can send anything it likes before the 200 response, even if the RFCs say they MUST NOT (as already pointed out in https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-optimistic-upgrade.html#name-guidance-for-http-connect).

For example, over in the HTTP API group, there's a draft about how to deal with people that uninentionally leak their API keys by sending them to a `http://` URL https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpapi-privacy-00.html. This is in spite of HTTP->HTTPS redirects or other mechanisms. One approach to solving that problem is to simply not listen on common plaintext ports, so that TCP would never establish and prevent application data. However, in a proxy setup, its easier to skirt that and accidentally send a request over the CONNECT stream before it would be established. 

Perhaps its worth a sentence to describe this sort of threat?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I don't understand the risk that you're considering here.

> in a proxy setup, its easier to skirt that and accidentally send a request over the CONNECT stream

Are you imagining a client that send a CONNECT request, incorrectly assumes that the CONNECT has failed (or will fail) without checking, and sends a followup request that is (unexpectedly) forwarded as TCP payload?

P.S. Plz review #2997

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Sort of the opposite, and that a client assumes a CONNECT will succeed, when the origin doesn't want it too. I think the risk is tenuous/marginal but to walk through some contrived examples to illustrate.

## Unproxied flow

1. User mistypes a URL as http://example.com/.
2. User Agent determines it should use plaintext TCP to port 80. 
3. Server has not been configured to listen on TCP port 80. This has been chosen explicitly to prevent plaintext clients sending credentials.
4. Client tries to connect() to the server IP. TCP handshake fails.
5. No HTTP data is exchanged, no secrets leaked.

## Proxied flow

1. User mistypes a URL as http://example.com/.
2. User Agent determines it should use plaintext TCP to port 80. 
3. Server has not been configured to listen on TCP port 80
4. Client asks proxy to CONNECT to the server IP. Erroneously sends HTTP request with secret credentials opportunistically
5. The server would not have allowed the handshake to succeed. That mitigation strategy is ineffective.
6. Proxy sees secrets that would not have been exchanged on the wire in unproxied flow.

This is admittedly contrived but could depend upon how a client network protocol stack is structured. For example, with proxying abstractions and async programming, it might to hard to spot this form of footgun. 

This could just be a case that we can't police every problem and broken software, so there's nothing to say. Just wanted to float the scenario.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
OK, interesting scenario.  The client is (1) attempting to reveal private information in TCP plaintext, but is protected from passive attack because (2) the destination does not actually exist ... but if (3) they also implement CONNECT incorrectly, they might still reveal this information to their chosen proxy server.

This seems like a bug, counteracted by another bug, and then potentially re-enabled by a third bug.  My inclination is to leave it out of the draft unless we see evidence of this problem in running code.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Leaving it out seems like a reasonable choice to me. Happy to close this issue unless others want to provide strong evidence it needs to be documented.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: As we haven't gotten any further comments, I'm going to mark this closed.

issues.title: Resolve how to signal TCP RST vs. FIN
issues.author: bemasc
issues.body:
In the current Editor's Copy of `connect-tcp`, TCP FIN and RST are distinguished by HTTP Stream Errors, or (especially in HTTP/1.1, where there is no such thing) by injecting a deliberate syntax error in the Capsule Protocol or an unclean termination of the HTTP connection itself.  This approach is likely simplest for recipients, as it avoids the need for new codepaths (beyond the error handling already required for broken connections), but it might be difficult to implement for senders, who would need detailed access to the HTTP stream, Capsule Protocol, TLS, or TCP connection (in order to inject an error).

PR #2949 draws up an alternative: a FINAL_DATA capsule that represents the FIN bit.  Streams that end without FINAL_DATA are presumed to be unclean (timeout, RST, etc.) and are converted to RST.    This approach matches the abstraction used by WebTransport and avoids the need for error injection, at the cost of some additional complexity.

Some reviewers have asked for an explicit RST signal as well.  This would allow a sender to terminate a stream explicitly, whether by FIN or RST, and then send additional capsules to communicate some metadata about the connection (e.g. summary statistics).  This could be encoded by an additional capsule type (e.g. "ERROR") or by a more flexible version of FINAL_DATA with a boolean flag for clean/unclean shutdown ("END_DATA").  One could even imagine a TCP_FLAGS_DATA that carries the entire TCP flags field, allowing senders to convey FIN, RST, PSH, and URG.

These are the 5 options that I am aware of: implicit (current editor's copy), FINAL_DATA (#2949), FINAL_DATA+ERROR, END_DATA, TCP_FLAGS_DATA.  We need to make a choice to unblock progress on this draft.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: Personally, I don't see a material advantage to the FINAL_DATA+ERROR or END_DATA proposals.  In the FINAL_DATA proposal, if we imagine a client that receives DATA, DATA, CONNECTION_METADATA, (end stream), it seems easy for the client to see that the connection was closed uncleanly with some metadata.  The ERROR capsule only adds value if the CONNECTION_METADATA capsule is substantially delayed, and I don't know of a realistic use case where that would happen.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I agree, I think there's value in having a way to communicate graceful end (FINAL_DATA) but I'm not sure what I'd do with the other information (and that can always be added as another capsule later). Though you linked #2997 and that seems unrelated, did you mean another PR?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
> Though you linked https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2997 and that seems unrelated, did you mean another PR?

You're right, I meant #2949.  Corrected.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Thanks. Looks like my opinion is already on that one :-) Yup I support adding that signal.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: @kazuho @PiotrSikora You both expressed interest in an explicit RST signal in #2949.  Are you still interested in that, or should we move forward with #2949 as-is?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
A TCP RST makes no guarantee about what might be delivered.  QUIC RESET_STREAM is similar.  What you get is what you get.  If our goal is to signal that, then resetting the stream is fine for RST; closing the stream is fine for termination.

There was a question about what to do with the TCP connection with HTTP/1.1.  https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38507586/reset-a-tcp-socket-connection-from-application might help.

QUIC has the RESET_STREAM_AT as well, which makes it possible to ensure that data is delivered, if you care about that.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
I think there's value in adding an explicit signal of FIN/RST inside the stream without closing the stream, to leave room for future work communicating information from the proxy later. The drawback of #2949 as it stands is that you can't relay a TCP RST without using RST_STREAM -- that means the proxy either cannot send further capsules on the stream _or_ the proxy must delay sending the RST signal until it knows the size of the metadata.

To me, this argues for an END_DATA that carries the FIN/RST outcome and removing the stream reset behavior entirely, or at least giving the server the option to do that. (Servers can still abort streams including for other reasons, so clients will still need a code path treating that as a RST or network error as well.)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I firmly believe that if you are concerned in communicating supplementary data for a closed thing, then that has some use, but we risk making this more complex just to accommodate a theoretical use case.  There are ways to gain that feature if it was considered important enough, even if we had streams reset.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
> There was a question about what to do with the TCP connection with HTTP/1.1. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38507586/reset-a-tcp-socket-connection-from-application might help.

This StackOverflow answer strikes me as evidence that a large fraction of implementors will give up and just bleach the RST in HTTP/1.1.  Also, note that sending a TCP RST on an "https" connection is insecure (violating privacy and integrity guarantees).  To propagate a RST securely, the endpoints must send a TLS alert or a malformed capsule.

I don't believe injecting an alert is possible in Golang TLS, or most other high-level TLS APIs.  I conclude that in the absence of a new capsule type such as FINAL_DATA/END_DATA, we will need Capsule Protocol implementations in languages like Golang to support injecting an incomplete (i.e. malformed) capsule.

Given the lack of interest among Capsule Protocol Enthusiasts in supporting deliberate syntax errors, I think this might be a pretty good argument for adding a new capsule type.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
> The drawback of [#2949](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2949) as it stands is that you can't relay a TCP RST without using RST_STREAM

This is not correct.  A stream that ends gracefully but without FINAL_DATA signals a TCP RST*.

*Technically, it signals an unclean shutdown, which could be a timeout or other error but is propagated as RST.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
@bemasc: Right, which means that the signal can't be sent until you've sent all the post-connection frames you wish to. That may well be acceptable, certainly given that we don't have a firm plan to send such data right now. But we should explicitly decide to accept that delay if we go that route.

@martinthomson: Believe me, I am completely sympathetic to the answer of YAGNI. If we want to leave room for this, we should do it as simply as possible unless/until we need it.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
There's often some confusion between FIN and RST when it comes to TCP. Many see them as roughly identical while they're absolutely not. FIN means "I have nothing more to say". RST means "I want you to stop talking to me". These are fundamentally different. TCP does have deficiencies on this, like the usual close-before-the-end that causes RSTs when redirecting HTTP POST requests for example. A not-so-uncommon sequence that exhibits both FIN and RST is the following:

- client sends a POST request to a server
- the server acknowledges the request, processes it and sends a final response to the client due to insufficient authentication. A 401 or a redirect is sent, along with a FIN.
- the server then closes the connection
- if the client had sent everything, the client will receive the message and the FIN only. If the client continues sending, the extra data in flight will trigger an RST from the server
- that RST from the server may reach the client before it had a chance to read the response message and the FIN, and destroy them in network buffers (possibly even on the sender side) so that the response will never be received while it was properly sent.

All that to say that improper handling of both signals can easily result in confusion on the receiver end by the loss of important data. But not having the distinction between these signals can also be problematic. For example having only the FIN would mean that the server would have no way to tell the client "please stop sending me your payload now". And using only RST wouldn't allow the client to know that the response might have been truncated in case where content-length is not used.

Thus I think that it's a good practice in general to consider them as two distinct signals for distinct use cases.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I think we are all discussing a simple model with three states for each leg: open, complete, and truncated.  There are only two allowed transitions: open->complete (FIN) and open->truncated (RST).  FINAL_DATA (#2949) only allows the sender to drive these transitions.  @wtarreau, it sounds like you're suggesting that it's worthwhile to have a higher-fidelity model of TCP, where the receiver can also drive the open->truncated transition.

In HTTP/2, this can be accomplished by sending RST_STREAM after sending a FINAL_DATA capsule.  RST_STREAM is bidirectional, so it doesn't provide a way to say "stop sending but I'm still sending".  For better or worse, this maps well to TCP RST.

QUIC can express "stop sending but I'm still sending" as well, thanks to a distinction between RESET_STREAM (send-side) and STOP_SENDING (receive-side).

In HTTP/1.1, one could imagine sending a truncated capsule after FINAL_DATA to force a connection error.

If we try to solve this purely at the Capsule layer, it could be done using two capsules like FINAL_DATA and "STOP_SENDING_DATA".  STOP_SENDING_DATA means "I am discarding the content of any further DATA frames".  (You MUST NOT send STOP_SENDING_DATA after receiving a FINAL_DATA.)

STOP_SENDING_DATA seems fairly appealing to me, as it creates a reusable abstract CloseRead/CloseWrite distinction that parallels QUIC and covers more of the TCP state machine without getting too far into details of TCP.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Note, I'm not necessarily advocating for a higher-fidelity model of TCP, I'm just expressing that there are two distinct use cases for a final vs aborted termination and that we at least need to support conveying this difference.

Regarding "stop sending but I'm still sending", I'm not seeing any valid use case for this, and from a protocol perspective this would be an anti-pattern that easily leads to deadlocks because if each peer does the same within half an RTT, then you get a stuck communication (except if it only applies to payload and not control-level of course).

I generally agree with your vision of STOP_SENDING_DATA and FINAL_DATA. However the "MUST NOT" rule regarding sending STOP_SENDING_DATA after receiving FINAL_DATA is not necessary because it cannot be enforced on the receiver's side: again it's a matter of timing. By the time the STOP_SENDING_DATA message arrives to the other end, it might have already sent its FINAL_DATA. I'd just say that doing that is useless (it doesn't change the final state).

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I've significantly updated #2949 based on feedback from @wtarreau.  #2949 now enables this distinction without adding any significant mandatory requirements.

Please review #2949.  I'll plan to merge it in 48 hours if there are no more comments.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: Merged.  Thanks all for your input on this topic.

issues.title: QUERY: use GET params for a (stored) query
issues.author: reschke
issues.body: Is this allowed? Recommended? Do we want to talk about it?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
So, with the XSLT example in <https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-08.html#more-query-formats>... Would it be allowed/useful for the XSLT to be parametrized, and to obtain the parameters from the query component of the request URI?

For instance:

~~~
QUERY /errata.json?from-year=1234 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: application/xslt+xml
Accept: application/xml, text/csv
Location: /x/42

<transform xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
  xmlns:j="http://www.w3.org/2005/xpath-functions"
  version="3.0">

  <output method="text"/>

  <param name="from-year">1970</param>

  <param name="input"/>
...
~~~

So the actual query would be determined by *both* query parameters and the payload.

If the server decides to return a "Location" field, providing a "stored query", would that be based both on payload and request parameters (I'd expect that), or would it still depend on request parameters, such as in...:

~~~
GET x/42?from-year=1234 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
~~~

Do we need to discuss this?

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
If you want to supply more parameters, the more likely method on a Location: response field might be a QUERY.
(Otherwise it is not clear to me which kind of URI arithmetic is needed to massage the Location: response field into a modified GET URI.  It does not help that the term "query parameters" is a bit wobbly in the draft.)

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
>  It does not help that the term "query parameters" is a bit wobbly in the draft.)

Good catch. Let's fix that first. -> #3019 and #3020

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> ...the more likely method on a Location: response field might be a QUERY.

I'm not sure whether the choice of method matters here, but if it's not GET we better define what it means. For GET we currently say:

> A server MAY create or locate a resource that identifies the query operation for future use. If the server does so, the URI of the resource can be included in the Location header field of the response (see [Section 10.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-10.2.2) of [HTTP]. This represents a claim that a client can send a GET request to the indicated URI to repeat the query operation just performed without resending the query parameters. This resource might be temporary; if a future request fails, the client can retry using the original QUERY resource and the previously submitted parameters again.

So this is an instance of "query parameters" that #3020 wants to clarify. If, in the Location response field, the server includes the URI request parameters from the original request, would that make *that* resource parametrized? That would make the example above:

~~~
QUERY /errata.json?from-year=1234 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: application/xslt+xml
Accept: application/xml, text/csv
Location: /x/42?from-year=1234
~~~

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body: While reading the spec I also found that the proximity of the examples involving GET/POST/QUERY naturally made me wonder how query-string parameters ought to be handled with QUERY (and I have not found text regarding this in the draft). I have no strong opinion on either choice but I think it should be mentioned (at least to say that it's unspecified) so that adopters are careful about how they want to use this. The temptation to turn either GET or POST directly to QUERY might be strong enough to make such cases appear.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Discussed at IETF 122 Bangkok. Feedback:

1. The query part in the request URI for QUERY works exactly the same way it does for other methods. So from the perspective of the protocol, adding a query part is a change of URI and thus a different resource is identified.
2. We should note that in the definition of the method.
3. This does not prevent implementations from doing this for specific query media types, but that's out of scope for this spec.

@MikeBishop , @martinthomson ?

issues.title: Tri-state
issues.author: kazuho
issues.body:
In https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/11, @martinthomson says:
> Ted Hardie suggested that we might have three states:
> 
> 1. Incremental is necessary
> 2. Incremental is preferred, but not essential
> 3. Incremental is not necessary
> 
> This seems like a better way than [#7](https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/7) and more general overall.
> 
> I suggest a/p/n for always/preferred/not preferred.

Rationale for having "preferred" is discussed in https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/8.
Rationale for having "not preferred" (or prefer buffered) is discussed in https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/7.

comments.author: PiotrSikora
comments.body:
> Rationale for having "not preferred" (or prefer buffered) is discussed in [kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http#7](https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/7).

My reading of [kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http#7](https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/7) is that it's asking for a strict (i.e. reject if cannot be fulfilled) fully buffered store-and-forward semantics, and not simply expressing a preference, so that OHTTP request is not interleaved with OHTTP response, since the privacy properties of OHTTP were proven with that assumption in mind.

cc @thibmeu to confirm

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@PiotrSikora Thank you for raising the point.

While we wait for confirmation from @thibmeu, generally speaking, we are talking about a 2x2 matrix:
||required|preferable|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|incremental|status quo||
|fully-buffered|||

Status quo is targeting only the top left corner, with the aim to improve interoperability.

Doing other three boxes does not necessarily improve interoperability. Applications that are fine with the signal being indications of preference (rather than a requirement) are using the signal for optimization. For OHTTP, it could make sense to require fully-buffered behavior for privacy reasons, though requiring that does not improve interoperability (because the functionality provided by OHTTP works perfectly when the messages are forwarded incrementally).

Therefore, I am concerned that there would be less appetite among the proxy developers to implement something other than the "require-incremental" mode.

Probably, one way of moving forward would be to define the "require-incremental" mode and keep room for adding other modes.

comments.author: PiotrSikora
comments.body:
> Doing other three boxes does not necessarily improve interoperability. Applications that are fine with the signal being indications of preference (rather than a requirement) are using the signal for optimization.

FWIW, I'm not convinced that the "preference" options are worth implementing, since clients shouldn't be in the business of optimizing and micro-managing the buffering behavior of the intermediaries.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
The comment on https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/7 is indeed trying to signal a preference from the client to not interleave request and response. If the server support Incremental, this is a requirement, but not all server will support it.
I have added that description to a rough update of the draft in a [fork](https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/compare/main...thibmeu:draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http:main?expand=1).

This should allow a proxy that does not want to buffer request/response to reject the request, possibly with a fallback to a non chunked variant on the client side.

This is different from @martinthomson proposal which is to have a [tri-state](https://github.com/kazuho/draft-kazuho-httpbis-incremental-http/issues/11) specifically for incremental. If I was to update your table

|                | required | preferred        | not-necessary    |
|:---------------|:---------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| incremental    | `?1`     | `martin-state-1` | `martin-state-2` |
| fully-buffered | `?0`     |                  |                  |

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Based on the discussion at IETF 122, my understanding is that we should close this issue without adopting the PR.

If we decide to have signals demanding (or prefering) fully-buffered mode in the future, we would have the room to add such a signal.

issues.title: CSRF mitigation and SameSite=Strict
issues.author: Jxck
issues.body:
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-20#section-5.6.7.1

> Lax enforcement provides reasonable defense in depth against CSRF attacks that rely on unsafe HTTP methods (like POST), but does not offer a robust defense against CSRF as a general category of attack:
>
> Attackers can still pop up new windows or trigger top-level navigations in order to create a "same-site" request (as described in [Section 5.2.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-20#document-requests)), which is only a speedbump along the road to exploitation.
> Features like <link rel='prerender'> [[prerendering](https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/prerender)] can be exploited to create "same-site" requests without the risk of user detection.



My understanding is that the only request that can be generated by this “1 and 2” attack is a GET. In other words, the attack implicitly relies on the service having an API that accepts GET requests with side effects.

In general, there is no fundamental countermeasure against “CSRF via GET” other than ensuring that side-effect APIs are not implemented in GET endpoints. Instead, those APIs should be implemented via POST (PUT/DELETE).

If a service has enough resources to classify cookies into “read” and “write” and add the `Strict` attribute to “write” cookies, it might be more effective simply to change any side-effecting GET endpoints to POST instead. According to the RFC, deploying `Strict` does offer robust defense in depth, but it does so only because “the request is sent but no cookie is granted.” This is not a valid final layer for a multi-layer defense, and it is questionable to recommend it as the primary measure.

Essentially, CSRF countermeasures should be prioritized as follows:

1. **Do not implement APIs with side effects in GET.**
2. **Check the `Origin` header for any API with side effects.**
   - Note that not only `fetch()` but also `<form>` submissions send the `Origin` header in all major browser now.
3. **Restrict cookie sending** (e.g., `SameSite=Lax` or stricter) so that cookies are not automatically included if the request originates from a different site by attack.

Given that points 1 and 2 are properly implemented, I wonder how much value there really is in separating cookies into “read” and “write” categories or distinguishing between Strict and Lax. It seems to me that there is no major problem with just making one Session cookie with `Lax` as before, but am I missing something?

I understand that this RFC is not a guideline for CSRF mitigation. However, if that were the case, the current use of Strict and the separation of “read”/“write” and the description as if it is important as a CSRF countermeasure seem to invite misleading.

comments.author: Jxck
comments.body:
any comments？
or are there any point I’m missing here ?

comments.author: johannhof
comments.body: Your priorities 1 and 2 are best practices, priority 3 (using SameSite) is technical enforcement. "Just don't do stupid things" works well if you're an experienced developer working on a small service, but that stops scaling quickly even for small teams. The best mitigation at scale is not trusting yourself or others and thus minimizing the default attack surface for your service, your company or ideally the Web as a whole :)

issues.title: Location
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
Currently, QUERY says:

>A server can create or locate a resource that identifies the query operation for future use. If the server does so, the URI of the resource can be included in the Location header field of the response (see [Section 10.2.2](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-10.2.2) of [[HTTP](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-09.html#HTTP)]). This represents a claim that a client can send a GET request to the indicated URI to repeat the query operation just performed without resending the query content. This resource might be temporary; if a future request fails, the client can retry using the original QUERY resource and the previously submitted content.

This defines blanket semantics for all QUERY responses regardless of status code.

However, 9110 says:

> The "Location" header field is used in some responses to refer to a specific resource in relation to the response. The type of relationship is defined by the combination of request method and status code semantics.

and goes on to give general guidelines:

> For [201 (Created)](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#status.201) responses, the Location value refers to the primary resource created by the request. For [3xx (Redirection)](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#status.3xx) responses, the Location value refers to the preferred target resource for automatically redirecting the request.

The `201` semantics are mostly aligned, but I really wonder about the `3xx` semantics here -- it's easy to imagine a case where a server redirects a request without understanding the specific semantics of QUERY, and the resource on the other end of `Location` won't be prepared to handle those future GETs.

So I suspect that this statement needs to be narrowed to specific status codes (likely, `201`).

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body: That's a good point, because authenticating intermediaries tend to use 3xx quite a bit with very little understanding of the application semantics. Usually it's as simple as "received a request without a valid cookie -> redirect to authentication portal". Same can happen with domain redirections (company A acquires company B and the site redirects all requests to the new domain on the same server).

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> The "Location" header field is used in some responses to refer to a specific resource in relation to the response. The type of relationship is defined by the combination of request method and status code semantics.

So yes, we can define this. We are not restricted to 201. We also discussed that it would be weird for a safe method to return 201 instead of 200.

Wrt 300 - point taken. Let's  overhaul *that* part.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
FWIW, the subsequent section about 3xx indeed says:

> In some cases, the server may choose to respond indirectly to the QUERY request by redirecting the user agent to a different URI (see [Section 15.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.4) of [[HTTP]](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-09.html#HTTP)). The semantics of the redirect response do not differ from other methods. For instance, a 303 (See Other) response would indicate that the Location field identifies an alternate URI from which the results can be retrieved using a GET request (this use case is also covered by the use of the Location response field in a 2xx response). On the other hand, response codes 307 (Temporary Redirect) and 308 (Permanent Redirect) can be used to request the user agent to redo the QUERY request on the URI specified by the Location field. Various non-normative examples of successful QUERY responses are illustrated in [Appendix A](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-09.html#examples).

So restricting this to 2xx would be consistent with that.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
@wtarreau ...:

> That's a good point, because authenticating intermediaries tend to use 3xx quite a bit with very little understanding of the application semantics. Usually it's as simple as "received a request without a valid cookie -> redirect to authentication portal". Same can happen with domain redirections (company A acquires company B and the site redirects all requests to the new domain on the same server).

For 3xx, the spec currently only defines additional behaviour for 303. OTOH, we did not define anything new for 301, 302, 307 or 308 - which of course we can't. So I believe we are safe here. If there is indeed a problem with 303 + Location, I would recommend to drop the whole concept of "indirect responses" to keep things simple.

Or use "Prefer". Or use a link relation. But that sounds like a lot of work for something that might not be used anyway.

issues.title: Content-Location

issues.body:
> Furthermore, a successful response can include a Content-Location header field (see [Section 8.7](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-8.7) of [[HTTP](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-09.html#HTTP)]) containing an identifier for a resource corresponding to the results of the operation.

issues.title: Adjust HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 malformed messages to be consistent with what implementations actually do
issues.author: DemiMarie
issues.body:
This arguably belongs in http-core or http2, but neither of those mentions HTTP/3.

RFC9113 (HTTP/2) and RFC9114 (HTTP/3) both consider a message to be malformed if it has any of the following:

- A field value with an invalid character.
- A field value with leading and/or trailing whitespace.
- Other characteristics not relevant here.

However, the handling of malformed field values varies widely among implementations:

1. Browsers only consider NUL, CR, and LF to be invalid field value characters.  I have not checked how they handle leading and/or trailing whitespace.
2. HAProxy strips leading and trailing whitespace and only considers NUL, CR, and LF to be invalid field value characters.
3. NGINX preserves leading and trailing whitespace and only considers NUL, CR, and LF to be invalid field value characters.
4. H2O and Varnish both perform strict validation, but H2O returns a 400 error instead of a stream error.
5. nghttp2 performs strict validation by default, but this can be relaxed to some degree
6. nghttp3 silently discards a field if the value is malformed.

I think 1, 2, 4, and 5 should be permitted, but 3 and 6 should not be.  Text like the following could make sense.

> Implementations MUST NOT send a message with leading and/or trailing LWS in a field value.  If such a message is received, implementations MUST either strip the leading and/or trailing LWS before doing any processing, or else treat the entire message as malformed.  Implementations MUST NOT discard the field value or preserve the leading and/or trailing LWS.
> 
> Implementations MUST NOT send a message with NUL, CR, or LF in a field value.  A message with NUL, CR, or LF in a field value MUST be treated as malformed.
> 
> Implementations SHOULD NOT send a message with other CTRLs in a field value.  Implementations that receive such a message MUST either treat the entire message as malformed, treat the CTRLs as ordinary characters, or replace them with SP.  Implementations MUST NOT silently discard the field value.
> 
> Clients that receive a malformed message MUST send a stream error.  Servers that receive a malformed message MUST send a stream error or a 400 response.

issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
(follow up to https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2896)

Currently:

>[2.4. ](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-11.html#section-2.4)[Caching](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-11.html#name-caching)

>The response to a QUERY method is cacheable; a cache MAY use it to satisfy subsequent QUERY requests as per [Section 4](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111#section-4) of [[HTTP-CACHING](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-11.html#HTTP-CACHING)]).
>The cache key for a QUERY request (see [Section 2](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111#section-2) of [[HTTP-CACHING](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-11.html#HTTP-CACHING)]) MUST incorporate the request content. When doing so, caches SHOULD first normalize request content to remove semantically insignificant differences, thereby improving cache efficiency, by:
>
>- Removing content encoding(s) ([Section 8.4](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-8.4) of [[HTTP](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-11.html#HTTP)]).
>- Normalizing based upon knowledge of format conventions, as indicated by any media subtype suffix in the request's Content-Type field (e.g., "+json", see [Section 4.2.8](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6838#section-4.2.8) of [[RFC6838](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-11.html#RFC6838)]).
>- Normalizing based upon knowledge of the semantics of the content itself, as indicated by the request's Content-Type field.
>
> Note that any such normalization is performed solely for the purpose of generating a cache key; it does not change the request itself.

Issues:

1. "... MUST incorporate the request content" - that's misleading, because any kind of stable indentifier (such as a SHA-256 of (normalized) content) should be good enough
2. "When doing so..." means "When responses are cached...", right?
3. "...SHOULD first normalize..." is misleading, as all the steps that follow are more or less optional ... "...can normalize..." or "...are encouraged to normalize..." maybe?
4. "remove semantically insignificant differences, thereby improving cache efficiency, by" -> "remove semantically insignificant differences, thereby improving cache efficiency. _For instance_,  by"

Anyways, thanks for teaching me about C14N.

issues.title: Cookies: combining multiple prefixes
issues.author: yoavweiss
issues.body:
Following up on a [discussion](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025AprJun/0192.html) from the mailing list.

As we're [planning to add](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3110) more prefixes, it'd be good to have a way to combine them.
After multiple proposals, I think the best way to do that is to extend the prefix syntax to have a single char delimiter (e.g. `_`), and extend the processing logic to split on that delimiter and process multiple prefixes.

An example cookie name may look like `__Host_Http_FlyingCars-cookiename`, which will imply that the cookie is host-scoped, http-only and also some future semantics we haven't defined yet (and which will be ignored until we would).

/cc @roryhewitt @annevk @johannhof @cfredric @DCtheTall

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: I'd like to better understand the benefit of a more complex scheme. Even today we are already removing certain possibilities, such as HttpOnly without Secure. I would expect that to continue to some extent. And even if we end up with 20-40 unique prefixes you need to keep in a lookup table, that still seems preferable to having to parse cookie names.

comments.author: yoavweiss
comments.body:
@cfrederic mentioned the `Unpartitioned` prefix as a potential candidate.

Let's explore what adding that would look like without a multi-prefix scheme.
One way in which we can reduce combinatorial options is by requiring the prefixes to be alphabetically ordered.

So in that case, we would have `__Secure` (which is orthogonal as it's implied by all other prefixes), `__Http`, `__Host`, `__Unpartitioned`, `__HostHttp`,  `__HostUnpartitioned`, `__HttpUnpartitioned`, and `__HostHttpUnpartitioned`.

I guess we can change the specification to define the semantics of each variant, and then easily define the combined semantics of e.g. `__HostHttpUnpartitioned` by pointing at the requirements for all 3.

At the same time, I'm not sure this is better than parsing cookie names.

comments.author: cfredric
comments.body:
I was using `Unpartitioned` as a placeholder "new prefix, unrelated to existing ones", I didn't mean that it should necessarily come next.

It just seemed to me the current approach feels a bit ad-hoc and is/would be a pain to extend, which would make it harder than necessary for websites that want to have certain guarantees about their cookies.

If I put myself in the shoes of a site developer (or web framework developer), I'd rather write a (linearly-growing) parsing routine instead of maintaining an (exponentially growing) table of unique prefixes. A table seems somewhat prone to typos unless you autogenerate it, and at that point, what's the benefit over parsing?

Making the "prefixes"/tags be order-independent also feels like the least footgunny option from a web developer's perspective; bugs due to supplying the tags in the wrong order (non-alphabetical, say) would be impossible.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
All this effort seems to be an attempt to resolve the same problem: that the UAs don't share a cookie's metadata/attribute when that cookie is read. So malicious cookies can masquerade as privileged ones.

The cookie prefixes were an effort to crowbar in some assurances about specific cookie attributes in a backwards compatible way. It mostly worked but:
- the server can't actually be sure the browser enforces the prefixes
- they were never widely adopted
- it's inelegant (imo)

Given that, adding more, especially with complicated semantic parsing for combinations, is a design-smell to me. Maybe it's the right choice, maybe there are better options.

Here's a ~bad~ first idea, what if the UA returns the metadata in some new request header field?
This would give us a couple nice properties:

- Backwards compatible
- The fields presence assures servers of UA support

Some open questions I can immediately think of:

- Correlating cookies with metadata?
  - The metadata could be returned in the same order as the cookies.
- Increased request size?
  - Make it opt-in. Servers that don't understand or care about this could simply not ask for it.
    - This could even be on a per-cookie basis, maybe with some `__metadata-` prefix.
- Which metadata to return?
  - Secure, http-only, domain, path? Lots of opportunity for discussions here.

This design obviously requires more effort on the server's part, and its cookie handling support, but sites interested in this information have control on whether or not they implement it.

I feel a more generic approach is cleaner and would reduce cognitive load

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
TBH I remain unconvinced we actually are going to need to turn the crank another time after HttpOnly but I agree with @sbingler that *if* we have to do it again, that's probably a better direction. We do need to worry about intermediaries mucking with the cookie header but this feels solvable.

That said, I don't think we need to solve this for HttpOnly, so I think it's also perfectly fine to defer this to the next round, if it ever comes.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I agree with David.  Remember why we have prefixes: it's redundancy to protect against attribute loss (from configuration errors and the like).

The case for more prefixes gets progressively weaker over time, not stronger.  That is, we didn't add a prefix for the attribute before, adding it is both more expensive now, and people have demonstrably been getting by without since then.  Maybe with strong evidence of misconfiguration, but I find it hard to believe that attributes are somehow being dropped.

comments.author: yoavweiss
comments.body:
Thanks all!

Also tagging @dveditz, who [commented](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025AprJun/0195.html) on the related mailing list thread.

I tend to agree with @davidben and @martinthomson on the [YAGNI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_aren%27t_gonna_need_it) potential of this discussion, as we don't know if and when we're going to need to add another prefix beyond `__Http`. Therefore, the shiny new mechanism that @sbingler suggests feels like an overkill to tackle right now.

Given that, maybe we should downscope this thread a bit, and just think of the combination of `__Host-` and `__Http-`.

That combination could be `__HostHttp-` which is shorter and may be future extensible by creating a lookup table as @annevk suggested.

It could also be `__Host_Http-` which is one char longer, and would enable future extensibility through parsing the delimiter.

Personally, either one of these would work, so it's a question of which option we want to keep open in the future, in case where new prefixes would come up, and we don't go with something like what @sbingler suggested.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
> it's redundancy to protect against attribute loss (from configuration errors and the like).

I don't think that's *quite* right. Prefixes are redundancy to protect against cookie injection. The problem is that http and https origins share a cookie jar, as do origins across the same eTLD+1.

Servers aren't told *how* a cookie was saved. If a request could mix cookies from sources that aren't equally trusted, the less trusted source could inject cookies into a request that assumed the more trusted one.

But that's still a very specific situation, and not all that generally applicable. We're mostly dealing with the gap between same origin policy and cookies' weird predecessor security policy.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
It's fine by me if this is the chosen design, I just wanted us to consider some alternative approaches before settling. It's been a bit since I last saw this proposal and the idea of permutations of the prefixes stuck out to me.

If these really are the last prefixes then great. Somehow though it seems like a new prefix is proposed every few years.

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: Let's go with `__HostHttp-` and we can revisit this discussion if the need for more prefixes arises.

comments.author: yoavweiss
comments.body: SG. I'll bring back `__HostHttp-` to https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3110

comments.author: AKJUS
comments.body: very helpful thankyou

comments.author: yoavweiss
comments.body: Closing this, as we decided to punt on the larger question and landed on `__HostHttp-` for the immediate need.

issues.title: Cookies: local and server clock out-of-sync
issues.author: annevk
issues.body:
https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1909980#c5

> Chrome computes the expiration time by adding the delta between the local and server times. If your computer is 10 hours in the future, the cookie expiration time will be increased by 10 hours. As far as I know, this is not part of the cookie spec (rfc6265bis), but we should implement the same logic.
