issues.title: Cookies: do we need to byte-lowercase case-senitive cookie prefixes?
issues.author: miketaylr
issues.body:
https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3110#discussion_r2159165691


Cookies talks about cookie prefixes as being case-sensitive:

> If a cookie's name begins with a case-sensitive match for the string __Secure-

https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/blob/main/draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies.md#the-__secure--prefix

But then later byte-lowercases the prefixes:

> If cookie's name, byte-lowercased, starts with __secure- and cookie's secure-only is false, then return null.

https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/blob/main/draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies.md#the-__secure--prefix:~:text=If%20cookie%27s%20name%2C%20byte%2Dlowercased%2C%20starts%20with%20__secure%2D%20and%20cookie%27s%20secure%2Donly%20is%20false%2C%20then%20return%20null.

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: As explained in that thread, this is by design. Different requirements for producers and consumers.

comments.author: miketaylr
comments.body: OK - I misread the thread then.

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: Well I did offer that if we wanted to make them match we could open an issue for that, but it wasn't entirely clear to me if that's what you were going for here.

comments.author: dveditz
comments.body: In earlier drafts of rfc6265bis prefixes were case-sensitive, but we discovered some common server platforms treated cookie names as case-insensitive despite the earlier specs. The whole point of the ugly name hack was that fast-moving browsers could offer protective features to front-end web developers who couldn't otherwise replace their underlying server stack, so we had to change it. We made enforcement case-insensitive in issue #2231

issues.title: QUERY: HTTPDIR/RF review - conditional requests
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
> 2.3.  Conditional Requests
>
>    A conditional QUERY requests that the selected representation (i.e.,
>    the query results, after any content negotiation) be returned in the
>    response only under the circumstances described by the conditional
>    header field(s), as defined in Section 13 of [HTTP].

I think this is incorrect and requires more explanation and reference
to 3.2 [HTTP].  You might even want to quote the last paragraph of 3.2
and specifically define that, for QUERY, the response content is
influenced by content negotiation. I recommend a more extensive
discussion of content negotiation along with the examples.

The conditional request mechanisms, however, are defined by the
"selected representation" of GET semantics. Specifically, things like
last-modified and etag comparisons are done before the query
is processed, not after, since the condition says "do not proceed". 

A resource that responds to QUERY is almost certain to also respond
to GET (usually with an empty form/instructions). The existing
conditional mechanisms will work on that empty form, which is
probably not what is desired.

In theory, new condition fields could be defined that operate after the
query has been processed, but that would be silly given the instructions
for the query are already located within the request content and
can include their own conditions for when to limit or what to exclude.
Use the query's conditions instead of HTTP conditionals.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: High-level comment: the good thing is that if the server allocates a new GETtable resource, things get easy.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Related to: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1917

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
OTOH, if QUERY is going to remain defined as a cacheable method, then my above comment is incorrect and all of the conditional field mechanisms and ordering algorithm need to be updated to treat QUERY in the same way as GET. 

Note that this might not be compatible with servers that have not yet implemented QUERY, but I suspect those will all respond with "not implemented" first before trying to process conditional fields.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
I can imagine two ways in which conditional requests might be used:

- Don't execute the query if the state of the underlying resource (database) hasn't changed since it was last executed, to save server effort
- Don't transfer the results if the results of executing the query are the same as the last execution, to save bandwidth

The advantage of the first is that it probably doesn't require modifying the 9110 language, since it would consider the condition before executing the instruction, but it would require stating what ETag and Last-Modified represent in relation to QUERY results. If a server wants the latter semantics, it can allocate a GET-able resource, where the existing rules about GET would cause that behavior.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Thoughts:

- all these things get irrelevant once the server exposes a GETtable URI for the current result. If that's the case, in a perfect world the user agent will not resend the same QUERY again, and all the semantics for GET can be applied.
- ETag - this again is based on the concept of "selected representation", so that's what we need to understand.
- yes, at least one example will be needed, or two: QUERY -> QUERY and QUERY -> GET

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> OTOH, if QUERY is going to remain defined as a cacheable method, then my above comment is incorrect and all of the conditional field mechanisms and ordering algorithm need to be updated to treat QUERY in the same way as GET.

So should we put this on hold until we have an answer for #3120?

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
They are intertwined. It's hard to come to a conclusion without discussing all of the tradeoffs.

The conditional request mechanisms had three essential purposes in HTTP:

  1) efficient cache updates (my original motivation for If-Modified-Since);
  2) optimistic overwrite protection (Henrik's pre-DAV authoring motivation), plus later WebDAV pessimistic If;
  3) recomposition of partial responses (Jeff Mogul's If-Range motivation).

QUERY can exclude (2). Maybe we just need to define what "selected representation" means for QUERY and let the other definitions cascade from there. But, no matter how we look at it, we are still talking about proposed changes to how the same fields/algorithms are defined in 9110.

I think it's borderline unsafe for the Internet to encourage QUERY be used instead of GET without having a caching solution that is at least capable of efficient cache updates.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Observation: we _could_ say that when a server mints a GETtable resource (via `Location`), ETags and last modified dates will be the same as for QUERY. With that, we can delegate the definitions for QUERY completely to GET (even if the server does not _actually_ does not support that mechanism).

Let's try that.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Overtaken by https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3255

issues.title: QUERY: HTTPDIR/RF review - Content-Location, Location
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
> 2.1.  Content-Location and Location Fields
>
>    A successful response (2xx, Section 15.3 of [HTTP]) can include a
>    Content-Location header field containing an identifier for a resource
>    corresponding to the results of the operation; see Section 8.7 of
>    [HTTP] for details.  This represents a claim from the server that a
>    client can send a GET request for the indicated URI to retrieve the
>    results of the query operation just performed.  The indicated
>    resource might be temporary.

That paragraph needs to be above in the description of a 200 response
to QUERY, or at least referred to as such, since it is just repeating
the definition of Content-Location.

>    A server can create or locate a resource that identifies the query
>    operation for future use.  If the server does so, the URI of the
>    resource can be included in the Location header field of the 2xx
>    response (see Section 10.2.2 of [HTTP]).  This represents a claim
>    that a client can send a GET request to the indicated URI to repeat
>    the query operation just performed without resending the query
>    content.  This resource might be temporary; if a future request
>    fails, the client can retry using the original QUERY resource and the
>    previously submitted content.

Again, this is part of the protocol definition and belongs above as
generally applying for all 2xx responses (even 204).

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Whether these are discussed as sub paragraphs (2.1 and 2.2), or inlined into the main section 2) seems to be entirely editorial to me.

(and if we move them into the parent section, somebody else will come along and complain about lack of structure...)

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: @royfielding - can I close this one?

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body: It is editorial, but note that it differs from the way we defined other methods in 9110. If you follow the same pattern as 9110, it becomes relatively easy to understand the semantics in terms of "this is a new method, here's how it is processed, this is how to interpret specific response codes". And, yes, it is deliberately less structured in 9110 because we already define the specifics where those fields are defined. But feel free to close this if you really want the extra structures.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: ok, thanks.

issues.title: QUERY: HTTPDIR/RF review - Redirection
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
> 2.2.  Redirection
>
>    In some cases, the server may choose to respond indirectly to the
>    QUERY request by redirecting the user agent to a different URI (see
>    Section 15.4 of [HTTP]).  The semantics of the redirect response do
>    not differ from other methods.
>
>    For instance, a 303 (See Other, Section 15.4.4 of [HTTP]) response
>    would indicate that the Location field identifies an alternate URI
>    from which the results can be retrieved using a GET request (this use
>    case is also covered by the use of the Location response field in a
>    2xx response).

No, that is incorrect. In a 303 response, the Location field identifies
a replacement target resource that will perform the same query when it
receives a GET request. To complete processing of the original QUERY, the
user agent will need to perform a GET request on the resource referenced
by Location. This allows the original query to be identified for reuse as
a normal resource and for the results to be cached.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Hmmm.

https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc9110.html#status.303 says:

> The 303 (See Other) status code indicates that the server is redirecting the user agent to a different resource, as indicated by a URI in the [Location](https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc9110.html#field.location) header field, which is intended to provide an indirect response to the original request. A user agent can perform a retrieval request targeting that URI (a GET or HEAD request if using HTTP), which might also be redirected, and _present the eventual result as an answer to the original request_. Note that the new URI in the Location header field is not considered equivalent to the target URI.

(emphasis mine)

To me that means that "Location" identifies a GETTtable resource that represents the query result, not the query.

Am I missing something here?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: FWIW, for a POST request, a 303 Location points to the result of *that* request, not the one you'd get when repeating the POST request. Right? Why would that be different? (yes, I know POST is neither safe not idempotent, but that is not mentioned in the definition of 303).

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: @royfielding - can I close this one with no action?

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
That's not what it means. A POST 👉 GET transition cannot be equivalent because the first request is unsafe, but the GET response itself is a cacheable response (and thus can be reused after each 303).

A QUERY -> 303 can be defined as resource equivalence because this spec is doing the definition and Location is explicitly defined as having method-specific semantics. You are seeking a consistency here for Location on POST that doesn't exist by design.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
Historically, 303 was the redirect with changed method (given in a header field). Since that was unsafe in general, we changed it to just 303 -> GET. Later there were unending discussions about resources that shouldn't be retrieved (Semantic Web), so we added the GET -> 303 -> GET semantics of description. Now we are adding QUERY -> 303 -> GET and it will require some tweaks to 303 description in semantics.

The alternative would be to define a new 3XX code, which has proven to be less successful in the past.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Okkk.

The definition of Location indeed says in <https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc9110.html#rfc.section.10.2.2.p.1>:

> The "Location" header field is used in some responses to refer to a specific resource in relation to the response. The type of relationship is defined by the combination of request method and status code semantics.

So, yes, we can define Location on 303 to mean the same things as Location on 2xx. This is indeed good and makes it consistent and more useful. Any objections to this from other interested parties? (cc @mnot, @MikeBishop, @martinthomson)

What I'm not understanding yet is how we would need to tweak the definition of 303 in RFC 9110. If we have to, wouldn't we have to _update_ RFC 9110? That makes me nervous. If that's the case, I'd be in favor of dropping the whole 303 thing, because it seems less useful that 2xx + Location anyway.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Sounds reasonable to me.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
You could also leave 303 as is for "a resource that supplies information about the results of the query" and define a new 3XX code for a "stored query that will perform the same query when accessed with GET".

I doubt that this spec will get through RFC review without the metadata for "updates: RFC9110, RFC9111". Dive in.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
The primary reason for doing 303, IIUC, is so that the response payload (which is potentially large) gets delivered in a cacheable chunk for that URL which we expect to get future GETs as well. I'm really not inclined to mint new status codes in this spec; if we need that, I'd want it to be applicable more broadly than just QUERY and be defined in its own document.

I'm unclear why we need to update anything new for Location on 303, however. 9110 says this:

> A user agent can perform a retrieval request targeting that URI (a GET or HEAD request if using HTTP), which might also be redirected, and present the eventual result as an answer to the original request. Note that the new URI in the Location header field is not considered equivalent to the target URI.
> 
> This status code is applicable to any HTTP method. It is primarily used to allow the output of a POST action to redirect the user agent to a different resource, since doing so provides the information corresponding to the POST response as a resource that can be separately identified, bookmarked, and cached.

The "any method" behavior is exactly what we want -- GET the indicated URI and present it as a response to the initial QUERY.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> I doubt that this spec will get through RFC review without the metadata for "updates: RFC9110, RFC9111". Dive in.

Wow, that makes me very nervous. We carelly cleaned up / clarified extension points in HTTP over they years. If we can't define QUERY as idempotent & safe POST - which really should be trivial - there's something very wrong going on.

I'd rather drop non-essential features from the spec if those are in the way.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
It can be defined as idempotent and safe, and it can be defined as having the GET-equivalent caching and conditional mechanisms, but the latter are defined by the core spec (not by extension methods).

Because we can't know the meaning of new methods, the default behavior when processing conditional request fields is tied to the PUT/POST semantics (i.e, we assume an unknown request is unsafe and needs overwrite protection). GET/HEAD is the exception here and is defined as such in 9110. Hence, to create another exception, the algorithms defined in 9110/9111 have to be changed.

Maybe we should have defined them the same way for all safe&idempotent methods, but it's kind of hard to generalize when there is only one working example.

For example, in [If-None-Match](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-if-none-match):

> An origin server that evaluates an If-None-Match condition MUST NOT perform the requested method if the condition evaluates to false; instead, the origin server MUST respond with either a) the [304 (Not Modified)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.304) status code if the request method is GET or HEAD or b) the [412 (Precondition Failed)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.412) status code for all other request methods.

and to get past that requirement, *this* spec needs to update 9110 to include QUERY with GET (as an exception) both in the conditional fields and in [section 13.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-evaluation-of-preconditions). Just "update" the semantics with the sections listed, not a full spec revision.

I have not checked if something similar would be need to be updated for 9111. It would surprise me if we actually managed to cleanly separate the two specs and didn't include any requirements specific to GET.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> You could also leave 303 as is for "a resource that supplies information about the results of the query" and define a new 3XX code for a "stored query that will perform the same query when accessed with GET".
> 
> I doubt that this spec will get through RFC review without the metadata for "updates: RFC9110, RFC9111". Dive in.

I hear you saying that what the spec currently says is indeed correct?

FWIW, I don't think we need a new status code; we already have most of this functionality in 2xx/Location. _A spec is only ready when there's nothing to take out anymore_, I heard a long time ago.

If we *absolutely* need this functionality for a redirect, I'd rather define a Link relation.

A new status code should be generally applicable (maybe to all safe methods), and defined in it's own spec.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> Because we can't know the meaning of new methods, the default behavior when processing conditional request fields is tied to the PUT/POST semantics (i.e, we assume an unknown request is unsafe and needs overwrite protection). GET/HEAD is the exception here and is defined as such in 9110. Hence, to create another exception, the algorithms defined in 9110/9111 have to be changed.

Let's discuss that in #3117.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
My takeaway is: we *can* define 303/Location for a new method; we just need to pick one of the two alternatives. 

We currently use the behaviour defined for 2xx/Content-Location, but _could_ switch to the 2xx/Location behaviour instead. TODOs would be:

- switch the definition
- clarify that we _can_ do this based on RFC 9110
- update examples

Thoughts?

issues.title: QUERY: HTTPDIR/RF review - Caching
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
**_QUOTED FROM SPEC TEXT, COMMENTS ARE ROY'S (@royfielding)_**

> 2.4.  Caching
>
>    The response to a QUERY method is cacheable; a cache MAY use it to
>    satisfy subsequent QUERY requests as per Section 4 of
>    [HTTP-CACHING]).

No, just no. A cache does not have access to the request content when
making a hit/miss decision. Use the 303 response, as designed.

The reason why this is not allowed in HTTP is because routing decisions
are based on the connection context, host, and entire target URI.
A cache cannot know what parts may apply. The origin doesn't know either.

The actual server recipient of a request containing query parameters
might have been passed along a completely different internal routing
path, with its own security filtering, from the same request with
those parameters hidden within the request content.

Allowing a cache to change the key by moving identifiers from the
content would allow a generic resource to poison the cache for other,
more specific resources.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: See also https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3122#issuecomment-3025288750

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
As much as I disagree with the idea, the way forward here is to clearly document how QUERY caching differs from (or is the same as) existing GET caches, in all respects. If the specification accurately describes the tradeoffs for implementation, I won't have a problem with it.

That means define QUERY in the same level of detail as we define GET for HTTP. In addition to defining how to construct the key, It means going through all of the conditional request header fields and defining how they are to be interpreted (mostly like GET does for testing when to send the response, not like PUT and POST does as a precondition for performing the method). It means demonstrating how a client would make a conditional QUERY request, why it would do so, and what to do for each significant status code returned (i.e., 304). Likewise for Range requests.

Note that all of the above will have to be defined as updates to 9110, since HTTP semantics assumes (for a reason) that there will never be another method like GET. This spec needs to redefine that, for its own reasons, and seriously discuss the negative tradeoffs for existing deployments of the Web and caching.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
9111 requires that the server "implements all specified caching-related behavior" for the method, which makes it seem to me like we don't need to update 9110 or 9111 to get any behavior that's specific to QUERY, only if we need to update general properties of caching. What is the general property that we're changing here?

The primary difference I'm aware of is that the (potentially normalized) request content forms part of the cache key. As @royfielding notes, that's unprecedented in HTTP, but it's not prohibited. Nothing in 9110 or 9111 says that the request content can't be part of the cache key if the method defines it that way.

Instead, 9110 says:

> If the new method is cacheable, its definition ought to describe how, and under what conditions, a cache can store a response and use it to satisfy a subsequent request. The new method ought to describe whether it can be made conditional ([Section 13.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#preconditions)) and, if so, how a server responds when the condition is false. Likewise, if the new method might have some use for partial response semantics ([Section 14.2](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.range)), it ought to document this, too.

I think Roy is correct that we need more detailed text defining what conditionals and partial responses look like, but I haven't yet seen a compelling argument that this changes anything in base 9110 or 9111.

comments.author: gabesullice
comments.body:
Forgive me in this was already discussed and rejected, I read this thread and the linked threads here on GitHub, but haven't seen it mentioned.

To make caching optional without an additional round trip, can a new `query-digest` header (or trailer) be introduced with specifics for how clients must compute a hash of the request body? Caches would then use the URI+digest to synthesize a cache key for the response without needing to read the message body (as if the request were `QUERY /some/path?query-digest={digest-value}`). Given that `QUERY` is an addition to the protocol, it seems acceptable to introduce additional burdens on clients, intermediaries and origin servers that intend to support it.

Origins would also be required to:

1. Verify the digest
2. Compute a new hash of the request digest + their recomputed digest
3. Return their own `query-digest` response header for _client_ verification.

Clients would be required to verify that the response header digest is correct for the digest+request body that they sent.

The implementation burden would be on browser developers and lower level client maintainers (such as curl), meaning it would be practically invisible to the vast majority of web developers. And the digest could be computed at the binary level to circumvent media type/encoding/compression concerns (those variants would each have unique digests).

Importantly, this could be entirely optional. The fallback is simple: treat the request/response as uncacheable.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: If an origin server is willing to compute a digest, why not instead use it in a URI of a GETtable resource, which will work without any other changes for caching, conditionals and potentially range requests?

comments.author: gabesullice
comments.body:
I hear you, and I see the elegance you're defending with your question. URIs for unique resources is at the heart of the web. We don't want to break that, but it also doesn't make sense to neuter the method before it's even standardized.

First, allow me to answer with another rhetorical question:

If the client is willing to send a request that can't possibly be cached in expectation of a certain redirect to follow, why not instead send a POST request?

Now, to answer your question directly: because it adds a round-trip.

However, the premise that the origin is "willing" to compute the digest is a little unfair. They _have_ to read the body, parse it, and interpret it in order to respond. They could easily compute the digest with a streaming hash function with practically imperceptible cost as the bytes are pumped into the parser. Moreover, most origins will be hashing the body to compute a cache key _regardless_—even if they're responding with a `303` and a `Location` header because they'll want to serve that redirect without generating a fresh response if possible.

My proposal was intended to offer a pragmatic compromise by creating a sort of virtual URI for intermediaries.

We can go one step further and preserve URIs though :)

`201` provides a precedent for responding with a resource locatable by the `Location` response header without a redirect. Could a new `2XX` or `3XX` statis code provide a cacheable response to the original query located at the location identified by the `Location` header without an additional round trip?

Would that address your concern?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
That's

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-11.html#section-2.1-2

no?

Re:

> If the client is willing to send a request that can't possibly be cached in expectation of a certain redirect to follow, why not instead send a POST request?

Because it's neither safe nor idempotent?

comments.author: gabesullice
comments.body:
I appreciate the link, thank you. I didn't make the connection.

> Because it's neither safe nor idempotent?

And `QUERY` is, which begs the question, why can it not also be cacheable?

Let me see if I can explain your concern correctly via an example because I'm worried it's above my head.

1. Client sends a query for `value=true`
2. Origin servers responds with all entities with a value of "true"
3. Cache normalizes the query content to `value=1` and stores it accordingly
4. Another client sends a query for `value=1`
5. Cache HIT

However, the origin server does not consider those values to be equivalent and the user isn't authorized to access `value=true` entities, just `value=1` entities, and/or they're not the entities the client expected.

Is that all of it or have I missed some other important considerations?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> And QUERY is, which begs the question, why can it not also be cacheable?

Did I say that?

Note that the text starting this issue is taken from @royfielding 's review.

> However, the origin server does not consider those values to be equivalent and the user isn't authorized to access value=true entities, just value=1 entities, and/or they're not the entities the client expected.

That would be a case of incorrect normalization.

comments.author: gabesullice
comments.body:
> Did I say that? 

I'm feeling gaslit. Yes? See:

>> 2.4. Caching: … a cache MAY use it to … satisfy subsequent QUERY requests
>
> No, just no.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
That was a quote from my review on the mailing list. Lost context.

I cannot reiterate this enough: the potential round trip cost for creating an initial query is completely irrelevant to high performance sites. It's just one subrequest.

The repeated queries after the initial query is built is what needs to be efficient. The shared queries. The instructions that get pasted on a popular website and suddenly trigger large, repetitive requests. That's how caching works.

QUERY can be cacheable if we redeploy the Internet to make it so. I don't think that's a good idea. If the authors think it is a good idea, they should explain why in the draft, address the potential damage (or alternatives), and provide advice regarding things like query size vs efficient encoding.

It's not sufficient to provide the technology and hope people don't misuse it.

Julian is using this issue to track my comment so that it isn't lost, even the WG decides to do nothing. It's not his fault.

comments.author: gabesullice
comments.body:
Thank you for that context @royfielding. I think that explains a lot of the confusion I felt.

@reschke: I'm sorry if you felt I was being combative. And I apologize for coming in with a "what if we just" as a random internet stranger. I tried to make sense of the problem before I posted.

---

> It's not sufficient to provide the technology and hope people don't misuse it.

100% agreed @royfielding. A good design should be inherently hard to misuse. The current design of the `QUERY` parameter doesn't have any extra hoops to jump through to make a developer wonder: "wait, am I doing this wrong?"

I think the most convincing argument against a cacheable `QUERY` method, maybe even damning, is that it supports a request like this:

```
QUERY / HTTP/1.1
Host: yolo.xyz

id=/article/42
```

So, to be clear, I am not advocating that the current caching story of this draft be accepted as-is. Nor do I think it would be enough to address your concerns with non-normative advice/recommendations.

That said, I feel removing the `QUERY` method's cacheability would be a mistake. So I'm trying to offer an engineered approach that addresses your concerns in a normative way.

---

> I cannot reiterate this enough: the potential round trip cost for creating an initial query is completely irrelevant to high performance sites. It's just one subrequest.

I'll defer to you, but my understanding of a "subrequest" is that it's a request for a subresource like a stylesheet or script not a second, blocking request for a primary resource.

Accepting that it's just one subrequest, thousands of developer-hours have been spent trying to reduce the collective time end-users must wait for subrequests.[^1]

Perhaps all of that dev effort was misplaced, however I feel certain that if `QUERY` is standardized without a cache story, practitioners and service providers will find a way to cache it. Just as they already [cache POST responses](https://techdocs.akamai.com/property-mgr/docs/cache-post-responses).

The draft ought to get in front of that with a design that promotes the desirable properties of the web architecture that would otherwise be broken by poorly designed sites/APIs as shown in the example above.

How?

---

#### 1. Useful URIs via Content-Location

Consider a query against a library's site under degraded network conditions:

1. A teacher navigates the site by genre and finally builds a unique query in that section: `/genres/teen/fantasy`
2. The teacher then searches by year, # of pages, price, and a number of other facets not listed here.
3. The teacher waits for the response.
4. Finally, the teacher saves the URL and emails it to his or her class as a summer reading list.

Using a `303` would double the waiting time in step 3 (I admit that under good conditions, that's not much).

I think one of your concerns with `QUERY` is that the shared URL would be `/genres/teen/fantasy` instead of `/genres/teen/fantasy?year=1984&…`, thus making it effectively uncacheable without accessing the request body. Is that accurate?

If so, I think the authors attempted to address that concern via the `Content-Location` header as @reschke [helpfully pointed out](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3120#issuecomment-3124540691).

Perhaps `Content-Location` could be added as a mandatory response field for the response to be cache-eligible?

---

#### 2. Fast & safe cache key generation via Query-Digest

> The repeated queries after the initial query is built is what needs to be efficient. The shared queries. The instructions that get pasted on a popular website and suddenly trigger large, repetitive requests. That's how caching works.

This would be partially addressed by the `Content-Location` header since the first user would copy the URL returned to their first successful query. However, there's another use case: consider a similar story to the above example but instead of a library, the site is a massively scaled online bookstore where users are _not_ sharing URLs, but they _are_ making the same query. For the sake of example, assume it's for an old book that recently went viral on social media.

In that case, nearly every searcher is sending the same query but they aren't coordinating as in your example of copying and pasting instructions.

If the initial `303` can't be cached, the origin server must service every request. This implies origin servers will inevitably implement their own procedures to normalize and hash the query so that it can cache the `303` redirect internally.

Wouldn't it be ideal if caching intermediaries could service those requests too? And wouldn't it be better if a framework for that technique were standardized instead of different vendors inventing their own techniques for it?

If so, the obvious design challenge to overcome would be that caches shouldn't need to understand how to normalize and hash the query content/request body, which, as you've said (and I agree with), wouldn't be acceptable.

Hence, the `Query-Digest` [proposal above](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3120#issuecomment-3124415575) which allows intermediaries on the hot path to ignore the request body.

Just as the `Content-Location` field could be a mandatory field to make the request/response cache-eligible, the `Query-Digest` request/response fields could be mandatory as well.

--- 

#### A design that's hard to misuse

Those two field requirements, I believe, would serve this purpose:

>> It's not sufficient to provide the technology and hope people don't misuse it.
>
> 100% agreed. A good design should be hard to misuse and the current design of the `QUERY` parameter doesn't have any extra hoops that might trigger a developer's spidey-sense and cause them to ask: "am I doing this wrong?"

Normative cache-eligibility criteria would create two "hoops" to push developers in the direction of `GET` to avoid them, when possible.

In the case where it _not_ possible or discouraged[^2], those hoops may be worth jumping through.

And finally, in cases that only need a safe and idempotent `POST`, the hoops could be ignored and the response wouldn't be cached.

[^1]: Inline styles, HTTP/2 server push, code "bundling", server-side rendering of SPAs, 103 Early Hints, etc.

[^2]: Query length limitations, privacy concerns, query syntax complexity, the uncoordinated mobbed query interface case outlined above, etc.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
> > I cannot reiterate this enough: the potential round trip cost for creating an initial query is completely irrelevant to high performance sites. It's just one subrequest.
> 
> I'll defer to you, but my understanding of a "subrequest" is that it's a request for a subresource like a stylesheet or script not a second, blocking request for a primary resource.

A subrequest is any additional requests in the process of the user agent completing a user-requested action. Some are blocking and some are not. Yes, the blocking ones are the primary concern for web vitals.

Technically speaking, a user's conceptual model of "handling a request" is substantially longer for queries than for following links (i.e., their expectations are different).

> Accepting that it's just one subrequest, thousands of developer-hours have been spent trying to reduce the collective time end-users must wait for subrequests.[1](#user-content-fn-1-164dad0745a8cbe63cd144e5ebd2f001)

Yes, that's my day job. It's not relevant to QUERY because browsers do not use QUERY now, and would not use QUERY in the future without a corresponding query builder (script). Such a script provided by the origin server is already capable of generating encoded parameters prior to the initial QUERY request, assuming the query itself isn't super long/complicated enough to defy encoding. OTOH, if a QUERY is super long and complicated in the body then it isn't safe/efficient to create a cache key, let alone use that cache key as some kind of short-hand for a second request after reading the long and complicated QUERY body again. It's better to only send the body once (creating a temporary resource in the server) and then invoke that resource normally (using GET) from that point on. That's what Location can provide for 2XX and 303 responses.

For API uses, the scripts are replaced by other APIs (or just SDKs) that construct a query prior to sending. The effect is the same. In general, it is safer to manage the construction of an Internet request prior to sending it, as opposed to just publishing an open-ended interface and hoping that user agents use it correctly. There are going to be edge cases where an open interface is also useful, but those cases don't need to be as efficient.

Hence, the better solution, in all cases, is to run a query builder on the client side and let it decide whether to use an encoded or hashed GET request (efficient and cacheable) or a very long QUERY request (inefficient and not cacheable, but potentially reusable if the server responds with a corresponding Location or some kind of URI template). This applies to both browser and API applications.

One of those potential solutions could be for the origin-provided query builder to produce a hash that could be used as a cache key instead of a QUERY body, but Julian's point is that, if such a solution exists, the query builder with hashing process can just send a GET (with hash in target URI) immediately, or at least after seeding the origin with the query itself so that the origin knows which query body corresponds with the hash. This entire process can be done in the background while the query builder is constructing the query via the UI. Zero added delay, and we don't even need a new method for that.

> Using a `303` would double the waiting time in step 3 (I admit that under good conditions, that's not much).

No. "double the waiting time" assumes running the query on the data set takes no time.  In good conditions, a short cached CDN response to a well-connected client is less than 25ms round trip (fiber to my home in California). Bad conditions would be 500ms or more, but those are typically due to cell networks or lost/corrupted packet errors, both of which are mostly caused by longer messages and processing delays. Most uncached subrequests are somewhere in the 150-300ms range plus however long it takes to read, process, and send the data.

Try a query in real life and measure how long it takes for you to anticipate a response. I'll bet you will perceive a 3 second query response (3000ms) as being "fast", whereas it would be considered too slow for a linked GET. In fact, many users are dissatisfied by a query response that is "too fast" because they think the service didn't try hard enough. Of course, this only applies to user-perceived performance, not something like a blind API query.

> I think one of your concerns with `QUERY` is that the shared URL would be `/genres/teen/fantasy` instead of `/genres/teen/fantasy?year=1984&…`, thus making it effectively uncacheable without accessing the request body. Is that accurate?

No. It isn't cacheable without reading the request body because the method definition requires the body to be part of the cache key. The key needs to be known prior to making a HIT/MISS decision. Regardless, a cache has to read the entire request message or close the connection after responding, so large request messages are a big deal. Small queries (even those with variable parameter values) are less of a concern, but they also don't need QUERY: small queries are easy to encode as GET parameters even if they need to be tokenized or encrypted.

> If so, I think the authors attempted to address that concern via the `Content-Location` header as [@reschke](https://github.com/reschke) [helpfully pointed out](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3120#issuecomment-3124540691).

Content-Location is for requesting a past result. Location is for running the query again.

My concern (after I pointed out the Location bits in a prior review) is that providing both QUERY method caching and Location-redirection based caching is not a good idea given that GET caching is already deployed and works better than sending a QUERY body on every request. We *can* specify both, but we *don't need to*.

The tradeoff is that QUERY method caching allows the first response from service to client to be cached for later reuse by a later QUERY request containing exactly the same query body, whereas Location-based caching either redirects the initial request to a GET (forcing a clean request without body) or directly responds to the initial request but doesn't bother to cache those first results. In both cases, Location can be provided in the response to supply a URI for future GET requests, so future reusable/shared requests would only use the GET method and thus be easily cached.

> If so, the obvious design challenge to overcome would be that caches shouldn't need to understand how to normalize and hash the query content/request body, which, as you've said (and I agree with), wouldn't be acceptable.
> 
> Hence, the `Query-Digest` [proposal above](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3120#issuecomment-3124415575) which allows intermediaries on the hot path to ignore the request body.

No, because even if they don't use the request body, they can't ignore it. They would have to read it anyway just to parse the protocol, and they would have to verify it just to avoid cache poisoning attacks. Reading a request body isn't easy; it takes far longer than reading the initial control data found in the front of each HTTP request, and thus delays the processing of each request in a non-linear fashion due to window effects. On every request. The net result is that caches would have to do more work than what is currently specified for QUERY, which is already far more work than simply redirecting to a GET as soon as the origin server believes the request could be reusable as a resource.

Hence, my advice is to not allow QUERY to be directly cacheable, but rather encourage it to be used as a query builder for stored queries (a.k.a., resources).

But that's just my advice. If the WG chooses to go ahead and make QUERY directly cacheable (for reasons), I expect to see more of this discussion and the rationale reflected in the final specification.

Right now, the spec just ignores what we learned over 30 years ago, as if sending queries to servers wasn't part of Web history (e.g., see WAIS, the original SEARCH method, etc.) and wasn't deliberately excluded from HTTP/1.0 in 1994 in favor of using GET for all reusable retrievals.

comments.author: gabesullice
comments.body:
> Yes, that's my day job.

I suspected; your reputation precedes you :slightly_smiling_face:.[^1]

> It's not relevant to QUERY because browsers do not use QUERY now, and would not use QUERY in the future without a corresponding query builder (script).

This is a dangerous assumption. We should proceed as if the WHATWG might add `QUERY` as an allowed `method` value of the `<form>` element, merely for its safe and idemptotent properties. Also because, for better or worse, web applications ship scripts that replace HTML dynamically, which many users perceive to be a primary navigation event.[^2]

> Hence, the better solution, in all cases, is to run a query builder on the client side and let it decide whether to use an encoded or hashed GET request (efficient and cacheable) or a very long QUERY request (inefficient and not cacheable, but potentially reusable if the server responds with a corresponding Location or some kind of URI template). This applies to both browser and API applications.
>
> One of those potential solutions could be for the origin-provided query builder to produce a hash that could be used as a cache key instead of a QUERY body, but Julian's point is that, if such a solution exists, the query builder with hashing process can just send a GET (with hash in target URI) immediately, or at least after seeding the origin with the query itself so that the origin knows which query body corresponds with the hash. This entire process can be done in the background while the query builder is constructing the query via the UI. Zero added delay, and we don't even need a new method for that.

What you're describing is an unstandardized workaround to acheive practically the same result as the `Query-Digest` proposal with additional chattiness and implementation complexity.

> Julian's point is that, if such a solution exists, the query builder with hashing process can just send a GET (with hash in target URI) immediately, or at least _after seeding the origin with the query itself so that the origin knows which query body corresponds with the hash_. (emphasis mine)

The emphasized portion admits the flaw in the that approach: every client must assume that their query has never been sent before and so they _must_ always seed it first, or test for it with a `GET`/`HEAD`. Even in the oversimplified example below, the script shouldn't decide to use a hashed `GET` because the space of possible results is so vast (>16 million excluding the `personalization` param) that it must assume the server won't have a cached response.

```
GET /item/42/designer?queryDigest={hash(color=f00&personalization=political+slogan)} HTTP/1.1
Host: tshirts.example.com
```

The flow I'm proposing as a modification to the draft is:

```
QUERY /item/42/designer HTTP/1.1
Host: tshirts.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Query-Digest={hash(color=f00&personalization=political+slogan)}

normalizedByScriptOrMediaTypeSpec(color=ff0000&personalization=political+slogan)
```

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Host: tshirts.example.com
Content-Type: text/html
Query-Digest={hash(hashVerified(color=f00&personalization=political+slogan),hashReceived(Query-Digest))}
Content-Location=/item/42/style/design/some-uuid

<… content …>
```

> No. "double the waiting time" assumes running the query on the data set takes no time. In good conditions, [it's irrelevant]...

That's why I made the admission about "good conditions" in the text you quoted.

> No. It isn't cacheable without reading the request body because the method definition requires the body to be part of the cache key. The key needs to be known prior to making a HIT/MISS decision.

Hence, a `Query-Digest` field, which is a hash of the body, so that the key is available to caches in the HEADERS frame (I will address the cache poisoning issue further below).

> Regardless, a cache has to read the entire request message or close the connection after responding, so large request messages are a big deal.

I _think_ this is an orthogonal concern. If `QUERY` is uncacheable, or the client uses `POST` instead, doesn't the cache need to either stream the body to the origin server, read it into `/dev/null`, or close the connection regardless? I don't see how a cacheable `QUERY` method makes the problem worse unless your concern is that it encourages larger message bodies in general. Since this is your field of expertise (and your day job :wink:), I would appreciate your correction if I'm missing important nuance (I mean this very sincerely).

> The tradeoff … In both cases, Location can be provided in the response to supply a URI for future GET requests, so future reusable/shared requests would only use the GET method and thus be easily cached.

We agree on the tradeoff. Where we seem to be talking at cross purposes is that your focus is on a single client's repeated request or a multiple clients making the same request for a URL shared out-of-band, whereas I'm foccused on uncoordinated clients sending the same initial query.

The relative weight we assign to those two purposes is, I assume, why we see the tradeoff differently.

> No, because even if they don't use the request body, they can't ignore it. They would have to read it anyway just to parse the protocol …  The net result is that caches would have to do more work than what is currently specified for QUERY … If the WG chooses to go ahead and make QUERY directly cacheable (for reasons), I expect to see more of this discussion and the rationale reflected in the final specification.

My intent in this discussion is to suggest an alternative to the current draft, in response to your review, which might _pass_ your review. Not to argue why the current draft should move forward as-is.

With that in mind, I don't fee that we've adequately explored why the `Query-Digest` proposal is infeasible. You've described why the current draft requires caches to read the body and why that's unacceptable (which I've already agreed is a problem), but I disagree that it would be necessary reason below.

> and they would have to verify it just to avoid cache poisoning attacks.

In the proposal, the client and service would be responsible for normalization (if not handled by the media type) and the origin server would be responsible for verification. This mitigates (but does not eliminate) the cache poisoning problem.

Only responses that the origin server has designated as cache-eligible via a returned `Query-Digest` header would be stored in the cache. If caches suspect a misbehaving backend, they can read the body to audit the request/response digests and act accordingly.

[^1]: I hope you'll appreciate [a little humor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AJXKVOxqkWM). Frankly, I'm honored you replied to me.
[^2]: This practice is already supported by other standards, cf. [the History interface](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/nav-history-apis.html#the-history-interface).

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
> Where we seem to be talking at cross purposes is that your focus is on a single client's repeated request or a multiple clients making the same request for a URL shared out-of-band, whereas I'm foccused on uncoordinated clients sending the same initial query.
> 
> The relative weight we assign to those two purposes is, I assume, why we see the tradeoff differently.

I am focused on using a cache to improve latency **and** safely reduce peak demand spikes, whether that's because one client is making a million repeated queries (this happens all the time) or a million uncoordinated clients getting lucky on the same query (this only happens when some event triggers all of the clients to query for the same thing, such as a sporting event or earthquake).

Your suggestion is to add more data to the critical path of each QUERY request, in the form of a computed hash of the actual query which is being sent in the same message, so that the header field can be key-checked by a shared cache prior to reading the body.

The only problem that solves is the latency between reading the body and header field, and it does that by adding latency via a new field, hash data, and hash processing. It doesn't help with consistent routing of the request if that routing is dependent on the contents of the query. It doesn't help identify common queries that could be given a URI, reused as bookmarks/links, and grow the Web. It describes a new field for new QUERY caches that haven't already been deployed.

Whereas my alternative, linking to stored procedures, already exists and is consistent with the deployed Web architecture.

The right place for discussion of a Query-Digest header field is on the mailing list, with a subject specific to the draft that defines the field, not within a github issue about someone else's comments on some other draft.

In any case, as I posted on the list, the last two paragraphs of my comment were a misunderstanding on my part. I thought that section specified reuse of the QUERY response for later GET requests by allowing a cache to move the query from the body into a cache key for later GET requests (i.e., manufacture a URI for GET), whereas it actually specifies QUERY caching for reuse by later QUERY requests.

issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
> Abstract
>
>    This specification defines a new HTTP method, QUERY, as a safe,
>    idempotent request method that can carry request content.

The above is too generic. It should say why it is being defined:

   This specification defines the QUERY method for HTTP.
   A QUERY requests that the request target process the enclosed
   content in a safe/idempotent manner and then respond with the
   result of that processing. This is similar to POST requests but
   can be automatically repeated or restarted without concern for
   partial state changes. The kind of processing desired to perform
   the QUERY is indicated by the Content-Type header field value
   enclosed with the request.

issues.body:
**_QUOTED FROM SPEC TEXT, COMMENTS ARE ROY'S (@royfielding)_**

> 1.  Introduction
>
>    This specification defines the HTTP QUERY request method as a means
>    of making a safe, idempotent request (Section 9.2 of [HTTP]) that
>    contains content.

"that contains content" --> "containing content that describes
how the request is to be processed by the target resource"

-> https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3122#issuecomment-3025327459

>    Most often, this is desirable when the data conveyed in a request is
>    too voluminous to be encoded into the request's URI.  For example,
>    this is a common query pattern:
>
>    GET /feed?q=foo&limit=10&sort=-published HTTP/1.1
>    Host: example.org
>
>    However, for a query with parameters that are complex or large,
>    encoding it in the request URI may not be the best option because
>
>    *  often size limits are not known ahead of time because a request
>       can pass through many uncoordinated systems (but note that
>       Section 4.1 of [HTTP] recommends senders and recipients to support
>       at least 8000 octets),
>
>    *  expressing certain kinds of data in the target URI is inefficient
>       because of the overhead of encoding that data into a valid URI,
>       and
>
>    *  encoding queries directly into the request URI effectively casts
>       every possible combination of query inputs as distinct resources.
>
>    As an alternative to using GET, many implementations make use of the
>    HTTP POST method to perform queries, as illustrated in the example
>    below.  In this case, the input to the query operation is passed as
>    the request content as opposed to using the request URI's query
>    component.
>
>    A typical use of HTTP POST for requesting a query is:
>
>    POST /feed HTTP/1.1
>    Host: example.org
>    Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
>
>    q=foo&limit=10&sort=-published
>
>    This variation, however, suffers from the same basic limitation as
>    GET in that it is not readily apparent -- absent specific knowledge
>    of the resource and server to which the request is being sent -- that
>    a safe, idempotent query is being performed.
>
>    The QUERY method provides a solution that spans the gap between the
>    use of GET and POST, with the example above being expressed as:
>
>    QUERY /feed HTTP/1.1
>    Host: example.org
>    Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
>
>    q=foo&limit=10&sort=-published
>
>    As with POST, the input to the query operation is passed as the
>    content of the request rather than as part of the request URI.
>    Unlike POST, however, the method is explicitly safe and idempotent,

Yes, that's fine. These are all motivating statements but they just aren't illustrated by the two examples. It certainly impacts the choice of implementation, but there are plenty of implementations to choose from that handle up to 8KB URLs. The user-provided data in the query is a more common concern, though it is limited to bookmarks these days (current services routinely log request bodies too, especially when that's where the dangerous bits are supplied).

The reason people shouldn't build systems like this is because reading and processing the request query (whether in URL or in body) is on the critical path of every request, which is just horrible at scale when compared to creating a stored procedure that the server can compile, analyze, make more efficient, and then pass a name back that can be used as a URL. But we all know that developers have to learn that lesson on their own every decade or so (e.g., GraphQL).

issues.title: QUERY: HTTPDIR/RF review - QUERY method definition
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
**_QUOTED FROM SPEC TEXT, COMMENTS ARE ROY'S (@royfielding)_**

> 2.  QUERY
>
>    The QUERY method is used to initiate a server-side query.  Unlike the
>    HTTP GET method, which requests that a server return a representation
>    of the resource identified by the target URI (as defined by
>    Section 7.1 of [HTTP]), the QUERY method is used to ask the server to
>    perform a query operation (described by the request content) over
>    some set of data at the resource.  The content returned in response
>    to a QUERY cannot be assumed to be a representation of the resource
>    identified by the target URI.

Let's say there are two resources on a server, "/a" and "/b".
Is the same QUERY sent to "/a" going to mean the same to "/b"?
Are we expecting those two queries to result in the same response?
If not, the QUERY is being sent to the targeted resource, which is
doing all of those things above that are being described as "the server".

"HTTP GET" --> "GET"
"requests that a server return a representation" -->
     "requests a representation"
"to ask the server to perform a query operation" -->
     "to ask the target resource to perform a query operation"
"over some set of data at the resource" -->
     "within the scope of that target resource (as defined by its origin)."

"target URI" should be cited somewhere else [this looks like a citation
for GET].

The last sentence "cannot be assumed" isn't useful.
What is needed is a definition of what is returned for each kind
of response.  I believe that should at least include:

   A 200 (OK) response to a QUERY request indicates that the query
   was successfully processed and the results of that processing are
   enclosed as the response content.

   A 303 (See Other) response to a QUERY request indicates that the query
   is equivalent to the resource identified in the response's Location
   header field. The client can obtain a result of the query by performing
   a GET request on the referenced Location, which will then be cacheable
   and reusable like any other GET request.

   [you may want to describe other common codes as well if they have a
   particular meaning unique to QUERY. I particularly suggest highlighting
   the difference for 200, 204, 206, 400, 406, 415, and 422.]

>    The content of the request and it's media type define the query.
>    Implementations MAY use a request content of any media type with the
>    QUERY method, provided that it has appropriate query semantics.

This is ambiguous. For security filtering reasons, the request header
field Content-Type MUST be consistent with the request content. IOW,
if they differ the server MUST fail (400) the request. As such, the
media type defines the query processing and the request content MUST
adhere to the media type requirements to be successfully processed.

>    As for all HTTP methods in general, the target URI's query part takes
>    part in identifying the resource being queried and therefore is not
>    part of the actual query.  Whether and how the URI's query part
>    directly affects the result of the query is implementation specific
>    and out of scope for this specification.

Strike "and therefore is not part of the actual query" because it
contradicts the next sentence. I would say it is resource-specific,
since the implementation doesn't limit such things.

>    QUERY requests are both safe and idempotent with regard to the
>    resource identified by the request URI.  That is, QUERY requests do
>    not alter the state of the identified resource.  However, while
>    processing a QUERY request, a server can be expected to allocate
>    computing and memory resources or even create additional HTTP
>    resources through which the response can be retrieved.

No, no, no. Do not even think about redefining

  https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-safe-methods

here. Just reference it. Both the "That is" and "However" are wrong in
very subtle ways.

If you want to clarify a very specific point (like safe doesn't mean a
server can't create a new resource if it wants to) then do that in
a separate sentence after referencing the definition of "safe".

This should also mention the good thing about idempotent being that a
client can retry or repeat the request after connection failure.

>    A successful response to a QUERY request is expected to provide some
>    indication as to the final disposition of the operation.  For
>    instance, a successful query that yields no results can be
>    represented by a 204 (No Content, Section 15.3.5 of [HTTP]) response.
>    If the response includes content, it is expected to describe the
>    results of the operation.

I am not sure what this is attempting to clarify. Maybe that an
empty set of results is a 200, not a 404? But doesn't that depend
on the query itself?

EDIT (JR): see also https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3124#issuecomment-3020987715

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
@royfielding 

> [you may want to describe other common codes as well if they have a
particular meaning unique to QUERY. I particularly suggest highlighting
the difference for 200, 204, 206, 400, 406, 415, and 422.]

I'm not sure which of these actually _have_ a different meaning for QUERY (and, if that was the case, that would be bad, no?)

- 204: empty content in response
- 206: we currently say that Range Requests are the same as for GET (with only Byte Ranges defined for now). We currently do not say a lot about Range Requests; maybe we should explain that in many cases, this can be achieved better with the semantics of the query type (think paging in SQL) - https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3151
- 4xx: I don't see anything special here, but we illustrate 406, 415, 422 in the examples section. -https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3152

With that, we can simplify that to just a mention that these have the same meaning as define by RFC 9110, and then point to 4xx examples in the appendix.

WDYT?

cc @MikeBishop @mnot @martinthomson

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Closed per https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3148

issues.title: Purpose of the server algorithm
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
[Section 9.3.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-compression-dictionary-19#section-9.3.2) of the compression dictionary draft defines an algorithm, but it isn't clear who runs that algorithm.  It appears to be a version of the algorithm that a client might use to determine whether the content of a response is readable.  Sort of.  Note: "sort of" is not a great way to describe something that might be normatively defined elsewhere.

It's unclear to me what purpose this serves or why it would be included in a section entitled "Server Responsibilities".

If the goal here is to describe the things a server might need to consider before making a response readable (thereby activating a resource as a dictionary), then this is not as helpful as it seems.  For a server, the considerations are very different from what is defined here.  The server needs to consider whether the content of the resource is conditioned on information that the requester (via `Origin`) might not otherwise have.  It might then decide to participate in CORS (assuming it wants to make the resource available) only if the contents are safe to publish.

Even there, this algorithm does not help a server.  Better to describe what the server logic might be.  That's far simpler: if the resource includes secrets, don't participate in CORS.

The section is pretty confusing otherwise.  This promises requirements that never appear:

> In addition, the following requirements on a server are intended to disable dictionary-aware compression when the client provides CORS request header fields that indicate a cross-origin request context.

This might be better as:

> A server that produces a representation that contains information that might be secret can ensure that client does not use that content as a dictionary by not participating in CORS [FETCH].  In particular, this means not including `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` in responses (CORS includes other conditions to make a response readable in a cross-origin context, but this is the pivotal one).
