issues.title: QUERY: define what the selected representation is for QUERY
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
See https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#representations

> A [target resource](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#target.resource) might be provided with, or be capable of generating, multiple representations that are each intended to reflect the resource's current state. An algorithm, usually based on [content negotiation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#content.negotiation) ([Section 12](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#content.negotiation)), would be used to select one of those representations as being most applicable to a given request. This "selected representation" provides the data and metadata for evaluating conditional requests ([Section 13](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#conditional.requests)) and constructing the content for [200 (OK)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.200), [206 (Partial Content)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.206), and [304 (Not Modified)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.304) responses to GET ([Section 9.3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#GET)).

It seems that this affects other issues such as #3117.

Thoughts:

- should be the same for all "new" methods, in particular, but not limited to all, safe and idempotent methods including request content.
- what precisely is it for POST, and can the definition for QUERY be derived from that?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
The definition of Content-Location provides additional context on the selected representation for POST:
> - For a response to a GET or HEAD request, this is an indication that the target URI refers to a resource that is subject to content negotiation and the Content-Location field value is a more specific identifier for the [selected representation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#selected.representation).
> - [...]
> - Otherwise, such a Content-Location indicates that this content is a representation reporting on the requested action's status and that the same report is available (for future access with GET) at the given URI. For example, a purchase transaction made via a POST request might include a receipt document as the content of the [200 (OK)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.200) response; the Content-Location field value provides an identifier for retrieving a copy of that same receipt in the future.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: @MikeBishop - how does the point about POST help here?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: For POST, and I'd expect for QUERY, it suggests that the selected representation is the result of the target resource processing the request payload, not a representation of the resource itself as it would be for GET. (I don't think that's a general statement for all new methods, though.)

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
What we know:

- as for GET, the selected representation takes conneg into account - so if a response could be either application/json or application/xml, we'd have two selected selected representations

What we don't know (yet):

- for a resource that supports both GET (which is not optional) and QUERY, do we have *two* sets of selected representations (in which case the method name would contribute to the process of selecting a representation)?
- how exactly does the answer affect conditionals and range requests (and maybe caching)?

What I'd like to see:

- an answer that does not require updating the base specs, and which is the same for all "new" methods - or at least for all *classes* of new methods (safe/idempotent/content-carrying)

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
@martinthomson - if we made that "the same as GET except the server needs to take the content into account", we'd still have the problem that GET and QUERY would share the same set of selected representations.

*Could* we state that QUERY-without-content actually MUST be the *same thing* as a GET request (for the same conneg properties otherwise)?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Proposal 1:

1. REQUIRE that the server treats QUERY requests without content the same way as GET; make them synonymous (EDIT: made that https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3147)
2. define that in the context of selected representations (and all that depends on that), QUERY is the same thing as GET (if request content was allowed/defined for GET)
3. with that, all that's left is to say that the *selected represention* now needs to take the request content into account (that probably requires updating RFC 9110)

*This essentially makes QUERY a slightly extended form of the standard HTTP retrieval method.*

Slightly different Proposal 2:

- as Proposal 1, but without point 2. In that case, 3. would need to be extended to say that the request method name affects the representation selection as well

I *believe* that both proposals would automatically explain how conditionals work (and probably range requests as well)

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
The "pessimistic" approach:

Don't do anything like that; just say that if you want the benefits of conditionals/range requests (and maybe caching), you'll have to hand out a GETtable resource to the client.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I prefer your first proposal.  The layman's version of this is: QUERY is GET where the response depends on the URL *plus the content* as opposed to just the URL.  In that setting, the set of selected representations, conditions, and everything else follows on from that.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
I think the above is gazing too much at the navel instead of the reason why these definitions exist.

The term "selected representation" is a conceptual definition for some mid-point(s) in the request mapping logic wherein the server has figured out how to map the request given the target resource but not yet whether it should do so (i.e., perform the method semantics). Behind the server interface, there are actually many different selected representations that are being tested in sequence as the server makes decisions about the request, such as during the internal (GET) redirections that generate content or supply custom error message, but those are not included in the definition.

A problem is that it is easy to confuse "selected representation" with response content, but I think we got that right in the specs. For example, see the discussion on [Preconditions](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-preconditions).

The definition doesn't change according to the request method. GET, PUT, POST, DELETE, et al are made conditional by testing how the server would respond to a GET at the time of request, since the conditions we have defined (for 911X) are based on the resource state as perceived by changes to the selected representation (not changes to the response content).

What differs by request method is the result: what the method requires of the server when a precondition fails while handling the request. Unfortunately, we defined that by listing each method instead of by safe/unsafe characteristics.

I would not change the definition of selected representation for the sake of QUERY.

I would change the limitations on when/where preconditions are evaluated,
include evaluation of the request content as part of the mapping for QUERY (only),
and define the result of precondition failure for safe methods in general.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
It seems important to state that it depends not only on the request payload, but also the request content-type, since the server will be interpreting the payload in order to know what to do with the data in that resource.

Conceptually, if the resource represents the underlying dataset, then would the entire dataset be the selected representation?

I'm not sure we would actually return the full dataset to the client if they made a GET request with no query parameters to that URL -- at the least, they'd probably get a paginated response (first X results) and in many systems, I'd think a web page that helps them formulate a query would be more likely.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> It seems important to state that it depends not only on the request payload, but also the request content-type, since the server will be interpreting the payload in order to know what to do with the data in that resource.

Yes, we could repeat that.

> Conceptually, if the resource represents the underlying dataset, then would the entire dataset be the selected representation?

It depends on the actual query, right? Not every query necessarily depends on the full dataset.

Is this really different for GET?

> I'm not sure we would actually return the full dataset to the client if they made a GET request with no query parameters to that URL -- at the least, they'd probably get a paginated response (first X results) and in many systems, I'd think a web page that helps them formulate a query would be more likely.

Both are possible. If the query essentially is a filter, it might return everything.

But it depends, and again is the same for GET. That's why I would like to align QUERY-without-content completely with GET.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
@royfielding - looking at your conclusions...:

> I would not change the definition of selected representation for the sake of QUERY.

But do you agree that completely aligning QUERY-without-content with GET (as normative requirement) is good in any case? Should that go into separate ticket?

> I would change the limitations on when/where preconditions are evaluated, include evaluation of the request content as part of the mapping for QUERY (only), and define the result of precondition failure for safe methods in general.

That sounds ... complicated. 

The options we have discussed so far appear to be:

1. Give up on conditional requests for now, and push clients and servers to use/support the GETtable equivalents - conditionals are mostly useful for clients when they repeat requests, in which case using the GETtable resource in subsequent requests should be acceptable.
2. Try to adjust the concept of selected representation, and let conditional semantics follow from that.
3. Leave selected representations alone, and adjust conditionals to work with QUERY.

Options 2 and 3 require updating RFC 9110.  Option 1 is simple and allows us to move on without losing too much functionality.

And for option 1, we could also file enhancement requests/TODOs for a revision to RFC 9110 to make things more flexible.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Agreeing with Roy - the definition of selected representation doesn't need to change, but the rat's nest of conditionals do. Less convinced that we need to update 9110 - we can monkey-patch that in the current spec and 9110 implementations doesn't need to change UNLESS they're implementing this spec.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Who is "they" in this context?

And would it be a great loss if we said that if you want conditionals, use the GETtable version?

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
> ... we can monkey-patch that in the current spec and 9110 implementations doesn't need to change UNLESS they're implementing this spec.

@mnot - that sounds like we want to define `if-modfied-since` and `if-none-match` for QUERY and then we are done (except for range requests)?

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Think so.

issues.title: Potential security implication of incremental requests
issues.author: wtarreau
issues.body:
While thinking about what it would imply to implement incremental in haproxy (seems trivial at first glance, basically disable Nagle and kernel buffering to avoid the 200ms pauses, and disable compression), I figured that it can have a security impact on the request path: we do support buffering all or up to a certain size of a message for analysis purposes, and this is essentially used by many intermediaries on the request path in various forms of WAF (web application firewall) filtering, to detect and block malicious attacks.

Then we're facing a dilemma: if we conclude that "Incremental: ?1" is sufficient to disable buffering hence bypass such filtering, it will be used by all sort of attacks to try to evade request inspection and directly touch servers. And if we mention that local policy always has precedence, it will make Incremental fail from the client on the vast majority of infrastructures since WAFs are everywhere nowadays.

I'm tempted to think that we should suggest a few deployment approaches (not sure which ones are good, just enumerating on the top of my head):
  - intermediaries may decide to ignore incremental in a specific direction for security analysis purposes
  - intermediaries may decide to only support incremental on a configurable subset of URIs
  - intermediaries may arbitrarily decide to only enable incremental after a certain quantity was buffered

I think the least intrusive might possibly be the second one (by-URI), though it would require some configuration effort. In any case the impact of disabling content analysis should be reminded in the security considerations section.

At the moment I'm embarrassed because in haproxy we do support a rule allowing to buffer part of a message for analysis, and it's used both for analysis and for optimal processing of data. If I'd bypass this rule when seeing Incremental, it would open a big security hole in all deployments where users rely on this for analysis. And if I don't do it, it would not allow such rules to be automatically disabled when they're implemented only for transfer optimization. Still, this last option for now sounds like the sanest one.

Do we have examples of concrete request messages that require incremental ? I'm interested in seeing when and how they are used. For example maybe there are a number of fixed parameters followed by a specific one that needs to be streamed ? If so, maybe it would be sufficient for intermediaries to instead look for certain configured params and only allow incremental on a configured param. And maybe in this case the incremental header field could instead designate the name of the parameter which requires incremental forwarding, since it always knows it anyway ? Just a thought (not necessarily easy to implement for intermediaries).

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Thank you for the great feedback.

When an intermediary receives an HTTP request with `Incremental: ?1`, the intermediary can apply one of the two strategies: a) buffer the request and wait for more, or b) reject the request.

Based on the understanding that the Incremental header field indicates the reliance on incremental delivery, I think what we want to recommend is _b_. In fact, we already state that intermediaries SHOULD reject when there are no slots left for incremental delivery. I think we can expand that section and state that intermediaries should behave similarly when they cannot obey to the signal.

As undesirable HTTP errors are, they are still better than timeouts, clearly indicating _why_ a successful response was not received.

PS. In reality, WAFs might buffer for a few seconds to collect necessary information to validate the request, then based on that information being collected, either obey to the Incremental signal or reject the request.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Hi Kazuho!

I'm fine with the option of rejecting (and I continue to think that it might make sense for intermediaries to do that based on URIs only). However here we should reject with a 4xx, not a 503, since it's the request that cannot be satisfied (i.e. if the client retries without incremental the request will be fulfilled).

Also regarding WAFs, they don't buffer a few seconds but up to a certain size to perform analysis, after which they are reasonably confident the request is safe or malicious. Typically they'll be looking for certain fields. What I'm not sure about is what type of interactivity clients expect with Incremental. I.e. do they periodically send encapsulated request/response pairs (i.e. a few hundred bytes once in a while), more (i.e. bidirectional audio/video), or less (e.g. just a few keep-alive bytes), or is it just short-lived (e.g. auto-completion in a form field for the time it takes the user to type) ?

For example in haproxy we have an option to buffer up to the min of the message body and a configurable buffer size, or a delay, and the user can write rules to decide how to act when one of these limits is reached. Some will inspect a "user" field if present for example, etc. Here doing so would cause possibly undesirable delays. If we can be sure that sending a status to the client is sufficient to make it try again without incremental, that would be clean IMHO. But if it results in a non-working service, people will just associate incremental to other failed mechanisms we've accumulated over the years and that would be bad.

I'm also wondering if we couldn't use a 1xx from the intermediary to the client to say "No, I won't be passing your bytes that way, please go ahead and send what you have all at once". We could even imagine that the intermediary says "I need at least XXXX bytes or the full message before forwarding incrementally". Not sure if clients could make a good use of this though (except using padding). Just some ideas...

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
BTW even for the regular case I think the 503 is inappropriate: 5xx are errors the client cannot do anything about. That's why sometimes there's even a "retry-after" field there: it's pointless to trying again immediately, it solely depends on the server. Here the issue is related to the presence of incremental that the client can decide to disable and see the request immediately processed (possibly with incremental on the other direction by the way).

However the 503 makes sense if the server requires incremental when there are already too many, since it's a case the client has no control over.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Regarding the status code to be sent when the intermediary desides to reject the request, I agree we should use 4xx. Probably a 403 with a new Proxy-Status name?

> Also regarding WAFs, they don't buffer a few seconds but up to a certain size to perform analysis, after which they are reasonably confident the request is safe or malicious.

This approach will not work as-is for Incremental.

The Incremental field is not an optimization. It is intended to be used by applications that would fail if the intermediaries buffer HTTP messages, hoping that the sender would send all the message.

Consider Chunked OHTTP. Intermediaries must not wait for the entire request, but forward each "chunk" of the request; otherwise the backend server cannot respond to each chunk.

Therefore, intermediaries have to either obey to the signal, or reject the request in a timely manner to avoid timeouts. They cannot wait and hope that the client would provide more input.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
403 is forbidden. It's a bit hard. Usually it's what you get when some rules deny you access to a resource. I think that "422 Unprocessable Content" would be more suitable.

In fact I'm even thinking that your mechanism very closely matches what's usually done using Expect. We could have "Expect: incremental" and have 417 in response if it fails. But that wouldn't help for response processing and I think it's better to keep the mechanism symmetrical between request and response messages.

Regarding the issue with buffering, I well understand that this cannot work as-is, that's exactly why I explained how usually such things are handled, because the reality remains there, such requests will not pass through such components. And I definitely agree with immediate rejection to let the client adapt / find a different communication method instead of waiting till a timeout strikes. At least the use cases you have in mind make it clear that no 1xx interim responses will help the client either, so we can ditch that one.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> 403 is forbidden. It's a bit hard. Usually it's what you get when some rules deny you access to a resource. I think that "422 Unprocessable Content" would be more suitable.

My argument for 403 would be that we have a precedence for using it to indicate rejection by intermediaries; see https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9209.html#http-request-denied.

422 also works for me, though it's a bit odd for a proxy, without the knowledge of the content-type, to produce that error code.

FWIW, we did consider use of Expect but avoided it due to the same reason :+1:.

Sounds like the only thing we need to converge is the status code for rejection. IOW, we are making good progress!

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Just a brief note on this:

> disable Nagle and kernel buffering to avoid the 200ms pauses, and disable compression

You don't *have* to disable Nagle.  The goal of `Incremental: ?1` is to avoid *unbounded* buffering, not all buffering.  So a 200ms pause is probably no good and it probably degrades performance, a shorter Nagle delay might be acceptable.

The same might apply to compression, though I suspect the safest thing to do there is disable it unless the compressor understands that it needs to release bytes on a (short) timer.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Looking into this more closely, I think that 429 (Too Many Requests) is more appropriate than any of the status codes suggested here.

I also think that the proxy status code is not exactly right; I wonder whether we should define a new one for this.  Something like incremental_unsupported (Incremental Forwarding Not Supported).

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Hi Martin!

regarding Nagle, we don't *have to* indeed, but we know by experience that every time we messed up and forgot to disable it with interactive sessions, users quickly complained, so they do really notice it. Usually you don't choose the delay (at least I'm not aware of an OS allowing you to set it).

For compression, it really depends IMHO. Do you think that there are some use cases where we'd want to deliver a server response ASAP while it's heavy and would benefit from being compressed ? I still don't know the intended use cases, that's why I'm asking. We do have lightweight zero-latency compression in haproxy so we could definitely afford to say "compress what you have without waiting for more", that sounds easy and could be a good compromise if still relevant.

For status, "too many requests" sounds odd when it does this from the very first one :-/

I was also thinking about definiting a status code which could be a better match, but maybe it shouldn't be too tight though, so that it can be reused for something else. For example 417 is extremely close to what we're looking for except that it's tied to Expect. I was thinking about something like "Request constraints not satisfiable" so that it could be reused later for anything else using the same model.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
You are right that 429 for the very first request is going to be confusing, but I suggested it because it involves enforcement of a limit: the server has some number of requests that it might be willing to forward incrementally.

Still, it looks like there isn't a good status code, other than 400.  Maybe 400 is the best we have.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body: Same, the request is not bad (i.e. it parses properly). Keep in mind that servers and intermediaries are used to returning customized errors for specific status codes, and if an errorp age for 400 says "please fix your broken browser that sends invalid requests", it will not be great for users. Here we're dealing with something that cannot satisfy both a client and an intermediary (or server) constraint at the same time. One wants not to buffer and the other one wants to buffer, they're no way to reconcile them, but nothing is invalid once taken apart. For me the closest semantically speaking is the 417. The client expects something that the server cannot satisfy. Or we create a new one. It wouldn't be the first time.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> I also think that the proxy status code is not exactly right; I wonder whether we should define a new one for this. Something like incremental_unsupported (Incremental Forwarding Not Supported).

I think the current use of connection_limit_used is appropriate, as the case is about proxies receiving too many incremental requests.

For the case we are discussing in this issue, a new proxy status code is needed. `incremental_unsuppported` sounds good to me.

Regarding the status code, I think 429 is fine. After all, Incremental is a new extension and users using Incremental would refer to the specification. Moreever, we have Proxy-Status which is more specific.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @kazuho do you think that you could take the task to define `incremental_unsupported`?

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Editors, are we moving towards resolution here? This is the only thing I see preventing WGLC.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: @mnot Sorry for the delay. Merged the resolution and submitted -01.

issues.title: QUERY: require that QUERY with empty content errors with 400
issues.author: reschke
issues.body:
Define:

_An origin server **MUST** treat a QUERY request with no content exactly as a GET request._

That ensures that we do not introduce a new HTTP method that does not match what happens for GET. (Of course, that does not affect QUERY requests with content)

WDYT, @MikeBishop  @mnot @martinthomson @royfielding ?

(we could even expand that further to say that the same is true for requests *with* content, should the server happen to "support" GET with content - would that conflict with https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc9110.html#rfc.section.9.3.1.p.6???)

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body: I don't see why this would be desirable from an implementation perspective. I would prefer that a QUERY request without content be a 400 error. That is, prevent QUERY from being used as an alias for GET because the infrastructure for GET is more efficient.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Ah, even better.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Wouldn't this be defined by the query's content-type? While I'd expect most query formats would define some structure even in the most minimalist case (e.g. `{}` or `""`), I'm not sure that's for this specification to impose. I think it's sufficient to say that a QUERY without content is not equivalent to a GET, but is still interpreted. If the content-type doesn't permit an empty document to be valid, _then_ it's a 400.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
That would require the protocol engine to know all content type semantics. The reason to introduce this method is to send content as the query. If the content is empty, the method has no query even if an empty body means something to the content type.

It's better to say: When a client that is in the process of constructing a QUERY request finds that the content would empty, the client should either abort the request or change the method to GET.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
Q: what's the meaning of "Content-Type" when there is no content?

@MikeBishop - what we want to avoid here is that a new type of message exists in parallel to GET but with different semantics.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Empty is just one of many possible sequences of bytes.  That might be valid in a given content type (Mike's JSON examples do not permit empty content, but they show that it is possible to carry almost no information with more than zero bytes).  But this is no different than POST with an empty body, which is also valid.  So, while I appreciate the desire to say "use GET if you don't have enough QUERY for it to matter", that involves the exercise of discretion, so I don't think that it's good as the basis of a specification.  It's fine advice, to be sure, but not sound with respect to determining what is or isn't good for the protocol.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
>  So, while I appreciate the desire to say "use GET if you don't have enough QUERY for it to matter",...

That's not the primary intention.

The intent is to avoid having two retrieval methods in HTTP that do the same, even if there is no request content. And it would be consistent with the base idea if "QUERY is like GET, except that it can have request content".

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
But a QUERY of a resource, even with empty content, does have different semantics to a GET for that resource. I think it's consistent to say that it's equivalent to a GET for _some_ resource, but it's not necessarily the same as a GET for _the same_ resource.

As a naive example, I'd expect a GET of the resource to potentially return a web form for constructing a query, while a QUERY providing no filters might return all records.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
> That would require the protocol engine to know all content type semantics. The reason to introduce this method is to send content as the query. If the content is empty, the method has no query even if an empty body means something to the content type.

Not for caching. It only needs to know if the content-type and the content are the same as the cached response. That can be accomplished with e.g. hashing them together and checking for matches. If it's not in cache, then it's up to whatever implements the resource to interpret the payload, empty or not.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
I think what's clear is that we forbid any type of "content sniffing" .

In general, any problem with the contents (or metadata) of a request is a 4xx - we don't need to be more specific here -> and that would go into the definition of QUERY.

For specific cases, we can describe them in an example appendix about conneg, such as:

- If the media type (Content-Type) is missing from a request, that's a hard error (4xx -> 400, I don't think 415 is applicable here).
- If the media type is specified but not supported by the resource -> 415. (that includes the case where the media type is "understood", but has no defined query semantics, such as application/json).
- If the media type is specified and understood, but is inconsistent with the content -> 400 (this is somewhat in between 415 and 422?)
- If the media type is specified and understood and the content is consistent with the type, but the query can not be processed due to actual query semantics (say a database table name which does not exist), that's a 422.
- If the client requests the response in a format  (media type) not supported by the server, that's a 406.

With that @martinthomson and @MikeBishop - how can a zero-length content ever be consistent with a media type _**with**_ defined query semantics???

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Let's say that your query is text/csv.  Maybe each row in the CSV is something to add to the response.  But there might be some baseline information (like status).  Maybe adding nothing is acceptable.  That would run the gauntlet of your conditions all the way to a 2xx.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
The query can't be "text/csv", unless you define query semantics for it.

>  Maybe each row in the CSV is something to add to the response. But there might be some baseline information (like status). Maybe adding nothing is acceptable. That would run the gauntlet of your conditions all the way to a 2xx.

But what's the query then?

Could you provide a concrete example?

issues.title: RESUMABLE: what does backward-compatible with conventional HTTP uploads mean?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt the Introduction section

> "backwards-compatible with conventional HTTP uploads"
What does that mean?  Is that a relic of tus-v2?
Resumable uploads purportedly aim to extend the accumulation of
a single request body across multiple requests, but the draft does
not say that concisely.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Opened #3239 to resolve this issue. The intention is that a client can still try to negotiate resumable uploads even when it doesn't know whether the server supports it. I think "bootstrap" is more clear.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: proposal to change the design to support parallel uploads
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt the Introduction section

> "Unlike ranged downloads, this protocol does not support transferring an upload as multiple requests in parallel."
That is an application limitation due to over-specified implementation details
and flaws in the resumable upload protocol design.  The client should manage the state of the resource through successful upload of chunks.  If a chunk fails for any reason, the chunk should be resent, perhaps in multiple smaller chunks.

This is a proposal to change the technical design established during the development of the document.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
The ability to upload in parallel is a nice feature, but is not the primary point I was trying to make here

The primary point I am trying to make about this is that if the client manages the temporary resource, much of the current resumable upload complexity can be removed.  Upload-Offset would not be needed to be sent in responses by server.  The client would upload chunks of data.  If uploading a chunk of data was unsuccessful, the client would re-upload the whole chunk, perhaps in a set of multiple smaller chunks.  In contrast, the current extra round trips required for resumable upload recovery can exhibit worst-case behavior more frequently than not, and the recommendations for the server to write as much partial data as possible before being killed by a different request (?!) is suboptimal and messy.  That is not in the spirit of independent HTTP requests.

Were the client managing the temporary resource, and the client would always know the state of the temporary resource.  There would be no need for the very, **very** questionable recommendation in resumable uploads that an idempotent request for temporary resource state should kill a different, already in progress non-idempotent PATCH which may have hung.  Instead, the client would ignore the hung request and re-upload the data to the same offset in the temporary resource.  Even if not hung, the previous request would write the same data to that offset, and so there would not be any file corruption in the temporary resource.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
When you say "manage", what do you mean?  Do you mean choosing the URL?

The design is as it is because it is the server's URL space to manage, so it needs to be the one to allocate resources and resource identifiers for the upload process.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> When you say "manage", what do you mean? Do you mean choosing the URL?

I mean not relying on the server to tell the client Upload-Offset or other state of the temporary resource.  The client should know which chunks it uploaded successfully and should know when the temporary resource has been completely uploaded.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: A client can know this and not rely on the server's representation of this state, but only if requests succeed.  The design needs to allow for cases where connections break and requests fail.  How else can a client recover in that case?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> The design needs to allow for cases where connections break and requests fail. How else can a client recover in that case?

If the client is uploading in reasonably-sized chunks, that should be sufficient.  If there is more loss, the client can use smaller chunks to progress.  (This is much more reasonable when the client can upload many chunks, filling the bandwidth, rather than resumable upload requiring serial upload)

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body: To my prior post, a client updating a temporary resource -- and not restricted by resumable uploads as drafted -- could send an HTTP/1.1 pipeline or multiple HTTP/2 streams loading chunks serially or in parallel (does not matter).  If a request or connection fails, reconnect and send the chunks for which client has not received a successful HTTP response.  A client can abandon a connection if the client deems it hung or too much loss, and can resend chunks on a different network path.  All this is possible when the client is responsible for uploading the temporary resource and the client is able to do so across multiple requests and without having to ask the server for state.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> it is the server's URL space to manage, so it needs to be the one to allocate resources and resource identifiers for the upload process.

I fully agree that the server should control creation/allocation of the temporary resource and resource identifiers.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Most of the discussion is besides the point of the issue I created. Please stay on topic. The proposal is to change the design and that would allow parallel upload.

Authors need to hear from the WG to understand if this is a property that they want or not.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Closing this as the authors have not heard enough support to meet the bar of such a large technical design.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: resources do not manage things
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4

> "This upload resources is responsible for handling ..."
> The server is required to maintain server-side state for the upload resource.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: the original target cannot be updated
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4

> Related, the server is required to maintain server-side state including the original target.  The target is then unable to be later changed, e.g. a date in the title of the doc or blog post.  That does not matter in all case, but might matter in some.  In any case, it would be better if the target was required with Upload-Complete: ?1.  The target could still be provided in the initial request, in order for the server to do some early checks, but those checks should be repeated immediately before processing after Upload-Complete: ?1

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
The comment also questions how much state the server is required to store on the initial request, and suggests that it might be better for the client to be required to provide some/all of that state when the temporary resource is complete.  My comment is not so much a request for a feature to change the target, but more an overall questioning of the design.

There can be a large amount of time between the initial request to create the temporary resource and the completion of upload of the temporary resource.  The server should revalidate the request against all appropriate policies when the temporary resource is submitted to the target resource for processing.  (The draft also mentions this briefly in Security Considerations, but might also mention that the entire request, including headers, is untrusted.)

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> There can be a large amount of time between the initial request to create the temporary resource and the completion of upload of the temporary resource. The server should revalidate the request against all appropriate policies when the temporary resource is submitted to the target resource for processing.

That's a valuable suggestion we should add to the draft. Thank you for bringing this up!

issues.title: RESUMABLE: conjecture if the authors have written any server-side code

> I wonder if the authors of this have written and maintained any server-side code.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Yes they have.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: design change proposal to allow uploads of full representation without requiring Upload-Complete with a true value
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following (slightly edited) feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4

> Therefore, the server SHOULD keep the upload resource available for a reasonable amount of time after the upload is complete.
> This is over-specified.  If you need a transaction, then implement a transaction and job queue and the ability to check the status of completed jobs.  To increase certainty that the resource has uploaded properly, upload the resource fully with Upload-Complete: ?0.  Once complete, send Upload-Complete: ?1 as a separate request containing an empty body.  If for some reason you do not get a response, resend Upload-Complete: ?1 with an empty body until you do.  If you receive a 2xx response, you're done.  If you get an error that the upload is already complete, or that the upload resource is no longer available, then the server likely processed the result and you might verify by accessing the target resource.

This appears to be a proposal to change the design of the upload creation behaviour in Section 4.2

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body: The comment documents a robust way for clients to *know* that the temporary resource has been successfully uploaded before triggering processing by the target resource.  Yes, it suggests two separate requests and may incur additional latency for RTT between the requests, but adds more robustness/determinism to the behavior.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Some targets are upload dropboxes, which vend you a ticket once they receive the upload. If the upload resource disappears immediately after completion and offset retrieving yields 404, it is not possible to recover the lost final response, and the client has to try again.

I think we could make this non-normative given that the loss of the final response might be recoverable through different strategies. What do you all think?

issues.title: RESUMABLE: rephrase requirements on URI reuse in section 4
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4

> "An upload resource SHOULD NOT reuse the URI from a previous upload resource ..."
It would be better to specify a positive, not a negative.  "An upload resource SHOULD be unique.  Reuse of a URI for a different upload resource SHOULD be avoided to reduce the chance of misdirected or corrupted upload resources."  This is even more important it light of recommendation earlier in doc to keep upload resources around "for a reasonable amount of time after the upload is complete."

This would be an editorial change to ensure the intent is maintained while the text is rephrased to be clearer.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Thanks for the suggestion, I also mentioned security considerations in #3240

issues.title: RESUMABLE: proposed rename section headers discussing state concepts
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.1

> These headings are misnamed
> * 4.1.1 Offset        ->  Upload-Offset
> * 4.1.2 Completeness  ->  Upload-Complete
> * 4.1.3 Length        ->  Upload-Length
> * 4.1.4 Limits        ->  Upload-Limit
> 
> Considering the doc states that the server is required to keep state, such as the target resource, it appears that important state items are not all clearly defined under the topic "State".

Section 4.1 defines properties of the state of an upload. It also defines headers to transfer state information between endpoints. Therefore this is a subjective editorial issue.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I made one, rather large, proposal for this on https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3199 but happy to entertain other options to weigh up the right choice

issues.title: RESUMABLE: definition of Upload-Length for both requests and responses is unclear
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.1.3

> "The request can include the Upload-Length request and response header field."  What is "and response" header field supposed to mean in the context of the request?
> With HTTP/1.1 Transfer-Encoding: chunked and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 framing, the lenght might never be specified.  That is okay, though its absense means that it can not be cross-checked with the upload resource size.

At the point the header is defined, it is not clear on how it is used in requests or responses. Text later in the document fills in some gaps but this is not sufficent. The definition at the time of declaration can be can be improved, most likely through editorial changes.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: poor definition of stopping behaviour
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.1.4

> "The upload resource can stop the upload ..."
Do you mean the server?  The upload resource is a resource.
What do you mean by "stop"?  Abort?  Discard?  Invalidate?  Cancel?

This text is ambigiuous and does not go into sufficient detail. Most likely new text about normative behaviour will be required (even if cross referenced to other sections or other documents).

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I changed the wording to "deactivate" which was already used in Upload Cancellation (#3241). I prefer not adding anything normative for limits since they are all advisory.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: proposal to relax the requirements on changes to limits
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.1.4

> "... the existence of a limit or its value MUST NOT change ..."
Over-specified.  Maybe SHOULD NOT.  A more intelligent server might want to supply hints or make adjustments to adapt to changing conditions.  Many of these "limits" are over-specified and might be better as hints.

To add:

* The current text does not specify how to deal with a change in limits, which might be an indicator that this MUST NOT requirement is not being adhered to
* There is no rationale provided about why changes are prohibited in this way. Explanation could help, whether or not the MUST NOT is changed to a SHOULD not. Text could cover things such as whether limit decreases are worse than limit increases.

Changes in this topic would be a (marginal) design change

issues.title: RESUMABLE: text about defined/undefined Upload-Limit dict entries is unclear
issues.author: LPardue

issues.title: RESUMABLE: questions about server requirements for dealing with an OPTIONS request
issues.author: LPardue

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
For example, the definition of [Accept-Patch](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789#section-3.1) states:

issues.title: RESUMABLE: question "why create Content-Type: application/partial-upload?"
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.1.4

> Related, why create Content-Type: application/partial-upload?  That does not match the Content-Type of the temporary resource.  Is Content-Type from the original upload also required to be kept in server-side state alongside the upload resource?  (Yes.)  Accept-Patch could theoretically be extended with a new patch type, "foo" which could be defined to require and use Upload-Offset request header.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: What's the underlying issue here?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
Sorry.  I was thinking about partial-PUT Content-Range and perhaps defining a new token other than `bytes` to indicate a resumable upload (and the range could replace Upload-Offset), but I withdraw that specific suggestion.

I think partial-PUT is already well-defined in https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#partial.PUT  HOWEVER, what I think might be missing is a standardized mechanism to determine that a server supports partial-PUT.  I suppose `Accept-Patch: application/partial-put` might be an abuse of `Accept-Patch`. :)

If partial-PUT is not the preferred method, then I am suggesting `OPTIONS` response with `Accept-Patch: application/partial-upload` -- or something with a better name, but let's not bikeshed right now -- be a recommended discovery mechanism for resumable uploads.

(A 'partial-upload' can also be described as a 'patch', so `application/partial-upload` is not particularly meaningful to me.)

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Is sounds like this could be resolved by changes to text to clarify what is returned in OPTIONS, per #3174.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I added Accept-Patch in #3242. For the naming of the media type, I agree that `application/partial-upload` is vague. Maybe `application/upload-append` or `application/bytes-append`?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> For the naming of the media type, I agree that `application/partial-upload` is vague. Maybe `application/upload-append` or `application/bytes-append`?

A similar name was also suggested in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2962#issuecomment-2499693237. As far as I understand, media types have been named so that the name describes their content rather than how the document is intended to be handled. I'm unsure if there are any naming conventions written down somewhere.

We have application/partial-upload for now as it was one of the first ideas that felt good enough to go ahead with. So we could consider alternatives.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: That makes sense. I guess something like `application/resumable-upload` could also fit that criteria while being slightly less generic. We can also mark this as a dup of #2962 since it has already been discussed there.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: proposal to do different discovery mechanisms
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.1.4

> More broadly, I think that there could be many better ways to do "discovery" of the resumable-upload application rather than what is defined in the doc, and I hope more isolated, too.  An independent request to create a temporary resource would be my starting point, maybe to a target under /.well-known/.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: At this stage we need to see a more detailed proposal and support for adopting it.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
Sample (not too detailed)
* Step 1: send request to create temporary resource via well-known URI.
* Step 2: send multiple requests to populate temporary resource.  Partial-PUT is well-defined for modifying a file-based resource, in this case a temporary resource created in Step 1.
* Step 3: send request to submit temporary resource for processing.  Once temporary resource is complete, define generic HTTP mechanism to ask server to use alternative URI for request body.  I'll call this `Alt-Body` below.

Request:
```
GET /.well-known/temporary-resource HTTP/1.1
Destination: /target/processing
```
Response:
```
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /tmp/unique-hex-id-abcdef012345679
```
(Successful response indicates that server supports (made-up) Alt-Body for /target/processing URI.)

Request:
```
PUT /tmp/unique-hex-id-abcdef012345679 HTTP/1.1
...
```
(partial-PUT repeated in chunks, and let's assume for this sample that response is 204 for all partial-PUT requests)

Once client knows that temporary resource is complete:
Request:
```
POST /target/processing HTTP/1.1
Alt-Body: /tmp/unique-hex-id-abcdef012345679
```
Alt-Body to indicate that server use the given URI instead of request body.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: How is this proposal better than the current solution?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body: I should add that with happy-eye-balls, a request to the target resource with the request body could be made in parallel to a request for a temporary resource.  If the original request succeeds, send a follow-up request to delete/abandon the temporary resource.  If the original request fails due to disconnect, and the request can be safely repeated, start sending the request body to the temporary resource.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> How is this proposal better than the current solution?

Infinitely.

* Much more robust.  There is a separation of concerns between temporary resource creation and submission.
* Temporary resource population is under the full direction of the client and can be performed in parallel, in as many chunks as the client needs, and can be done using existing standards, i.e. partial PUT.
* There is room for extension to handle what resumable uploads does not handle, which is more robust transactional semantics or at least job queue submission and status retrieval.  Right now, resumable uploads says confusingly that with `Upload-Complete: ?1`, the upload resource belongs to the target URI.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: This does not sound infinitely better to me. The client is asking the server to create state without any indication of the properties of the upload object.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
There's no reason the request could not also include a structured field with parameters to more precisely communicate with the server the intended properties and use of the generic temporary resource.  Similarly, headers besides Destination could be provided for the server to check policy before creating the temporary resource.

Regardless, the server policy should be rechecked at the point that the temporary resource is submitted to the target for processing.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I suggest writing a full design out to ensure that all aspects of your proposal are laid out and understood, such as by writing an Internet-Draft that can be read in whole and iterated on. Progressive design elaboration via comments is too hard for people to keep context on.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body: I might not have time to submit that until mid-Sept.  I hope I have submitted enough actionable feedback that more discussion is warranted with the WG and last call on draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-09 can be extended.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thats a decision for the chairs to make.

The authors plan to address the editorial and minor design issues that have been raised by mid-september.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Closing this as the authors have not heard enough support to meet the bar of such a large technical design change.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: opportunity to improve text on server behavior
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.2.2

> "The resource targeted by this initial request is responsible for processing the representation data transferred in the resumable uload according to the method and header fields in the initial request..."
> 
> This wording is confusing with wording earlier in the doc that the upload resource is responsible for keeping state.  The upload resource must keep state, including the original target resource.  Once the upload resource is complete, only then does the server pass the complete upload resoure to the original target resource for processing.
> 
> That is quite a requirement to be so subtle!  This suggests that the server MUST save the *ENTIRE* set of request headers of the initial request alongside the upload resource, and then manipulate the request headers with final length, possibly remove Upload-*, or more, before finally sending a complete upload resource to the initial resource target for processing.

Further analysis is need to figure out if changes on this topic would be editorial (ensuring wording matches current intent) or if there are other normative changes that get surfaced.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body: OT: I sketched a different design for resumable uploads in #3176 but am linking since it might provide context to my thinking when reading others issues like this one.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> This suggests that the server MUST save the _ENTIRE_ set of request headers of the initial request alongside the upload resource, and then manipulate the request headers with final length, possibly remove Upload-*, or more, before finally sending a complete upload resource to the initial resource target for processing.

This would be one way to implement the upload handling, but other implementation approaches also exist. For me, this is an implementation detail and does not have to be mandated by the specification. Instead, the text tries to define the expected behavior that is necessary to achieve interoperability between clients and server. At least that was the intention, but we should look over the text and see if the wording can be improved.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: My mental model of resumable upload is that it's just a prolonged regular upload. Request headers should be supplied at the beginning, and maybe consider trailers if some fields need to be updated at the end of the upload, or perform a separate transaction. I think the requirement should be kept as is.

comments.body: I agree with @guoye-zhang on this one. Could we get an example to highlight the issue described in the original email?

issues.title: RESUMABLE: proposal to change the requirements related to 104 Upload Resumption Supported and Location header
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following (slightly edited) feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.2.2

> "These interim responses MUST NOT include the Location header field"
Over-specified.  MUST NOT should be SHOULD NOT, and/or the doc should say that Location should not be included in any 104 response other than in the initial 104 response when the upload resource is created, and that a client SHOULD ignore Location in any 104 response besides the initial 104 response for the upload resource.  Icky.  It would also be okay to say the Location of the upload resource MUST NOT change if Location is sent more than once. A more robust approach would be a request for creation of a temporary resource with a 0-length request body, which is separate from requests sending the request body to the upload resource.

This sounds like it would be design change, albeit a minor one.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Regarding the latter point above:

> A more robust approach would be a request for creation of a temporary resource with a 0-length request body, which is separate from requests sending the request body to the upload resource.

This is possible and described in [Section 4.2.1](
https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.2.1). There may be some text/cross referencing we could add to ensure readers have a clear understanding of options.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
This issue also relates to the append operation in Section 4.4.2. @gstrauss highlights in 

> "These interim responses MUST NOT include the Location header field."
Over-specified again?  Why MUST NOT?  This is in section 4.4 Upload Append.  Would it be clearer to suggest that 104 responses to PATCH should not include Location?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
If creation of temporary resource was separate from populating the temporary resource (with PATCH), then 104 might not be needed at all.  If client knows which request chunks succeeded, and if client sends multiple requests in small chunks, then the server response to each chunk obviates the need for 104 intermediate status while bytes are sent.

If an application-level signal for "are you still there and are you receiving bytes in a timely manner" is needed, a specific response should be created for that, e.g. 105 I am still here, keep-alive.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
PR #3203 attempts to solve the requirements for 104.

Discussion about whether we should use 104 at all is basically a separate larger topic, so that should be split into a different ticket if the proposers would like to continue it.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: proposal - requirements on tying HTTP requests together create a fragile design and this should stop the document leaving the WG for publication
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.2.2.

> Not only is this fragile, but it imposes a requirement that the server maintain state for exclusive access to the upload resource, and have a new request affect a different request -- which are big implementation requirements -- tying together multiple HTTP requests which are supposed to be independent in HTTP.
** This is a huge failure and should immediately disqualify this draft from proceeding passed last call. **

>Related is the fragile behavior specified in 4.3 Offset Retrieval:
"The client MUST NOT perform offset retrieval while creation (Seciton 4.2) or appending (Section 4.4) is in progress as this can cause the previous request to be terminated by the server as described in Section 4.6."

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: More detail as to why this is fragile would help. Hyperbolic statements do not.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> More detail as to why this is fragile would help. Hyperbolic statements do not.

Section 4.6 Concurrency
>   The RECOMMENDED approach is as follows: If an upload resource
   receives a new request to retrieve the offset (Section 4.3), append
   representation data (Section 4.4), or cancel the upload (Section 4.5)
   while a previous request for creating the upload (Section 4.2) or
   appending representation data (Section 4.4) is still ongoing, the
   resource SHOULD prevent race conditions, data loss, and corruption by
   terminating the previous request before processing the new request.

I think I said it well in #3159 

An *idempotent* HEAD request to retrieve the offset should not cause a non-idempotent PATCH request -- on the same server or on another server -- to be cancelled.  Specifying such recommended behavior does not strike me as in the spirit of independent HTTP requests, and also not *idempotent* HEAD requests.

This would not be necessary to recover from hung requests with my alternative proposal to remove the complexity and restrictions imposed by having the server report Upload-Offset to the client.  Instead, the client should send reasonably-sized chunks and should resend the chunk (perhaps in multiple smaller chunk requests) if sending the chunk fails (or hangs).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The proposal to keep uploading chunks of data that might have been received and processed (in whole or in-part) sounds to me like it could create conditions where a client spends bandwidth on uploading duplicate data that is not necessary, and a server spends resources handling such requests. 

Does your proposal offer any way to avoid such resource spending by allowing a a client to get an accurate view of precisely how much data has been received and processed by the server at any point in time?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body: My proposal side-steps all the complexity by suggesting that the client adjust the data chunk size of the representation that it chooses to send.  By not requiring serial upload, the client can choose how much data to pipeline in how many requests.  Yes, failed requests will need to be resent in my proposal.  Multiple requests can be sent with smaller chunk sizes.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
So the answer to my question 

> Does your proposal offer any way to avoid such resource spending by allowing a a client to get an accurate view of precisely how much data has been received and processed by the server at any point in time?

Is no?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> So the answer to my question
> 
> > Does your proposal offer any way to avoid such resource spending by allowing a a client to get an accurate view of precisely how much data has been received and processed by the server at any point in time?
> 
> Is no?

Incorrect: If the client is uploading sequentially, then sending a HEAD request to the server for the temporary resource gives the client an accurate view of precisely how much data has been received.

*However, in my proposal, there is no need to ask the server with a separate request and RTT cost.*

The client already knows how much data has been received by the server by the successful HTTP response(s) to each request containing a chunk of the representation sent by the client.  It does not matter if the client is uploading sequentially, in parallel, and/or pipelining.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
What is the client is sending in parallel? Is there a way to query the precise ranges that have been processed and received? 

A server can respond prior to receiving the full payload of a request. You would probably want to state a server MUST NOT do that in your design.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> What is the client is sending in parallel? Is there a way to query the precise ranges that have been processed and received?
> 
> A server can respond prior to receiving the full payload of a request. You would probably want to state a server MUST NOT do that in your design.

That is an implementation detail and could be supported.  If the server stores the temporary resource in a file on a filesystem which supports holes, then it would be possible to send back to the client a list of ranges of data, and by extension, the holes.  In another possible implementation, if the temporary resource was stored in a database, the ranges could be reported from the database.

Aside: I do not understand what you mean by "processed" as in both resumable uploads and my temporary resource proposal, the temporary resource is collected until Upload-Complete: ?1 (or equivalent) before being submitted to the target resource for processing.  I am responding to your question about portions of the representation "received".

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> Aside: I do not understand what you mean by "processed" as in both resumable uploads and my temporary resource proposal, the temporary resource is collected until Upload-Complete: ?1 (or equivalent) before being submitted to the target resource for processing.

Your design, IIUC, requires a 2xx to confirm the chunks are received in whole. It's all or nothing. Draft 09 supports capturing whatever message content was received and processed by the server prior to the upload creation or append failing, no 104 or 200 is strictly necessary, since the offset is retrievable.

Client strategies for dealing with these situation are probably not too dissimilar - follow up chunk size, potential for backtracking, etc.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> Your design, IIUC, requires a 2xx to confirm the chunks are received in whole. It's all or nothing.

One might say very HTTP-like.

The difference from all-or-nothing is that my temporary resource proposal allows the client to send the data in chunks in multiple requests.  Partial-PUT is already an established means to do this.  An intelligent client might measure the RTT for the temporary resource creation request and then use that timing, as well as subsequent partial-PUT requests to calculate BDP and adapt chunk sizes and number of requests.

> Draft 09 supports capturing whatever message content was received and processed by the server prior to the upload creation or append failing, no 104 or 200 is strictly necessary, since the offset is retrievable.

When the offset is not updated by 104 (due to 104 not being passed), then a full RTT is required to recover from *each and every* request failure.  Draft 09 requires sequential upload.  Combined, in the face of unstable/flaky/changing connections, Draft 09 will likely exhibit *much worse* performance recovering.  On top of that, the protocol is more complex than my proposal.

In the face of no network connectivity issues and low packet loss, there will not be a huge difference between the solutions, except that Draft 09 does have an advantage of fewer round trips for tiny request bodies.  I conjecture that if an application can tolerate a resubmission (e.g. POST with the same request body is "safe"), then an intelligent client may try to send a tiny request body all at once, falling back to resumable uploads only on failure.  In that case, neither Draft 09 or my solution are used, and so the Draft 09 advantage for tiny requests is lessened.  Additionally, my proposal could optionally be extended to accept an initial request body in the temporary resource creation request, further reducing the Draft 09 perceived advantage for tiny requests.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The issue with your proposed design is, it can consume additional bandwidth due to needing to send duplicated data that was already delivered to server but not confirmed as such by a 200 response. Eating an RTT to save on bandwidth is a reasonable tradeoff to make.

Client environments may not be in control of request dispatch to their connection pool, nor able to access information about the network (such as TCP or QUIC connection statistics). Parallelizing chunk uploads for the same resource can lead to all requests being pooled into the same connection, with little control over the client-side send scheduling. Sharing bandwidth over multiple chunks means that when a connection terminates, each chunk would have made slower parallel progress. If a client picks large chunks, the impact of a connection failure in this design is high, because the bandwidth spent to send those chunks is wasted until a server returns a 200. 

Using fallback and/or smaller chunks increases the total count of requests required, which is also a tradeoff because some deployment models bill by request count. A server operator can limit this, to some extent, by declaring a minimum chunk size. However, there will then be tension between the operator and the client needs.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: It would be remiss to not mention that fetching the upload offset, as described in 09, is also a request that would count against total requests. However, the nature of the request is different (no request message content) , which may factor into costs calculations on the server side.

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> Client environments may not be in control of request dispatch to their connection pool, nor able to access information about the network (such as TCP or QUIC connection statistics). Parallelizing chunk uploads for the same resource can lead to all requests being pooled into the same connection, with little control over the client-side send scheduling. Sharing bandwidth over multiple chunks means that when a connection terminates, each chunk would have made slower parallel progress. If a client picks large chunks, the impact of a connection failure in this design is high, because the bandwidth spent to send those chunks is wasted until a server returns a 200.

I have no doubt that each individual point that you make is true somewhere, but together I am less certain.  If parallelizing will lead to terrible behavior, don't parallelize.  If pipelining will lead to terrible behavior, don't pipeline.  Send sequentially.  However, if a software stack is going to implement resumable uploads, then I hope it might recognize the pattern and not choose the most suboptimal steps.  If not, the client should send those requests one-at-a-time, which would effectively slow my proposal down to the speed of resumable uploads.  However, without those constraints, my proposal could be much faster.  If the parallelization behavior is desirable, it could utilize the network bandwidth with multiple requests of multiple chunks of data, potential over multiple different network paths, and would still be able to recover if some of those requests failed.

> Using fallback and/or smaller chunks increases the total count of requests required, which is also a tradeoff because some deployment models bill by request count. A server operator can limit this, to some extent, by declaring a minimum chunk size. However, there will then be tension between the operator and the client needs.

These sound like they heavily influenced the design choices.  Are these documented somewhere?  I'm sorry I must admit that I have not followed every IETF meeting where Resumable Uploads was discussed, but I have tried to read the meeting notes from most of the meetings.  If request count is billed in such a way that more smaller requests would have a substantial impact, then that sounds like some businesses may want to change to a provider with a fairer resource-based billing.

How rampant is such billing that is billed in such a way that would have a substantial impact for larger requests which are split into, say, 256KB chunks versus 2MB chunks?  While I can now see why the draft tries to get as much bytes written as possible, the billing problem is not a technical problem, and so the billing problem should not be addressed with a technical kludge.  The billing problem is still a problem, but I think there are different pressures which might lead to better solutions.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
It sounds like parralelization is an optimization that can be fragile.

There's a lot of open questions and tradeoffs here for both the current design and the proposal. 

I suggest the way to make progress is to implement and gather data on the respective approaches under varying network conditions such as low/high RTT, low/high bandwidth, network loss / disconnects, client disconnects, and server disconnects.

There are several client and server implementations of draft 09. If we have one or more implementations of the proposed design, it would allow us to more concretely compare the two. The testbed can be a collaborative effort.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Closing this as the authors have not heard enough support to meet the bar of such a large technical design change.

The client could send chunks of representation data, and then resend the whole chunk on failure.  (Maybe try to recover by sending smaller chunks.)  The server would manage the upload resource per-request and apply policies per-request.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: "MUST if" is a poor normative construction
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt 4.3.2

> "MUST include the length in the Upload-Length header field if known"
Over-specified.  If it is okay to exclude it if not known, then this should be SHOULD, not MUST.

Stating how the client deals with a missing field probably would not go amiss either. Borderline editorial/minor design change.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: This is clearly editorial - at least to the extent of the feedback. Many hold that best practice is to use "MUST... unless" rather than "SHOULD... unless" constructions.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
No hats, just my opinion:

There is a distinction between the two, but I agree it's subtle. SHOULD means the behavior is truly optional, though recommended. We want to explain the circumstances where an implementation might reasonably skip the behavior and why it's a Really Good Idea the rest of the time.

"MUST... unless" is truly mandatory outside of the indicated circumstance.

In general, I tend to prefer MUST when the peer can validate and SHOULD when the peer just has to trust you did the best you could. You can read it through the lens that MUST implies the peer MAY treat any violation as an error, while SHOULD implies the peer MUST NOT consider a violation an error.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I tend to prefer being precise about what the counterparty might be permitted or required to do, rather than fixate on one side.  It's a protocol, after all.

So if there is a condition where you would say "MUST ... if", you can flip that around and say that in the same circumstances, the peer MAY or MUST reject the opposite choice.  So if the action is non-discretionary, you can say "MUST ... if", but you would also setup consequences, such that you improve the chances that someone bothers to follow the rules.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks for the discussion, very helpful. On balance, I've opted for the MUST unless variant in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3204. 

In a nutshell, the interaction is to echo back a value a client SHOULD send you. Adding more optionality to that interaction via a server SHOULD seems of little value to me.

I resisted the urge to flip requirements around here, due to the sequence of interactions. I think the new text makes it clear enough if you page in the full context (but that doesn't preclude us applying that advice in other areas as a separate followup).

issues.title: RESUMABLE: proposal - revisit partial upload vs. PATCH discussion
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
@gstrauss provided the following feedback on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0094.html wrt Section 4.4.1

> "A client can continue the upload and append representation data by sending a PATCH request with the application/partial-upload media type ..."
> Why Content-Type: application/partial-upload ?
Could instead use Range request header and a proper Content-Type (or application/octet-stream) since the PATCH request is a byte range, already defined by the RFC.
With OPTIONS, could use Accept-Patch.  See the RFC 5789 for PATCH.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2962. Is there any new information to warrant revisting this?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
Iff the WG reconsiders some of the design limitations and reduces complexity by eliminating requirements for serial upload and Upload-Offset, then yes, it may make sense to also revisit the PATCH discussion.

As I posted in a different issue, perhaps the hesitation to using partial-PUT is the lack of a standardized discovery mechanism that a server supports RFC9110 partial-PUT.

comments.author: reschke

comments.author: reschke
