issues.title: RESUMABLE: Section 10.1 description of how to use Repr-Digest seems wrong
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
During WGLC review, @MikeBishop raised the following issue on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0123.html

> In Section 10.1, regarding integrity verification, could Repr-Digest also be on the HEAD of the upload resource?

However, looking even further at the text I'm not 100% sure the suggested interactions are correct (and I probably should have caught this earler). 

First, we state this use case which seems fine

> If the client knows the integrity digest of the entire representation data before creating an upload resource, it can include the Repr-Digest header field when creating an upload ([Section 4.2](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/new#upload-creation)). Once the upload is completed, the server can compute the integrity digest of the received representation data and compare it to the provided digest. If the digests don't match, the server SHOULD consider the upload failed, not process the representation further, and signal the failure to the client. This way, the integrity of the entire representation data can be protected.

In other words, the client knew the full data and sent it over for the server to eventually use once it has all the data.

The bit I'm less sure about is 

> the server can compute the digest continuously during the upload and include the Repr-Digest header field in responses to upload creation ([Section 4.2](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/new#upload-creation)) and upload appending requests ([Section 4.4](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/new#upload-appending)) even when the upload is not completed yet.

If the upload is, for example, 1000 bytes of content but the server only received 500 bytes, the hash it would produce over 500 bytes is not the same as over 1000. So is this the representation of the upload resource? Does HTTP allow that to change over time (I think it does). If we agree, the text could probably be clearer on that point. Then, we can answer Mike's original point that Offset Retrieval (HEAD request) returns the state of the upload resource including a Repr-Digest.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: This got me thinging about some security implications there might be wrt content negotiaton, see https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3213#issuecomment-3217520588

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> If the upload is, for example, 1000 bytes of content but the server only received 500 bytes, the hash it would produce over 500 bytes is not the same as over 1000. So is this the representation of the upload resource? Does HTTP allow that to change over time (I think it does).

That has been my interpretation so far, yes. The representation on the server-side changes during the upload as data is appended to it.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I was actually planning on relying on the interpretation of the representation as "what has been uploaded so far", rather than "what will be uploaded in total". It seemed to me very useful to be able to send a digest of the entire content that has been uploaded up to the current point, to continually ensure the server has the right data in total throughout the entire upload. The digest for "what will be uploaded in total" could simply be transferred in the final `Upload-Complete: ?1` request, making it strictly more useful to interpret it that way for `Repr-Digest`. When I read "Alternatively, the server can compute the digest continuously ...", I was quite happy.

The only argument against this being strictly more useful that I can think of is if a server implementation wants to rely on `Repr-Digest` for deduplication before the upload even starts. Knowing the hash of the entire upload ahead of time would make this simpler. But arguably, that information could simply be transferred in the `Content-Disposition` instead, albeit less interoperably.

Perhaps this should be clarified one way or another so that it can be relied on by client implementations? Right now, I'm under the impression that an interoperable client can't really choose either.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I think this can work on the server side, its patching a representation and hence keeps calculating a new one. On the client side its harder, the patch document is the representation; see https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9530.html#section-3.1-5

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: I see. Then I suppose that's another argument in favor of #2962, haha. Assuming the same does not apply to `POST` requests, that is.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
A client can set the Repr-Digest header in the initial request if it attempts to transfer the entire representation data in this request. I'm not sure if the same applies if the transfer is intentionally split across multiple requests.

That being said, the approach where the server computes a running hash over the entire received representation and includes it in responses should still work. The client can then verify that the digest matches its value. I think we agree that this idea is sound and only have to tweak the wording a bit to make this point clearer.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
To summarise my thinking:

1. An upload creation for the entire representation could use Repr-Digest just fine
2. An upload creation using a partial PUT (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#partial.PUT) could in theory use Repr-Digest. Although due to the nature of the resumable upload protocol, partial PUT would seem to have rough edges. In the introduction we already say "While partial PUT is one method for uploading a partial representation (via Content-Range in the request), there are caveats that affect its deployability; see [Section 14.5](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-14.5) of [[HTTP](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#HTTP)].". For simplicity we might want to consider stating these two things are entirely incompatible - that seems like a new issue to consider tangentially. Lets assume we'll do that for the purposes of this thread.
3. Upload creation using less than the entire representation cannout use Repr-Digest. We'd need to communicate the representation's full length but not send it, that places us straight back into partial PUT territory.
4. Upload append uses PATCH. The patch document is a different resource and hence representation. Repr-Digest applies to the patch document not the upload resource. There is no current way to communicate "Apply this patch document and it should produce a representation with a digest X". I started a conversation on the list; see https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2026AprJun/0037.html and based on current responses I don't think will happen any time soon
5. The upload resource is mutated over time. 
  5a. The upload append can return the state of the representation in the response
  5b. Offset retrieval can return the state of the representation in the response.
  5c. Repr-Digest can be returned in 5a and 5b no matter the offset of the upload resource. The client can verify the Repr-Digest based on the `upload-offset` value, which will let it know the byte range over which to calculate the digest (always starting at 0, ending at the offset). However, see point 6.
6. Does an offset retrieval or upload append response contain a header that articulates the full length of the upload resource in either the `content-length` or `content-range` headers? I can't find a clear answer to that in the document and it would have a bearing on what a client might be able to do (and also raises questions on whether `upload-offset` has to strictly match the full length values sent in either `content-length` or `content-range`.

Based on the above, I could probably open a simple PR to address point 5 and make it a bit clearer about how a client might do things. However, point 6 probably intereferes and would benefit from an answer first.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
For 1-4, I agree.

For 5, I don't know what representation that digest would be referring to. All of the data uploaded so far? These responses themselves don't have any expected content, so surely not the representation communicated by the response content. Are you suggesting that the protocol be updated to specify the repesentation that digest would refer to? In particular, that it would refer to the data acknowledged by the server so far up to the upload offset?

For 6, what do you mean by "full length of the upload resource"? If you mean the length of the total representation data uploaded so far, is that not the `Upload-Offset`? If you mean the total length of the complete upload, is that not the `Upload-Length`? I'm also not sure what bearing you think this would have.

As a side note, setting aside semantics and speaking pragmatically, at least for my use case, it would be ideal if the digest could be checked by the server, so that it can reject the digested representation data and ask for it to be resent without restarting the entire upload. Otherwise, if the client checks the digest after the server already acknowledged an upload creation/append, the only thing the client can do to handle a mismatch is restart the upload. It can't backtrack the offset. Just wanted to throw that out there in case it becomes relevant.

Also, regarding the running hash use case I mentioned earlier, I would be willing to compromise and go with a hash of the representation communicated by each request's content instead. That includes incomplete upload creation requests, which aren't patch documents, so what `Repr-Digest` refers to in that case may have to be clarified.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> 3\. Upload creation using less than the entire representation cannout use Repr-Digest. We'd need to communicate the representation's full length but not send it, that places us straight back into partial PUT territory.

That makes sense. It's not semantically correct for the client to include the Repr-Digest of the full representation if it doesn't include the entire representation. We can probably adjust the text to say that Repr-Digest should be accompanied by `Upload-Complete: ?1` in upload creation requests.

> 5\. The upload resource is mutated over time.
>         5a. The upload append can return the state of the representation in the response
>         5b. Offset retrieval can return the state of the representation in the response.

This touches on a question I've been thinking about. I agree with you that the representation on the server-side changes over time as the upload progresses and that HEAD/GET and PATCH requests return the corresponding state. Can these responses include the Repr-Digest over the received representation data, although the responses do not include said representation on its own? As clarified in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3467, we don't require upload resources to provide the uploaded representation back to the client.

This could also lead to a contradiction: If HEAD responses include the Repr-Digest of the uploaded representation, GET responses should include it to. The spec doesn't place restrictions on the GET response content, so it could be anything, whose digest might not match Repr-Digest. Or can we get out of trouble by defining that the selected representation for upload resources is always the uploaded representation data (since Repr-Digest is defined as the digest of the selected representation)? 

> 6\. Does an offset retrieval or upload append response contain a header that articulates the full length of the upload resource in either the `content-length` or `content-range` headers? I can't find a clear answer to that in the document and it would have a bearing on what a client might be able to do (and also raises questions on whether `upload-offset` has to strictly match the full length values sent in either `content-length` or `content-range`.

As Grant said, offset retrieval responses include the length in Upload-Length, if the length is known to the server. But there are no considerations for Content-Length since the server can respond with any content it likes for HEAD and PATCH requests.

That being said, I think that the most useful case for digests here is for the client to communicate the expected digests to the servers, who then validates them and might stop processing the representation if integrity is violated. I see less immediate use cases for communicating the digests from the server to the client. I originally added text for this because I thought it could easily be done through the headers defined in RFC 9530. But if this raises more questions than it answers, we should also consider removing the problematic text.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> That being said, I think that the most useful case for digests here is for the client to communicate the expected digests to the servers, who then validates them and might stop processing the representation if integrity is violated. I see less immediate use cases for communicating the digests from the server to the client. I originally added text for this because I thought it could easily be done through the headers defined in RFC 9530. But if this raises more questions than it answers, we should also consider removing the problematic text.

So looking at what text we have already, the nuances or edge cases related to core protocol elements or interactions, the forthcoming unencoded-digest, etc. I agree it keeps raising more questions.

It leads me to think we stand the best chance of gathering consensus on the resumable upload protocol doc if we were to drop section 10. its better to say nothing than to say the wrong thing. If digests are valuable in practice, a follow up document spun out from this one could make sense. (It wouldn't be the first time the WG does a spin off).

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: That stance is understandable, though I'd be a bit sad that incomplete upload creation requests sent to my server by interoperable clients won't include `Repr-Digest` due to the lack of clarity surrounding that. `Content-Digest` is just not as useful.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks Grant, thats useful information to capture and present to the WG as a motivator for it to consider adopting new work if the integrity aspects are spun out. I'll be sure to reflect it in comms.

The  area of integrity for uploads was researched as part of RFC 9530. I don't have the full context paged in but I recall extant approaches in S3 and Google cloud seemed quite cursed when compared to standardized HTTP semantics. For example, the use of Content-MD5 in https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/resumable-uploads#integrity_checks (there were more details beyond whats shown at that link)

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: I would love to contribute to work on the integrity aspects of resumable uploads. There's a _lot_ to consider, so it makes sense we wouldn't want to just rush this and get it wrong (both semantically and practically). I believe integrity checking is an extremely important aspect of resumable uploads for most use cases; every large-scale implementer of a proprietary resumable upload protocol in the wild (such as S3 and GCS) has considerable documentation just regarding integrity verification. If we want to push that off to a follow-up document, I personally have no problem with that, but my only hope would be that work can start on that as soon as possible after this protocol is stabilized, to maximize the usefulness of this protocol. Without deliberate mechanisms for integrity verification, I suspect adoption of resumable uploads won't be nearly as high.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I wonder if @danielresnick might have any opinion on the matter of integrity and uploads from a Google perspective.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: when appending and the offset matches the upload length, clarify what the server does
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
During WGLC review, @MikeBishop raised the following issue as a nit on https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2025JulSep/0123.html

> 4.4.2: "stopping to append bytes..., rejecting the request" => "rejecting requests to append..." perhaps?

While Mike classes this as a nit, I think its a little bigger. My read is that were currently recommending that the server process the appending data up to the point the upload length is reached, then discard any data after that. Is that a right interpretation?

Think we need some editorial work here to be sure.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
The paragraph in question is:

> If the length is known, the upload resource MUST prevent the offset from exceeding the upload length by stopping to append bytes once the offset reaches the length, rejecting the request, marking the upload resource invalid and rejecting any further interaction with it. It is not sufficient to rely on the Content-Length header field for enforcement because the header field might not be present.

(https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.4.2-8)

> My read is that were currently recommending that the server process the appending data up to the point the upload length is reached, then discard any data after that. Is that a right interpretation?

To me it reads as if the server should not process the representation at all if its length exceeds the announced value (or try to undo whatever changes the prcessing of the representarion yielded). Just discarding the additional bytes isn't allowed. That's similar to how newer HTTP version mark the entire request malformed if the content is larger than Content-Length.

I think Mike's suggestion would also work as it keeps the same intention.

Preserving this suggestion so it doesn't get lost; the PR might have been merged before it came in?

issues.title: RESUMABLE: diagram shows client waiting on 104
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
During WGLC review, @wtarreau raised the comment in https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/httpbisa/JjZSzo1siwNKqsilcw8Gz8WE6tc/:

> 
> I was initially confused by the first diagram in 3.1:
>   ```
>    Client                                  Server
>    |                                            |
>    | POST /project/123/files                    |
>    | Upload-Complete: ?1                        |
>    |------------------------------------------->|
>    |                                            |
>    |                                            | Reserve resources
>    |                                            | for upload
>    |                                            |-----------------.
>    |                                            |                 |
>    |                                            |<----------------'
>    |                                            |
>    |            104 Upload Resumption Supported |
>    |            Location: /uploads/abc          |
>    |<-------------------------------------------|
>    |                                            |
>    X--------------Flow Interrupted--------------X
>    ```
> Which I've read as:
> 
> - client sends POST with headers
> - server returns 104
> - client the possibly uploads data
> - transfer is interrupted
> 
> As an intermediary implemented it worried me that we'd have a new header
> that would cause uploads to wait for an interim response. When reading
> the rest I figured it does not make sense and is just my incorrect
> interpretation of the diagram. But it also means that others could
> possibly implement it like this (especially clients which could then
> wait for the 104 before sending data).
>
> I don't know how we could fix the diagram. Maybe adding an arrow from the
> client to the server in the middle, like this:
> 
> ```
>    Client                                  Server
>    |                                            |
>    | POST /project/123/files                    |
>    | Upload-Complete: ?1                        |
>    |------------------------------------------->|
>    | body                                       |
>    |------------------------------------------->| Reserve resources
>    |                                            | for upload
>    |                                            |-----------------.
>    |                                            |                 |
>    |                                            |<----------------'
>    |                                            |
>    |            104 Upload Resumption Supported |
>    |            Location: /uploads/abc          |
>    |<-------------------------------------------|
>    |                                            |
> ```

While a client could in theory be waiting on a 104 response to check for Upload-Limit, I don't expect most client to behave that way. They will likely just start transferring the data as soon as the request is opened. Therefore, we should update the diagram to make this clearer.

issues.title: Key sort should be stable
issues.author: ricea
issues.body:
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-no-vary-search-03#section-6-2.8.2.2.1 says

> 2. Set searchParamsA to the result of sorting searchParamsA in ascending order with keyLessThan.
> 3. Set searchParamsB to the result of sorting searchParamsB in ascending order with keyLessThan.

I think it should explicitly mention that the sorts should be stable, otherwise implementations might accidentally change the order of multiple values with the same key, resulting in erroneous matches or mismatches.

It could either say "sorting ... in ascending order with keyLessThan preserving the existing order of pairs with identical keys" or just "stably sorting".

Chromium is already using a stable sort in practice.

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: I think the real problem here is that the document says it's using the Infra Standard and uses inline references for algorithms used from that standard, but then doesn't actually do it for this operation. https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list-sort-in-ascending-order is quite clear this is supposed to be stable.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: What happens when a POST request is made for an already-created incomplete resource?
issues.author: mertalev
issues.body:
My use-case is that a given user can only make one resource with a given checksum. This checksum is provided in the Repr-Digest header in the initial request and validated on upload completion. The resource URI itself is not a checksum, but a UUID. Once the client has created the resource with the initial POST request, it should either complete it (possibly in multiple parts) or cancel it. Once cancelled, the user is allowed to create a new resource with a different UUID for the same checksum.

The spec is clear enough that a complete resource should not be modified and provides a response to use for this case. However, what should happen if the client creates this resource without completing it, then tries to create it again?
* Should it be rejected with a 400 code?
* Should it cause the incomplete resource to be invalidated?
* Should it include a Location header to direct it to the existing resource?
* Should it truncate the existing resource and start over?

Given the client needs to know the resource in order to resume or cancel it in this case, I think it makes sense to include the Location header with an error status code to allow them to take further action, possibly also including the Upload-Offset.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
A good way to think of the resumable upload is that it's just an in-progress regular upload. What do you do if a user performs 2 concurrent POSTs with the same checksum without using resumable upload? Whatever you decide to do should apply here as well.

In general, we recommend that the new attempt overrides the old attempt since the client might have recovered from a crash and unaware of the old attempt. Yes, you could design something to try to recover the state, but I'm not certain that we need to add the complexity to the protocol. Essentially this would be adding a lookup mechanism of the temporary resource from the file checksum.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body:
As I understand it, the spec as written doesn't seem to have a way for the client to resume an upload if it doesn't know or forgets the URI provided by the server, such as if it crashes or restarts, unless it persists this somewhere. This would be a way for the client to retrieve this URI from the server based on some criteria (in this case the user ID and checksum). It would also mean the upload could be resumed from a different client with the same file.

It's of course possible to have a custom design that does this when the client and server agree on this behavior, but it'd be nice to have a standard way to do this that all RUFH clients can understand.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
It is achievable today with a 104 response followed immediately by a 5xx response. The client would perform offset retrieving and upload appending. We might want to change this sentence in "Offset Retrieval" but it's not a MUST:

> The offset can be less than or equal to the number of bytes of representation data that the client has already sent.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: That's clever! It's maybe semantically incorrect since it isn't *really* a server error, but it addresses the use-case in question.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Yeah we could in theory define a separate status code for "please retry", but the workaround above should already work with the implementation today on iOS/macOS

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> It is achievable today with a 104 response followed immediately by a 5xx response. The client would perform offset retrieving and upload appending. We might want to change this sentence in "Offset Retrieval" but it's not a MUST:
> 
> > The offset can be less than or equal to the number of bytes of representation data that the client has already sent.

The spec doesn't prohibit the offset from jumping ahead (from the client's perspective), but it explicitly allows clients to error out in such cases:

> The client MAY reject an offset which is greater than the number of bytes it has already sent during this upload.

Therefore, I would assume that this server behavior won't work with every client.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: *Should* it allow the client to reject a greater offset? Even a streamed input can work with a greater offset.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Allowing clients to reject greater offsets can make their implementation simpler, especially if they are uploading streaming data. In addition, the offset should not jump ahead for usual uploads where one client uploads a representation independently of previous uploads. That was the reason behind allowing this client behavior so far.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: I can say that as a server implementer, although supporting all RUFH clients is ideal, my priority is targeting URLSession and probably one or two more clients for other platforms. So long as it works for those target clients, I will consider the approach viable. If I did want to handle other clients as a server, I would need to go by user agent or something to detect what the client supports and behave differently for them. Allowing clients to reject this thus comes with the caveat of potentially fractured interoperability.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: URLSession passes the responsibility to its users. If they are uploading a file, arbitrary offset is supported automatically. Otherwise they are asked to provide a request body stream from a certain offset which they might be able to do or decline.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: I suppose that would still be fine as long as the client `DELETE`'s the upload resource if declined. The only issue is if they both can't accept the offset and also take no action, since it would just get stuck at that point.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: We haven't implemented upload cancellation in URLSession yet, so yeah it will be stuck

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body:
> We haven't implemented upload cancellation in URLSession yet, so yeah it will be stuck

Hmm, perhaps it should be an opt-in behavior through a request header to be safe. If it isn't provided, the server can assume it won't support the offset and overwrite the earlier attempt instead.

Out of curiosity, is the RUFH handling open source? I might be able to contribute some spec functionality if so, mainly cancellation and limits in mind.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: URLSession is not open source unfortunately. Please file feedbacks requesting this and send me the FB number, so it can be prioritized.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body:
> URLSession is not open source unfortunately. Please file feedbacks requesting this and send me the FB number, so it can be prioritized.

Thank you for prioritizing this! I made the feedbacks FB20751965 and FB20752104. I'm happy to provide more details if needed or participate in dev betas to give more feedback.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Can we close this issue or are there inquiries to adapt the resumable upload process? To me it seems that the questions have been answered and no further action is necessary for now.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: The spec could probably use different wording to acknowledge that the server is allowed to send a greater offset and that the client should accept it if it's able. The 5xx status is also a bit awkward and might benefit from a more explicit response. These are the main things that come to mind for this issue.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3319 proposed text for handling 409 on the client-side.

issues.title: Redundant requirements for secondary certs on a non-control stream
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
The draft states both

> The SERVER_CERTIFICATE frame MUST be sent on the control stream. A SERVER_CERTIFICATE frame received on any other stream MUST not be used for server authentication.

and 

> The SERVER_CERTIFICATE frame applies to the connection, not a specific stream. An endpoint MUST treat a SERVER_CERTIFICATE frame received on any stream other than the control stream as a connection error.

This seems a bit redundant. If you trigger a connection error, then you don't process the frame and so the "MUST not be used for server authentication" can't apply. Consider combining and condensing the requirement text.

comments.author: egorbaty
comments.body: Agreed, both of these requirements are basically stating the same thing. Will condense these.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Retrieving the lost final response after a completed upload
issues.author: guoye-zhang
issues.body:
The draft currently states that

> The server SHOULD keep the upload resource available for a reasonable amount of time after the upload is complete.

However, it does not define a mechanism for retrieving the final response. Interacting with the temporary response would result in a failure with the "completed-upload" problem type.

For a well-behaving client, if the connection is lost before a response is received, it would attempt to perform offset retrieval followed by upload appending. If the server resends the final response for a 0-length complete append, the upload would complete successfully with no additional effort on the client side. If the server is unwilling to keep the final response for resending, I'm not sure if there is a value in keeping the temporary resource available, either.

We can eliminate the "completed-upload" problem type altogether if we allow this.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Would you suggest that if an upload resource persists after the upload is complete, it should always resend the final response after completion? Should the server cache the response similar to implementations using idempotency keys to prevent duplicate requests? Or would that just be an implementation detail?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: If the server keeps the upload resource alive, it should replay the final response when processing a 0-length append at the final offset. It doesn't need to process the request again, so I don't think it needs idempotency key since the URL is already uniquely identifying the upload.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: I'm open to that idea but would like to hear what others think as well.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body:
I think caching is an implementation detail. Ultimately, the important thing is that the response is the same. For instance, my server can make the same response based on DB metadata without explicit caching. 

Personally, I don't see a need for an idempotency key either, but I'm unsure if there are any situations where it'd be useful.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
Yes please, I'm in favor of this. The "last response lost" problem has been a recurring issue in the tus protocol and if we can solve it here I would be happy. It seems like the last piece of the puzzle for from my point of view.

I agree with others that there is probably no need for idempotency keys unless anyone else can come up with a reason? Also agree that the exact implementation details (caching or reprocessing) should be left up to the server.

comments.author: awwright
comments.body:
I think the proposal makes sense: Partial uploads should be idempotent, so if the server receives the final segment of the upload—even if it’s zero length—the server should be permitted to re-send the same response.

However, this expands the scope a little bit, and still wouldn't cover all cases where a response might be lost.

First, if recovery of responses is a feature, it's quite a useful one, so I think the introduction text should mention this.

And second, if the document is going to address lost responses, the client can also lose the "upload resumption supported" URL. The server may receive the full request and process it, without the client knowing if any part was received at all.

Solving that problem would require some sort of client-generated request identifier ([Idempotency-Key](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/)); or (if the request content is non-empty) the use of “Expect: 100-continue” to ensure that the server does not commit any changes until the client acknowledges it has received a resumption URL.

Overall, how comprehensive should resumable uploads be in recovering from lost responses?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
I agree that we do not need to solve all cases of lost responses. The draft currently recommends that the temporary resource being kept alive after upload finishes in case the final response is lost, but it's not super useful since there is no way to retrieve the final response, and interacting with the temporary resource always leads to 409.

If we think this is not in scope of the protocol, the server should just invalidate the temporary resource as soon as the upload completes.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body: +1 to supporting retrieval of final response via a zero-byte PATCH with Upload-Complete: ?1. I think this should probably be SHOULD rather than MUST though for server implementors, and they should be free to decide how to implement as long as it's idempotent (e.g. save final response from first "finalization" and replay it, vs re-process the request and achieve the same outcome). It should be expected that the upload resource can still disappear after a period of time.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
After discussing this at the IETF 124, I think we go with this route and make the final, 0-length PATCH request idempotent. It should generate the same response, although the language has to agnostic of any implementation details.

> We can eliminate the "completed-upload" problem type altogether if we allow this.

Yes, but we then might want to have a problem type for when the client sends a PATCH request with Upload-Complete: ?0 after the server already received a PATCH request with Upload-Complete: ?1.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Regarding #3405, I would like to provide a rebuttal to what was brought up at IETF 125. (Unfortunately, I wasn't able to attend the meeting.) The argument was that recovering the final response is out of scope for this protocol, because lost final responses are a problem for all HTTP requests in general, and that could be generalized to a separate protocol rather than being specific to resumable uploads. If such a protocol were to be created, the support provided by resumable uploads would be redundant.

This is a reasonable objection, but I would argue the problem actually is in scope. To me, much of the point of resumable uploads is to create the expectation that an upload can be resumed no matter the unfavorable client, server, or network conditions, and the final response is just another arbitrary part of that. Why should the final response be the only out-of-scope part of a resumable upload's resumability? Either way, I think the tangible real-world benefits of simply allowing an interoperable way to recover that final response outweigh the abstract mismatch in scope some may perceive.

Furthermore, real-world server implementers that benefit significantly from being able to recover final responses will still have to create a custom protocol for handling that, and general resumable upload clients won't be able to take advantage of that feature. In fact, it may end up being simpler for a server that cares about this issue to avoid the resumable upload protocol entirely, since using a custom protocol alone may enable a better-integrated solution.

On a more personal level, the solution suggested here seems to actually simplify my client's implementation, since I believe I can use the same retry logic I use everywhere else for the final append, rather than having to propagate an error instead, which is an unusual edge case. The fact that adding this feature may _simplify_ the client implementation further compels me to think this is the right way. That is, it fits right in with the rest of the protocol's behavior.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I think the protocol already naturally allows the retrieval of the lost response with no extra work on the client-side, but we over-specified error scenarios, accidentally preventing it from working. The way out is to stop defining appending to complete uploads errors, allowing the server the freedom to reject or replay.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Oh, I misunderstood the PR! Didn't notice it added language supporting this feature too. That sounds great then. :)

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Clarify client recovery behavior for 409 Conflict responses
issues.author: danielresnick
issues.body:
This issue is a spin-off from the discussion in #3193 regarding chunk granularity, as suggested by @guoye-zhang.

The core issue is that the current specification is ambiguous about whether clients need to handle a 409 Conflict response. This ambiguity can lead to upload failures in recoverable scenarios, undermining the specs goals.

**Problem**

A fully spec complaint client can receive a 409 Conflict response due to factors outside the client's direct control e.g. a network interruption causing the client and server to become desynchronized regarding the current Upload-Offset (client thinks a PATCH request has failed, but it actually succeeded).

The Concurrency section of the spec discusses this, and RECOMMENDS an approach to avoid ever serving clients 409 Conflict responses (latest request wins; previous requests are cancelled), however this is a non-binding recommendation and is acknowledged to be onerous / potentially impractical for servers to implement. A more realistic approach for large-scale servers to meet the requirements of the Concurrency section would be to use a strongly consistent database to maintain session state (current offset, etc) along with optimistic concurrency control to ensure versioning.

Even a proactive client can't avoid this race condition. Consider a scenario where a client's PATCH request times out locally, but is still in-flight to the server. To recover, the client sends a HEAD request to get the current offset. The server might respond to this HEAD request before it has processed the original, in-flight PATCH. By the time the client acts on that HEAD response and sends a new PATCH, the original one may have finally completed, advancing the server's offset and causing the new PATCH to be correctly rejected with a 409 Conflict.

As confirmed by @guoye-zhang, major client implementations like Apple's NSURLSession today treat all 4xx responses as fatal errors and do not attempt to retry / recover.

If a client gives up on a recoverable 409 Conflict, the protocol fails to deliver on its promise of reliable uploads over unreliable connections.

**Proposed Solution**

The spec should be updated to unambiguously state that a client MUST (or at least SHOULD) treat a 409 Conflict response as a recoverable signal.

The recovery mechanism would be via Upload-Offset in the 409 Conflict response and/or the Offset Retrieval mechanism.

Mandating this recovery logic (or at least strongly recommending it) would ensure that it is baked into foundational libraries, providing robust, out-of-the-box reliability for application developers who may not be aware of this specific failure case.


Keen for feedback from others as I’m not sure to what extent this has been discussed previously.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Today, the draft intends that 409 to be used for the cases where the server is certain that the client is non-compliant. E.g. resumed from a different offset from the preceding offset retrieval. It puts the burden on the server to ensure that a conflict can't occur when talking to a spec-compliant client.

If the server is uncertain that the client is compliant and simply wants it to try resuming an again, maybe a different status code can be used?

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body: We have discussed status codes and conflicts before and while I agree that the current spec idea with closing/ignoring older connections is ideal I do agree with @danielresnick here that there are some cases where some 4xx responses should be retriable, 409 being one and possibly even 412 Precondition failed in some cases. These are kind of oddballs not fitting into the whole "It's the client's fault" and I think they should be excluded from the list of status codes that should cause the client to abandon the upload. The only alternative as I see it is for the server to return a 5xx error on conflict, which is doable but will make it harder to debug what is going on. Just my 2 cents.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body:
> Today, the draft intends that 409 to be used for the cases where the server is certain that the client is non-compliant. E.g. resumed from a different offset from the preceding offset retrieval. It puts the burden on the server to ensure that a conflict can't occur when talking to a spec-compliant client.

Interesting. FWIW I didn't read the spec this way, so maybe the wording needs tweaking if this is the intention?

My core point though is that putting the entire burden on the server to prevent conflicts is unworkable for any large-scale service. The required statefulness (e.g., via exclusive locks or request cancellation) makes the system partition intolerant. During a network partition, such a system would be forced to sacrifice availability to maintain its state guarantees, which is a difficult trade-off for a global / large-scale upload service. As an example, AFAICT, resumeable upload services from both Google and Cloudflare don't offer such guarantees.

I guess it'd be possible to use a different status code but I'm not sure what it'd buy us over 409 Conflict which seems like the intended code for this sort of "state desynchronization" situation. Either way I think we need a mechanism for clients to handle this scenario gracefully and I agree with @smatsson that 5xx is less desirable.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Yeah, the draft may not be super clear on this. It treats state desynchronization as a server bug or a client bug, so does not allow the client to retry.

We could definitely retry 409, but let's think about the scenarios of desynchronization so we can design a retry strategy that works. The issue described in "Concurrency" is especially problematic since for example, the client switches from a high latency cellular network to a fast wifi network and decides to resume the upload over wifi, if the server is not able to discard the in-progress transfer, offset retrieving can keep returning invalid offsets. Currently URLSession performs 3 retries, and if none of them makes any forward progress, it considers the resumable upload failed.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body:
Thanks @guoye-zhang!  Apologies for the slow reply here - lots been going on. 

In your example I agree the server should abort the in-flight (cellular) request as soon as it's aware of the new (wifi) one in order to meet the requirements of the spec around avoiding data corruption, etc. 

I've drafted up a PR to (hopefully) help drive alignment on a path forward here. I've kept out specific retry strategies (backoff, num retries, etc) as I don't see a logical place for it in the spec at the moment, but curious if you think it's worth including.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I'm confused why we'd want to make normative statements about how clients should handle 409 responses in general. What if the server wants to respond to the upload request with a 409 for reasons unrelated to resumable uploads? For example, perhaps the client specified a filename that's already taken, and the server doesn't allow multiple files with the same name. 409 is an appropriate response status code for that situation, and the request should absolutely not be infinitely retried by any generic resumable upload client following the spec's recommendation.

More generally, I don't think recommendations for retrying should be coupled with specific 4xx status codes, or else those codes will run into the same infinite-retry problem. I think this should be coupled with other information instead, such as the presence of an `Upload-Offset` response header in the 4xx response that doesn't match the offset expected by the client. Or perhaps a new header just to specify that the upload should be retried/resumed. The right approach may depend on the semantics of 4xx responses for resumable uploads in general, which is not entirely clear to me (possibly related suggestion: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3226#issuecomment-3990133093).

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: We generally use `Upload-Complete: ?1` to distinguish between the final response and the intermediate responses from the resumable upload protocol.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
@guoye-zhang [Section 4.4.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.1-5) says,

> If the client received a final response with the Upload-Complete: ?0 header field or the header field missing, the next step depends on the status code

after which, the recommendation to retry on 409 is being added. The error may be returned from a different part of the server which isn't aware of resumable upload support, and that would still result in the infinite-retry problem with the header missing. Furthermore, I'm not aware that the draft ever recommends final error responses contain `Upload-Complete: ?1`, though I'm not sure that would be useful anyway for the reason I just mentioned.

(Also, I was not aware of that until you said so. I think it may help to emphasize that in [section 4.1.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#name-completeness), which only states completeness represents whether the request content was fully processed after the client requests the complete upload. I can open a separate issue for that.)

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Yeah, it's a good point that `upload-complete` is confusing. I think of resumable upload as a middleware that can allow a regular upload to be upgraded to a resumable upload. The responses it generates on its own all have `upload-complete: ?0`, and the final response it forwards has `upload-complete: ?1`.

Now how should we treat responses without `upload-complete`? It was brought up that 5xx can be emitted by middleboxes that have no knowledge of the resumable upload protocol, so it should be retried. However, that's not safe for 409 as you mentioned. I think it would overcomplicate the protocol if we have different retry rules per status code. Maybe we should claim that missing `upload-complete` should be treated as ?1. This would align with the request-side as well where missing `upload-complete` means it's a regular complete upload.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body: I think a simpler compromise might be to tweak the proposed retry handling for 409 Conflict in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3319 to narrowly focus on the state desynchronization problem this issue is trying to address. E.g. saying something like: "For a 409 (Conflict) status code, if the Upload-Offset header field is present and differs from the client's expected offset, the client SHOULD attempt to resume the upload using the provided offset. Otherwise, the client SHOULD NOT automatically retry the request."

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: @guoye-zhang I don't think missing `Upload-Complete` should be treated as `?1`, because 5xx errors are likely to omit the header and shouldn't require restarting the upload to retry. The same goes for error 429, to give an example of a 4xx error code with the same property.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
@danielresnick This definitely resolves my concern and was one of the solutions I initially suggested, but why make it specific to 409 responses? Why can't any 4xx status use the `Upload-Offset` header for the same purpose? 413 responses can greatly benefit from that too, for example, and I wouldn't be surprised if there were others.

Another alternative is to recommend retrying when `Upload-Complete: ?0` is present, which would be simpler to implement. Either way, there would be benefit from generalizing it to all 4xx responses.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body:
@GrantGryczan That’s a fair question. I agree that 413 Payload Too Large is an interesting case where an offset could be useful for recovery.

But applying this logic to any 4xx status feels risky because it overrides fundamental HTTP semantics. IMO the status code needs to take precedence.

If we use the presence of Upload-Offset as a blanket signal to retry any 4xx response, clients might end up blindly retrying fatal errors e.g. 400 Bad Request, 401/403, 404 Not Found. In these cases, even if a server (perhaps erroneously) includes an Upload-Offset, the client should absolutely not retry as it indicates something more fundamentally wrong.

If we want to expand beyond 409 Conflict, I think the safer approach is an explicitly allowlisted set of status codes (e.g., 409, maybe 412 Precondition Failed, and 413) where an Upload-Offset mismatch has a defined recovery path in the spec. Curious for your (and others thoughts)

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I see where you're coming from.

If the only problem were overriding fundamental HTTP semantics, I would probably recommend adding normative language _requiring_ that servers do not include retry indication for responses with semantics that don't allow retries.

But your concern regarding possibly erroneous servers makes sense and is harder to address. The downside of allowlisting is that it would complicate client implementations that want to gracefully handle retries, and it isn't automatically future-proof against new status codes that might benefit from this, so old clients might become slightly less interoperable over time. But perhaps that's not a big deal because it's very limited (and it might just be an inherent drawback of building an interoperable protocol on top of HTTP). More opinions would be valuable.

Another alternative (that I initially suggested) was adding a new response header just to explicitly indicate that an error response should be retried, which is less likely to be included erroneously. But in retrospect, that might be redundant (and not really specific to resumable uploads) since arguably status code semantics _are_ the way to communicate that. But resumable uploads are unusual because requests can be partially accepted, so they are "more retriable" than typical HTTP requests. I dunno, doesn't feel right. And there may still be situations where clients would want to retry from responses that omitted that header, making the header seem like not the best generalization.

My overall view is that I wouldn't be upset with allowlisted status codes for client retry logic, contingent on the presence of a resumable upload response header like mismatched `Upload-Offset` and/or `Upload-Complete: ?0`.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I'm wondering if it's easier to stay with the original text: 4xx for non-retriable errors and 5xx for retriable errors. The client logic is simple and unambiguous. The server can still use a 5xx status code for a recoverable conflict.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I think requiring 5xx for retriable requests is semantically incorrect. But after recommending against retrying for 4xx responses, the current text does say "unless the semantics of the response allow or recommend the client to retry the request" in order to account for that, which is fine. The problem is that it doesn't clarify very important conditions under which semantics do allow/recommend a retry, such as the one described in this issue, so servers won't be able to count on most clients retrying for otherwise retriable 4xx responses.

Implementers, including myself, would certainly benefit from having more specific conditions clarified. I wouldn't want to get the retry logic wrong in my client. It seems like a fairly easy thing to get wrong, especially because the current phrasing might make it seem like _all_ 4xx responses should result in a failure, which as this issue justifies, is certainly false. I personally think making client implementations more complex in order to solve this is the better compromise.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
413 and 429 can be returned by intermediaries sitting in front of the resumable upload logic, hence the client should be allowed to continue the upload after taking the necessary adjustments regardless of the presence of any `Upload-*` header field in the response.

I think we should tweak the text so the following is possible:
- 409 + Upload-Complete: ?0 -> resume with new offset
- 409 and no Upload-Complete -> probably want to stop the upload
- 409 and Upload-Complete: ?1 -> upload done; this is your final response
- 413 + Upload-Complete: ?0 or missing -> resume after adjusting content size
- ~~423~~ 429 + Upload-Complete: ?0 or missing -> resume after delay
- 5XX and no Upload-Complete: ?1 -> safe to resume

So, yes, there are a few different conditions and the response handling does not solely depend on Upload-Complete's presence and its value. Resumable uploads may be implemented on different layer on the client and server-side, so we have to consider whatever sits in between them. But that should be doable in the text, even if gets a bit involved. In an ideal world, the decision to retry could only depend on the status code, but that doesn't appear feasible given the current HTTP ecosystem.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Good points! Though I think you meant 429, not 423. I personally would be very happy to see all this made explicit in the draft.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Though I think you meant 429, not 423.

You're right, thanks for correcting me :)

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> - 409 and Upload-Complete: ?1 -> upload done; this is your final response

I don't think this alone can be used to determine that the upload is done. If servers can use `Upload-Complete: ?1` to communicate that the error response relates to the original resource rather than the resumable upload (as per https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-3993667232), clients need a way to distinguish whether this kind of response means the upload failed or the upload succeeded.

You might suggest that the client additionally check that the response's `Upload-Offset` matches the upload length, but that doesn't work if the length is unknown, and even if the length is known, it still doesn't work because the offset can be at the end without the upload succeeding.

Perhaps the fix here is to check the presence of `Upload-Offset`, and add normative language that error responses indicating upload failure MUST NOT include the `Upload-Offset` response header? That also just semantically makes sense, since there is no more upload offset if there is no more upload, after all.

(Furthermore, shouldn't the [paragraph of the draft that requires `Upload-Offset` for the kind of 409 response you were thinking of](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-3) also require `Upload-Complete`, so that this client check works?)

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Actually, I realize that while the additions in my previous comment help, they alone still wouldn't guarantee the ability to immediately distinguish a final 409 response with `Upload-Complete: ?1` and `Upload-Offset` returned from the original resource after the upload is completed successfully from a 409 response due to appending nonempty data after the upload was already completed.

#3270 would allow a means to distinguish this. A client running into a 409 response with both `Upload-Complete: ?1` and `Upload-Offset` will naturally send another empty append in order to retrieve the final response, and if that final response is still a 409, the client can tell it relates to the original resource. Although, an erroneous client might not realize this, and might just interpret it as another offset mismatch response, resulting in infinite retries.

Alternatively, to save a round trip and simplify client logic (and make it less prone to infinite retries), `Upload-Offset` could just be forbidden entirely on error responses with `Upload-Complete: ?1`, with the exception of 409 offset mismatches. I think this would be the ideal solution, because then the client doesn't have to hold in memory which kind of request the response came from.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> wouldn't guarantee the ability to immediately distinguish a final 409 response with `Upload-Complete: ?1` and `Upload-Offset` returned from the original resource after the upload is completed successfully from a 409 response due to appending nonempty data after the upload was already completed.

An alternative would be to not use a 409 in the later situation, but just a regular 400 response, for example. Or we could consider minting an new 4XX response code for mismatching offsets, which would free 409 of that meaning when appending to an upload resource. The benefit would be that the response semantics don't get overloaded through the presence of specific response headers and mostly depend on the status code. The client wouldn't have to check for an Upload-Offset response header field to identify whether the error response belongs to the upload itself or the processing of the representation.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I just realized some great news: thanks to the new `Upload-Complete` response header semantics from #3404, 409 responses due to offset mismatches no longer have any ambiguity! `Upload-Complete: ?0` is required for offset mismatch response regardless of whether the upload has been completed, so the following handling is always correct:

- 409 with `Upload-Complete` false -> attempt upload resumption
- 409 with `Upload-Complete` true or missing -> upload failed

(Side note: That's awesome. A solution nobody thought of, but that naturally popped right out of an improvement to semantics in a tangential area! Super happy about this. Thanks for the improvement, @guoye-zhang! I'm feeling more confident about that change.)

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: That's great to hear. It sounds like we can close this issue then, can't we?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: This issue is more general than that; it's about documenting the ways that clients should handle 409 responses. There's still an open PR for it. It's just that the correct handling is no longer uncertain. :)

issues.title: incremental: remove header when not delivering incrementally
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
Should the draft include a recommendation (or requirement) that intermediaries, which recognize the Incremental header field but won't deliver the message content incrementally, should remove the header field when forwarding the message?

On the one side, this would remove a wrong signal as the content won't be delivered incrementally end-to-end. On the other hand, the removal might not be necessary as intermediaries cannot trust the presence of the header anyways, because of upstream intermediaries that don't recognize the Incremental header field.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Thank you for raising the issue.

As the draft notes in [§4.1](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-incremental.html#name-permanent-rejection) and [§4.2](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-incremental.html#name-temporary-rejection), if an intermediary recognizes Incremental but will not forward the message incrementally, it should reject the request and indicate why via Proxy-Status.

The rationale is that messages that depend on incremental delivery are better served by an explicit failure with a reason than by being implicitly treated as bufferable. The latter typically surfaces as a timeout or other opaque error, with no indication of what went wrong.

For that reason, I believe explicit rejection is preferable to silently amending the effective properties of the request based on how it is delivered.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Thanks for the clarification!

> As the draft notes in [§4.1](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-incremental.html#name-permanent-rejection) and [§4.2](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-incremental.html#name-temporary-rejection), if an intermediary recognizes Incremental but will not forward the message incrementally, it should reject the request and indicate why via Proxy-Status.

That's good to know! I didn't deduce the expectation that intermediaries should reject requests with Incremental: ?1 if they can't fulfil it. On first thought, I do agree that explicit rejection is better in the long term.

Maybe this expectation could be stated more clearly and prominently. For me, the security considerations only lay out how and why intermediaries might reject requests, but not that they have to do so if they cannot deliver incrementally.

issues.title: resumable: Upload-Limit language is ambiguous
issues.author: danielresnick
issues.body:
Spinning off from https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3193#issuecomment-3469842535

The spec as is (draft 10) is unclear on whether clients MUST respect limits a server sends down via a Upload-Limit header.

"The client SHOULD respect any limits (Section 4.1.4) announced in the Upload-Limit header field in interim or final responses" -> implies optional but strongly recommended

"max-append-size: Specifies a maximum size counted in bytes for the request content in a single upload append request (Section 4.4). The server might reject requests exceeding this limit. A client that is aware of this limit MUST NOT send larger upload append requests. The value is an Integer." -> implies clients are required to respect this limit (since why wouldn't they be "aware" of it? It's included in the spec, and clients are guaranteed to have received it in the Upload Creation response if the server sets it).

Overall I'd be keen to make as clear as possible that it's (at least) strongly recommended that clients which intend to be maximally interoperable with a variety of servers respect all known Upload-Limits. 

I'm happy to take a stab at rewording to try to remove this ambiguity if helpful, but lets first align on the desired end state.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Thank you for the feedback! I can understand that this language is not very clear.

> "The client SHOULD respect any limits (Section 4.1.4) announced in the Upload-Limit header field in interim or final responses" -> implies optional but strongly recommended

IIRC, the intention behind SHOULD is that in some cases the client does not know the limit before starting to transfer data. For example, if the upload creation request carries representation data, the client starts sending this data before it receives the limits. Hence it's not able to know what the resources's max-size, min-append-size and max-append-size limits are.

That being said, by the time the first append request is started, the client should have had the opportunity to discover the limits. Either through the upload creation response or a HEAD response.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body: That interpretation sounds reasonable to me though I think @guoye-zhang had a different one (see https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3193#issuecomment-3469526528). @guoye-zhang do you think it's realistic  and not too onerous for clients like UrlSession to support limits after optimistic upload creation?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I think it would be possible to support, but we cannot comment on future plans. I have the feedbacks you filed, and if you have official channels to escalate this through the management chain, it would definitely help us prioritizing the work.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body: Thanks that makes sense, mostly just looking for signal on whether you have strong feelings about what direction the spec goes here as an owner of a key client impl

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Implementing Upload-Limit support will definitely add additional work and complexity, but enabling more interop is more important.

On the topic of interop, maybe we need an explicit signal that the client supports certain limits, e.g. a request header `Upload-Limit-Supported: min-append-size, max-append-size, append-granularity`. The server could be more confident sending a 409 to reject the upload creation and get a compliant append. (We don't need to include it in the current spec to delay it further, but can do it as an experiment for a future extension)

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: I'm not entirely sure how we can make this clearer, but I took a stab at this in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3470. Let me know what you think.

issues.title: query-method: no mention of how to handle query components
issues.author: jeremyfiel
issues.body:
Can you clarify the behavior of a QUERY with query components? 

```http
QUERY /dogs?dog_id=123
content-type: application/json

{"age": 10}
```

Should this query the `dogs` collection for any dog `age: 10` and ignore the query component or should it narrow the search to the dog identifier and then parse the request content and return the result based on if `dog_id: 123` has an equivalent age value?

issues.title: Allow sending SameSite=Lax cookies for certain POST requests
issues.author: cbiesinger
issues.body:
(context: https://github.com/w3c-fedid/FedCM/issues/587)

While SameSite behavior seems to be specified in the [fetch spec](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#cookie-infrastructure) now, I wanted to keep this group updated on this proposal:

For credentialed [FedCM](https://w3c-fedid.github.io/FedCM/) requests (using `Sec-Fetch-Dest: webidentity`), we would like to send SameSite=Lax cookies in addition to SameSite=Strict, including the post-user confirmation POST request.

# Motivation

Currently, many identity providers implement signing in to a website using redirects (from the relying party to the identity provider, and after user confirmation back to the relying party with a signed token).

Because this is using toplevel redirects, these sites can and often do use SameSite=Lax cookies for this purpose. This increases security over SameSite=None because they will not get send for any other cross-site requests such as subresource requests.

However, as currently specified and implemented, this makes it impossible to migrate to FedCM. FedCM provides various desirable privacy properties and a better user experience, so it would be desirable to allow this so that more identity providers can adopt FedCM without lowering their cookie security properties.

# Why this is safe

FedCM requires "opt in" by having [a file](https://w3c-fedid.github.io/FedCM/#idp-api-well-known) at the eTLD+1 at `/.well-known/web-identity` with the correct content.

Requests to this file are made without credentials. If this file does not exist, or does not have the correct content, browsers abort the request and do not send any further credentialed FedCM requests for this flow.

Therefore, the scope of this change is very limited: Only servers who have specifically opted in to FedCM on their eTLD+1 will see any changes to the sent cookies. (and of course, from a caller perspective this only affects requests made due to a navigator.credentials.get() call for an `identity` credential).

By eTLD+1 I specifically mean https://example.tld; https://accounts.example.tld/ is not sufficient, although we do follow redirects for this specific file.

Note: FedCM is currently implemented in Blink (i.e. Chrome/Edge/other derived browsers). Firefox has prototyped an implementation but is not currently pursuing shipping FedCM.

Please share any feedback you may have on this proposal.

comments.author: johannhof
comments.body:
From my perspective I think this is a good idea - it actually improves security in practice by allowing servers to avoid setting their cookies to SameSite=None (making all their endpoints potentially vulnerable to CSRF) to make FedCM work.

It comes with the slight compromise of adding a precedent for extending SameSite=Lax to cover new functionality. While it's safe in this instance, I think we should be very explicit that this is NOT meant as an invitation for others to revisit SameSite rules and that future attempts to change SameSite should be viewed with the same level of scrutiny as before.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
To be clear: you're proposing that `SameSite=Strict` and `SameSite=Lax` cookies for the IdP's server will be sent cross-site during, and only during, a valid FedCM login flow; thus allowing the IdP server to avoid having to store its state in `SameSite=None` cookies?

I agree with Johann, this seems reasonable (even if it does complicate the story of when SameSite cookies get sent).

>  I think we should be very explicit that this is NOT meant as an invitation for others to revisit SameSite rules and that future attempts to change SameSite should be viewed with the same level of scrutiny as before.

I strongly agree

comments.author: cbiesinger
comments.body:
> To be clear: you're proposing that `SameSite=Strict` and `SameSite=Lax` cookies for the IdP's server will be sent cross-site during, and only during, a valid FedCM login flow; thus allowing the IdP server to avoid having to store its state in `SameSite=None` cookies?

Yes that's correct, a better summary than I was able to write!

issues.title: Reversablilty of encoding wrt unencoded-digest
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
During WGLC @martinthomson noted:

> There is one thing that occurred to me reading this, which might be worth noting.  This depends on having codings that produce exactly one sequence of bytes when decoded.
>
> RFC 9110 says that a content coding transforms the content "without losing the identity of its underlying media type and without loss of information".  I can think of any number of codings that would not always transform back into the same sequence of bytes.

This is an astute observation. I think we can capture some high-level consiseration(s) to help implementers understand such cases. Even if the likelihood of a reversible yet non-identical-output encoding is niche today.

comments.body:

issues.title: Formally updating RFC 9530 "Integrity Fields" and "Integrity Preference Fields"?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
A fair while back, @Acconut raised the point that the `Unencoded-Digest` and `Want-Unencoded-Digest` fields are being added into the mix to compliment other fields and that it might make sense to formally update RFC 9530's defintion of "Integrity Fields" and "Integrity Preference Fields" terms to include these two new ones. 

This came up because in the HTTPAPI WG, we're close to done on the [Problem Types for Digest Fields](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-digest-fields-problem-types/02/) doc that imports the "Integrity Fields" and "Integrity Preference Fields" terms. The concepts there will work equally well for the new things. A formal update would help square the circle and ensure people know the general applicability.

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
I agree on updating the list of "Integrity fields", since it's an useful forward-link that allows RFC9530 readers to discover new integrity fields.

Maybe in RFC9530 we could have been a bit more generic (e.g., it seems to me that RFC9110 uses "Representation header fields" without an explicit enumeration https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#section-8.2 ).
Still, I don't know whether adding a new Representation header field requires updating RFC9110.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I can live with how we did things in the past, this isn't some huge extension point and massive applicability. I think we made the right call to be specific in 9530.

issues.author: LPardue

issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
_Comment by @MikeBishop_

2119 keywords can't really be applied to future documents. I presume this really is intended to say "This specification does not define any Parameters; future extensions might do so."

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
For background, the offending text was added to address https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3132 . I don't have an issue with adapting to the proposed text.

Tangentially: From #3132 I was go back over the [notes of IETF 123](https://github.com/httpwg/wg-materials/blob/gh-pages/ietf123/minutes.md) where we discussed that RFC 9530 is missing a similar definition. The outcome of that seems to be to open an errata on that document, which I'll go do.
