issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
_Comment by @MikeBishop_

This document updates RFC9530, but does not seem to include explanatory text about this in the abstract.

issues.title: Section 1, paragraph 4
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
_Comment by @MikeBishop_

~~~ 
     A more complex example involves HTTP Range Requests (Section 14 of [HTTP]), where a client fetches multiple partial representations from
     different origins and "stitches" them back into a whole.
~~~
I don't see anything in that about different origins, only about separate requests for a given resource. If the origins differ, they are not the same resource (from HTTP's perspective).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Good observation about my looseness with the term "origin". I think substituting the example to be across multiple requests is clear enough at a high level, so I'll prep a PR for that.

issues.title: Section 3, paragraph 3
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
_Comment by @MikeBishop_

I assume there was discussion about whether repeating the definition here was worthwhile rather than simply saying it's identically structured?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I wouldn't assume anything here 😄 

In RFC 9530, the Repr-Digest and Content-Digest fields both define themselves individually with very similar text. Having Unencoded-Digest do the same follows the pattern, and avoids a level of indirection. One of the prime use cases for Unencoded-Digest is signature-based integrity and I don't think they care about Repr-Digest, making them go read a different draft might cause more confusion if the reader can't separate header structure from semantics.

We also have the "fun" around the parameters oversight I mentioned over on https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3350#issuecomment-3639632258. We can do better now than we did in RFC 9530, and a reference to that doc with new rules seems like it could also complicate things.

As an author, I think this issue is editorial and that the current text strikes the right balance. Therefore I would propose to close with no action.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: That's fine. Just wanted to make sure the decision had been thought through!

issues.title: Section 3, paragraph 13
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
_Comment by @MikeBishop_

Please reword to be clear that you don't mean the Security Considerations section of the current document. Perhaps "[DIGEST-FIELDS] discusses some of the issues...."

issues.title: Section 4, paragraph 3
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
_Comment by @MikeBishop_

It's difficult to know whether the recipient "ignored" what you sent or considered it but made a different choice. Consider being more precise here, that receiving an Unencoded-Digest which does not conform to the Want-Unencoded-Digest you sent is not (MUST NOT be?) treated as an error.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
So this text was intended to strictly mirror what was in RFC 9530 (coincidentally also in [Section 4](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9530.html#rfc.section.4), para 3. I've just spotted we omitted a sentence and have opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3364 to make it fully consistent. I'm not sure if this addresses your comment (I suspect not though)

For broader context, the whole situation with these preferences was awkward in RFC 9530 since we were obsoleting RFC 3230 but could not find any implementers that could provide input on how to deal with this sort of situation. (Personally, I think the preferences are a waste of time, but the process in 9530 drove us towards feature parity with the old stuff).

I'd really prefer not to deviate from the language in RFC 9530. That has the potential to raise questions on whether there is any actual difference between Want-Unencoded-Digest vs. Want-[Repr|Content]-Digest. 

Propose close with no action (even if I tend to agree with the comment when considered without the above baggage).

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I'm okay with that decision, though I wouldn't be shocked to get a similar comment during IESG review.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I'll also add that our expectation is that digest fields can't really be used in isolation of context - their usage needs to be profiled. HTTP provides the means to pass the stuff around but dealing with expectations, especially around dealing with validation failure, needs to be specified elsewhere. 

We can see what the IESG say on the matter. But I am going to hold a high bar to any proposed changes to deviate from the strategy already standardised in RFC 9530.

issues.title: Section 5, paragraph 2
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
_Comment by @MikeBishop_

This is a subtle distinction; thank you for calling it out. A content-coding is defined to operate "without loss of information", but that doesn't necessarily mean byte-for-byte equivalence.

comments.body:
> RFC6266 suggests that "inline" means "behave as if the Content-Disposition header field wasn't present" which I think is appropriate for this use case

I agree. Furthermore, [RFC 6226 section 4.2](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6266.html#rfc.section.4.2) says the following:

> If the disposition type matches "attachment" (case-insensitively), this indicates that the recipient should prompt the user to save the response locally, rather than process it normally (as per its media type).
> 
> On the other hand, if it matches "inline" (case-insensitively), this implies default processing. Therefore, the disposition type "inline" is only useful when it is augmented with additional parameters, such as the filename (see below).
> 
> Unknown or unhandled disposition types SHOULD be handled by recipients the same way as "attachment" (see also [[RFC2183]](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6266.html#RFC2183), [Section 2.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2183.html#section-2.8)).

In the context of uploads, "prompt the user to save the response" doesn't even make sense, so I don't think we should use the "attachment" disposition type. The user is making the request, not receiving a response they can save. Even if you interpret "user" to mean the server receiving the request, that would be contradictory to calling it a "response", and the server might not even necessarily be performing a "save" on the upload, but rather some in-memory processing.

On the other hand, "inline" merely "implies default processing", which certainly can apply in any context.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: In any case, I think there should be normative language describing which disposition types **MUST** or **SHOULD** be sent by the client, and **MUST** or **SHOULD** be accepted, ignored, or rejected by the server, provided there is a `Content-Disposition` header present. Otherwise, I'd argue interoperability could more easily become a problem. It's apparent that the correct decisions here aren't unambiguous, and we wouldn't want different implementations making different decisions in an incompatible way.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thanks for your input. I think we can definitely include an example for this, but have to be careful around the normative text. Some server applications don't need filename and want to just ignore the header. Likewise, there are client use cases, where no filename exists and the client doesn't want to send one. Considering these, the use and handling of Content-Disposition is rather optional, making hard requirements rather unsuitable.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Yeah, I agree. That's why I said the normative language would only be conditional on "provided there is a `Content-Disposition` header present". But if that's also unsuitable, clear examples would at least be better than nothing.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: I opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3394. Please take a look at it and let me know.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Awesome! Thanks for your work.

issues.title: Max-Age=0
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis#section-4.1.1 --

> Servers conforming to this profile MUST NOT send Set-Cookie header fields that deviate from the following grammar:
[...]
> max-age-av        = "Max-Age" BWS "=" BWS non-zero-digit *DIGIT

This has the effect of disallowing `Max-Age=0`, even though [later](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis#name-the-max-age-attribute-2):

> If delta-seconds is less than or equal to zero (0), let expiry-time be the earliest representable date and time. Otherwise, let the expiry-time be the current date and time plus delta-seconds seconds.

comments.author: mikewest
comments.body:
At first, I thought this was simply a distinction between the server-side requirements and the (more forgiving) client-side requirements. Here, though, I think we really do want to accept `max-age=0` as a way of deleting cookies (see e.g. [this MDN article's recommendation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies#:~:text=To%20immediately%20remove%20a%20cookie%2C%20set%20the%20cookie%20again%20with%20the%20same%20name%2C%20path%2C%20and%20domain%20(if%20specified)%2C%20and%20set%20its%20Expires%20attribute%20to%20a%20date%20in%20the%20past%20or%20its%20Max%2DAge%20attribute%20to%200%20or%20negative.%20This%20instructs%20the%20browser%20to%20delete%20the%20cookie%20right%20away.%20For%20example%3A)).

I think we can drop the `non-zero-digit` definition and use `1*DIGIT` instead in this grammar rule. That seems to better match what clients are doing today.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body: I like this. I'm generally wary of loosening the server syntax but in this case I think this behavior is very useful and something the spec should explicitly allow.

comments.author: mikewest
comments.body: The change in #3376 seems like enough to me. @mnot, do you think more explanation is necessary for the remaining discrepancy between the server-side grammar and the client-side handling for negative numbers?

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Not really.

comments.author: johannhof
comments.body:
It probably makes sense to port this to layered-cookies as well

cc @annevk

issues.title: QUERY: Potential ambiguity in QUERY safety wording
issues.author: tillsc
issues.body:
In `draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body`, the text says:

> "QUERY requests are safe with regard to the target resource ... This does not prevent the server from creating additional HTTP resources ..."

I think the intent is “QUERY is safe per RFC 9110 Section 9.2.1”, and that auxiliary server-side side effects (incl. creating derivative/aux resources) are still compatible with safety.

However, the phrasing “safe with regard to the target resource” could be read as introducing a *relative* notion of safety, and might inadvertently suggest that intended state changes to other resources are compatible with QUERY, as long as the target resource is not changed.

Would you consider tightening the wording to align more directly with RFC 9110 semantics, for example by explicitly stating that QUERY is a safe method as defined by RFC 9110 Section 9.2.1, which already permits such side effects, and that any resource creation described in Sections 2.3/2.4 is an allowed side effect rather than an intended state change?

Happy to propose concrete text if that helps.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
We already cite RFC 9110 in that sequence.

I understand your concern, but the timing is bad. We are post all Last Calls and IESG approval, and the document is already in the publication queue. That makes changes really hard.

comments.author: tillsc
comments.body:
Thanks for the clarification and for the context around timing.

That makes sense. Given the stage of the document, I agree this is not the right moment to pursue wording changes. Happy to close this.

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: Thanks.

issues.title: "## Cookie Header" should be "Cookie Field" or "Cookie Header Field"
issues.author: Jxck
issues.body:
In https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3329, "Header" was added to the "Cookie" section to address some reviewer comments.

Diff: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/commit/07e51519113ed658e7e96b974f2193eca44fcb12#diff-c96f4fab694f25d91c3ae6f4cd68ae735dbcb33dcbb2f4b79a13675b293caa7bL553

Current:
```
4.  Server Requirements
  4.1.  Set-Cookie Header
    4.1.1.  Syntax
    ...
  4.2.  Cookie Header
    4.2.1.  Syntax
    ...
```

As defined in HTTP Semantics [RFC9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-field-names), "Cookie Header" should be explicitly written as "Cookie Header Field". Alternatively, if it's not intended to apply only to headers (but also to trailers), it could be "Cookie Field".

Sections 4.1 and 4.2 cover general syntax and semantics, so using just "Field" seems reasonable:

```
4.  Server Requirements
  4.1.  Set-Cookie Field
    4.1.1.  Syntax
    ...
  4.2.  Cookie Field
    4.2.1.  Syntax
    ...
```

However, this draft only mentions "Cookie/Set-Cookie Header Fields" and does not reference trailers. (I'm not sure if cookies work with trailer fields.)

Using "Header Field" also seems reasonable, but in that case:

```
4.  Server Requirements
  4.1.  Set-Cookie Header Field
    4.1.1.  Syntax
    ...
  4.2.  Cookie Header Field
    4.2.1.  Syntax
    ...
5.  User Agent Requirements
  5.1.  Subcomponent Algorithms
  ...
  5.6.  The Set-Cookie Header Field
  5.7.  Storage Model
  5.8.  Retrieval Model
     5.8.1.  The Cookie Header Field
```

Having the same section titles with or without "The" is a bit confusing to me.

comments.author: johannhof
comments.body: @sbingler are we still making changes to 6265bis?

comments.body: No, but for a very minor change like this we may be able to work it in alongside an editorial change from the review process, if one comes up.

issues.title: [QUESTION] Using multiple dictionaries for a singular resource
issues.author: TheArcaneBrony
issues.body:
I'm not sure if this would make any sense, but could it be possible to support using multiple dictionaries for a single resource?

Concrete example: Say I run an online communication service (ie. a chat service) - It might make sense for me to use a shared (& likely static) dictionary for protocol layer compression, but it might also make sense to use a separate dictionary - which would be gated by access controls - to have a dictionary of very frequently re-occuring data, such as user IDs of members of a private channel, the first few digits of a timestamp, etc

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I'm guessing that this is about compression dictionaries.

I'm also quite sure that [this](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9842) is too late to change in the way you describe.  Work on an alternative or extension is possible if you can demonstrate value, but I suspect that the bar is pretty high.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
It was an intentional design decision to only allow for a single dictionary to be available at a given point in time and for the client to pick the "best" from the ones it has available for a given request at the time the request is made (for a bunch of reasons, but the biggest is to minimize the cache key explosion for server-side caches that can come from `vary: available-dictionary`.

What you're describing, if I understand it correctly, could be handled by having the "separate dictionary" include the protocol-layer patterns as well as the data patterns and use the basic dictionary to compress the more-advanced (and specific) one. The advanced one could be scoped to individual channels/whatever based on URL pattern matching so you could have different advanced dictionaries for different channels.

issues.title: Trailers with "connect-tcp"?
issues.author: bemasc
issues.body:
RFC 9209 specifically calls out some [use cases for Proxy-Status as a trailer](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9209.html#section-2-11).  draft-ietf-connect-tcp says

> In HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, proxies MAY additionally send a "Proxy-Status" trailer in the event of an abrupt stream closure.

However, RFC 9113 (HTTP/2) [says](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#section-8.5-6)

> Frame types other than [DATA](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#DATA) or stream management frames ([RST_STREAM](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#RST_STREAM), [WINDOW_UPDATE](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#WINDOW_UPDATE), and [PRIORITY](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#PRIORITY)) MUST NOT be sent on a connected stream and MUST be treated as a [stream error](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#StreamErrorHandler) ([Section 5.4.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#StreamErrorHandler)) if received.

and RFC 9114 (HTTP/3) [says](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#section-8.5-6)

> Once the CONNECT method has completed, only [DATA](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#frame-data) frames are permitted to be sent on the stream. Extension frames MAY be used if specifically permitted by the definition of the extension. Receipt of any other known frame type MUST be treated as a [connection error](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#errors) of type [H3_FRAME_UNEXPECTED](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#H3_FRAME_UNEXPECTED).


Possible ways forward:
1. Drop this text from connect-tcp.
  - This leaves no way to convey details of why a connection closed uncleanly (e.g. "this proxy instance is shutting down" vs. "connection timeout" vs. "you have exceeded your monthly transfer quota") for debugging.
2. Define a new Capsule to convey shutdown metadata (generally) or Proxy-Status (specifically).
  - Allows HTTP/1.1 support
  - Creates redundancy with trailers and/or Proxy-Status in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.  Adds some complexity when chaining proxies.
3. Interpret ":protocol" values as "extensions" for the purpose of HTTP/3 ("Extension frames MAY be used if specifically permitted by the definition of the extension"), and assume a similar extensibility rule in HTTP/2.  Add text noting that "connect-tcp" permits trailers.
  - Adds complexity to ["HTTP version translation" of the Capsule Protocol](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-kb-capsule-conversion/), if this behavior is only permitted for a subset of Capsule Protocol requests.
4. Allow trailers in all Capsule-Protocol or all Extended-CONNECT responses.
  - Theoretically constitutes a non-backward-compatible change to published RFCs.  (Unclear if this would have any practical consequence.)
  - Probably requires a separate draft.

See also [the mailing list thread](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2026JanMar/0043.html).

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
The Working Group concluded that it would be best to disallow the use of trailers with "connect-tcp".  I have changed this text to say:

> Clients and proxies MUST NOT send trailer fields on "connect-tcp" streams.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Impossible restriction on `max-age`
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body:
@GrantGryczan found a mistake in the draft. The `max-age` limit is defined as:

> Specifies the remaining lifetime of the upload resource in seconds counted from the generation of the response.

Later on we say:

> In particular, whereas the values for `max-size`, `max-append-size`, and `max-age` can increase without harm, they SHOULD NOT decrease as they can cause ongoing uploads to fail.

If `max-age` cannot be decreased, the upload resource would never expire, which is obviously not the desired outcome. The sentence from the last quote stems from a draft version where `max-age` was an absolute timestamp. The restriction made sense back then, because an upload resource shouldn't expire sooner that previously announced or otherwise the client might run into issues. With the value now being a relative duration, the restriction is problematic and has to be rephrased.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Early response handling
issues.author: guoye-zhang
issues.body:
It was brought up in #3275 that `Upload-Complete` in the response might not match the request due to the possibility of early responses.

Should `Upload-Complete` be true in the response if the server wants to terminate an incomplete upload (early response from the original resource)? Or when HTTP is used for bidirectional streaming.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I think this is definitely useful, but needs to be handled carefully. Without this, clients often have no means of distinguishing whether an error response relates to the original resource or the upload resource.

I was actually just about to submit an issue going over how I'd approach specifying the requirements around this. I'll just add it as a comment here instead, once I finish writing it.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I tagged this "discuss" to talk about during IETF 125

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
@guoye-zhang pointed out the following in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-3993667232, in relation to early error responses:

> We generally use `Upload-Complete: ?1` to distinguish between the final response and the intermediate responses from the resumable upload protocol.

If this is the case, it's important to have specific normative language on the usage of headers in early responses. For example, this would allow clients to distinguish between an error response relating to the original resource vs. the upload resource. It would also facilitate clients receiving more information that they can use to reduce round trips when handling errors or deciding whether and how to retry. See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-4000016898 for examples of how clients could use headers to handle error responses.

I'd propose the following, which I'm happy to refine and organize into a PR if desirable (though it'll have to be towards the end of the month).

---

For 4xx responses to creation requests:

- If the request failed because it violated upload limits, then the response SHOULD include `Upload-Limit`.
- If the upload was completed, and no upload resource was created, then the response SHOULD include `Upload-Complete: ?1` and MUST NOT include `Upload-Offset`.
  - Note that servers that don't support resumable uploads won't include `Upload-Complete`. Nevertheless, it helps clients when possible.
  - See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-4010621810 for rationale on "MUST NOT" (in particular simplifying client logic and mitigating erroneous infinite retries).
- If the upload was completed, and an upload resource was created, then the response MUST include `Upload-Complete: ?1` and MUST NOT include `Upload-Offset`.
  - This can be a hard requirement since successful upload resource completion necessarily implies the part of the server generating this response is aware of resumable uploads. Note that append responses already require this ([section 4.4.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-6)).
  - Same as previous rationale for "MUST NOT".
- If the upload was not completed, and no upload resource was created, then the response SHOULD include `Upload-Complete: ?1` and MUST NOT include `Upload-Offset`.
  - See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-4006617617 for (different) rationale on "MUST NOT".
- If the upload was not completed, and an upload resource was created and not deactivated, then the response SHOULD include `Upload-Complete: ?0` and SHOULD include `Upload-Offset`.
- If the upload was not completed, and an upload resource was created and deactivated, then the response MUST include `Upload-Complete: ?1` and MUST NOT include `Upload-Offset`.
  - This can be a hard requirement since upload resource deactivation necessarily implies the part of the server generating this response is aware of resumable uploads.
  - Same as previous rationale for "MUST NOT".

For 4xx responses to append requests:

- If the request failed because it violated upload limits, then the response SHOULD include `Upload-Limit`.
- If the upload was completed, then the response MUST include `Upload-Complete: ?1` and, unless it's a 409 offset mismatch response, MUST NOT include `Upload-Offset`.
  - The "MUST include" is already a requirement from [section 4.4.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-6).
  - See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-4010621810 for rationale on "MUST NOT".
- If the upload was not completed, and the upload resource is still activated, then the response SHOULD include `Upload-Complete: ?0` and SHOULD include `Upload-Offset`.
- If the upload was not completed, and the upload resource was deactivated, then the response MUST include `Upload-Complete: ?1` and, unless it's a 409 offset mismatch response, MUST NOT include `Upload-Offset`.
  - Same rationales as the last point under creation responses.
  - "it's a 409 mismatch response" might not be possible here, but I'm including it for clarity just in case.

Despite the verbosity of all of the above, I expect the implementation to be very simple, since it mostly boils down to just including whatever information the server has on the upload in the response. I also wouldn't be surprised if some statements can be consolidated.

5xx responses are exceptionally likely to be returned from a part of the server unaware of resumable uploads, even as a result of internal errors arising directly from resumable uploads, so they should follow the same as all of the above, but with each "MUST include" treated as "SHOULD include". Note that this (intentionally) loosens the current [section 4.4.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-6) requirement, which I'd argue isn't realistic for 5xx responses.

The current draft already covers 2xx responses well enough. Phrasing just needs to be expanded to allow them to be returned before the client marks the upload as completed.

I think all early 1xx responses can just be transparently passed on with no changes, since clients can easily distinguish an early 1xx response by whether it's 104. The spec probably just needs to clarify 1xx responses are allowed.

I believe early 3xx responses don't make sense, since semantically, that would tell the client to restart or continue the upload at the new location, which is already what non-early 3xx responses do. So I don't think anything needs to be added for 3xx.

---

The reason to use "SHOULD"s rather than "MUST"s is that in those situations, unfortunately, responses may be returned from a part of the server which isn't aware of resumable uploads. The draft already covers some situations where the server is certainly aware of resumable uploads in an error response, such as [here](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-3) and [here](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-6), and those do use "MUST" rather than "SHOULD" as expected. It may be useful to rephrase things to avoid server implementers interpreting these "SHOULD"s for error responses in general as conflicting with the "MUST" for the specific kind of 409 response described in [section 4.4.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.2-3).

The reason to use "SHOULD"s rather than "MAY"s (and, where possible, "MUST"s rather than "SHOULD"s) is simply that more information is better for clients, and arguably, clients are going to need all the information they can get. (See the last paragraph of this comment for more on that.)

Other more trivial changes would likely be necessary to support early responses, such as in [section 4.1.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#name-completeness) on completeness, allowing servers to mark an upload as complete before the client does. This may require distinguishing between "fully complete" and "early complete", or something like that. Not sure.

Lastly, it's equally important to get the specifics right on how clients should handle these responses. Unfortunately, I don't see any possible way to allow clients to certainly distinguish, in every situation, whether the response is related to the resumable upload itself or the processing of the upload representation. As far as I know, the most we can do is recommend servers give the client as much information as possible (as I outlined above). I'd elaborate on best-effort heuristics that I think would be wise to recommend, but I'm out of time for now. Perhaps another time, but https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-4000016898 is a good starting point.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Thank you for the detailed response, @GrantGryczan! Overall, an approach that doesn't use the presence of the Upload-Offset header field to determine the response semantics would be preferable. Otherwise the semantics depend on the status code, Upload-Complete and Upload-Offset header fields. If I understand correctly, the distinction is only necessary for status codes that have a special meaning in the upload process itself, but I believe there are other alternatives as well for handling these (see https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-4085702924).

When starting an upload, the client's next step in the case of a 4XX also depends on whether the client knows that the resource supports resumable uploads. If so, any response missing Upload-Complete can be interpreted as a failure of the upload process itself. Depending on the resource, it might be safe to just retry, but that is application-specific. If the client optimistically upgrades an upload to resumable, such a response would have to be counted as the final response for the upload.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: I agree that the reliance on a response header isn't ideal! I thought of using a new 4xx code, but I dismissed the idea because I'm not sure how feasible that is. I had the feeling that 4xx codes are scarce. But if not, I think that would be an excellent solution to have more well-defined semantics, simplify implementations, and loosen unintuitive requirements.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Defining new status codes has a very high bar. It not necessarily about scaracity but the impact they have to HTTP.

We should attempt to resolve this using other means such as headers etc

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> We should attempt to resolve this using other means such as headers etc

@LPardue Never mind, no need! See https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3275#issuecomment-4527570486.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Servers should be required to allow empty upload creation requests
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
In order to support clients that can't handle interim responses (e.g., browser JS clients), the draft allows clients to submit an upload creation request with `Upload-Complete: ?0` and no content. But because of a server's upload limits, this request may be rejected, and the client can't do anything to reliably obtain an upload resource URI.

I propose that servers MUST NOT enforce the ~~`min-size` and~~ `min-append-size` upload limits for empty upload creation requests.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I think it would be easier if the min-size was defined with a clear relationship to the Upload-Length request header.

That way, a client can learn the limits (if any) and create an upload resource that is compatible. An upload creation request does not need to send content to satisfy that. 

For example, if the client uses an OPTIONS request to learn a limit of min-size value of 100 and then sends a creation request with Upload-Length: 100 and Content-Length: 0. Thats ok. 
If the client sends Upload-Length: 50 and Content-Length: 0, that's not OK.

Levying the proposed MUST NOT on the server severely affects its abilities. I suspect it would be ignored by implementations.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
@LPardue My bad, this isn't about the upload length. I made a mistake by mentioning `min-size`, because that wouldn't be enforced in an empty, incomplete upload creation request anyway, assuming the `Upload-Length` isn't outside the limit. I'm only talking about `min-append-size` here.

I'm not concerned about the client being able to learn the limits and comply with them; I'm concerned about the client being able to reliably obtain the upload resource URI. If a client that can't read 104 responses starts an upload that's interrupted, it can't do anything to resume it.

The best workaround for this would be to send an `OPTIONS` request to get the `min-append-size`, and then send a single upload request with just that much data before sending the rest of the upload in a separate request. That's minimum 3 round trips for every upload above the `min-append-size` (unless the client wants to risk being unable to resume the upload, which largely defeats the point of the protocol).

I'm pretty sure TUS already has this requirement, and in fact, transferring upload data in the first request is an optional extension, so I don't think this would be burdensome for server implementers.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
min-append-size is currntly defined as

> Specifies a minimum size counted in bytes for the request content in a single upload append ([Section 4.4](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#upload-appending)) or upload creation ([Section 4.2](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#upload-creation)) request.

I can't recall the reason why this is claimed as being applicable to the upload creation. It might just be a copy/paste mistake. Removing that requirement seems natural to me. We just dont need to state it in MUST NOT terms

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Well, the limit should definitely apply when the upload creation request is nonempty ~~or complete~~.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The definition also states

> Requests completing the upload by including the Upload-Complete: ?1 header field are exempt from this limit.

What if that were rephrase to

> There are cases exempt from this limit: when a request creation has no content and includes an Upload-Complete: ?0, or when a request completes an upload by including Upload-Complete: ?1

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
That could work! Though I personally went for a "MUST NOT" to emphasize that not doing this should be strictly considered a violation of the protocol. Although, I would say the same for the existing exempt case for a final append. The difference in semantics is not clear to me.

Let's make sure there isn't some practical issue with this requirement that I didn't consider though, and wait for other opinions. I find it odd that this property of TUS wasn't already carried over, so that could be intentional.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Cool, I thibk we are aligned on the spirit of the issue then. Lets see if others are.

One of the lesser well understood aspects of IETF documents is that text is normative even without the use of BCP keywords. Non-nornative text, examples etc tend to be called out explicitly

While it can seem to read clearer to use very explicit language, it can be difficult to articulate all of the possible scenarios, current or future.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Oh, I also just realized that "and includes an Upload-Complete: ?0" doesn't need to be specified, because if it doesn't include that (i.e., the upload is to be completed), it's exempt from the `min-append-size` anyway.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thanks for bringing this up, @GrantGryczan! I agree that the `min-append-size` limit shouldn't be enforced for empty upload creations. The text proposed by Lucas seems like a good starting point for this. I don't think we have to use explicit MUSTs here. The exemption from this limit if `Upload-Complete: ?1` is set also doesn't use MUST and doesn't seem to have caused confusion or interoperability issues, even though it's an important piece to make sure uploads work.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body: I agree, removing the `min‑append‑size` requirement for empty creation requests makes sense and aligns with how clients behave in practice.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: Oops, this was an oversight on my part. I was mainly thinking about `max-append-size` and figured `min-append-size` should be consistent with it. Preventing empty requests definitely wasn't the intent.

issues.title: Unencoded-Digest: Unable to reproduce example
issues.author: Acconut

issues.title: Scope of semantics
issues.author: mnot
issues.body: The initial draft suggests 'Preliminary Request Denied', which is fairly specific. In subsequent discussion, a broader semantic, such as 'Purpose Declined' was suggested.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
My 2c:

Maybe its just me but I really struggle with the word preliminary. The draft since conception has had to define what a "premilinary request" is and the only thing it used to do so was to tie it to Sec-Purpose via `A preliminary request is one that contains a Sec-Purpose header field [FETCH] with the value "prefetch".`.  

While the term preliminary is general, if its tied so closely only to Sec-Purpose: prefetch, the scope remains the same. Is the issue here about the shaking out whether we want to support request of other similar nature?

Part of what I struggled with is that the word `preliminary` implies the thing wasn't full, final, or conclusive. My undersstanding is that a prefetch is not an attempt to get a partial or minimal view of a resource, its an attempt by a client to get the thing and use it at a time, for a purpose it believes is "good" but the server disagrees at that moment.

One reason a server might reject a prefetch or preload is because its too early in the timeline. Sad that we already have [425 Too Early](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc8470.html#rfc.section.5.2) for an entirely different case 😄 

I recall a little while back talking to folks about [Fetch metadata](https://www.w3.org/TR/fetch-metadata/), expanding scope to accomodate those things seems like expanding the scope too far.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
One reason to deny a prefetch is that the serving of the content might have side-effects (consider the display of ads as an example, which often involves payment or at least the recording of an impression).  So the use case is fine.  And 400 series is right.

The question about scope is the hard one.  "Purpose Declined" is a reasonable thing to expand it to, though it might not be expanding it at all unless there are other purposes that are eventually defined.

I wonder whether this couldn't be expanded to include `Sec-Fetch-Dest` as well, perhaps even `Sec-Fetch-Mode`.  The idea here is that the context into which the response will be placed is not compatible with the expectations of the server.

issues.title: Status Code
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
A specific status code needs to be selected.

The initial draft suggests one in the 4xx range. That seems to be appropriate given the semantics desired (whether broad or narrow; see #3409). 

If that holds, we should select a code that is unregistered and relatively unused.

The next unassigned 4xx status code is 419. No use is documented in MDN or wikipedia, but I see a few resources that mention a single PHP framework is squatting on it to indicate that a session token is expired.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Nit: Update or remove draft references
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11 contains the following text

> For interoperability testing of this draft version, implementations SHALL use the value "connect-tcp-07".

> For this draft version of the protocol, the Capsule Type values 0x2028d7f0 and 0x2028d7f1 shall be used provisionally for testing, under the names "DATA-08" and "FINAL_DATA-08".

We should probably update/remove these.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Clarify "in-stream metadata" and extensibility via capsules
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
Section 1.2 cites as a problem:

> Classic HTTP CONNECT requests cannot carry in-stream metadata. For example, the WRAP_UP capsule [[I-D.schinazi-httpbis-wrap-up](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#I-D.schinazi-httpbis-wrap-up)] cannot be used with Classic HTTP CONNECT.

We then define DATA and FINAL_DATA capsules, each of which _also_ cannot carry in-stream metadata. That's fine, since you can interleave other capsules, but as far as I can tell, that's mostly just hinted at in the document (e.g. references to other capsules between DATA capsules). 

Perhaps we should have a brief mention that future metadata should be conveyed by extending with additional capsules per RFC 9297, just to make that extensibility pathway clear.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] How do 100 Continue and optimistic data interact?
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
I very much like the ability to send data optimistically. However, it doesn't seem super clear how that's expected to interact with `Expect: 100-continue`.

What happens if I'm using H2 or H3, I send optimistic data that fits within flow control limits, and I also send `Expect: 100-continue`? 

> This specification supports the "Expect: 100-continue" request header ([[RFC9110](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC9110)], [Section 10.1.1](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-10.1.1)) in any HTTP version. The "100 (Continue)" status code confirms receipt of a request at the proxy without waiting for the proxy-destination TCP handshake to succeed or fail. This might be particularly helpful when the destination host is not responding, as TCP handshakes can hang for several minutes before failing. Clients MAY send "Expect: 100-continue", and proxies MUST respect it by returning "100 (Continue)" if the request is not immediately rejected.

If I'm already sending optimistic data, there's not a lot of point in sending something that signals that I'm waiting before sending content.

Should we say that clients SHOULD NOT combine both? Define the flow of events for when both are combined?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I think the flow is well-defined, and using them together might be unusual but not unreasonable.  I can add a sentence clarifying that, maybe:

> A 100 (Continue) response could be useful to let the client estimate network path delays, initiate optimistic payload data with less risk of wasted effort, or provide a clearer status indication while waiting for the destination host to respond.

comments.author: ekinnear
comments.body:
> initiate optimistic payload data with less risk of wasted effort

Are you thinking of a use case where I first wait for 100 (Continue) and then start sending my optimistic data?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: Yes

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Are proxies expected to allow the default template URI?
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
We define a default template URI and say that clients SHOULD fall back to it: 

> If the client infers that classic HTTP CONNECT is not supported, it SHOULD retry the request using the registered default template for "connect-tcp":

And [RFC 9298 Section 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9298.html#section-2) says:
> UDP proxy deployments SHOULD offer service at this location if they need to interoperate with such clients.

Should we state something similar in this document that "deployments SHOULD offer service at the default template URI", just for completeness?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I don't think we should make a recommendation like that.

For RFC 9298, using the .well-known/ template is required for interoperability with an anticipated class of potential clients (clients that start with a domain for Classic CONNECT, and want to discover CONNECT-UDP).  For this draft, using .well-known is not required for compatibility with any anticipated class of clients, because any clients that are bootstrapping from a bare hostname are expected to try Classic CONNECT first.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: I think it's OK to not recommend this with a SHOULD; I'd be OK to close this without a change (speaking as individual)

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: OK, closing.  See #3435 for some related adjustments.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] When is it okay to use Proxy-Status?
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
We say: 
> Proxies implementing this specification SHOULD include a "Proxy-Status" response header field [[RFC9209](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC9209)] in any success or failure response (i.e., status codes 101, 2XX, 4XX, or 5XX) to support advanced client behaviors and diagnostics. Clients and proxies MUST NOT send trailer fields on "connect-tcp" streams.

Just out of curiosity, what about 100 Continue? Or 3xx responses?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
RFC 9209 doesn't address the applicability of Proxy-Status to 100 or 3xx responses, so I'm inclined to remain silent on that question here as well.

In my personal view:

* 3xx means "this endpoint isn't your proxy", so Proxy-Status is not applicable
* 100 means "all good but proxying hasn't started yet", so there's nothing to say about proxying yet.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: I think we can be silent as well; I don't see it applying to 100 or 3xx well, and this document is probably not the place to define it.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Mention Happy Eyeballs?
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
Given that Happy Eyeballs (existing versions as well) provides real benefits, but also introduces some interesting caveats surrounding handling of optimistic data, should we have some mention here that helps explain what to do with any optimistic data?

Perhaps something like: 
> When target_host resolves to multiple addresses, proxies SHOULD use an algorithm such as Happy Eyeballs [RFC8305] to minimize connection latency. Proxies that race multiple connection attempts MUST buffer any optimistic content until a connection succeeds and discard such content for any failed or unused attempts.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Nit: Normative and informative reference for CONNECT-UDP
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body: The document references RFC9298 both normatively and informatively, perhaps worth consolidating?

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Editorial: Explain Proxy Authentication reasoning
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
We've discussed using/not using `Proxy Authentication Required`, but not a lot of that reasoning made it into the document. Would it be worth including something in the document to explain?

Current text:
> A templated TCP proxy does not use the "407 (Proxy Authentication Required)" response code and related header fields ([[RFC9110](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC9110)], [Section 11.7](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-11.7)) because they do not traverse HTTP gateways (see [Section 7](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#operational-considerations)).

Perhaps we could add something like:
> Unlike a classic HTTP CONNECT proxy, which is identified only by a host and port, a template-driven proxy is an ordinary HTTP origin resource identified by a URI. Accordingly, authentication follows the standard HTTP origin authentication model rather than the proxy authentication model.

To help implementors understand the design a bit more than "do not traverse HTTP gateways"?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: I'm open to providing more rationale here, but I'm not sure that Extended CONNECT or Upgrade targets are "ordinary HTTP origin resources".

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I can't think of anything else to say here.  In my view:

* 407, Proxy-Authorization et. al. were invented to disambiguate them from the end-to-end authentication headers, when using an HTTP Request Proxy (which mixes all these header fields together).
* When HTTP CONNECT was introduced, either 401 or 407 (etc.) could have been used, but the 407 style was used for consistency with request proxies.
* "connect-tcp" could have used either style, and we considered both, but we settled on 401 because it reduces the amount of work needed to set up a gateway for "connect-tcp".

I don't think the existence of a URI or resource corresponding to the "connect-tcp" request is especially a determining factor here.

I guess one additional possible argument for using 401 (etc.) is that it allows "connect-tcp" to traverse an authenticated forward request proxy ... but this seems like a bit of a stretch.

Assigning to @ekinnear for any additional thoughts on what needs improvement in this text.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @ekinnear anything more, or should we try to close?

comments.author: ekinnear
comments.body:
Yeah, I was thinking something more than "because they do not traverse HTTP gateways" could help to explain why this thing that one might, at face-value, think was a proxy, doesn't do the regular proxy thing. 

We don't have to go super far towards calling them "ordinary resources", just wanted something that made it clear this was intentional and helped the reader reason about it.

Not a huge deal.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Graceful vs. abrupt closure for HTTP/1.1
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
We define a per-version set of behaviors for graceful vs. abrupt TCP closure handling (previously discussed in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3000): 

> When a TCP connection reaches the TIME-WAIT or CLOSED state, the associated endpoint MUST close its send stream.

> If the connection closed gracefully, the endpoint MUST close the send stream gracefully.
> Otherwise, the endpoint SHOULD close the send stream abruptly, using a mechanism appropriate to the HTTP version:

> HTTP/3: reset the stream with H3_CONNECT_ERROR; see [[RFC9000](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC9000)], [Section 19.4](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000#section-19.4) and [[RFC9114](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC9114)], [Section 8.1](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114#section-8.1)
HTTP/2: reset the stream with CONNECT_ERROR; see [[RFC9113](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC9113)], Sections 6.4 and 7
HTTP/1.1 over TLS: TCP shutdown without a TLS closure alert; see [[RFC8446](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC8446)], [Section 6.1](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446#section-6.1).
HTTP/1.1 without TLS: TCP RST

But then we also say: 
> The graceful and abrupt closure signals ([Section 3.4](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#closing-connections)) are more likely to be missing or corrupted:

> Some implementations may be unable to emit the recommended abrupt closure signals, due to limitations in their TCP and TLS subsystems.

> Faulty implementations may fail to send a TLS closure alert during graceful shutdown, or fail to report an error when the expected closure alert is not received. These misbehaviors are not compliant with [[RFC8446](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#RFC8446)], but they are common nonetheless among HTTP/1.1 implementations today.

If I get one of these signals via HTTP/1.1, how do I know what the endpoint on the other end is actually doing? 

Should we: 
1. Leave as-is.
2. Just say that HTTP/1.1 can't reliably propagate this distinction, instead of saying "here's how it works, but also it might not work".
3. Maybe make FINAL_DATA the primary signal for HTTP/1.1? If you get FINAL_DATA then it's a graceful closure, regardless of if you got a TLS alert. If you don't get FINAL_DATA, then treat it as an abrupt closure, regardless of other layers.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I would prefer to leave this as-is.  This is all SHOULD-strength stuff, and none of it is even visible via ordinary TCP APIs.

The main value I see is for deployments like
```
Client <-----> Gateway <-------> Proxy <-----> Destination
        HTTP/2          HTTP/1.1         TCP
```
The Gateway and Proxy, which may represent a single operator or a close commercial relatinoship, have a defined protocol that they can choose to implement in order to preserve this signal.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @ekinnear thoughts?

comments.author: ekinnear
comments.body: We could adjust editorial text to help explain what's actually available, but I don't feel strongly -- would be okay to leave as-is.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Capsule forwarding and intermediaries
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
[RFC 9297 Section 3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9297.html#section-3.2) says: 
> Because new protocols or extensions might define new Capsule Types, intermediaries that wish to allow for future extensibility SHOULD forward Capsules without modification unless the definition of the Capsule Type in use specifies additional intermediary processing. One such Capsule Type is the DATAGRAM Capsule; see [Section 3.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9297.html#datagram-capsule). In particular, intermediaries SHOULD forward Capsules with an unknown Capsule Type without modification.

This document says: 
> An intermediary MAY merge and split successive DATA and FINAL_DATA capsules, subject to the following requirements:
> - There are no intervening capsules of other types.
> - The order of payload content is preserved.
> - The final emitted capsule uses the same capsule type (DATA or FINAL_DATA) as the final input capsule, and all others use the DATA capsule type.

So we're defining "additional intermediary processing", but would it be worth adding a little bit of text to make it clear that applies in the context of just `connect-tcp` and not anyone who might reuse DATA and FINAL_DATA for other reasons? 

Perhaps: 
> Intermediaries that forward capsules per [RFC9297] Section 3.2 without implementing the “connect-tcp” protocol MUST forward DATA and FINAL_DATA capsules without modification.

Or did we intend for that to be something intermediaries can do any time they see DATA or FINAL_DATA capsules?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: Capsules are generally defined independently of the :protocol.  So yes, this is a general property of DATA/FINAL_DATA, for any :protocol that uses them.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: @ekinnear Does this answer your question, or do you think we need more text to emphasize that the capsule definition is :protocol-independent?

comments.author: ekinnear
comments.body: Thanks, I think that answers it. So we're saying that DATA and FINAL_DATA are always mergable and splittable, and if an intermediary doesn't understand it then it should be forwarding it unmodified by default anyway.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Nit: DATA and FINAL_DATA names
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
Similar to https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3420, thought I'd ask about names if we're making it clear that the `DATA` and `FINAL_DATA` capsules represent TCP stream data that can be combined and split. 

Would it make sense to name them: 
- `TCP_DATA` and `TCP_FINAL_DATA`
- `STREAM_DATA` and `FINAL_STREAM_DATA` / `STREAM_FINAL_DATA`

The latter seems nicer if we're saying that merging and splitting is a generic property of any stream, not just TCP. The former seems nicer if we're saying that merging and splitting can be done only in the context of `connect-tcp`.

This would also help to distinguish them from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 `DATA` frames that they are carried within.

If we keep the existing names, can we add an editorial note for implementors that they should not confuse them with the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 frames of the same name?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
In the current text, these capsules are intended to be reusable for future stream-like use cases, so that would rule out `TCP_DATA`.

Currently, we have a capsule called `DATAGRAM` that is meant to be equivalent to an HTTP/3 Datagram, so using `DATA` for the capsule that is like a `DATA` frame seemed natural, but I am not wedded to the name.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Anyone else have feedback here, or more from @ekinnear ? Warning: potential bike shed...

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: Speaking personally (no hats on) I prefer the current names of `DATA` and `FINAL_DATA` to mirror `DATAGRAM`, instead of anything with `TCP` in the name. I could see some value in calling them `STREAM_DATA` and `FINAL_STREAM_DATA` to be very clear, but I don't have any strong opinion there.

comments.author: ekinnear
comments.body:
Yeah, I have a slight preference for `STREAM_DATA` and `FINAL_STREAM_DATA` (especially given that they can be merged and split), but I have a very strong preference for avoiding the bikeshed entirely. `DATA` and `FINAL_DATA` are good enough.

> If we keep the existing names, can we add an editorial note for implementors that they should not confuse them with the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 frames of the same name?

If we do rev the doc, this would be nice-to-have, but doesn't seem like a blocker.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
In my view the distinction from HTTP DATA frames is already emphasized sufficiently in this sentence:

> The boundaries between DATA and FINAL_DATA capsules are not significant, and are not expected to match TCP segments, TLS records, HTTP DATA frames, QUIC STREAM frames, etc.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: FWIW I also prefer DATA and FINAL_DATA

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Edge cases for FINAL_DATA
issues.author: ekinnear
issues.body:
A few (potentially editorial) questions about FINAL_DATA that might be worth clarifying in the document text: 

1. What happens if I get duplicate FINAL_DATA. We say: 

> After sending a FINAL_DATA capsule, an endpoint MUST NOT send any more DATA or FINAL_DATA capsules on this data stream. (See [Section 3.4](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-11.html#closing-connections) for related requirements.)

But there is nothing that says what to do as a receiver if you receive a second FINAL_DATA. Is that an error? Do you ignore it?

2. HTTP stream FIN, but no FINAL_DATA. We say: 

> When the receive stream is closed abruptly or without a FINAL_DATA capsule received, the endpoint SHOULD send a TCP RST if the TCP subsystem permits it.

Given that this potentially means data is truncated, should we upgrade this to a "MUST, if", rather than a "SHOULD, if"? It'd be nice if this signal were as likely as possible to propagate.

3. FINAL_DATA, but no HTTP stream closure. 

We say that an endpoint "MUST close its send stream", but what do I do as a receiver if I get FINAL_DATA but the HTTP stream stays open? Should I have a timeout? Is that an error? Do I just ignore it and decide the other endpoint is taking up some of its stream flow control credit, so it probably shouldn't do that, but it's fine if it does (I like this last one, personally)?

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
For point 2, I think SHOULD is preferable. RST is not always easy to produce and most frameworks will probably not expose this possibility at all. Also "closed abruptly" corresponds to the detection of a null read() before FINAL_DATA, and sending just a FIN will reproduce exactly that. Finally, sending an RST will result in truncation of bytes already sent down the send path which in certain circumstances might not necessarily be desirable, and some implementations might prefer to stick to a regular FIN instead.

Same question as you regarding points 1 and 3 however.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
On 1: IMHO, as a general rule, if party A detects that party B has violated a mandatory requirement, party A is permitted to abort and report unless there is an explicit prohibition.

On 3: I wouldn't want to complicate the state machine by addressing this explicitly.  It's certainly weird, and I can imagine that production implementations might well have some kind of idle timeout, but that's also true at every other stage of the connection.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: @ekinnear @wtarreau Are your questions answered?  Do you think we need additional text in the draft?

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body: Thanks Ben for the ping. I'm actually re-reading the draft to see if I can spot anything.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: @wtarreau Did you reach any conclusion about this after your review?

comments.author: ekinnear
comments.body:
> party A is permitted to abort and report unless there is an explicit prohibition.

We've often been saying "party A is *required* to abort" for these.

> RST is not always easy to produce and most frameworks will probably not expose this possibility at all.

I think that's fair, it's not necessarily a requirement that everyone can fulfill, and having the RST there instead of a FIN may not always be the best answer anyway.

> I wouldn't want to complicate the state machine by addressing this explicitly. It's certainly weird, and I can imagine that production implementations might well have some kind of idle timeout, but that's also true at every other stage of the connection.

Isn't the state machine already complicated by reality here? Why does having the document not address it help anything be less surprising or less complicated for implementers? I was thinking about this especially since it seemed a bit rapid-reset adjacent.

comments.author: ekinnear
comments.body:
Trying to come up with some concrete suggested text, for (1) perhaps something like: 

  > An endpoint that receives a DATA or FINAL_DATA capsule after a FINAL_DATA
  > capsule on the same data stream MUST treat this as an error on that stream.
  > Because the endpoint has already sent a TCP FIN toward its destination, 
  > it cannot forward the additional payload, and it therefore MUST abort the 
  > stream using an abrupt closure mechanism appropriate to the HTTP version
  > (Section 3.4). It SHOULD also send a TCP RST toward the destination if able.

And for (3), how about: 

In 3.4: 

  > Note: A FINAL_DATA capsule closes only the sending endpoint's direction of
  > the data stream, analogous to a TCP half-close, so the receiving endpoint
  > can continue to use the stream sending data in the opposite direction.
  > If an endpoint sends FINAL_DATA but leaves the underlying stream open
  > in the same direction, the receiving endpoint MUST ensure that stream is
  > subject to idle-timeouts or other resource management strategies (see Section 6.1).

And then in 6.1: 

  > - Idle Stream Resource Growth: A malicious client can signal that a proxied
  >   connection is finished, for example by sending FINAL_DATA, while
  >   deliberately holding the CONNECT stream open. This ties up stream state
  >   and proxy buffers at little cost to the attacker and can evade limits that only
  >   account for streams with active data flow.
  >   - Mitigation: Ensure there is an idle timeout for streams with no active 
  >     data flow and count half-closed or otherwise drained streams against the
  >     per-client concurrency limits described above.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I've posted #3480 and #3481 to capture your first two points.  On point 3, let me see if I understand the attack.

Here's how I understand the attack scenario:
1. Client->Proxy: FINAL_DATA("foo")
2. Proxy->Dest: "foo",FIN.  Proxy is in FIN-WAIT-1
3. Dest->Proxy: FINACK,"bar",FIN.
4. Proxy->Dest: FINACK.
5. Proxy->Client: FINAL_DATA("bar")
6. Proxy is in TIME-WAIT.  Buffers are deallocated but the kernel reserves the 5-tuple for up to 4 minutes.
7. Client holds the request open indefinitely.  Client and proxy both have HTTP state, and neither has TCP state.

The interesting point here is step 4.  The proxy has sent FINACK, even though it isn't sure that "bar" will be received.  Ideally, the FINACK would be withheld until the client closes the request cleanly.  However, in POSIX APIs it is probably impossible for an application to delay the FINACK in this way.

If we remove step 4 (an ideal proxy that withholds FINACK), then the proxy is stuck in FIN-WAIT-2 instead of TIME-WAIT.  This also wouldn't really require holding any buffers open AFAICS.

Either way, I think the resource usage is captured by the existing "WAIT-Abuse" attack, so I don't think we need "Idle Stream Resource Growth".

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
> [@wtarreau](https://github.com/wtarreau) Did you reach any conclusion about this after your review?

sorry @bemasc, I've been dragged away from it, I'll restart with the rest of the conversation above in mind.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Note that step 4 is in fact just the final ACK since the FIN was already sent at step 2. Also in step 3 the dest is not forced to respond with a FIN, it can also just ack and continue to send data. It will send its FIN once it has nothing to say anymore.

Another point to keep in mind is to discourage applications from abusing this approach of making the client close first (there's already a warning about this for CONNECT in 9110 or 9112 I don't remember), because this will indeed leave TIME_WAITs on the proxy, and can very quickly deplete its ports.

One effective way to discourage from doing this is to say that depending on local configuration, a proxy having to send a FIN first MAY instead send an RST to preserve its source ports, but that this may result in in-flight data being truncated and any non-received response being lost. This way the client is prepared to take this risk by sending FINAL_DATA first. IMHO it's better to officially suggest it because the reality will be that this is what will be implemented to avoid a trivial DoS.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body: @bemask, #3480 and #3481 look good to me and indeed seem to address my earlier questions above.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
> One effective way to discourage from doing this is to say that depending on local configuration, a proxy having to send a FIN first MAY instead send an RST to preserve its source ports, but that this may result in in-flight data being truncated and any non-received response being lost. This way the client is prepared to take this risk by sending FINAL_DATA first. IMHO it's better to officially suggest it because the reality will be that this is what will be implemented to avoid a trivial DoS.

We discussed the question of what happens after sending RST last year (https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2949#issuecomment-2816611442).  RFC 9293 says the sender "should" enter TIME-WAIT, but you explained that this instruction is usually ignored.  This puts us in a tricky position when making a recommendation; I wouldn't want to contradict RFC 9293.

However, while looking into this question, I learned about Linux's `tcp_tw_reuse=1` option, which uses a variant of the PAWS optimization to disambiguate packets from the old and new connections.  That seems like a very clean and quite strong defense against this attack.  Please review proposed text in #3488.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Ah I didn't remember we already talked about it, sorry. Yeah I've seen your proposal in #3488, that could be a reasonable mitigation approach that is not portable though. I'm still thinking we should suggest implementations exploring possibilities. For example breaking an association using connect(AF_UNSPEC) does usually cause an RST to be emitted, but more as a result of the connection being instantly destroyed, not the other way around. I have not seen yet a platform where we'd keep TIME_WAIT on client side after this. Maybe we should add another bullet point after your proposed addition along the lines of:
* resort to any platform-specific mechanism that allows to reliably destroy the connection association
This way it remains clean from a protocol perspective (i.e. we do our best to mimic what we see on the other side) while suggesting that implementers do their homework to figure the best ways at their disposal for this.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body: I like the wording you adopted, thanks!

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] TLS considerations
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
I think it would make sense to either require TLS or at least recommend it with a SHOULD and provide appropriate security considerations.

FWIW, CONNECT-IP mandates TLS or QUIC.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: I don't think a "MUST" is reasonable here.  "SHOULD" is possible, but I don't see that recommendation in RFC 9298, and I don't know of any reason to deviate from 9298 here.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
Looks like we don't have consistency - RFC9484 and draft-ietf-masque-connect-ethernet (currently with IESG) mandate encryption while RFC9298 does not mention it.

I think we should cover this with a SHOULD in security considerations.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Why do those drafts bother mandating anything? Seems like boilerplate security theatre to me.

The documents are fundamentally HTTP extensions, what makes it critical to the extension usage that TLS or QUIC security is needed? It seems an anti-pattern for every new HTTP extension to have to stste the same requirement over and over

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body: I'd agree that if RFC 9298 doesn't mandate anything, we shouldn't need to either here.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] server applicability
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
Statements in first paragraph of 5.1 apply only when comparing templated CONNECT-TCP with CONNECT over cleartext HTTP/1.
When TLS or QUIC is involved virtual servers are distinguished through SNI.

Also, I really don't think URI should be a recommended authorisation technique.

It may also be worth mentioning draft-ietf-intarea-proxy-config as a discovery mechanism.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
I don't believe that SNI would be a suitable or correct way to implement this kind of virtual hosting.  HTTP connections can be used for requests to any origin matching the certificate (if DNS agrees) but the SNI only indicates a single hostname.

> It may also be worth mentioning draft-ietf-intarea-proxy-config as a discovery mechanism.

Yes, we can mention that.

comments.author: bemasc
bemasc
comments.body:
#3435 and #3436 are now merged.  The remaining topic for this issue is "Applicability > Server" pg. 1:

> For server operators, template-driven TCP proxies are particularly valuable in situations where virtual-hosting is needed, or where multiple proxies must share an origin. For example, the proxy might benefit from sharing an HTTP gateway that provides DDoS defense, performs request sanitization, or enforces user authorization.

As noted at the top, it is possible to share an IP address among multiple classic CONNECT proxies using TLS SNI.  However, in my experience demultiplexing TLS by SNI is not a recommended arrangement, and is not considered a valid form of HTTP virtual hosting.  As such, I think the current text is correct and sufficient.

This text is not normative.  If anyone would like to see it adjusted, feel free to suggest an improvement.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @yaroslavros any further feedback?

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body: Looks good to me. Thank you for your exemplary work, @bemasc !

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] mTLS authentication
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body: Client Certificate authentication (aka mTLS) should be mentioned as a valid technique in section 3.3.2. This is a common approach for managed devices.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Capsules format
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
From implementers perspective DATA/FINAL_DATA capsules are somewhat loosely defined.
It would be good to follow the pattern of Capsules defined in other specifications and add easy to read figures - similarly to Figures 11/12, 9/10, 7/8 of RFC9484 or Figure 4 of RFC9297.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] What's the point of splitting capsules?
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
Last paragraph of Section 3 talks about splitting and merging capsules by intermediaries as long as they do not inject capsules of other types in between.

So... what's the point of splitting or merging if everything is streamed anyway and data could be processed regardless of capsule boundaries?

I think this paragraph could be removed.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
This option serves a few purposes:

1. It matches the expectations for HTTP DATA frames.
2. It enforces the rule that DATA boundaries are not semantically meaningful.
3. It enables an optimization to merge small DATA capsules when they are buffered together at the intermediary.
4. With certain additional restrictions (e.g. assuming no other capsule types are in use), it gives implementations the flexibility to implement the specification by reconstructing the TCP stream and forward the stream, which will then be reconstructed into CONNECT-TCP later on.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @yaroslavros any further feedback? Otherwise it sounds like we'll close with no action.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
Personally, I still find it a bit confusing and I think that clarification (similar to https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3427#issuecomment-4270937500) in the document would be useful.

But I am not going to stand in the way. Feel free to close with no action.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
@yaroslavros I've proposed a sentence describing the capsule merging optimization in #3443.  Please review.

The other motivations are more subjective or speculative, so I did not include them.  Overall, I do agree that splitting capsules is less likely to be useful, but forbidding splitting while allowing merging strikes me as semantically odd -- better to make the capsule boundaries truly arbitrary for simplicity.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body: I think this is the right balance. Thank you for working on this, @bemasc !

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Remove HPKP
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
As we have learned HPKP ([RFC7469]) causes a lot of operational pain and currently is virtually unsupported by anyone.

I don't think we should be mentioning it in a new specification.

issues.title: [Connect-TCP WGLC] Streaming considerations
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
I think it is worth spelling out that TCP segment boundaries, capsule boundaries, HTTP DATA frame boundaries and lower layer boundaries do not have to align.
Endpoints should be processing data as it arrives without waiting for capsule, data frame or any other construct to be fully delivered.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Unclear how server should handle completing request with insufficient length
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
If the client sends an upload creation or append request with `Upload-Complete: ?1` whose content isn't large enough to meet the upload length expected by the server, what should the server do? I don't think this edge case is ever explicitly commented on in the draft. If it is, I can't find it.

Some options I can think of:

1. ~~Mark the upload as completed, process the content, and adjust the upload length accordingly. (Can the upload length change? Opened #3431)~~
2. Don't mark the upload as completed, but respond with success, and otherwise process the content as if there's no issue.
3. Don't mark the upload as completed, and respond with an error, but otherwise process the content as if there's no issue.
4. Don't mark the upload as completed, respond with an error, and don't comment on whether the content should be processed.
5. Don't mark the upload as completed, respond with an error, and recommend against processing the content.

I personally would suggest either option 4 or 5.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
I agree with you and would propose option 5 here as this is clearly a client error given how the current spec is written. The server should not process this content as it's not completely uploaded.

Food for thought though: should `Upload-Length` be treated as an exact value (as currently specified) or as a maximum? If the latter is allowed this case wouldn't be an error. The client estimated 100 bytes but it turned out to be 90 and that seems reasonable to handle gracefully. The current wording does create some inconsistency: if `Upload-Complete` is what finalizes the upload then `Upload-Length` being an exact value is somewhat redundant in the completing request (unless we want to support a zero-byte finalizing request for some reason, e.g. making sure that the last response is received).

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
The situation we have is comparable to HTTP/2. The request body is transmitted as one or many DATA frames where the final frame has the END_STREAM flag set. The request header can optionally contain the Content-Length header, but RFC 9113 clearly says that a request is malformed if the value from the header doesn't match the amount from the DATA frames (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#section-8.1.1-2):

> A request or response is also malformed if the value of a content-length header field does not equal the sum of the [DATA](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#DATA) frame payload lengths that form the content, unless the message is defined as having no content.

The Content-Length header in HTTP/2 is not used for message delimitation as in HTTP/1.1, but to indicate the content length to the receiver.

That's how I see Upload-Length as well. It's a signal how much data the client will send, but it's not responsible for upload termination. Any inconsistency between Upload-Length and the actual data amount should render the upload invalid. The upload length is not a vague signal, but a value that server can rely on if the client decides to set it.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thinking more about this, the situation is the same as in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3431: the client first indicates the length via `Upload-Length`, but then provides a different (smaller) value using `Upload-Complete: ?1` + `Content-Length` + `Upload-Offset`. And the spec already disallows this as mentioned in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3431#issuecomment-4435075561. I think we can close this one as well.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Maybe. Currently, the draft doesn't list `Upload-Offset` as tying into the indication for the upload length. I think that would need to be added for this issue to be resolved that way.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
The text does take the offset into consideration:

> If the request includes the Upload-Complete field value set to true and a valid Content-Length header field, the request content is the remaining representation data.
