The length is then the sum of the current offset ([Section 4.1.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#upload-offset)) and the Content-Length header field value.

(https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.3-3.1.1)

The only loophole is that this is only specified for requests with Content-Length. This header isn't always present (e.g. when Transfer-Encoding: chunked is used), so this case isn't prohibited at the moment:
1. Empty POST request with Upload-Length: 1000 and Upload-Complete: ?0
2. PATCH request with Upload-Complete: ?1, no Content-Length, but 500 bytes of content

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Ah, good catch! That can easily be mended.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3463 for this. It also explicitly spells out that the indicated length must be correct for the upload to complete.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Unclear if changing upload length is allowed
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body: Is the client allowed to send a request with an `Upload-Length` field (or upload offset + `Content-Length` with `Upload-Complete: ?1`) set to a value different from the value expected by the server? And regardless of whether it's allowed, what should the server do upon receipt of such a request? I don't think this edge case is ever explicitly commented on in the draft. If it is, I can't find it.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: This shouldn't be allowed. If the client is uncertain about the length, it shouldn't set the corresponding headers in the first place. We can add a sentence to the upload append section that such requests are malformed. Thank you for raising this!

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Would there need to be a corresponding problem type for this? Or would it be appropriate to reuse `https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#inconsistent-upload-length`? Or should a server assume a client will never do this by ignoring any new length?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Reusing the `https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#inconsistent-upload-length` problem type seems fine to me. Servers shouldn't ignore mismatches since it clearly indicates a mistake by one of the peers.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
The document already includes this restriction, which should cover the case of changing upload length values:

> If multiple requests include indicators, their indicated values MUST match. A server can use the problem type [[PROBLEM](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#PROBLEM)] of "https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#inconsistent-upload-length" ([Section 7.3](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#inconsistent-length)) in responses to indicate inconsistent length values.

(from https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.3-5)

Does that cover the case you had in mind, @GrantGryczan?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: I don't think so. This is saying the two indicators mentioned just before that quote (`Upload-Complete: ?1` + `Content-Length`, and `Upload-Length`) must be consistent with each other if both are present on an individual request. It doesn't assert anything about consistency across multiple requests. A simple tweak could probably be made to this to fix that.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
The cited paragraph mentions both. Two mismatching indicators in the same request:

> If indicators (1) and (2) are both present in the same request, their indicated lengths MUST match.

Separate requests with mismatching values between them:

> If multiple requests include indicators, their indicated values MUST match.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Oh, I see! I missed that. In that case, we're good.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: How to request with unknown completeness
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
While implementing a general-purpose client for the latest draft, I ran into a problem that I'm struggling to come up with a great solution for.

During a streaming upload where the representation data is divided into one creation and multiple append requests (which I'll call chunks), the upload length may be unknown to the client. This is fine, because the client can simply omit the `Upload-Length` header if it doesn't know it. But the same is not true for `Upload-Complete`, even though the client has to know the upload length to know whether the upload will be completed by the current chunk.

I thought to simply set `Upload-Complete: ?0` if the upload length is unknown, and then if that chunk ends up being the last, send an empty upload append request with `Upload-Complete: ?1` afterwards. But this doesn't work, because what if the final chunk is below the `min-append-size` limit? The `min-append-size` limit does not (and, I think, cannot) exempt this second-to-last request, so that final nonempty chunk would often fail.

This too can be worked around by resending the same rejected content in a new append request, but with `Upload-Complete: ?1`. But this isn't ideal because it wastes bandwidth and time, depending on the `min-append-size`. I'm wondering if this problem should be solved in the spec itself.

Some half-baked ideas, just to spitball:

- Require servers to only enforce the `min-append-size` on the next request. New chunks can't be added if the last chunk was too small. This what AWS S3 seems to do for its multipart upload API's minimum part size, though I haven't tested and only judge that from documentation examples.
- Make any upload append request below the `min-append-size` limit automatically imply marking the upload as completed. I don't like this because the semantics aren't intuitive, but it follows naturally from and has the same effect as the previous suggestion.
- Add a new request header that means "if the content doesn't reach this length, mark the upload as completed" (`Upload-Chunk-Length`?). I don't like this because it will increase server complexity while being rarely used.

It's arguably far more important to avoid moving the complexity to server implementations, and to find a solution that isn't error-prone and likely to lead to interoperability issues due to iffy semantics. And I'm not confident either of these accomplish that satisfactorily, as opposed to just resending the data. But I'm also not satisfied with resending the data. I don't have a strong opinion here. More thoughts are definitely needed.

Also worth asking: what does the official TUS client do? Does it handle this situation?

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
Interesting problem indeed!

>During a streaming upload where the representation data is divided into multiple creation and append requests (which I'll call chunks),

Is this a typo? Or do you mean that you split your streaming upload into multiple upload resources by doing multiple creation requests? 

>Also worth asking: what does the official TUS client do? Does it handle this situation?

Tus doesn't have a `Upload-Complete` header but instead uses `Upload-Length` to determine if the upload is complete. The upload is complete when the data received matches the value in `Upload-Length`. For streaming uploads one would use `Upload-Defer-Length: 1` which indicates that the length is currently not known and will be provided later. The `Upload-Length` would then be included in the last chunk or you would send a zero byte PATCH with the `Upload-Length` header set to the entire size of the upload (which the client needs to track).

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> Is this a typo? Or do you mean that you split your streaming upload into multiple upload resources by doing multiple creation requests?

Edited for clarification! 

Regarding your explanation of TUS, that makes sense. I guess TUS implementations aren't concerned about this because they don't have an equivalent to the `min-append-size` limit. But the official TUS client also supports this protocol (or at least an older version of it), which I am curious about as well.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Why is it only a problem for second-to-last chunk? How are you ensuing that previous chunks meet the min-append-size?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
The chunk size can be decided based on the limits provided by the server. The last chunk is a problem for `min-append-size` because the last chunk's size is just the remainder after subtracting the sizes of all previous chunks from the upload length, so there's nothing the server can do to make it larger like all the other chunks. This is why the limit has an exemption for completing requests [in the draft](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.4-3.8.1):

> Requests completing the upload by including the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header field are exempt from this limit.

All of that makes a lot of sense. But when the completeness is unknown, it seems the last chunk must be uploaded with `Upload-Complete: ?0` (making it the second-to-last chunk), so it isn't exempted.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: When you are uploading a file, you would know that the last chunk is the last right? I'm not understanding how it is possible for the client to simultaneously 1. guarantee that only the last chunk is smaller than min-append-size, and 2. not know that it's the last chunk. If `<min-append-size` is the signal to complete the upload, the client could simply set `Upload-Complete: ?1` itself and not asking the server to infer it right?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Let me try to give an example. A stream of 1200 bytes is being sent through the client, but the client doesn't know the total length will be 1200 bytes until the stream has closed. It starts with an empty upload creation request, and the server replies saying its `min-append-size` is 250. The client decides to send as many chunks as possible at 500 bytes each, which complies with the limit. Each chunk is sent with `Upload-Complete: ?0`, because `?1` would be invalid without certainty that it's the last chunk. It sends one chunk, and then the next. It starts to send the third chunk, but the stream suddenly closes after 200 bytes. So the server rejects the request because 200 is under the `min-append-size` of 250.

According to the workaround I described, the client would then resend the last chunk of 200 bytes with `Upload-Complete: ?1`, which is wasteful, especially if these numbers are much larger.

If sending under the `min-append-size` were a signal to complete the upload, the last chunk would instead succeed, and the server wouldn't need to send an extra append request marking the upload as completed. If the last chunk were instead 400 bytes, so not violating the limit, the server would simply send an empty append request to complete the upload, which has less overhead. But to be clear, I think that suggestion is a bad idea; I was only throwing ideas around to get the ball rolling.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: What if the 1200 is not actually the total length of stream and more data comes in afterwards? Would your implementation still send 200 bytes which violates the min-append-size?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
No, as I said:

> If the last chunk were instead 400 bytes, so not violating the limit, the server would simply send an empty append request to complete the upload, which has less overhead.

This would happen if it were 2900 bytes, for example: 5 chunks of 500, then 1 chunk of 400. While sending each chunk, the client waits for either the content to reach the chunk size (500 in this case) or the stream to close before ending the request. I'm not sure what makes you think it might still send 200 bytes if the stream didn't close after 200 bytes.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Oh you are doing streaming chunked upload. Current protocol requires chunks to be buffered to the boundary, and streaming upload only works with a single complete request.

Perhaps a trailer? But that’s not necessarily supported everywhere. I think the min size isn’t easily enforceable since we had to carve so many holes already.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> Current protocol requires chunks to be buffered to the boundary

Yes, but the stream can be buffered while it's initially transmitted, so that's not a problem and doesn't add any performance overhead to the upload. It only adds client memory usage.

> streaming upload only works with a single complete request.

Generally, as far as I can tell, a streaming resumable upload must be chunked and cannot be sent with a single complete request. Otherwise, the client might have to buffer the entire stream in order to be able to play it back from the beginning in the event of a failure, resulting in unbounded memory usage. Ending a request at each chunk boundary lets the client force the server to confirm each chunk was fully received, allowing the client to discard (or retransmit) it.

This is true even if the client can read the 1xx responses (which browser-based web clients [can't](https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/1913)), because the client can't know the server will actually send 104 responses often enough to let the client ever flush its buffer. Servers aren't even required to send 104 responses, so clients (other than extremely optimistic ones that don't care about unbounded memory usage in the event they're wrong) must send chunks with `Upload-Complete: ?0`.

> Perhaps a trailer? But that’s not necessarily supported everywhere.

Yeah, support is definitely not good enough for servers or clients (another thing browser-based web clients [can't do](https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/981)). Otherwise, that'd be great.

> I think the min size isn’t easily enforceable since we had to carve so many holes already.

I want to be extremely clear that the problem here is not the fault of `min-append-size`. `min-append-size` is very important. Every S3-compatible API in the wild that I know of enforces a limit like this for its multipart uploads, for example. To me, the source of the problem is that completeness must be known and communicated ahead of time. Which is why my (again, half-baked) ideas focus on some way to communicate completeness conditional on the number of bytes sent, or adjusting the failure condition.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
The best solution in this case might just be to collect sufficient data on the client-side until it clearly knows that the correct value for `Upload-Complete` should be. If no `min-append-size` applies or more data has been collected, it can send `Upload-Complete: ?0`. If the source ended before `min-append-size` was reached, `Upload-Complete: ?1` is included. While this isn't the most efficient solution, it's the approach that doesn't add even more complexity to the spec. But I would argue that's fine. `min-append-size` is a compromise. It enables constrained servers to pass these restrictions to the client, so a successful upload becomes possible in the first place. But this still comes at the cost of using non-optimal data handling methods. 

My proposal is to close this for now. If this turns out to be major hassle in real production deployments, we can revisit it in the future.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: That's fine by me.

issues.title: Host-only cookie retrieval
issues.author: will-bartlett
issues.body:
[FedCM](https://github.com/w3c-fedid/FedCM) has some additional privacy complexities that are motivated by the current cookie retrieval algorithm. In particular, FedCM retrieves metadata from the _registrable domain_ rather than the _origin_ (like most specifications) because cookies are scoped to registrable domains and not origins. See [FedCM section 5.3.1 Manifest Fingerprinting](https://w3c-fedid.github.io/FedCM/#manifest-fingerprinting) for motivation and https://github.com/w3c-fedid/FedCM/issues/809 and https://github.com/w3c-fedid/FedCM/pull/821 for the problems this causes and an attempt to resolve them.

Some participants [observed](https://github.com/w3c-fedid/FedCM/pull/821#issuecomment-4239660472) that only retrieving host-only cookies would resolve this issue cleanly. FedCM could switch to metadata on the _origin_ (like most specifications) if cookies were origin scoped. 

Proposal: The retrieve cookie algorithm from draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies takes five inputs ("To Retrieve Cookies given a boolean isSecure, host host, URL path path, boolean httpOnlyAllowed, and string sameSite"). Add a sixth input boolean originScoped and update the retrieval algorithm such that, when originScoped is true, cookies are only retrieved if the host-only flag is true or if host exact-matches cookie's host.

Once in the cookie specification, fetch can consume it as a new credential mode, and FedCM consume it through fetch.

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: How does that make it origin-only? What about the port for instance?

comments.author: will-bartlett
comments.body:
> How does that make it origin-only? What about the port for instance?

I will rename the issue - host-only is the right name for this, not origin-only. My goal is to expose the existing host-only semantics available as a storage algorithm additionally as a retrieval algorithm for fetch (and thereby for FedCM), not to define new semantics.

comments.author: samuelgoto
comments.body:
> Some participants observed that only retrieving host-only cookies would resolve this issue cleanly. 

Can you expand on this a bit more? How it is that constraining the cookies to be host-only / origin-only help resolve the issue of fingerprinting?

comments.author: will-bartlett
comments.body:
> > Some participants observed that only retrieving host-only cookies would resolve this issue cleanly.
> 
> Can you expand on this a bit more? How it is that constraining the cookies to be host-only / origin-only help resolve the issue of fingerprinting?

Fingerprinting in FedCM happens when foo.example uses foo-example.login.idp.example and bar.example uses bar-example.login.idp.example and foo-example.login.idp.example and bar-example.login.idp.example share cookies. Here, login.idp.example receives both the relying party identity and the shared user cookie in a single request pre-consent.

Constraining cookies to be host-only reduces fingerprinting by preventing shared cookies between subdomains. It doesn't resolve the issue fully - but it makes the domain where a singleton endpoint is required to prevent fingerprinting be the host (login.idp.example) instead the registrable domain (idp.example).

comments.author: annevk
comments.body: cc @bvandersloot @sysrqb

comments.author: samuelgoto
comments.body:
> foo-example.login.idp.example and bar-example.login.idp.example share cookies

What's special about `login.idp.example`? Wouldn't an attacker be able to use `foo-example.idp.example` and `bar-example.idp.example` equally well and still meet the following attack  "receives both the relying party identity and the shared user cookie in a single request pre-consent."?

Or, are you working under the assumption that we'd still have some sort of well-known file somewhere that guarantees that there is only 1 `login.idp.example` per registrable domain?

comments.author: will-bartlett
comments.body:
> > foo-example.login.idp.example and bar-example.login.idp.example share cookies
> 
> What's special about `login.idp.example`? Wouldn't an attacker be able to use `foo-example.idp.example` and `bar-example.idp.example` equally well and still meet the following attack "receives both the relying party identity and the shared user cookie in a single request pre-consent."?
> 
> Or, are you working under the assumption that we'd still have some sort of well-known file somewhere that guarantees that there is only 1 `login.idp.example` per registrable domain?

Not per registrable domain.

Today, FedCM prevents manifest fingerprinting in both host and path by using a well known file at the registrable domain. If we could specify FedCM to only use host-only cookies, FedCM would only need to prevent manifest fingerprinting in the path but not the host, because there would be no shared data between hosts. Then, we could host the well known file in the same host as the config file instead of using the registrable domain.

PS - this issue is in http-extensions github, not FedCM, so we may way to take the conversation to FedCM github or slack. We already have a conversation in FedCM slack. Just not sure how interested these folks are in details of FedCM.

comments.author: will-bartlett
comments.body:
Maybe another way of looking at this `protocol://subdomain.registrabledomain/path`.

FedCM today prevents manifest fingerprinting in the "subdomain" portion and the "path" portion, but not the "registrabledomain" portion (no shared data) nor the "protocol://" portion (fixed to `https` by spec).

I am suggesting FedCM could prevent fingerprinting only in the "/path" portion by removing the shared data in the "subdomain" portion. My understanding is that cookies are the only type of shared data in that portion and that limiting cookie retrieval to host-only would make the subdomain and registrabledomain portions equivalent, from a privacy perspective. Keep in mind that it is already approximately free to obtain infinite registrabledomains through the use of PSL.

comments.author: npm1
comments.body:
> Today, FedCM prevents manifest fingerprinting in both host and path by using a well known file at the registrable domain. If we could specify FedCM to only use host-only cookies, FedCM would only need to prevent manifest fingerprinting in the path but not the host, because there would be no shared data between hosts. Then, we could host the well known file in the same host as the config file instead of using the registrable domain.

I think this does not actually prevent fingerprinting. Even if FedCM fetches are restricted to origin-scoped cookies, there is nothing preventing IDP1 from later writing those origin-scoped cookie contents into domain-scoped cookies, IDP2 doing the same, and the IDP domain then cross-referencing those cookies to get all of the information.
 
> PS - this issue is in http-extensions github, not FedCM, so we may way to take the conversation to FedCM github or slack. We already have a conversation in FedCM slack. Just not sure how interested these folks are in details of FedCM.

Isn't FedCM the motivation of this issue? It is not in the title but it is the only use case mentioned in the issue description.

comments.body:
> I think this does not actually prevent fingerprinting. Even if FedCM fetches are restricted to origin-scoped cookies, there is nothing preventing IDP1 from later writing those origin-scoped cookie contents into domain-scoped cookies, IDP2 doing the same, and the IDP domain then cross-referencing those cookies to get all of the information.

Interesting. I was thinking host-only was equivalent to PSL, but it isn't, because browser bounce tracking operates at the level of the registrable domain. That is, the browser will keep idp.foo.example, idp2.foo.example, and foo.example storage around if the user only interacts with idp.foo.example, unless foo.example is on the PSL, and then it requires interaction with the specific subdomains and parent domain separately to keep the storage around.

That's probably kills this idea for FedCM then.

I was thinking this idea was generally useful - folks have been talking about making cookies origin only for decades to reduce the inclusion of unnecessary data. But FedCM was the case I was primarily interested in, of course.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Should `OPTIONS` method be supported?
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
Currently, the draft [indicates](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.2.1) that a resumable upload can be created with the `OPTIONS` method:

> A client can start a resumable upload from any request that can carry content by including the `Upload-Complete` header field ([Section 4.1.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#upload-complete)). As a consequence, all request methods that allow content are possible, such as `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH`.

This is because `OPTIONS` requests can carry content, as per [RFC 9110](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#OPTIONS):

> A client that generates an OPTIONS request containing content MUST send a valid [Content-Type](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.content-type) header field describing the representation media type. Note that this specification does not define any use for such content.

But I'm not sure this is intentional, considering the draft [later says](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.4-7) `OPTIONS` requests can be used to determine support for the protocol in the first place:

> A client can use an `OPTIONS` request to discover support for resumable uploads and potential limits before creating an upload resource.

This begs the question: how do you check whether the `OPTIONS` request itself supports resumable uploads? Since `OPTIONS` content semantics are implementation-dependent (so the implementation can define semantics that account for this), I don't think this is necessarily problematic, and therefore, there's no reason `OPTIONS` requests should be excluded. But in any case, this needs clarification: either add `OPTIONS` to the list of examples (along with "`POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH`"), or explicitly exclude the `OPTIONS` method if there's a good reason to.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> But in any case, this needs clarification: either add `OPTIONS` to the list of examples (along with "`POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH`"), or explicitly exclude the `OPTIONS` method if there's a good reason to.

I don't think either is necessary. The list isn't meant to be exhaustive, but is there to indicate readers that the upload creation isn't tied to one request method by naming the most commonly used ones. For example, is doesn't include DELETE and doesn't have to IMO.

Excluding OPTIONS also isn't necessary. Without an Upload-Complete request header, the server won't create an upload resource and just falls back to the normal handling of the requests, where it responds with the endpoint's capabilities. I agree with you that although uncommon, there is nothing that prevents OPTIONS requests from using resumable uploads.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I just thought it might be unclear whether it's even allowed. Yeah, it's not technically necessary, but I think it would help clarity since it's a weird edge case. It could just be me though, so if you don't think this would confuse others, then feel free to disregard and close this.

I should be clear that it's not the listing of the other methods that makes this confusing to me, but the fact that the draft adds requirements for the `OPTIONS` method.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Yeah this is an interesting edge case. When responding to an upload creation request, Upload-Limits isn't required, but when responding to OPTIONS, Upload-Limits is even if the value is `min-size=0` (after #3440). Some implementations might get confused where it's both upload creation and OPTIONS.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: It might be cleaner to exclude OPTIONS, or more clearly define when OPTIONS requests have special requirements (ones without Upload-Complete / with Upload-Complete: ?1), or align the Upload-Limits header requirements everywhere so OPTIONS are not special.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Confusion about `Accept-Patch` compliance
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
The section on [limits](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.4-6) says the following:

> A server that supports the creation of a resumable upload resource ([Section 4.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#upload-creation)) for a target URI MUST include the `Accept-Patch` ([Section 3.1](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789#section-3.1) of [[PATCH](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#PATCH)]) header field in response to an `OPTIONS` request for the target URI.

But [RFC 5789](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789#section-3.1) says the following:

> The presence of the Accept-Patch header in response to any method is an implicit indication that PATCH is allowed on the resource identified by the Request-URI.

It sounds to me like the draft requires servers to be non-compliant with RFC 5789 in the case that the resource which handles upload creation requests doesn't allow the `PATCH` method. The draft requires `PATCH` requests be accepted by the upload resource URI, not the initial target URI.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: That's a good point, thanks for raising it. Given the wording in RFC 5789, Accept-Patch doesn't seem usable to convey the intended information. Maybe it's best to revert https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3242, which introduced the cited paragraph.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Mention `Incremental: ?1`
issues.author: Acconut
issues.body: Resumable uploads work best if request content is delivered incrementally, so the partial content can be processed even if the entire request doesn't complete. We should consider recommending the inclusion of `Incremental: ?1` from [draft-ietf-httpbis-incremental](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-incremental/) in content-transferring requests to encourage intermediaries to not buffer.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Yeah. I don't think there's _much_ to say. We should not duplicate text for sure. However, we probably want to highlight why incremental can be useful in this use case.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3461 for this.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Addressed in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3462.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Clarification on `min-size`
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
@Acconut wrote the following in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3408#issuecomment-4439012488:

> The purpose of min-size is mainly to let the client know that the server won't offer resumable uploads for representations outside of those boundaries. But this doesn't mean the representation will be rejected when uploading via a traditional POST request, for example. A server may decide to only use resumable uploads for larger files as there is a cost of holding state involved for upload resources.

And the following in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3408#issuecomment-4439173526:

> The definitions of max-size and min-size state that the server might not create an upload resource if the indicated representation size falls outside of these boundaries:
> 
> > ...
> 
> It doesn't say that upload creation requests with sizes outside of these limits must be rejected. The server can still process the included representation without involving resumable uploads, which is a feature IMO, but a bug :)

I didn't know this! If this is true, this seems important to clarify in the draft. Right now, the definition of `min-size` _also_ says that it is "a minimum size for the representation data", which is a stronger requirement that I thought disallowed this.

~~I'd argue having an uncommunicated, separate (or a lack of a) limit for non-resumable uploads is pointless, because a server could just use `min-append-size` to ensure the entire upload is done in one request under a certain size. The server could even loosen the `min-append-size` limit after the first request if it only needs that restriction for the purpose of avoiding creating an upload resource.~~ In my opinion, using `min-size` for this ~~is redundant and~~ may make `min-size` less reliable for the purpose of restricting the representation data size.

EDIT: Struck through most of my previous argument because I realize `min-append-size` can't be used to restrict upload resource creation, since it doesn't apply to empty upload creation requests. Is there any common situation where a server would want an actual, final minimum restriction on the total size of an upload, resumable or not? I guess I can't really think of anything.

Lastly, I also wanted to ask for clarification on whether `min-size` can be enforced by servers during upload append requests rather than during upload creation, since I'm not sure whether a previous comment hinted that it might only be enforced on upload creation. The current phrasing as "a minimum size for the representation data", as opposed to a minimum upload length to allow upload resource creation, makes it seem like it would always be enforced.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Is there any common situation where a server would want an actual, final minimum restriction on the total size of an upload, resumable or not? I guess I can't really think of anything.

I can't think generic reason either. That's why min-size is intended to indicate what the minimum size is to start a resumable uploads. Server might not want to pay the cost of resumable uploads for representations below that limit, while still accepting and processing these representations when they are uploaded without resumablity using traditional uploads.

> Lastly, I also wanted to ask for clarification on whether `min-size` can be enforced by servers during upload append requests rather than during upload creation, since I'm not sure whether a previous comment hinted that it might only be enforced on upload creation. The current phrasing as "a minimum size for the representation data", as opposed to a minimum upload length to allow upload resource creation, makes it seem like it would always be enforced.

At the end of the day, the server has ultimate control over how/if the uploaded representation is processed. It can stop the upload at any time and discard data as it wants, regardless of what we say the spec. If you want to check the representation's size once the upload's done, that fine as well. `min-size` isn't a requirement on the server when to assert the limit, but a hint to the client that resumability is likely not available if the representation is below this limit. The client can then decide to use a traditional upload method or stop entirely.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Fair enough! Thanks for the clarification. In that case, can we change and/or add some phrasing to communicate this? This makes sense but wasn't at all clear from the draft IMO. I'm going to want to change some code around in my client implementation to fall back to non-resumable uploads when under the `min-size`. Or perhaps I should do the whole upload in a single `Upload-Complete: ?1` request under the `min-size`, since that would be simpler?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3460 to address this.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Recover lost early response
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
As of some recent changes, clients can now recover a lost final response (if supported by the server), and servers can send responses before the client finishes uploading the full representation data. But the combination of these may or may not have been considered: recovering a lost early response.

The relevant text is as follows:

> Even if the upload is complete ({{upload-complete}}) in the server's perspective and the final response from the targeted resource has already been sent, the client might still perform an upload append ({{upload-appending}}) after an offset retrieval ({{offset-retrieving}}) due to the response being lost during transmission. The server can choose to replay the final response to the client if the request to append to the completed upload is valid.

The condition to allow a request to replay a final response is "if the request to append to the completed upload is valid." Does this exclude a nonempty upload append request with `Upload-Complete: ?0`? I can't think of a reason it would, but I just want to confirm with others. And perhaps an explicit note could be added that that's allowed, since it's a potentially surprising edge case?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: We aren't officially supporting retrieving lost final response in the draft based on working group feedback, and this entire paragraph is informational and up for implementation interpretation. Feel free to suggest some clarification here, but yes this is allowed by the current spec. It is just a regular upload resumption in the client's perspective, and the server can choose to replay if it still has the final response (or don't, which is also allowed).

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Recommend `Upload-Limits` in all 4xx responses caused by limit violations
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
I suggest we recommend servers include the `Upload-Limits` header in all 4xx responses produced because of a client's violation of upload limits. This recommendation already exists for 413 responses, but I ran into a situation where this would be greatly useful for other status codes:

If a server doesn't want to pay the cost of resumable uploads below a certain `min-size` (as per #3446), I'd expect the server to reject any empty upload creation request that has an `Upload-Length` under that `min-size`, since the overhead of an upload resource may be an undesirable. Ideally, an optimistic client should be able to handle that rejection response by resubmitting the request in one non-resumable request rather than as an upload append.

The problem is, the server has no means to communicate that the response failure was due to a `min-size` violation. Therefore, it seems a generalized, optimistic client has no choice but to handle all 4xx upload creation failures by requesting the upload limits and possibly trying again. Most of the time, this results in extra round trips with no benefit. If the client could see the `Upload-Limits` in that response, another round trip wouldn't be needed.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Yeah that makes sense. All failures resulted from a limit violation should advertise the limits, and it doesn't hurt if other responses carry the limits as well.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> If a server doesn't want to pay the cost of resumable uploads below a certain `min-size` (as per [#3446](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3446)), I'd expect the server to reject any empty upload creation request that has an `Upload-Length` under that `min-size`, since the overhead of an upload resource may be an undesirable.

The server doesn't have to reject the upload outright when it's below the minimum size. If the request doesn't include `Upload-Complete: ?0` it can just accept the representation without offering resumability and its corresponding overhead.

That being said, including the limits when they were violated is a helpful improvement.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Yeah, I meant an empty upload creation request with `Upload-Complete: ?0`, since that'll be a common pattern from clients.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3466 for this.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Client-side upload offset handling seems under-specified
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
While implementing my generalized resumable upload client, I ran into several edge cases related to `Upload-Offset` as a response header that I seeked for guidance from the draft on, but the draft doesn't say anything about them.

1. _(This is the only purely editorial issue.)_ In a 2xx response to a creation/append request, a client can determine the new upload offset for the `Upload-Offset` response header based on the length of the content it uploaded added to the previous offset. For example, if the client sent `Upload-Offset: 100` and `Content-Length: 50`, the client knows from a 2xx response that the new offset should be 150. This is implied by the [definition of upload offset](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.1-1). It's also specified that the client can [free previous resources](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.1-4) upon receipt of a new `Upload-Offset` value, but the same is not specified for changes to the upload offset in general. I think this suggestion may be better communicated if generalized to the offset implied by responses in general (e.g., as implied by a 2xx response), rather than specific to the `Upload-Offset` header.
2. In a 2xx response to a creation/append request, how should a client treat an `Upload-Offset` value inconsistent with what the client requested? Reusing the previous example, what should the client do if the server replies to that request with `Upload-Offset: 125` or `Upload-Offset: 200` instead of the correct `Upload-Offset: 150`?
3. In an offset retrieval response, how should a client treat an `Upload-Offset` value below its current known offset? In other words, what should the client do if the server tells it that the offset moved backwards?
4. Similarly, should a client handle the case that the offset moved forward further ahead than it knows it ever uploaded the representation, since that implies the server messed up? Or should the client just take that for granted, since that allows a simpler implementation?
5. In an offset retrieval response, how should a client treat a missing or invalid `Upload-Offset`? The [definition of the `Upload-Offset` header](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.1-3) currently says syntactically invalid or negative values "MUST cause the entire header field to be ignored", but ignoring the header on offset retrieval responses is unacceptable, which seems like an oversight in this definition.

I'm guessing that, for some of these, we'd want the client to abort its current request and cancel the upload, similarly to [when the server messes up](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.2.2-7) the `Location` response header.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
For 1, we can rephrase this to clarify in Upload Append Client Behavior:

>The client MUST indicate the offset of the request content inside the representation data by including the `Upload-Offset` header field. To ensure that the upload resource will accept the request, the offset SHOULD be taken from an immediate previous response for retrieving the offset ({{offset-retrieving}}) or the end offset of the immediate previous successful incomplete append ({{upload-appending}}).

For 2, since the information is redundant and not required on responses, most client implementations probably won't read it. I think it's fine to leave it just for debugging purposes and not define any actions on it

For 3, there are 2 types of backtracking. The draft mentioned backtracking if it's caused by the loss of inflight data, but doesn't specify if an explicit backtrack (from offset retrieval or 104 progress updates) is allowed. I would say that a robust generic server implementation shouldn't backtrack since the client might have freed the dynamic generated request stream, but if the body is known to be seekable for a specific application, backtrack is fine.

4 used to be banned but was allowed in #3317. Same reasoning, seekable body for specific applications.

For 5, yeah an invalid field can be treated the same way as a missing field. We could say that the client shouldn't try to resume, but it doesn't matter much if the upload is cancelled or not since this is just a bug on the server.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
guoye-zhang
comments.body:
> If the correct behavior isn't specified, every client that supports this optimization still has to make a decision on the order here. I'm not confident that every implementer will choose correctly, since this is an edge case that requires a faulty or malicious server implementation in order to run into, and one order isn't more natural than the other.
> 
> Then again, perhaps it doesn't matter which the client prefers when the server is already faulty or malicious, but it may nevertheless be nice to let client implementers know the preferable behavior so they don't have to think about this.

We could recommend to do something here. However, our implementation never looks at the Upload-Offset on the creation or the append responses. When retrying, we always perform an offset retrieval. I think that should be allowed as a valid implementation.

> Interesting, I didn't think of that. There may still be value in specifying 3 and 4 though, for the clients that don't support backtracking or forward-tracking, perhaps by simply saying they MAY cancel the upload (or MAY support backtracking/forward-tracking?). It would have sped up decision-making for my own implementation, at least, but I understand if that kind of specificity is out of scope.

I believe it's already addressed in the draft:

>> If the client is not able to provide the representation data at the given offset, the upload MUST be considered a failure. The client then MUST NOT continue the upload and SHOULD cancel the upload ({{upload-cancellation}}).

> But how should a missing `Upload-Offset` be treated for an offset retrieval request? The whole point of making this request is that you want the upload offset, so if it's missing, I can only guess that the client should cancel the upload. Following the same reasoning as my previous point (just facilitating less decision-making burden for implementers), would it be useful to say clients MAY cancel the upload? Clients are going to have to do _something_, and hopefully that something isn't to crash and burn, so a note on this matter may remind implementers to do something about it.

Our current implementation treats it the same way as the HTTP message failing to parse. So it's throwing an error immediately and does not cancel the upload. I could see that other implementations performing a retry on 5xx which is also valid. I don't know if we have consensus on the best way to handle this.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> I think that should be allowed as a valid implementation.

Absolutely. My suggestions in #3454 don't force clients to violate requirements or recommendations in order to be able to perform offset retrieval every time.

> I believe it's already addressed in the draft:
> 
> > If the client is not able to provide the representation data at the given offset, the upload MUST be considered a failure. The client then MUST NOT continue the upload and SHOULD cancel the upload ({{upload-cancellation}}).

This doesn't cover cases where the client is _able_ to provide the representation data at the given offset, but it just isn't appropriate behavior for the application. But again, I don't know how broadly valuable or in-scope this is. It's just something that would have helped me personally.

> So it's throwing an error immediately and does not cancel the upload.

Hm, then how does the upload continue when the offset needs to be retrieved? Do you just hope the server doesn't keep making the same mistake for further retries?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> 1\. (This is the only purely editorial issue.) In a 2xx response to a creation/append request, a client can determine the new upload offset for the Upload-Offset response header based on the length of the content it uploaded added to the previous offset. For example, if the client sent Upload-Offset: 100 and Content-Length: 50, the client knows from a 2xx response that the new offset should be 150. This is implied by the [definition of upload offset](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.1-1). It's also specified that the client can [free previous resources](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.1-4) upon receipt of a new Upload-Offset value, but the same is not specified for changes to the upload offset in general. I think this suggestion may be better communicated if generalized to the offset implied by responses in general (e.g., as implied by a 2xx response), rather than specific to the Upload-Offset header.

Good point, we can spell that out more explicitly.

> 2\. In a 2xx response to a creation/append request, how should a client treat an `Upload-Offset` value inconsistent with what the client requested? Reusing the previous example, what should the client do if the server replies to that request with `Upload-Offset: 125` or `Upload-Offset: 200` instead of the correct `Upload-Offset: 150`?

The client should treat the offset the same way it would handle HEAD responses. We recently adjusted the draft to allow the offset to advance without the transfer of additional representation data: https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.3.1-2. In that case the client follows the offset (unless it doesn't want to, of course).

This also answers your question 4.

> 3\. In an offset retrieval response, how should a client treat an Upload-Offset value below its current known offset? In other words, what should the client do if the server tells it that the offset moved backwards?

As Guoye said, the client should backtrack if in-flight data was lost. If acknowledged data was lost, the upload resource is in an unrecoverable state: https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.1.1-3

> 5\. In an offset retrieval response, how should a client treat a missing or invalid Upload-Offset? The [definition of the Upload-Offset header](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.1.1-3) currently says syntactically invalid or negative values "MUST cause the entire header field to be ignored", but ignoring the header on offset retrieval responses is unacceptable, which seems like an oversight in this definition.

The client could retry the offset retrieval, like it would do for a 5XX response.

comments.body:

Makes sense, but then that does need to be specified so that generalized clients use the `Upload-Offset` header from 2xx responses instead of strictly assuming the offset from the 2xx status and request content length, assuming I'm understanding correctly. This is very likely to end up as inconsistent behavior between clients if not specified; in fact, my own pseudo-code above made the mistake of prioritizing 2xx's implied offset over the `Upload-Offset` response header, which would have ended up a bug in my implementation had you not clarified this.

This looks more like it's talking about in-flight data being lost, not data that the server acknowledged.

> If acknowledged data was lost, the upload resource is in an unrecoverable state: https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.1.1-3

Oh, I thought Guoye was saying some applications can backtrack acknowledged data. Either way, that paragraph describes that the server is required to deactivate the resource, but doesn't specify what the client should do if the server violates the spec and gives the client an offset backtracked from previously acknowledged data.

> The client could retry the offset retrieval, like it would do for a 5XX response.

That's reasonable. Again, do we want to specify some behaviors the client may do here, to help clarify and facilitate implementers considering how to handle this edge case?

I think the difference between unwilling and unable is minor, and not enforceable by a protocol spec. For all intents and purposes, you don't want to provide the data from the offset is the same as you can't provide the data.

We don't retry, but it might be the case that the 5xx was sent by a load balancer and not the resumable upload server.

> Oh, I thought Guoye was saying some applications can backtrack acknowledged data. Either way, that paragraph describes that the server is required to deactivate the resource, but doesn't specify what the client should do if the server violates the spec and gives the client an offset backtracked from previously acknowledged data.

Oh I didn't remember this paragraph. Yeah it's not allowed. Our current implementation doesn't check though and we would happily resend the data if available.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> In a 2xx response to a creation/append request, how should a client treat an Upload-Offset value inconsistent with what the client requested? Reusing the previous example, what should the client do if the server replies to that request with Upload-Offset: 125 or Upload-Offset: 200 instead of the correct Upload-Offset: 150?

I was a bit wrong about this question, I think. The current draft doesn't mention that 2XX responses for creating or appending include Upload-Offset. So clients shouldn't check this header for these requests. Or did we agree to change this in another issue?

I don't think we can say much in these cases as it really depends on your application and circumstances where you want to restart the upload, retry the upload without resumability or abort and bubble up the errors. It probably also depends on whether your implementation is a standalone client (e.g. tus-js-client) or a transparent layer in the HTTP stack (e.g. URLSession).

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Recommend `Upload-Offset` in 4xx responses with `Upload-Complete: ?0`
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
For a client handling a 4xx creation/append response with `Upload-Complete: ?0`, it can resume the upload by sending an offset retrieval request, waiting for the response, and then submitting an append request at the retrieved offset. But this isn't necessary if the response includes an up-to-date `Upload-Offset` value already; then, a client can just use that and save a round trip, immediately resuming the upload at the given offset without performing offset retrieval.

This is especially problematic for servers that require that incomplete appends conform to a particular chunk granularity. Since clients have no way to tell what a server's chunk granularity is, a server with a chunk granularity requirement will respond to nearly every incomplete creation/append with a non-completing 4xx response (as per https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3193#issuecomment-3893170872), since most request content lengths won't be a multiple of the server's chunk granularity. Then the client has to perform offset retrieval to send every single chunk but the first and last. This puts unnecessary load on clients and servers wherever chunk granularity is involved.

I'd strongly argue we should recommend servers include the `Upload-Offset` header in 4xx responses with `Upload-Complete: ?0`. We don't have to recommend clients actually use this information, since as Guoye Zhang said in [a comment](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3319#discussion_r2474114941), that would make client implementations more complex. But clients should at least have the option to opt into that sometimes-very-significant performance optimization, and I expect it to be very simple for servers to include that information.

~~[This paragraph](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-4.4.1-2) should also be modified to mention this as one of the sources clients are recommended to take the offset from, though I'm not sure how I'd phrase that.~~ EDIT: I'm not sure why I thought any change was needed there. Looking at it again, it seems like it already covers this.

This could also be extended to ~~3xx-5xx~~ 3xx responses that contain the `Upload-Complete: ?0` header. There is no point in recommending this for 2xx since the offset after a non-completing 2xx response can be inferred from the previous known offset + the requested content length. I also wouldn't recommend extending this to any responses without the `Upload-Complete` header, since those responses are often generated without awareness of resumable uploads.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
I think this was discussed before, and the conclusion back then was that supporting multiple signaling paths (HEAD vs. inline response headers) would add unnecessary complexity. I agree it could help in cases like minimum chunk size, but I’m not sure how common that scenario actually is?

> This could also be extended to 3xx-5xx responses that contain the Upload-Complete: ?0 header. 

I would be very cautious here. A 5xx response means the server is in an error state, so trusting metadata in that situation feels unreliable. It becomes a bit contradictory: “Something went wrong, but here’s information you should trust.” That seems risky to formalize.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> I think this was discussed before, and the conclusion back then was that supporting multiple signaling paths (HEAD vs. inline response headers) would add unnecessary complexity.

Unnecessary complexity for the client or the server? I addressed client complexity in my third paragraph (in short, this isn't a recommendation for clients), and I really don't think this would add any server complexity in most cases. The server already has the offset; it just has to pass it into an HTTP response header in probably the same place it sets `Upload-Complete: ?0`. In every high-level language, that's just 1 extra line of code on each response, maybe wrapped in a condition to check the status code if it's generalized to all responses. In the rare case that it is somehow very complex on the server, they can simply not follow the recommendation, as it wouldn't be a requirement.

> I agree it could help in cases like minimum chunk size, but I’m not sure how common that scenario actually is?

Well, this would save round trips for any 4xx response in general. The chunk granularity case is just an extreme example where every response is 4xx. Round trips really matter on slow or unstable connections.

> A 5xx response means the server is in an error state, so trusting metadata in that situation feels unreliable.

That makes sense. I wasn't super confident about 5xx, nor am I about 3xx. Clients should definitely be _allowed_ to use the header information from 5xx responses though, because in my case for example, I know that any 5xx response returned from the server will actually have correct header values. All my server's 5xx response cases are explicit and controlled, with the exception of 5xx responses from my CDN, which I expect to never contain these headers. That doesn't have to be formalized though, as long as it's not formally discouraged.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> I think this was discussed before, and the conclusion back then was that supporting multiple signaling paths (HEAD vs. inline response headers) would add unnecessary complexity.

Just found the change where this happened. Prior to https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3018, the Upload-Offset header was part of the responses when appending to an upload resource

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
Thanks @Acconut for finding it. I tried but couldn't remember what to search for.

@GrantGryczan 
>  That doesn't have to be formalized though, as long as it's not formally discouraged.

If it’s available in the response, I don’t see a reason to discourage using it. It still feels a bit conceptually odd to me for the reasons I mentioned earlier, but I’m not strongly against it.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> Just found the change where this happened. Prior to https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3018, the Upload-Offset header was part of the responses when appending to an upload resource

Ah, I see. It makes sense to remove it as a requirement, but I only suggest we make it a recommendation, and only for 3xx-4xx responses with `Upload-Complete: ?0`. Servers that don't want to implement it don't have to.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: I'm not convinced we need additional text for this. The server can respond with a 409 and include the Upload-Offset header if wants the client to continue from a certain offset, essentially synchronizing their views of the upload's offset. This works when the client attempts to append to the wrong offset, but I don't see a reason why this couldn't also be used when the server didn't append all data from a PATCH request.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
The spec doesn't say to do that, and I'd say 409 is semantically inappropriate in the chunk granularity example. I'd consider 400 to be more appropriate in that case.

I am just now realizing though that the reason you say this is because we're only recommending clients retry for 409, 413, and 429 (as per https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3319#issuecomment-4433360637), which I had forgotten. In retrospect, that seems a little strange.

Perhaps a better approach than this issue would be to change client retry semantics such that the client can retry for any semantically appropriate 4xx response with the `Upload-Offset` header? The `Upload-Offset` header would be interpreted as a general instruction to "continue at this offset". This would save round trips, let any appropriate status code be retriable, and possibly simplify the specification of client retry behavior for 409, since it won't be tied to 409 anymore.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> I am just now realizing though that the reason you say this is because we're only recommending clients retry for 409, 413, and 429 (as per [#3319 (comment)](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3319#issuecomment-4433360637)), which I had forgotten. In retrospect, that seems a little strange.

Besides including recommendations for handling these status codes, I think the document should include a phrase to allow retries for other, appropriate 4xx codes, like it currently does.

> Perhaps a better approach than this issue would be to change client retry semantics such that the client can retry for any semantically appropriate 4xx response with the Upload-Offset header? The Upload-Offset header would be interpreted as a general instruction to "continue at this offset". This would save round trips, let any appropriate status code be retriable, and possibly simplify the specification of client retry behavior for 409, since it won't be tied to 409 anymore.

I don't think we improve the document by increasing the response conditions that a client has to check against to determine the next step. Response handling is already getting complex, and we should avoid adding more conditions to this, especially if the document already includes methods for the server to trigger the desired client behavior.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
> I don't think we improve the document by increasing the response conditions that a client has to check against to determine the next step.

As I said, I think this could simplify the client implementation since it no longer has to check for status 409 (those responses already MUST include `Upload-Offset`), while also covering any other status codes independent of the application. Clients doing this would check just as many or fewer conditions to retry. I believe this would simplify my own generalized client implementation.

And as I said, that behavior may fit in with the existing `Upload-Offset` semantics, so it makes sense that the implementation would be simpler because of it. I think there may be other concerns with the semantics of my suggestion, but I'm not convinced on client complexity. Can you explain how this behavior could increase complexity? The new recommendations would look like this:

```
Upload-Complete: ?1 -> do not resume
413 (Content Too Large) -> resume with smaller chunk
429 (Too Many Requests) -> resume with delay
Upload-Offset -> resume
5xx -> resume
```

I'll note that the client doesn't even have to use the value of the header if it considers that too complex; it could just get the value from offset retrieval instead as usual.

> especially if the document already includes methods for the server to trigger the desired client behavior.

Without some general recommended condition, I don't think there's a workaround servers can rely on to enable retrying for other status codes. Only application-specific clients would be able to handle resumable uploads gracefully for servers that use other statuses, which isn't interoperable. In practice, this prohibits the chunk granularity use case unless the server wants to abuse status 409, which I think is incorrect.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
A rule saying that the client should retry on any 4XX that includes the Upload-Offset is too generic and leaves too many questions open. Why should the client retry on a 403 or 404 response? Retrying won't help in those cases. What about a 429 with Upload-Offset? Retry after a delay at the provided offset? Answering these questions in a watertight in the spec is possible, but I fear it will make the text more complex.

My point is that the spec already includes a way to trigger the client to resume from a provided offset and we should add more ways to achieve the same. Others are welcome to join this discussion if they believe otherwise.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I don't think this would really complicate the spec.

> Why should the client retry on a 403 or 404 response? Retrying won't help in those cases.

We would simply say something like "on status codes appropriate for retrying" when defining these semantics. Either way, a server doing this would be violating HTTP.

> What about a 429 with Upload-Offset? Retry after a delay at the provided offset?

These checks are already planned to be specified in a certain order. Just as you have to check for `Upload-Complete: ?1` first before checking any status codes to know if we have the final response, we also have to check for `Upload-Offset` after checking for 4xx status codes. The description of the process here is equally complicated, just in a different order, no?

> My point is that the spec already includes a way to trigger the client to resume from a provided offset and we should add more ways to achieve the same. Others are welcome to join this discussion if they believe otherwise.

(Assuming you mean "shouldn't",) I understand where you're coming from, but do we really want to abuse 409 for that? 409 already has a meaning in HTTP. Just because our spec defines one case where 409 is appropriate doesn't mean every case that wants retriability should have to use 409.

I understand why you'd want these semantics to be tied to a status code instead of a header, but it seems the only reason 409 is able to be used here is because it's less common, so very unlikely to conflict with a server that needs 409 with `Upload-Complete: ?0` for a different reason, even though it would be semantically correct to use 409 for a situation inappropriate for retrying. The server isn't even going to make sure this is actually an inconsistent offset response before retrying; it's just going to check for 409. I don't see how those semantics are better. The presence of `Upload-Offset` makes much more sense to me because it only makes sense to include, and realistically will naturally only be included, when it should be retried.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: By the way, I would be willing to compromise on this with some added clarification that servers MAY include `Upload-Offset` in non-completing 3xx-5xx responses in order to save some clients a round trip from offset retrieval. My current concern is mostly that servers currently don't even know they can do this, and that it helps. But if we go with that, I'd still like to know the rationale against making it a recommendation.

issues.title: Deb Cooley's IESG feedback on unencoded-digest
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Source: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/2026JanMar/0184.html

Original statement from Deb

> Please note that while I am balloting 'no obj', I do feel like some minor
> tweaks make sense.  I am happy to have a conversation (in avoidance of the 'd'
> word).
> 
> Section 7, para 2:  I expected a 'SHOULD NOT' use an Unencoded-Digest in this
> circumstance.
> 
> Section 7, para 2:  I'm not sure I would call the inference of 'details about
> the unencrypted content with out decrypting it' a 'side channel' per se. Most
> commonly, we talk about side channels leaking key, not leaking plain text. 
> With no loss of clarity, I would suggest merely deleting this sentence:  'This
> could be used as a side channel'.  Notes:  I would hope that any digest
> algorithm used in this capacity was strong enough to obscure whatever structure
> was in the plain text.  I would also hope that in this circumstance, an
> Unencoded-Digest field would not be utilized.


In response, I said

> This has come up a few times, so happy to (small d) discuss more. 
> 
> aes128gcm is defined in RFC 8188 and has a section on leaking information in header fields [1] . It uses the term "side-channel information". I think perhaps we've conflated our terminology a little. If striking the sentence is ok by your judgement we can do that, or attempt to use the term "side-channel information" to tie it closer to RFC 8118. Please let us know if you have a preference.
> 
> Similarly, RFC 8188 Section 4.6 also explains how to deal with the threats. A blanket SHOULD NOT could be at odds with that advice IMHO. For example, one of the mitigations described in RFCF 8188 is to "encapsulate the HTTP message using the application/http media type", and in that case sending the field within the encapsulation would be ok. Would a statement such as the following work?
> 
> Old:
> 
> > When the "aes128gcm" content coding is used, the security considerations in Section 4 of [RFC8188] apply.
> 
> > When the "aes128gm" content coding is used, the security considerations in Section 4 of [RFC8188] apply. Namely, the Unencoded-Digest is considered sensitive information and SHOULD be omitted unless a means of encrypted the Unencoded-Digest field is used.

To which Deb responded

> side channel sentence:  Section 4 para 2 of RFC 8188 uses side channel in the way that I normally see it used, while Section 4.6 uses side-channel (w/ a hyphen) differently. Given this conflicting use (does the hyphen make that big of a difference?), I think dropping the sentence is the best option.
> 
> SHOULD NOT?:  The rework of this sentence into two sentences looks much better.

issues.title: RESUMABLE: Inconsistent status code for `completed-upload` problem type
issues.author: GrantGryczan
issues.body:
[Here](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-14.4-4.6.1) suggests 410:

> If the server retains knowledge of the upload resource but it is not available, the `410 (Gone)` status code can be used; the response could also contain a `Location` header field to indicate the location of the completed upload. The server can use the problem type [[PROBLEM](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#PROBLEM)] of "https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#completed-upload" ([Section 7.2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#completed-upload)) in the response.

[Here](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-7.2-2) shows an example with 400:

> ```
> HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
> Content-Type: application/problem+json
> 
> {
>   "type":"https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#\
>     completed-upload",
>   "title": "upload is already completed"
> }
> ```

[Here](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-11.html#section-14.4-4.6.1) recommends 400:

> Type URI: https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#completed-upload
> Title: Upload Is Completed
> Recommended HTTP status code: 400

As far as I can think of, this problem type can only be used in the scenario where the server knows about the upload resource but it isn't available, which is described in the first reference I cited. So it seems to me 410 would be most appropriate.

Being consistent here would let clients handle this kind of response more reliably. In my client, I'd want to check for status 410 with the `Location` header, but I'm not sure I'd want to do the same for 400 since 400 is more broad.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Thank you for bringing this up. The completed-upload problem type has been removed in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3405, so this issue no longer persists.

The latest draft version on datatracker is -11, but many changes have been merged since then without publishing a new version on datatracker. For the time being, I recommend you to consult https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html for a rendering of the latest iteration from this repository.

issues.title: QUERY: interest in avoiding request-content re-transmission on cache hits?
issues.author: jeswr
issues.body:
**This is a request for interest, not a proposal — I'm gauging whether this is worth pursuing before drafting anything formal.**

RFC 10008 (Section 2.7) puts the request content in a QUERY response's cache key. Unlike GET, a cache cannot tell a hit from a miss until the client has uploaded the (possibly large) content — the very cost caching should avoid. A client cannot avoid this alone, and a shared cache or origin cannot be consulted without receiving the content.

One fix, using only existing fields: the client sends a `Content-Digest` (RFC 9530) and `Expect: 100-continue` and withholds the body; a cache holding a matching result answers without `100 (Continue)`, so the body is never sent. On a miss the cache sends `100 (Continue)`, verifies the content against the digest, and stores. It adds one rule — a request-content digest may key a QUERY response — works on HTTP/2+, and is opportunistic.

Questions:

1. Is this worth solving in the WG, or out of scope?
2. Is `Expect: 100-continue` the right primitive, or a dedicated request precondition?
3. An RFC 10008 companion, or an independent extension?

A rough sketch (kramdown-rfc source) is here: https://gist.github.com/jeswr/7425f74439733762eb347f0a0c199339 — if there's interest I'll develop it into a proper draft.
