pulls.title: rough in server scheduling guidance
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
This tries to address two sets of comments on "what signals are subsumed by priority hints" and "how should a server implement things". 

One aspect of this is setting client expectations straight; they should have a vague idea what will happen if a server plays ball but also expect that servers can and will do whatever they want.

The other aspect of this is describing what signals servers have at their disposal, and presenting some of the gotchas or tradeoffs that might happen if the extensible priority scheme is implemented too matter-of-fact. Some people would like to see more explicit guidance for servers, that's a fine request. However, I don't see how any single scheduling algorithm would work for the range of vendors and deployments that have shown an interest Priorities, so I've focused on the common criteria.

While adding this section, the thought did cross my mind to move the sections on scheduling. We can always do that as a followup.

Closes #1216 and #1232.

pulls.author: jricher
pulls.body: Originally in #1235

reviews.author: ioggstream
reviews.body: imho this PR introduces a very weak normative part. I'd ask for feedback from the community/ML.

comments.body:
At first, thanks @jricher  for asking me to review!

In this paragraph imho we are giving information that does not help interoperability:
- the first sentence states that "the verifier MUST comply with their own requirements, that depend on the use case", but it does not make a clear statement on those requirements;
- the fact that an "expired" signature MAY be accepted can be perceived as an abuse from a signer which instead wants to be in control of the data he signed.

I think that using fields like `nbf`,`iat`,`exp` allows to implement the very same behavior without removing control from the signer, and  putting a solid interoperability ground instead: signer and verifier just have to agree about the interval they accept.

This is clearly IMHO, and probably @martinthomson or @jyasskin can give more useful guidance than me on this subject.

Thanks for the feedback!

There are three objectives that this paragraph is trying to achieve:

- 1st Sentence: Require implementers' time-related constraints to be enforced relative to the Creation Time and Expiration Time properties defined by the spec (as opposed to the Date header, or some proprietary property embedded in the request somewhere).
- 2nd Sentence: Allow verifiers to account for clock skew between the signer and verifier, which may be significant.
- 3rd Sentence: Allow verifiers to reject signatures based on their own requirements, i.e., "I don't care if you're telling me this 2 year old signature fine, I'm not going to accept it."

Open to suggestions on rewording to make these objectives clearer.

> the first sentence states that "the verifier MUST comply with their own requirements, that depend on the use case", but it does not make a clear statement on those requirements;

Explained above, but restating for clarity: the purpose is to ensure that verifiers use the spec-defined Creation Time and Expiration Time properties to evaluate time-related constraints. Would it help to give example constraints? (e.g., a maximum signature age)

> the fact that an "expired" signature MAY be accepted can be perceived as an abuse from a signer which instead wants to be in control of the data he signed.

It may be necessary for a verifier to accept a signature whose Expiration Time is after the current time as measured by the verifier, in order to allow verifiers to account for clock skew between signer and verifier. Maybe it would be better to reframe this as a verifier may offset their current time by some amount to account for clock skew, at least for the purposes of evaluating time-related constraints? That would allow us to bring back in the prohibition on accepting signatures past their Expiration Time.

> I think that using fields like nbf, iat, exp allows to implement the very same behavior

I'm not sure how to interpret this in the context of this spec, since it does not use JWTs.

@richanna can we split the sentences over multiple lines? I'd find it easier to discuss them, eg.

```suggestion
The verifier MUST examine the signature's Creation Time and Expiration Time and evaluate whether they meet the verifier's requirements.  These requirements may vary depending on the use case. 
When comparing Creation Time and/or Expiration Time to a timestamp obtained from another source (e.g., testing that the Expiration Time is later than the local time at the verifier), the verifier MAY allow for some variability due to clock skew between the two timestamp sources (e.g., the signer and the verifier). 
The verifier MAY impose its own maximum age limits, and reject signatures that are too old (i.e., have a Creation Time too far in the past) regardless of whether the signer gave the signatures an Expiration Time.
```

I'd rephrase with something like the following. the 2119 keywords can be tuned, and the rest is just an example... your feedback is welcome!

The passage below ensures the verifier cannot take action beyond the will of the signer.

```
[addition] To take into account clock skew, the signer MAY provide the NotBefore Time parameter
indicating that the signature is valid prior to the Creation Time.

The verifier MUST NOT process a signature where:
- the Expiration Time is in the past;
- the lowest value between NotBefore and Creation Time is in the future.
```

This second sentence ensures that the verifier is free to impose further requirements that may relate - but not limit to - Time parameters, thus giving more freedom to invalidate to the verifier that the previous version:

```
The verifier MAY impose further requirements depending on the use case, including:
- maximum age limits;
- constraints between Creation Time and Exipration Time, or on other signature parameter values;
- (insert here some examples).
```

Some guidance for implementers about how to communicate further requirements could be helpful, because providing extensive information on why a signature is invalid may expose the peers to attacks

```
Those requirements SHOULD be communicated out-of-band or when it is safe to do so MAY be communicated on the wire (eg. in the response payload or headers).
```

I don't have a firm suggestion here, but here are a couple thoughts in the hope that they might help:

* The discussion of "the verifier's requirements" might really be talking about how this header is embedded into a higher-level protocol. The CBOR spec explicitly puts [constraints on CBOR-based protocols](https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-ietf-cbor-7049bis-16.html#name-creating-cbor-based-protoco) and mandates that they specify certain things. For example ["The first layer that does process the semantics of an invalid CBOR item MUST take one of two choices: …. A CBOR-based protocol MUST specify which of these options its decoders take"](https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-ietf-cbor-7049bis-16.html#name-validity-of-items). Maybe this spec could just say that
    > A protocol using HTTP Message Signatures MUST define how it uses 
    >
    > 1. the verifier's current time,
    > 1. the verifier's estimate of any clock skew between the verifier and the signer,
    > 1. the Creation Time, and
    > 1. the Expiration Time 
    >
    > to determine whether the signature is currently valid.

* Handling clock skew is probably more complicated than just offsetting the verifier's current time, and checking that the new time is between the creation and expiration times. Clock skew is inherently uncertain and the verifier's estimate of it might be vulnerable to attack, especially if the verifier is a client. The signed exchange [spec](https://wicg.github.io/webpackage/loading.html#validating-signature) currently says clients may adjust the creation time for skew but mustn't adjust the expiration time. The current Chromium implementation [doesn't adjust for skew at all](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/master:content/browser/web_package/signed_exchange_signature_verifier.cc;l=213;drc=7a942548e0af7397f79bf07b4ca03ade10d04019). Leaving it open for protocols to experiment with, as the current PR text does, is probably the right answer for this PR. 

* My reading of [JWT's "nbf"](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519#section-4.1.5) indicates that they don't take the earliest of the not-before and the creation times when comparing to the current time. Instead, it looks like the ["Issued At"](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519#section-4.1.6) value is used for allowing a signature to be created some time before it's supposed to be valid. The signer also can't prevent the verifier from using whatever "now" value it wants, so I don't think it's worthwhile to add complexity to attempt to prevent that.

* I'm intrigued by the suggestion that saying why a signature was invalid could help attackers. Saying "when it is safe to do so" probably doesn't help protocol designers much, but it could be useful to have some more detail in the Security Considerations. On the other hand, most of the time, saying "the requirements are in the higher-level protocol definition" is likely to be enough.

* I like the examples of constraints verifiers might impose, like "MAY impose its own maximum age limits".

"not before" is not really helpful when dealing with clock skew as it falls under the same limitations. 

I'm personally in favor of defining only the "signature creation time" and having everything else be decided by the verifier. Look at it from the signer's perspective: Why should I be able to tell you how long to accept my signature? I don't have the security context for that, and you can override it anyway and reject it even if I tell you it's not expired yet. 

Better, I think, to mark the creation time and have guidelines on reasonable default expiration and lifetimes for validators, especially if we can state them in terms of a delta from the current time (and possibly the "date" header).

@jyasskin thanks for your feedback!

> A protocol using HTTP Message Signatures MUST define how it uses
> ... to determine whether the signature is currently valid.

This approach is  a good starting point

> The signed exchange spec currently says clients may adjust the creation time for skew
> but mustn't adjust the expiration time
> Chromium implementation doesn't adjust for skew at all

I think that this spec should allow to implement this behavior.

> My reading of JWT's "nbf" indicates that they don't take the earliest

Right, but still it's useful to account for clock skew.

> The signer also can't prevent the verifier from using whatever "now" value it wants

It is true if the verifier purposedly wants to accept expired signatures. OTOH if the verifier 
have a very large skew tolerance the protocol could become vulnerable to replay attacks.

> ... when it is safe to do so ...

This part  was just a placeholder to highlight that security considerations are required. 

@jricher 

> reasonable default expiration and lifetimes

you know my opinion :D  there can be no reasonable default value, because imho it's for the signer to say :D 
not supporting expiration will hinder adoption of this spec in all cases where an expiration is mandatory...

I like the idea of including guidance/requirements for profiling specs, though I would want to aggregate those under a separate "Considerations for Profiling Specifications" (e.g.) section, rather than have them distributed across the document. That makes it easier for profilers to understand what's needed of them, and for non-profilers to ignore stuff that's irrelevant to them.

> Why should [the signer] be able to tell [the verifier] how long to accept [the signer's] signature?

Think of it instead as the signer saying how long they will acknowledge the signature, from a non-repudiation standpoint. That also serves as an implicit recommendation to the verifier – "I'm not trusting this after X, so you probably shouldn't either." The value of X may be informed by how the signer manages their signing keys, or knowledge about the network environment between signer and verifier that the verifier may not have.

At the same time, the signer may not know how the verifier will process the signed message. It may verify the signature on receipt, then forward the whole message (with signature) to an async workflow, which might revalidate the signature minutes or hours later. In such a scenario, the async workflow may need to be looser with expiration time enforcement than recommended by the signer.

There are very few absolute statements we can make about time-related signature validity checks, at least at this level of abstraction. I'm 100% in favor of providing examples, and requiring profiling specifications to define requirements and/or provide guidance. 

With all of this, here is what I think needs to go into the spec:

1. Define Expiration Time as the signer's statement/recommendation to the verifier.
2. Explicitly state that this spec does not impose any limits on how verifier considers Expiration Time (examples of scenarios where a verifier might apply a higher or lower Expiration Time).

pulls.title: Add definition and semantics of applied parameter.
pulls.author: roger-on-github
pulls.body:
Define an 'applied' parameter for Priority HTTP Header Field (responses only). The presence of this parameter indicates that a Priority HTTP Header Field was recognized in the request. Its value indicates that the requested prioritization was applied to the scheduling of the response (or not).

This parameter will be useful to clients whose optimal behavior depends on whether prioritization controls are available. For example, consider a media client that plays a live stream by successively downloading and displaying short media segments as they are produced. The standard model is to assume a connection whose bandwidth is just slightly above the media bit rate. If each media segment is 400ms, the RTT is 100ms, and the client is playing 3 segments behind the live edge, overall performance can be improved by pipelining successive segment requests to amortize the RTT cost -- but only if the remote end does not send responses in parallel (incremental=0). If responses are sent in parallel then the next segment to play will share bandwidth with subsequent response(s) and take longer than 400ms to arrive, causing playback to stall. A client that requests pipelining and discovers that it is not available can then issue future requests in serial, without pipelining them.

In time, it became evident that if people want that sort of resolution, they can create their own X-Header (or the like... High-Precision-Expiration: 234.3342).

Thanks for sharing the historic reasons behind this!

A non-standard `High-Precision-Expiration` header field doesn't enable sub-second expiration precision. The signature's expiration time is defined by the `*expires` parameter. Profiling specs can't change that, they can only add additional expiration semantics on top of that. We should not encourage that though, as it introduces confusion – which expiration rules apply? Do they both have to pass, or just one? etc.

If we want to eliminate decimals, let's express both `*created` and `*expires` in milliseconds.
I'm amazed.  Is the implication here that signers and verifiers have clocks synchronized with sub-second precision?

@martinthomson 

1-  I agree with your consideration
2- In this PR I just wanted to get rid of duplicate definitions leaving the semantic discussion to other issues. Specifically, there are other parts defining expires as a decimal. 
3- We should - in other PRs - discuss the precision of *created and *expires which imho should be expressed with `seconds` precision, but I don't think should be discussed in this PR :D 





 this PR is mostly an editorial one which just removes redundant definitions. 

Once we agree we can delegate definitions

@martinthomson wrote:
> I'm amazed. Is the implication here that signers and verifiers have clocks synchronized with sub-second precision?

Yes, this is true in high-frequency trading systems (for example)... some of which have highly tuned HTTP stacks and are looking at QUIC + HTTP/3 with interest. The legal implications here are that, in some of those systems, that you're supposed to execute orders as you receive them and sometimes the digital signature time matters (from a contractual basis). Here's what a couple of hundred milliseconds in a high-frequency trading system looked like back in 2013 (when we started on this spec):

https://youtu.be/B_k_elbBz8c?t=103

Things move much more quickly now, which is why we might want to drop this use case and get them to create and sign over their own header that has nanosecond (or better) precision. 

All that to say, we could probably back off on the millisecond precision and go to second-based precision if we wanted to support constrained devices that may not be able to do 64-bit integers?

Also, agree with @ioggstream -- all of this is for another PR.

@richanna wrote:
> A non-standard High-Precision-Expiration header field doesn't enable sub-second expiration precision. The signature's expiration time is defined by the *expires parameter. Profiling specs can't change that, they can only add additional expiration semantics on top of that. We should not encourage that though, as it introduces confusion – which expiration rules apply? Do they both have to pass, or just one?

Hmm, I wish things worked like that. :)

For example, the high frequency traders won't create a profiling spec, they'll do whatever they want to with this spec as it's base. Notably, they won't sign over `expires` (since it's optional) and will instead add their own header with nanosecond precision, sign over that, and use the standard signature verification thing PLUS their own verification algorithm that takes their header into account.

That's not necessarily a bad thing, per se... and I admit that this is a corner case... but we should be careful to not prevent this sort of usage of the specification.

> Is the implication here that signers and verifiers have clocks synchronized with sub-second precision?

Yes. In addition to @msporny's high-frequency trading example, this level of clock synchronization is not uncommon within distributed systems.

> For example, the high frequency traders won't create a profiling spec, they'll do whatever they want to with this spec as it's base. Notably, they won't sign over expires (since it's optional) and will instead add their own header with nanosecond precision, sign over that, and use the standard signature verification thing PLUS their own verification algorithm that takes their header into account.

Yes, and that results in a non-standard, non-interoperable implementation. That's what I want to avoid by including support for sub-second expiration times in the spec.

The definition of `created` refers to the canonicalized value, so referring to `created` creates a circular reference. Small change to fix that:

Its canonicalized value is an `sf-integer` containing the signature's Creation Time expressed as the number of seconds since the Epoch, as defined in [Section 4.16](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/V1_chap04.html#tag_04_16) of {{POSIX.1}}.
```

Removing circular reference as mentioned above.

Its canonicalized value is an `sf-decimal` containing the signature's Expiration Time expressed as the number of seconds since the Epoch, as defined in [Section 4.16](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/V1_chap04.html#tag_04_16) of {{POSIX.1}}.

     Zx/Kdrq32DrfakQ6bPsvB9aqZqognNT6be4olHROIkeV879RrsrObury8L9SCEibe

    FquQrXRlmYOh+Hx5D9fJkXcXe5tmAg==:
~~~

Here, the inner list in `Signature-Input` requires folding to insert a whitespace, otherwise you lose delimitation; but `Signature` requires it to be withheld. 

Addressing this with (1) means that you'd need to specify different whitespace folding rules for different headers, which is beyond ugly. It's also likely to cause bugs from people who only read examples...

Also, base64 implementations already ignore whitespace; e.g., 

~~~ python
>>> base64.encodestring(b"foo bar baz")
b'Zm9vIGJhciBiYXo=\n'
>>> base64.decodestring(b'Zm9vIGJhciBiYXo=\n')
b'foo bar baz'
>>> base64.decodestring(b'Zm9vIGJhciBiY Xo=\n')
b'foo bar baz'
>>> base64.decodestring(b'Zm9vIGJhciBiY    Xo=\n')
b'foo bar baz'
~~~

... which means that all we need to do is make a small change to allow whitespace [here](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-header-structure.html#name-byte-sequences) and [here](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-header-structure.html#name-parsing-a-byte-sequence).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks for putting this together. However, I'm not sure if all the text really helps address #1221 now that we obsoleted parameters.

An endpoint that receives a digest field with more than one `digest-algorithm` of the same type has a couple of options. Ignore it altogether (no validation); or do validation and pick the first, pick the last, pick them all, etc. Obviously if you have the same `digest-algorithm` and different `digest-values` there is a chance that your pick could be wrong and validation might fail. We already describe a similar case wrt SRI, saying `This document specifies no requirements or guidance for user agents that experience such cases.`. I think what to do is best left as an implementation choice.

I don't see the value in talking about hypotheticals. We removed parameters because of lack evidence of usage, if someone wants to go that route they can design their own solution, which is what we recommend in Section 8 already.

So in summary, I think at most all we can do is document that it is an implementation decision to pick which entries in the possible set of digests should be verified.

pulls.title: priority: HTTP/2 doesn't have stream limits
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
Fixes #1261.

When the ID discusses PRIORITY_UPDATE frame element ID for HTTP/2,
@MikeBishop rightly pointed out that HTTP/2 doesn't have HTTP/3's 
notion of stream limits. So this text tries to reframe things in
terms of the concurrency window.

I might have gone too far here. Given the guidance we give about
buffering PRIORITY_UPDATE, and the fuziness of concurrency window and
upper limts to idle but openable streams, I don't think its right
to recommend that servers treat it as a conenction error. 

Interested to see what others think of the PR/

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
What about:

> The Prioritized Stream ID SHOULD refer to a stream in the "open", "half-closed (local)", or "idle" state.  Frames where the Prioritized Stream ID refers to a stream in the "half-closed (remote)" or "closed" state can be discarded upon receipt.  The number of streams which have been prioritized but remain in the "idle" state plus the number of active streams (those in the "open" or "half-closed" states; see section 5.1.2 of RFC 7540) MUST NOT exceed the value of the SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS parameter.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: When you talk about "half-closed (local)", are you talking about for the sender or receiver?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I'm talking about for the receiver, but an equivalent formulation for the sender would be possible.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Thanks for the suggestion. I think it makes things clearer. However, I'm wary of getting something wrong with with accounting of different limits that apply to requests and pushes. Does the suggestion accommodate e.g. wanting to reprioritize the 250th push while 250 requests are being made concurrently?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Thank you folks for working on this. I think we are heading towards the right direction, but I have one concern.

@MikeBishop 
>  The number of streams which have been prioritized but remain in the "idle" state plus the number of active streams (those in the "open" or "half-closed" states; see section 5.1.2 of RFC 7540) MUST NOT exceed the value of the SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS parameter.

I'm not fully sure if we can have this MUST. To be precise, I have concerns regarding the possibility of the receiver enforcing this.

IIRC, our design is based on the premise that clients might send a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame on stream zero before sending the request that the PRIORITY_UPDATE frame refers to. If such kind of overtaking is to be permitted (i.e. a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame overtaking the HEADERS frame of the request), I think we have to also allow a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame associated to a new request overtaking a RST_STREAM frame of an old request. If so, a server cannot enforce.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> I'm not fully sure if we can have this MUST.

+1. The present document has a MUST, while preparing this PR my thinking got leaning towards it being a SHOULD.

comments.author: MikeBishop
MikeBishop
comments.body:
> IIRC, our design is based on the premise that clients might send a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame on stream zero before sending the request that the PRIORITY_UPDATE frame refers to.

Also, while this is true, that principle only goes so far.  You can only prioritize a request you _could_ send, even if you haven't yet.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@MikeBishop The question is what assumptions that we can have for HTTP/2 implementations.

When discussing about frame ordering in HTTP/3, I heard these two arguments:
* There is no ordering guarantee between HTTP/3 frames being sent on different streams, because frames (carried by packets) can be dropped.
* HTTP emits bytes to each stream, then the multiplexing layer (i.e. QUIC stack in case of HTTP/3) sends stream bytes being buffered. Therefore, even when packets are not lost, there is no ordering guarantee across multiple streams.

The first argument is specific to QUIC. But the second argument might not be.

Let's assume that we have a HTTP/2 stack designed using that approach (i.e. the one described in the second bullet point). Then, when such a HTTP/2 stack emits a RST_STREAM frame for an existing stream and then a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame for a new stream, the multiplexing layer might send the PRIORITY_UPDATE frame before the RST_STREAM frame. If that happens, the number of open streams observed by the receiver might go above the concurrency limit.

To paraphrase, the side effect of using a MUST is that we'd prohibit the aforementioned this type of design. For me it's not a problem, but I think we need to make sure that everybody is fine with that.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: @kazuho, by that logic, the HEADERS of the new stream might be serialized to the wire before the RST_STREAM of the old one, which would violate the stream limit on the server.  I don't believe that implementation style would be capable of guaranteeing stream limit compliance without a similar level of synchronization to what I'm suggesting.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: @MikeBishop That's a good argument. While I think that an HTTP/2 implementation might be written in a way that it buffers and sends data of control stream asynchronously from other request streams, I do not think we need to be too concerned about potential esoteric designs. In other words, I agree that MUST is fine (and preferable) here.

pulls.title: Describe considerations for server push prioritisation
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
Fixes #1056.

There's been a fair amount of discussion on how a server should 
treat server push prioritization. This PR attempts to be highlight
some of the consideration a server should make and highlight that
there is no general advice, and ergo no safe default.﻿

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> I'm still not happy about moving away from any form of concrete guidance in this document. We're basically saying "we don't know either, figure it out yourself", all but ensuring we will have inconsistent server-side behavior even with this simpler scheme. This will be less problematic for client-side requested resources, but for things like Push it'll be worse if we don't explicitly provide defaults imo.

I'm willing to review PRs that add more guidance without causing other issues. The last attempt I saw fell into the trap of describing a solution that would not be implementable for a wide range of cases or implementations. But that doesn't mean all proposals suffer a similar fate.

That aside, this PR riffs on @kazuho's comments on the issue (#1056), which highlight that server push is a server-driven decision - so implementations should use everything in their toolbox to decide how to multiplex pushed responses with normal responses. Furthermore, based on the differing opinions on #1056 (and that I've heard elsewhere), I don't think there is a safe, commonly-applicable solution to server push defaults. We could arbitrarily pick something for consistency but we risk picking a bad default for some cases.

comments.author: rmarx
comments.body:
@LPardue you really have a knack for rewriting suggested text, the new commit looks great! 

wrt the usefulness of concrete guidance, I agree it's difficult to specify a default that works for all cases. However, then deciding it's better not to specify a default at all is strange to me. 

I feel you have two types of users/implementers here: a) those who really know what they're doing and b) those who don't. If you specify a default, the first type is free to re-imagine that as they see fit, while the second will at least fall back to something consistent/reproducible/predictable. If you don't the first type will still do whatever they please, but the second will come up with very different approaches, making debugging/reasoning harder. 

I feel this is the case for prioritization in general, but especially here for push, as I believe https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1056#issuecomment-593496441 has it right that push is an optimization mainly for web page loads to utilize idle time. From that perspective, I do believe a decent default can be proposed/defined. Even some text like this at the end of the first paragraph in this PR could help:

> When in doubt, it is best to assign a pushed resource a low priority, as push is considered an optional optimization to better utilize idle time and should not interfere with explicit (client-)side signals

Finally though, as said above, I acknowledge the general approach has gone in a different direction for the extensible priorities proposal and don't want to push this too hard in general (at least not at this point in time ;) ).

comments.author: englehardt
comments.body:
@chlily1 Would you mind taking another look at this post-merge with #1384? I've simplified the language in the same-site section regarding how we calculate same-site for requests which are reload navigations resulting from UI. Previously you had:

>  whether that request is same-site or cross-site should be evaluated based on the client of the request that originally navigated to the reloaded page, rather than the client of the request itself.

But consider the example of a user that types in B.com in the address bar (i.e., no client), B.com HTTP redirects to A.com, and then the user manually refreshes A.com. The B.com to A.com redirect makes the initial load cross-site, and thus we'd expect the user-initiated reload to still be cross-site. But if we followed the quoted text above, we'd use the client of the initial load (i.e., null) and conclude the new request should be same-site. I've instead opted to use the criteria you added later in the draft:

> Requests which are the result of a reload navigation triggered through a user interface element are same-site if the reloaded document was originally navigated to via a same-site request.

IMO this is guidance, and therefore should become part of the guidance section that is being added below (maybe as the last paragraph).

I think that this paragraph calls out two design constraints:
* New parameters should not adversely interfere with existing ones.
* Nnew parameters cannot modify the meaning of existing ones.

It might be possible to derive the second point from the first point, though I agree that it's worth pointing out.

OTOH, I tend to think that
* We should better discuss about endpoints and intermediaries.
* Negotiation can be performed in a hop-by-hop manner, so I am hesitant to state that as the requirement. The problem in the design space is the multi-hop nature of HTTP, therefore we should call that out instead.
* This guidance will apply to any existing parameter rather than just "u" and "i."

So how about something like:
_When defining new parameters, care must be taken so that they do not adversely interfere with prioritization performed by existing endpoints or intermediaries that do not understand the newly defined parameter. Since unknown parameters are ignored, new parameters should not change the interpretation of or modify the predefined parameters in a way that is not backwards compatible or fallback safe._

comments.author: PiotrSikora
comments.body:
> So, what's the difference to `http_response_incomplete`, then? Should we just remove `http_response_incomplete` perhaps?

`connection_terminated` can be also sent if the connection is terminated before or when sending HTTP request.

`http_response_incomplete` is more generic and can be sent in response to other events as well (e.g. read/write timeouts).

But more importantly, either can be sent in response to the same event (i.e. connection terminated when receiving HTTP response), depending on the existing proxy implementation or various policies, i.e. "proxy should be as specific as it wants to be" from your last email.

pulls.title: [6265bis] Refactor cookie retrieval algorithm to support non-HTTP APIs
pulls.author: englehardt
pulls.body:
This PR refactors the cookie retrieval algorithm that formerly lived in `The Cookie Header` section to a new `Retrieval Model` section that mirrors the more generic `Storage Model` section for cookie setting.

This didn't require too much legwork in the end. Of note, I've moved us over from working with a [request-target](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-5.3) to [target URI](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-5.1). A request target may not be a full URI (i.e., the "origin form" is a path + query), but we want a full URI so we can call the retrieval algorithm with a Document's URI for non-HTTP APIs. This was mostly a drop-in replacement in the rest of the doc, but I did remove one section that elaborated on extracting a path from the different forms of a request target.

I'm wondering whether we want to keep the `non-HTTP API` section at all. This only specifies one type of non-HTTP API (i.e., those with an associated Document); I'm not sure if there are any other non-HTTP APIs that user agents implement? And that functionality is already specified in more detail in HTML [here](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-document-cookie). I wonder whether it's better to just update HTML with a reference to the new Retrieval Algorithm once we release a new version of the draft. cc/ @annevk for input.

Addresses #1233, #769, and #1163.

reviews.author: kazuho
reviews.body:
@yangchi Thank you for your efforts.

Aside from what @LPardue says, I think that we might want to use QUIC v1 as an example of transport that allows the application to transmit something else than what has been deemed lost. Otherwise, when QUIC v2 comes out, we'd have to update the priority draft just to allow such behavior.

I like your point about PTO - I wonder if we could generalize that altogether, possibly to something like:
* application may send something new rather than what has been deemed lost, and
* application may retransmit data when it is probable that that data has been lost

by using the guidelines of QUIC v1 as examples.

comments.body:
```suggestion
Transport protocols such as TCP and QUIC provide reliability by detecting packet
losses and retransmitting lost information. While this document specifies
HTTP-layer prioritization, its effectiveness can be further enhanced if the
transport layer factors priority into scheduling both new data and
retransmission data. The remainder of this section discusses considerations when
using QUIC.
```

This text you proposed is good. This suggestion is editorial to tighten things up a little. 

~~I've also removed the MAY since levying requirements on a transport protocol seems odd for this draft. IMO it should be enough to demonstrate the advantages and let people make up their own minds on what to do.~~

Update: actually I think we can levy the requirement on how an HTTP/3 application uses QUIC, but we can do that below.

```suggestion
{{!I-D.ietf-quic-transport}}, Section 13.3 states "Endpoints SHOULD prioritize
retransmission of data over sending new data, unless priorities specified by the
application indicate otherwise". When an HTTP/3 application uses the priority
scheme defined in this document, the QUIC transport implementation SHOULD
consider the relative priority of streams when scheduling of new data and
retransmission data. For example, if one stream with higher urgency has new data
to send and another stream with lower urgency has retransmission data to send, a
QUIC transport is more likely to fulfil the application's intent if it chooses
to schedule the higher urgency new data before the lower urgency retransmission
data. While there is no requirement on QUIC implementations to implement the
extensible priority scheme, an aligned prioritization model can help
applications manage scheduling expectations.
```

I actually think we can be more direct here and state that QUIC implementations that support application-indicated priorities SHOULD factor them into retransmission decisions. Maybe @rmarx has an opinion here.

The rest of this is just some editorializing.

```suggestion
{{?I-D.ietf-quic-recovery}}, Section 6.2.4 also highlights consideration of
application priorities when sending probe packets after PTO timer expiration. An
QUIC implementation supporting application-indicated priorities might use the
relative priority of streams when choosing probe data. 
```

I think it is clearer to just make this a consideration point that implementers should be aware of, so removing normative language.

I'm not sure we have enough data at this point to know if it should be a SHOULD or a MAY... AFAIK nobody has really researched the impact of this. IIUC FB implemented this, but hasn't looked too closely at metric impact yet (though I assume it's not massive in either direction or it would have been spotted). 

I'm mainly thinking about (theoretical) situations where there's just a single packet lost of a low prio stream and that's the only outstanding/remaining data for that stream, where it might make sense to retrans that packet before higher prio data etc. (you can extrapolate that to X packets, where X is a certain percentage of estimated cwnd etc.). Similar remarks can be made for potential starvation, app-layer logic that might abort streams if they take too long to complete, etc. 

I'm also not sure how this could cascade in a persistent-quic-tunnel-from-edge-to-origin setup where this connection multiplexes data for many clients at the same time (though that can be generally said from this new prioritization setup).

I would say it's probably best to go with the conservative MAY for now, mainly to make sure people are aware of this possibility.

Thanks Robin. 

Since we don't have much info I agree it's hard to make any recommendation. We should be wary of suggsting something that turns out to be bad.

 To paraphrase the point I was trying to communicate, QUIC transport says "SHOULD prioritize restransmissions unless there's some communicated application-intent" and here we are saying "if the transport layer speaks a compatible model, it really SHOULD factor in stream priorities, but what chooses to do is still up to it". 

If you agree with the premise of that point, I think I can highlight it better by changing words around a bit such as

> 
            When an HTTP/3 application uses the priority
            scheme defined in this document and the QUIC transport implementation
            supports application indicated stream priority, a transport that considers
            the relative priority of streams when scheduling both new data and
            retransmission data might better match the expectations of the application.
            However, here are no requirements on how it chooses to schedule based on
            this information because the decision depends on several factors and trade-offs,
            A transport could prioritize new data for a higher urgency stream over retransmission data
            for a lower priority stream, or it could prioritize retransmission data over new data 
            irrespective of urgencies.
I think this newer text indeed better reflects what we should be saying here, and also highlights the tradeoffs.

```suggestion
application indicate otherwise". When an HTTP/3 application uses the priority
scheme defined in this document and the QUIC transport implementation supports
application indicated stream priority, a transport that considers the relative
priority of streams when scheduling both new data and retransmission data might
better match the expectations of the application. However, here are no
requirements on how a transport chooses to schedule based on this information
because the decision depends on several factors and trade-offs, It could
prioritize new data for a higher urgency stream over retransmission data for a
lower priority stream, or it could prioritize retransmission data over new data

```suggestion

@LPardue  thoughts?

thanks, this helps.

I think this is actually a good example of a danger we point out in the Server scheduling section

> At the same urgency level, an incremental request of indeterminate length followed by a non-incremental large resource.

So how about tweaking your suggestion to say something like 

"When a request stream carries the CONNECT method, the scheduling guidance in this document applies to all DATA frames on the stream. If the request is unsuccesful, there might be DATA frames that carry HTTP content. If the request is successful, DATA frames carry payload related to a TCP connection. This is often handled as an unstructured byte stream of indeterminate length, where chunks are processed incrementally. Clients can send CONNECT requests with the incremental parameter. Servers can use the incremental parameter, the CONNECT method itself, the response status, and other factors as input into their scheduling; see {{server-scheduling}}."

Maybe just "all frames on the stream", not making DATA special in any way.  Then you don't need to talk about the protocol bits (which other documents cover).

Regarding incremental, I would just give permission to treat CONNECT as incremental even if the priority didn't indicate that it was.  Nothing else makes sense really.

> Regarding incremental, I would just give permission to treat CONNECT as incremental even if the priority didn't indicate that it was. Nothing else makes sense really.

I'm not entirely sure. A client could do interesting things like create one CONNECT tunnel for each priority level, and when it is about to send a HTTP request, choose one of the tunnel based on the request priority.

EDIT. I'm not saying that clients should do such clever things, but it's better to recommend clients explicitly express their intentions (e.g., incremental), to give room for them to do clever things.

The tunnel doesn't know that you are using this for HTTP requests.

The problem I have with non-incremental is that you can't use the CONNECT tunnel for anything.  It's fundamentally TCP, which requires that you have a continuous exchange of bytes.  There is no sense in saying non-incremental because while that implies a very particular exchange pattern: this stream is not useful to me unless I have all of it.  

As soon as you have TLS inside a tunnel, non-incremental is non-viable.

I can see value in having priority on different tunnels, that's a good way of (somewhat) dealing with remote nodes who aren't able to do proper prioritization.  But non-incremental: that implies a very particular interaction model.

I think we agree that some sort of bandwidth sharing is necessary for CONNECT requests, as TCP connections often have idle timeouts. The question is if incremental is sufficient and adequate.

Regarding sufficiency, there is at least one corner case. Consider the case where one H3 stream is used to carry GET (u=0) and CONNECT (u=3,i). GET (u=0) would absorb all available bandwidth until that response is complete. This is not good, therefore, we need to give some more advice than "assume incremental."

Regarding adequacy, incremental assumes a particular way of bandwidth sharing; i.e. treat all streams equal. As stated above, that might not always what we'd want.

Taking a step back, idle timeout is an issue even for intermediaries forwarding HTTP messages. Let's say that the intermediary is connected to upstream using HTTP/1.1. If that intermediary does not read more data from upstream for some amount of time, the upstream might consider that the HTTP/1.1 connection has stalled, and close it. To prevent that, the intermediary has to give a small amount of bandwidth to that HTTP message, even when another message of higher precedence is inflight.

To summarize, I think the advice that we might want to give are:
* servers SHOULD give some bandwidth to streams for which idle timeout is a concern (regardless of they carry HTTP messages or CONNECT data)
* CONNECT clients can set the incremental flag if it wants the server to provide fairness between the CONNECT requests that the client issues.
Regarding the first bullet point, I've opened https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1562. I would appreciate your feedback. Thank you in advance.

```suggestion
An intermediary serving an HTTP connection might split requests over multiple
backend connections. When it applies prioritization rules strictly, low priority

If you have to start guessing for ANYTHING it's a bad idea to sign it. We haven't filled out the security considerations section yet but this is a key point for this protocol.

If they do not ignore it, they are broken already.

I agree with the concerns about signing individual parameters in a lot of cases, but I also think that the tradeoffs are going to be worth it for a lot of applications.

```suggestion
The `Accept-Signature` HTTP header field is a Dictionary Structured Header {{!RFC8941}} containing the metadata for one or more requested message signatures to be generated from content within the target HTTP message. Each member describes a single message signature. The member's name is an identifier that uniquely identifies the requested message signature within the context of the target HTTP message. The member's value is the serialization of the desired covered content of the target message, including any allowed signature metadata parameters, using the serialization process defined in {{signature-params}}.
```
It might be good to mention that responses which are the result of negotiation need to either be uncacheable, or carry a `Vary` header field.

All responses from resources that support such signature negotiation SHOULD either be uncacheable or contain a `Vary` header field that lists `Accept-Signature`, in order to prevent a cache from returning a response with a signature intended for a different request.
```

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body: @LPardue now it's Specification Required :)
Mark's feedback on case-sensitivity of checksum.

```suggestion
defined in {{algorithms}}.
```

With the sentence above, it wasn't clear to me what was supposed to be compared and how. Hence this suggestion.

```suggestion
Every digest-algorithm defines its computation procedure and
encoding output. Unless specified otherwise, comparison of
encoded output is case-sensitive.  
```

as per my comment on the issue, I think specification required is fine. So the suggestion here is

```suggestion
Registrations or this registry use the Specification
Required policy (Section 4.6 of {{!RFC8126}}).
The designated expert or experts verify that a
specification exists and is readily accessible.
```

+1 to Specification Required. You could also shorten it to "This registry uses the Specification
Required policy (Section 4.6 of {{!RFC8126}}).

In case of "Specification Required", how to ensure interoperability with the overall HTTP work if the Specification is published outside IETF (eg. W3C, OASIS, ...) ? 

Further notes are here https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1533#issuecomment-916462729

You don't.  It might be nice in theory to insist on people only deploying things that have been carefully designed and vetted, but that doesn't happen.  If you make the requirements on registrations very difficult to achieve, what you end up with is people not registering things.  They will still use the codepoints and deploy the code, so what you end up with is no reliable record of what codepoints are safe to use.  Even "Specification Required" can be too much to avoid that happening, but we should at least encourage people to write down what they are doing.

```suggestion
This registry uses the Specification
Required policy (Section 4.6 of {{!RFC8126}}).
```

Thanks, I see. I think my concerns are:
* The paragraph proposed is a mixture of problem statement and solution. That does not fit well into the current structure of the section that writes down the problems and then explaining the solution in the final paragraph below. I think we'd better cut down this paragraph to a problem statement, at the same time adding text to the final paragraph of the section to explain why the particular solution was chosen (if necessary).
* As a problem statement, I'm not sure if it suites the most to state that the problem as about intermediaries. The insight that we have is that the crux of the problem is that Semantics does not have the concept of a "connection." Not only intermediaries but also HTTP client library API suffer from the problem. I'm fine with using intermediaries as an example.

So maybe something like: _HTTP/2 priority signal of an HTTP request is expressed as a value relative to that of other requests sharing the same HTTP/2 connection. Such design requires the understanding of the underlying protocol version and how the requests are coalesced in order to use priority signals. This has been a burden to HTTP endpoints that generate or forward requests at the HTTP Semantic layer._
I'm happy with whatever you two prefer.

pulls.title: Standardize maximum Expires/Max-Age
pulls.author: arichiv
pulls.body:
The current spec is ambiguous on (1) what the maximum `Expires`/`Max-Age` attribute values can be and (2) whether the two must be consistent. This resolves both by requiring:

1. The maximum attribute value to be 400 days in the future or less
2. The maximum set for Max-Age and Expires be consistent.

Why 400 days? The goal was to get close to 13 months so that functions one might perform annually (e.g., selecting insurance benefits for the next year) would work even as specific dates varied slightly. Since `Expires` deals in a specific date while `Max-Age` deals in delta-seconds, it seems ideal to select a value with an unambiguous meaning. If the cap were set at 13 months (instead of 400 days) in the future, the maximum TTL varies by the month it was set in and whether or not it's a leap year.

Who is compliant with this modification? Currently, only Safari sets a cap lower than 400 days (one week).

closes #1600

comments.body:
Not sure that I fully grok this sentence.  What are you intended to say here?  That is might be hard to set a stream limit?  That's true, but you don't really need to say it unless you are about to offer some advice.

If you are saying that the stream limits live in the QUIC stack such that an HTTP/3 implementation can't know if PRIORITY_UPDATE was permitted, that's a very interesting point I hadn't considered.  It's a real one though.  What are you going to do about that?  Say that endpoints might buffer unpaired PRIORITY_UPDATE up to their own limit and discard any extra?  Recommend expanding the API surface from the transport piece?

The comment about concurrency limits has been there a while. I know I wrote it but struggling to remember the exact motivation. It did seem important at the time but also a bit weasly, so it had a TODO next to it. On the path towards WGLC I extracted the TODO into issue https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1569 and, for lack of any feedback ever on the TODO, I removed it it as resolution to the issue.

Paging @kazuho in case this was something related to his implementation. 

Speaking for Cloudflare's quiche, we added an API to query how many streams you could open on the  peer (the other side's limits) but don't have one to query local concurrency. A user would configure limits at the start of a connection with initial_streams_{uni, bidi} and we attempt to use that as the target for how many stream credits to allow (issuing credits when streams are closed). At lot of this happens transparently to the application layer.

Thanks for the context Lucas.

We widened the interface to the transport for that too.  But not everyone will have that option.  This depends on a new interface that is not described in [RFC 9000](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/rfc9000.html#name-operations-on-streams).

Regarding the number of PRIORITY_UPDATE frames that a server should buffer, I think we need to state three things:
* Most recently-received PRIORITY_UPDATE frame for each request stream yet to be opened SHOULD be buffered.
* There should be enough slots in that buffer, so that prioritization information would not be lost when the client tries to fully utilize the concurrency.
* The number of slots MUST be bounded to avoid attacks.

I think that the first two points are already stated in Section 7. Regarding this paragraph, I think the problem with the text that we have is that it is discussing interoperability issues rather than security issues. This is Security Considerations section and what we need to state here is the attack and the mitigation (i.e. the third bullet point).

EDIT. Regarding what we do in h2o (our HTTP/3 stack), we [error-close the connection when receiving a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame carrying a Stream ID that it above the current limit](https://github.com/h2o/h2o/blob/6f6ecfc734dfaf30f3be9d62de81b7a327259ea9/lib/http3/server.c#L1441-L1443). But as you might have pointed out, QUIC stacks might not provide an API that allows HTTP/3 clients to prevent such PRIORITY_UPDATE frames from being sent.

> The number of slots MUST be bounded to avoid attacks.

Section 7 says:

> Holding PRIORITY_UPDATE frames for each stream requires server resources, which can can be bound by local implementation policy.

and so what I'm hearing here is we should consider boosting that `can be bound` to `MUST be bound` and then we can note the practical problems that might exist.

Then, in the security considerations, we'll simply reference to section 7.

Sounds like a new issue to me, so I'll do that.

pulls.title: Split the HTTP Priority Parameters registry in two
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
Fixes #1717.

We want registration policies that encourage extensions. We also need to bear in mind the existing guidance about how the base scheme, urgency and incremental, are used/applied by clients, servers and intermediaries. The scheme is malleable but it can't implementations are unlikely to be able to swap out prioritization wholesale.  This puts reviewers into an awkward position, so we should document clear guidance on registration review and how or when it might be rejected (airing on the side of permissiveness).

Fortunately, we had some of these considerations already written down. So this change makes those criteria more specific and actionable.

The other important part is that keys are strings, so clashes are less likely. However, given the constraints above and the attractiveness of short key lengths for repeated information, there might be pressure on the finite supply of the 25 remaining single-character keys. So split the IANA registry in two, and place additional Specification Required policy on those precious keys.

reviews.author: martinthomson
reviews.body: Seems like a good idea.

comments.body:
This is going to be a bone of contention in future.

Any person arguing for inclusion of a new parameter can argue that degradation of performance due to their new thing not being understood is why it needs to be added.

I would avoid this clause entirely.  Let people break things; trying to stop them is futile.

I see your point. But this clause is based on the spirit of what we intended in the registration guidance section. Due to the nature of this extension mechanism, we should always expect new parameters to be ignored by some subset. The "invariants" of this scheme are urgency and incremental. Implementations of this specification are expected to know how those apply, even if they choose to ignore them. 

We want to encourage compatible extension and guide folks away from incompatible extension that realistically might struggle to work across the intended deployment targets. The further the elastic band stretches from the basic scheme we have here, the harder it might snaps back. (Luke's comments on the challenges of extension, with no other negotiation mechanism, that alter the design premises of this scheme (for the valid application of his use case) highlight how hard it might get).

Now I admit the reviewer might not be the right person to do the guidance bit. But if then by that argument we give no instruction for how the reviewer can reject anything, which seems like a lame duck. 

Would it make any difference to lower the barrier for a provisional registration of extensions?

This is classic registry philosophy.  That is: do you expect your experts to act as police?

Let's say that someone adds a new field called "inv".  What is does is invert the urgency value.  Clearly this would create some interesting behaviour.  Should the experts be responsible for blocking the registration?

My answer there is "no".  The idea is bad, but if someone is using that parameter to mean that, then the marginal utility gained by avoiding multiple conflicting uses is greater than the harm caused by having a bad idea in the registry.  It is easy to ignore bad ideas.

I would expect experts to push back here.  They might ask questions and even provide some guidance.  But these rules exist to give them a solid footing when they come to reject something.  If someone is resolute in registering a bad idea we should thank them for registering it.  Many people will not register.  More so if you throw up hurdles.

When it comes to encouraging people to do the right thing, my answer is to build a library of good options.  I can think of several and the draft even mentions a couple.  Lead by example.

```suggestion
Since each HTTP request can have associated priority signals, there is value
```

While I do like the idea of the protocol police, I'm a big fan of [preventative policing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preventive_police) through educational outreach and community engagement. 

Since we are using Structured Fields here, the only real registry danger is name conflict, DoS, or tragedy of the short-name commons. 

I accept your points and think losing this clause for experts (but keeping it in the extender's guidance pack) is a good path forward.
@martinthomson  I went 180 in the clause, in order to make it abundantly clear that reviewers are not enforcers in this area.

This PR add a grammar that corresponds to the algorithm parsing section.  

A grammar currently exists in section 4.4.1 but it's much stricter than what user agents actually enforce, and there have been several instances where that grammar was assumed to correspond with the cookie parsing algorithm defined in section 5. ```
Ignoring the attribute would cause it to have a `SameSite` of `Strict`, but per the spec it should have a `SameSite` of `Default`.

I'll update this to be something like `samesite-value     = "Strict" / "Lax" / "None" / *optional-value`
We'll need to update this to reflect that `Domain` and `Domain=` are valid and must not be ignored (Ex: `name=value; Domain=example.com; Domain=`)
Same with `Domain=.`

Actually I think I like using `ignored-value` instead of `optional-value` here, since anything but the three listed aren't used directly (but still constitute a valid `SameSite` attribute). 

@sbingler you are correct that we could omit the string literals, although IMO the grammar is more immediately useful to readers if we include them. Let me know if you feel strongly otherwise, though.

```suggestion
case-insensitive (e.g. "Secure" is equivalent to "secure" and "sEcUrE").
```

This is a pattern of ABNF definition we're not using in http-core anymore. Note that by defintion, any valid cookie-av will match extension-av (right?).

It would be better to just define the common syntax of any cookie-av, and then define seperate ABNFs for the individual values.
Good point - I moved the attribute grammars into separate ABNFs. Thanks for the feedback!

At the time of parsing when "Expires" is detected, the parsing into name and value has already happened.

Thus, I would just define the syntax for the value, as in:

~~~
expires-v = cookie-date
~~~

Note this is how multi-level grammars are defined in the core HTTP specs as well.

Ah, I see - thank you for the example @reschke.

It seems like we'd lose a bit of completeness if we only include the attribute value in the grammar.  For instance, the grammar wouldn't explicitly tie the "Expires" keyword to the Expires attribute, and wouldn't convey whether "ExPiReS" is treated the same way as "Expires".  Having the grammar format used here align with the convention in the core HTTP specs seems desirable as well, though.

Does anyone else have thoughts on this?

> . For instance, the grammar wouldn't explicitly tie the "Expires" keyword to the Expires attribute

It by definition can't do that anyway, as long as the grammar allows for extensibilty - an ABNF-driven parser would simply switch to the code branch for new attributes, and then the value syntax would remain unconstrained.

You really can't do this in ABNF; it needs to be done in prose.

If our goal is to have an ABNF-driven parser function correctly, it seems like we'd need to go back to the using the previous definition of `cookie-av`. To address the original concern of "any valid cookie-av will match extension-av", maybe we could do something like the following:
```
cookie-av          = expires-av / max-age-av / domain-av /
                     path-av / secure-av / httponly-av /
                     samesite-av / extension-av

extension-av       = 1*cookie-name-octet BWS extension-eq-value BWS
extension-eq-value = "" / ("=" BWS optional-value)
    ; attributes solely matching extension-av should be treated as unrecognized by
    ; cookie parsers strictly conforming to this RFC
```

What do you think?

I don't think you can solve this by adding prose (comments) to the ABNF.

The ABNF should be something that can translate to how a parser processes the input. Parsers in general parse first generic structures, then look at specific micro syntaxes of values.

That's what we're doing in the base spec, and that's what I'll keep suggesting to do.

pulls.title: Security and Privacy Considerations for Signatures
pulls.author: jricher
pulls.body: Adds security and privacy considerations and applies various cleanups including those suggested by early security review

comments.body: Would it make sense to recommend that signature verifiers be structured to return a whole message instead of a boolean result, so that they can strip out the unverified components?

I think "the verifier processes the message as a whole" conflates two components of the system: the piece that verifies the signature, and the piece that then processes the message. Could you introduce separate terms for those?

```suggestion
A common attack against signature systems is to force a signature collision, where the same signature value can be applied to multiple different inputs. Since this specification relies on reconstruction of the input string based on an HTTP message, and the list of components signed is fixed in the signature, it is difficult but not impossible for an attacker to effect such a collision. An attacker would need to manipulate the HTTP message and its covered message components in order to make the collision effective.
```
And I'm not sure that "be applied to" is the right term here ... "where the same signature value can verify multiple different inputs"?
I don't understand "could lead to the verifier signature checking".

```suggestion
However, the HTTP Message Signature standard allows for flexibility in determining which components are signed precisely so that a given application can choose the appropriate portions of the message that need to be signed, avoiding problematic components. For example, a web application framework that relies on rewriting query parameters might avoid use of the `@query` content in favor of sub-indexing it using `@query-params` instead.
```
I think?

In systems that allow both symmetric and asymmetric signatures in the same format, there have also been attacks where the attacker replaces, say, RSA with HMAC and uses the public key to generate a "valid" signature: https://auth0.com/blog/critical-vulnerabilities-in-json-web-token-libraries/#RSA-or-HMAC-.

https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html#name-application-of-http-message mentions this kind of consideration, but I think it should also be in the security considerations.
Good catch, that is supposed to be "lead to the verifier skipping signature checking". Very important verb there...
I think that works, we'll play with the language here.

By "verifier" we mean "the party that verifies the message with its signature" and not "the verification function". The function returns a boolean with the message as input, so the caller of that function would have access to the whole message anyway. I think having more precise terms isn't a bad idea, as long as we're using them consistently.

Should have been:

```suggestion
However, the HTTP Message Signature standard allows for flexibility in determining which components are signed precisely so that a given application can choose the appropriate portions of the message that need to be signed, avoiding problematic components. For example, a web application framework that relies on rewriting query parameters might avoid use of the `@query` content in favor of sub-indexing the query value using `@query-params` instead.
```
That's what this section was getting at, but I think it's worth calling out this specific example as well. Thanks!
See other comment: the verifier calls the verification function and so the boolean response makes sense here, but more precise term usage is a good call.

reviews.author: martinthomson
reviews.body: This is very long.  I'm afraid I ran out of time and didn't read it all.  Maybe I'll get back to it later.

comments.body: Is your goal to include the quotes in the string that is appended? Maybe you want "\`\n\`" instead.
This is only true if your attacker is not involved in the exchange.

Consider reading (or even paraphrasing) [Section 8.1 of RFC 3275](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3275#section-8.1).  That is a poor mechanism - mostly for the reasons I think that this message signing approach is poor - but that text is very much relevant.
Are you talking about weak cryptography or the ability of an attacker to - given a signature - generate a new key pair under which that signature will validate successfully?

```suggestion
While it is possible for an attacker to substitute the signature parameters value or the signature value separately, the [signature input generation algorithm](#create-sig-input) always covers the signature parameters as the final value in the input string. This strongly binds the signature input with the signature value in a way that makes it much more difficult for an attacker to perform a partial substitution of inputs.
```
This is a good point to talk about key validity lifetimes and other countermeasures for theft.

This is the second time that you have mentioned "just turn it off".  I get that you want to acknowledge this tension that is created by security mechanisms that make things not work, but I think that you should be a little more careful in phrasing these to avoid creating the wrong impression.
The assumption on the use of TLS is that TLS is not itself compromised. Can this be stated more clearly? This section does still need to point to BCP195.

Ah thanks -- the other section was added after we wrote this paragraph, we can remove that text here. And I agree, it does need to be phrased carefully. However, I have seen too many security systems not acknowledge the fact that when security gets in the way of functionality, functionality naturally wins. I think that's particularly true for something like this, as described in the other section.

These security considerations make me want to reframe signature verification as "verify a signature against your requirements" rather than just "verify a signature against its input". E.g., verification steps are:
1. Identify the set of message components required/expected/allowed to be signed, keys and algs permitted, etc.
2. Verify that the signature input matches requirements.
3. Verify that the corresponding signature matches signature input and message. (i.e., existing verification instructions)

This highlights the importance of identifying requirements and testing against those first and foremost - a "valid" signature that doesn't cover what's needed is irrelevant - and emphasizes this as a critical part of the verifier's job. As it is, this is tacked on at the end of the verification process. I want to encourage library interfaces that look like `verify(message, required_components)` not `verify(message)`.

I agree with that in principle, and I get where it's coming from. We've got some precedent in the world of JOSE implementations where you send not only the JWS but also the required header and (sometimes) body claims for a JWT. My only concern is that there is a separate definitive step of doing the signature verification calculation, and we don't want that to get lost in the overall discussion. How can we frame it so that we mostly talk about the larger piece but still can call out the smaller piece when necessary? Namely when we define how the algorithms are applied.
typo: `The intermediary can ad its own signature` => `The intermediary can add its own signature`

My experience with inline links is that xml2rfc makes a real hash of this format.  Try this:

```suggestion
A targeted field for a particular class of cache can be defined by requesting registration in the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Field Name Registry ([](https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-fields/)), listing this specification as the specification document. The Comments field of the registration should clearly define the class of caches that the targeted field applies to.
```

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I recall the comments about the security section in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/1724 but not any issue specific to bashing in the motivation section, maybe it was done on the mailing list? Either way, thanks for making the PR. I think there are some useful edits in there but do think that some of the statements should remain. I've noted those in line.
It seems odd to link to HTTP/2 when this section states disabling RFC 7540.

This paragraph reflects reality, I don't see it as bashing. I would like to keep something along these lines but can live with an edited down version. The difficulty for servers in interpreting or operating with relationship-based trees is one core part of the extensible priorities scheme. Some of the following edits in this PR also present text that overlooks tree troubles, I suspect we editors might want to keep that. @kazuho any thoughts?
I can live without this paragraph
I can live without this paragraph.
This is a nice simplification of the existing text.
My mistake.  I will revert this piece.

I wasn't pointing to this in particular as bashing, but more the overall effect of the section.

I thought that I addressed the most pertinent points in the text about request relationships.  More importantly, I think that h2bis covers this topic adequately and we don't need redundant text about the many ways in which RFC 7540 failed.

```suggestion
signals.

Prioritization can use information that servers have about resources or the
order in which requests are generated. For example, a server, with knowledge of
an HTML document structure, might want to prioritize the delivery of images
that are critical to user experience above other images. But with RFC 7540
trees, it is difficult for servers to understand their intent and act or
intervene accordingly, because clients build their priority tree in a unique
way.
```

I might change these paragraphs like above with the intent being:
* It's better to divide the paragraph after pointing out one problem.
* Lack of signalling method is a result of a prioritization scheme that cannot be intervened by the server. We should point out the latter rather than the former.
* Therefore, we can move the argument about intervention (coordination) from the removed paragraph at the top to here.

I think we can remove this sentence, by moving the point made by the last sentence below (please see my review comment below).

Regarding other sentences, I'm not sure if they are a problem related to Extensible Priorities, and do not have an argument against removing them. Also, I'd point out that the last paragraph of this PR might imply the discussion here; it says that rich flexibility was deemed unnecessary for the web use-case.

```suggestion
alternative to RFC 7540 stream priority (see {{Section 5.3 of RFC7540}}).
```

The split in the paragraph is good.

I'm less sure about the addition.  Though I think I can agree with your intent, I don't think that the proposed scheme fixes this problem.  Overselling this is worse than the h2 bashing.

What I think you might reasonably say is that the complex/rich signals in h2 were often too complicated to act on directly, which forced servers to interpret the signals and translate them into something the server could understand and use.  But as different clients produced under the same conditions, this meant that there was no standard (some would create a chain, some would weight then, some would use placeholder nodes, it was a mess). The result was just a series of proprietary signals that only *appeared* to share the same mechanism.  The goal of this document is to produce a signal that is simple enough to be acted upon directly, with no translation.

Now, whether it is worth saying all that, when so much else has been said in criticism of the design, and the design here is already well justified, I don't know.  It's a fairly difficult concept to explain well. I concluded that it is better to just not bother.

I might argue that without the added text, existing text is just verbose, because it talks about server-driven prioritization without any relation to RFC 7540 priority trees or Extensible Priorities.

That said, I might agree that we can be even more concise. IMO the two points we have to state are:
* Extensible Priorities defines a method for combining client- and server-driven prioritization signals.
* Some servers did not fully support RFC 7540 priority trees.

The second point can be left to http2bis, but I think that the former have to be kept here, as the intent of this section is to describe the key differences between the two prioritization signals.

I'd be fine with just listing these points without going into the detailed explanation that we have now.

I see your point.  How about:

> With RFC 7540 it is difficult for servers to integrate signals from clients into prioritization as the same conditions could result in very different signaling from different clients. This document describes signaling that is simpler and more constrained, requiring less interpretation and allowing less variation.
I like how concise the text is :+1: Thank you.

+1 strong and concise. If you could update the PR with that text, I think we are good to go.

(I hesitate to push the suggestion myself in case I mangle it, but I'll do that if your short on time)
Mangling complete.
Thank you.

Fixup script that I used:

```py

import fileinput, re

label = re.compile('^github-issue-label: (\S+)')
note = re.compile('^--- note_')
middle = re.compile('^--- middle')

is_note = False

for line in fileinput.input():
    m = label.match(line)
    if m:
        print(f"""venue:
  group: HTTP
  type: Working Group
  home: https://httpwg.github.io/
  mail: ietf-http-wg@w3.org
  arch: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/ietf-http-wg/
  repo: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/labels/{m[1]}""")
    elif note.match(line):
        is_note = True
    elif middle.match(line):
        is_note = False
    if not is_note:
        print(line.rstrip())
```
