comments.body:
The point I believe @jricher made in #1841 is that it's just as easy to downgrade to weak algorithms by stripping off better ones. Since digest has no in built mechanisms to prevent downgrade, if people care then they should protect the digest fields. That could be done, for example, by using TLS or digital signatures. It could also be done by endpoints restricting the algorithms that they support - potentially rejecting processing of messages that do not contain a digest contained in their supported set,

The algorithm substitution attack mentioned in the next paragraph and described in RFC6211 seems to be something a bit different. It seems to predicate on the verification depending on the length of the hash, not the so much algorithm itself. Since the algorithm identifier is always included in digest, I don't know how much this one applies. Perhaps if there is a digest algorithm that encodes its parameters in the representation-data-digest, as we suggest in Section 1.3. But again the only way to protect from manipulation of field values is to use something like TLS or sigs.

So how about rephrasing the paragraph addition to something like:

While algorithm agility allows the migration to stronger algorithms it does not prevent the use of weaker algorithms. Digest and Content-Digest do not provide any mitigiations for downgrade or substitution (see Section 1 of {{?RFC6211}} attacks of the digest-algorithm. To protect against such attacks, endpoints could restrict their set of supported algorithms to stronger ones and protect the value of Digest and Content-Digest by using TLS and/or digital signatures.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
If you are talking about the standard assumptions about what a cryptographic hash function provides, you need to talk about what properties you are getting (or, conversely, what the not-secure options don't provide).  So not just collisions, but first- and second-preimage resistance.

Justin also points out that you need to consider the target security level in making any recommendation.  As in, it might be that a 256-bit hash suffices in some cases, but not others.  I think that is secondary to what I think we need to be saying here, but it's probably worth including something.

> The "standard" algorithms listed in this document are suitable for many purposes, including adversarial situations where hash functions might need to provide resistance to collision, first-preimage and second-preimage attacks.  Algorithms listed as "insecure" either provide none of these properties, or are known to be weak (see {{NO-MD5}} and {{NO-SHA1}}).
>
> For adversarial situations, which of the "standard" algorithms are acceptable will depend on the level of protection the circumstances demand. As there is no negotiation, endpoints that depend on a (digest|hash) for security will be vulnerable to attacks on the weakest algorithm they are willing to accept.

reviews.body: As mentioned in the linked issue, this PR is not complete: there needs to be a discussion of collisions and, more broadly, algorithm selection in the security considerations, since this draft leaves the choice of which algorithms to accept entirely up to the implementor. I would also expect to see a discussion of the danger of a receiver of Digest headers blindly accepting "all" algorithms defined in the draft or registry, even if they aren't deprecated. For example, a system in which all "good" clients use SHA512 but still accepts SHA256 is only really protected by SHA256 since that's the lightest weight item an attacker can make use of.

pulls.title: H2 PRIORITY_UPDATE type field is 8 bits
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
During IESG review, Éric Vyncke noted that the prose for the HTTP/2 PRIORITY_UPDATE frame used a type value written as `0x10` while the diagram used `10`. That inconsistency stems from 7540bis and I opened https://github.com/httpwg/http2-spec/pull/1002/files to fix that there.

While looking again at our type definition, we incorrectly stated `Type(i) = 10`. By convention, that suggest the type is a QUIC variable length integer. But that was never the intention. HTTP/2 frame type is part of the HTTP/2 frame header, which is an 8-bit field. In this draft, we are not changing the definition of HTTP/2 frame headers. Therefore the diagram is currently wrong. 

This change is editorial to address the above two issues.

pulls.title: Client certificate chain
pulls.author: MikeBishop
pulls.body: Fixes #1521, based on #1873.

comments.author: b---c
comments.body: This PR would address both #1521 and #1551

comments.author: b---c
comments.body: also would fix #1596

Arbitrary ordering worries me here -- I think we can have a well-defined _order_ without necessarily having it be a complete (as in, no-gaps) certificate chain with specific endpoints. Maybe something like:

> The certificates in the `Cient-Cert-Chain` header field MUST be increasingly general, with the later certificates signing earlier certificates in the list.

... Or something along those lines. I think the warning about extraneous (and missing) certificates is reasonable, but I think the order should be predictable.

Omitting the trust anchor, for the reasons mentioned, seems like a very reasonable thing. But I don't really see reason or value in allowing for gaps elsewhere, extraneous unrelated certificates, or unpredictable ordering. I plan to take editing pass over this section and try to tighten it up as such.

I took the text here almost verbatim from TLS 1.3.  It recommends the proper ordering, but does not require it.  It certainly could be that they have constraints we don't -- legacy code being one, obviously -- but I'd want to have a concrete reason to diverge from what TLS uses in transferring the same thing.

reviews.author: MikeBishop
reviews.body: @b---c, thanks for building on this.

comments.body:
```suggestion
fields SHOULD be configurable
```

Replied in the now-obsolete thread, but the SHOULDs come from RFC 8446's version of these requirements.  If we're making this mandatory (implicit MUST), this needs to specify what happens when it's violated.

SHOULD means exactly that -- it's better to do it this way, and things might go wrong if you don't.

I am blissfully ignorant of the constraints and objectives that went into that bit of TLS 1.3 but, while the same thing is being transferred, the context of use is quite different. In TLS it's part of the elaborate authentication ceremony during the establishment of a connection.  With the Cient-Cert-Chain header, it's conveying the information post-authentication to another entity on every request on the established connection. My reasoning is more: why wouldn't we have the TTRP convey that information in a defined and predictable way?

My hope/goal was to place constraints on the sender here that lead to a predictable output. Do it this way. Full stop. 

I'm not sure what happens when it's violated with must or should. I see what you are saying but the implicit MUSTs are meat to mean - do it this way, otherwise it's wrong.
I agree with @b---c here, if this spec can be tighter in its generation requirements, I think it should be. Reaching out to the TLS community is not a bad idea though.

This is the result of the way in which certification paths are constructed in practice, with co-signing and other things causing the ordering to be non-obvious.

Clearly, the order in which certificates appear can be linear, at least in the sense that the certificates can form a tree rooted on the EE certificate.  The problem is that it often needs to be a tree and not a chain because of the way in which different trust anchors accumulate in different endpoints.

This is far less likely to be a problem with client certificates as servers tend to carry the compatibility burdens, but I can't imagine that client certificates are completely immune to those sorts of compatibility problems either.

More fundamentally though: if the list of certificates that come out of TLS is not validated by the intermediary that inserts the header field, why do you think we can specify validation rules?  That is, if the certification path is constructed and validated by the back end system, the header field might be inserted with no knowledge of its contents. The only rule that makes any sense here is that the list of certificates match what the client included in its TLS handshake (or post-handshake authentication if you want to go there).

My expectation of what Cient-Cert-Chain header is supposed to carry, which I think the text (largely from Mike) in the PR is in line with and is consistent with the thrust of the document in general, it that it's the chain/path that was used by the intermediary to validate the client's EE certificate. The intermediary that inserts the header field does the validation during the TLS handshake and the cert path that was constructed during the handshake is the chain that is conveyed to the back end.

I don't think that you can assume that the intermediary will be performing path construction and validation, nor can you assume that the back-end server trusts it to do that.  While the backend might need to trust that the intermediary validates the in-TLS signature relative to the EE certificate, this design allows the backend to perform all the path construction independently.

If the back-end has different trust anchors then the intermediary, it will want to have all the information presented in the TLS handshake.

Honestly, I'm at a bit of a loss as to how to respond (and have spent way more time than I'd like trying to do so). That is exactly the assumption I want to make and what I view as an objective of the document to facilitate - where the proxy does the validation work and only exposes the information to back end. I view separating out the validation responsibilities like that as being rife with potential for subtle unexpected problems.  But maybe I'm in the weeds on this. I was rather skeptical of the purported need to expose more than the client's EE cert in the first place. Yet a number of folks expressed a need/want for it. And here we are. 

I also tried to look at docs of a few proxies and TLS implementations to get an idea of existing practice and/or what's even generally possible. And, to me anyway, everything is pretty ambiguous about what is exposed - what the client provided or what the server constructed. I suppose that if one reads the text of this PR without the bias I came with, it's consistent with that. 

All of this rambling is to say that l relent and I'll put that sentence back as well as the SHOULDs in the paragraph prior.
b251935ece5105c3b98aa078610e0fdeed9581bd puts that sentence back in the text as well as the SHOULDs into the paragraph prior.

I'm concerned about the general direction of this PR and the document in general. A reliable method of sharing information between data controllers is needed to enable smaller organisations to band together to offer comparable services to larger organisations that are able to operate their services under a single domain or origin or have sufficient brand presence to nudge users to login across multiple services.

This PR emphasis unspecified concerns in the industry and appears to endorse a direction set by internet gatekeepers without evidence of those concerns and without providing any specifics concerning the equivalent guidance for user agents to support lawful use cases.

James, this isn't a competition regulator or a courtroom -- it's recording the consensus of the technical community, which has had a long history of balancing privacy concerns against technical capabilities. comments.author: jwrosewell
comments.body:
*Completeness*
 
> The proposed text is largely a statement of fact and history, not creating policy.

In which case it should reflect all the facts and all the history rather than being selective.

*Experiment*

The latest PR contains the following text.

> …ongoing developments in user agents are best characterised as *experiments* that can provide input into that eventual consensus.

Checking the meaning of the word experiment with Websters provides the following definition.

-	test or trial
-	a tentative procedure or policy
-	an operation or procedure carried out under controlled conditions in order to discover an unknown effect or law, to test or establish a hypothesis, or to illustrate a known law

All web browser vendors have adopted concrete and widely communicated policies on the subject and many have widely deployed implementations. There is nothing experimental.

*Established practice*

The IETF considers factors beyond the text of past specifications. RFC 8890 is one such example. The sharing of state between different origins or domains via HTTP and other methods has enabled a great deal of innovation and benefits to end users including free and easy access to services. End users have many service providers to choose from. We have moved on from the days of closed services such as Compuserve, Prodigy and AOL. The guidance in future specifications must show how benefits to end users are preserved and enhanced by mitigating the potential harms.

pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
This PR attempts to capture my interpretation of the discussion during the HTTP Interim meeting Feb 2022. Editorial judgement has been applied with judicious KISS.

Executive summary:

1. Obsolete 3230.
  *  The suggestion was to put this in an appendix. However, if we are obsoleting Digest, I don't see much benefit in talking through many details. Stop using it and use the substitutes we spend lots of text on. The text ended up as half a page and I kept it in the Introductory section 1
2. Having a mix of sf-dictionary and sf-list that need to reference each other is really annoying. I'm sure there's a way to square the circle about using List items as lookups for Dictionary keys but after already spending hours noodling on it, it seems like an accident waiting to happen.
  * So I cheated. I switched Want-Representation-Digest and Want-Content-Digest to be Dictionaries too. It's just that the member value is an integer between 0 and 10 that expresses a preference weight. (Thanks MT for the suggestion to use int)
  * Using a dictionary here disposes of the 'q' parameter qvalue problem I mentioned in the meeting
3. New IANA table for the new headers
  * This is another slight cheat that lets us avoid updating a table that implementers of an obsolete RFC might still rely on.
  * It imports all the old headers from before, including insecure stuff that people previously said they wanted.

What this doesn't do is bikeshed on the header name. I suggest we try to find consensus on the general changes in the draft and follow up with issues for any bikeshed issues.

pulls.title: Add support for absent header fields
pulls.author: jricher
pulls.body:
Closes #1864
﻿

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
No, the signature input would be:

```
Signature-Input: sig=("absent-field";absent);created=1645056898;alg="rsa-pss-sha512"
```

And then the line would be added to the signature input as:

```
"absent-field";absent: 
```

Just like any other content identifier. The value is an empty string, which is what shows up after the colon and space.

If the header is in the message when the string is created, it's an error, explicitly. The signer is declaring that the field will not be present in the message, and if it's been added, then something has gone wrong. For a normal field:

```
Signature-Input: sig=("absent-field");created=1645056898;alg="rsa-pss-sha512"
```

If you can't find "absent-field" in the message, then :that: is an error, since you can't calculate the value for the string. It is absolutely not crossing the two (signal the field is covered then have a special "empty" value if it's not present).

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: My usual question: why does `absent` apply to regular headers but not to dictionary members, or to query params?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Ok, this is probably just me, but I have something of a visceral reaction to:

```
Signature-Input: sig=("absent-field";absent);created=1645056898;alg="rsa-pss-sha512"
```

Why does this need to be specified there?  Either the field is present or absent.  The signature will guarantee that.  It doesn't need to be distinguished any place other than in the input to the signature.  That might address Yaron's concern as well, I think.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: It's to ensure a field is not injected by an intermediary.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
@martinthomson The draft does not allow to have a field name in the signature params unless the corresponding header has a non-empty value. So this solution adds the ability to sign *optional* fields securely.

Having said that, I think a cleaner alternative is an `optional` parameter that lets you sign both absent and present fields.

`Signature-Input: sig=("optional-field";optional);created=1645056898;alg="rsa-pss-sha512"`

Where depending on whether the field exists or not, the input is either:

`"optional-field";optional: `

or

`"optional-field";optional: some value`

This would IMO simplify the process both for signers and verifiers, because it would move the (minor) complexity from the application into the signature/verification code. 

And then, of course, you can also have:

`"@query-params";name="param1";optional`

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
@yaronf this PR is about **prohibited** fields, not optional ones. If they're tagged "absent" then they MUST NOT show up in the resulting message. Honestly "optional" feels like it's opening up a door for security bugs and implementation quirks. And the signer is going to know whether the field is there or not, and what its value is.  If that's changed by the time it hits the verifier, then the signature fails. Any decision on the optionality of a component needs to happen before the covered components are chosen, and the state of that field is fixed by the time the signature creation process is started.

Also note, an empty field value is allowed and has a defined value syntax, see https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures-08.html#section-2.1-10 for the details.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
@jricher I've forgotten about empty fields, thanks for the reminder.

But given that they exist, I will join Martin's question: Ideally the list of covered fields should be constant per use case, and the recipient should only trust covered-and-signed fields (which sometimes have an empty value). Having an "absent" indicator for a field implies that the recipient intends to use this field's value, even though it is not covered. This sounds like an insecure practice.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
@yaronf it's an indication that if the field shows up, the verifier can assume that something unexpected happened. It's increased security. Think of it as an extra layer of enforcement on the guidelines of "don't trust a value that isn't signed" that are already listed in the security considerations. This is a way for the signer to say "I guarantee this wasn't here when I signed the message so if you see it, something's wrong."

Let's take a another example: a request is sent to a system that does LAN authentication (with apologies if this gives anyone flashbacks of dealing with SiteMinder). You have a proxy that strips off incoming headers for sanitization purposes before handing the request over to the siteminder installation -- with this you can sign the proxied request with `"sm-auth";absent` in the component list, which the siteminder install can check that it's not present. Or you can have your client sign with `"sm-auth";absent` to prove that it didn't do header injection at the time of signature.

There were some other use cases brought up when this function was first discussed, and it seemed at the time that there was enough interest to have this kind of signal.

I'm not against having it also apply to other items (including derived components like dictionary keys and named query parameters), but that wasn't the driving use case that started this.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
I also want to note about the alternate encoding suggestions: remember that the HTTP signature input is never parsed by any party. The signature input parameters are not reconstructed from the input string -- and it should be considered a write-only buffer by the generator. As such, as long as a given line is unique for a given message and can be created deterministically, it doesn't need to use any different constructions for a given line. I think this greatly simplifies the code. Right now, ever single line is of the form:

```
sf-string params ":" SP component-value
```

Where "component-value" is defined by the component and its parameters.

Tagging a header field as "absent" here already creates a different line than when it's present but without a value:

```
"header": 
"header";absent: 
```

So a signer or verifier will never create the wrong line, as the flagging is explicit.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
> @yaronf it's an indication that if the field shows up, the verifier can assume that something unexpected happened. It's increased security. Think of it as an extra layer of enforcement on the guidelines of "don't trust a value that isn't signed" that are already listed in the security considerations.

I think we have a disconnect on the goals of the verifier. To me, a typical verifier is not out to detect malicious injections. All they want is to provide a simple policy (a list of assertions, and in the simplest case a list of required fields) and then leave it to the signature verification layer to ensure the message is trustworthy, before it can be sent to the rest of the application.

Seen this way, if all I want is to enforce the assertion "field X is absent", the verifier library can do it just fine without any signature syntax. Just check that the thing doesn't exist!

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: @yaronf I agree that a verifier can check for absence of a field, and will need to do so if the application requires it, but without the signature syntax it won't know **that the intent of the signer is that the field is absent**. comments.body: @martinthomson Because it's a detached signature on an object that can be changed in the middle between the signer and verifier, I believe this is a useful signal. Signing an present header says "This field is here and I know its value". Signing an absent header says "this field is not there". If I sign a present header and it's not there anymore when the verifier gets it, that's an error. If I sign an absent header and it's there when the verifier gets it, that's an error. Yes of course they both know that a field is there or not when they sign or verify the message -- the important thing here is whether that field was still there or not at the other end.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
With the current serialization format plus this PR, a (syntactically valid) value of `Example: :` you get:

```
"example": :\n   (present)
"example": \n    (empty)
"example";absent: \n (absent)
```

If we remove the space and adopt the no-value absent line we get:

```
"example"::\n   (present)
"example":\n    (empty)
"example"\n (absent)
```

While still distinct, I'd argue it's easier for someone developing and debugging something like this to look at the first one and think it's probably an error, and overcorrect it to look like the second value, especially if one side has already made the mistake and you're trying to just make things work. This is about making it clear to an implementor what to do in every case at every step, especially when things go wrong -- which they will.

So let's talk about parameter names, which as a token can include the colon character unescaped. So somebody adds the parameter "a=b:" to a field and you end up with the even more confusing:

```
"example";a=b:::\n   (present)
"example";a=b::\n    (empty)
"example";a=b:\n (absent)
```

And then things get fun, because with that parameter added, you now have a case where the presence of the parameter `;a=b:` and a field value of `:` now serializes to the same as a parameter value of `;a=b` and a field value of `::`, both of them are:

```
"example";a=b:::
```

If you leave off both the space and colon it's not any better:

```
"example";a=b::
```

With or without that colon, using the space, which can neither end a parameter name/value nor start the field value, prevents that. This is a small collision, and it's the kind of collision that's unlikely to happen on its own, but it's the kind of thing that can act as a foothold for other kinds of injection and manipulation.

We can avoid this entire class of problems by having a clear and unambiguous serialization for each distinct case. Using the space and colon we end up with two different things:

```
"example";a=b: ::\n
"example";a=b:: :\n
```

So as I said above, it's the colon that's redundant, and the space is needed to stave off this kind of collision. Without that extra colon but with a space we still have unambiguous encodings:

```
"example";a=b ::\n
"example";a=b: :\n
```

But, the colon isn't really raising any issues on its own here, and getting rid of it and the space doesn't get rid of the ambiguity of creating:

```
"example";a=b::\n
```

While we don't have to worry about ambiguous parsing, we do need to be concerned about ambiguous generation. Anything you can give an attacker to force a change that they control into the input of the signature that's different from what's intended is a bad design. This is all just for the signature base string -- hopefully the rest of the application will be checking for things like valid parameter names and values and valid field values, but if they aren't and you can get the signature to pass with something other than what was used on the signer's end, then you've undermined the whole system.

And finally, I still do not see the value of changing the core serialization mechanic at this point without really good reason to do so. The proposed solutions make the input string prettier, but do not make it easier or less ambiguous to create. Remember, this string is never seen except in debugging situations (and the draft examples), and it is never sent over the wire. Deterministic generation is absolutely important here.

Now: This whole conversation does raise the question: does an empty field (present with no value) have a semantic difference from an absent field? My reading of SEMANTICS points to "yes", or at least "it could depending on the field definition". If that isn't the case, and they are equivalent, they should be serialized the same way. But that's separate from the underlying question of how to encode all the values in the string.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I thought that we'd already resolved the present vs. empty thing.  There is a semantic difference.

As for the parameters thing, why?  Field values might have parameters, but why would the name need a value?  I know that the grammar of Inner List supports the notion, but why would you allow that here?

I'm happy to concede that we simply disagree about signaling absence in the `Signature-Input`, but isn't this the essence of that disagreement?  That is, why seek to make things more complicated: ban the use of parameters in this instance (or at least say that there are currently none and refuse to define what to do with them for the moment) and avoid the complications.

comments.author: richanna
comments.body:
> And then things get fun, because with that parameter added, you now have a case where the presence of the parameter ;a=b: and a field value of : now serializes to the same as a parameter value of ;a=b and a field value of ::

The value of the `@signature-input` component is different for each of those, so the signatures will still be different. So technically that's still safe, but it makes me nervous. I'd definitely prefer it if there were no serialization collisions between semantically distinct components.

> This whole conversation does raise the question: does an empty field (present with no value) have a semantic difference from an absent field?

It can, depending on the field definition. For example, see [`Accept-Encoding`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-5.3.4):

```
A request without an Accept-Encoding header field implies that the
user agent has no preferences regarding content-codings.
...
An Accept-Encoding header field with a combined field-value that is
empty implies that the user agent does not want any content-coding in
response.
```
(hat-tip: Willy Tarreau on the mailing list for pointing out this example)

---

I want to step back and consider use cases and failure modes involving absent header fields. With the published draft, signature input generation fails at [step 2.4](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures.html#section-2.3-4.2.2.4.2.2) if the component list includes an absent header field. There is no way for the the signer to explicitly signal that they did not include a particular header field. If the header field is present in the message, the verifier has no way to determine if it was included by the signer or injected along the way. But this is true of all unsigned components. Message signatures provide the verifier with information about the components that were included in the signature input. They do not provide information on components not included in the signature input.

This PR changes that by allowing the message signature to assert something about a component that is not covered – specifically, `example-header;absent` asserts that that any `example-header` present in the message did not come from the signer. Is this useful information to the verifier? Since `example-header` is absent from the signature input, the verifier already knows that the signature provides no information about its value. But is there a meaningful difference between "this signature doesn't tell me anything about this value" and "this signature tells me this value didn't come from the signer"? Under what circumstances would that difference trigger a change in a verifier's behavior?

Given the degree to which proxies can modify messages, including this information might cause more harm than good. Consider an overzealous client that includes `Accept-Encoding;absent` in their signature input. Suppose requests pass through a proxy that adds `Accept-Encoding: compress, gzip`, as a bandwidth optimization. Now the service receives a request with an invalid signature. The service could decide that since `Accept-Encoding` isn't in its list of meaningful, must-be-signed components, that it will ignore the value for the purposes of signature verification and build the input string as if it were absent. That might even be safe, but it's awfully complicated and seems like the kind of code that shows up as the root cause of a CVE a year later.

Here's another example: a client developer heard about bad guys spoofing `X-Forwarded-For`, so they decide to include `X-Forwarded-For;absent` so no one can replay their signatures in requests with `X-Forwarded-For` header fields. Take that, bad guys. ...Except the service's load balancer adds `X-Forwarded-For`, and even adds a signature over it. So now just like the earlier example the service host receives a request with an invalid signature.

The fundamental issue here is that the signer is presuming that a header field being injected by an intermediary is necessarily an error state, and in so doing they are making an unfounded assertion about content they have not seen and know nothing about. It is neither the signer's responsibility nor place to dictate to the verifier how it should treat unsigned components.

pulls.author: bobby-stripe
pulls.body:
I'm not sure what the current digest is, but it doesn't match the 23-byte HTTP body of that message.
We can verify the expected/new digest with:

```
$ echo -n '{"message": "good dog"}' | sha512sum | cut -d ' ' -f 1 | xxd -r -p | base64
mEWXIS7MaLRuGgxOBdODa3xqM1XdEvxoYhvlCFJ41QJgJc4GTsPp29l5oGX69wWdXymyU0rjJuahq4l5aGgfLQ==
```

(also verified in a go implementation of message signatures)

As the digest changed, the Signature for the ECDSA P-256 example also changed, I've included a new signature over the updated digest that verifies based on the key in the spec.

Thanks!

pulls.title: Mention HTTP Message Signatures as an illustration
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
Editorial change @jricher and I talked about over lunch in IETF 113.

Initially I was going to include an example of a Signature that covered content-digest, but I stepped back from doing that for a few reasons:

* the sigs draft already has a few examples that contain a content-digest
* I don't want to have to explain all the items or concepts that appear in HTTP signatures examples, that belongs in the sigs draft itself and we shouldn't duplicate it
* we probably aren't running the same infrastructure to make sure the examples stay correct

What might work is for the sigs doc to provide some slimmed-down examples that focus on signing `Content-Digest` and `Repr-Digest` and then we could reference them from this draft. But I'm open to other ideas.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
I think an example of a signed request or response with Content-Digest would be reasonable, and it honestly doesn't have to go into explaining how the signatures work against the digest, just showing the digest in the signed components list would be sufficient.

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Digest: \
  sha-256=:X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=:
Signature-Input: cdsigex=("content-digest" "content-type" "@status")
Signature: cdsigex=:7ajtA8nCss0JpwEjvSzvwShEC1csS8pquZJ0vrAnM\
  2mRw+lEropP5Ea/+5tx9gAOZDzuU0talUe357Yf3VG/2g==:

{"hello": "world"}
```

This doesn't even have parameters like key and alg, but can be introduced with "This example shows covering the content digest field in a response using HTTP Message Signatures [reference here]", and I think that's probably good enough. Yes, it's not directly verifiable from the digest spec, but doing so would require a lot more information than is necessary -- this isn't about showing how signatures work, it's about showing how the signatures cover the digest. I think just showing the Content-Digest in the signature's content is enough to make the point.

comments.author: ioggstream
comments.body:
Agree with mentioning signatures without examples.

Signatures i-d is the correct place for examples containing a signed *-digest field.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: To be clear, I'm recommending an example and not a test vector.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Thanks for the example Justin. To me, it raises more questions than it answers though. Primarily because it's not clear what the example shows (to the reader that is uninformed about sigs) unless we describe to some extent Signature-Input and the process of signature generation. If the argument is to just give an example of how to include a field in the Signature-Input, that seems so trivial I'm not sure the value. 

Instead, my thinking was we could modify https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2098/files#diff-de34152d297a9eb29b85b24962949ba2e309478a5c32e1d94fd4c3ee27b4584dR508 to deep link into the Signature's draft, for example saying something like 

> one possible approach is to include them as part of HTTP Message Signatures, as shown in {{Section X.Y of SIGNATURES}}.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Going to merge this as is, any possible future changes can be one additively without massive change.

pulls.title: Document Style updates for Signatures
pulls.author: jricher
pulls.body:
This updates the document to comply with the style guides:

- clean up structured field references and remove ABNF
- format field names per style guide
- update semantics and messaging references
- udpate self-references
- update registry tables

This does not (yet) modify the registry initial contents from tables to dictionary lists because I'm not sure how to format those for adding multiple 
entries at once.

comments.body:
```suggestion
For a variety of reasons, it is impractical to strictly define what constitutes a safe change versus an unsafe one.  Applications use HTTP in a wide variety of ways, and may disagree on whether a particular piece of information in a message (e.g., the body, or the Date header field) is relevant.  Thus a general purpose solution must provide signers with some degree of control over which message components are signed.
```

```suggestion
An individual member value of a Dictionary Structured Field is canonicalized by applying the serialization algorithm described in {{Section 4.1.2 of STRUCTURED-FIELDS}} on the `member_value` and its parameters, without the dictionary key. Specifically, the value is serialized as an Item or Inner List (the two possible values of a Dictionary member).
```

"Member value" at the top of the sentence is just plain English.
The result of which constraint? Why not say simply that each signature (named by a signature label) is associated with exactly one signature input?
I think the SHOULD should be a MUST if this is a security concern.
This list is missing the `Status` column.

```suggestion
in order to facilitate parallelism with this value's inclusion in the Signature-Input field,
```

```suggestion
This document defines component identifiers, which can be parameterized in specific circumstances to provide unique modified behavior. IANA is asked to create and maintain a new registry typed "HTTP Signature Component Parameters" to record and maintain the set of parameters for component identifiers, and the methods to produce their associated parameter values. Initial values for this registry are given in {{iana-component-param-contents}}.  Future assignments and modifications to existing assignments are to be made through the Expert Review registration policy {{?RFC8126}} and shall follow the template presented in {{iana-component-param-template}}.
```
Can we reference Structured Fields here, instead of specifying the allowed characters?
I was specifically referencing the variable from the algorithm in structured-fields, but I think you're right here.
@mnot I believe you had a reason that this can't be a MUST, right?
This is actually a smaller list than what's allowed for the `key` production rule in structured fields. I don't remember if there's a compelling reason for this though.

Is it a security concern or an interoperability one?

I'm not strongly against MUST, but wonder why it's a requirement at all - mentioning caching is fine, but making it a requirement is akin to saying 'Messages MUST be well-formed'.
The constraint is that a signature uses both fields. The goal of the language change here is to show that there's a 1:1 mapping, and anything else is an error in the signature headers.

I do think there are some security implications -- if I'm requesting a signed response but I'm getting a cache hit for the signature then I'm going to have a higher level of confidence in the incorrect result than I would have otherwise. It's only a security risk if the cached signature is valid for a different message -- but that's more a case of the signature not covering an appropriately large amount of the message.

But I think this can even be addressed by recommending use of the `created` field on the signature parameters and letting the validator figure it out. I'm fine with it being listed as a consideration but removing the normative requirement here. I'll be the first to admit I'm not an expert on cache semantics and will defer to those who are.

```suggestion
Status:
: A brief text description of the status of the parameter. The description MUST begin with one of "Active" or "Deprecated", and MAY provide further context or explanation as to the reason for the status.

Target:
```

Ugh, copy-paste mistakes here. Changing it to this instead:

```suggestion
This document defines several kinds of component identifiers, some of which can be parameterized in specific circumstances to provide unique modified behavior. IANA is asked to create and maintain a new registry typed "HTTP Signature Component Parameters" to record and maintain the set of parameters names, the component identifiers they are associated with, and the modifications these parameters make to the component value. Initial values for this registry are given in {{iana-component-param-contents}}.  Future assignments and modifications to existing assignments are to be made through the Expert Review registration policy {{?RFC8126}} and shall follow the template presented in {{iana-component-param-template}}.
```
I just find it hard to understand from the text, specifically what does "constraint" refer to.

Looking again, it actually doesn't comply with the requirements for S-F parameter keys, since S-F does not allow parameter keys to start with numbers or hyphens. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941#section-3.1.2-3

I think that's a solid argument for referencing S-F here.
Left this text as is, since the text in question was not actually changed from a previous version. We can potentially add a recommendation for how to handle cache in a future PR.

pulls.title: Wrapping problematic fields for signatures
pulls.author: jricher
pulls.body:
This adds a binary wrapper for fields that don't follow the List or Dictionary format for multiple values, such as Set-Cookie. The wrapper is selected 
using the `bs` parameter, and the component value is made by wrapping each individual field value in a Byte Sequence and putting them into a List, then 
doing a strict serialization on those values.

Closes #2166

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: In general, is this even needed or are we over-engineering here? If the main use case is `Set-Cookie`, do we think it is likely to be signed?

```suggestion
: A boolean flag indicating that the component value is derived from the request that triggered this response message and not from the response message directly.
```
This is not a MAY, it's at least a SHOULD because not using it would result in a security issue.
If we are aware of other common fields that need to be handled this way, let's list them in {{security-non-list}} as well.

What does this mean? Maybe: encode the list as a structured field Byte Sequence using the list's ASCII representation. (This assumes that only ASCII is allowed, but that's really part of the problem.)
Set-Cookie is the only common one that I found that fits this, but I didn't want the language to preclude other weirdness out there.

@mnot is this an accurate way to say "take the header value as a binary"? To create the examples I encoded the strings, and field values are already a subset of ASCII characters allowed.

```suggestion
    2. Encode the resulting field value's ASCII representation as a Byte Sequence
```

I'm actually fine with this being a SHOULD for the reasons given.

```suggestion
If the value of the the HTTP field in question is known by the application to cause problems with serialization, particularly with combination of multiple values as discussed in {{security-non-list}}, the signer SHOULD include the `bs` parameter in a component identifier to indicate the values of the fields need to be wrapped as binary structures before being combined.
```

pulls.title: Add signature context
pulls.author: jricher
pulls.body:
Adds an optional `context` parameter to signatures, to allow applications to signal specific usage between the signer and verifier.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: @richanna @yaronf I've walked the language in the definition back a bit and added it to an example. I think this is sufficient to include as a new feature.

```suggestion
* `context`: A context for the signature as a String value. This value is used by applications to help identify the signature's validity in specific applications or protocols. Context is often needed for avoiding cross-protocol attacks.
```

IMO the value does not identify the signature (which the "sig1" name is doing), rather it clarifies within which context the signature is valid.

reviews.author: richanna
reviews.body: I remain unconvinced that `context` provides any real value, so I'm against including it in the spec. If we do end up including it anyway, we must not imply that it provides security benefits that it does not.

comments.body:
```suggestion
* `context`: A context for the signature as a String value. This value may be used by applications to help identify the intended usage of the signature.
```

I'm still not thrilled by the second sentence, but this wording seems more accurate to me. The third sentence is simply not true. Signing all components that are semantically meaningful to the application will prevent cross-protocol attacks in most cases; in the remaining cases, there is no reason to assume context will provide any additional mitigation.

The third sentence was added by @yaronf in [1c081b0](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2222/commits/1c081b0df5983d58a80a3568c6ae2096fe48132d). I'm actually fine with backing it off from here because the discussion really should be in a larger space about using the context, in security considerations or something like that.

This non-normative proposal is:

- Not well defined.
- Contradicts the normative definition of `@authority`.
- And requires the server/verifier to simulate some of the logic of the reverse proxy.

pulls.title: client-cert: certificate chain in the same order as it appears in TLS
pulls.author: bc-pi
pulls.body: attempt @martinthomson's "simple alternative" in #1927 to say the chain is in the same order as it appears in TLS rather than copying the language from TLS

comments.body: Can you explain your reasoning behind this "might or might not" clause?

That text was from 0a7210f7d644dea399f0fc4d1b5119acb436d1db when @MikeBishop added the Client-Cert-Chain header and I was trying not to step on his work too much. Also the text allows for the case that the proxy assembles the chain and conveys it.

This seems problematic as it invites a query about why that might (or might not) be the case.

I would prefer to say that the proxy can add certificates to this field.  It provides the certificates in the order in which they appear in the TLS handshake, unless it has cause to provide other information.

What about even less invitation of questions by making that last sentence this? 

"The order of the certificates is the same as the ordering in TLS (such as described in {{Section 4.4.2 of RFC8446}})."

That would work for me, but I got the impression that you are aware of cases where that is not the case.  I don't think that there is any harm in saying "..., unless the server and proxy agree otherwise." or similar.

Honestly don't remember what my logic was in writing that; it appears to have been from my first pass at this text and not touched in any of the feedback.

I *think* that was based on TLS 1.3 saying that "...a certificate that specifies a trust anchor MAY be omitted from the chain, provided that supported peers are known to possess any omitted certificates."  If the proxy possesses certificates the origin might not, the client might omit them from the handshake, but the proxy could append them for the origin's information.

I don't think there's harm in allowing for private agreement here, but I don't feel strongly either way.

As I remember things, there was some disagreement when the initial text for `Cient-Cert-Chain` was added/proposed about whether the proxy would construct and validate the chain and convey the constructed chain to the origin or whether the proxy would pass through what the client sent as-is and defer validation and construction to the origin. Some of this discussion is captured in PR #1874. AFAIK most of the time the chain would look the same. But I've tried to adjust the text such that either would be okay. The sentence above about the order being the same was intended to mean only that ordering is the same but not that they *are* the same.

[5fb237a](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2258/commits/5fb237a7dbb030ab323710a1d254d442cd41f35d) is another pass at this that removes the "might or might not" and tries to better articulate ordering.

pulls.title: Update cookie-value definition to reflect browser behavior
pulls.author: april
pulls.body:
I recently ran into a problem where browsers were allowing cookies to be set containing values that standard libraries were failing to parse. These libraries are mostly following the relatively obsolete published RFC6265 (with tweaks), which limits a lot of characters that browsers allow and frequently appear inside cookies.

As such, this updates section 4.1.1 to reflect the characters that browsers allow to be set inside cookie values: any 8-bit octet except for control characters and semicolons.

For reference as to how browsers handle cookie setting:

* Chromium: [any octet except control characters and semicolons](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:net/cookies/parsed_cookie.cc;drc=796d9f7be35cc8f766fabc6e84df424046460890;l=495)
* Firefox: [any octet except control characters and semicolons, but allowing 0x09 (htab) and 0x7F (del)](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/source/netwerk/cookie/CookieCommons.cpp#210)
* Safari: seems to be any ASCII (7-bit) character except control characters (which includes htab) and semicolons

I was led down this rabbit hole by Golang:
* Golang: [any ASCII (7-bit) character except control characters, double quotes, semicolons, and backslashes](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/net/http/cookie.go;l=414)
* Python: too many regular expressions for me to read through, but seems to behave the same as Golang

As for servers:
* nginx: lets you set a `Set-Cookie` with the characters listed above, so every browser accepts commas, semicolons, and backslashes, Firefox and Chromium allow unicode, etc.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
Hi,

> I recently ran into a problem where browsers were allowing cookies to be set containing values that standard libraries were failing to parse.

Section 4 is meant to be a subset of the characters that the spec asks user agents (browsers) to support. This is almost entirely due to historical reasons and the sub-set was selected to maximize a server's compatibility with all user agents (including more minor UAs). I.e.: If a server stays within Section 4's guidelines then their cookies are the most likely to be accepted by all UAs.

UAs, on the other hand, are meant to implement Section 5 which includes the larger set of characters you've identified.

So it sounds like the behavior you're seeing is not unexpected. Can you provide more information on your problem? That may help us come to a resolution.

comments.author: april
comments.body:
Sorry, I'm a bit confused by your response.

> Section 4 is meant to be a subset of the characters that the spec asks user agents (browsers) to support.

Browsers _do_ support what is specified, and quite a bit more, including double quotes and other characters, which is why I've been running into issues. This is an attempt to align section 4.1.1 with what browsers actually accept (and send to servers). As well as what servers send, and browsers seem to happily accept.

We are in an awkward state at the moment where browsers will accept characters inside cookie values (such as dquotes) but then they will fail downstream because standard libraries are very limited in what they accept because they kinda-sorta follow 4.1.1 from the published RFC and then fail in numerous ways. It would be great if all sides of this equation are aligned on what values are allowed inside cookie values.

The exact issue I'm running into is that a popular piece of vendor software that handles EU cookie laws is setting cookies with a value that contains quotation marks, as it's using JSON. Browsers happily accept it, servers pass it along, and then the standard library (often invisibly) fails to parse it because it is using the rules as defined in 4.1.1.

Note that I just tested nginx and it happily allows me to use `Set-Cookie` with a quotation mark which browsers happily accept, also in violation section 4.1.1. It's rare for anything to follow 4.1.1 except when they follow pieces of it and break things randomly.

If 4.1.1 is meant to reflect what browsers will accept from servers, then it should reflect what they actually accept from servers in the present, which is listed above.

comments.body:
To add: even if we updated 4.1.1 to reflect what the most proscriptive browser (Safari) allows, that would still mean that commas, backslashes, and double quotes are allowed inside cookie values.

But Chromium and Firefox will happily accept server-set cookies with things like unicode in them just fine.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
> Sorry, I'm a bit confused by your response.

Whoops, I may have mangled my reply a bit with some errant and accidental cut/pasting.

> If 4.1.1 is meant to reflect what browsers will accept from servers

It is not.
Section 4 is the "Server Requirements" section, so everything in there is tailored to inform a server how to be the most compatible with every UA. As you've seen not every server follows those recommendations, but they remain good practice nonetheless.

(The definition of servers is a bit hand wavy in the spec. It might be more helpful to think of "servers" as anything that produces cookies.)

Section 5 "User Agent Requirements" details what browsers (and other UAs) should accept. And given that many servers have previously, and still do, deviate from Section 4's recommendation, the UAs are strongly encouraged to accept those deviations in the name of compatibility and dealing with historical baggage. Many of these accepted deviations are footguns or have had issues with consistent processing among different UAs which is why they're discouraged.

As an example: one such troublesome deviation is the ability to create a nameless cookie `Set-Cookie: =foobar`. Trying to remove that ability in the past broke important sites and so many UAs still support it. However it's a giant footgun and so section 4 disallows it. (And I'm hoping to remove it from Section 5 in the not too distant future)

> they kinda-sorta follow 4.1.1

Yes, this has long been a problem :/ Hence section 5.

> The exact issue I'm running into is that a popular piece of vendor software that handles EU cookie laws is setting cookies with a value that contains quotation marks, as it's using JSON. Browsers happily accept it, servers pass it along, and then the standard library (often invisibly) fails to parse it because it is using the rules as defined in 4.1.1.

The spec has mostly operated under the assumption that if a given server can produce a cookie, then that same server must also accept the cookie. Nowadays with SaaS and various frameworks being as popular as they are that isn't always the case. 
But I don't believe this is a problem for the spec to solve, it's not that the spec is giving incorrect information but rather that one of both sides is in noncompliance of the spec. Afaict if both the vendor software and the library implemented 4.1.1 fully this wouldn't be an issue.

Furthermore, expanding the character set in 4.1.1 could result in more servers producing those characters then they would've if we left 4.1.1. as-is. But unless 100% of every other UA/library/software also implements support then that results in more incompatibility across the web ecosystem.

comments.author: sbingler
comments.body:
Section 4 is framed around maximizing compatibility. Changes to what we tell servers to do can affect every web ecosystem component that the server communicates with or along: Major/minor browsers, old/new browsers, CLI utilities, internet infrastructure, etc. Some of these components support different sets of characters from the others. Since we want to encourage a server to be the most compatible across the entire ecosystem we want to take the intersection of all the supported characters among those components which leads to a set that is less-than-or-equal to what a given UA might support. If we have such a maximally compatible character set already, any additions must then reduce compatibility. So we should have a good reason to.

(Some servers may deviate from our suggestion and that will exclude some UAs; that's something the server does at its own risk.)

On the other hand: what we tell browsers, and other UAs, to do in section 5 is framed around supporting as many servers as reasonably possible. Since we know that some servers deviate from section 4 for whatever reasons, this necessitates supporting a larger set than section 4.

There’s a recent example of this:

Cookie prefixes, `__Secure-` and `__Host-`, were originally specified to be case sensitive. It turned out that some servers would send `__HOST-` and `__secure-` cookies. So section 5 (UA) was updated to specify that prefixes should be checked case-insensitively in order to still gain the benefits of the prefixes with those servers. However, section 4 continues to specify that servers should send case sensitive prefixes in order to support UAs that don’t do case-insensitive checks.

> Can you help me understand what the criteria is for determining when it's safe to make this change?

Enough benefit to the change such that it outweighs potential compatibility loss.
So the change should be very positive, or we should have some data that the potential compatibility loss is very small.

Security related changes are a good example.

> Is there a test suite where we test against clients to determine when it would be safe to change?

Not that I'm aware of. The closest I know of would be the [web platform tests](https://web-platform-tests.org/), but that is primarily focused on testing web platform features.

> Would it be possible to change Section 4, which seems to indicate that this behavior belongs to both sides

I'm in favor of clarifying section 4.

> should we update Section 5 to forbid user agents from accepting cookies and/or sending cookies with [%x80-FF]

There is some interest in deprecating this historical cruft, so in the longer term hopefully yes.

In the short term though, I think not. While we want to encourage servers not to use them, some of them do. In this case, if the UA is able to receive the character then it obviously was able to make it to the user's device and so it's probably fine to send it back.

comments.author: dveditz
comments.body:
> Browsers accept those characters both from `Set-Cookie` (where it would probably be fine to reflect as `Cookie`) but also from Javascript. Which the server had nothing to do with [...]

From the browser's POV the server had _everything_ to do with that script. The browser won't create any cookies on its own!

It's of course a complication that web documents can be amalgamations of scripts from different servers with different cookie behavior, but even in a pure single-server document (e.g. CSP `default-src 'self'`) this isn't the only way a web application's code can conflict with the server layer it's running on.

I'm not saying this problem is purely the server's fault; I'm pushing back on the implication that it's purely the browser's fault. It's complicated.

pulls.title: Proposal of server-generated upload URLs
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
The current draft -00 of the resumable upload protocol uses a client-generated token to identify which procedures belong together. There has been valid criticism of this methodology, especially that the server is not able to control this identifier, which fits badly into the typical request-response schema of HTTP APIs. There seems to be a majority supporting the use of server-generated identifiers over client-generated ones.

That being said, the original intention of these tokens was two-folded and is still desirable:

1. Allow clients to upload small files in a single request, without the need of additional roundtrips.
2. Allow clients to resume an upload before receiving a response for the server by using the client-generated token.

We believe it is possible to achieve these two goals even when using server-generated uploads URLs by utilizing the Idempotency-Key header, whose draft is currently being discussed by the httpapi working group (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/).

This PR proposes to move from client-generated tokens to server-generated URLs. The role of Idempotency-Key is not included here and is laid out in a separate issue: https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2293

Any feedback is welcome!

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> That being said, the original intention of these tokens was two-folded and is still desirable:
>
> *  Allow clients to upload small files in a single request, without the need of additional roundtrips.
> *  Allow clients to resume an upload before receiving a response for the server by using the client-generated token.

For a small file, how are resumable-uploads useful?  If a disconnect occurs, the data can be re-sent with little overhead.
For multiple small files, are HTTP/2 streams somehow insufficient?  Why?
For a large file, why is round-trip delay time a problem for an upload that will presumably take order(s) of magnitude longer than the round-trip delay time to upload?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> For a small file, how are resumable-uploads useful? If a disconnect occurs, the data can be re-sent with little overhead.

Good question! The benefit of resumable uploads (or retryable uploads in this case) for small files is that the client and server can use one API for all uploads, regardless of their size. For example, in our use case, customers can upload files of any size and type to our server. Often, these files are uploaded simultaneously in the same session. It would be helpful if big and small files could use the same mechanism for uploads and therefore reduce the complexity in the our entire uploading infrastructure (clients, proxies, servers etc).

In addition, it makes it possible for the client to decide what a big and small file is. The threshold for when a file is big depends on the available network and is best judged by the client. So if the server supports this hybrid approach, the client can decide if it wants to go the save route and create the upload in a separate request, or try to transfer the file in a single request. For example, a 10MB file might be small if you have a fast fiber connection or big if you are on a spotty mobile network.

> For a large file, why is round-trip delay time a problem for an upload that will presumably take order(s) of magnitude longer than the round-trip delay time to upload?

You are correct that the additional request is not a huge concern for big uploads. In these situations, the client would prefer to create the upload in a separate request. Only in cases of small uploads, it makes sense to combine the creation and data transfer in a single request.

Does that make sense?

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
> You are correct that the additional request is not a huge concern for big uploads. In these situations, the client would prefer to create the upload in a separate request. Only in cases of small uploads, it makes sense to combine the creation and data transfer in a single request.

It sounds like you are trying to optimize for a case where it should not matter.  In the case of a small file -- as determined by the client -- if upload fails, then send it again.  If your failure rate is high in the common case *for small files*, then that sounds like a different problem.  As you agreed above, when the file is not small, the round-trip latency is not relevant.

Also, HTTP/1.1 pipelining has been around for over 20 years, and HTTP/2 is even better.  For a small file to be created, you send an HTTP request using HTTP.  If you get a 201 or 200 response, you are done.  If you did not, then you may choose to retry.  If you are using resumable-uploads, you have to keep the file around to be able to resume, which is no different than keeping the small file around to resend in total, so I do not see any added value.

If you must upload the file once and only once, then that sounds like a different problem.  You have mentioned Idempotency-Key as one option.  Another is that if you must upload the file once and only once, then that is an application-level requirement and can be solved by application-level communication of a unique token or the like.

reviews.author: guoye-zhang
reviews.body: Finally got a chance to go through this. Thank you for doing this! Looks good in general

comments.body: I think of `Upload-Incomplete` as an advanced feature for people who need to do chunked uploads. Using it to identify resumable upload feels a bit wrong. Also `Upload-Incomplete = false` is a double negative which can be confusing. If we go this route, I prefer flipping it to `Upload-Complete` instead. (Also don't forget to update the examples)
Is `SHOULD` too strong for feature detection? I used `MAY` since it's optional, but we could update it all to `SHOULD`.
I think we could get rid of this entire section. It's no longer ambiguous what the procedure is since the server determines the URL for appending, retrieving and cancelling.
Let's also recommend the URL to be strong and non-guessable. Even one bit of info leak (whether an upload exists or not) could be detrimental.
Personally, I think SHOULD is better here. Yes, it is optional, but I do think that there is a benefit to using it and hence we should recommend it instead of just providing this mechanism.

I get where you are coming from and the relevancy of this section has decreased with this PR, yes. I do think that this section is helpful for people looking to start a server-side implementation. However, I am not sure if such content is best placed in the draft itself.

You touch on two good points here. I abuse the Upload-Incomplete header for feature detection here. This may or may not be a smart choice. Maybe we use a more explicit header as mentioned in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2295 and keep Upload-Incomplete optional.

Removing the double-negative also sounds good but maybe let's do this in a separate PR.
Good idea!

```suggestion
The definition of HTTP field names does not allow for the use of the `@` character anywhere in the name. As such, since all derived component names start with the `@` character, these namespaces should be completely separate. However, some HTTP implementations are not sufficiently strict about the characters accepted in HTTP field names. In such implementations, a sender (or attacker) could inject a header field starting with an `@` character and have it passed through to the application code. These invalid header fields could be used to override a portion of the derived message content and substitute an arbitrary value, providing a potential place for an attacker to mount a [signature collision](#security-collision) attack or other functional substitution attack (such as using the signature from a GET request on a crafted POST request).
```

There are stimm multiple issues here:

- this not just about "list based" fields, but any case where there are multiple instances of the same field name - that may soundlike nitpicking, but the combination rule applies to *any* field
- "Note that intermediaries are allowed to separate values of list-based HTTP fields with any amount of whitespace between commas." - that sounds a bit like if this was about uncombining lists, but that's no whay you mean here , right?
- "For robustness, it is RECOMMENDED that messages include only a single value for any field covered under the signature, with the value for list-based fields serialized using the algorithm below." - once it's a single value, the actua algorithm doesn't matter at all.
- "This approach increases the chances of the field value remaining untouched through intermediaries." - it sort of guarantees it, unless the intermediary rewrites values it shouldn't touch (in which case we want the sig to fail)
- "Where that approach is not possible and multiple field lines need to be sent separately, it is RECOMMENDED that signers and verifiers process list-based fields starting with the individual field values based on the strict algorithm below, where possible, to account for possible intermediary behavior." - that makes it sound as if that would help - but if the intermediary combines in a different way (such as no SP), the sig will definitively fail.

Thanks, I think I'm still getting hung up on getting the precise terminology here -- noted about "list-based" fields, but I do think it's worth pointing it out as these are the fields that specifically fall into this category.

One thing I'm confused about: Aren't intermediaries allowed to process lists _as lists_? Part of the concern here is that I send `Foo: a, b` (one space) and an intermediary turns that into `Foo: a,b` (no space) in transit, which would fail the signature w/o the semantics of the field changing. I believe this is allowed, but am I wrong here? If I'm wrong then we can lean harder on the single field instance's value. The algorithm given is for *creating* the single field value.

The final recommendation is actually to split the values apart and re-combine them with "comma <SP>", so an intermediary messing with the spacing actually wouldn't affect the value in the signature base, since it would be re-created.
No, intermediaries are not supposed to rewrite field values. In particular, an intermediary cannot assume that a comma is indeed a list delimiter in general -- consider quoted strings. Or ETags.
I've taken another shot at this -- please take a look at the new text.

In the above example we have that:

1. content-digest is signed
2. content-encoding is not present
3. content-encoding is not signed

If I add a content-encoding header, the signature is still valid, since content-encoding is not signed and the client does not know whether:

1. content-encoding in the original request was present but not signed by accident
2. content-encoding was missing and the request was tampered

Correct, you cannot sign an absent header. That feature was discussed at length and rejected by the wg. The original message could have a content encoding header, whether or not that's covered by the signature. Absence from the signature does not imply absence from the message, as you claim above. These are independent.

If you add a content encoding header, and this changes the content, the signature is not valid because the digest is no longer valid - while the signature itself would pass the digest would not, as is pointed out in this section. Now this is assuming you change the content and don't just add a meaningless header. If you don't change the content but claim a different encoding, this should fail when the message is processed because the encoding makes no sense. Signature and digest won't fix a badly formed http message.

In all of these cases, I believe the system is behaving as intended and failing where we'd expect it to fail, and how we expect it to fail. So, I am with @reschke here in that I don't see what the issue is with this situation.

I'm with Julian and Justin here. Not signing a field is tangential to that field applying to the message.

Signatures doesn't support covering the absence of a field. And it's sad that there's no formal definition that allows "Content-encoding: nothing". But these are things we are stuck with. The rough edge, of signing content-digest and having someone screw up the message isn't nice but will fail closed and will be quickly noticeable. The workaround is gzip (or whatever) the content if your application really can't live this sharp edge, then you have a proper content-encoding to send.

 I don't think Signstures needs to do anything special here. There's lots of ways applications can screw up signing unrelated to content digest.
I agree that the issue is we can't say `content-encoding: nothing`. The example could use a content-encoding as a workaround.

pulls.title: [WIP] RFC6265bis: "Lax-Allowing-Unsafe" applies to cross-site redirect
pulls.author: sbingler
pulls.body:
This PR is a WIP while waiting on data to show us that this is the correct approach.

Until https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1348, the spec mistakenly didn't define the same-site-ness to include the redirect chain. When some UAs, such as Chrome, attempted to apply the changes in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/1348 they found that users complained of breakage. Bug reports hinted that this occurred during similar situations as Lax+POST, i.e.: young cookies with an unsafe method.

This changes modifies lax-allowing-unsafe to also include cookies that being blocked due a cross-site redirect with an unsafe method. It retains the suggested 2 min limit on cookie age.

Update the semantics of parameters in Accept-Signature to be more fully defined and explicit.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
I think the new text adds complexity and potential security issues. Specifically, the client/signer (which is in some cases the weakest link) now needs to handle a complicated request from the server and resolve potential conflicts. What if `keyid` does not match `alg`?

Some of these flags are not useful, since there's no harm done if the signer _always_ sends `created` and `expires`, and the verifier is free to respect or ignore them. But `alg` is actively harmful -- the algorithm should be determined by `keyid`. (Thinking of well known JWT security issues.)

comments.author: jricher
comments.body:
@yaronf the ability to send `alg` and `keyid` is not new with this text -- in fact those were the ones that were previously allowed, the other parameters were prohibited before. There's already a security consideration about choosing algorithms and matching the algorithm to the key ID, both of which the signer has to do :anyway: when signing a message -- this is not added or changed by the Accept-Signature field.

I do think that perhaps it warrants calling out specifically in a security consideration about Accept Signature, though, to hopefully prevent naive processing of Accept-Signature requests.

A suggestion you might consider...  I think that it would be helpful to include a more complete example here.

There is a hazard here in that any inconsistency how processing occurs creates interesting effects.  That is, the field is destroyed if a Date if observed.  That might lead to [Heisenbug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heisenbug)s.

Let's say you have a WAF that uses SF to parse, but it only looks at certain things.  Maybe it doesn't look at parameters.  This might ignore a Date on something like:

```
Example: ?0;t=@4098543601
```

Code that processes the `t` parameter might (rightfully) discard the field if it sees the Date.

comments.body:
```suggestion

The effect of upgrading a Structured Fields implementation is that some field values that were invalid according to RFC 8941 might become valid when processed.  For instance, though it would not be valid for a field defined against RFC 8941, a field might include include a Date value. An RFC 8941 implementation would reject the entire field, whereas an updated Structured Field implementation might permit the value. In some cases, the resulting Date value will be rejected by field-specific logic, but values in fields that are otherwise ignored (such as extension parameters) might not be detected and the field might subsequently be accepted and processed.

```
Hm, that's very wordy, and this section is already quite wordy.
I know. I don’t like it much for that reason. But maybe this is worth the text. Slapping a section header on might help. “Backwards Compatibility” might be a good title.

I cannot in good confidence say that any of this adds clarity, but I will not go as far as to call it surpluage, because there is a point to be made here.

I think what bugs me, is that having a SFbis parser return an unexpected and illegal sf-date is not materially different from having a 8941 parser return sf-decimal where sf-integer was expected.

In the end, the responsibility for validating the header can only fall on the application code.

Maybe we should simply write that, and use the 8941-defined-SFbis-parser-returning-sf-date example to illustrate a detail people might otherwise miss ?

```suggestion
Because this specification effectively extends RFC 8941, deployments that use implementations of it need to be aware of the effects of adding a new type on error handling when that type is sent erroneously. If the application does not check the type of the result and reject the Date value, it could lead to interoperability issues, since it was relying on parser behaviour that has changed.
```
See proposal below.

However, this document is designed to be backwards-compatible with RFC 8941; a parser that implements the requirements here can also parse valid Structured Fields whose definitions reference RFC 8941, but if the parser output contains any Date values, the caller must reject it as invalid, to remain RFC 8941 compliant.

Content coding mechanisms can support different encoding parameters, meaning that the same input content can produce different outputs. For example, GZIP supports mulitple compression levels. pulls.title: Clarify that hashing bytes are base-64 encoded and give examples
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
With Digest, the encoding of the digest value was based on the digest
algorithm. For different algorithms, this varied between base64, hex
encoding or decimal encoding.

In this spec, we removed the variablilty by using SF Byte Sequence,
which is always serialized as a base-64 encoding of the input bytes. All
algorithms are now expected to use this format.

This change tries to make it more clear that we expect the input of the
Byte Sequence to be. For example, we really don't want people accidentally
base-64'ing the textual hex represenation output of cksum - that can
lead to interop pain.

To help implementers further, add a new appendix with some samples that
can be used as test vectors.

Closes #2385
