pulls.author: jricher
pulls.body: A signature over another signature does not provide the transitive protection that it seems it should. The examples and advice have been updated to accomodate this.

comments.author: jricher
comments.body: @bblfish @yaronf can you please verify the signatures on the updated examples in this PR?
Does this need to say "client's signature value" given the attacks that Dennis describes?

@martinthomson not sure I understand the comment -- are you saying the signature value shouldn't be included in the proxy's signature at all, or that where it says "original signature" it should instead read "the client's signature"? If the former, the attack surface is a little bit different here because the proxy is a trusted party that's making a different kind of statement than the request-response-binding non-repudiation. This is mitigated by covering additional portions of the message, including the signature input line and any items that didn't change, along with items that did change at the proxy.

As below, I think that saying that the server signs the signature is a problem.  It can sign the request, including the signature-input field, which would be sufficient.  In that case, signing the signature is - as I understand it - OK, but it is worth making it clear that signing the signature alone is what leads to attacks.

I'm having trouble identifying what criteria you are using to decide what is signed or not in this example.

It's a little distressing that the signature doesn't cover the body of either message.  Is there a reason for that?  It seems though you could make an argument that the content of the request has no material impact on the outcome (the server being busy could be true for any request and you have included method and authority).  The content of the busy message itself seems material - or at least more important than the length of that message.

With intermediaries involved - a key motivation behind this design - it might be worth pointing out that if the server signs something that an intermediary added the client is unlikely to be able to validate the signature.

I guess the problem here is that the specific example is hard to follow.  Is it fair to say that the proxy has two goals: 1. it wants to cover the request that arrives at the server and 2. it also wants to transitively attest to what the client requested of it (maybe because the server can also validate that, but this is not entirely clear from context).

The former does not require that the signature or signature input from the client needs to be covered at all.  The latter is more interesting and requires that the proxy not change anything that the client signed, it can only add things that it additionally signs.  But in that case, the proxy can simply sign the same stuff the client did (and anything extra).  The only thing that is left is signing the fact that it knows that the client signed the message or signing to signal that it validated the client's signature (what signing a signature means here between those two, I don't know, maybe the difference is encoded in the difference between signing `signature-input` and signing `signature`).

Either way, the emphasis on including the signature is probably not really advancing a particular goal and should be de-emphasized.
The body could be covered by also signing a content-digest header, but we just didn't add that to this example because that's not what the example is trying to showcase and emphasize.

I think framing it in terms of signing the request, including portions of the request, is fine.

The criteria here is simply to pick a few things to showcase the function. This isn't a real application, it's a strawman example.
I'm just looking for plausible.  I'm having a little bit of a hard time suspending disbelief with this one, that's all.

comments.author: bsdphk
comments.body:
I am, as amply communicated previously, very firmly against this very idea.

I am against it in principle because the last two decades have seen the HTTP protocol systematically move away from being UX-adjecent to being pure IPC messaging, to the extent that "HTTP is the new TCP" has become a meme.

This is why H2 and H3 wisely, and explicitly, dropped the "reason phrase" from the response status message, to avoid wading into the I18N sump at the protocol handling level.

Adding a Yet Another Escape Mechanism, when we already have a well defined sf-blob to safely transfer arbitrary byte-sequences is also a blatant violation of Getty's first rule:

»Do not add new functionality unless an implementor cannot complete a real application without it.«

Precisely what is it, that who cannot do, using sf-blob to transfer these byte-sequences ?!

Second, the specific proposal contains the kind of half-assery which time and time again has come back to haunt us as security issues.

Is the contents UTF8 sequence or not ?

Who can tell ?

The proposed text makes this entirely up to the sender, and makes no requirement for them declare it in the message.

We're supposed to take a byte sequence and "present it to users", but we're not told if it is UTF8, BAUDOT or EBCDIC ?

And dont forget that validating Unicode requires an up-to-date copy of the Unicode registry.

How can that possibly go wrong...

And reusing %xx encoding in a place where it has never before been used ?

How many pieces of code will unintentionally interpret %xx encoding and emit random byte-values where they are not supposed to go ?

You can bet your sweet arse that there are places out there which do %xx substitution on the entire HTTP message because the URI field needs it:  Now add a couple of %0d%0a in a HTTP message and you have a smugling attack.

If we want to provide a mechanism for "strings to be presented to users" in HTTP fields, we should do it properly.

As the absolute minimum, that requires nailing down the encoding and a negotiation mechanism for cultural choices of language and dialect.

But in my world, that does certainly not belong at the "HTTP is the new TCP" level of the stack.

Summary:

* Needless addition of complexity, all uses cases are already covered by sf-blob.
* Half-assed specification invites security issues down the road.
* Wrong level of the protocol stack to be doing this.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I am not concerned about encodings (it is UTF-8, always, and a failure to convert to a string or validate as UTF-8 should be treated as a parse error).  We can note that this can encode any byte sequence, but that non-UTF-8 sequences are invalid.  We don't need to validate that the characters are valid or in any particular form in order for them to be useful; UTF-8 decoding is simple, easy, and sufficient at this layer.

I am not concerned about NUL, though we should definitely note that it is possible to encode `%00`, which might be surprising.

I'm not concerned about display requirements.  Software always needs to be careful with unsanitized or untrustworthy inputs, this is no different.  Encoding strings as binary and interpreting them that way has exactly the same problem.

I'm not concerned about smuggling.  Or rather, I think we should note the possibility and say "don't serialize display strings back into messages without escaping them properly".

So I think that PHK has pointed out where the security considerations on this change are insufficient, but that insufficiency only exists to the extent that this change isn't highlighting the risks involved.

In addition to those, we should also note that language tagging (it is often a requirement when handling Unicode data that language choice determines how that handling is performed) is not directly provided.  We can point out that parameters could be used for this purpose, if necessary, though there are obviously other ways to obtain that information as well (like `Content-Language`).

pulls.author: DavidSchinazi
pulls.body: Fixes #2490

comments.body:
I think that you want to be clearer about what is going on here.  In prose.  That is, 48 bytes is output, then the first 32 bytes is input to the signature and the next 16 bytes are sent along with the signature (to allow the recipient to confirm that the exporter produces the right values).

@dennisjackson, could you just transmit half the nonce instead of extending the KDF output?  The other half should be hard to guess, but confirming that way would save an extra invocation of HMAC.  (I'm not particularly concerned about the cost; I'm just asking to improve my understanding.)
I don't like this word, as we've previously discussed.  "Signature Input" would work.

Why not simply send the nonce on the wire? The server could then check that (1) the nonce is as expected and (2) the signature is valid. I realize that would result in more bytes on the wire, but splitting up the nonce/verification just seems odd to me. The `verification` value is like a proxy for the actual message being signed, so I thought to myself, why not just send the actual message that's signed?
Ah, I see @martinthomson had basically the same thought.
Why not just send the entire nonce?

If we send the entire nonce, then a lazy implementer could use that as the value for signature checking instead of properly computing the key exporter. The current design (or MT's proposal to only send part of the nonce) avoid that risk.

My gut feeling is that using another part of the key exporter would make security analysis easier than using part of the nonce, but I'll let @dennisjackson comment on that
Signature Input sounds good to me. I'll address this as an editorial change after I land the current train of PRs to avoid having to deal with 17 merge conflicts
See other comment thread
I'm not sure I buy the lazy implementer argument, but I also think sending half the nonce would be sufficient here.

I agree that sending half the nonce would work, but what's the benefit? We need to transmit some sort of verification bit regardless, so the only benefit I see to reusing the start of the nonce instead of getting some more key exporter output is that it saves an HKDP operation. I'd rather take the minimal CPU hit to avoid bit reuse if there's no other benefit
It just seems like the most obvious thing to do: send the message that is being signed.
Filed #2578 to track this

Sorry for the slow response. 

Short answer: @chris-wood is right that from a formal analysis perspective sending the entire message or a hash of the entire message would also be fine and this is the generic fix to this kind of signature attack. @martinthomson's suggestion of sending half the signature input also works in this specific case. However, for pragmatic reasons I think @DavidSchinazi's solution is nicest overall. 

Longer answer: 

From the perspective of a formal analysis, using the full or half signature input is fine. The positive property we're looking for is that the sender is committed to a single message input, so the full message obviously achieves that. The half input is only going to match with prob 2^128 so also fine. Thinking about negative consequences, we're going from transmitting the signature of the authenticator to the authenticator itself. In a formal analysis, this isn't ever going to be a problem because signature schemes are assumed to be unforgeable (EUF-CMA) but nothing more, so an attacker in 'proof world' can do things like take a signature and reverse it to learn the message (even though that's typically hard in the real world).   

Pragmatically though, I like @DavidSchinazi's solution best. It lessens the risk of a lazy implementer using the sender's value by mistake in the signature verification or trying to save a `memcmp` by skipping the second check of the signature input. 

Another *very* minor benefit that in some signature schemes like Ed25519, the attacker can't reverse it in practice as they only learn `h(pk || m)` and in this case `m` is high entropy. So in the case the implementer uses Ed25519, by using the extra KDF output you make it intractable for an attacker who has witnessed an unprompted auth header to extract the authenticator value.

pulls.title: Switch to URLPattern for request matching
pulls.author: pmeenan
pulls.body:
This switches the custom wildcard matching to use [URLPattern](https://wicg.github.io/urlpattern/) with regexp support disabled. URLPattern is being used by the service worker routing API's and is what the web side is standardizing on for anything that pattern-matches URLs.

This splits the match pattern into explicit path and search (query param) components and forces the origin to be inherited from the dictionary request URL.

Also included here is a new `Use-As-Dictionary` field for `match-dest` to allow for matching on request destinations. The biggest use case for that will be for allowing site-wide HTML dictionaries to do something like `Use-As-Dictionary: match-path="/*", match-dest="document"` and for the dictionary to not be sent for every request across the site (images, etc).

See issues #2639, #2638, #2625

It might be worth talking to @wanderview about whether this has any hope of turning into a REC, hopefully through a working group.  It might be possible to get this particular piece of work done in the IETF, which might be easier than trying to find a home for it in W3C-land.

pulls.title: Improve consistency of request variations
pulls.author: pmeenan
pulls.body:
This set of changes should reduce the number of variants that caches end up seeing from clients requesting dictionary-compressed resources with `Vary: accept-encoding, available-dictionary".

The default `ttl` is reduced to 7 days and the language is updated to refresh the expiration time whenever the dictionary is loaded from a local cache. That way the dictionary will default to being usable for up to 7 days after the last time a given client loaded the dictionary (as part of a page load or otherwise). This is independent of when it was last sent as "available" so if a page rotates dictionaries or JS libraries, the old one that is being used as a dictionary by clients won't be "loaded" any more, even if it isn't replaced so it will age out.

The `Accept-Encoding` header was updated to require `br` when `br-d` and `zstd` when `zstd-d` are advertised as well as specifying that the order be sorted alphabetically. This is an attempt to inject some cross-client consistency in the Accept-Encoding header when the same compression schemes are supported.

There will still be some fan-out for clients that support dictionaries but different sets of encodings but it should be a better baseline than we have today where they are not normalized.

See #2635

pulls.title: Upload progress via informational responses
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Based on the discussion in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2291, this PR would allow servers to repeatedly generate 104 responses to inform the client about the upload progress. The formulation allows the client to free associated resources (e.g. file buffers) because the server guarantees that the upload offset will never be less than the last reported value.

Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2291.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: If this is not a mandatory part of the protocol, I wonder how the client would know that the server supports it. It's possible that the client has already forgot about the initial bytes beyond the first ACK when the ACK is received.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
I don't think the client must know in advance whether the server will send these additional informational responses. This mechanism is an additional enhancement, but not much should be lost if the server does not implement it.

> It's possible that the client has already forgot about the initial bytes beyond the first ACK when the ACK is received.

Yes, that can happen, but this can also occur in the current draft version. If the client forgot bytes that come before the `Upload-Offset` reported by the server, it cannot continue the upload. The only save way for the client to regularly forget data is by chunking the upload into multiple requests using `Upload-Complete: ?0` and thereby getting a confirmation from the server about the new upload offset.

The addition of 104 for progress information does not change much about this approach. If you want to be sure about the offset, you should chunk the upload. But the 104s provide a slight improvement, where the client can already forget data before the request is completed. In a sense, the client should never forget data before the request is completed or a 104 is received if the client wants to recover from upload failures.

This PR should just be an enhancement for the client, but not pose any additional issues for it. Does that make sense?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Based on the feedback from #2291 and IETF 118, I adjust the text in this PR to clarify what header fields can be present in informational responses:

Upload creation:
- Server may send one or more 104 responses
- The first 104 response must contain the Location header, subsequent responses must not.
- The Upload-Offset header is optional

Upload appending:
- Server may send one or more 104 responses
- The 104 response must not contain the Location header.
- The Upload-Offset header is optional

In theory, this allows a 104 to be generated with no Location or Upload-Offset header, but I don't see a reason against disallowing this. The text now also ensures that the client knows the upload resource URL before it receives a 104 with Upload-Offset. This avoids implementation issues where the client might free upload data before it knows the upload resource URL to resume the upload in cases of failure.

Please let me know if these changes improve the draft's readability.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: If we are adding strict incrementing requirement to 104 responses, should we also do so for plain offset retrieving?

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
> If we are adding strict incrementing requirement to 104 responses, should we also do so for plain offset retrieving?

I would prefer so for consistency.

To me, the text seems a bit vague regarding if it mandates the inclusion of upload-offset header in the first 104 response.

My preference would go to mandate inclusion of `upload-offset` header field in all 104 responses (even with the first one, which would typically carry a value of `0`), or say that use of that header is optional in all 104 responses.

Maybe it would make sense to go with the latter, considering that `upload-offset` is an optimization that we consider optional.

Good point, the language could be refined to make the possible headers in 104 more clear. Keeping Upload-Offset optional in 104 would be my preference because a `Upload-Offset: 0` looks like no data was saved at all, which might not be true. So I agree with your preference here.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: @martinthomson this adds the dictionary hash to the HTTP response when used.  Right now it is a `SHOULD`. Let me know if you think it should be a `MUST` instead.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
> If this field carries binary data, why aren't you using structured fields?

Mostly for developer ergonomics to make it easier to deploy. In the case of static resources using previous versions as dictionaries (v1 to v2 of main.js), one method for enabling that is to compress the new version using the old version on the cli as part of the push to production and store the dictionary-compressed artifact as a file on the server next to the full file.  Then at serving time, compare the value of the `Available-Dictionary` request header with the file names on the server for the given URL to see if a delta-compressed artifact is available.

Structured fields encode the binary data as base-64 encoded strings which aren't filesystem-friendly so there would need to be some steps at serving time to decode the header, convert it to ascii and then check. It's not insurmountable but it's a bit more processing and a straight string match could be handled directly with templating in server config.

Lowercase hex was picked since that's what all of the cli tools for generating hashes emit.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: Is `Content-Dictionary` a reasonable name for the response header?  I'd actually prefer `Dictionary` but it felt like that might be over-stepping since there could be some other generic need for associating a dictionary with a HTTP-response but maybe I'm being overly-cautious.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I don't think that authoring convenience outweighs the advantages of having a unified grammar here.  It's not like base64 is some esoteric function.  If you are talking about sha256sum, here's a toy: https://github.com/martinthomson/shabase64

comments.author: reschke
comments.body: I agree with @martinthomson - don't. To make the sf value filesystem friendly, you just need to strip a few characters and remap "/".

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
> Lowercase hex was picked since that's what all of the cli tools for generating hashes emit.

Keep in mind that hashes are not hex strings. A SHA-256 hash is 32 bytes of binary data. The hex thing is just what some tools happen to output. But anything consuming this programmatically to, e.g., compare the hash against something would be best served by the underlying bytes.

Using base64 is also slightly more compact on the wire. And if binary structured fields gets off the ground, it can be even more compact.

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
My main concern is trading off a unified grammer of using sf-binary in the headers vs consistency with tooling and how the dictionaries are represented once it gets out of the protocol.

In the dynamic case, this could be something like the web server checking to see if the requested dictionary is available (on disk) in response to a request. I don't know how each web server will choose to build that but having files named with the hash is an easy common starting point. Otherwise each chooses what the ascii representation of the 32-byte hash should be for their case.

On the static case, I'm not so much worried about not having a tool that can create base64-encoded strings of sha256 hashes (it's trivial as you pointed out). I'm more concerned about the transformations that need to happen at serving time to decode the hash, convert it into an ascii representation and then check if that variant of the encoded file is available. It's certainly all doable, but it requires base64decode and binhex (or some equivalents) to be available in the layer where the checks are being done - or to rely on application code.

Specifically, I was thinking that it would be easy enough in VCL or an existing Nginx or Apache config to do something like:

* If `Available-Dictionary` request header is present and validates against a [0-9a-f]+ regex
* and 'br-d' is available in the `Accept-Encoding` request header
* try returning `<path>` + '.' + request['Accept-Encoding'] + '.br-d' (and add relevant response headers)
* otherwise return `<path>`

Doing similar processing with base64-encoded hashes has a step to convert it into an unspecified format that is platform-specific and may not be doable without either running application code or updating the server with base64decode + binhex support.

It likely doesn't matter for the case of applications and servers that are dictionary-aware and can operate on the raw hashes (and enjoy the ~20 byte request header savings) but it is a tradeoff that pushes complexity further up the stack so I just want to make sure that is the tradeoff that we want to make.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
Having a finally consistent grammar for HTTP is the precursor to get consistent tooling. It may be more convenient to do something else in the short term, but in the long term we'd just be adding to the mess of inconsistency in HTTP. In the long term, I would hope that these config language DSLs would be able to process structured fields natively. (Although, it may be on this WG to demonstrate this being possible, since the data model for structured fields is slightly interesting...)

I also don't think we should be encouraging, much less designing for, folks trying to process HTTP headers with regexps. There's a well-defined grammar and inventing other parsers is a great way to not quite get things right. We already have a pretty hard time with HTTP extensibility due to folks parsing it wrong.

The path-unfriendliness is a little unfortunate. Possibly we should have picked the URL-safe version of base64, but too late for that. But since byte strings and text strings aren't the same type, I imagine any sf-binary-aware config language DSL would also have hex and base64 functions available. Indeed taking attacker-supplied input and mapping it to a path component, without running it through some very restrictive encoding, seems a pretty bad idea!

At the end of the day, SHA-256 hashes are byte strings, and sf-binary is the way HTTP decided to say byte string.

We could say that, although SHA-256 hashes are byte strings, dictionary names are ASCII strings computed by hex(sha256). Then these headers should be sf-string (with quotes). But that would be less efficient on the wire, and our [mandate](https://www.w3.org/TR/design-principles/#priority-of-constituencies) on the web is to put user needs (bandwidth, in this case) first, so I think this is the wrong tradeoff.

That said, I see `Available-Dictionary` also uses this format. It wouldn't make sense for `Available-Dictionary` and `Content-Dictionary` to use different formats, so perhaps switching away from the less consistent and less efficient format should probably be handled separately from this PR?

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body: I switched `Available-Dictionary` and `Content-Dictionary` both to sf-binary.  The plan is to update the ID and then send out a summary of changes for discussion on the listserv and since this PR is about the dictionary in the headers anyway it should be fine to update both of them at the same time.  Happy to split it out if it helps with history tracking.

comments.author: yoavweiss
comments.body:
I think this change adds significant complexity, and I'm not sure regarding its benefits.

I very recently played around with prototyping a compression dictionaries deployment and was very happy with the simplicity of it:
* You generate diff files at build time with some naming convention
* Then at serving time, you configure your routing logic (similarly to how @pmeenan [pointed out](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2680#issuecomment-1810759792)) to those diffs

That can be done today in almost any deployed routing layer.

Once this change lands in implementations, a similar deployment would require me to add custom logic to transform that header value to something that is file system friendly. 
It doesn't matter if that transformation is to base64 decode the binary data and then to hex encode it, or to 'just.. strip a few characters and remap "/"'. It is an operation that is not necessarily supported in many layers that developers currently operate in.

To take just one example - if I were to implement this as a [Cloudflare transform rule](https://developers.cloudflare.com/rules/transform/url-rewrite/), I'm not even sure it's feasible to do that. (although it might be,  with a creative [`regex_replace`](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ruleset-engine/rules-language/functions/#function-regex_replace)).

Can you elaborate on the advantages of moving to base64, beyond theoretical purity?

reviews.author: martinthomson
reviews.body: If this field carries binary data, why aren't you using structured fields?

comments.body: This isn't lowercase.  Strings in ABNF are case-insensitive.  You need to use `%x61-66`.
A "MUST NOT" here doesn't really help.  "cannot" is probably the word you want.
Usually when we use "SHOULD", there is a discussion about what sort of reasons might lead to the recommendation being ignored.  What might cause a server to choose not to include this field?
Thanks. Updated.
I changed it to MUST since there isn't really a good case for when you wouldn't send the dictionary used in the response.

Is "cannot" the right way to phrase it when it is technically possible but bad things could happen? i.e. You can decompress a resource using a dictionary other than the one that was used to compress it but you will get the wrong output (level of brokenness depends on how much the dictionaries varied).  So it's "possible" to do but you absolutely must not do it or you'll get corrupt data.
"cannot decode or use" would probably be correct. The client could _attempt_ to decode, but the decoding will not be successful, and a content-digest would reveal that.

Thanks.  Changed to cannot.  I was just worried that it was a technical barrier that people might try to rely on (decode and trust that it would fail if the dictionary didn't match) instead of failing silently by generating garbage.

reviews.body: Thanks!

pulls.title: Add security consideration regarding request filtering
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
As brought up in #2681, resumable uploads may interfere with intermediaries scanning the request content. This PR adds a paragraph in the security considerations.

Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2681.

comments.body: For reviewers: I combined line 397 and 399 into one paragraph without modifying the sentences, but the git diff displays this in a more complex way.

```suggestion
Some servers or intermediaries provide scanning of content uploaded by clients. Any scanning mechanism that relies on receiving a complete file in a single request message can be defeated by resumable uploads because content can be split across multiple messages. Servers or intermediaries wishing to perform content scanning SHOULD consider how resumable uploads can circumvent scanning and take appropriate measures. Possible strategies include waiting for the upload to complete before scanning a full file, or disabling resumable uploads.
```

basically a slight rewrite of the text to sound more like stating what some servers do and warning them why their implementations might get circumvented if they don't accomodate for resumable uploads. As much as we might not like it, disabling resumable uploads in such servers is a valid solution to the new problem we've created.
Thank you very much, Lucas!

This adds support for a server-provided sf-string "id" of up to 1024 characters that is echoed back in a "Dictionary-ID" request header when the dictionary is advertised as being available.

This allows for a server to use something other than the hash to retrieve the dictionary (i.e. a cache key). This should be more flexible than the client sending the original request URL and will allow for servers to store arbitrary context information with the dictionary.

It doesn't open up any additional privacy or security concerns because the dictionary hash was already being treated as if it was user-identifiable information.

For #2633

comments.body: You can use https://urlpattern.spec.whatwg.org/#urlpattern-has-regexp-groups as of this morning :)

@jeremyroman points out this is almost certainly not correct, since by default the hash is `"*"`, so you're requiring authors to explicitly have the pattern include `#` at the end.

I don't think this check is necessary. If the author includes a pattern like `/foo#bar`, this will simply never match. There's no reason to reject that at this stage; it will cause line 255 to return false.

I'm not sure these steps are necessary. If the author includes another origin, then I believe this will fail to match, since `input=URL` (line 255) will not match the pattern due to protocol/username/password/hostname/port mismatches there.

If for some reason different-origin URLs are a possible input into line 255, then the simplest way to handle that would be to add a check before line 255 which checks the URL's origin before doing the URL pattern matching, to exclude them from matching any dictionaries. Thanks. switched over to it.

pulls.title: Discuss the proxy's origin in more detail
pulls.author: bemasc
pulls.body: Fixes #2643

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: After looking harder, I found that RFC 9110 [says](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-7.3.2-1) that a proxy "is usually identified by an "http" or "https" URI".  I'm not sure that's 100% accurate, but it conveniently resolves the wording problem, and who am I to argue with RFC 9110?

reviews.author: DavidSchinazi
reviews.body: Overall this is going in the right direction. A few comments inline.

comments.body:
```suggestion
Ordinarily, HTTP allows multiple origin hostnames to share a single server IP address and port number (i.e., virtual-hosting), by specifying the applicable hostname in the "Host" or ":authority" header field.  However, classic HTTP CONNECT proxies use these fields to indicate the CONNECT request's destination ({{?RFC9112, Section 3.2.3}}), leaving no way to distinguish multiple proxy origins on one server.  As a result, classic HTTP CONNECT proxies cannot be deployed using virtual-hosting, nor can they apply the usual defenses against server port misdirection attacks (see {{Section 7.4 of ?RFC9110}}).  The absence of an explicit origin for the proxy also creates ambiguity about the use of origin-scoped response header fields such as Alt-Svc {{?RFC7838}} and Strict-Transport-Security {{?RFC6797}}.
```

Classic HTTP CONNECT proxies don't have a scheme.

```suggestion
Classic HTTP CONNECT proxies are identified by a host and port.  The proxy does not have a path of its own.  This prevents any origin from hosting multiple distinct proxy services.
```

```suggestion
A templated TCP proxy has an unambiguous origin of its own.  Origin-scoped HTTP header fields such as Alt-Svc {{?RFC7838}} and Strict-Transport-Security {{?RFC6797}} apply to this origin when they are associated with a templated TCP proxy request or response.
```

I have a few concerns related to this paragraph. First, this isn't specific to Web browsers. Second, this should be written as normative text, as it isn't clear to me if it is trying to convey MUST or SHOULD. Third, I think both Proxy-Authorization and Authorization make sense here just like they both make sense for GET - because you can have an intermediary between the client and proxy. But overall, this topic warrants its own discussion. Can we split this off to its own issue and PR?
Hm. Don't they essentially have a scheme? We have both 'HTTP' and 'HTTPS' CONNECT proxies, so that *seems* like a scheme.

Yeah maybe "host, port, and use of TLS"?

Scheme is part of URI, but CONNECT does not deal with an URI.

I actually prefer @bemasc's text here. The term "Proxy origin" sounds confusing to me, as origin is the CONNECT destination in case of traditional CONNECT. "Proxy" is more succinct and serves the purpose.

Agreed that if we are to add this paragraph we need to open a specific issue.

FWIW, [RFC 9110 Section 11.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-authenticating-users-to-ori) states that WWW-Authenticate, Authorization, and 401 deals with origins (or the target resource). I would personally be surprised if we are to use the proxy variants here.
I changed this to "a host, a port number, and optionally a security protocol".
OK, I removed this paragraph and opened #2694 to discuss.

```suggestion
Classic HTTP CONNECT proxies are identified by a host, a port number, and whether a security protocol is used or not.  The proxy does not have a path of its own.  This prevents any HTTP origin from hosting multiple distinct proxy services.
```
If we want to keep the term "proxy", then we should define it in this document. This usage of proxy feels odd to me but perhaps with an appropriate definition it works.

Yeah "proxy" is a term defined in https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-3.7-5, I think we might want to refer to that definition, considering that this is an HTTP extension.

Regarding how we talk, I think things might become clearer if we talk about "HTTP proxies" here. HTTP proxies are identified by host, port, and use of TLS. Traditional CONNECT is just one way of using the HTTP proxies.

We could point that out, then go on to explain explain that this extension defines the way to establish a TCP tunnel "through HTTP origin."

Expanding on my comment above, how about something like:
```suggestion
An ordinary HTTP request involves a URI, which includes an origin as a property. Since clients specify origins in HTTP requests using the "Host" or ":authority" header field, servers can colocate multiple origins on a single server IP address and port number, a practice known as virtual hosting. However, the classic CONNECT method is an exception. It targets a proxy, and the hostname of the proxy is not included in the HTTP request. As a result, classic CONNECT cannot be deployed using virtual hosting, nor can it implement the usual defenses against server port misdirection attacks (see {{Section 7.4 of ?RFC9110}}). The absence of an explicit origin for the proxy also creates ambiguity about the use of origin-scoped response header fields such as Alt-Svc {{?RFC7838}} and Strict-Transport-Security {{?RFC6797}}.
```
OK, I've added a reference to that section and clarified that we mean "HTTP proxy".

reviews.author: kazuho
reviews.body:
Re RFC 9110 Section 7.3.2, well found!

The PR looks good modulo the nitpick below.

comments.body:
I'm not sure if the second and third sentence are accurate. It's not only the path; none of the proxy's URI component are conveyed by a CONNECT request. A CONNECT proxy is not an origin in terms of HTTP, it is a proxy.

Maybe something like:
```suggestion
HTTP proxies are usually identified by an "http" or "https" URI ({{?RFC9110, Section 7.3.2}}).  However, HTTP requests do not convey any of the proxy's URI components.  Instead, they only carry the URI of the request target (i.e., the origin) or, in the case of CONNECT requests, the host and port of the target.  This prevents any HTTP server from hosting multiple distinct proxy services.
```

This text in 9110 is about proxies in general, but doesn't apply to CONNECT proxies. When sending a GET request to a proxy, the scheme is present - but not for CONNECT. I think we were better off with the previous wording.

GET requests to an HTTP request proxy carry the scheme of the target origin, not the proxy.  I don't see any indication that the text in 9110 is about request proxies but excludes CONNECT proxies, especially since CONNECT was always designed to be used alongside HTTP request proxying with the same proxy server (for "https" and "http" target origins, respectively).

Section 7.3.2 of 9110 (and 7.3 more broadly) are specifically about routing _requests_. CONNECT is a means to establish a connection, not a way to send requests. From that section:
> the client connects inbound by establishing (or reusing) a connection to that proxy and then sending it an HTTP request message containing a request target that matches the client's target URI.

In the use-case of HTTPS-over-TLS-over-CONNECT-over-HTTP, the request message to the CONNECT proxy contains a request target that does *not* match the end-to-end target URI. So this section doesn't apply to CONNECT.

But perhaps a more productive path forward would be to focus on the fact that regular CONNECT doesn't carry a scheme nor path, and make some assertions specific to templated CONNECT. We might not agree on the details of what 9110 says, but I think we all agree that (1) regular CONNECT has pitfalls and (2) we know how to fix them in templated CONNECT - so might be best to focus on those points

@DavidSchinazi 
> So this section doesn't apply to CONNECT.

This is true, but I wonder if the fact requires any changes to the text being proposed.

FWIW, the text says that "(the requests) only indicate the URI of the request target (i.e., the origin) or, in the case of CONNECT requests, the host and port of the target," which is accurate for CONNECT.

I think we agree on the pitfalls, and this paragraph is trying specifically to explain one of the pitfalls (i.e., why virtual hosting is impossible).

Is it the case that the proposed text is hard to digest?

I think it's just the first sentence that bugs me because it doesn't match my understanding of CONNECT. A minimal change could be:

```suggestion
HTTP clients can be configured to use proxies by selecting a proxy hostname, a port, and whether to use a security protocol. However, CONNECT requests using the proxy do not carry this configuration information. Instead, they only indicate the hostname and port of the target. This prevents any HTTP server from hosting multiple distinct proxy services, as the server cannot distinguish them by path (as with distinct resources) or by origin (as in "virtual hosting").
```
@DavidSchinazi Yeah, I get the confusion. While people may repurpose URIs for specifying proxies, it is questionable if everyone is used to thinking that way. In that sense I like your text.

reviews.body: Thanks for the discussion!

pulls.title: [connect-tcp] Specify WWW-Authenticate as The One Way to authenticate
pulls.author: bemasc
pulls.body: Fixes #2694

comments.body:
```suggestion
A templated TCP proxy has an unambiguous origin of its own.

Origin-scoped HTTP header fields such as "Alt-Svc" {{?RFC7838}} and "Strict-Transport-Security" {{?RFC6797}} apply to this origin when they are associated with a templated TCP proxy request or response.
```

Maybe it would make sense to split the paragraph here, considering the use of Alt-Svc, Strict-Transport-Securuity, 401, WWW-Authenticate, Authorization are examples of the effects of the templated TCP proxy being an origin.

Regarding the last sentence, I think the intent is to state that the unit of authentication is the template proxy rather than the URI that includes the target host and port, and I think that's a reasonable assumption to make.

At the same time, I'm not sure what this means in practice, or if it is in accord with RFC 9110. The problem is that 401 is not cacheable unless the server says so, see [RFC 9000 Section 15.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.1-2).

Considering that, I think it might make sense to either:
* drop the sentence for simplicity, with the rationale being that clients can always decide not to use the template proxy for whatever reason, and a protocol specification does not need to specify when, or
* explain that clients might make such decision without using RFC 2119 key words.

This is true, but I'm specifically trying to emphasize the applicability of origin-scoped headers, and WWW-Authenticate is not origin-scoped.  I've expanded this section to clarify what "origin-scoped" means and include more examples.

I've rewritten this recommendation in terms of authentication realms, which hopefully dodges some of the caching questions.  Note that 9110 says Authorization is "usually, but not necessarily, [sent] after receiving a 401 (Unauthorized) response", so sending it more aggressively is not a violation of HTTP.

reviews.author: kazuho
reviews.body: Looks good! :+1:

comments.body:
If we have a topology like `Client -- Gateway -- Templated-Proxy`, then
* `Templated-Proxy` can require auth by using `401` / `WWW-Authenticate` / `Authorization`
* `Gateway` can require auth by using `407` / `Proxy-Authenticate` / `Proxy-Authorization`

I wouldn't say that "407 and related are not used", just that they're used by gateways and not origins.

```suggestion
Clients SHOULD assume that all proxy resources generated by a single template share a protection space (realm) ({{?RFC9110, Section 11.5}}).  For many authentication schemes, this will allow the client to avoid waiting for a "401 (Unauthorized)" response before each new connection through the proxy.
```
I've changed the instruction to active voice, to be clear that the templated proxy doesn't use 407.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Explain empty requests
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
This PR adds explanations helping readers to understand when empty requests for upload creation or appending might be useful and why server should support them.

Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2728.

reviews.author: LPardue
reviews.body: Thanks for this. A couple of suggestions to build on what you've put in.

comments.body:
While the statement is correct, I don't think we want to promote the idea that 1xx can fail, how about something like

```suggestion
The request content MAY be empty. If the `Upload-Complete` header field is then set to true, the client intends to upload an empty entity. An `Upload-Complete` header field is set to false is also valid. This can be used to create an upload resource URL before transferring data, which can save client or server resources. Since informational responses are optional, this technique provides another mechanism to learn the URL, at the cost of an additional round-trip before data upload can commence.
```

This is good. Its reminds me a bit of the slow loris treatment in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#section-21.6, so let's ~steal~ borrow some of that

We should cite [SLOWLORIS ](https://web.archive.org/web/20150315054838/http://ha.ckers.org/slowloris/) but I'm too lazy right now and in a web editor.

```suggestion
Resumable uploads are vulnerable to Slowloris-style attacks [SLOWLORIS]. A malicious client may create upload resources and keep them alive by regularly sending `PATCH` requests with no or small content to the upload resources. This could be abused to exhaust server resources by creating and holding open uploads indefinately with minimal work.

Servers SHOULD provide mitigations for Slowloris attacks, such as increasing the maximum number of clients the server will allow, limiting the number of uploads a single client is allowed to make, imposing restrictions on the minimum transfer speed an uploads is allowed to have, and restricting the length of time an upload resource can exist.
```

Is it common to refer to specific attacks in a spec like this? It's probably not the case with Slowloris but I imagine it being possible that a referenced attack is no longer applicable due to other reasons?

Good suggestion, thank you! I didn't want to imply that the transmission of a 1xx can fail, but rather wanted to highlight situations where the client is incapable of receiving them because the HTTP interface does not expose them. But your change expresses that better.
It's probably better to name and link to similar attacks to help the reader understand the topic and related issues better. So it doesn't do any harm, I guess.

Security considerations are always more advisory than strict. There's things that will be stale and, and new things we can't predicte. QUIC links to SlowLoris, H2 links to Netflix-discovered DoS attacks. The important thing is to be clear the sorts of problems, with examples , that there can be.

pulls.title: Resumable Uploads: `application/partial-upload` media type
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
As discussed in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2501 and https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2610, the PATCH requests needs a suiting media type to describe the message content.

Since there does not seem to be an existing, suitable media type, [we proposed the `application/partial-upload` media type on the media-types mailing list](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/media-types/XoF-_vBDWWS4KjLFjLlrbnuO8bw/). This PR is a first, rough attempt at including such a media type in the draft.

comments.body:
I feel that this sentence is a bit off, probably due to language barriers on my end. 

Suggested edit:
>  The request MUST use the `PATCH` method with `application/partial-upload` as content type and be sent to the upload resource. The `Upload-Offset` field value ({{upload-offset}}) MUST be set to the resumption offset.

To me "unmodified" reads as "take the entire thing and apply it without changes" which is probably not what is intended here? The server is not allowed to pick bytes that it appends, but I think we need to clarify that the entire request must not complete for the server to append data. I.e. if the connection breaks down after 100 bytes then as much as possible of those 100 bytes _should_ be appended and what is appended _must_ be appended without modification.

Minor nit: 

> The start and end of *THE* block of data might align with the start and end of the file that should be uploaded, but are not required to do so.

or 

> The start and end of *THE* data might align with the start and end of the file that should be uploaded, but are not required to do so.


Should we avoid using "file" as the thing to be uploaded and use something more generic like "resource that should be uploaded"?
Good idea, thank you.

You are right with the missing _the_.

Regarding file/resource: I am also struggling with the same question of what the call the thing that we want to upload. _File_ might not be the best choice as it might be confused with a file that is saved on disk as seen from an operating system's point of view. With resumable uploads, you can also upload streaming data that is not such a file but is generated on-demand. _Resource_ is also problematic as it has a special meaning in HTTP: https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#resources

We could use the term _file_ if we stat at the beginning of the document that it not only refers to files on disks, but all kinds of data sources (streaming or not).

pulls.title: Resumable Uploads: Subsequent resources using `Content-Location`
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
In https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2312 we discussed how a server could provide the client with access to information and resources that are generated based on the uploaded data. One solution that emerged was a `Content-Location` header the pointed to another resource, where the client could download data, fetch extracted information etc. This PR adds a small section explaining this possibility and its interaction with resumable uploads.

Closes #2312

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Is there a reason for the server to return a Content-Location before the upload is complete? I'm wondering if both Location and Content-Location together might be confusing.

```
HTTP/1.1 104 Upload Resumption Supported
Upload-Draft-Interop-Version: 5
Location: https://example.com/upload/b530ce8ff
Content-Location: https://example.com/uploaded/b530ce8ff
```

Also since we aren't defining what you can do with this resource, it might not help with interop today, so it's mainly a future extension point?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Is there a reason for the server to return a Content-Location before the upload is complete?

I think so, yes. A server might already process the uploaded data while the upload is still ongoing and make derived information available at the same time under the resource that Content-Location points to.

> I'm wondering if both Location and Content-Location together might be confusing.

I agree that it's a bit confusing, but I don't see a reason against it. RFC 9110 also includes some guides on how to interpret responses that include both header fields: https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.content-location

> Also since we aren't defining what you can do with this resource, it might not help with interop today, so it's mainly a future extension point?

Kind of, yes. This addition is indented to be a guide for people who are interested in how a server can indicate additional resources belonging to an upload. The exact handling is probably outside of the draft's scope and might already be covered enough by the HTTP semantics itself.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Allow 200 in response for retrieving offset
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
A server might allow GET requests to be sent to an upload resource and serve content, in which case a 200 status code is more appropriate for responses to HEAD requests. This PR lifts the requirement that a successful response must be a 200.

Closes #2662.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Add details about Transfer-Encoding and Content-Encoding
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
With this PR, I attempt to clarify the role of content and transfer encoding in resumable upload that is:
- the bytes for offsets are counted on a representation, where Content-Encoding might be applied, but not Transfer-Encoding because that is a property of the transfer and not the representation itself.
- an upload retain the same content coding throughout its lifecycle, meaning that requests to resume the upload should target the same representation with the same content coding. Otherwise, data might end up invalid on the server if the content coding is switched during the upload. 

Closes #2679 and #2674.

comments.body: Minor nit, but is "coding" and "encoding" the same thing? Google doesn't give a straight answer and English is not my first language.
Good addition! :) Same with coding vs encoding here

I took the language from [RFC 9110](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.content-encoding):
> The "Content-Encoding" header field indicates what content codings have been applied to the representation

So Content-Encoding is the header field name and its value identifies the used content codings, if I understood it correctly.
Same as above, but from RFC 9112: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9112#name-transfer-codings
Thanks for looking it up! Seems reasonable. Ignore my minor nit :)

pulls.title: Resumable Uploads: Resource-specific upload limits
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body: As discussed in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2741, this mechanism allows the server to send an Upload-Limit header in informational and final responses. The header indicates a maximum upload size that the server accepts. If the upload exceeds the size, the server may abort it depending on its preference. A client should not continue upload if it knows that its upload won't fit into that size.

> Can the upload limit change during am upload? I don't think we should allow that

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Do we want Upload-Limit to be a dictionary structured field so it can support additional information in the future? E.g. `Upload-Limit: bytes=100000000, concurrency=4`

I don't see a reason against this. We could also use this to indicate a limit on the lifetime of an upload resource or the minimum and maximum sizes of individual PATCH requests. Since we get dictionaries for free from structured fields, we can make it a dictionary easily.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Added the changes. Let me know what you think

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Making it a dictionary is going to need more text than that I'm afraid. You're going to need an IANA registry etc . But most importantly we then need to define a framework for limits and what the expectations are for setting them. Immediately I can see from Guoye's example we are conflating limits on the upload resource with limits on the server more generally, and that sort of generic capability is an interop concern

We're also treading near to the rate limit headers in httpapi. The uses cases are distinct but there was a lot of friction about how to express these things over there so we need to be wary.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
That makes sense. Maybe we are better of with individual headers to represent the individual limits. I see that individual headers are also more in line with how messages in HTTP are laid as this allows reuse etc.

On the top of my head, I can think of the following limits applying to an upload resource:
- total size
- minimum and maximum size of an upload creation or append request (e.g. limited by proxies or buffers)
- lifetime of the resource
- concurrent upload request (if that's specified in another document in the future)

For some of these there already seem to be existing headers. For example, lifetime could be expressed using the Sunset header.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: At IETF 119, we discussed upload limits and there were no concerns raised about utilizing a dictionary for upload limits. As long as we include language for handling future extensions/changes of the header field, we also apparently don't need a separate registry.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
I extended this PR to include more upload limits. Most of these are already used in production system for resumable uploads, but are only documented in the provider's website, inaccessible to the clients themselves:

- `max-size` is the maximum size for a single uploaded file.
- `min-size` is the minimum size. A server might not want to create a resumable upload for a 1KB file and instead use traditional uploads for this.
- `min-append-size` and `max-append-size` is the minimum and maximum size of an append request. Many deployments put a limit on this, likely to cap the duration of a single request and help with proxies and other intermediaries. For example, [CloudFlare](https://developers.cloudflare.com/stream/uploading-videos/upload-video-file/#resumable-uploads-with-tus-for-large-files) has an lower (5 MiB) and upper (200 MiB) limit (search for chunk size on the linked pages).
- `expires` is the remaining lifetime of an upload in seconds and let's the client know how long it can resume the upload.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Would be hesitant defining a min append size. What if the last remaining part is smaller than the min append size?

The min size might also interact badly if we are doing automatic upgrades. The client wouldn't know it beforehand and we don't want the upload to get rejected.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> What if the last remaining part is smaller than the min append size?

Good point, which should be addressed. The last append request (which includes `Upload-Complete: ?1`) would be allowed to surpass the minimum append size. This is also similar to how multipart uploads to S3 work. Each part must be larger than 5MB, except for the last part, which might be smaller.

> The min size might also interact badly if we are doing automatic upgrades. The client wouldn't know it beforehand and we don't want the upload to get rejected.

The minimum append size shouldn't be a problem for automatic upgrades as the client should try to upload the entire file is one request anyway, as far as I understand it. The maximum append size on the other hand, might cause a problem, indeed. However, hopefully the client received in the informational response and is able to resume the upload while abiding to the min/max append sizes. But of course, limits on the append sizes can make the uploads less efficient. In my experience, some services do implement the limits, so I thought it would be better to provide a standardized way to discover those limits. Or do you think it is better to not include such append limits in the protocol to encourage implementers to handle append requests without limits?

pulls.title: Resumable Uploads: Describe interaction with Digest Fields
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
This PR adds a section describing a possible interaction between resumable uploads and digest fields. I am not yet entirely sure whether this style is appropriate in such a draft at all. The intention is to help readers understand how digests could help in certain use cases and how implementation should handle interaction between resumable uploads and digests.

Closes #2408

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The digest spec is very loose with any rules for what to do in failure and punts that up to other specs. 

The text here seems technically correct but raises a few questions, mainly to do with reacting to failure. For example, if an append fails an integrity check on the server side, how does it signal *back* to the client and what are the expectations on the client to recover?

The PR currently opens more questions than it answers, which might lead to hard to troubleshoot interop problems. So a bit more thought and discussion is needed. For example, can we survey how s3, Google drive etc expect integrity fsilures to be handled?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> For example, if an append fails an integrity check on the server side, how does it signal _back_ to the client and what are the expectations on the client to recover?

I agree, these points should be mentioned. The draft could recommend that servers respond with a 400 status code. As far as I know, there is no status code specifically to indicate failure with integrity check and RFC 9530 does not make any recommendation (which might be on purpose, I assume). On the other hand, a 400 makes it challenging for the client to discover that the underlying cause was a failed integrity check.

I am unsure what the best reaction of the client would be if it discovers a failed integrity check. It could try to retransmit the upload part in the hope that the integrity failure was caused by a fault in the transmission (e.g. bit flip). Although it is questionable how often this occurs in practice. In most situation, the client would bubble up the error to the end as a integrity check failure often points to bugs in the implementation in my experience. Would you have any other recommendation?

> For example, can we survey how s3, Google drive etc expect integrity fsilures to be handled?

I looked into S3 and the client can supply a checksum in the request headers or trailers (see https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity.html). If the request content's checksum calculated by the server does match the provided value, it will reject the request with a 400 response code (see BadDigest at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/ErrorResponses.html)

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> > For example, if an append fails an integrity check on the server side, how does it signal _back_ to the client and what are the expectations on the client to recover?
> 
> I agree, these points should be mentioned. The draft could recommend that servers respond with a 400 status code. As far as I know, there is no status code specifically to indicate failure with integrity check and RFC 9530 does not make any recommendation (which might be on purpose, I assume). On the other hand, a 400 makes it challenging for the client to discover that the underlying cause was a failed integrity check.

We could use problem details in the response; see https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html. This actually seems aligned with how S3 responds with BadDigest in your example, except it would be a standard approach that cite. If going that route, we might want to consider defining [problem type extensions](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html#section-3.2) specifi to digest, such as returning the failed calculated digest value.

> 
> I am unsure what the best reaction of the client would be if it discovers a failed integrity check. It could try to retransmit the upload part in the hope that the integrity failure was caused by a fault in the transmission (e.g. bit flip). Although it is questionable how often this occurs in practice. In most situation, the client would bubble up the error to the end as a integrity check failure often points to bugs in the implementation in my experience. Would you have any other recommendation?

 If the client is speaking "directly" to an upload server, I suspect a content-digest for an append has low risk of failing due to transport protocol integrity (e.g. TLS or QUIC). However, any cases of intermediation increase the number of processing steps and transport hops, and so the risks increase. Allowing an upload server sat behind N levels of intermediation to detect some form of corruption and signal that back seems of potential value to me.
 
 Regarding bubbling up of errors: the upload append section currently states:
 
 > The client SHOULD NOT automatically retry if a client error status code between 400 and 499 (inclusive) is received.

It's an interesting thought if a user would want to be pestered with errors of dialog boxes to retry a failed upload append due to a digest failure, or whether their user agent could attempt like 3 retries automatically before giving up and flagging a problem.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> We could use problem details in the response; see https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html. This actually seems aligned with how S3 responds with BadDigest in your example, except it would be a standard approach that cite. If going that route, we might want to consider defining [problem type extensions](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html#section-3.2) specifi to digest, such as returning the failed calculated digest value.

Problem details would be a great fit here and be better suited than a status code to indicate mismatching digests. I am interested in exploring possible problem types for digest fields in general, which can also be used for use cases like resumable uploads.

I could also imagine that we define specific problem types for resumable uploads, for example to indicate details about mismatching offsets.

> Regarding bubbling up of errors: the upload append section currently states:
> 
> > The client SHOULD NOT automatically retry if a client error status code between 400 and 499 (inclusive) is received.
> 
> It's an interesting thought if a user would want to be pestered with errors of dialog boxes to retry a failed upload append due to a digest failure, or whether their user agent could attempt like 3 retries automatically before giving up and flagging a problem.

The recommendation to not retry on 4xx was mainly motivated by 404 or 403 responses. In these cases, retrying without modifying the request will likely not help because the upload resource doesn't exist at all or is not accessible by the end user. However, there are also some 4xx status codes where a retry of the same request could be beneficial, such as 408 Request Timeout, 423 Locked, 429 Too Many Requests. This was also an experience from a few tus implementations where we arrived at a situation where the client only retries on 423 and 429, while also allowing the end user to override this behavior. I think we should also update the text in this draft to include these considerations.

Is there case for the situation where the server doesn't want to verify repr-digest itself but can calculate one and make it available for the client to obtain? For example, over a series of upload appends it combines ranges (content) into a representation. Then once upload is complete, the server can calculate the complete repr-digest and return that, allowing the client to perform a comparison of the local and remote views.

> Then once upload is complete, the server can calculate the complete repr-digest and return that, allowing the client to perform a comparison of the local and remote views.

Yes, I could image that very well. A client may calculate the checksum while uploading the data and thus cannot include it in the request header fields. In addition, comparing the complete repr-digest has the benefit that it verifies that the messages from the upload append requests were properly combined into a final representation, whereas comparing the repr-digest of a single upload append request only verifies the integrity of the message. If there is a bug on the server-side combining the upload appends, then this would be caught be the comparison of the complete repr-digest.

Overall, I could image that Repr-Digest is more helpful than Content-Digest for resumable uploads. If an upload append (or an upload creation) uses Content-Digest to secure the integrity of the message and the request transmission is interrupted in the middle, the server likely received just a partial message content and its digest won't match the digest of the entire message content that the client included in Content-Digest. A server may then reject the partial message due to the failure in validating the integrity, forcing the client to re-transmit the data.

The use of Repr-Digest helps in this case because the upload can interrupted and resumed multiple times while also accepting partial messages. Only once the upload is finished, the Repr-Digest of the entire representation is compared (either by the client or the server).

On re-reading, I don't think the use of `Want-Content-Digest` as described is standard. A client's "want-content-digest" would request that the server add `Content-Digest` over the response message content. Unless the response contains the bytes that were uploaded, the content-digest won't meet the expectations in your proposed text. Requiring a server to echo the actual upload chunk doesn't seem helpful to me. Can we punt on this suggestion and consider it in a follow up?
Thank you for pointing out this mistake, Lucas! I have removed the mention of `Want-Content-Digest` now and I will open a new issue to discuss methods for indicating client's interest in digests.

pulls.title: [compression-dictionary] Moved the dictionary hash into the body
pulls.author: pmeenan
pulls.body:
This eliminates the `Content-Dictionary` response header and moves the hash of the dictionary into the payload of the response.

Specifically, it adds 36-byte header in front of the compressed stream which is a 4 or 8-byte signature followed by the 32-byte SHA-256 hash digest.

The signature is different for the two different compressions:
* Dictionary-Compressed Brotli: `\xFF\x44\x43\x42` (0xFF followed by `DCB`)
* Dictionary-Compressed Zstandard: `\x5e\x2a\x4d\x18\x20\x00\x00\x00` (32-byte skippable Zstandard frame)

This also changes the content-encoding names for the different schemes to make it clear that they are a new format and not a raw brotli or Zstandard stream (`dcb` and `dcz`).

From the cli, the stream is equivalent to:

```sh
echo -en '\xffDCB' > data.txt.dcb && \
openssl dgst -sha256 -binary dictionary.txt >> data.txt.dcb && \
brotli --stdout -D dictionary.txt data.txt >> data.txt.dcb
```

or 

```sh
echo -en '\x5e\x2a\x4d\x18\x20\x00\x00\x00' > data.txt.dcz && \
openssl dgst -sha256 -binary dictionary.txt >> data.txt.dcz && \
zstd -D dictionary.txt -f -o tmp.zstd data.txt && \
cat tmp.zstd >> data.txt.dcz
```

Fix #2770

comments.author: pmeenan
comments.body:
FWIW, it doesn't look like it would be particularly difficult to use a skippable frame instead of a custom header in the Zstandard case if that's the way we want to go.  It's 4-bytes bigger (for the frame size) so it will essentially have an 8-byte "magic number" (since the size will always be the same).

It won't help with the creation of the files but if there's benefit to have the existing tooling be able to decode them (without verifying the hash because it will just skip it) we can go that route.

On the client side, it feels like it will be cleaner on the implementation to use the same flow for verifying the dictionary hash and magic number for both encodings without having to deal with different sized magic numbers (and always buffer and remove the first 36 bytes) but it's not a significant difference.

The new language is much better, but I think it still misses the point. We don't need to be shy about why these requirements are in the spec and under what circumstances they are necessary. I suggest starting with an explanation:

> As with any usage of compressed content in a secure context, a potential timing attack exists if the attacker can control any part of the dictionary, or if it can read the dictionary and control any part of the content being compressed, while performing multiple requests that vary the dictionary or injected content. Under such an attack, the processing time and/or changing size of the response reveals information about the content, which might be sufficient to decode the supposedly secure response.
> 
> In general, a server can mitigate such attacks by preventing variations per request, as in preventing active use of multiple dictionaries for the same content, disabling compression when any portion of the content comes from uncontrolled sources, and securing access and control over the dictionary content in the same way as the response content. In addition, the following requirements on a server are intended to disable dictionary-aware compression when the client provides CORS request header fields that indicate a cross-origin request context.

We have registries so that the same name is not being used for two different things. We don't need to deprecate things that are not used. If they are used where they shouldn't be, that would be a note placed on their specification by full IETF review, not on their name registry.

I do not agree with this suggestion.

Upgrade is intended to support a not-yet-defined future. Limits placed upon it must be evaluated in terms of what will be excluded from future use, not what is currently being used in practice.

If you want to limit what can be sent in a body, do that instead. The entire premise of this document is that a client will send something incredibly stupid and uncontrolled in a request body while asking for an upgrade. Just forbid that and be done.

In any case, Upgrade with GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS has no such issues. Upgrade should also be possible to use with QUERY with any compliant server.
