This latency cost is unfortunate, and could be avoided by making Capsule Protocol mandatory to implement for servers.  However, that would increase the implementation complexity for a minimal compliant server, and should not be done lightly.

@DavidSchinazi @mnot

Yeah, current design allows you to do various optimisations such calling splice (2) to avoid making copies to / from userspace, or pass the socket to some other process (with TLS being offloaded to the kernel). If we are to mandate the use of Caspules, those optimisations become impossible.

A middle ground would be to keep this text, and later define a way for servers to commit to supporting the Capsule Protocol.  Note that the HTTPS record would likely not work for this commitment, because it must be fully authenticated.

2nd sentence seems to seems broken. Maybe what you meant to state is:
```suggestion
When the use of the Capsule Protocol is negotiated, TCP data is sent using a new Capsule Type named DATA ({{data-capsule}}).  It conveys a payload that should be processed in the same way as ordinary stream contents when the Capsule Protocol is not in use.
```

I share the performance concerns. Something Ilthat came up when I talked about this with @DavidSchinazi is the possibility of having a $humongous data frame that extends to the end of the stream, so that endpoints can opt out of needing capsule framing if they don't believe they need to send any other capsules.

I havent thought exactly about how that works across intermediaries for the different use cases we discussed during the IETF 120 neeting
OK, I've reframed this in a way that is hopefully clearer.
Thank you for the changes! 29f03cc looks good to me.

Decoding capsules is pretty trivial. We're already decoding HTTP/3 frames and QUIC frames by the time we're reading this data stream.

> Yeah, current design allows you to do various optimisations such calling splice (2) to avoid making copies to / from userspace, or pass the socket to some other process (with TLS being offloaded to the kernel). If we are to mandate the use of Caspules, those optimisations become impossible.

That's not true when you're using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, and there is no reason to optimize HTTP/1.1 at this point.

I really do care about allowing the client to send data with the request. And we can't do that without requiring capsule support on the server: we just need to say that any server implementing this specification MUST NOT read the data stream if it doesn't agree with the value of the Capsule-Protocol header sent by the client.

> Future specifications may establish the meaning of DATA capsules with other Upgrade Tokens.

Capsules aren't scoped to an upgrade token, so this should work out of the box for other methods or upgrade tokens. Not sure if we should forbid it though
I think we need a bit more text to explain this capsule than just the sentence on line 151.

> I really do care about allowing the client to send data with the request.

OK, I've reworked this text to make that safe while keeping capsule support optional, based on your suggestion.

> there is no reason to optimize HTTP/1.1 at this point.

I have heard that HTTP/3->HTTP/1.1 conversion at a gateway is a common pattern, so the performance of HTTP/1.1 may be significant even if it is not heavily used over the open internet.
OK, I've attempted to future-proof the definition of DATA.  It's a bit abstract but hopefully it's comprehensible.
I've expanded that text and added a section reference to this table entry.

```suggestion
Server support for the Capsule Protocol is also OPTIONAL.  If the request includes "Capsule-Protocol: ?1", and the server does not support the Capsule Protocol, the server MUST respond with a 4xx (Client Error) status and a "Capsule-Protocol: ?0" response header field, and subsequently discard any received data stream on this request stream.  Upon receiving such a response, the client MUST disable use of the Capsule Protocol with this URI Template for the remainder of the session and retry the request.
```

```suggestion
When using the Capsule Protocol, TCP payload data is sent in the payload of a new Capsule Type named DATA ({{data-capsule}}).  The concatenation of ordered DATA capsule payloads has the same semantics as what would have been sent on the data stream, were the Capsule Protocol not in use.  It is applicable whenever use of the Capsule Protocol is optional.
```
Can you add a randomly generated 4-byte capsule type so we can test interop? (make sure to avoid grease values)
OK, done.  I've also added a note defining "connect-tcp-05" for interop.

You can't infer what end-to-end extensions a server supports from one request, because different requests can be routed to different backends even if they are sent over the same client-intermediary connection. For this to work I think we need to mandate server support.

That's fine in this case.  The client uses the capsule protocol until it encounters a request where that is rejected.  Then, for the rest of the "session" it sticks to baseline.  Once your server fleet is finished upgrading to capsule support, clients will use it reliably (if they support it).

If you want, we could soften the notion of a "session" to indicate that clients can retry after a reasonable amount of time.

"MUST disable for the rest of the session" is a bit strong.  "MUST retry without the Capsule Protocol and MAY disable for all future requests" is all that's actually needed. Let implementations decide how aggressive they want to be about backing off in a heterogeneous environment.
@MikeBishop OK, I've made that change.

The current text still uses the word "session" without defining what that means. But at this point we're in the weeds, I'm ok with merging this and then figuring out the details in separate smaller issues/PRs

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Add guidance on upload creation strategy
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
The definition of upload creation requests allows the client to include the entire file, some file data or no data at all. While we provide this flexibility, we don't give guidance on when which approach is best suited.

This PR adds this missing piece and explains how an optimistic client can attempt to upload the file in one request and how a careful client uses a separate request for creating the upload. In addition, it also mentions how to transparently upgrade to resumable uploads, which wasn't explained in detail before.

Let me know if you have any feedback on this.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Are "Optimistic Upload Creation" and "Upgrading To Resumable Uploads" the exact same way?

Maybe the 3rd way could be checking `Upload-Limit` first before uploading?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Are "Optimistic Upload Creation" and "Upgrading To Resumable Uploads" the exact same way?

The way they are described right now they are similar, yes. In theory, an optimistic upload creation can also be used where the client doesn't upload the entire file, but just a large part of it (think 500 MB of a 10 GB file). When upgrading a non-resumable request to a resumable upload, this act of division is not allowed. But I am not sure if we should go into that much detail here. If not, then we can merge these two sections.

> Maybe the 3rd way could be checking `Upload-Limit` first before uploading?

Upload limits are a good point! With the careful upload, the client also knows the limits before sending the first PATCH request. The optimistic client must be prepared to receive a 104 response with limits that it has to adapt to.

We can mention that a careful client may also send an OPTIONS request before hand if it deems that necessary.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I think upload-limit can just be enforced on the server side. If it sends a 104 and a 5xx response, the client would automatically retry. We have deployed a client-side implementation that is not aware of the upload-limit header field.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Thanks for all of your comments! I updated the PR to put the section about upgrading to resumable uploads under the optimistic upload creation since they are similar. I also added a brief mention of Upload-Limit and shortened the text a bit.

Let me know if you think the text needs more adjustments.

reviews.author: smatsson
reviews.body:
Just a minor nit. Otherwise I think this is a very good addition and agree with @guoye-zhang   that we should add some text with regards to the `Upload-Limit`.

Proposal for optimistic: The client needs to adapt to the `Upload-Limit` header provided in the `104 (Upload Resumption Supported)` intermediate response and fail the request if the file is larger than the maximum allowed size.

Proposal for Careful: The client can use the  `Upload-Limit` header provided in the `104 (Upload Resumption Supported)` to verify that the file is allowed to be uploaded before sending any data.

comments.body:
>... because the client assumes that the file will be transferred without interruptions.

> ... because the client assumes that the file will be transferred without interruptions or resumed if an interruption occurs.

reviews.author: martinthomson
reviews.body:
Some editorial suggestions, but one big question:

What is the material difference between the first and third strategy?  Could these be the same strategy?

comments.body:
```suggestion
The definition of the upload creation request ({{upload-creation}}) provides the client with flexibility to choose whether the file is fully or partially transferred in the first request, or if no file data is included at all. Which behavior is best largely depends on the client's capabilities, its intention to avoid data transmission, and its knowledge about the server's support for resumable uploads.
```

```suggestion
The benefit of this method is that if the upload creation request succeeds, the file was transferred in a single request without additional round trips.

A possible drawback is that the client might be unable to resume an upload. If an upload is interrupted before the client received a `104 (Upload Resumption Supported)` intermediate response with the upload URL, the client cannot resume that upload due to the missing upload URL. The intermediate response might not be received if the interruption happens too early in the message exchange, the server does not support sending the 104 (Upload Resumption Supported) intermediate response, or an intermediary dropped the intermediate response. Without a 104 response, the client needs to either treat the upload as failed or retry the entire upload creation request if this is allowed by the application.
```

I'll note that if the 104 doesn't have time to arrive, then the client isn't really losing much progress.  As long as they are able to start over, this seems like a very reasonable approach.

```suggestion
```

This is redundant.

```suggestion
To perform an upgrade, the client adds the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header field to the original request, which attempts to transmit the entire file in one request. A server that supports resumable uploads at the target URI, can create a resumable upload resource and send its upload URL in a 104 (Upload Resumption Supported) intermediate response for the client to resume the upload after interruptions.

A server that does not support resumable uploads or does not want to upgrade to a resumable upload for this request can ignore the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header and treat the request as a non-resumable upload.
```
This seems indistinguishable from the optimistic approach to me.  The use of Upload-Complete might distinguish it, but I don't see how these are functionally different.
You're correct. I merged them.

> assumes that the server supports resumable uploads under the target URI

This seems to be a bit in conflict with the "Upgrading To Resumable Uploads" subsection now that they are merged. Maybe we can say "assumes that the server supports resumable uploads under the target URI, or has no knowledge of the server support", but then that sentence doesn't really say anything.

"Careful Upload Creation" is where the server must support resumable uploads. "Optimistic Upload Creation" is OK if the server doesn't.

Yes, the client's knowledge about the server support was a difference of the two sections at first. Now that they are merged, the text gets a bit more unwieldy, but a added https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/commit/de5992146b5957168dc2c7e0af2a2dbe64086ab5 to correct the statements about the client's knowledge. What do you think? Is that sufficient or do we need more significant changes?
Looks good, thanks

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Discover upload limits through OPTIONS request
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
This change allows client to discover support for resumable uploads and potential limits via an OPTIONS request.

Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2833.

A brief comment on this sentence:

> The limits announced in an `OPTIONS` response SHOULD NOT be less restrictive than the limits applied to an upload once the upload resource has been created.

Once the server has created an upload resource it might have more information available (user details, file metadata etc) and apply different limits than it would have known upfront for an OPTIONS request where this information was not available. We allow this difference but recommend that the upfront announced limits are not looser than the limits after the upload resource has been created. The client can then assume that it can create an upload resource if it obeys to the upfront announced limits even if looser limits will then apply later. Does this make sense? Or is this addition rather unnecessary?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Is OPTIONS a required feature on the server side? What about `OPTIONS *` requests?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Is OPTIONS a required feature on the server side?

Yes, I think a server should be required to support this. If it only wants to provide resumable uploads for specific users, it does not have to announce this for unauthorized users.

> What about `OPTIONS *` requests?

If a server supports resumable uploads for all target URIs, then it should respond with `Upload-Limit` to an `OPTIONS *` request. But I am unsure how often this actually happens.

pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2832.

During the IETF 120 session, we saw support for a header to indicate the length during upload creation. A server can deduce the length from Content-Length, but this is not possible of chunked transfer coding is used or the upload is split across multiple requests. This PR adds the advisory `Upload-Length` header to fill this gap.

> * Update the examples

Done!

> * Mention that the server should reject the request in situations where Content-Length and Upload-Length mismatch (Content-Length > Upload-Length, or Upload-Offset + Content-Length != Upload-Length if complete is true)

For upload creation, this PR requires Content-Length and Upload-Length to be consistent:

> The request can indicate the upload's final size in two different ways. Both indicators may be present in the same request as long as they convey the same size. If the sizes are inconsistent, the server MUST reject the request by responding with a `400 (Bad Request)` status code.

For upload appending, we already have this text:

> If the request includes the `Upload-Complete` field value set to true and a valid `Content-Length` header field, the client attempts to upload the remaining resource in one request. In this case, the upload's final size is the sum of the upload's offset and the `Content-Length` header field. If the server does not have a record of the upload's final size from creation or the previous append, the server MUST record the upload's final size to ensure its consistency. If the server does have a previous record, that value MUST match the upload's final size. If they do not match, the server MUST reject the request with a `400 (Bad Request)` status code.

I think this covers all cases where Content-Length and Upload-Length mismatch. Did we miss anything else so far?

If so, there would be two values that can influence the completeness of an upload. And that seemed to be the worse evil than allow uploads to be completely full but not completed.
Yeah agreed. It's good enough as it is now.

> As mentioned in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2916#issuecomment-2414644750, the document includes text that requires the server to stop the upload if the client exceeds its own upload length. Does that cover what you had in mind?

The quoted part in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2916#issuecomment-2414644750 is more about how to handle mismatches between the header values. Edge case but still.

Preliminary feedback:

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thank you for the feedback, Roberto. I added subsections for representation and content digests in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/2917/commits/664679150c9ece5f5f5cb3b89b3b398fb225841b. I think this division helps the reader and also makes sense since representation digests can cover the entire upload, while content digests only cover one request. Let me know if you think differently.

```suggestion
When creating an upload (see {{upload-creation}}),
the client MAY ask the server to compute and return the integrity digests using a `Want-Repr-Digest` field conveying the preferred algorithms.
The response SHOULD include at least one of the requested digests,
but MAY not include it. <!-- e.g., if the server is overloaded -->

<!-- Use more lines to ease diff/patch -->
The server SHOULD compute the representation digests using the preferred algorithms once the upload is complete and include the corresponding `Repr-Digest` header field in the response.
Alternatively, the server MAY compute the digest continuously during the upload and include the `Repr-Digest` header field in responses to upload creation ({{upload-creation}}) and upload appending requests ({{upload-appending}}) even when the upload is not completed yet.
This allows the client to simultaneously compute the digest of the transmitted upload data, compare its digest to the server's digest, and spot data integrity issues.
If an upload is spread across multiple requests, data integrity issues can be found even before the upload is fully completed.
```

pulls.title: no-vary-search: Allow more efficient caches by assuming consistency
pulls.author: jeremyroman
pulls.body:
For most known use cases, a particular resource is consistently invariant to the same query parameters (i.e., either only certain parameters are ever meaningful, or certain parameters are always meaningless).

In such cases, it is possible to avoid searching several stored responses and take a more efficient approach. This shortcut might be desirable in, for example, browser disk cache implementations, where the number of accesses is known to affect cache latency significantly.

Implementations are not required (neither servers nor caches) to take this shortcut; the worst consequence is an avoidable cache miss. Incorrect stored responses are never used.

Resolves #2908.

comments.author: jeremyroman

comments.body:
The final sentence here is so long. It is very hard to follow. And as noted, it's kind of modifying a caching integration that doesn't exist.

My attempt at clearing this up would be something like the following:

This specification modifies the "Constructing Responses from Caches" section of RFC 9911 by replacing the statement that a cache must not reuse a stored response unless "the presented target URI and that of the stored response match". Instead, cache implementations use the condition that **the cache URIs match** given the presented target URI and the stored response.

The **cache URIs match**, given a URL |url| and a stored response |response|, if the following algorithm returns true:

1. An implementation may perform the following step:
   1. If all of the following are true:
      - The cache has more recently stored a response |moreRecentResponse| with a target URI which is equal, excluding the query, to |url|;
      - |moreRecentResponse|'s `No-Vary-Search` field is non-empty; and
      - |moreRecentResponse|'s `No-Vary-Search` field does not equal |response|'s `No-Vary-Search` field,
     
      then return true if |response|'s target URI equals |url|. Otherwise return false.
1. Let |urlSearchVariance| be the result of obtaining a URL search variance given |response|.
1. Return whether |url| is equivalent modulo URL search variance to |response|'s target URI, given |urlSearchVariance|.

pulls.title: [connect-tcp] Remove bare TCP payload mode
pulls.author: bemasc
pulls.body:
This leaves only the Capsule Protocol mode

Fixes #2855

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I do think we should add FINAL_DATA, but I'm fine with merging this first and then discussing that in #2949

Two suggested changes here:
1. I think it would help to reuse the data stream concept from [the capsule document](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9297#section-3.1)
2. I know this predates this PR, but the notion of "in any protocol where this is well-defined" is not fully clear to me. I think if we just cite the data stream then this becomes well defined anywhere where there is a data stream, which is anywhere there are no HTTP messages.

```suggestion
When using "connect-tcp", TCP payload data is sent in the payload of a new Capsule Type named DATA (see registration in {{data-capsule}}).  The ordered concatenation of DATA capsule payloads represents the data stream (as defined in {{Section 3.1 of !RFC9297}}).  Intermediaries MAY split or merge DATA capsules.
```

I don't think we can say this.  All capsules live _inside_ the data stream, including DATA.  DATA creates something like a new "nested" data stream whose meaning is specific to the Upgrade Token, but connect-tcp is the first Capsule Protocol Upgrade Token that has a stream of this kind.

I've rephrased this paragraph to avoid "in any protocol where this is well-defined" and tried to separate the speculative future applications from the specific use in this draft.

Nitpicking, but perhaps using `merge continuous stream of DATA capsules` to make sure that implementations don't merge `DATA` capsules across  e.g. `DATA`, `FLUSH` (or another imaginary capsule type), `DATA` into merged `DATA`, `FLUSH` or similar would be useful?

I believe that @DavidSchinazi mentioned that making this header optional was a mistake in RFC9297.

Should this be a `MUST` instead or do we want to double-down on `SHOULD`?
What's "incomplete DATA capsule"?
Thinking about this... should we add a `FLUSH` capsule to force intermediates to flush data and prevent them from buffering / concatenating the payload?
Intermediaries should not be buffering for no reason - we could add guidance for that but I don't see a need for an explicit flush signal

If intermediaries have a chance to merge multiple `DATA` capsules, then it seems like they are buffering for one reason or another (slow endpoint, rate limiting, pacing, overhead optimizations, etc.), and a flush signal could be used to preserve a record boundary across multiple layers.

I agree, we probably don't want intermediaries reordering DATA chunks around other capsules in the stream.  I've added the word "adjacent" to prevent that.

This limitation makes me question the value of the split/merge permission.  I think it makes sense for consistency with H2 DATA frames, but I don't know why anyone would actually implement it.

In addition to the TCP payload data stream, TCP also has a bunch of other obscure features like the "Push" flag (which is pretty much like a flush) and "Urgent" (which is even weirder).  We mostly ignore that stuff, and Classic HTTP CONNECT just bleaches it all.

With Capsules we have the option of bringing some of that stuff back, but I think we can leave that all to future extensions.

I'm open to `MUST` or `SHOULD`.  `SHOULD` is more consistent with CONNECT-UDP (etc.), but `MUST` would be more convenient for draft-kb-capsule-conversion (https://github.com/bemasc/capsule-conversion).
A DATA capsule is incomplete if it is truncated by the end of the underlying data stream.  This concept is defined in RFC 9297, so I've added a reference here.
What if there is no data in-flight (i.e. an idle connection)? Should intermediaries inject malformed `DATA` frame?

Yes, the recommendation is to inject a truncated DATA capsule by sending a DATA capsule header indicating nonzero length, then close the stream without sending any payload.

An alternative would be to define a new capsule type that serves as an explicit error indication.

An explicit error indication is much more powerful, may support easier debugging of connection failures, and may be easier to implement on the sender side.  However, it is more work to implement on the receiver side, and opens up a major design bikeshed.  The parsimony of having fewer ways to fail also might increase the odds of those failures being handled correctly.

I'm open to either approach.

Since we're now always using capsules, I think there's value in making this an explicit signal. How about adding a DATA_END capsule of length_zero and requiring to send that? If the stream closes without receiving that, then it means it was aborted.

Alternate encoding: is to have two capsule types for DATA and a FIN bit, like we do for STREAM frames in QUIC.

BIKESHED TIME

There are a bunch of different ways a TCP connection can end.  At a minimum, there's the distinction between FIN and RST, but there's also timeout (dead air), interface going down, ICMP Unreachable, proxy-injected errors like "quota exceeded", etc.  We have to decide how much detail to encode, and how to encode it.

The simplest option, as you say, would probably be something like an empty DATA_END capsule indicating clean shutdown, with RST assumed otherwise.
FIN vs RST is a useful distinction. It's something we accomodate in H2 and H3 CONNECT. I'd be happy to consider those in scope to address but punt on others

I don't think we need `DATA_END` capsule to signal a clean shutdown, we could use an empty `DATA` for that. This is how BSD sockets and other applications transmit `FIN` to userland.

But yes, using either empty `DATA` or adding a `flags` field with a `FIN` bit to signal a clean shutdown, and using the lack of that signal and a termination of the underlying transport to signal connection reset seems better than injecting malformed `DATA` frames.

AFAIK, the push flag is heavily used and added to TCP flags of the packet containing the last bit of data sent from the userland, so it would be unfortunate to lose it.

Notably, I want to avoid situation where things work without when communicating directly, but stop working (or work in degraded fashion) with added intermediary, because we start dropping flags for no reason.

> There are a bunch of different ways a TCP connection can end. At a minimum, there's the distinction between FIN and RST, but there's also timeout (dead air), interface going down, ICMP Unreachable, proxy-injected errors like "quota exceeded", etc. We have to decide how much detail to encode, and how to encode it.

We have to be able to emit those back to TCP endpoints, so the amount of details and bike-sheding that we can do here is limited.

I'm pretty sure that the "push" flag is already "bleached" by all existing implementations of HTTP CONNECT over TLS, so I don't think we need to reintroduce it in this draft.  I believe we're in a good position to add support for "push" later if needed.

DID SOMEONE SAY BIKESHED??? I'M ENTHUSIASTIC

I never liked the fact that reading 0 on a BSD socket means "end of stream" for TCP. It's odd, and inconsistent with other uses (e.g., for UDP it means "I received a UDP packet with no payload").

We should definitely separate between "clean termination" (TCP FIN) and "abortive termination" (TCP RST, timeout, etc.) but I don't think we need to separate RST from timeout. That would match what classic CONNECT does.

So, +1 for DATA capsule with a FIN bit :)
Sure, fine with me. This was mostly a side-comment wrt merged DATA capsules, anyway.
@DavidSchinazi?

A FIN bit adds overhead to every DATA capsule, which seems unappealing to me. reviews.body: Thanks!

comments.body: Sorry to be late, but is there a strong reason to add FINAL_DATA when in H2 and H3 we have clear distinction between streams being reset (RST_STREAM and RESET_STREAM) vs. clean shutdown (FIN bit)?

The strongest argument I see for FINAL_DATA is that it guarantees* correct shutdown handling through semi-compliant HTTP/1.1 intermediaries.  In particular, unclean shutdown signalling is often difficult to implement in HTTP/1.1, where (absent a signal in the Capsule Protocol) it requires injecting a TLS alert (or TCP RST), but TLS and TCP APIs don't always offer this ability.  Previous versions of this draft suggested signalling by sending a truncated capsule, but this requires piercing an abstraction barrier that might reasonably be exposed by a Capsule Protocol implementation.

Even if the client and server are both speaking HTTP/3, there could be an HTTP/1.1 "hop" in between that "bleaches" the stream error.

*Nothing is ever guaranteed.

Yeah I do not think people have complained that as a problem with the traditional CONNECT. TCP shutdown is murky, so applications tend to have their own ways of marking the end.

Therefore, the only case where having FINAL_DATA helps is when HTTP/1.1 is used for connect-tcp and when an application protocol that does not have its own way of marking the end but is vulnerable to truncation is being used.

Is that something we need to care?

I would not mind seeing this PR getting merged as-is, but I think FINAL_DATA needs its own issue and that we need to discuss at the WG.

OK, I have moved FINAL_DATA out of this PR and into a separate one (#2949).

I can say that I have personally fought with (1) applications that silently lost data due to truncation and (2) broken Happy Eyeballs with proxies that reported successful connection because the implementation had no way to report failure, so I do believe these issues are real, though maybe not the most common.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Thank you for opening the new issue dedicated to FINAL_DATA.

@DavidSchinazi 
> I do think we should add a FINAL_DATA. It allows for example sending metadata after the stream is gracefully closed. I can imagine using that to send capsules that contain TCP performance info

I think the question is if we would benefit from being able to observe the ordering between close and metadata; if there is, then it makes sense to have a frame indicating close. Otherwise, it is waste, considering that most underlying layers (HTTP/2, HTTP/3, TLS) already provide ways to distinguish between graceful shutdown and abrupt close.

For things like performance information, I don't think there would be material difference in sending them right before or after signalling the closure. I'd assume that we would allow such information to be sent at any moment during the lifetime of the tunnel, and that receivers would record whatever they receive. Senders that want to emit most recent information can send performance information at the moment they notice the TCP tunnel getting closed, and close the tunnel.

Separately, if we have the interest in sending metadata after closure, I am not sure if such interest applies only to graceful close and not to resets? To paraphrase, it might make more sense to define a frame that conveys closure and how it is closed (i.e., graceful or reset), rather than FINAL_DATA that only signals graceful shutdown.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
> Otherwise, it is waste

What is wasted? This just requires registering a capsule type, which is a 2^62 registry. In most cases, the proxy will send the last bit of data inside a FINAL_DATA capsule. In the unusual scenario where it learns about the FIN after it sent its last DATA capsule, then it does need to send 2 bytes.

> allow such information to be sent at any moment during the lifetime of the tunnel

FWIW, the lifetime of the tunnel is already somewhat disconnected from the TCP FIN since a FIN only closes one side of the connection. I see a value in telling the peer that TCP closed gracefully while reserving the right to send future capsules in response to something the peer sends.

> it might make more sense to define a frame that conveys closure and how it is closed (i.e., graceful or reset), rather than FINAL_DATA that only signals graceful shutdown.

Having a third capsule like DATA_ABORTED doesn't seem unreasonable to me.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Nice! It looks clean to me. I'm just having one nit here:

>     - HTTP/1.1 over TLS: a TLS Error Alert

I'd instead say:

>     - HTTP/1.1 over TLS: a TLS Error Alert or TCP RST

The rationale for this is the following: sending a TCP RST doesn't cost anything for the sender, so a client could easily send hundreds of thousands of them per second. However, the gateway dealing with protocol translation would face a risk of trivial denial of service by sending a TLS alert, because that means you need to be the last one sending before closing, with the connection ending in TIME_WAIT on its outgoing side, something that must never ever happen, otherwise it ends up depleting its source ports in a fraction of second and fails to connect to the servers for a minute or more. The only way to avoid this is to close the TCP connection abrubptly as well, but that results in the loss of the TLS alert for the other one (data queued in network buffers are destroyed by the system as soon as the connection is reset). As such, the next hop cannot reliably expect to see the TLS alert, and must be prepared to just see the TCP connection being reset.

We could suggest that the TLS alert be a SHOULD that eases debugging and is more polite, but that the TCP RST is the final way of closing in any case. I.e. depending on timing the endpoint must be prepared to receive a TCP RST for all protocols ultimately transported over TCP. Some might have the chance to see an RST_STREAM or TLS alert before that.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
@wtarreau It sounds like you're concerned about a malicious client and destination executing an asymmetric resource exhaustion attack against the proxy.  The more I thought about this class of attacks, the more I realized there seemed to be a lot of them.  I've added a section discussing these attacks and how to mitigate them.

I don't think we need to change the guidance on TLS Alerts.  Sending a TCP RST in that case would not fix all the "WAIT Abuse" port exhaustion attacks, and it would violate the confidentiality promise of the "https://" URI scheme.  Instead, I think these attacks must be addressed by doing resource accounting more carefully, as noted in the new text.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
> @wtarreau It sounds like you're concerned about a malicious client and destination executing an asymmetric resource exhaustion attack against the proxy. The more I thought about this class of attacks, the more I realized there seemed to be a lot of them. I've added a section discussing these attacks and how to mitigate them.

Not just attacks actually, even regular usage. The most common cases I've seen port exhaustion was on pretty valid traffic relying misdesigned protocols (e.g. SQL stuff where the client closes first). Once you have many clients doing just a few short connections, as soon as this happens more often than the the number of ephemeral ports over the time_wait duration, you're stuck. On a default linux setup, you have 28232 ports and 60s time_wait, that's an abysmally load of 470 conn/s that suffices to block them all. It doesn't require many clients, and actually a single firewall reboot or edge proxy restart in production can be sufficient to cause this. Thus for me the mitigation doesn't address accidents, it only addresses the most trivial case of a bad actor.

> I don't think we need to change the guidance on TLS Alerts. Sending a TCP RST in that case would not fix all the "WAIT Abuse" port exhaustion attacks,

Yes it does because it avoids the TIME_WAIT.

> and it would violate the confidentiality promise of the "https://" URI scheme.

I don't see how. Otherwise TCP would violate TLS, since an RST can happen for many reasons, the first one being just the gateway crashing or being restarted in the middle of transfers.

> Instead, I think these attacks must be addressed by doing resource accounting more carefully, as noted in the new text.

Attacks do have to be mitigated, but it's also our responsibility to make sure that protocols and their extensions are designed in a way that doesn't cause domino effects on production equipment or that they amplify the consequences of minor accidents (e.g. a first layer of proxy being restarted before the gateway that performs the conversion).

comments.body:
> > @wtarreau It sounds like you're concerned about a malicious client and destination executing an asymmetric resource exhaustion attack against the proxy. The more I thought about this class of attacks, the more I realized there seemed to be a lot of them. I've added a section discussing these attacks and how to mitigate them.

Once you have many clients doing just a few short connections, as soon as this happens more often than the the number of ephemeral ports over the time_wait duration, you're stuck. On a default linux setup, you have 28232 ports and 60s time_wait, that's an abysmally load of 470 conn/s that suffices to block them all. It doesn't require many clients, and actually a single firewall reboot or edge proxy restart in production can be sufficient to cause this. Thus for me the mitigation doesn't address accidents, it only addresses the most trivial case of a bad actor.

I'm not sure I understand this problem.  [TIME-WAIT is per-4-tuple](https://serverfault.com/questions/844317/can-time-wait-port-be-reused-for-different-remote-server), so the 470 conn/s limit is at each client, not at the proxy.  (Or maybe you're thinking of 470 conn/s from the proxy to any single destination?  But that would not be affected by how we structure the client<->proxy protocol.)

> > I don't think we need to change the guidance on TLS Alerts. Sending a TCP RST in that case would not fix all the "WAIT Abuse" port exhaustion attacks,
> 
> Yes it does because it avoids the TIME_WAIT.

The TCP RFC says that [sending RST means you _enter_ TIME-WAIT](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.5.2-1).  Regardless, TIME-WAIT is by 4-tuple, so it primarily applies when the _client_ closes.

> > and it would violate the confidentiality promise of the "https://" URI scheme.
> 
> I don't see how. Otherwise TCP would violate TLS, since an RST can happen for many reasons, the first one being just the gateway crashing or being restarted in the middle of transfers.

These RSTs are HTTP response content, and cannot leak outside the TLS envelope. If a standard HTTP gateway receives a TCP RST from upstream, it forwards it as an HTTP 5XX or stream error inside TLS.

BTW, using a TCP RST here also violates the "https://" integrity guarantees: a middlebox can (and often does) convert the RST to a FIN, losing the error signal.

> > Instead, I think these attacks must be addressed by doing resource accounting more carefully, as noted in the new text.
> 
> Attacks do have to be mitigated, but it's also our responsibility to make sure that protocols and their extensions are designed in a way that doesn't cause domino effects on production equipment or that they amplify the consequences of minor accidents (e.g. a first layer of proxy being restarted before the gateway that performs the conversion).

Definitely!  If we have a convincing way to make this protocol safer to deploy, I'm all for it.  Otherwise, perhaps you can contribute some text to the Operational Considerations.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
> The TCP RFC says that [sending RST means you enter TIME-WAIT](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.5.2-1).

In fact not really, that's a non-normative "should". In practices all stacks I've dealt with till now don't do that, and for a good reason, which is that the only ways for a userland application to trigger an RST are 1) breaking the association by connecting to AF_UNSPEC , leaving no trace of the connection in the TCP table, or 2) disabling lingering and closing, in which case the RST is more a consequence of the destruction of pending unsent data. The only case an application needs to force an RST is to close an outgoing connection precisely to avoid monopolizing an ephemeral port to a destination.

Regarding the direction of the RST, I think we were not talking about the same since you're speaking about responses. I agree that with responses generally an intermediary will send a 5xx (if the RST was received before the intermediary started to send headers), or break TLS to the client. I was speaking about the other direction: a TCP client reaches a gateway that encapsulates the connection over HTTP. In this case the client can close using RST at no cost, and it must not incur a cost for the gateway. If the gateway is forced to emit a TLS alert, it will have to keep the ephemeral port open to the next hop. My point is that for such directions the intermediary must be allowed to close using RST (and the next hop to detect that as well, just as if the gateway crashed after all).

>  If we have a convincing way to make this protocol safer to deploy, I'm all for it. Otherwise, perhaps you can contribute some text to the Operational Considerations.

I think that just using this does the job:

    HTTP/1.1 over TLS: a TLS Error Alert, or TCP RST as a last resort

comments.body:
@wtarreau OK, it sounds like your main concern is about shared clients being left in the TIME-WAIT state on the client<->proxy connection.  After thinking about this a bit, I believe there are many ways that this can happen, even when connections are closed cleanly.

Ultimately, this is just one of several major downsides of using HTTP/1.1 for this purpose.  I've added Operational Considerations text recommending against use of HTTP/1.1 for this kind of deployment and enumerating several concerns, including this one.

comments.body:
Yeah I think my point is that _if_ we are to give advise regarding how proxies should handle TCP resets, we ought to state that it is a bidirectional reset and that stream has to be tear down in both directions.

The mechanism can be different within each HTTP versions (or depending on the extensions in play).

The TCP RFC defines the TIME-WAIT timeout as [2 * MSL](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.10.7.4-2.5.2.2.2.9.2.1), which is [2 minutes](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-4-1.40).

There's a distinction here between the "connect-tcp" state machine and the "TCP" state machine.  Together they generate the correct behavior:

* "connect-tcp" endpoint A converts incoming RST into outgoing RESET_STREAM.
* "connect-tcp" endpoint B converts incoming RESET_STREAM into outgoing RST.
* Sending a RST causes the TCP connection for B to close, if it is not already closed.
* Endpoint B "MUST close its send stream when the corresponding TCP connection reaches the TIME-WAIT or CLOSED state".

I would prefer to avoid duplicating functionality between these two state machines.  That can get very complicated and doesn't seem to offer any benefit.


I'm also not clear on why this isn't the correct advice.

The statement says that you should not produce `set-cookie: a=b;c=d` from `set-cookie: a=b` and `set-cookie: c=d`.  It justifies that by saying that the usual combining rules for fields don't work.  However, the advice you want is: if you combine `set-cookie`, use a semicolon rather than a comma.

The thing that got me to react here was the implication that leaving the cookie fields alone carries a risk that an intermediary might combine fields without knowing that `set-cookie` is special.  In THAT case, combining (using ";") at the origin server would be an excellent idea because it would avoid that happening.

(There are other concerns, like the effect of combining on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 header compression efficiency.  But maybe we don't need to get into that level of detail.)

It's possible that this is just poor wording.  Maybe if you say that implementations (origin servers, any servers, intermediaries, clients, anyone) ~~should~~MUST not combine `set-cookie` using ",".  That this specifically names origin servers invokes all of the above questions.  (If you agree, we should open an issue to clarify, rather than continuing here, where it will definitely be lost.)

> However, the advice you want is: if you combine set-cookie, use a semicolon rather than a comma.

We don't want to give that advice either.
Within a set-cookie string any values separated by a semicolon will be treated as attributes for the first `name=value` pair. 

From Section 5.6

> 2. If the set-cookie-string contains a %x3B (";") character:
>   1. The name-value-pair string consists of the characters up to, but not including, the first %x3B (";"), and the unparsed-attributes consist of the remainder of the set-cookie-string (including the %x3B (";") in question).

So `set-cookie: a=b;c=d ` would set a cookie `a=b` with some attribute `c` that has a value of `d`. Since `c` is an unrecognized attribute it'll be ignored and a default `a=b` cookie will be set.

> The thing that got me to react here was the implication that leaving the cookie fields alone carries a risk that an intermediary might combine fields without knowing that set-cookie is special. 

Presumably an intermediary would have implemented the [HTTP spec](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-field-order) which specifically calls out `Set-Cookie` as special. Granted that's specified with an "ought".

> That this specifically names origin servers invokes all of the above questions

Fair.

I think we can resolve this ambiguity by calling out origin servers and intermediaries. Something like 

`Origin servers and intermediaries MUST NOT each combine multiple Set-Cookie header fields into a...`
Not sure how clear the "MUST NOT each" phrasing is, open to suggestions. This should take care of that ambiguity.

I'll upload a patch

reviews.author: mikewest
reviews.body: This LGTM, but I think we could add a little more clarification of the problem since I'm not sure we're on the same page about that.

comments.body: I'm not sure "each" does much work here. "A and B must not X." seems clear enough.

Perhaps we could clarify the problem here, as I think the discussion in this issue doesn't match my understanding of the reason for this admonition. In short, `Set-Cookie`'s grammar allows `,` to be used as part of the cookie's definition. Both `path-value` and `extension-av` accept any character other than CTLs or `;`, so `Set-Cookie: a=b;path=/c,d=e` is ambiguous. It might be a cookie named `a` with a value of `b` and a path of `/c`, followed by another cookie named `d`. Or it might be a single cookie with a path of `/c,d=e`. It's impossible to tell at this point (though browsers, at least, parse it as the latter).

I'm trying to avoid any implied relation between the origin servers and intermediaries. With the phrasing "Origin servers *and* intermediaries MUST NOT combine" or "Origin servers *or* intermediaries MUST NOT combine" could suggest that the behavior depends on what the origin servers and the intermediaries are doing in relation to each other.
Good suggestion
On second thought I agree. Removed.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Correct terminology around representations
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
The current draft mixes the use of _representation (data)_, _file_, or just _data_ when referring to the bytes being uploaded. This inconsistency is confusing and the use of _file_ is not entirely correct because resumable uploads can transfer non-file representations as well, as was rightfully [mentioned by Roy Fielding on the mailing list](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/httpbisa/m-iXTJQGdb8XpxGjZWxXGj6Siic/).

This PR attempts to unify the terminology and embrace the HTTP terms _representation_ and _representation data_ where possible.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Upload Resource Section
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
This PR tries to improve the draft's readability by introducing a dedicated section about the upload resource. This resource is the main component that enables resumable uploads but is not directly described in the document so far. Additionally, some of the section in the current draft are too long and would benefit from being broken up.

The new section about the upload resource houses a brief description of its responsibilities and the state that the resource needs to keep track of (offset, completeness, length, limits). I also moved the definition of the corresponding headers (Upload-Offset etc) in there as it made sense to me to describe the values and their presentations in the same space. Let me know if you disagree here.

The upload resource section then includes the definition of how the different requests for creating and resuming uploads are handled. Each description is further divided into behavior for the client and server break the huge wall of text into more digestible sections.

In addtion:
- I added a dedicated section about handling concurrent requests, so that the corresponding text does not have to be duplicated in the creation and appending sections.
- I removed the section "Feature Detection" since this is covered by "Upgrading To Resumable Uploads".
- The "Offset values" section has been merged into the "Offset" section.

Since the diff is rather confusing, I recommend to review this PR by reading the rendered section at https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/resumable-upload/upload-resource/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#name-upload-resource.

Note that this PR is intended to be editorial. Please let me know if I included normative changes by accident.

The last response received by the client is considered the response for the entire file upload and should be presented to the user.

In my thinking, the last request to `/uploads/1234` that completes the upload (through the use of `Upload-Complete: ?1`, which is why I mentioned this header in my comment above) would produce the response indicating the h264 codec. pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Require client to adhere to limits in `Upload-Limit`
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body: Currently, the client is not required to adhere to limits announced in the `Upload-Limit` header field in responses. As discussed in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3006#discussion_r1959738722, it doesn't make a lot of sense to give the client the option to willingly ignore limits that the server announces. Hence, this PR changes the normative language to require the client to adhere to any limits that the client received and recognizes.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
I'm hesitant about making this a MUST. Currently, our client does not parse `Upload-Limit` at all, as we only operate in the mode where we upgrade a traditional upload to a resumable upload. Let's suppose that the upload itself is larger than `max-size`, it might not be resumable but it might still be fine to continue as a traditional upload. And respecting `max-append-size` requires a lot of additional work on the client side since we currently only do `Upload-Complete: ?1`.

The server can always enforce the limits by sending a `413 Content Too Large` response, or a 5xx response so the client would try to resume. I'm not sure if it's worth the additional complexity to adhere to the limits on the client side since the server has to enforce it anyway.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I tend to agree with Guoye. I'd treat this as an advisory header, in the vein of Retry-After https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-10.2.3. 

In fact, removing the SHOULD might be closer to reality. Instead, we can explain why clients benefit from consuming the hint and taking some action. Then we can leave it up to them to make their own call.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
I understand that implementing the client behavior can be challenging, especially `max-append-size`. My main concern is that making it optional for the client to follow limits could result in interoperability issues. Our experience with tus has been that a sizeable number of server deployments for resumable uploads enforce a maximum request content size. Usually to accommodate for restrictions in proxies or other parts of the infrastructure. I would assume that similar restrictions will exist if people deploy resumable uploads as defined in this draft.

A client that ignores Upload-Limit can then run into issues uploading files that are larger than the server's maximum request size. Proxies usually reject requests that are too large with a 413, preventing the client from resuming, causing the upload to fail. As Guoye mentioned, the upload would work if the proxy consumes request content until reaching the size limit and then responding with a 5xx. The client will resume and the upload can continue, but I'm unsure if such a proxy behavior is feasible in reality.

If a client respects the limits announced by the server, it can directly adjust to the server's restrictions and increase interoperability.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I agree with these points. However, isn't that pretty much the situation we're already in today? 

I know that I operate proxy servers that have variable upload limits, and variable behaviour when it comes to buffering of upload before responding vs. Responding immediately and allowing uploads to continue unbuffered (aka streamed).

The language in the Upload Limits section is currently that a server `MAY` not do something if the action exceeds a limit it advertised. I don't think it's acceptable to levy a MUST requirement on a client if a server might be more flexible in how it applies limits it advertised. 

I know it feels like it might help to be strict but HTTP is generally quite loose. The market will decide what it wants to do. And if people are already saying "it's easier for me to deal with rejection staus codes like I do with all HTTP upload services than use Upload-Limit" the a MUST probably won't change their mind.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> However, isn't that pretty much the situation we're already in today?

Yes, leaving adherence to upload limits optional won't make interoperability less likely than it currently is. With this new draft we would have the opportunity to improve the chance of interoperability by learning from shortcomings in current deployments.

That being said, this PR might not have the impact that I imagine. There will likely be two kinds of clients in production environments:

- People using RUFH clients to upload to known servers (like most tus setups today). They therefore know which limits the server imposes and can configure the client accordingly in advance. Or they know that their client automatically adjusts to limits on the fly. Forcing adherence to limits won't change anything here.
- Clients that automatically upgrade traditional uploads to resumable uploads (like URLSession on iOS). They don't usually know the server limits upfront. But a server that would accept a representation transferred in one request as a traditional upload is probably just as likely to accept the same representation as a resumable upload in one request. It would be odd if the server accepts a 1GB traditional request but requires the equivalent resumable upload to be split across multiple requests. Hence, forcing adherence to limits will unlikely improve interoperability.

Considering that, I am also fine with leaving the SHOULD as is.

> I don't think it's acceptable to levy a MUST requirement on a client if a server might be more flexible in how it applies limits it advertised.

Fair point. We could consider making the limits more strict on the server-side. But then again, I consider the limits as hints from the server to client about what it will likely be able to handle, not as an enforceable contract.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Closing this for now as I don't see strong support for this.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Rename `expires` limit to `max-age`
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Closes #2940.

The Upload-Limit header can provide the remain lifetime of the upload resource in number of seconds under the `expires` key. However, this name is misleading as it implies that the value is an absolute timestamp. A better name could be `max-age`, which is already used in the [Cache-Control](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#name-max-age), [Set-Cookie](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265#autoid-13), and [Alt-Svc](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7838#section-3.1) header fields to denominate the lifetime of cookies and cache entries.

reviews.body: Lgtm

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Clarify handling of different status codes
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
This PR attempts to make the text clearer on how the client should react to different status code, especially in which cases it should stop resuming at all, retry the same request or resume the upload by retrieving the offset. Most of this was already implied before, but the explicit mention makes implementing a client easier.

I also merged the text from the dedicated "Redirection" section into the other, corresponding sections.

Currently, the draft is clear that clients should not retry on 4xx, but do so for all 5xx responses. I wonder if this strict rule makes sense, in particular:

- Should the client retry on 408 Request Timeout? The server might have received some representation data and the upload could continue.
- Would it be better if the server didn't resume on 501 Not Implemented? Retries will likely not change the status.
- How about 409 Conflict? Appending to an upload resource produces this status code when a request includes the wrong offset. In theory, a well behaving client does not trigger this status code. Yet I see them from time-to-time in production tus deployments. If the client resumes the upload by fetching the correct offset first, the upload has a good chance of completing. Should the client be allowed to resume on 409?

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: URI instead of URL
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
The document incorrectly used the term URL where it should have been URI. This PR corrects this issue and adds a reference to RFC 9110 as a source, [as recommended by Roy Fielding](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/httpbisa/m-iXTJQGdb8XpxGjZWxXGj6Siic/):

> URL is also being used without a reference. For this draft, it
should be URI and reference Section 4 of [HTTP].

reviews.author: martinthomson
reviews.body: This seems good.  Both dimensions seem large enough that most uses will fit well within.  I can see how someone might want a 10-20 character label, but not 10-20 of them, so maybe the total number of groups could be 16 instead, to reduce this to a <<1k max, but we can afford a little generosity.  After all, the 1k this requires is not that significant relative to other metadata necessary to operate a good cache.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Clear up definitions
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2874

In the past, the document used the term "target resource" to denote the resource that the initial request was sent to. This term is quite confusing, so since then we moved away from this term and used other descriptions. In this PR, the last two occurrences are removed.

In addition, it puts a brief mention of "upload resource" in the "Conventions and Definitions" section, so readers know early on what it is.

pulls.title: Require less response headers for upload creation and appending
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Currently, the draft requires responses for upload creation and appending requests to include the `Upload-Complete` and `Upload-Offset` header fields. The original intention was to make the resource signal the new upload state back to the client. However, this isn't necessary for resumable uploads to work. If the client received a successful response, it can assume that the upload state was updated accordingly. If it didn't get a response, it retrieves the state using a HEAD request.

So make this document less restrictive, this PR removes the requirement to send `Upload-Offset` ~~and `Upload-Complete`~~ in responses to upload creation and append. The append response also doesn't have to include the `Upload-Limit` anymore. If one exists, the client has already received it in the upload creation or offset retrieval response.

EDIT: `Upload-Complete` is still necessary to identify whether a response is related to the resumable upload or the processing of the representation.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Probably need to bump the interop version for this change since I think our client is checking the presence of these header fields

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: @guoye-zhang We can definitely bump the interop version. How do you feel about this PR in general?

comments.author: jbaehr
comments.body:
While the `Upload-Complete` response header may not be required in the case of a successful response or in case of no response, it is currently needed in the case of an unsuccessful response: Specifically the `409 (Conflict)` response becomes ambiguous if concerning the last/final request. There are two ways of interpreting it:
- The `Upload-Offset` provided by the client *does not match* the server's value, so the chunk uploaded with this request cannot be used. In turn the upload stays incomplete. A client may retry with the `Upload-Offset` provided in the response, which may results in a success.
- The  `Upload-Offset` provided by the client *does match* the server's value and the upload gets finalized. Now quoting [the current draft version](https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/blob/021878764a05a901c3b2958105995c4447edddd9/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.md?plain=1#L491):
  > the upload is marked as complete and the upload resource SHOULD generate the response that matches what the resource, that was targeted by the initial upload creation ({{upload-creation}}), would have generated if it had received the entire representation in the initial request.

  In this step, while processing the entire resource, the server may want to reply with a 409 as well. This time however meaning that the new target resource conflicts. Any retry attempt made by the client is likely to fail as well, either because appending to an already finalized upload resource results in a subsequent `400 Bad Request`, a `404 File Not Found` because the upload resource is already gone, or when redoing the entire upload the `409 Conflict` will show up again. Because the upload itself was not the problem.

My preference would be to have the server reply with a `400 Bad Request` in the first case (just like when appending to an already completed upload). The current way of using the `Upload-Complete` response header field to figure out the meaning of the HTTP status code is not ideal. And with this PR here even becomes impossible.

Has this already been discusses somewhere? I haven't found anything in the issues labeled "resumable-upload". Shall I create a dedicated issue for this discussion? Although triggered by this PR, it may be a bit beyond the scope of the proposed changes here.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
@jbaehr The draft currently requires a 409 Conflict response to be accompanied with the correct offset in the Upload-Offset header field:

> If the Upload-Offset request header field value does not match the current offset ({{upload-offset}}), the upload resource MUST reject the request with a 409 (Conflict) status code. The response MUST include the correct offset in the Upload-Offset header field.

This would allow a client to distinguish whether a 409 is related to the resumable upload itself or the processing of the uploaded representation after the upload is complete.

That being said, the document also currently says that a client should not try to resume an upload if it received a 4xx, including a 409. Just like any other 4xx response, a 409 is treated as a terminal state regarding the upload. The reasoning behind this is that a well-behaving client and server should never trigger a 409. A 409 indicates that the offset counted by the client has diverged from the correct offset of the upload resource, which can only be the result of a bug (in the client or server) or an intermediary fiddling with the messages. When a client resumes an upload after an interruption, it fetches the current offset via a HEAD request instead of guessing the correct offset in a PATCH request.

However, with this argumentation, there is no reason to use 409 for mismatching offsets instead of a 400, I agree with you.

I am open to discussing
- whether 409 should be replaced with a 400, while continuing to say that clients shouldn't resume in these cases, or
- whether 409 + Upload-Offset is kept, and clients are allows to resume in those cases (diverging from the current wording in the spec).

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Using `Upload-Complete: ?1` to distinguish the final response is the only way today. I don’t think changing 409 to 400 is sufficient since it can also be the final response. We will have to register a new 4xx status code exclusively for resumable upload failures for that to work.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Can't a client detect mismatching offsets by looking for 409 and the Upload-Offset header in the response? If the client gets a 409 without Upload-Offset, the error response is not related to the uploading itself. Or am I missing the point here?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Technically, we don’t disallow the final response to include Upload-Offset. Our current server implementation in NIO puts Upload-Offset on all responses.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
You're right, we don't disallow it. If we want to allow clients to resume an upload after they attempted to append at a wrong offset, we could either use a new 4xx status code (as @guoye-zhang suggested) or make the server return a 5xx, so that the client retrieves the new offset. 5xx feels a bit odd at first, but if we frame the mismatching offsets as "server cannot write data at that position", it could technically be interpreted as a server error.

But this requires that we want clients to resume after mismatching offsets (which the spec currently doesn't allow). Do we want to allow that?

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I don't think we should. Upload-Offset in the 409 is merely for debugging purposes. Not something that people write code to handle.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
I'm fine with keeping it that way but would also be open to changing that. At the end of the day, I have to admit that I wrote client code that explicitly retries on 409, mostly to make uploads work with weird setups that I don't control.

> @jbaehr Has this already been discusses somewhere? I haven't found anything in the issues labeled "resumable-upload". Shall I create a dedicated issue for this discussion? Although triggered by this PR, it may be a bit beyond the scope of the proposed changes here.

Yes, please! Feel free to open a separate issue to discuss this.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
@guoye-zhang @jbaehr Thank you for your feedback. I updated the PR to ensure that responses for append requests always include the `Upload-Complete` header so the client can distinguish whether error responses belonging the resumable upload versus the representation processing. Please let me know what you think.

I will bump the interop version in a separate PR to keep this diff readable.

comments.author: jbaehr
comments.body:
> However, with this argumentation, there is no reason to use 409 for mismatching offsets instead of a 400, I agree with you.
> 
> I am open to discussing
> -  whether 409 should be replaced with a 400, while continuing to say that clients shouldn't resume in these cases, or
> -  whether 409 + Upload-Offset is kept, and clients are allows to resume in those cases (diverging from the current wording in the spec).

I guess the tradeoff here is between one additional request (HEAD, as in "resume after interruption") and the ease to retrofit existing protocols with resumeability (where the 409 status is already well-established).

To my liking there are several places in the current draft that seem to have this retrofitting use case in mind. The section I quoted above or §17.1.1 "Upgrading To Resumable Uploads". Let's make this a first-class concept and remove the last remaining roadblock of conflicting error codes.

---

> Using `Upload-Complete: ?1` to distinguish the final response is the only way today.

Yes. And reinterpreting the very same status code based on the (non-)existence of some other headers is far from straight forward.

> I don’t think changing 409 to 400 is sufficient since it can also be the final response. We will have to register a new 4xx status code exclusively for resumable upload failures for that to work.

That's also true. One could argue that only one potentially clashing status is better than having two of them. Or that the likelihood of encountering a 409 further down the pipeline (when the entire upload is done and the payload processing starts) is higher than a 400 (which by definition is only scoped to a request, not a resource)...
At the end of the day it's just me who happens to encounter the problem with 409, not 400 -- so a subjective choice. The objective way is to register a new 4xx status. Similar to `411 Length Required`.

---

> I updated the PR to ensure that responses for append requests always include the Upload-Complete header so the client can distinguish whether error responses belonging the resumable upload versus the representation processing. Please let me know what you think.

We do have now (again, but this time explicitly) a way to distinguish between errors from the upload itself and from processing the uploaded resource (as it would be processed without resume capabilities). This is good.

I still find it odd to have to look into other headers to determine the definite meaning of a status code, though. However, this is better discussed separately. I'll open a dedicated issue for that, but it may take a few days.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thank you for the feedback, @jbaehr. Let's discuss this in a separate issue (or on the mailing list)!

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: Closing; see https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3041#issuecomment-2819853292.
Nitpicking, but doesn't SHOULD (instead of MUST) make "always" effectively the same as "preferred"?
Isn't this effectively the same as absent header?
Shouldn't we also have "never" (enforcing store-and-forward semantics)?

The difference is in how the intermediaries behave when they refuse (or cannot).

In case of `always`, the intermediaries generate errors (because they know that things break by not delivering incremental). In case of `preferred` the intermediaries just buffer the message (because they know that incremental delivery is nothing more than a preference).

Yeah, there's definitely the question of what is the default and if we need store-and-forward as a preference.

FWIW, I'm kind of inclined to keeping the scope of the extension to just adding deliver-incremental-or-reject mode as an alternative to the default behavior that we already have.
Right, that's my understanding as well. But doesn't it mean that "always" should be a normative MUST instead of SHOULD?
That's fair. Even though the Incremental header is advisory (as HTTP stacks are not required to implement every HTTP extension), for those that understand Incremental it is better to use MUSTs.

I agree that SHOULD sounds a bit odd for "always". However, thinking of when it would be violated, it would mainly be a case where incremental delivery doesn't actually make sense (too short to break up into chunks, all available at the same time, not able to send until the whole thing is available). In such a case, the message might not be delivered incrementally, but still isn't an error case.
Is it ever "impossible", or is it something that the server is just unwilling to support?
Sounds like we agree that portions of the HTTP message ought to be delivered in a timely manner. Assuming that is the case, I think we should use a MUST that covers the cases that Tommy brought up.

This really puts a lie to the whole "always" thing for me.  Because an intermediary might not implement, the value is pretty low value.

On the other hand, a simple Boolean has the benefit of asking for, but not expecting, the non-buffered forwarding.  Obviously, if buffering occurs, the request will go badly, but this is always a risk.

I think that our current approach is to strongly request incremental, but not completely depend on that happening.  That's most healthy for the endpoint requesting that treatment, because they need to think about what might happen if the proxy doesn't understand the request OR the proxy refuses the request.

```suggestion
incrementally with minimum buffering. If the intermediary is unwilling to forward incrementally,
```

> This really puts a lie to the whole "always" thing for me. Because an intermediary might not implement, the value is pretty low value.

We all agree that intermediaries might not understand the header and buffer the request.

But that point is orthogonal to what clients can expect when they know the intermediaries they are talking to have implemented the extension.

If the debate is between SHOULD vs. MUST, then I can live either ways. But I really think we should assure endpoints that, when talking through intermediaries that implement the extension, the endpoints can expect the they would see incremental delivery or get the request rejected.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: Closing; see https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3042#issuecomment-2819854354.
Considering that applications break if incremental delivery is refused by the intermediaries, I wonder if it would be more appropriate to use the Expect header.

```suggestion
# The Signaling Scheme
```

US English doesn't use the double-el

Is "Expect" available for use, or does it have basically the same properties as what we have here?  Not many resources pay attention to Expect.  Maybe intermediaries are generally better, but given that the only use for Expect that is even approximately used is 100-continue, I'm not confident that this is going to get you what you want any more than what we have now.

[RFC 9110 section 10.1.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-expect) states:
* The "Expect" header field in a request indicates a certain set of behaviors (expectations) that need to be supported by the server in order to properly handle this request.
* The only expectation defined by this specification is "100-continue" (with no defined parameters).

I would interpret these statements that we can define new tokens, and that the use of Expect header is correct for our purpose.

Semantics is silent in regard to how to process an unknown expectation, though considering that "100-continue" is an optional behavior, maybe the intent is to let endpoints ignore unknown expectations, but we do not know the reality.

To paraphrase, by using `expect` instead of `prefer`, we gain some theoretical correctness (because in the case of Incremental, clients are expecting certain behavior rather than preferring), at the cost of having the concern of some servers becoming confused.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Retries, rejections, and security
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
This PR addresses feedback received on the latest resumable upload draft:

- It clarifies what the server has to do when an upload append request provides too much data in the request content, exceeding the upload length. It has to reject the request, invalidate the upload resource, and reject further interaction. Such behavior is indicative of a client bug and has to be fixed on the client's end, so preventing resumption is not a problem.
- Clients are currently recommended to not resume the upload after 4xx responses. This PR relaxes this rule to allow retries for some 4xx responses, like 429 or 421.
- The security considerations are expanded to include additional recommendations based on experience from current and past implementations:
  - Upload resource URIs should not leak confidential information, e.g. the storage server where the representation is saved at.
  - Representation metadata should be properly sanitized before consulting it to determine how representations are processed (I witnessed people using non-sanitized filenames as the location of where to save uploads in the past)
  - Reiterate that uploaded data is untrusted input and has to be handled carefully.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Can we rephrase it so we don't explicitly mention 429? There is also 421 that clients can retry on a new connection.

In general, resumable upload implementations use 4xx to signal fatal errors, and 5xx to signal recoverable errors. I guess that's not true in general for HTTP, and different status codes can be handled by different layers of the stack.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Can we rephrase it so we don't explicitly mention 429? There is also 421 that clients can retry on a new connection.

Good point, I can try. How about something like this:

> [if the response has a] `4xx (Client Error)` status code, the client SHOULD NOT attempt to retry or resume the upload, unless the semantics of the response allow or recommend the client to retry the request.

Does this cover 429, 421 and potential future status codes sufficiently, yet precisely, enough?
