comments.body:
This is going to end up being confusing because it is close to the semantic of QUIC's STOP_SENDING, but not quite.

I understand that you might want to have this capability for HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1, where our model does not properly decouple send and receive sides of a bidirectional exchange.  This is a function that is already provided by the reset function in each protocol (RST_STREAM in HTTP/2, TCP RST in HTTP/1.1).  

While you might think that it is necessary to cover for those shortcomings, I don't see how that is necessary.  You are  only providing a redundant mechanism/signal.

A positive signal that a stream ended cleanly is useful, but the absence of that signal is sufficient to indicate truncation.

I agree with MT, I don't think we need STOP_SENDING_DATA. For h2 and h3, sending RST_STREAM/RESET_STREAM without sending FINAL_DATA is enough to indicate an abortive close. For h1, we have a mechanism (TCP RST / TLS error alert) that's good enough even if it's not possible to implement for everyone.

comments.body: @bemasc Thoughts?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
This seems clear, thanks!

Personally, I find the idea of "bidirectional streaming POST" kind of semantically offensive.  I would prefer that we push all of these bidirectional streaming use cases over to Extended CONNECT, for the sake of having meaningful semantics for method names and status codes.  (What does it mean to "200 OK" a POST that could later be truncated by a transport error?  What is the Content-Type of content that is actually a protocol?)

But if the consensus demands this capability, this text makes it pretty clear.

comments.author: kazuho
martinthomson
comments.body: I agree with @kazuho.  Even though I think that using POST to establish a bidirectional exchange is gross for the same reasons @bemasc does, it is something that the protocol enabled.  I don't think that Incremental should aim to make THAT better, but if we do so while making useful things better (streaming upload, streaming download), then so be it.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
As a technical matter, we would be free to do the opposite: i.e. declaring that Incremental (in the request) means "stream each message but **don't** forward the response until the request is complete".  Then setting this header would acknowledge and commit to the preferred(?) behavior.

Assuming we're unlikely to take that approach, I think it still might be worthwhile to add some cautionary language, such as "(although Extended CONNECT {{?RFC8441}}{{?RFC9220}} is generally preferred for this purpose)".

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@bemasc I get the sentiment but I'm not sure if there's one preferred way.

IMO, the two approaches (i.e., extended CONNECT and using HTTP as bidirectional stream) have their own pros and cons.

Extended CONNECT is more extensible and reliable, at the cost of requiring every endpoint and intermediary involved to have the knowledge of how the extended protocol work. We might consider it as a tool for designing _protocols_ on top of HTTP.

For developers building _applications_ on top of HTTP, they rarely have the chance to change the protocol stack that they use, or the intermediaries that they have to deal with. They need something that works through endpoints and intermediaries that are often maintained by a third party. It is very difficult if not impossible for such developers to teach their HTTP stacks (consider web browsers) and intermediaries what the semantics of their application is. They have to rely on incremental forwarding, be it unidirectional of bidirectional.

I am not opposed to writing down something like this in the draft, though I wonder it is kind of verbose... it would be like having a section dedicated to the topic. Maybe we can just point out the similarities and stop there?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
> Extended CONNECT is more extensible and reliable, at the cost of requiring every endpoint and intermediary involved to have the knowledge of how the extended protocol work. We might consider it as a tool for designing _protocols_ on top of HTTP.

I agree.  But in my view, bidirectional streaming is, by definition, a protocol, not a "message" as described in RFC 9110:
"HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol for exchanging "messages" across a connection. ... A client sends requests to a server in the form of a "request" message".

> For developers building _applications_ on top of HTTP, they rarely have the chance to change the protocol stack that they use, or the intermediaries that they have to deal with.

Yes, but they do have a suite of tools, including Extended CONNECT, WebSocket, and WebTransport.  Do we really need to bless protocols over POST, given the other tools available?

> They need something that works through endpoints and intermediaries that are often maintained by a third party. 

This could just as easily be accomplished with Extended CONNECT as with this draft.  I see at least two ways:

* Define a new Upgrade Token named "stream", meaning "trivially forwardable generic bytestream".
* Define a new request header like "Trivially-Forwardable: ?1" (very similar to [draft-kb-capsule-conversion](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-kb-capsule-conversion/)).

> It is very difficult if not impossible for such developers to teach their HTTP stacks (consider web browsers) and intermediaries what the semantics of their application is. They have to rely on incremental forwarding, be it unidirectional of bidirectional.

Nit: [bidirectional forwarding is not possible in web browsers today](https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/1254).  Those use cases are on WebSocket, etc.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
> we would be free to do the opposite: i.e. declaring that Incremental (in the request) means "stream each message but don't forward the response until the request is complete". 

For the record, I don't believe that we are free to do that.  I realize that we can constrain behaviour of endpoints that agree to implement this new feature, but I don't believe that anyone would pay attention if we decided to bundle that constraint with this (otherwise useful) addition.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> But in my view, bidirectional streaming is, by definition, a protocol, not a "message" as described in RFC 9110:
> "HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol for exchanging "messages" across a connection. ... A client sends requests to a server in the form of a "request" message".

Yeah, the protocol allows streaming requests or responses. And in some cases, it makes sense to stream in both directions.

Consider an application that transforms a message. That transformation could be compression, or something else. Such applications can be implemented in a blocking manner, but depending on the size or due to other deployment considerations, they sometimes end up being implemented (or become reimplemented) using streaming.

To summarize, streaming (incl. bidirectional) is a natural part of HTTP permitted by the core specification. That ship has sailed a long time ago, and I do not think we can restrict people from doing that.

People occasionally switch to streaming not knowing that it is unreliable, and it is often too late for them to change.

I've tried many times to convince application developers that people should not be relying on streaming behavior. It is very unproductive; please see https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/121/materials/slides-121-httpbis-incremental-http-messages-00.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Ben was confused, so I'll restate.  Streaming requests and responses is an important feature of HTTP.  Early responses are an important feature of HTTP.  That unavoidably leads to the possibility of bidirectional exchanges.  Attempting to prevent people from exploiting that possibility is not something I'm interested in doing, even if I personally think that the practice is not consistent with the protocol architecture.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Correct usage of BCP14 keywords
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
In his [review](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/httpbisa/9dsNnPwl3j3TCuv1o7jL5Em5380/), Julian rightfully called out some incorrect uses of BCP14 keywords in the document.

This PR attempts to address these point by

- turning MAYs into "can"s where they just express a possibility,
- turning SHOULDs into MUSTs where appropriate,
- explaining SHOULD to aid reader in the decision process of whether to follow the advice or not.

Some of these changes are normative:

- Handling `OPTIONS *` is now optional
- Server must announce limits using `Upload-Limit`
- Clients must adhere to limits that they are aware of
- Server must prevent issues from concurrent requests, but are not required to achieve this by terminating previous requests. This gives server the ability to implement the approach that works best while focusing on the outcome.
- 204 response is no longer mandated for DELETE responses 

Some additional paragraphs or sentences have been added to provide more context where helpful.

pulls.title: Resumable Upload: Replace section 'Subsequent Resources'
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Resumable uploads have the problem that if the client misses the response to the last PATCH request, it has no direct way of recovering this specific response. For that reason, the draft currently includes a section about subsequent resources that tries to explain how an additional resource can be used to make the final response available for later retrieval. However, the paragraph doesn't explain the actual root problem well and provides little context in general.

Therefore, this PR replaces this section with one that attempts to describe the issue properly, as well as different approaches using existing HTTP mechanism to work around the problem. It also gets rid of the odd term of _subsequent resources_.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
I'll merge this for now as I believe it's an improvement of the current text and only changes non-normative parts.

We have discussed the problem of lost final responses in the past. In my memory, the outcome was that this isn't necessarily something that this draft should address. If someone feels differently and that we need a solution, please let us know and we can talk about it again.

EDIT: The paragraph starting on line 733, I accidentally marked to much, sorry. The rest is good.

I found this section a bit hard to read. Could we simplify it? 

Suggestion:
> To fix this issue, the server can send the needed information in headers that are included in both the final response 
 and also in responses when the client queries the upload state with a HEAD request. Additionally, if the server sends a representation and wants to make it available for later, it can include the `Content-Location` header field in both the final response and in responses when checking the upload state. This allows the client to get the information even if it didn't receive the final response.

Responses to HEAD are not allowed to contain bodies, so it does not make sense to use offset retrieving to retrieve the final response if it has a body. I would just recommend that the server accepting a 0-length upload as a way to retrieve the final response again. Our client already does that.

>Responses to HEAD are not allowed to contain bodies, so it does not make sense to use offset retrieving to retrieve the final response if it has a body.

The HEAD response cannot but the GET response from the URL in the Content-Location header can. I think it does make sense as this is a common pattern for servers when they want to cache a response for later use. 

> I would just recommend that the server accepting a 0-length upload as a way to retrieve the final response again. Our client already does that.

While this is an interesting approach it seems very custom for this protocol as most servers already uses the Content-Location header for other setups. I'm not against your approach here but from experience I haven't seen any servers that actually implement it this way (for this protocol or others). It will need to be documented in the specification if we want wide adoption of it.

The reason we used 0-length append is that it's the least implementation effort on the client side. We already handle connection interruptions by doing an offset retrieving and an append. And we don't currently look at the Content-Location header in the offset retrieving response.

The server can always use a 303 redirect as the append response, and we will follow the Location header with a new GET request.

> I would just recommend that the server accepting a 0-length upload as a way to retrieve the final response again.

I think that would currently cause problems as the draft doesn't allow append requests to completed uploads, even if the request content is empty: https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.4.2-4

The Content-Location header can also be replaced with a Link header if that fits more appropriately. The idea here is not that the client itself handles this header, but instead the user of the client. In your case, I would imagine that the URLSession API just passes the last response to the caller of the API, who can then look for either a response body or the Content-Location or Link header and resolve the URI if they are interested in the resource.

> The server can always use a 303 redirect as the append response, and we will follow the Location header with a new GET request.

This could work for append requests, but I'm not sure about HEAD requests. If the server redirects the client when trying to retrieve the upload state, the process would likely fail.
Thanks, I incorporated this into the PR

comments.body: closed in favor of https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3131
s/are encouraged to/may/ (lower-case may at that)
s/is/should be/

See @vidraj's recent commentary.  @vidraj believes (and I suspect they're right) that request-side `no-transform` has long been in HTTP and RFC 9110's failure to mention it is accidental.
See RFC9111.
@mnot ah, I was searching for `cache-request-directive`.
Still, I encourage you to say "may" (lower case) rather than "are encouraged to".  I don't see the need to "encourage".
"encouraged to" is supposed to be between "may" and "should". Saying "may" wouldn't de facto mean anything, because a cache doesn't need permission for this in any case.
No, it does not change the request at all.

"is" is a statement of fact.

If we would say "should", we'd have to consider under which circumstances it would be ok to ignore the requirement.

Let's be specific and exact.  A change to the request body's byte sequence can be not-a-change of the request's logical contents and semantics, but it _is_ a change of the request.  To say that the permissible normalizations are those that do not change the request's semantics is quite correct, precise, sufficient, and necessary.  To try to further distinguish what sort of change is allowed seems pointless given that not changing the _semantics_ of the request is enough.

For example, a proxy could change the encoding of the request if the point of the proxy is to do just that because some clients have an encoding impedance mismatch with the server.  But it would be quite wrong to change the semantics of the request query.

"Econraged to" is not closer to "should" as far as RFC 2119 is concerned -- neither "encouraged to" nor "should" nor "may" are recognized by RFC 2119.  So to a point we're splitting hairs.

But!  I don't see a need to encourage these transformations.  Especially given that I have serious doubts that any cache will ever implement them because it's between `ETOOHARD` and `ENOTWORTHWHILE` (because users won't be ~~posting~~ sending the same queries anyways).  You don't have running code to demonstrate it either.

Incidentally, I work with a [proprietary] RESTful directory service that has caching for non-query end-points (because these have an ORM N+1 problem and there are commonly-requested entities) and no caching for query end-points precisely because there is no point to caching random queries that are very fast (because those do not have an ORM N+1 problem) (also it is difficult to invalidate _bulk_ query cached results, so any caching of those must be very short-lived).  Thus my skepticism.

If you have experience contrary to mine it'd be good to hear about it.
"should" not being normative, I disagree, but we can split this by using "would".  "Note that any such transformation _would be_ performed solely for ...".
The cache does not change the request. The whole paragraph is about generating the cache key.
I don't think this changes the meaning of the statement in any way.

You are now again questioning normalization in general it seems.

We had this discussion before, and the conclusion was to keep it but to clarify the description. This is what this PR is about.

It does change the request from the point of view of the client who came second and got a cached response originally generated for a different – even if semantically identical – request.

What's the rationale for requiring the first request to be passed on unchanged? I think it would be better to require caches to send the transformed (normalized / canonicalized) request if they perform such changes.

This would ensure that every client gets the same response no matter who came first, that the transformation is something sane (as opposed to whatever suboptimal or borderline broken thing the first client happened to generate), and that the server operators get to see the transformation in action (good for inspecting buggy / misconfigured proxies).

> You are now again questioning normalization in general it seems.

> We had this discussion before, and the conclusion was to keep it but to clarify the description. This is what this PR is about.

That was _your_ conclusion.  You yourself indicated that you had no idea how to normalize things like SQL.  You've also not indicated whether you have running code, which I assume means you don't have any.  I think at this point this matter has to be brought to the [ietf-http-wg@w3.org](mailto:ietf-http-wg@w3.org) list for a consensus call.

I don't want to give the impression that this is something that caches should do.  You want exactly that near as I can tell.  Clearly we differ on this.  I think we've reached the end of productive discussion on GitHub issues commentary.

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
Splitting the section is an improvement, but that's really not what I was requesting. The existing text reads like it is redefining HTTP semantics (i.e., like what we were doing in 9110).

This spec only needs to use those semantics. It should be motivating their use, not defining fields. For example, instead of
```
<section title="Content-Location Response Field" anchor="content-location">
      <t>
        A successful response (2xx, <xref target="HTTP" section="15.3"/>)
        can include a Content-Location
        header field containing an
        identifier for a resource corresponding to the results of the
        operation; see <xref target="HTTP" section="8.7"/> for details. This represents a claim from the server that a client can send
        a GET request for the indicated URI to retrieve the results of the query
        operation just performed. The indicated resource might be temporary.
      </t>
      <t>
        See <xref target="example.content-location"/> for an example.
      </t>
    </section>
```
try instead:
```
<section title="Identifying query results using Content-Location" anchor="content-location">
      <t>
        A successful (2xx) response that includes a Content-Location (<xref target="HTTP" section="8.7"/> )
        header field indicates that the resource referenced by the field value can be used as an identifier for the enclosed
        results of this QUERY request. A recipient can expect that a future GET request on the referenced resource
        would retrieve those same results (without performing the query anew).
      </t>
      <t>
        Note that supplying an identifier does not imply that the referenced resource will remain available forever,
        nor that it will be accessible to all recipients of the field.
      </t>
    </section>
```
and likewise
```
<section title="Identifying a stored query using Location" anchor="location">
      <t>
        A successful (2xx) or "See Other" (303) response to QUERY that includes a
        Location (<xref target="HTTP" section="10.2.2"/>) header field indicates that
        the resource referenced by the field value can be used as an identifier for that QUERY.
        A recipient can repeat the same semantics as the current QUERY request by performing a subsequent
        GET request on that referenced resource. In essence, the server is informing the client that
        the query semantics have a name, similar to a stored query function within a database, and
        can be accessed as a normal resource.
      </t>
      <t>
        For a 303 response, the user agent is being told to obtain the immediate QUERY results by
        performing a GET request on the referenced resource. In many cases, this indirect mechanism for
        providing results to a QUERY is preferable if the query is common, likely to be shared, or the
        content is more efficiently distributed as a response to GET.
      </t>
      <t>
        Note that supplying an identifier does not imply that the referenced resource will remain available forever,
        nor that it will be accessible to all recipients of the field.
      </t>
    </section>
```

comments.author: reschke
comments.body:
@royfielding - thanks a lot for the feedback.

@mnot , @MikeBishop , @martinthomson - I believe this is ready now.

```suggestion
        response are defined by the particular status code.
```
I think this needs elaboration because of 301/302 (what that history means for QUERY given that the historical notes are only about POST) and the reasons for choosing particular codes. It isn't useful to make statements ambiguous with "In some cases" and "such as". 

For example, I suggest:

The redirect status code semantics are the same as for GET except for the following distinctions:
  1) 301 indicates the resource motivating the query has permanently moved (i.e., the form or context that guides construction of a query for this resource has moved to a different Location); the user agent is expected to perform a GET request on the identified Location resource for further instruction.
  2) 302 indicates that the results for this QUERY are not enclosed, but can be obtained or described by performing a retrieval request (a GET request if using HTTP) targeting the URI reference supplied in the [Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.location) header field. Note that this redirection URI is not considered equivalent to the original QUERY target URI because it might only reflect the results of that specific query, not the results of similar future queries.
  3) 303 indicates that the results for this QUERY are not enclosed, but the same query can be performed via a retrieval request (a GET request if using HTTP) targeting the URI reference supplied in the [Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.location) header field. Note that this redirection URI is intended to be equivalent to the original QUERY request as a whole, much like a stored procedure for a database, and accessed via GET to improve cacheability and subsequent reuse as a linkable resource.
  4) 307 indicates a temporary redirect to the resource identified in Location; the user agent MAY continue the request by sending the same QUERY to the resource identified in Location but should not assume that the new location is a permanent replacement for the original request URI.
  5) 308 indicates a permanent redirect to the resource identified in Location; the user agent MAY continue the request by sending the same QUERY to the resource identified in Location and can use this new identifier as a permanent replacement for the original request URI.

I hear you, but that interpretation of 301/302 is inconsistent with RFC 9110. We should stick with what we say there ~; we don't _expect_ a client to do a GET request, but we allow that. On all other aspects, 301/302 are the same as 308/307~.

In particular, we carefully said in the current RFCs, that for 301 and 302, _only_ POST can be rewritten to GET - and that actually was tested with user agents.

Thus, trying to special-case these for POST seems to be entirely unproductive.

What you suggest for 307 and 308 appears to be exactly what RFC 9110 says.

We can certainly tune the text for 303/307/308 when needed. We could also say that for the case of QUERY, 301/302 mean exacly the same thing as 308/307.

I have update the PR slightly - but I still believe that adding detailed definitions of 301/302/307/308 does not make any sense here, in particular if these details conflict with that RFC 9110 says.

Next step would be to add one more example wrt 301/302/307/308.

```suggestion
        <xref target="HTTP" section="15.4"/>).
```
The sentence doesn't say anything useful.

Since we aren't changing the definition, these can be simplified 
```suggestion
        A response with either of the status codes
        301 (Moved Permanently, <xref target="HTTP" format="comma" section="15.4.2"/>) or
        308 (Permanent Redirect, <xref target="HTTP" format="comma" section="15.4.9"/>)
        indicates that the target resource has permanently moved to a different URI referenced by the
        Location response field (<xref target="HTTP" sectionFormat="comma" section="10.2.2"/>).
        Likewise, a response with either
        302 (Found, <xref target="HTTP" format="comma" section="15.4.3"/> or
        307 (Temporary Redirect, <xref target="HTTP" format="comma" section="15.4.8"/>)
        indicates that the target resource has temporarily moved. In all four cases, the server is
        suggesting that the user agent can accomplish its original QUERY request by sending a
        similar QUERY request to the new target URI referenced by Location.
```

```suggestion
        Note that the exceptions for redirecting a POST as a GET request after a 301 or 302 response
        do not apply to QUERY requests.
```

```suggestion
        A response to QUERY with the status code 303 (See Other, <xref target="HTTP" section="15.4.4"/>)
        indicates that the original query can be accomplished via a normal retrieval request on the URI referenced
        by the Location response field (<xref target="HTTP" sectionFormat="comma" section="10.2.2"/>).
        For HTTP, this means sending a GET request to the new target URI, as illustrated by the example
        in <xref target="example.indirect"/>.
```

pulls.title: [connect-tcp] Improve recommendation for abrupt TLS termination
pulls.author: bemasc
pulls.body: The current recommendation, to send a TLS Error Alert, is very difficult to implement.  The new, relaxed recommendation allows a broader range of implementations, is much easier to implement, and is equally effective and secure.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: @martinthomson Do you still have concerns about this text change?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
As discussed at IETF 124, I would like to see if we can close out this discussion.  Please review the latest version of this PR and leave a comment so we can see if there is a rough consensus.

It seem like the main active topic is how to signal failure after half-close (i.e. "RST after FIN") in HTTP/1.1 over TLS.  In my view, the current text does a good job of (1) defining a clear path for those who care about this case, (2) minimizing loss of functionality when it's not implemented as recommended, and (3) providing a clear rationale to avoid HTTP/1.1 entirely.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
> As discussed at IETF 124, I would like to see if we can close out this discussion. Please review the latest version of this PR and leave a comment so we can see if there is a rough consensus.

The proposed changes look sane to me as they adapt the requirements to what is technically feasible.

> It seem like the main active topic is how to signal failure after half-close (i.e. "RST after FIN") in HTTP/1.1 over TLS. 

We face similar difficulties in haproxy a few years ago during a rework of our error notifications. A failure after half-close is in fact a failure to send data in the other direction. At the implementation level, it will be reported to the send() call only. If we have a way to detect a send() failure (native or over TLS) then the half-close status will not be an issue since it won't affect the send path. The thing that you cannot easily detect is an error on the wire after the last successful send(), which happens on buffered data that's sent later. There are some OS-specific ways to query the state of pending output data on a socket but that's not pollable anyway. So in practice you have to assume that after the last successful send() and shutdown() on a half-closed socket, the data are on their own, and good luck to them.

The concern is not that TLS stacks do graceful closes even when asked to terminate a connection, but more that they do not use close_notify to terminate flows that end in normal circumstances, such that you cannot distinguish between a successful close (which is supposed to include close_notify) and an abortive close (which is supposed to exclude close_notify).

Now, if you are saying that it is ALSO hard to guarantee that an abortive close doesn't result in close_notify in other stacks, that's useful information.  That further motivates the inclusion of FINAL_DATA.  But it doesn't mean that you need to say anything here:

```suggestion
```

After all, the stream is treated as incomplete unless a complete FINAL_DATA capsule is received.

Failing that, is "unclean" really the word that you want to use for this?  Consider "abortive close" or "abrupt closure" or something along those lines.

```suggestion
* It may be difficult to implement an abortive close ({{closing-connections}}), as TLS subsystems may close connections gracefully even when this is not desired.
```
Wasn't this a TCP RST?  It's true that a TCP shutdown will produce a similar effect, but a RST matches what you use for unsecured HTTP over TCP.

Is this needed given that you are saying /without/ a TLS alert?

```suggestion
```

```suggestion
    - HTTP/1.1 (with or without TLS): TCP RST
```

```suggestion
      see {{!RFC9113}}, Sections 6.4 and 7
```

Sending a TCP RST (without sending close_notify) would be compliant here, but it is not the only option.

I wouldn't want to recommend TCP RST specifically.  Sending a TCP RST on the outer connection breaks the usual confidentiality guarantees of "https" (e.g. revealing that this connection is likely a "connect-tcp" proxy, not a WebSocket).  It's also harder to implement, unauthenticated, and [increases the amount of data that is likely to be lost](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9112#section-9.6-9).

> RST matches what you use for unsecured HTTP over TCP

In my view, each of these 4 recommendations describes how to signal an abrupt closure using the transport layer immediately below "connect-tcp".

"TLS closure alert" is a term of art that is not widely known outside of TLS.  To know what a TLS closure alert is, and what it means to avoid sending one, I think we need a reference to the definition, which is in RFC 8446, Section 6.1.

Ideally I would hyperlink all of these references to the relevant sections without the explicit references (at least in the HTML output), but I couldn't figure out how to make kramdown-rfc do that.

> The concern is not that TLS stacks do graceful closes even when asked to terminate a connection, but more that they do not use close_notify to terminate flows that end in normal circumstances

OK, I've added this to the list of reasons to avoid HTTP/1.1.

> After all, the stream is treated as incomplete unless a complete FINAL_DATA capsule is received.

The purpose of abrupt closure is not to inform you that the incoming stream was truncated.  FINAL_DATA indeed covers that.  The purpose of abrupt closure is to inform you that your _outgoing_ stream was truncated (or in reverse, that it was [delivered in full](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.6-1)).  This can occur _after_ the incoming FINAL_DATA, so it needs a separate signal.

> Failing that, is "unclean" really the word that you want to use for this? Consider "abortive close" or "abrupt closure" or something along those lines.

Changed to "abrupt closure" throughout.

reviews.author: kazuho
reviews.body: I have an editorial question but otherwise the PR looks good!

That seems like an improvement to me.  Done.

reviews.author: martinthomson
reviews.body: Sorry for not tracking this closely enough.  I don't think that where you landed is self-consistent.

comments.body:
Many implementation will treat this as a normal stream termination.  That's because this is indistinguishable from a successful termination in the case that the TLS close_notify doesn't get sent (or doesn't make it through).

I would not show any message being exchanged here at all.

```suggestion
```

Of course, this is based on you RECOMMENDING that no close_notify be sent.  That's not something I would endorse.

The right way to deal with this in HTTP/1.1 is to use chunked encoding or Content-Length properly.  If the connection ends before the request is terminated, then it's an abortive close.

This doesn't seem to be consistent with what you are recommending above.

So rather than this, note that premature message termination might be hard to distinguish from successfully terminated messages, especially if there is no Content-Length or the terminal chunked encoding piece.

Including advice that you can't rely on the presence or absence of a TLS closure alert for clean message termination is useful.  Then say that the best way to avoid that is to use Content-Length or chunked encoding.  As long as TLS is involved and you have proof positive that the message is complete, then the nature of the abortive close is far less important.

> Many implementation will treat this as a normal stream termination.

Do you mean implementations of TLS, or of "connect-tcp"?  I assume that the major implementations of TLS correctly surface an error when close_notify is omitted at shutdown; otherwise some uses would be vulnerable to truncation attacks.  Implementations of "connect-tcp" do not yet exist, and can be asked to conform.  My main concern would be about TLS-terminating load balancers that _always_ send close_notify.

> I would not show any message being exchanged here at all.

I don't understand.  When `A` times out the TCP connection, what should it do with the HTTP connection?

> Of course, this is based on you RECOMMENDING that no close_notify be sent. That's not something I would endorse.

Is there a reason why this recommendation is dangerous or problematic?

> The right way to deal with this in HTTP/1.1 is to use chunked encoding or Content-Length properly.

In HTTP/1.1, "connect-tcp" uses HTTP Upgrade, so Content-Length and chunked encoding are not available.  Instead, it uses the Capsule Protocol (similar to chunked encoding).

> If the connection ends before the request is terminated, then it's an abortive close.

"connect-tcp" employs a FINAL_DATA capsule to represent the TCP FIN (end of incoming data), without any reliance on the HTTP transport/stream.  However, [according to RFC 9293](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.6-1:~:text=a%20user%20who%20expects%20no%20data%20in%20return%20need%20only%20wait%20to%20hear%20the%20connection%20was%20CLOSED%20successfully%20to%20know%20that%20all%20their%20data%20was%20received%20at%20the%20destination%20TCP%20endpoint) that's not the same as "closed":

> "a user who expects no data in return need only wait to hear the connection was CLOSED successfully to know that all their data was received at the destination TCP endpoint."

To get to the CLOSED state, you need a signal for ["received ACK of FIN"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#figure-5).  In H2/H3, the draft uses graceful stream closure for that.  In H1 over TLS, close_notify seems to be the equivalent signal.

> note that premature message termination might be hard to distinguish from successfully terminated messages

How is this different from the current text: "The abrupt closure signals ... are more likely to be missing or corrupted"?

> As long as TLS is involved and you have proof positive that the message is complete, then the nature of the abortive close is far less important.

I agree.  The draft [notes this distinction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-connect-tcp-09.html#section-3.4-4) by making the former mandatory, and the latter recommended.

Since the POSIX TCP APIs don't even really expose the CLOSING vs. CLOSED distinction, and applications should never rely on it, I'm not too concerned if it often gets lost in HTTP/1.1.  However, I do think it is worth defining the distinction here to support debugging, allow propagation of this signal across HTTP version translating intermediaries, minimize the impact of transparent proxies, etc.

Closure with a close_notify after receiving a FINAL_DATA capsule (representing FIN) would indicate graceful close.  The purpose of this line is to provide a signal of ungraceful close (i.e. RST or timeout) that can be used after receiving the FIN (but before the connection is closed).

> > Many implementation will treat this as a normal stream termination.
> 
> Do you mean implementations of TLS, or of "connect-tcp"? I assume that the major implementations of TLS correctly surface an error when close_notify is omitted at shutdown; otherwise some uses would be vulnerable to truncation attacks. Implementations of "connect-tcp" do not yet exist, and can be asked to conform. My main concern would be about TLS-terminating load balancers that _always_ send close_notify.
> [...]
> I don't understand. When `A` times out the TCP connection, what should it do with the HTTP connection?

I was talking about HTTP generally.

In the timeout case, you don't need to mandate any particular behaviour.  Because a timeout can be many things, including a clean termination (FINAL_DATA included) or not.  You are attempting to proscribe actions that don't need that.

> > Of course, this is based on you RECOMMENDING that no close_notify be sent. That's not something I would endorse.
> 
> Is there a reason why this recommendation is dangerous or problematic?

Because that's not how HTTP has worked so far and you are attempting to levy implementation requirements where they are most likely unwelcome.  It might be appealing to have all implementations do the same thing here, but our experience is that they don't and they probably won't change just because it would be nicer if they would.

(ignore the stuff about message termination; that's what I get for not pulling in enough context)
As noted above, either works if you don't have FINAL_DATA, so why attempt to fix implementations.

The apparent inconsistency was

> unable to omit the TLS closure alert or send a TCP RST, as recommended

with

> - HTTP/1.1 over TLS: TCP shutdown without a TLS closure alert;

It wasn't clear to me that the "as recommended" applied to both the closure alert and TCP RST, due to English not being clear about whether such clauses distribute. 

Ignore the other piece.

> a timeout can be many things, including a clean termination

I'm referring to a TCP user timeout, which [is an error](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.10.8) in TCP terms.  It cannot be a clean shutdown because the endpoint does not know if all data was successfully received in both directions.

My point in showing this example was partly to show that even with this level of detail, some information is still lost: all errors are collapsed into RST.

> that's not how HTTP has worked so far and you are attempting to levy implementation requirements where they are most likely unwelcome

1. It's not really "HTTP".  This is Upgrade, so the HTTP session is over, and the connection is now owned by a new protocol named "connect-tcp".
2. It's a recommendation, not a requirement.  If you ignore it, everything will mostly be fine, but debugging failures will be a bit harder and you'll lose this signal in HTTP/3 (where abrupt closure is not as controversial) if you have version-translating intermediaries.
3. In at least some implementations, it's extremely easy to implement.  In my Go prototype it's [one line](https://github.com/bemasc/masque-go/commit/0bf68f13c564ffee0ec2eebc69509717cc804c26#diff-fd4820e2c415e0057b0e67d294303bdde3b98c2731b6dbd1e2b0f79349744499R638): `tlsConn.NetConn().Close()`.  If a behavior is helpful but not crucial, sometimes easy to implement and sometimes not worth the bother, that seems like a good case for RECOMMENDED.  (Lowering this to OPTIONAL in HTTP/1.1, while it's still RECOMMENDED in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, seems like extra text and complexity with no discernible benefit.)

OK, I've changed the text to

* The graceful and abrupt closure signals ({{closing-connections}}) are more likely to be missing or corrupted:
  - Some implementations may be unable to emit the recommended abrupt closure signals, due to limitations in their TCP and TLS subsystems.
  - Faulty implementations may fail to send a TLS closure alert during graceful shutdown, or fail to report an error when the expected closure alert is not received.  These misbehaviors are not compliant with {{RFC8446}}, but they are common nonetheless among HTTP/1.1 implementations today.

pulls.title: WAFs might reject requests permanently
pulls.author: kazuho
pulls.body:
This pull request splits the Security Considerations section, retaining the existing case of sending `connection-limit-reached` as an example of temporary rejection, and adding the WAF case discussed in #3143 as an example of permanent rejection.

For the WAF case, I've chosen 403 + `Proxy-Status: http_request_denied`, as this combination is defined to indicate policy-based rejection by an intermediary; see https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9209.html#http-request-denied. Though I think we can discuss defining a new Proxy-Status error specific to incremental requests.

Closes #3143.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
So my concern with 403 is that 403 denotes a violation of the policy, while here we are unable to apply the policy. WAF owners typically monitor the number of 403 per client IP address and will just block them permanently after they cause too many because normally they are attackers violating the policy. Here innocent clients just trying to perform incremental requests will be confused as attackers. And in general this makes the system less observable.  I think it is important to distinguish "I cannot accept this request because I cannot analyze it" from "I cannot accept this request which tries to violate our filtering policy".

I continue to think that even codes like "417 Expectation failed" are much closer to this need. In addition it would really make sense that a client trying to engage into an incremental request would use an "Expect: 100-continue" in order to avoid sending data and be able to reuse their connection. Indeed, in HTTP/1 if you try incremental and start sending data of infinite length, and you get a rejection from the server or intermediary, it's difficult to finish. With chunk encoding it's doable but some servers/intermediaries still do not like them much on requests. With Expect, the client can wait for the server's agreement before starting to send the data and is able to give up before starting to send. And in this case we'd have exactly 417 expectation failed (i.e. the server is not willing to accept that request since it requires incremental).

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@wtarreau While I think that rejecting due to insufficient information is part of a policy, you make a good point about how 403 could be used in practice and that might interfere with what we want to see happen with incremental requests.

However, thinking a bit more, I think I have to disagree with using 417 or Expect as the mechanism.

The problem with expectations of HTTP is that it is an opt-in. Assume we define `Expect: incremental`. Servers that do not recognize "incremental" as an expectation token are supposed to reject such requests with 417.

This is not the behavior we want. Between end clients and end servers, HTTP messages are already exchanged in an incremental manner; we do not want to prohibit that from happening. What we want to define is a signal that changes the behavior of intermediaries. Therefore, the type of the signal is opt-out; i.e., a signal ignored by endpoints that do not understand Incremental.

To this end, I think we should go with 400 and a new Proxy-Status error, or even select a new status code.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Please note, I wasn't clear, I wasn't suggesting `Expect: incremental` but:
```
POST ...
Incremental: ?1
Expect: 100-continue
```
I suspect that regardless of what the spec will define, it will be what clients will do due to the risk of seeing the request rejected, because in HTTP/1 there is no way to abort the upload without breaking the connection. The 100-continue will offer them this ability, and in this case this is already 100% supported by existing infrastructure, and maybe we should encourage using this as the normal way to use incremental. And probably that in this case the fall back to 403 when not using 417 would make more sense: the intermediary offers the ability to present the request without the payload and get a status (417). If the client wants to go full throttle without asking, and the intermediary doesn't support it, 403 can make sense (with the impact described above). But why would a client do this if we document that 100-continue is the recommended way to use it ?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@wtarreau 
> And probably that in this case the fall back to 403 when not using 417 would make more sense: the intermediary offers the ability to present the request without the payload and get a status (417). If the client wants to go full throttle without asking, and the intermediary doesn't support it, 403 can make sense (with the impact described above). But why would a client do this if we document that 100-continue is the recommended way to use it ?

Am I correct to understand that you are suggesting for a server to return 417, when that server received a request with both `Expect: 100-continue` and `Incremental: ?1` and decides to refuse the request based on the existence of the Incremental header field?

I'm not sure if that is the intended use of expectations.

IIUC, when a server receives a request with an `expect: 100-continue` and is capable of determining the final response just by looking at the request headers, it should generate _that_ final response, whereas 417 is meant to be sent only when there is a problem in the Expect header field. Quoting from [Section 15.5.18 of RFC 9110](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-417-expectation-failed), 417 is sent when _the expectation given in the request's **Expect header field** could not be met_.

To paraphrase, the status code to be used for refusing Incremental requests should be the same regardless of if `Expect: 100-continue` is used.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
> Quoting from [Section 15.5.18 of RFC 9110](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-417-expectation-failed), 417 is sent when _the expectation given in the request's **Expect header field** could not be met_

Indeed! Though (with a bit of a stretch) the 100-continue cannot be fulfilled with incremental since the server will not be able to deal with that body. But I get your point, you're right. Martin already suggested that we should create a specific status and I think that all this discussion just demonstrates this. I really think that "I cannot process that request without buffering the body", or "I cannot process that request without significantly degrading the user's experience" is what we need here.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Thank you for the input, folks.

As of 77aba65, the reponse used to reject Incremental -  for both request and response - is 501 Not Implemented + incremental_refused Proxy-Status error.

The rationale for choosing 501 is as follows:

When refusing to forward an incremental _response_, the status code must be a permanent 5xx, and the status code should indicate that a feature is unavailable.

The closest status code we have is 501, which has the following definition: "The 501 (Not Implemented) status code _indicates that the server does not support the functionality required to fulfill the request_. This is the appropriate response when the server does not recognize the request method and is not capable of supporting it for any resource" ([section 15.6.2 of RFC 9110](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-501-not-implemented); emphasis mine).

Note 503 and 504 are inappropriate, as they are temporary errors.

When refusing to forward an incremental _request_, it might be possible to argue for either 4xx or 5xx. But in the case of Incremental, the request that the client has generated is correct and it is the proxy that decides to _reject_ the request. If we think along these lines, 5xx, specifically 501 for the same reasons stated above, becomes appropriate.

For both incremental requests and rejections, the response will be accompanied by the incremental_refused Proxy-Status error. Therefore, clients can refer to the header field to find out the cause.

WDYT?

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Let me just paste my response here again so that it doesn't get lost above in the threaded conversation:

--

I think I'm fine with 501, as it indeed matches an incompatibility between what the client desires and what the server is able to do, i.e. one of them has to change something for the request to be accepted. So yeah, that's fine for me.

I'm less sure that it's suitable for the response, because in order to block the response, the server needs to have already processed the request and started to respond. But 501 normally implies that the request was not processed. IMHO the 502 bad gateway is more suitable there as it's a deployment issue: the server is trying to do stuff that is incompatible with the hosting infrastructure. That's typically what's returned when a server response is invalid or blocked by an intermediary by policy (e.g. after detecting a risk of information leak etc).

Also I do think that we should support "Incremental: ?0" so that intermediaries can warn servers "don't try to do that, I'm not compatible" in order for servers to degrade nicely or return a clean message to the user instead of failing hard on a 502. And the 502 would be even more suitable there as it would be clear that the server didn't consider the advertised limitation.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> I think I'm fine with 501, ...

:+1: to converge on how to indicate refusal of incremental requests.

As to incremental responses, both 501 and 502 have their own merits and disadvantages. I do not have an opinion.

501 is better in sense that it indicates that a capability is missing. 502 is better as implies that (at least a portion of) the request was processed. Though I would also argue that, as these error codes indicate permanent errors, the failed request will never be replayed and hence it does not matter a whole lot if the request reached the origin.

> Also I do think that we should support "Incremental: ?0" so that intermediaries can warn servers "don't try to do that, I'm not compatible" in order for servers to degrade nicely or return a clean message to the user instead of failing hard on a 502.

That sounds like an issue that we closed separately (#3043).

We can revisit the issue, though I would argue that,
* Incremental responses would rarely be interpreted by humans, therefore, a beautiful rendering of the problem is unneeded. What we need is an error indicator that can be processed automatically, and to fulfill the need, we have defined a dedicated Proxy-Status error.
* Regardless of it the proxy indicates its unwillingness to allow incremental responses, the server might provide one. To paraphrase, #3043 (proxy indicating support for incremental responses) is an issue orthogonal to this one.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Regarding 501, maybe we can use in each direction in combination with the proxy-status header indicating where it failed: "proxy-status: incremental-request" or "proxy-status: incremental-response", since only one will cause the processing to stop. And in this case it's unambiguous and that might be OK.

For the lack of retry, I'm not sure it will not happen. Don't you think that clients right now have other ways to access the service in a slightly degraded way ? E.g. try to fetch everything at once with a longer delay instead of doing it in a progressive way for example ?

Even if the response is not for humans (sorry but I'm still not clear on the intended exact use case of this extension), I think that servers often have multiple options to respond, with higher or lower degrees of quality, and that being able to respond in a degraded way is usually better than seeing the response totally blocked.

Also, do you know if clients/servers will send only incremental data as part of the payload or if they might send *some* payload then want to continue with incremental ? I'm asking because it could make a big difference to make WAFs and analyzers more transparent to this. For example, if a WAF wants to analyze, say, 10kB of payload minimum, and the client uploads a large block followed by an incremental body, if instead of just saying "incremental: ?1" it said "incremental: 12000" to indicate that it hopes to switch to incremental after that length, then it could allow the WAF to observe what it wants and let the rest pass through incrementally. But if the client said "incremental: 8000", then the waf would return the 501 since it cannot analyze enough. I'm not certain it's a good idea, but I prefer to expose it in case it sparks another one in someone else's head. I'm still keeping in mind that the first goal is to fail fast.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Sorry I dropped the ball. I've merged the PR, and will rev a new draft.

Responding to @wtarreau's points:

> Regarding 501, maybe we can use in each direction in combination with the proxy-status header indicating where it failed: "proxy-status: incremental-request" or "proxy-status: incremental-response", since only one will cause the processing to stop. And in this case it's unambiguous and that might be OK.

As much as I like having fine-grained errors, I doubt how much benefit we'd have by having the distinction between requests and response here.

In the case of endpoints without fallbacks, what users can do does not change by having that distinction. 

Regardless of the distinction, the users can (and would) contact the operator of that intermediary, and ask them to fix. For these operators, I'd argue that the knowledge of the distinction by itself is insufficient to deem if incremental can allowed; they need to look at the application that is using incremental and decide on per-application basis.

In the case of endpoints with fallbacks, the typical approach would be to disable the use of incremental in all directions.

To paraphrase, IMO, having the distinction would be useful only for endpoints that start with using incremental in both directions that then fall back to using it in one direction should it receive an indication that incremental is unsupported in one direction.

That does not seem like worth the complexity to me.

> For the lack of retry, I'm not sure it will not happen. Don't you think that clients right now have other ways to access the service in a slightly degraded way ? E.g. try to fetch everything at once with a longer delay instead of doing it in a progressive way for example ?

I think it'd be up to the applications. As 501 indicates lack of support for a functionality, I think it is perfectly fine for applications to try a different approach.

> Also, do you know if clients/servers will send only incremental data as part of the payload or if they might send some payload then want to continue with incremental ? 

I do not think we can or should make these kind of assumptions.

WAFs would verify HTTP messages in various ways. If the application that they are dealing with sends enough information upfront, then they might forward the HTTP message. Otherwise, they can buffer it for a short period, hoping that they would receive enough to verify. If that expires, they should send an error.

comments.author: wtarreau
comments.body:
Hi @kazuho

> In the case of endpoints without fallbacks, what users can do does not change by having that distinction.

That was in fact my point: there's nothing the user can do if an unsupported incremental response is sent, however in case of failure on the request, the client can retry without incremental. That's why I thought the distinction is useful (i.e. "you may retry" vs "please do not retry, it will give the same result").

comments.body:
@wtarreau Ah I see, thank you for the clarification.

> That's why I thought the distinction is useful (i.e. "you may retry" vs "please do not retry, it will give the same result").

```suggestion
Some intermediaries inspect the payload of an HTTP messages and forward them only if
```

```suggestion
the content is deemed safe. Such intermediaries might decide to reject
```

(though see below)

```suggestion
the content is deemed safe. Any feature that depends on seeing the entirety
of the message in this way is incompatible with incremental delivery,
so these intermediaries need to reject requests unless the entire message
is received.
```

There are two cases here:

1. incremental requests, which this text assumes and for which 403 etc is fine.
2. incremental *responses*, which I think also get some sort of rejection, but it won't be a http_request_denied, maybe http_response_timeout with 504.

The suggestions above try to make that text more generic, but I don't quite know how to make this text more general without spelling that out.
Thanks, applied manually.

+1 to making the problem statement generic, so I've applied your suggestions against the previous paragraph.

Regarding what the signal should be, I think I'm more inclined to defining the `incremental_unsupported` Proxy-Status error, as that can be the source of truth for the rejection of both requests and responses.
Added as `incremental_refused` in commits up to 4b4bfc7.
Did you want to update this with the 504 response rejection case?

Please not 5xx. All infrastructure operators are monitoring those as a reliable metric for their infrastructure's health. 504 is a timeout, it happens when servers are too slow to respond (overloaded or depending on an overloaded database) and it's long been graphed and monitor as representing this. And ideally upon 504, a client should refrain from trying again too soon. Here the only reason for not processing is the presence of the incremental header in the request, i.e. if the client knows how to access the same feature without incremental, it will be immediately served.

The problem here is that the client might not have asked for an incremental *response*, but if the intermediary is unwilling to support the feature (and insists on buffering), it has to send the client *something*.  What should that be other than 504?

Ah you meant about the response, I thought you were speaking about the request. Yes the response in this case must necessarily be a 5xx since we've blocked between the intermediary and the server, i.e. the client cannot fix this. It could be a problem by the way that we reject valid server responses in this case without being able to warn them that we can't proceed with incremental, because the user will face a dirty error while the application could have degraded much more nicely instead (e.g. using redirects to a better capable server, switching to a less interactive but compatible mechanism, such as a Refresh header etc). We leave it no chance with the 5xx like this.

Wouldn't it be good first if we could suggest that intermediaries that *have* to buffer responses send "Incremental: ?0" to the server to say "don't ever think about trying this". Because then it would make sense to consider that the server trying it anyway is violating the rule, and many more 5xx would be suitable here (including 502 Bad Gateway in this case).

Thank you for your feedback; 7defc7aa adds a new paragraph clarifying how intermediaries SHOULD refuse to server incremental _response_.

I went with 501 Not Implemented, as I think neither 503 or 504 are appropriate. The problem with 503 and 504 are that they are both "temporary" errors, even though what we want is a permanent error. To me 501 seems more appropriate, as it is a generic signal of permanent errors indicating lack of certain features.

WDYT?

I think I'm fine with 501, as it indeed matches an incompatibility between what the client desires and what the server is able to do, i.e. one of them has to change something for the request to be accepted. So yeah, that's fine for me.

I'm less sure that it's suitable for the response, because in order to block the response, the server needs to have already processed the request and started to respond. But 501 normally implies that the request was not processed. IMHO the 502 bad gateway is more suitable there as it's a deployment issue: the server is trying to do stuff that is incompatible with the hosting infrastructure. That's typically what's returned when a server response is invalid or blocked by an intermediary by policy (e.g. after detecting a risk of information leak etc).

Also I **do** think that we should support "Incremental: ?0" so that intermediaries can warn servers "don't try to do that, I'm not compatible" in order for servers to degrade nicely or return a clean message to the user instead of failing hard on a 502. And the 502 would be even more suitable there as it would be clear that the server didn't consider the advertised limitation.

reviews.body: I can see @wtarreau's perspective on 502, but I think that 501 is a better *suggestion*.  The response from the server is valid in this case, but 502 would imply that it wasn't.

comments.body: I think this is consistent with the RFC we're updating, and that it's perfectly reasonable to leave clearer integration with HTML and DOM APIs to the `tre` layering document in progress.

We do now support `new Worker("data:application/javascript,...")`, which creates a dedicated Worker with an opaque origin. I'd suggest that we instead drop this note entirely, and change the dedicated worker text on lines 1154-1157 to support that case explicitly:

> Dedicated workers are simple, as each dedicated worker is bound to one and only one document. The worker's "site for cookies" is the document's "site for cookies" if the worker's origin is same-site with the document's "site for cookies", and an opaque origin otherwise.

This seems right, and is consistent with the use of opaque origin in HTML.  It's a shame that the use of opaque origin in HTML is just not very good.  It says that opaque origins can be compared for equality, then uses "an opaque origin" often, without specifying which other opaque origins qualify as equal.

In this case, the only opaque origin that would be equal to the opaque origin for this dedicated worker would be the result of any attempt to get the "site for cookies" for exactly the same worker.

That is, another call to `new Worker ("data:...")` would produce a different opaque origin.  I assume.  Otherwise, you might imagine that each attempt to get an origin produces a different opaque origin, which would never compare as equal.

comments.body:
```suggestion
Servers, including intermediaries, can (and often do) apply restrictions on the size of individual request message content. There is no standard mechanism to communicate such existing size restriction. A server that implements one can respond with a 413 Content Too Large status code; see {{Section 15.5.14 of HTTP}}. Appending to an upload resource, as a series of appends, can be used to upload data up to the `max-size` limit without encountering per-message limits. The `min-append-size` and `max-append-size` limits applies to the upload resource. Servers might apply restrictions that are smaller than the append limits, which would also result in a failed request. Clients could deal with such situations by retrying an upload append with a smaller size, as long as the new size resides between `min-append-size` and `max-append-size`. Cases where an append uses `min-append-size` fails with a 413 Content Too Large response might indicate a deployment mismatch that cannot be recovered from.
```

comments.body: Previously, receivers could error out if unknown keys held values with unexpected types. This now requires them to ignore these. I'm fine with that, but just something to be aware of.

Thanks for the callout. To explain a bit more my though process,

1. If the field is a valid `Dictionary` then it will pass https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9651#section-4.2
2. If the field in an invalid `Dictionary` then the requirements in https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9651#section-4.2-10 apply 

> If parsing fails, either the entire field value MUST be ignored (i.e., treated as if the field were not present in the section), or alternatively the complete HTTP message MUST be treated as malformed. This is intentionally strict to improve interoperability and safety, and field specifications that use Structured Fields are not allowed to loosen this requirement.

3. If the field is a valid `Dictionary`, then apply the additional requirements of this document on the member `value`. If you know the key, you can parse the value and apply this documents rules. If you don't know the key, then you can't know the rules and can't do validation.

When I first authored the commit, I took the opinion that we should ignore the individual members. However, revisiting now I wonder if we should state stricter text more akin to RFC 9651 e.g., 

```suggestion
Receivers of `Upload-Limit` parse the Dictionary as described in {{Section 4.2 of STRUCTURED-FIELDS}}. Where the Dictionary is successfully parsed, this document places the two additional requirements on Dictionary members. First, a member with an unknown key MUST be ignored. Second, a member with a known key but a value of unexpected type MUST cause the entire `Upload-Limit` header field to be ignored, or alternatively the complete HTTP message MUST be treated as malformed.
```

The stricter approach may help to avoid unintended consequences caused by ignoring individual dictionary members.
@Acconut I pushed the above text suggestion in a new commit, happy with it?

Your new suggestion looks good to me. This also seems to address @MikeBishop's comment on the WGLC that advocates for errors on unexpected value types for known keys:

> In 4.1.4, I'm surprised that keys with unexpected values are ignored rather than an error; does that mean I can include max-age="Really Long, I Swear" and the limit will still work? I commend the future-proofing of ignoring unknown keys, but I'd consider being stricter on keys you know the semantics of.

comments.body:
> 3. Section 8.3 lists security risks when cookies are sent in clear and clause 3
states: "A malicious client could alter the Cookie header before transmission,
with unpredictable results". I failed to understand how this is concerned with
the use of TLS. In my understanding, malicious clients can do this in any case,
regardless on whether TLS is used or not. Am I missing something?

This text has existed since draft-ietf-httpstate-cookie-00 but isn't present in rfc2965, so Adam Barth seems to have added it.

Perhaps Adam was considering a malicious client on the user's system? In that case, would TLS necessarily protect the cookies? If it was a malicious user agent then all bets are off.

I'm currently in agreement with the reviewer but I'm hoping someone else have a better understanding of why this is listed.

> 4. Section 7.1, last para states that "it is RECOMMENDED that user agents adopt
a policy for third-party cookies that is as restrictive as compatibility
constraints permit". This gives no concrete recommendations, and no examples,
thus making this requirement vague and subjective. I think this requirement
should be provided with more details how to deal with it.

My draft response for this is:

>This is difficult to do given the range of compatibility constraints among user agents. Some agents could strive for maximum compatibility while others for maximum user privacy. The third-party cookie policies will differ greatly between those two types of UAs.

Curious if anyone has other thoughts on how to handle this.

I agree that malicious client behavior has little to do with whether the client is sending information in an encrypted or unencrypted fashion. Dropping the third item here seems fine, as the risks listed in the first and second bullets seem exhaustive.

For this document, I agree with your approach. The primitives that user agents seem to be aligning around (CHIPS, etc) didn't make it into this document, so the advice we could provide here would be at best incomplete.

It might be reasonable to file this as feedback to https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies-00.html#name-third-party-cookies, however.

pulls.title: Update requirements on use of Location during upload creation
pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
Previously, there were "mixed" requirements on including a Location
in interim or final response to an upload creation request. This
created some annoying dealing with 104 responses depending on
if they were first or not.
   
The PR proposes more consistency. If you're going to generate a
Location, it must always be sent and must always be the same value
in all responses. Only a SHOULD requirement is levied on the client
to check these - making it MUST seems a bit too onerous.
    
Fixes #3183

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: @Acconut PTAL when you can

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body: I wholeheartedly agree to this change as I proposed the same thing some years ago ;) I agree with Marius question on how to handle the update location header value. Is there ever a reason for the server to change the location of the upload mid upload? The only thing I can think of is some kind of load balancing between servers but that seems like a risky implementation that just adds complexity. Any other ideas?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> Is there ever a reason for the server to change the location of the upload mid upload?

None that I can think of right now. Maybe in the future a use case arises, but this can then be specified in another document.

Should there be a recommendation for the client to abort the upload if it detects a changed Location value? How should a client react in this situation?

In addition, I'm wondering if this is too strict for the final response:

> Clients SHOULD verify the `Location` value does not change between response messages.

For example, the client uploads a large video in a single request. Since the file is large, the server offers a resumable upload via a 104 response and Location pointing to the upload resource. However, the upload completes fine and the server now wants to indicate the video's URI on the CDN to the client in the Location header. That value would then be different from the Location value in the 104 response. But that's OK because the upload is completed. Should we consider that as well as an exemption?
It feels to me we might want a little more input from the WG on this?

> It feels to me we might want a little more input from the WG on this?

We can prompt the WG for their opinions, but I don't think this is necessary to address my concern. That can also be done by stating explicitly that Location header field in responses with Upload-Complete: ?1 are exempt from this rule (these responses are the final ones after the upload is done and don't necessarily point to the upload resource).

How about something like this:


```suggestion
Where a response requires a `Location` header field to be included, all interim and final response messages for the same request MUST contain an identical `Location` value. Final responses including the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header field are exempt from this requirement as they are the result of processing the transferred representation. Clients SHOULD verify the `Location` value does not change between response messages. They SHOULD abort the current request and cancel the upload ({{upload-cancellation}}) if a change is detected.
```
Thanks, I'll take this but tweak it a bit. Give me a mo
@Acconut PTAL

reviews.author: Acconut
reviews.body: Great, thank you!

pulls.author: LPardue
pulls.body:
We have the requirement "if the client knows the representation data's length,
it SHOULD include the `Upload-Length`". Which means the server can be a position
to either know, or not know the value.

This change makes a minor tweak to the text to highlight that when the server
was given a length it really MUST respond with it but when it didn't get given

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I plan to rebase this and act on @Acconut's suggestion later today

The client can also specify the complete upload length implicitly through the combination of `Content-Length` and `Upload-Complete: ?1`. Wondering if the phrasing should be "unless the total length is unknown".
or `"unless the client has not supplied one (either by supplying its own upload-length or providing an Upload-Complete:?1 with a Content-Length)"`
Yeah, that works

The text could also just reference Section 4.1.3, which explains how the length of an upload can be discovered: 

> There are two different ways for the client to indicate and the upload resource to discover the length from requests for creating the upload resource ([Section 4.2](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#upload-creation)) or appending to it ([Section 4.4](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#upload-appending)):
> - If the request includes the Upload-Complete field value set to true and a valid Content-Length header field, the request content is the remaining representation data. The length is then the sum of the current offset ([Section 4.1.1](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#upload-offset)) and the Content-Length header field value.
> - The request can include the Upload-Length request and response header field. Upload-Length is an Item Structured Header Field ([[STRUCTURED-FIELDS](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#STRUCTURED-FIELDS)]). Its value is a non-negative Integer ([Section 3.3.1](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9651#section-3.3.1) of [[STRUCTURED-FIELDS](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#STRUCTURED-FIELDS)]) and indicates the number of bytes of the entire representation data. Other values MUST cause the entire header field to be ignored.

(from https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.1.3-2)

Maybe something along these lines:


```suggestion
- MUST include the length in the `Upload-Length` header field unless the client has not supplied one, by providing the corresponding headers as described in Section 4.1.3,
```

That might be a bit more watertight.

> While the values `*/*` and `application/*` indicate the acceptance of the `application/partial-upload` in PATCH requests, it does not necessarily indicate support for all aspects of resumable uploads as defined in this document.

For readability, perhaps we can tweak your wording a little such as

```suggestion
A server that supports the creation of a resumable upload resource ({{upload-creation}}) for a target URI MUST include the following header fields in response to an `OPTIONS` request for the target URI: `Upload-Limit` with the corresponding limits, and `Accept-Patch` ({{Section 3.1 of PATCH}}) with the value of `application/partial-upload`. ```

If a server supports the creation of upload resources for any target URI, it SHOULD include the following header fields in response to an `OPTIONS` request for the target `*` (if this target is supported): `Upload-Limit` with the corresponding limits, if limits apply, and `Accept-Patch` with the value of `application/partial-upload`.
