Achilles: Hmm. Well, maybe it’s used by the Web, just not identified. Like... a private thought in a mind that never speaks.

Tortoise: Exactly! Or like a turtle shell that exists, but no one has yet painted its pattern.

Achilles: Are you saying there are anonymous resources out there?

Tortoise: Oh, certainly. Some call them "blank nodes"—you might say they are resources that have no names, yet are woven into the Web’s fabric all the same.

Achilles: But without a URI, how do we refer to them?

Tortoise: By proximity. By structure. By implication. Sometimes, even by description. Imagine a house in a neighborhood you know, but you don’t know the address. You call it "the house with the green door next to the noisy dog."

Achilles: So it’s described, not named.

Tortoise: Precisely. It exists not because we named it, but because it plays a role in a larger structure. Much like characters in a novel that never get a name, yet shape the story.

(At this moment, a new character appears: a small, buzzing entity named Möbius.)

Möbius: Excuse me for intruding—but I couldn’t help overhearing your discussion. What if the URI is not absent, but merely inaccessible?

Achilles: Huh? What do you mean?

Möbius: Suppose I claim to represent a resource, but refuse to give you the address. I say: “Trust me, the resource exists. Just don’t ask where.”

Tortoise: Ah! The legendary phantom URI. It haunts the Web, existing in metadata but never resolving to a concrete destination.

Möbius: Like Schrödinger’s cat. It is referenced—but only in the abstract.

Achilles: This is starting to sound like theology.

Tortoise: Or quantum mechanics.

Möbius: Or both! Let me ask you something, Achilles: if a resource exists on the Web, but no one links to it, does it make a sound?

Achilles: Only if it’s described in RDF, I suppose.

Tortoise: Well said.

Achilles: So, to recap: a Web resource without a URI can exist, but only in the shadowy margins—described, implied, or embedded, but never pointed to directly.

Möbius: Or worse—it once had a URI, but the URI was lost in time. A digital ghost.

Tortoise: Or better—it never needed one. Like a fleeting idea, shared in passing, meaningful only in context.

Achilles: Then maybe URIs are overrated.

Tortoise: Careful, Achilles. That way lies anarchy. The Web stands on identifiers. Take them away, and all you have is whispers in the void.

Möbius: Beautiful whispers, though.

Tortoise: Yes. But still, whispers.

Achilles: So what do we do?

Tortoise: We keep listening. And when we find meaning—even in nameless things—we weave it into the Web. With or without a URI.

Möbius: And if you ever forget where something was, remember: the Web forgets too. But it does so gracefully.


... maybe this is an appendix? (Am I kidding? Not sure.)

comments.author: royfielding
comments.body:
That's a long walk off a short pier, and obviously ChatGPT has never talked to me.

People get confused by what a resource "is" even though what it "is" is never relevant to the Web. Hence, the definitions are about how a resource can be referenced, observed, acted upon, etc. There is no definition of a resource itself because there are no limitations on what a resource could be for the Web other than having or not having a URI through which it can be observed [and also because trying to define such a concept will instantly create a portal through which philosophers will appear and attempt to engage in standards].

Given that, a person might reason that a resource that has no URI is not, in fact, a resource: the word doesn't apply to things that do not have utility (the traditional English definition of resource). However, the Web is not the world, and there are obviously things/concepts without names in the real world. Those things are called "potential resources".

Maybe a bit more context would be helpful for readers:

```suggestion
When the client intents to create an upload resource, it can choose to not start transmitting the request content immediately and instead wait for a limited duration for a `104 (Upload Resumption Supported)` response as a sign that upload resumption is possible. In this case, the client MAY treat an interim response with the `104 (Upload Resumption Supported)` status code as fulfilling the 100-continue expectation and start sending the request content. pulls.title: RESUMABLE: Security consideration regarding time-of-check to time-of-use
```
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
This PR adds a security consideration addressing issues that can arise from the delay between the start and end of an upload. It was brought up in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3165. Not all implementations are vulnerable to this, but one has to be careful when a process is split up across multiple, long-running requests.

Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3165.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
I've actually heard the opposite view. The server wants to deliberately use this protocol to get around token expiry. If they use background upload on iOS, the system would retry the request up to 7 days by default, and it's possible that the auth token expires in less than a day, causing the upload to fail. However, the resumable upload protocol provides an escape hatch since the upload resource is tied to a previously authenticated request.

Maybe we can suggest setting the upload resource validity period to match their security policy?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
That's an interesting perspective. Token expiration is indeed a problem with resumable uploads, especially if they are running for extended periods. In the past, I've had a few inquiries from people seeking help with handling expired tokens in my client implementations.

That being said, resumable uploads shouldn't be able to circumvent access restrictions. For example, if an administrator removes my write privileges while my upload is ongoing, the file shouldn't be written to the destination once the upload is complete. Even if I had the privilege when the upload began. That was the motivation behind this change.

However, I don't think our perspectives are exclusive. Token validation is best performed when the upload begins, but privileges have to be checked at the end again. Let me update the text to account for that.

```suggestion

message before forwarding.

intermediaries might reject requests or responses.
```

pulls.title: resumable: clarify client behavior on 413 response
pulls.author: mertalev
pulls.body:
This PR aims to address https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3193#issuecomment-3394903322
* Makes min-append-size and max-append-size apply to upload creation requests as well
* Recommends retrying with body in this range after receiving a 413
* If limits are unknown, recommends discovering them with an OPTIONS request after a 413

These changes should make clients more resilient to server limits without giving up right away.

This is my first PR here, so sorry in advance if I made a mistake!

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body:
Something to consider is whether the server can make the resource and respond with 413 at some point later, or if it needs to respond upfront without doing anything. In the former case, the 413 response would need to include the Location header and maybe the Upload-Offset. A similar question is for upload append, as to whether the server can accept some of the body before responding or if it must reject immediately.

It would probably be simpler for the client to know these requests are no-ops, but there has been discussion on having the server accept up to its limits and ignore the rest, which implies that it can respond after processing part of the request.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Would prefer the server sending 104 with Location prior to 413. The only thing the client needs to do in that case is to allow 413 retry.

Based on the current spec, the server could send a 5xx after processing the request body to the limit, which would prompt the client to retry and resume. It's a hacky workaround though.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: The change looks OK to me. @Acconut what do you think?

We should probably require 413 to carry an `Upload-Limit` header if it's from a resumable upload server. Upload creation can be attempted without knowledge of server support, and clients can't retry a non-resumable upload.
The issue is that a proxy might respond with 413 based on the request's Content-Length, so even if the server is resumable it can't add the header in this case.
The OPTIONS request to learn the limits also doubles as a way to discover resumability. Maybe it should be emphasized here more, so as to avoid retrying without knowing about resumability.

As an implementor of a generic HTTP client, we can attempt resumable uploads for all uploads since it has little overhead and minimum risk, but we cannot perform an OPTIONS discovery step for all uploads that fail with 413. We need to know that the other side supports resumable uploads before doing something expensive.

The OPTIONS request wouldn't be a MUST - it's more that they MUST NOT retry if they don't know the server supports resumability. I suppose the only other way for a generic library to handle this proxy scenario would be to configure it to assume the server is resumable.

SHOULD is a recommendation and means that we think it's a good idea. I don't think it's feasible for us since you know there are unupgradable printers that would crash when it receives an OPTIONS request. We have to be as safe as possible when discovering resumable upload support.

Yeah, this has to be an opt-in feature, although a more desirable opt-in behavior probably is to always send OPTIONS to detect Upload-Limit first instead of relying on 413.

That makes sense. To summarize:
* If 413 contains Upload-Limit header, the client SHOULD try again within these limits
* If not, the client MAY try OPTIONS to learn limits and try again
* Client MUST NOT retry if it isn't aware of server resumable upload support, either from the above or from prior knowledge

Do those changes sound good?

Yes, looks good. I believe the reason we didn't tackle upload creation originally was the complexity of its interaction with discovery. Upload appending can only be performed if the server support is confirmed so its behavior is easier to define.

Minor nit: we stopped using the phrase "prior knowledge" based on the feedback in #3215.

This is a good addition overall! Thank you for the PR. The phrasing MUST + "unless unable" seems a bit odd to me. Would it be better to use SHOULD here in the first place?


```suggestion
A server responding with a 413 Content Too Large status code as a result of its upload limits SHOULD include the Upload-Limit header in this response if possible. This might not be possible if intermediaries enforce content size restrictions. When a client receives a response with a 413 Content Too Large status code during upload creation ({{upload-creation}}) or append ({{upload-appending}}), it SHOULD retry the request with a smaller size residing between `min-append-size` and `max-append-size`. If these limits are unknown at the time of receiving such a response, the client MAY attempt to discover them through an `OPTIONS` request. The client MUST NOT retry the upload request without knowledge of server support of resumable uploads. Cases where a request uses `min-append-size` yet fails with a 413 Content Too Large response might indicate a deployment mismatch that cannot be recovered from.
```
Thanks! I agree SHOULD makes sense there since the server is already allowed to not add it if it can't.

```suggestion
A server responding with a `413 (Content Too Large)` status code as a result of its upload limits SHOULD include the `Upload-Limit` header field in this response if possible. This might not be possible if intermediaries enforce content size restrictions. When a client receives a response with a `413 (Content Too Large)` status code during upload creation ({{upload-creation}}) or append ({{upload-appending}}), it SHOULD retry the request with a smaller size residing between `min-append-size` and `max-append-size`. If these limits are unknown at the time of receiving such a response, the client can attempt to discover them through an `OPTIONS` request. Retrying with the same request content size will likely yield the same error response. Cases where the request content size matches the `min-append-size` limit yet fails with a `413 (Content Too Large)` response might indicate a deployment mismatch that cannot be recovered from.
```

I think we can reduce the normative language here since it won't help with interoperability much here. It's better to describe the resulting situation, so implementers will know what not to do and why.

After that we can merge this :)

pulls.title: resumable: clarify greater offset
pulls.author: mertalev
pulls.body: Resolves #3268, making it more explicit that the resource offset is allowed to be greater than what the client sent in its current upload. It also consolidates the rejection behavior for lesser and greater offsets.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Thank you proposing this text. However, I think that this paragraph is a bit too ambiguous about how clients react to suddenly increasing offsets? Are they expected to follow the offset (i.e. MUST)? Are they recommended to do so (i.e. SHOULD)? Can they decide what to do?

The current text allows clients to abort of offset jumps, but doesn't require this behavior. A client that follows offset jumps would still be compliant with the current text. From that perspective it seems like this PR doesn't change much in the end yet.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: The intent is that they have to jump to the provided offset to continue the upload, or else the upload is a failure. I can see how that's a bit ambiguous in the text. My thought would be to make it a MUST to follow the jump since the server is the source of truth for the current offset. Does that seem reasonable?

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
If the intention is to require clients to follow offset jump, then MUST should be used in my opinion.

That being said, I want to discuss this topic at the upcoming httpbis meeting on Wednesday and collect opinions. The draft assumes that there's only one client uploading to a given upload resource and mandatory support for offset jumps is a deviation from this assumption.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
There are cases where jumping ahead doesn't make sense, e.g. uploading a continuous video stream.

This is targeting a specific use case where the client crashed and forgot about the resume URL, the server could look up the resume URL based on the creation request to recover the in-progress upload. The main question is whether this is a failure mode in scope for the spec.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> This is targeting a specific use case where the client crashed and forgot about the resume URL, [..]

Or in cases where the client never learned the upload resource URL in the first place because it didn't receive the interim or final response for the upload creation request. If the client is aware of the server's support for resumable upload and includes an application-specific header to deduplicate uploads (e.g. an idempotency key or hash), this could allow the client to re-send the upload creation request while being redirected to the previously created upload resource. From there it can then continue the upload. That was also my reasoning behind opening https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/2293 some time ago.

To make this work, we don't have to include details on which headers can be used to deduplicate uploads. That's up to the application. But we need a client that can follow an offset jump, which most clients likely have to implement anyways. If a client wants to resume an upload from a previous session, it has to seek to the correct offset anyways after discovering it via a HEAD requests. So it wouldn't be too much additional implementation work.

That being said, I'm unsure if this has to be mandatory for clients or optional as it currently is.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: The main issue with making the jump optional is that the server won't know whether the client implemented this, so will have to consider both possibilities or risk interop issues.

comments.author: mertalev
comments.body: I tried to clarify the client behavior here, let me know how you feel about the wording!

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: This was discussed during IETF 124 and received supportive feedback from the WG. The argument is that if the forward jump follows with the client's intention, then there is no reason against supporting this. Let's make sure that the language fits.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thank you, @mertalev!

I think we can lose a few more words from this paragraph now that clients can't make any assumption about the relation between the offset and the bytes sent. This should also help with not being too restrictive. 

```suggestion
The offset can be less than or equal to the number of bytes of representation data that the client has already sent. The client is expected to handle backtracking of a reasonable length. On the other hand, the offset can be greater than the amount of sent representation data if the upload resource obtained additional representation data on behalf of the client. If the client is not able to provide the representation data at the given offset, the upload MUST be considered a failure. The client then MUST NOT continue the upload and SHOULD cancel the upload ({{upload-cancellation}}).
```

What do you think, @guoye-zhang?
Looks good, yes
Looks good to me too!

reviews.author: guoye-zhang
reviews.body: Thanks for opening this PR, the text looks good. Left a few minor comments.

comments.body: I think it's better to keep this flow the same as 5xx: recommending doing an offset retrieval before resuming. Otherwise this creates a new code path, and the text in "Upload Append" about picking the offset is also inconsistent with the recommendation here.

SGTM, removed for now
Updated, how does this look?  It feels wrong to completely omit the option to leverage the Upload-Offset from the response since it's called out as a MUST for the server to return it just below

They both match, but which content is appended to the upload resource? Did you mean to say that the content should be appended in one transaction together with the offset check? But that would make this the same as the pessimistic locking, I think.

The server would receive two requests with the same offset (why though, really?) and one is slightly faster than the other i.e. it will get the exclusive lock and the thus the second request would fail. I had a go at rewording this to be clearer as it was both too vague and overly specific in different areas - is this any better?  The key distinction between 2 & 3 is that servers don't need to acquire an exclusive lock for the resource which means they're able to achieve higher availability during network partitions
Yes much better, thanks!

I'm wondering how this would be achieved in practice on the server-side. Does the server read the entire request content first and then tries to apply it in one atomic operation that checks the offset and appends the content? The offset would then be validated after receiving the request content, not when the headers are sent. Not a problem, but a different angle to the task.

Small suggestion:

```suggestion
3.  **Optimistic Concurrency Control**: The server handles concurrent modifications by checking the resource's state and applying changes together in one atomic operation. If a conflict is detected, the server rejects the request with a 409 (Conflict) status code, ensuring that only one of multiple parallel requests can succeed. Upload cancellation is implemented through a similar atomic operation.
```
I think this paragraph isn't necessary as it restates normative language that appeared previously in the section without adding new information.

I think we should keep more context from the original wording that explains why this works:

> Since the client is not allowed to perform multiple transfers in parallel, the upload resource can assume that the previous attempt has already failed. Therefore, the server MAY abruptly terminate the previous HTTP connection or stream.

Similarly, the text would benefit from emphasizing the downsides of this (simple) approach:

> However, since network interruptions can occur in ways that cause the request to hang from the server's perspective, it might take the server significant time to realize the interruption and time out the request. Yeah good point, removed

pulls.title: resumable: introduce new append-granularity limit
pulls.author: danielresnick
pulls.body: See discussion on #3193

comments.author: gstrauss
comments.body:
@danielresnick There should be an exception for the size of the final chunk at the end of the file.

Requiring upload-complete be set for the final chunk would take away the ability of a robust client to send chunks, and then *separately* without any additional body content, to send Upload-Complete.  The ability to send a separate message separates the uploading from marking the upload as complete.

The authors of resumable uploads have made many premature optimizations and I hope that they do not downplay or ignore the robustness of separation of concerns when evaluating this append-granularity feature.

---

Personally, I would prefer that the granularity be a hint, and not a hard error, especially since according to the resumable uploads draft, a server *may* accept part of an upload even if the upload gets disconnected.  If there was a *part* of the granularity chunk committed and the offset is no longer a multiple of the granularity, then a client might wish to send a smaller chunk (smaller than the granularity) even in the middle of an upload in order to re-align with the granularity for further chunks.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body:
Thanks for the feedback @gstrauss. Just to make sure I'm understanding, you're suggesting that the proposed carve out for final chunks ("Requests completing the upload by including the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header field are exempt from this limit.") be generalised to not necessarily require Upload-Complete: ?1, but rather be applicable to any append request which would result in the reaching of the declared Upload-Length (if there is one), is that right?  If so I'm open to this idea, though am interested in others' thoughts also. It's definitely more difficult to express concisely, but I can see how it might improve separation of concepts.

Re: hint vs hard error, as I mentioned on https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3193 I'm open to expressing this as SHOULD rather than MUST, but I do think it's important to be clear that a client intending to be widely interoperable with a variety of servers needs to be aware/respectful of potential granularity requirements.

Re: "a server may accept part of an upload even if the upload gets disconnected", I think the onus should be on the server which is advertising an append-granularity to avoid committing partial state that isn't aligned with that granularity. In fact the whole motivation for append-granularity's existence is server-side limitations that make it technically difficult to commit on non-aligned boundaries. Or to put it another way: clients shouldn't need to worry about re-aligning granularity. Open to suggestions on how I might make this clearer in the PR!  Thanks again for the detailed feedback!

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thank you for this proposal! We'll bring up the general topic of handling granularities during the IETF 124 httpbis meeting next Wednesday.

comments.author: danielresnick
comments.body: Noting before I forget: assuming I understood @gstrauss 's feedback correctly I think min-append-size also has this discrepancy as-is, so we should aim to be consistent for both. That is either only exempt requests with Upload-Complete:?1 from the limit, or exempt any request which contains the final bytes of the representation data as indicated by Upload-Length (in the current or a previous request).

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
Closing this as mentioned in https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3193#issuecomment-3893170872:

> This was discussed at the IETF 124 and the outcome was that we want to support chunk granularity by allowing the server to drop trailing bytes and letting the client discover the correct offset to resume. We should make sure that the language in the draft explicitly enables this.
> However, there was no support for adding a dedicated value to Upload-Limit for chunk granularity. Getting this right would be tricky and the WGLC is not the right time to open such a discussion. That being said, we could introduce it at a large stage in a separate document if implementation experience proves that it would be useful.
How should a client act when receiving this response? The document currently recommends client to stop the upload once they receive a 400.

Technically the spec says "4xx (Client Error) status code, the client SHOULD NOT attempt to retry or resume the upload, _unless the semantics of the response allow or recommend the client to retry the request_."

I agree that's quite subtle though -- expecting a client dev to read this, and then trawl through all possible response_code+problem_type combinations to decide on resume vs abort behaviour. Particularly because even parsing out the problem type requires doing some json parsing. I'll have a think about the best path forward here.. the most obvious options in my mind are (in no particular order):

1) Switch to a 5xx response code. As discussed on the corresponding issue this is likely to improve client interop, but is a hacky / less pure solution since this isn't actually a server error.

2) Use a different / more specific 4xx response code and improve the wording to call this code out specifically. The problem is I don't see a super obvious pre-existing code in the 4xx space. Maybe 422 Unprocessable Content, but that feels slightly odd vs the suggestion that a server should partially process the provided response.

3) Keep using 400 (Bad Request) and try to improving the wording in the client section to be clearer (e.g. with some combination of improving cross-referencing with problem-types, marking problem-types more explicitly as retryable vs not, rephrasing the 4xx status code handling piece quoted above to lead with a discussion on what's retryable vs not).

I think 409 would be an option. If https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/pull/3319 lands, clients should resume the upload when they get a 409, which I think it desired in that case.

> 3\. Keep using 400 (Bad Request) and try to improving the wording in the client section to be clearer (e.g. with some combination of improving cross-referencing with problem-types, marking problem-types more explicitly as retryable vs not, rephrasing the 4xx status code handling piece quoted above to lead with a discussion on what's retryable vs not).

I wouldn't want to mandate clients to parse the response body. It would be great if we can keep using status codes as the definitive signal for clients.

Yeah that's a good point. I'd sort of dismissed that option as I was finding it hard to justify granularity mismatch as a state conflict (though I agree that if that PR lands it would solve the problem from a pure behaviour standpoint), but thinking some more I guess an argument could be made that partial acceptance of a chunk (e.g., accepting 256 KiB of a 300 KiB request) creates a direct mismatch between the client's perceived state and the server's actual state. And yes agreed leveraging status codes only is much more robust & likely to get adoption in practice

I don't follow what's being hashed in this example and the one above. Previously, it matched the `Repr-Digest` example in https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9530#section-3, which I thought was intentional given the note above that "When there is no content coding, Unencoded-Digest acts identically to Repr-Digest; for the same hashing algorithm the computed value would be the same."

In RFC 9530, the examples that accompany the field definition are intended to be minimal and to simply capture how the field in isolation might look. I.e. the field is a dictionary and this is what it looks like if there are two entries. A similar approach has been taken here.

Rather than have cross-document dependencies, the first version of this spec made a decision to break any overlap and base the examples in section 6 on `"An unexceptional string" following by an LF.`.

- Include sha-512 in Section 6 as well, so search for this value leads to Section 6.

pulls.title: RESUMABLE: Redefine Upload-Complete on the server side
pulls.author: guoye-zhang
pulls.body:
Discussed during IETF125. Refining the `Upload-Complete` response header to differentiate the final response from the responses from the upload resource. Also allowing the final response to arrive early.

Resolves #3398

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: @smatsson I updated one of the examples to show this in action. What do you think?

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
@guoye-zhang Thanks for the update! Still not convinced of the wording.

>The `Upload-Complete` response header field distinguishes the response from the initial targeted resource or the temporary upload resource. The value of true means the response is from the initial targeted resource, and the value of false means the response is from the temporary upload resource.

Why is this important to mention? It seems like an implementation detail to me. For an event based implementation (tusdotnet, tusd etc) the "teporary upload resource" could very well cause this case by user action in an event. Why not just simplify it and say that the server can cancel the entire upload by sending a response with `Upload-Complete: ?1`? 

It would not hurt to add a sentence on what the expectations are from the client as well, given that this is what started the discussion in the other issue, e.g. 
> `Upload-Complete: ?1` means that the request should not be retried regardless of what the response status code is.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: The reason I mentioned it is that we implemented resumable upload as a middleware. To the application at the top, it's just a regular upload and they don't need to be aware of the temporary upload resource at all. The responses with `Upload-Complete: ?0` and `Upload-Complete: ?1` are processed by different layers, so it's not just about ending the upload. Does that make sense? We could think of ways to clarify it more.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
@guoye-zhang Thanks for the clarification! While I understand that this makes sense for your specific middleware architecture, stating that the header "distinguishes the response from the initial targeted resource or the temporary upload resource" is completely irrelevant for other types of implementations. 

Including this kind of implementation specific detail in the specification only creates confusion for anyone who hasn't built their server with the exact same architecture. We should just strictly define the protocol behavior over the wire and not add internal details about how different software layers process headers in a specific system.

It would be much clearer if the entire mention of "initial targeted" and "temporary upload" resources were just dropped. It's confusing because the draft already uses the terms "temporary resource" and "upload resource" to mean the URL returned in the Location header, see 3. Overview: 
> Resumable uploads are supported in HTTP through use of a temporary
> resource, an upload resource (Section 4), that is separate from the
> resource being uploaded to and specific to that upload. By
> interacting with the upload resource, a client can retrieve the
> current offset of the upload (Section 4.3), append to the upload
> (Section 4.4), and cancel the upload (Section 4.5).

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I want to clarify that the phrasing isn't about implementation details; it's about response semantics and isn't irrelevant depending on architecture. Let's suppose you create an upload using `POST /files`, and you interact with the upload resource using `PATCH /uploads/1`. If the upload is complete, the final successful response is considered to have come from `/files`, not `/uploads/1`. These different endpoints have different semantics. This is true for early complete responses too: if an upload append fails, the client needs to know if the failure response is coming from `/uploads/1` or `/files`. If the latter, that means the entire upload has failed. Both resources may have entirely different semantics, so it needs to be distinguished which semantics we're working with given a response from the upload resource.

But I'm not arguing the phrasing is necessary, just adding this clarification about the intent behind it to inform your judgment. Personally, I am undecided on whether it's necessary. If we do keep it, it's probably a good idea to change the phrasing to make this clearer. Or alternatively, come up with different semantics that create the same effect.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
@GrantGryczan I completely understand the underlying use case here. The client needs to know whether an error occurred during the actual byte transfer (meaning they might be able to resume/retry) or during the final processing of the completed payload (meaning the transfer phase is over, but backend processing failed).

My issue is that the current phrasing in the draft is still unclear and messy. Trying to explain this by saying the response conceptually "comes from the initial targeted resource" rather than the "temporary upload resource" is an abstract and confusing way to describe it. Describing it this way leaks implementation details into the protocol, and as mentioned earlier, it also clashes with the terminology already established in Section 3.

Instead of describing which internal resource is supposedly answering, wouldn't it be much clearer to just describe what this means for the state of the upload? 

Something along the lines of:
> The Upload-Complete header indicates that the server considers the upload phase to be finalized. If Upload-Complete: ?1 is present on an error response, the client MUST NOT attempt to resume the upload, as the error originated from processing the completed payload rather than the transfer itself.

This achieves the exact same goal for the client but focuses on concrete protocol behavior rather than abstract backend architecture.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Again, this is completely independent from how it's implemented or any backend architecture. It's just about response semantics. It's saying:

- If the initial request is a `PUT` request that results in the creation of a resource, then the `Upload-Complete: ?1` response is required by RFC 9110 to use status 201, even though RFC 5789 doesn't specify any requirement for `PATCH` requests to respond with status 201.
- If the initial request was to `OPTIONS /whatever`, then an `Allow` header included in the `Upload-Complete: ?1` response specifies the allowed request methods for `/whatever`, not the upload resource.
- If the initial request uses the `Accept` header, then the `Upload-Complete: ?1` response ought to have a `Content-Type` that matches that media type, despite responding to a different request entirely.

These are just examples. The point is that _all_ semantics that would otherwise apply to a response from the initial resource must also apply to an `Upload-Complete: ?1` response from the upload resource.

To reiterate, this has nothing to do with backend architecture. In my backend implementation, I personally plan to implement the final complete response as coming from the same function that handles responses for the upload resource. There won't be any middleware or whatever. But the data that function generates for the response is still obliged to obey whatever semantics are defined for the initial resource.

Perhaps this is not the best way to communicate this effect, but my point is just that it's certainly not about implementation details. It's defining a contract that the interface must follow. Merely specifying whether the upload can be resumed or retried does not communicate the same contract.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Also, regarding @smatsson's initial feedback:

> The biggest issue for me is that `Upload-Complete: ?1` in a response no longer means what the name implies, that the upload is complete. It now means "Stop sending data, we are done here". I think that this change deserves more than a side note. A reader coming to this fresh will be confused.

This is a fair point. Would it be a good idea to rename `Upload-Complete` to more accurately reflect the concept it's trying to represent? Perhaps `Upload-Done` since an early-responded upload isn't "complete", but it is done (hence "we are done here")? Opinions needed.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
I thought about renaming it, ultimately concluded that keeping the same is the right decision for a few reasons:

1. All the options are synonymous to "Upload-Complete", e.g. "Upload-Final", "Upload-Done", "Upload-Finished", "Upload-Ended". It would probably be more confusing if we renamed it to a synonym.
2. Even though this change redefines the semantics of the header, most existing implementations already conform with little or no changes. It only affects servers that need to send early responses. Keeping the name avoids the churn.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: What about keeping both explanations? Saying that `Upload-Complete: ?1` on the response means that the response is final and the client should not interact with the upload resource further.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: That could work, but I still think the phrasing of the current explanation needs refining.

comments.author: smatsson
guoye-zhang
comments.body: What about now? @GrantGryczan @smatsson

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
This is better, but I think it still doesn't make much sense to say a response comes from the temporary upload resource. As I said in my previous review, if a client creates a resumable upload with `Upload-Complete: ?0`, then a server may respond with `Upload-Complete: ?0`, but the client doesn't know about the temporary upload resource before receiving that response, so saying it's "from" the temporary upload resource is incoherent to the client. Does that make sense?

Furthermore, I suspect Stefan's criticism still applies to the "distinguishes the response from the initial targeted resource or the temporary upload resource", "response is from", and "targeted resource decides to generate" phrasings. I think those should probably be replaced or removed entirely, because framing it in terms of which semantics apply is much less ambiguous. I'll defer to Stefan.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I rephrased it by avoiding mentioning the upload resource

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Nice work! I think this is great. Let's see what Stefan thinks.

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body: @guoye-zhang Much clearer now, thanks! The update resolves my concerns.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Something seems off about these new semantics. I'm concerned about the error responses specified by the resumable upload protocol: mismatching offset, completed upload, and inconsistent length. If the upload was already completed, then what should `Upload-Complete` be set to for these responses?

- If `Upload-Complete: ?1`, this change defines that the response comes from the initial targeted resource rather than following resumable upload semantics, which is not true. The initial targeted resource would have given a different response, so this value violates the new definition.
- If `Upload-Complete: ?0`, that would be consistent with the new definition, since these errors do follow resumable upload semantics rather than the semantics of the initial targeted resource. But on the other hand, this value is misleading since the upload _was_ completed. It could be argued that this misleading nature indicates a fundamental design flaw with doing early responses this way. But a client would discover the upload is already complete upon attempting upload resumption (via offset retrieval), so perhaps this is fine.
- If `Upload-Complete` is absent, a generalized client will probably treat the response similarly to if it included `Upload-Complete: ?0`, so refer to the above. Arguably, this is less misleading since it doesn't look like an assertion that the upload is incomplete. But it also has the downside of behavior being less predictable here, and clients being uncertain how to handle this, going only off of heuristics. Ideally, a compliant client should handle these errors reliably.

If we decide one of these is best, I think it should be recommended explicitly in the draft. I would not be surprised if servers mistakenly choose a bad value here, since this situation is confusing.

We could also carve out an exception in the new definition to allow just these error responses to use `Upload-Complete` to signal the current completeness state, but that seems needlessly inconsistent and again arguably hints at a fundamental design flaw. The underlying inconsistency is that `Upload-Complete` is used for two different purposes: to communicate which response semantics apply, and to signal whether the upload has been completed. In most cases, these purposes are aligned, but sometimes, they are at odds.

Another example of this is offset retrieval responses, which use `Upload-Complete` strictly informatively rather than in a way that affects response semantics. The definition may need to cover this as an exception case too, unless we want to change our approach.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body:
Yes, based on the new definition, Upload-Complete should be false in those situations. I can mention it somewhere. Since 409 with false Upload-Complete is retryable now, this might even be a good change.

We should have as few exceptions as possible. It makes implementations easier and more consistent.

Yes, completeness in offset retrieval is different, it’s whether the final response was sent. I’m wondering if the header can be removed since it’s not needed for the protocol to function.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Completeness in offset retrieval is certainly important. Otherwise, it's difficult for the client to tell in some edge cases whether the upload was completed, such as lost final response.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: Knowing that a final response was generated without getting the final response isn’t super useful IMO. The final response could be a 403 or some other error. The client really should use a 0-length append to retrieve the final response.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Hm... Possibly, but I'd want to finish implementing my own resumable upload client to be certain that it's not useful. If you (and others) don't think this indicates a design flaw with the new semantics here, then I think this is good as-is for now, and we could put offset retrieval's use of the header on the backburner. Clarification on use of the header in error responses is still needed though.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: OK I’ll add the clarification. To me, this is the only definition that makes sense: the bit to differentiate between the final response and upload responses, which is the only bit of information that a client couldn’t figure out on its own.

> It is worth noting that `Upload-Complete` can be true even if the upload is not complete

This is confusing, especially since arguably `Upload-Complete` being true _defines_ the notion that the upload was completed in some sense. How about this (also fixed a typo, "the the"):

```suggestion
The `Upload-Complete` response header field distinguishes the response from the initial targeted resource or the temporary upload resource. The value of true means the response is from the initial targeted resource, and the value of false means the response is from the temporary upload resource. It is worth noting that `Upload-Complete` can be true even when the full representation data was not received if the targeted resource decides to generate an early response.
```

reviews.author: smatsson
reviews.body:
I like the idea here but I think the PR needs a bit more to be fully understandable.

The biggest issue for me is that `Upload-Complete: ?1` in a response no longer means what the name implies, that the upload is complete. It now means "Stop sending data, we are done here". I think that this change deserves more than a side note. A reader coming to this fresh will be confused. 

It would definitely help to have some examples e.g. showing the early response case and what the client should do when it receives Upload-Complete: ?1 midway through the upload.

comments.body:
As per the above discussion, I think we can improve this. At the very least, the response should be described as responding to a particular request rather than from a particular resource, because the response semantics also depend on the request method, headers, and content, not just the resource. Furthermore, it doesn't make sense to say the response is from the upload resource for the very first `Upload-Complete: ?0` response, since the client doesn't even know about the upload resource at that point.

Regardless, I think we can be even clearer than that--something irks me about simply asserting the response is responding to something that it actually isn't. It's ambiguous, as is apparent from @smatsson's arguments above. I think we can probably find a way to define this in a way that follows typical HTTP semantics, where a response is directly related to the corresponding request sent by the client.

I'm not experienced enough with RFC 9110 to confidently phrase this well, but can we say something like the following? Please completely rephrase if so; this phrasing is not good at all.

> The value of false means the response is related to the request that immediately prompted it, as usual. The value of true means the response must follow the semantics a response to the initial upload creation request would follow had that request omitted the `Upload-Complete` header and transferred the representation data up to what has already been transferred by prior upload creation and upload append requests for the current upload.

Nit: "that" wasn't used in the same place for the value of false, so let's be consistent for the value of true's phrasing.

```suggestion
The `Upload-Complete` response header field distinguishes the response from the initial targeted resource or the temporary upload resource. The value of true means the response is from the initial targeted resource, and the semantics of the targeted resource apply; the value of false means the response is from the temporary upload resource, and the semantics of the resumable upload protocol apply. It is worth noting that `Upload-Complete` can be true even when the full representation data was not received if the targeted resource decides to generate an early response. The client SHOULD NOT perform upload resumption to the upload resource after receiving a response with the `Upload-Complete` field value set to true.
```

Fixed typo.

```suggestion
The `Upload-Complete` response header field signals whether the response comes from the initial targeted resource. The value of true means that the semantics of the targeted resource apply, and the value of false means that the semantics of the resumable upload protocol apply. It is worth noting that `Upload-Complete` can be true even when the full representation data was not transmitted in the case that the server decides to generate an early response when processing the targeted resource. The client SHOULD NOT perform upload resumption to the upload resource after receiving a response with the `Upload-Complete` field value set to true.
```

I think we need adjustments here as well. This sentence indicates to me that only the client can mark an upload as complete, which isn't the case anymore. 

```suggestion
An upload is incomplete until it is explicitly marked as completed by the client or the server. After this point, no representation data can be appended anymore.
```
Should we mention the possibility of an early response in the sections for PATCH and/or HEAD as well?

I'm unsure this is a good example for an early response. A 4XX response usually marks the end of an upload regardless of the presence of the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header. IMO the value of early responses isn't visible in error responses, but actually successful responses. Could we have an example where the early response is 2XX because the targeted resource already received all the representation it needed to generate a response?

I personally think an early 2XX response in the wild would be extremely rare. Supporting error responses that interrupt an upload is probably going to be the most common use case for early responses, and there's no reason an example couldn't reflect that well. Though I agree this in particular is not the best example of that, since the error response here is the very first response, so in a sense, it's not really "interrupting" the upload, just preventing it from starting in the first place.

Yes, the most common cases for early responses are failures (401 unauthorized for example), and it's usually at the very beginning of the request. I think this example is fine for showcasing that Upload-Complete can be false in the request but true in the response. Or do we want an edge case example showing a particular pattern?

> the most common cases for early responses are failures (401 unauthorized for example)

In my mental model, these authentication failures would be raised before an upload resource is even allocated. But this might be different depending on your implementation.

One example for an early error response that's slightly different is when a content-encoded representation (e.g. Content-Encoding: gzip) is uploaded and a decoding failure occurs. comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I suspect having the initial request bypass the limit would be unacceptable in nearly every case where a server would want this limit. It would certainly be unacceptable in the use cases I considered for my own implementation. Here are some examples of usage I considered for my implementation:

- The server is directly submitting each chunk to a multipart AWS S3 upload so it doesn't need its own buffer, and S3 has its own minimum part size that doesn't treat the first part of the upload any differently. This would fail, and the server would need a non-standard way to communicate to the client that they should follow this limit for the initial request.
- `min-append-size` and `max-append-size` are both set to the same value to improve the storage and seeking efficiency of each chunk before storing each chunk directly. Letting the first chunk be inconsistently small would increase complexity, waste storage, and harm random access performance.
- A compression algorithm is applied to each chunk before storing the compressed chunk directly, and it would increase complexity to support compression and decompression of variably sized chunks (other than the last one), as well as be wasteful for storage and performance.
- Similar to previous but encryption instead of compression.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: @tfpauly @yaroslavros I've rewritten this section to incorporate the perspectives you've shared here.  Please review.

I don't think this is a good suggestion. It may lead to ambiguities - especially given that some other proxy techniques (CONNECT-UDP) also leverage identical URI template.

I would suggest something along the following lines:


```suggestion
Clients that support both classic HTTP CONNECT proxies and template-driven TCP proxies SHOULD have proxy type explicitly configured. Client configured with the HTTP CONNECT proxy hostname MAY use a discovery mechanism described in {{Section 2.1 of ?I-D.ietf-intarea-proxy-config=PVD-PROXY-CONFIG}}.
```

If you insist on encouraging a single configuration string, I would slightly adjust the final bullet as suggested below

```suggestion
* Additionally, both types of proxies can be discovered using a mechanism specified in {{Section 2.1 of ?I-D.ietf-intarea-proxy-config=PVD-PROXY-CONFIG}} as long as configuration string contains a hostname.
```

I think configuration via a single string is extremely valuable.  There is already a maze of system-level configuration mechanisms and user interfaces that can pass an HTTP proxy string.  These mechanisms are unlikely to ever be updated to incorporate the proposed metadata tag, so we should plan to use them as-is.

The intent here is not to limit PvD use to HTTPS records.  Hosting multiple distinct proxies on a hostname and avoiding revealing their presence to unauthorized clients are key motivations for this draft, and hostname-based configuration is incompatible with these goals.

A single string input can support a wide range of configuration starting points that lead to PvD.  Even an IP address could be used, in combination with `.well-known/pvd`.  The most flexible (and in my view best) option would be a full "https://" URL for the PvD JSON.  The purpose of this line is to remind implementers that they can support all of these things without redesigning their configuration input system.

Practically, I'm assuming that if there is a string input field for configuring a proxy, one would generally need to assume it is going to be the legacy HTTP CONNECT. I certainly think we can say "if you enter a string that looks like a CONNECT-TCP template, then a system that knows about CONNECT-TCP needs to use this spec.", but have a warning that entering that on systems that don't know about it may lead to failures to use the proxy.

pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Closes #3430.

This PR clarifies that the offset and length must match when the upload is about to be completed. The draft had already requirements that the length derived from `Content-Length` is consistent, but there was a loophole when the header is missing:

> The only loophole is that this is only specified for requests with Content-Length. This header isn't always present (e.g. when Transfer-Encoding: chunked is used), so this case isn't prohibited at the moment:
> 
>  -  Empty POST request with Upload-Length: 1000 and Upload-Complete: ?0
>  -  PATCH request with Upload-Complete: ?1, no Content-Length, but 500 bytes of content

(from https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3430#issuecomment-4438288485)

This gap is closed by explicitly saying that the length must be consistent in the end.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Why do we deactivate the upload resource instead of simply responding with a 4xx error with `Upload-Complete: ?0`? Couldn't the client recover from this mistake by simply resending the correct final append? This seems particularly problematic if the inconsistent length is merely a transmission error, not some permanent bad client state. Why would such an error result in the entire upload failing?

I'd think we'd want to just make this fall under the existing inconsistent length problem type.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: You're right. We can adjust the language to meet the existing requirements on keeping the length consistent.

comments.author: guoye-zhang
comments.body: I think this should be a hard failure. It's unclear how this could be the result of a transmission error, other than TCP somehow corrupting the bytes which is outside the scope of the protocol to recover. However, I'm also fine with it being retryable since it doesn't complicate the implementation.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body: Even if it isn't a realistic transmission error, the server implementation may be able to be simpler if it can just reuse the inconsistent upload length 4xx response, rather than special-casing this one means that the upload length can be inconsistent.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
I've adjusted the section of length to use _representation's length_ instead of _upload length_. We introduced this term, but it has the same meaning as the representation's length, so I think this makes it easier for the reader to understand what value is communicated. It should also be clearer that the length must stay consistent over the upload. The `Upload-Length` header is left untouched since it's now just a way to communicate the representation's length.

Please let me know what you think.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
This may be out of scope, but do we want to rename the `Upload-Length` header field to `Repr-Length` if it's really just an indicator for the representation's length? This seems more broadly useful than just for resumable uploads, and if an HTTP header for that were ever added in the future, it would make `Upload-Length` completely redundant.

Basing this on `Content-Digest` vs. `Repr-Digest`, we have `Content-Length` but no `Repr-Length`.

comments.author: Acconut

> This may be out of scope, but do we want to rename the Upload-Length header field to Repr-Length if it's really just an indicator for the representation's length?

There's value in keeping the header naming consistent (Upload-Complete, Upload-Offset, Upload-Limit, Upload-Length), so the prefix serves a good purpose. In addition, renaming it to Repr-Length would raise more questions about its relation to Content-Length and its general use outside of uploads. I'm not sure there's much to gain here.

reviews.author: GrantGryczan
reviews.body: Other than these 2 questions which I'm uncertain of, this seems good.

comments.body:
I know this is an old clause, but what if the client or server fails? Does this account for that sufficiently? For example,

- if a client makes an `Upload-Complete: ?1` request with no `Content-Length` header that the server rejects after receiving only half its content,
- if the client makes a request with `Upload-Length` that has an invalid value for `Upload-Complete`,
- if the client's headers correctly indicate the length and go through to the server, but the body doesn't get sent due to the client losing connection,
- if the client indicates the length, but the server fails with a 5xx response and is unable to record the length.

It says indicators (1) and (2) MUST match, but just within indicator (1), what if the content length doesn't match the `Content-Length` header? Perhaps we don't need to comment on that since RFC 9110 already [prohibits this](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.content-length):

> a sender MUST NOT forward a message with a Content-Length header field value that is known to be incorrect.

I don't think we should include normative statements in this document about how messages with inaccurate Content-Length values ought to be handled. It's outside of this document's scope and overlaps with the version-specific details of HTTP. If I'm not mistaken, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 consider messages with an inaccurate Content-Length as malformed.

> * if a client makes an `Upload-Complete: ?1` request with no `Content-Length` header that the server rejects after receiving only half its content,
> * if the client makes a request with `Upload-Length` that has an invalid value for `Upload-Complete`,

Then the length is unknown.

> * if the client's headers correctly indicate the length and go through to the server, but the body doesn't get sent due to the client losing connection,
> * if the client indicates the length, but the server fails with a 5xx response and is unable to record the length.

The server can try to record the length based on the request header without the content, but if that process fails the length remains unknown.

In general, I don't think we have to go into every possible failure scenario in the text, as this makes it too verbose, rigid and restrictive. The document shouldn't be an implementation blueprint. It's good to think about these scenarios and it's great that you bring themup, but the document should focus on areas where interoperability matters. The examples you mentioned either reflect transient failures in the message exchange that can be recovered from using the resumption techniques, or are cases of the client emitting invalid messages, where the file upload will fail regardless of what we specify in the document.
That's what I figured, but just making sure.

I wasn't suggesting explicitly documenting these edge cases; I was only suggesting that the conditions under which the server is required to record the length are perhaps too restrictive. But if you think situations like the examples I gave are already naturally exempt from this requirement, then feel free to mark as resolved.

pulls.title: RESUMABLE: Describe GET request against upload resource
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3214.

This PR updates the document so GET requests are to be handled as HEAD requests. It's explicitly mentioned that no requirements on GET response content is placed:

> This document does not place any requirements on the response content for `GET` requests. In particular, the server is not required to respond with the transferred representation data.

Let me know if that's not needed.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body: Thank you for your the reviews, Grant and Lucas!

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
You guys are way too quick for me, please slow down a bit! :P 

I think this change brings some potentially unwanted situations. Before I go into it, I do understand _why_ this was added, but I'm not sure it really aligns with the definition in RFC 9110 anyway.

If we look at GET under RFC 9110, it states: "The GET method requests transfer of a current selected representation for the target resource." The representation of the target resource in this case is the uploaded data itself. Redefining what `GET` returns in this PR is, in my opinion, just as problematic as changing the definition (i.e., splitting) HEAD and GET, as was done previously.

From an implementation standpoint, the server code handling uploads would now also have to support/intercept GET. Since it is only RECOMMENDED that the client uses HEAD, there is a real risk that clients will actually use GET just to fetch the upload status/offset. 

In many implementations, the upload handling is built as a middleware that intercepts the upload flow, while simply passing along requests it shouldn't handle (like GET requests for downloading the data) to the underlying application. This means we are now implicitly dictating that a server cannot offer file downloads on the exact same URL where the upload takes place, without turning the code into spaghetti where the middleware has to intercept and rewrite responses from the user code. 

The alternative is that the middleware always responds with the full file data, but then there's a huge risk of transferring massive amounts of data back to a client that only intended to check the offset (again, because the client CAN use GET without a real reason). 

At the beginning of this draft process, when we had the concept of the client creating a token, we received criticism because we were dictating how/where the server should structure its resources. I feel that this change introduces the exact same problem.

comments.author: Acconut
comments.body:
> If we look at GET under RFC 9110, it states: "The GET method requests transfer of a current selected representation for the target resource." The representation of the target resource in this case is the uploaded data itself. Redefining what GET returns in this PR is, in my opinion, just as problematic as changing the definition (i.e., splitting) HEAD and GET, as was done previously.

This is not entirely correct. The representation of the upload resource does not have to be the representation that is uploaded. It can be (if that's the purpose of the server), but it can also just be an empty representation (what this draft aims at), a textual description of the upload progress or anything else. There is no text in RFC 9110 or this draft that requires a GET request to return what was previously uploaded and the server can choose what representation to serve.

> In many implementations, the upload handling is built as a middleware that intercepts the upload flow, while simply passing along requests it shouldn't handle (like GET requests for downloading the data) to the underlying application. This means we are now implicitly dictating that a server cannot offer file downloads on the exact same URL where the upload takes place, without turning the code into spaghetti where the middleware has to intercept and rewrite responses from the user code.

A middleware implementation is still able to pass the GET request to the origin server, as long as it adds the necessary Upload-* header fields to the response. This is how reverse proxies operate and shouldn't be an uncommon mode of operation in HTTP deployment. This normative change doesn't prevent origins from handling GET request against the upload resource in their own, custom ways.

Does that clear things up a bit for you?

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
I don't have a strong opinion one way or another here, but if you do then I believe it is undoubtedly worth discussing. Things can always be changed! :)

It _is_ recommended for clients to use `HEAD`, so I find it most likely performance wouldn't be an issue in practice. If the problem is mainly that you don't want to make the server deal with repeatedly sending the incomplete representation data for every offset retrieval from such a careless client, would it suffice just to change the recommendation for clients to use `HEAD` to a requirement? If not, I'm not sure what alternative you mean to propose.

As for the other server burden you mention, RFC 9110 already recommends that `HEAD` responses return the same headers as `GET` responses to the same resource, so realistically, I suspect servers would already want to support `GET` with these headers regardless, no?

comments.author: smatsson
comments.body:
> It is recommended for clients to use HEAD, so I find it most likely performance wouldn't be an issue in practice. If the problem is mainly that you don't want to make the server deal with repeatedly sending the incomplete representation data for every offset retrieval from such a careless client, would it suffice just to change the recommendation for clients to use HEAD to a requirement? If not, I'm not sure what alternative you mean to propose.

The core issue with keeping it as a "recommendation" is that server implementers still have to build support for `GET` during the upload phase to account for clients that don't follow the recommendation. 

This leaves servers with two choices:
1. Return the body upon `GET` just to deliver the offset headers, which is a significant waste of bandwidth (and honestly no proper implementation will do this)
2. Disallow file downloads entirely on the upload URL. 

While option 2 isn't a problem for simple one-off form submissions, many systems in the wild (like those running `tus` today) keep the upload URL around permanently as the actual URI of the file (similar to Dropbox folders). If the server has to intercept `GET` to serve upload offsets, it becomes very difficult to serve the actual file download on that same URL without adding a lot of architectural complexity to separate the two states. 

So yes, your suggestion to change the recommendation to a strict requirement (`MUST` use `HEAD` to check upload status, leaving `GET` undefined by this spec) would absolutely solve this problem and remove the burden from the servers.

> As for the other server burden you mention, RFC 9110 already recommends that HEAD responses return the same headers as GET responses to the same resource, so realistically, I suspect servers would already want to support GET with these headers regardless, no?

In my practical experience with these types of systems, this isn't typically how they are architected. Most implementations I've seen handle `HEAD` exclusively to manage the state machine during the upload phase (fetching the offset/status). `GET` is kept entirely separate and is strictly reserved for downloading or interacting with the final data/file. Blending upload-state headers into standard file retrieval `GET` responses isn't a common pattern in practice, which is why allowing `GET` to be co-opted for offset retrieval causes these architectural friction points.

As a minor process note: merging normative spec changes in under 16 hours makes it quite difficult for those of us in different time zones to participate in the review process before decisions are finalized. It would be great if we could leave PRs open a bit longer in the future to allow for async feedback!

pulls.title: RESUMABLE: Clarify when client cannot know limits
pulls.author: Acconut
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3321.

The current draft says:

> The client SHOULD respect any limits ([Section 4.1.4](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#upload-limit)) announced in the Upload-Limit header field in interim or final responses.

This statement is rather vague. Clients cannot always know the limits before starting an upload and we likely don't want to force clients to discover them via an OPTIONS request first. That's why we say that clients SHOULD respect any limit that they are aware of (either discovered via OPTIONS or in responses), while not forcing them to adhere via MUST.

This PR attempts to add a bit more context around this statement to hopefully clear this up.

comments.author: GrantGryczan
comments.body:
Servers implementing chunk granularity (#3193) will need to return a 4xx error that signals the upload can be resumed when the client submits a chunk that isn't a multiple of the granularity. What status code can they rely on for clients to interpret it that way?

- The semantically correct answer would be 400, but 400 isn't a retry condition documented here, so it can't be relied on.
- It seems that, functionally, the best status code would be 409. But semantically, that doesn't make sense and technically violates RFC 9110's definition of status 409. There isn't a "conflict" when a client sends content with an unexpected length.
- I also don't think 413 would be appropriate either, since if the client sent _more_ data, it could reach the next multiple and still work. This may cause clients to make incorrect assumptions and misbehave.

Furthermore, even if there hypothetically were a nice status code that indicates incorrect content length, I'm sure there are other situations where a server may want to signal interoperable clients to resume with other 4xx status codes. It seems semantically incorrect to me to only define these few specific status codes to be reliably retriable.

I talked about this in http://github.com/httpwg/http-extensions/issues/3454#issuecomment-4745876577 and the subsequent comments, but there isn't a great solution to this that I'm totally confident in. My suggestion there was to use `Upload-Offset` in 4xx responses as a signal that the upload can be resumed at that particular offset, so that the server can use any 4xx status code that complies with HTTP semantics. (Of course, the client could just check for the presence of that header and perform offset retrieval anyway if that's simpler.) This would also remove the need for clients to check for 409, since offset mismatch responses are [required](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload.html#section-4.4.2-3) to include `Upload-Offset` anyway. Then, servers can use non-completing 409 responses for non-retriable purposes too by not including `Upload-Offset`.

The current design mangles all these semantics together in my opinion, making certain use cases (like non-retriable 409 and chunk granularity 400) impossible. My concern isn't just about chunk granularity, it's about the conflated semantics overall leading to less broad utility and future extensibility. Chunk granularity is just an example.

If desired, I can open a new issue for this to save it for after this is merged. It isn't so important that I'd insist it blocks this PR.

Also, did you mean to say the _status code_ doesn't indicate success? I would think you meant the `Upload-Complete: ?1` field doesn't indicate success.

```suggestion
If the client received a final response with the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header field, the upload is complete and the corresponding response comes from the resource processing the representation according to the initial request ({{upload-complete}}). The server SHOULD NOT generate a response with the `301 (Moved Permanently)`, `302 (Found)`, or `303 (See Other)` status codes because clients might follow the redirect without preserving the `HEAD` method.
```

Inconsistent phrasing:

```suggestion
The server SHOULD NOT generate a response with the `301 (Moved Permanently)`, `302 (Found)`, or `303 (See Other)` status codes because clients might follow the redirect without preserving the `DELETE` method.
```

Isn't this a normative statement? If not, it should be rephrased to avoid using the word "should".

```suggestion
The client SHOULD limit the number of retries it performs before considering the upload a failure.
```
I didn't add `and` since `therefore` already broke the sentence apart

"Therefore" is an adverb (like "consequently"), not a conjunction (like "so"), so it cannot join sentences. You could also replace `therefore` with `so` if you want, assuming that complies with editorial guidelines (which it might not because I don't see that anywhere else). Or you could replace `, therefore` with `; therefore,` since semicolons can join sentences.

```suggestion
If the client received a final response with the `Upload-Complete: ?1` header field, the upload is complete and the corresponding response comes from the resource processing the representation according to the initial request ({{upload-complete}}). Note that this does not necessarily indicate success. `4xx (Client Error)` or `5xx (Server Error)` status codes indicate in this case an error occurred while processing the representation; therefore, resuming the upload would not resolve this error.
```

I think this would make it slightly more concise & clear.

```suggestion
If the client receives a 2xx successful final response with the `Upload-Complete` header field set to false or missing, the `Location` response header field points the client to the created upload resource. The client can continue appending representation data to it ({{upload-appending}}).
```

```suggestion
If the client receives a non-successful final response with the `Upload-Complete` header field set to false or missing, or if it did not receive a final response, it can apply the heuristics described in {{retry}} to retry or resume the upload.
```

```suggestion
If the client received a non-successful response with the `Upload-Complete` header field set to false or missing when creating the upload resource ({{upload-creation}}) or appending to it ({{upload-appending}}), it can apply the heuristics described below to retry or resume the upload.
```

```suggestion
- `409 (Conflict)` with the `Upload-Complete` header field set to false can be resumed with the correct offset ({{upload-offset}}). If no `Upload-Offset` header field is provided, the client SHOULD retrieve the offset ({{offset-retrieving}}) before resuming.
```

I don't know that it's clear what "appropriate" means in "appropriate limits" and "appropriate delays". Is it possible to phrase these more concretely? It doesn't have to be specific on how to determine the limits/delays, just something less ambiguous and possibly confusing.

The section on upload limits already goes into more detail on how to handle 413 and we shouldn't repeat ourselves.

I think don't we have to add more text for 429, as a way to discover the appropriate delays is already mentioned in its RFC: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6585#autoid-4.
